The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. 00243 metered-farm-architecture-comparison metered-solar-farms partly supported A small neural network sitting on top of a solar-farm power model forecasts a metered solar farm about as well as XGBoost and improves on the power model alone by 4.4% in the quantile score, when the network outputs the whole forecast band. Networks that adjust a single number (the scale, a correction, or the sunlight fed to the power model) gain under 1%. The hybrid is far better than XGBoost at the upper tail (0.99 quantile, 29% lower pinball loss), which matters for curtailment. The neural network without physics does better still at that tail (32% lower pinball loss than XGBoost). 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. 00237 dp-two-number-solar-summary-with-clip differentiable-physics-embedded-generation supported At D5, in one year of data, summarising the ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation keeps at least about 90% of its gain when the solar output is clipped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (110%, interval 91% to 141%). On the sunniest third of daylight rows the point estimate of the remaining gain is about half (interval -12% to 88%). A post hoc arm using the standard deviation alone kept the gain there, which suggests testing that form. 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. 00228 dp-bg-rolling-origin-stack-against-bg2 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the solar summary) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5% of BG2's 2.715; lower is better), and most of the gain comes from November to March. From April to June 2026 the stack is worse than BG2, and arm D without the neural network head is worse than BG2 in summer. The year-long gain is only just separable from zero, and we cannot test other years until BG2 is re-run for them. 00227 lsc-fewer-false-alarms-and-softer-use-part-2 lsc-detectors partly supported Keeping only the learned score's most confident alarms gives a mask that finds 21 of 35 real load shifts with 5 alarms per match, recovers most of the forecast gain after a load shift, and does no measurable harm on ordinary days. A gentler use of the alarm is not needed at that setting. The result rests on 11 load shifts after which the gain is measured, so the next step is to confirm it on more load shifts before porting it. 00220 dp-bg-stage4-assembly-with-drop-one differentiable-physics-forecast-engine partly supported Adding two parts to the best-guess demand forecast lowers its quantile score by 0.136 points (5%) of substation effective capacity. The parts are a small neural network that corrects the forecast's median, and a two-number summary of the 51 ensemble members' solar response. Each part's gain is almost exactly what it achieves alone, so the two parts remove different errors. The network's own 11 quantiles reached 0.904 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights without the hand-fitted band fixes, and scored 0.048 points better than the corrected forecast overall, mostly at one substation. The coast-and-widen rule for missing readings was not scored with the stack. 00214 dp-pv-clip-ceiling-as-of-and-screen differentiable-physics-embedded-generation partly supported Capping the solar output that the demand forecast subtracts from one Primary substation (D5) at 60% of its solar capacity lowers the forecast error on sunny days by about 0.13 MW. Almost all of that gain (97%) remains when the cap is chosen using only data from before each monthly retraining. The five other Primaries tested show no clear gain, so the cap should be treated as specific to D5 for now. 00211 dp-boosted-tree-calibrator-and-input-ablations differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A gradient-boosted tree model given the same inputs as the neural network, and no recent errors, lowers the error score of our best day-ahead forecast by about as much as the network does (0.098 against 0.100 points). The interval is wide, so a loss of up to 0.03 points against the network is not ruled out. The gain comes mostly from two inputs, the forecast level and the weather-data era. 00205 dp-gamk-gap-robustness-coast-or-frozen-gam differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive When readings stop for 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours, keep running the Kalman filter, which corrects the convex demand model using its recent forecast errors, without feeding it new readings, and widen the quantile bands. At each of those four gap lengths that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction (a quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better; the gain is 8% to 14% of the uncorrected model's score). At 72 hours the 99.4% bootstrap interval for the gain runs from 0.04 to 0.48 points, so the gain may be small. The data cannot show whether dropping only the filter beats coasting after a gap of about 72 hours: at every gap length the difference between the two forecasts is smaller than the variation between months. The forecast with the filter, winter night offset, and recipe R was still 0.025 points worse than its no-gap score 48 hours after a 24-hour gap ended. The filter alone was within 0.02 points of its no-gap score 24 hours after the gap ended. 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. 00195 switching-neural-plus-detector-features lsc-detectors partly supported A learned score on the features that RO-NC and the pair alarm already compute finds 22 to 24 of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, against 18 or 19 for RO-NC, at the same number of unexplained alarms. A plain logistic regression finds 22 even without any look-ahead feature, so most of the gain is in the features, and the extra transfers are small ones (under 1 MW each). The next step is to test whether the extra alarms help the gated mask, which this experiment did not run. 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. 00180 dp-sunny-daylight-fix-d5-solar-shape differentiable-physics-embedded-generation supported D5's net power flattens like an export limit: capping the solar output the forecast subtracts from demand at 60% of the capacity held for D5 cuts the best GAM's sunny-daylight loss to BG2 from 0.20 MW to 0.07 MW, and moves the two placebo substations, D10 and D16, by under 0.01 MW on sunny half-hours. A different panel tilt or azimuth does nothing measurable. D5 is the only one of the six substations whose site table marks an export clip, so the next question is whether the 60% ceiling is stable from year to year. 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift differentiable-physics-long-history-and-drift supported Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner calibration-and-uncertainty supported The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves differentiable-physics-pooling-across-substations partly supported In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. 00148 switching-end-rule-lookahead-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported On injected transfers, a live service needs only 6 hours of data after the candidate end to fix the end of a switching interval, with no loss of recall against the offline rule. The call then comes a median 30 hours after the true end, and 24 of those hours are the step statistic's own window, so a longer lookahead of 24 or 48 hours only delays the call to 48 or 72 hours without finding more. The 35 real transfers give the same 18 found at every lookahead from 1 hour up. A lookahead of 0 hours is wrong in six transfers in ten, because the end is called about 8 hours early. 00147 causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported The end of a switching interval can be called from data available at the time, with no loss of recall against the offline rule, by waiting until the step statistic falls to 0.8 of its running peak. The call comes a median 29 hours after the true end. Ending the interval at the first sign of a return step is wrong in about six transfers in ten, because it fires about 8 hours early. Merging overlapping alarms on one Primary substation cuts the share of transfers reported as 2 or more intervals from 0.57 to 0.03. 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k differentiable-physics-forecast-engine small gain Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step differentiable-physics-demand-calendar-and-weather inconclusive Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 differentiable-physics-forecast-engine partly supported Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand demand-inputs small gain The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). 00087 bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). 00082 sw2-18-19-combined-refit-offset-and-same-sign-count lsc-detectors supported Using the refit offset and the same-sign neighbour count together found 0.770 of the moved power on injected transfers, against 0.656 for the benchmark detector. The gain of 0.114 is about the sum of the gains of 0.056 and 0.050 from each change alone. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day the combined detector found 12 and the benchmark 8, which is a weak signal on a small sample, and transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days gain nothing. 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). 00078 pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages solar-disaggregation small gain Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowered the error of experiment 64's best forecast by only 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold, and by 0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012, an interval that includes zero) at leads under 48 hours. 00071 sw2-18-refit-offset-and-gap-bridging lsc-detectors supported The detector ignored every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its forecasting model, which lowered recall by about 5% of the moved power. Lifting that rule recovers the loss, and the second residual model added to replace the ignored alarms adds nothing on injected transfers. 00070 sw2-19-same-sign-neighbour-count lsc-detectors supported Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation found 0.048 more of the moved power on injected transfers than the single-series detector, at the same number of unexplained alarms. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain (7 found, against 8 for the benchmark), and the gain does not extend to transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar solar-disaggregation supported Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand retraining-and-training-history supported B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models calibration-and-uncertainty supported Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand retraining-and-training-history inconclusive C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). 00033 best-guess-architecture-vs-production production-reference-and-best-guess supported The best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), each wholly below its threshold. 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand demand-inputs inconclusive C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost hierarchy-and-pooling supported Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. 00020 solar-wind-stack-cams-stage0-spread-margin calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For wind, a starting guess from the turbine power curve lowered the error by 0.055 points of capacity (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), and adding a spread factor made the total 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014); the spread factor's extra -0.016 (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. For solar, no change helped detectably, and the full stack was 0.035 points higher with an interval that includes zero (-0.075 to +0.116). 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic production-reference-and-best-guess supported C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). 00016 pooled-mixture-calibration-solar-wind calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For solar, one spread factor brought the 5% to 95% band from covering 94.3% to 95.3% of cases down to 89.5% to 91.8%, with no detectable change in accuracy. For wind, no planned correction fixed the first two days, and a spread factor on two lead groups, added after seeing the results, brought every lead band to 90.7% to 92.5% coverage and has not been tested on another year. 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand weather-products-and-blending inconclusive C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep demand-inputs partly supported P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. 00002 stage2-calibrator-and-mixture-vs-ens-quantile calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported Pooling the ERA5-trained solar and wind quantiles over the 51 weather-forecast members beat a model trained on archived weather forecasts: wind by 0.62 points of capacity (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and solar by 0.24 (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. A second calibration model on top did not improve on the pooling and made solar worse by 0.40 points (+0.26 to +0.61). The result rests on 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and one validation year. 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained weather-products-and-blending supported P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond.

docs.title: What the experiments taught us so far
docs.text:
• Retrain the Primary demand model weekly, and do not add a 14-day error correction. Weekly retraining without the correction scored 0.20 points of capacity below the best-guess stack, whose frozen model has the correction (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035), and a 7-day correction on the weekly model raised the score by 0.16 (-0.06 to +0.36), unresolved (00048). Experiment 34 found the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained, and hurts at weekly and daily cadence. The 14-day correction (00019, 00021) was measured on a frozen model, and the retraining results supersede it for Primary demand.
  • The 14-day correction on a frozen model is a historical result. It lowered the quantile score of N1, a model frozen at its training end, by 0.99 points (00019). At 4 bulk and grid supply point series it did not lower the score (00021), and at the supply points in experiment 87 adding it raised the score by 0.305 points.
  • A weather product as accurate as ERA5 would lower the Primary demand score by 1.9%. ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score by 0.10 points, nearly all from shortwave radiation and none up to 2 days ahead (00022).
  • Check for calendar memorisation. When the same valid time repeats across many ENS runs, a model with calendar columns can memorise it. Give each experiment a climatology row, and group folds by valid time.
  • Choose a row set that covers every weekday. The 53 Tuesday runs of 00001 and 00002 put every case of the first day on a Tuesday or Wednesday, which does not suit demand.
  • Training on ERA5 weather helps solar and wind, but a longer history does not add to it, and for demand a long history hurt. The solar and wind gain appeared even when the ERA5-trained model saw only the ENS-era months, so the gain comes from the weather it was trained on and not from the years. For demand, training from 2019 was worse than training from 2023, probably because the customer mix and embedded generation drifted.
  • Put recent power in the stage 2 calibrator, and calibrate before judging it. For Primary substations, the calibrator with recent-origin inputs beat a stage 1b correction, and a lag-free calibrator is worth about 1 point of capacity at short leads (00005).
  • The term and return-to-work columns showed no detectable gain on top of the Christmas column for Primary demand. Over the three validation years, the return and term columns moved the Primary error by +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 at Easter (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half terms (-0.68 to +0.07), and Both was not 0.2 points better than a calendar shifted by 17 days (00011). The arm with the full history and the COVID indicator scored 0.26 points higher on the whole year than the base arm.
  • A change that helps the point forecast of solar or wind need not help the pooled mixture's CRPS. CAMS-trained solar lowered the member-average error by 0.14 points (00012) and the mixture's CRPS by 0.009 (00020), and a stage 0 mapping widened the member spread by a quarter. A power-curve base margin lowered the wind CRPS by 0.055 (00020).
  • Attach the forecast solar term to the XGBoost model as a base margin, with a weight fitted on the training window and zero beyond 10 days. The base-margin arm lowered the Primary demand quantile score by 0.152 points (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111) against the best guess d0 and 0.256 against d1l, where the fixed-coefficient shift of 00046 lowered d1l by 0.056, and subtracting the forecast solar from a model trained on gross demand was not shown to match the best guess (00064).
  • Do not expect a zero start to help the production XGBoost models. Experiment 78 found that a zero base margin lowered its reference model d0 by 0.071 points, but on the production recipe the zero start changed the Primary score by -0.017 (-0.072 to +0.054) and the solar score by -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028), and worsened wind models without a power-curve margin by 0.049 (00080).
  • Refresh the capacity table that feeds the base margin once per season-year. A table refreshed that often captured almost all of the gain from a current capacity (00078).

docs.title: Data processing to apply in future experiments and production
docs.text: The experiments so far show that the power readings, the switching log, and the embedded-solar capacity estimates all need processing before an XGBoost model trains or scores on them. This page lists each step as an instruction. Every entry says where the step applies (experiments, production, or both), links the experiments that are the evidence, and states the scope the evidence covers. An entry whose evidence is a first look at the data gives its confidence in words. A plan for an experiment begins by reading this page.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• D code: an anonymised series label, such as D4, used in the experiment write-ups (see experiment 51). The page also names a few substations (Stickney, Kirton, Wrangle T1, Wrangle T2, and Mount Bridge Boston) as the experiment write-ups name them. A D code and a substation name are different labels, and the page does not say which D code matches which name.
  • Primary: a Primary substation, which steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. Sixteen of the 32 trial series are Primaries.
  • Point of capacity: 1% of a series' capacity. Scores in points of capacity are smaller when the forecast is better.
  • Season-year: a 12-month period running from September to August.
  • Best guess: the project's current forecasting recipe, assembled in experiment 33.
  • Skill: the percentage by which the best guess's quantile score is lower than the score of the rule-based forecast manual_heuristic.
  • Dark row: a half-hour in which the irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) is below 1 W/m².
  • Closure: a period in NGED's switching log in which an operator closed a switch that is normally open.
  • Transfer: a switching operation that moves part of one Primary's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The Primary that loses the load is the donor substation, and the receiving load is the usual load of the substations that gain it.
  • Labeller: a language model that reads the power readings and judges whether a transfer is visible, as in experiment 41.
  • Residual panel: the stored table of residuals, each the measured power minus the power an XGBoost model predicted.
  • Error correction: the 14-day correction that adds the forecast's recent errors to the next forecast.
  • Abnormal running arrangement (ARA) and normal running arrangement (NRA): an ARA is a period in which an operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary carries load that belongs to a neighbour. The NRA is the usual layout.
  • Tail coverage at q95: the share of observed values that fall below the forecast's 95th percentile, which is 0.95 for a forecast with correct tails.
  • Curtailment cost: the avoidable cost, in pounds, of a forecast's errors when a node is held to a limit (experiment 84).

docs.title: Series and units
docs.text:
Count 32 time series in version 1 of the trial area. They are 16 Primary substations, 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, 2 grid supply points, 2 bulk supply points, and 3 other generators or storage units, as the home page lists. Applies to experiments and production.

Read each series' unit from the units column of the metadata table, and treat the Primaries metered in MVA as a different kind of series. A series is metered in MW (signed active power) or in MVA (apparent power, which is never negative). Eight of the 16 trial Primaries are metered only in MVA. Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: experiment 79 found no reverse flow at 7 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries from April to September, and experiment 56 could not tell the best guess's skill at the 8 MVA-only Primaries from its skill at the 8 MW Primaries (inconclusive). Experiment 110 fitted a power factor to only 2 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries (and recovered one of them, D12), because the other 6 have almost no reverse flow in their training rows. It held the power factor at 0.97 at those 6, and modelling the meter as apparent power scored 0.13 points of capacity better than reading it as real power. Experiment 204 summed the apparent-power children of two bulk supply points into the bulk supply point's reading: reading the magnitude as signed power or converting it with a fitted sign scored within 0.03 points at one bulk supply point and 0.02 to 0.03 points better with the sign at the other, where Stickney (D12) has reverse flow. Provisional.

Read power through the cleaned table, and read the raw table only when the question is about availability. The cleaned table holds only unflagged rows (nged_data.storage.scan_cleaned_power). Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: the data-cleaning roadmap page and experiment 6, which scores on cleaned power.

Count a series' history from its first unflagged row, which is later than its first row of any kind (high confidence). D9 starts in 2023-04 and its first unflagged row is in 2023-08. Only five Primaries hold long histories: D5, D10, and D11 start in 2019-09, D14 in 2019-10, and D16 in 2020-12. The late starters begin between 2023 and 2025. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

docs.title: Trim the start of each series
docs.text:
Cut the first months of most demand series (high confidence for D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18, medium to low for the rest). The first 1 to 19 months of a series often sit far from the same months in later years. A new meter can read near zero for days to weeks and then step up, and a new site can commission in stages. Cut until the level, the daily shape, and the share of rows present match the same months in later years. Cut more when the match is uncertain, and let a later look move a cut later and never earlier. Applies to experiments, and to production for a series that has just started reporting. The cuts found so far cover 16 of the 20 series examined (experiment 103, figure 4):

Series Cut Confidence Reason D4 19.4 months High Level 1.5 to 2 times too high, a stuck plateau, then too low, until a step on 2021-04-12 D14 8.3 months High Level about half of later years until a step of 2.2 MW on 2020-06-15 D17 5.6 months Medium Reads about 0, then 4 months of ramp and erratic swings D5 4.5 months Medium Night level 15% to 30% low until a step on 2020-01-09 D3 3.5 months High Night level 30% to 50% low and 15% to 60% of half-hours missing D18 2.6 months High Zeros, then a level near 0 to 1.5 MW with negative rows, then erratic D1, D10, D21 2.5 months Medium D1 unusually smooth then volatile; D10 and D21 have 30% to 70% of half-hours missing D22 1.5 months Low Gaps in most days and a night step D9, D16 1.3 months High Near zero, then a staged switch-on D13, D19 0.9 months Low Level steps in the first weeks D15 0.8 months Medium Erratic for 2 weeks while the meter was commissioned D12 7.4 months Low Night level 1.5 to 2 times later years; the start-of-series review recommends no cut, and the 15-point rule cuts it

Figure 1 shows the dropped months sitting far from the kept months at D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18. The figure draws 7 Primaries, and the cut dates come from the start-of-series review that experiment 103 confirmed. The grey dropped months are read from the raw power table, because the cleaned table removes flagged rows and the early months are often flagged. The blue kept months are read from the cleaned table. At D10 and D5 the dropped months look less different from the kept months, which fits their medium confidence.

An uncut start hurts a model without recent power far more than a model with it (high confidence for D18). In experiment 102, D18's training rows began with a late start at zero output. A weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three recent-power inputs forecast 20% of capacity in December 2025 against an actual of 75%, and its score at D18 was 5.7 points of capacity worse than the same model with the inputs. With the start cut (training from a later date), the difference at D18 fell to -0.03 points. The cost of removing the inputs across the 16 Primaries fell from 0.710 to 0.361 points. Applies to experiments, and to any comparison of a model with and without recent power. A comparison that cuts the start for one arm must cut it for every arm.

docs.title: Decide which rows are demand
docs.text:
Use a Primary metered in MVA for demand only on dark rows (high confidence). An MVA reading cannot show reverse flow, so the solar output behind the Primary reads as demand in daylight. A filter that keeps rows with irradiance below 100 W/m² still keeps rows with solar output, because the filter admits irradiance above 1 W/m². After the start cuts, the dark rows leave 2.4 to 3.3 site-years per MVA Primary with the 2020 lockdown kept, 2.3 to 2.7 with the fixed lockdown window removed, and 0.9 to 1.0 in 2023-07 to 2025-06. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Figure 2 shows that the daylight half-hours at an MVA-only Primary carry a solar dip that the dark half-hours lack. The grey daylight half-hours sit in the middle of each day, where embedded solar output reduces the net flow and the apparent power cannot show its sign. The blue dark half-hours form the smooth evening and night curve that holds demand alone. The figure draws one Primary (D2) for two weeks of July 2025.

Do not treat grid supply points or bulk supply points as clean demand (high confidence). The grid supply points are dominated by generation: D1 is below 5 points of capacity on 75% of nights. The bulk supply points sum the trial Primaries: D17 reverses flow on 51% of May to August days at midday. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Screen for embedded generation with the share of negative dark half-hours (high confidence). Series with 26% to 82% of their dark half-hours negative carry embedded generation or an exporting grid connection. The screen cannot work on an MVA Primary. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103, figure 9.

Count the half-hours that substation_zero flags before scoring a detector on a transfer. (Provisional.) The rule flags a reading of exactly 0 at a Primary substation, and a transformer that was switched out read exactly 0 in the 5 transfers we checked. At the series P12 and P13, the two transformers of one Primary substation, the rule flagged 426 half-hours inside 5 of the 6 labelled real transfers lasting more than 1 day, and the panel of residuals used to score detectors held no readings there. The cleaned power table keeps flagged rows with their original readings, and restoring those half-hours let the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) find 4 of the 6 transfers. This applies to experiments on switching. For production, the maintainer has to decide whether the rule should keep a zero reading when the other transformer of the same Primary substation carries the load of the switched-out transformer. Evidence: experiment 132. Confidence: medium, from 5 transfers at one Primary substation.

docs.title: Unlabelled jumps
docs.text:
Before reading flow on two substations with no interconnection (a placebo pair) as a fault of a method, check whether either substation has unlabelled jumps (low confidence). In experiment 131's replicate year (2024-25), the edge-flow fit with a drift term put 4.27 MW-days a year on D16 and D10. Of those, 1.58 lie inside the two D10 windows described under "Expect D10 to carry unlabelled jumps" below. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 131.

Do not train a learned load-shift score with every real candidate as a negative and then score it on the months it trained on (medium confidence). Real load shifts that start in the training months are then taught as negatives: the score trained that way found 0 of the 15 logged load shifts that start in training months, against 7 for the same score with logged and labelled spans removed from its negatives. In the 20 load shifts that start in other months both found 13 (post hoc, experiment 302). Applies to experiments; provisional.

docs.title: Fixed windows
docs.text:
Use the fixed lockdown window, 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, and do not detect the window from the data. Experiment 6 defines its indicator with these dates, and the indicator lowered the error by 0.26 points of capacity on the selection fold. A window found from the data picks up drift and solar growth as well (experiment 103, figure 12; medium confidence): a drift-removed fit finds April 2020 more than 5 points low only at D11 (-26 points) and D10 (-7 points), and August 2020 to September 2021 sits 5 to 17 points above the fit at D5, D10, D11, and D14. Applies to experiments and production.

A dataset of dated events that ends before 2021-07-20 cannot be compared with the demand-model fit's training rows, because the lockdown window removes every earlier row from training. The feed-in tariff register, a list of small solar installations, ends on 2021-03-24, so none of its dates falls in a month on which the fit trains (experiment 215). Applies to experiments.

Check how many days of training rows a demand-model fit kept after the lockdown window is removed, and flag a fit with fewer than 180 days (provisional; medium confidence). Leaving the lockdown window out of training left Christmas 2020-21 fits with 51 to 143 days of rows. Every substation's Christmas 2021-22 fit had the same 104 summer days and no winter, and D9's 2023-24 fit had 31 days. The fits with under 180 days scored 1.38 to 1.91 times their ordinary-weekday error pooled over substations at Christmas, and D9 alone scored 5.6 times, where fits with at least 180 days scored 0.97 to 1.22 times (experiment 173; the 180-day threshold was chosen after the scores were read, and thresholds of 90 and 270 days gave the same picture for 2022-23 onwards). The Kalman filter and recipe R in that experiment do not repair a fit that saw little or no winter. Applies to experiments and production.

Give the series that changed regime an individual start date or a flag (medium confidence). D8 weekday daytime demand falls from about 9 MW to about 3 MW between 2023-10 and 2025. D12 switches between a high-night and a low-night regime. D18 steps up about 1.1 MW at night around 2026-07-03 (a date after the experiment's window, not rechecked there), and D5 shows a flat midday floor since 2022. Month-mean steps of over three monthly standard deviations occur at D6 (a drop of 218 MW in 2023-07) and D11 (2020-04). Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103 for the step list and D8.

Treat D8's reading as including one gas engine's output until 2023-08-15, and as excluding it afterwards (provisional, medium confidence). The engine connected on 2023-06-13 and its own readings carry output from 2023-07-03. While those readings arrived, D8's residual rose by 0.02 MW per MW of engine output, where a reading without the output would fall by 1 MW per MW.

D8's share of half-hours with a residual below -2.5 MW then stepped from 0.010 to 0.257 in the week of 2023-08-14 and stayed between 0.10 and 0.46 in every month to January 2026. The share fell from 0.292 in January 2026 to 0.070 in March and 0.008 in April, with no matching change in the engine's own readings, so whether the engine is visible in D8 from 2026 is unknown. Applies to experiments; whether it applies to production awaits NGED's answer. Evidence: experiment 194.

Give a forecast the engine state it will have at forecast time, and train the engine term on that same lagged state (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. D8's engine detector gives a state for each half-hour that is built from that half-hour's own reading. A coefficient fitted on that contemporaneous state is 3.6 MW per half-hour with one or more units running, but the state of the last settled day is worth 0.15 MW (interval -0.06 to 0.32) out of sample, so applying the contemporaneous coefficient to the lagged state makes the quantile score 10% worse. Trained on the lagged state, the coefficient is 0.9 to 1.0 MW and the score is 3% better than a model without the term (experiment 294).

Do not fit calendar and seasonal terms exactly (by variable projection, which solves the linear coefficients exactly at each step) to a window of three months or shorter. An exact least-squares fit of a per-substation model with holiday, tent, harmonic, and profile terms to 4 weeks or 3 months of data extrapolates those terms badly: the per-site fits scored 70.6 and 48.4 points at the five decision substations, against 15.1 and 5.5 for the gradient fits that stop before convergence. No window between 3 months and 2 years was tested. The pooled model with its interaction network failed the same way on four days of the scored year, where an exact fit with weak penalties forecast up to 280 points too high (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.

Treat a heating threshold above a substation's highest temperature, and any per-site threshold of a pooled model, as unidentified. Above the highest temperature the heating hinge is always on, and the deviation absorbs a shift, so only the prior sets the threshold; at real noise (standard deviation 5 points) a synthetic fleet with a 14 degree threshold was recovered to 2.7 to 5.7 degrees with the interaction network off or on (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.

docs.title: Drift in demand over the years
docs.text:
Do not assume that one level shift removes drift, because drift differs by series and by hour band. In 12 of 13 series some band moves by at least 1 point of capacity a year. From April to September the pooled slope is -1.30 points a year at midday (95% interval -2.32 to -0.92), -0.88 in the evening, and +0.69 at night. The all-hours slope is +0.04 because series drift in both directions (experiment 92). Subtracting a trailing 365-day level removed 42% of the old training year's penalty only when the largest series was included, and none of the penalty without that series (experiment 93). Applies to experiments and production. Scope: 13 Primary series with at least 24 months of data.

Do not expect an older training year to become usable by matching its weather product. Changing the weather product from 18 km to 9 km grid spacing does not explain why an old training year scores worse than a recent one (experiment 95). Applies to experiments and production.

Allow for a demand drop shared across sites in season-year 2022 (medium confidence). Evening demand fell by 7 to 10 points and night demand by 2 to 7 points of capacity at D10, D11, and D5 against season-year 2021, and recovered partly by 2025 at D5 and D11 but not at D10, probably after the rise in energy prices. Evidence: experiment 103, the season-year means in report.txt. A model trained across years can read the drop as a trend. Applies to experiments.

Expect monthly night demand to move together across the long-history Primaries, and expect the winter heating slope of night power not to drift (medium confidence). Winter heating slopes of night power show no detectable drift between the first and last winter at the long-history sites. Monthly levels move together across sites, with a mean pairwise correlation of 0.56 at night and 0.47 in the evening after the seasonal cycle is removed (experiment 103, figure 8). Applies to experiments, before pooling sites.

Figure 3 shows the same seasonal swing at all 5 long-history Primaries, with D10 swinging furthest. The grey band is the fixed lockdown window. The figure does not isolate the shared month-to-month level that the correlations above describe, because the seasonal cycle dominates the figure.

Centre the residual quantiles of a replica fit before adding them to a forecast's mean. The raw quantiles carry the replica year's mean bias, so adding them shifts every quantile of the scored year by that bias. In experiment 104 the shift moved the median forecast by -21.3 to +3.6 points at the six long-history Primaries and reversed the sign of two contrasts (all years against 12 months, and drift against no drift) (experiment 104, Correction). Applies to experiments and to production. Confidence: high, because the centred and uncentred sets differ only in this shift.

For the convex demand model, tie a joint fit through a level-tracking filter to the two-stage coefficients (provisional). In a fit that minimises the error after a Kalman filter that tracks a level, the filter absorbs a constant shift of each slow term (the weekly profile, the tent, and the harmonics), so the loss leaves those terms to the penalty alone. The untied joint fit's weekly profile moved by a median of 19 points of capacity (up to 95) when the training cut-off moved back by 7 days, against 1 point for the two-stage fit, and its quantile score at 12 to 36 hours was 5.4 points of capacity worse (experiment 135). A ridge tie to the two-stage coefficients cut the weekly-profile movement to 1 point and left the score within 0.013 points of the two-stage fit. Applies to experiments. Evidence: five decision substations, the scored year, one model family. Confidence: medium, because the explanation was not tested by a variant of the loss.

Give a capacity increment only to a season-year with enough training rows (provisional). A fit whose cut is 2024-07-01 includes the half-hour that ends exactly at the cut, which belongs to season-year 2024, so that season-year has only 2 rows at D5. A free capacity increment for those 2 rows reached -56 points in an unconstrained fit. The N5 scripts drop any season-year with fewer than 1,000 training rows from the capacity columns, so the rows count towards the previous season-year's capacity (experiment 113). Applies to experiments that fit the convex model's capacity. Evidence: D5 at the 2024-07-01 cut. Confidence: high.

docs.title: Timestamps and availability
docs.text:
Treat ERA5 as available about 5 days after the event, so ERA5 at lag times is a ceiling and not an input that a live service can have. ERA5 is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) estimate of past weather. Name the weather source used at lag times in every write-up. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 37 and experiment 38 both state the delay and call their numbers retrospective.

Treat an ECMWF ensemble run as usable 9 hours after its init_time, and derive power_fcst_init_time from the run. The constant NWP_PUBLICATION_DELAY_HOURS in packages/ml_core/src/ml_core/features/_nwp.py is 9. A 00Z run reaches our disk at about 10:30 UTC, which is 10.5 hours after its init_time, so the 9 hours is not the time the run arrives. The delay is the earliest usable time of a slot: any delay above 6 hours and up to 12 hours selects the same run at each of the four 6-hourly slots, and 9 hours gives each slot the run that a healthy ingest has landed by that slot. Bulk-mode training uses the same constant to derive power_fcst_init_time, so changing the constant changes the training features. A replay of a past init_time must apply the delay, because joining a run that landed afterwards is lookahead bias. Applies to experiments and production. Source: the constant's docstring in that file.

Join power and CAMS timestamps on (time - 1 µs).truncate("1h") + 1h (medium to high confidence). A power timestamp marks the end of its half-hour, and a CAMS timestamp marks the end of its hour. A naive join on equal timestamps drops or misassigns half the rows, and shifting the join by 30 minutes earlier weakens the correlation between hourly power and irradiance by 0.04 (experiment 103, figure 10). Applies to experiments and production.

Do not shift power timestamps: the time column of the cleaned power table marks the end of the half-hour (high confidence that no 30-minute error exists). Power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of NGED's fix of 2026-03-26 08:30 UTC, and the ingest's correction of the earlier late stamps goes the right way by the right amount. The test used clear days and the change in net power against a sun-height predictor at sunrise and sunset, with an offset search from -120 to +120 minutes and 95% intervals from resampling days, on the aggregate of the 6 metered solar farms. Before the fix, the corrected stamps read 0.9 minutes late (series from -0.2 to +2.9), so the raw feed was about 31 minutes late and the 30-minute ingest correction is right to within about 3 minutes. After the fix, from April to 2026-09-10, the median is +4.7 minutes (+1.5 to +13.3). The same months before the fix read +2.0 (-3.3 to +5.4), so the two sides do not differ. Primaries metered in MW are a weaker test, because demand ramps bias the fit: only D5 and D18 gave usable fits (+7 to +18 minutes). A correlation-peak test on summer middays is uninformative, because the correlation is flat near -0.18 with peaks at +/-60 to 90 minutes, so use sunrise and sunset ramps on clear days (experiment 103, figure 13). Applies to experiments and production. Scope: all power series, 2019 to 2026. The limits are that the metered solar farms lie within one 25 km area, the side after the fix has under 50 clear days, and the only known-answer check is the 30-minute sign test.

Assume a power reading reaches the forecast 3.5 hours after the half-hour it covers, and treat the number as an assumption. The recent-level filter of experiment 106 sees only the residuals whose half-hour ended at least 3.5 hours before the 09:00 UTC initialisation, the delay that experiments 87 and 104 use for lagged power (3 hours plus the half-hour a reading covers). No experiment has measured the delay of the live telemetry. Readings 0 hours old instead of 3.5 lowered the score by 0.035 points (95% interval -0.060 to -0.016). Readings 9 hours old raised it by 0.026 (0.000 to 0.046), and readings 24 hours old raised it by 0.099 (0.059 to 0.142), on five Primaries in the scored year. Experiment 115 repeated the sweep on ensemble weather at day D+1 (scored year, five Primaries, difference of mean scores without an interval): readings 0 hours old lowered the score by 0.016 points, readings 24 hours old raised it by 0.088, and readings 33 hours old raised it by 0.120. Applies to experiments and production. Provisional: the delay was not measured on live telemetry. Confidence: low for the delay, medium for the size of its effect.

When power readings are missing, let the Kalman filter coast and widen the quantile bands; do not fall back to the convex demand model with no correction (provisional, low to medium confidence). Coasting means running the Kalman filter, which estimates the recent error of the demand model's forecast, without feeding it new readings, so its short-lived error component decays and its slowly varying error component holds steady. After injected gaps of 3 to 72 hours, coasting scored 0.245 to 0.439 points of quantile score better (in percent of effective capacity, lower is better) than the demand model with no correction, over leads of 0.5 to 168 hours. Widening each quantile's offset from the mean by the filter's variance growth since the last reading reduced the share of readings below the predicted 5% quantile from 7.7% to 5.5% after a 24-hour gap (the target is 5%), without worsening the quantile score. The data could not show whether, after about 72 hours, it would be better to drop the filter but keep the winter night offset and recipe R. Applies to production. Evidence: experiment 205, at five Primary substations (up to 56 injected gaps each, made by hiding readings in clean data).

docs.title: Weather products
docs.text:
Train each model on the history of the weather product that will serve it, and do not train on the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA) archive of the Met Office's UKV forecast and then serve the live UKV. UKV is the Met Office's UK Variable-resolution forecast, on a 2 km grid. The CEDA archive and the live product are statistically different, and the archive is licensed for non-commercial use (experiment 53). Applies to experiments and production.

Calibrate the ECMWF ensemble's temperature and irradiance before it drives a model trained on ERA5 and CAMS, and expect shifts of up to about 2 K in temperature and 20% in irradiance (medium confidence). Per substation, season, lead band, and hour band, the ensemble-mean temperature needed a shift of -1.15 to +2.05 K (mean +0.20) and the daylight irradiance a ratio of 0.80 to 1.11 (mean 0.95) at five Primary substations, fitted on the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06. Shrinking the forecast solar anomaly towards CAMS's month-by-half-hour climatology did not help in any lead band (experiment 111). Applies to experiments, and to production if a model trained on past weather serves ensemble forecasts.

Drop an ensemble member that has a missing weather value from its run at that substation, and refuse a run whose control member is incomplete (medium confidence). Member 36 of the run of 2025-06-04 has 12 missing shortwave values at two Primaries, which would fail every half-hour of the run at those substations; the ensemble mixture then pools the remaining 50 members' forecasts (experiment 111). Applies to experiments and production.

Treat the ECMWF ensemble's shortwave radiation as a 6-hour mean after lead 144 hours. Applies to: experiments and production. "Lead" is the hours after the ensemble run's start time. The ensemble store's stamps are 3-hourly up to lead 144 hours and 6-hourly from lead 150 to 360 hours, and each downward shortwave value is a mean over the period that ends at the stamp. A pipeline that assumes 3-hour periods misplaces the daily peak after lead 144 hours (experiment 310). The evidence is a build for six solar farms in the trial area at leads of 12 to 252 hours. The confidence is moderate, and the entry is provisional until the experiment has had its reviews.

Drop observations that were not known at run time when building the manual_heuristic and climatology references. Applies to: experiments and production. manual_heuristic takes the quantiles of 13 earlier observed powers, 1 to 6 weeks and 49 to 55 weeks before the half-hour. When the lead exceeds 7 days, the observation 1 week before the half-hour is not yet known at run time. Drop that observation at those leads (experiment 310). The confidence is moderate, and the entry is provisional until the experiment has had its reviews.

Do not assume the unit PV shape rises with irradiance at low sun. Applies to: experiments. SunGeometry.pv_shape_and_ghi returned a unit PV shape that fell from 0.124 to 0.090 as half-hourly irradiance rose from 150 to 227 W/m2 at an elevation of about 14 degrees, in a fake ensemble that scaled the irradiance of one substation by 0.6 to 1.4. The response of the T-all fit to member irradiance was therefore not monotone on 1.8% of the daylight rows with a physical clear-sky index, all at elevations of 14 to 16 degrees (experiment 184). The scored contrast did not change when rows under 17 degrees were dropped. The confidence is moderate, and the entry is provisional until the experiment has had its reviews.

docs.title: Wind farms
docs.text:
Do not compute air density from the ECMWF ensemble's surface pressure for a model trained on ERA5 surface pressure (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments and production. The ensemble's surface pressure at the three metered wind farms is 0.7 to 7.0 hPa above ERA5's in the monthly mean (about +2.7 hPa on average, because the two products use different terrain heights), and a density column built from the ensemble pressure scored 0.049 points worse than temperature alone (95% interval 0.015 to 0.091). Evidence: experiment 256, three farms, July 2025 to June 2026.

Drop the rows in mask.parquet of experiment 210 before training or scoring on the three metered wind farms, and do not expect ERA5 wind speed alone to find idle rows (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. The idle floor is a set of near-zero readings with repeated values (W1 and W3 in MVA) or small negative readings (W2 in MW, down to -0.071 MW). At ERA5 100 m wind of 5 to 8 m/s, 11% to 50% of half-hours are in the idle band, and a wind-speed threshold that keeps false drops under 5% misses 51% to 69% of idle-band half-hours out of sample. The mask adds runs of at least 12 hours in the idle band at high ERA5 wind (suspected outages), which total 160 hours at W1, 428 at W2, and 2,742 at W3. W3's idle share at wind above 10 m/s is 6.2% over all years and 1.5% from 2021, so its first 2 years differ from the later ones. Evidence: experiment 210, three farms, 2019-09 to 2026-09. The mask is built on ERA5, which arrives about 5 days late, so it is for training and evaluation rows and not for live use. Removing the mask's rows from training lowered the quantile score of both the physics core and the XGBoost model when the weather was the 51 ensemble members (by 0.075 and 0.062 points on the kept rows, intervals excluding zero), and worsened it by under 0.015 points when the weather was ERA5 (experiment 276, three farms, July 2025 to June 2026).

Build the ensemble hindcast member rows with the production feature engineer, and expect a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm to lower the wind forecast's quantile score (provisional, low confidence). Applies to: experiments. The production TabularFeatureEngineer reproduced the stored scored-year frames of experiment 230 exactly and built 442 daily runs (April 2024 to June 2025) for the three metered wind farms in a few minutes. On the scored year, a table of offsets fitted on those runs lowered the quantile score of the physics-core forecast by 0.60 points, and a neural head given the ensemble's wind summaries did no better. The observed power was below the physics-core forecast's median on 31% to 40% of rows in every scored quarter and 33% in the first hindcast quarter, so the offsets correct a stable low bias in the ensemble mixture's median, whose cause the experiment did not identify. Evidence: experiment 259, three farms, July 2025 to June 2026.

Do not fit a wind-forecast correction to the single year of ensemble hindcast runs without checking that the speed-to-power relation of the hindcast year matches the scored year (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments and production. At the three metered wind farms, observed power at the same ensemble-mean 100 m wind speed was higher in the scored year (July 2025 to June 2026) than in the hindcast runs (April 2024 to June 2025) in most speed bins, and the mean observed fraction of capacity rose from 0.20 to 0.25 at W1, from 0.25 to 0.28 at W2, and from 0.21 to 0.25 at W3, while the ensemble-mean speed rose by 0.3 m/s. A neural adapter fitted to the hindcast runs scored 0.21 to 1.04 points worse than the same adapter fitted to ERA5 and then given an offset table, and an offset table fitted to the hindcast runs still helped. Evidence: experiment 303, three farms, July 2025 to June 2026; the cause of the shift is not identified.

Correct the ECMWF ensemble's 10 m and 100 m wind speeds before a wind-power model fitted to ERA5 reads them, and expect the uncorrected input to lower the median forecast by about 10 points of capacity (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments and production. At the three metered wind farms the ensemble-mean 100 m wind was 1.0 m/s slower than ERA5's in July 2025 to June 2026 (0.7 m/s in the hindcast), growing from 0.4 m/s at days 0 to 2 to 1.3 m/s from day 7, and 1.5 m/s slower at ERA5 speeds of 8 to 12 m/s. The 10 m wind was 1.3 m/s slower at those speeds. A physics-based wind-power model fitted to ERA5 had 52.8% of rows below its median when fed ERA5 wind (after dropping the idle rows of experiment 210's mask), and 36.6% when fed the ensemble-mean wind. The swap lowered the median by 10.2 points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity), and the 10 m and 100 m speeds each explained about 7 points alone. Evidence: experiment 261, three farms, July 2025 to June 2026.

Do not drop half-hours when the final physical notification exceeds metered output by more than 5% of capacity, when cleaning public wind farms' Elexon output (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. A wind farm's physical notification is the operator's own forecast. It correlates with metered output at only 0.7 to 0.8, and exceeds metered output in 35% of half-hours at the median of the 40 kept farms. The rule therefore removed 20% to 83% of the kept farms' half-hours, and kept the half-hours where the farm outproduced its forecast. Dropping only the half-hours with a bid-offer acceptance removed 3.6% of half-hours at the median kept farm and at most 10.4%. Evidence: experiment 288, 65 candidate Elexon wind units, of which 40 were kept, 2019-09 to 2026-06.

Leave capacity, turbine rating, and hub height out of a correction head trained on a pool of farms (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. Each of the 40 kept public wind farms has a distinct combination of those three values. A head given 3 random numbers per farm fitted the training farms as well as one given the real values. With the real values, a head trained on four fifths of the farms scored 12.8% worse on the held-out fifth than the head trained on all 40 farms, and beat the XGBoost forecast (R0) on 11 of 40 held-out farms. Without them, the held-out head scored 4.4% worse and beat R0 on 24 of 40. Evidence: experiment 288, 39 Scottish and 1 English wind farms, July 2025 to June 2026. Covers the pooled correction head only.

Score a wind-farm head on the idle half-hours before using it (provisional). The idle half-hours are the ones experiment 210's idle-band mask removes, where wind is near zero and the metered series holds a reactive-power floor. Where it applies: experiments that train a head on wind-farm rows after dropping those half-hours. Evidence: in experiment 324, a mixture-density head trained without the idle half-hours scored 0.27 points better than XGBoost plus the offset table on the other half-hours and 2.1 points worse on the 10,642 idle half-hours, so on all rows the gain was 0.04 points (95% interval -0.12 to 0.05). We did not test training with the idle half-hours included. Covers the three metered wind farms, July 2025 to June 2026. Confidence: medium.

docs.title: Embedded solar capacity
docs.text:
Hold embedded-solar capacity as one value per Primary per season-year, and do not estimate it weekly. In experiment 45, no pair of penalties on the grid was both quiet on noise and responsive to a real fall. The frozen weekly fit had a path error of 0.040 against 0.027 for the season-year constant on the semi-synthetic baseline, and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year against a limit of 0.5. Refreshing the table once per season-year captured almost all of the gain from a current capacity in experiment 78, which lowered the quantile score by 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004, where a negative value means a lower error). Applies to experiments and production. Scope: 8 Primaries metered in MW.

Feed the forecast a capacity built only from data before the run, keyed by the run's date. A capacity fitted on all the data leaks the future. The latest week of a real-time capacity had 3.63 times the path error of the same week in the final fit (experiment 45), so do not read the newest week as a measurement. Applies to experiments and production.

Mask the weeks with no usable observation, and never read them as zero capacity. One Primary (Mount Bridge Boston) has 198 unobserved weeks of 354, and its season-year constant falls to about 0 MW from 2023-09-04 to 2025-08-25, all in unobserved weeks (experiment 45). Applies to any capacity table.

Exclude the MVA-only Primaries from capacity fits. The MVA reading folds the solar output into positive demand, and experiment 39 fitted a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. A fit that unfolds the sign recovered capacity with a median error of 0.09 against 0.29 for the fit that ignores the sign. The unfolding fit found the direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78, where 0.5 is a guess, and the 75% to 87% reverse flow at Stickney from 2021 cannot be checked without signed power (experiment 79). Applies to experiments. Confidence: medium.

Drive the solar shape with CAMS irradiance, and report capacity as the 99th percentile of the half-hourly output in AC power. CAMS irradiance recovered an injected 99th-percentile capacity in experiment 39, and experiment 45 defines capacity the same way. Applies to experiments and capacity tables.

Treat Wrangle T1 and Wrangle T2 as one area for any outside solar count, and use the Primary's polygon and not its point. The two share one polygon, and one Primary's point lies 95 m outside its own polygon (experiment 45). Applies to experiments and production.

Flag the Primaries whose capacity is confounded, and carry the error bound of each unflagged one. Kirton is flagged in 6 of 7 season-years. A day-long cloud-driven load is detected in only 0.35 of simulated trials, so the bound on the capacity at the seven unflagged Primaries is 0.18 to 0.71 and not 0.10 (experiment 40). In experiment 39, 6 of the 8 Primaries passed all four real-data checks, and the placebo-sky check failed at Wrangle T1. Applies to experiments.

Do not fit the panel orientation mix or the ratio of direct-current to alternating-current rating from a Primary's power, and use a fixed menu instead. The orientation mix is not identified on injected mixes (experiment 73). A fitted east-south-west shape lowered the held-out fit error by 1.3% in experiment 73, but gave no forecast gain in experiment 77, which keeps the all-south shape. Applies to experiments.

Shrink the forecast solar anomaly, and do not rely on the anomaly beyond about 2 days. The residual of the ensemble-based median has a slope of -0.42 to -0.69 on the oracle shift in every month and hour bin (experiment 51), and -0.771 overall in experiment 46, so a coefficient of 1 is too large. The ensemble forecast of the solar anomaly carries skill only to about 2 days ahead (experiment 46). Shifting the ensemble mean scored 0.129 points (0.057 to 0.212) better than shifting each member (experiment 51). Applies to experiments, in summer daylight hours.

Remove the logged switching, padded by 24 hours, from every capacity fit. A transfer moves the donor substation's solar output and looks like a capacity step (experiment 45 applies this mask). Applies to experiments. Confidence: medium, because the write-up states the rule and does not test the rule.

Do not treat the real-time frozen capacity vintage as the season-year constant. The vintage is experiment 45's weekly capacity estimate made with data up to each origin date. Over the weeks that it and the hindsight season-year constant share, the two differ in every week, by a ratio of 0.30 to 1.48 in the early weeks of 2020 and 2021 and by up to about 10% in the weeks near the end of the data (experiment 104). Each origin lists weekly capacities back to 2019-09, but the first origin is 2023-08, so a training cut before then has no real-time capacity. Take the latest origin on or before the cut, hold its last week afterwards, and hold the last observed value through unobserved weeks. Applies to experiments. Scope: six MW Primaries. Confidence: high for the difference, which was measured week by week; medium for the size near the cut, which comes from five Primaries.

Pin the capacity in a model to the real-time vintage. A capacity fitted together with the other terms moves with the optimiser's starting point (experiment 105's pooled model reached different capacities at nearly the same fit). Experiment 106 therefore takes the weekly capacity from the latest frozen vintage whose origin is on or before the cut, holds the median of the last 13 weeks up to the cut afterwards, and holds the last observed value through unobserved weeks. The latest week's capacity has 3.63 times the path error of the final fit's capacity for the same week (experiment 45), which is why the median of 13 weeks is held and not the last week. Applies to experiments. Scope: the six MW Primaries and D18. Confidence: medium. The fitted capacity scored 0.04 points better in the scored year and 0.16 worse in the replicate year, so the two choices are not separable on this evidence.

A cut before the first real-time origin uses hindsight, and the amount differs by substation. The first origin is 2023-08-07 at the five long-history Primaries. A cut up to 6 weeks before an origin uses that vintage as it is (5 weeks at the tuning cut of 2023-07-01). A cut more than 6 weeks before the first origin takes the median of the vintage's last 13 weeks and scales it back at 5% a year, the median of 12 season-year (1 July to 30 June) increments at five Primaries. That level is hindsight: D9 at 2024-07-01 looks 9.5 months ahead, D15 at 2025-07-01 370 days, D18 at every cut up to the whole scored year, and every Primary at the tuning year's replica (2022-07-01) 13 months. D14's vintage stops at 2023-04-17 at every origin, so its capacity is held from then.

Leave a substation out of a joint (pooled) fit at any cut where its pinned capacity is a late vintage (provisional). A hindsight capacity in one substation's target would move the fleet mean and so every other substation's forecast. In experiment 158, D9's capacity is a late vintage at every cut before 2025-04, so D9 was fitted alone at those cuts and joined the fleet from 2025-04. Applies to experiments and production. Confidence: medium; the rule follows studies.dp_gam_pooled's refusal, and no experiment measured the size of the effect.

With the capacity pinned, a drift term absorbs an injected solar farm in the hours the farm produces. The morning, midday, and evening bands move, and the night band does not (0.004 to 0.011 points in experiment 106's test). Applies to experiments.

Do not count a season-year as trained because a few half-hours of it precede the cut. A season-year runs from 1 July to 30 June. A training cut at 1 July 00:00 UTC leaves two night-time half-hours of the next season-year in the training data, because local time is an hour ahead in summer, so a model would count a whole extra season-year as trained and give it a capacity and a centring mean from those two rows. Count a season-year as trained only when it holds enough rows (experiment 104 uses 30 days of half-hours for centring, and any solar signal for capacity). Applies to experiments. Confidence: high, because a test of the training rows shows it.

Treat the ERA5 half-hourly file's :30 values as interpolated. Each :30 value is the mean of the hourly values either side of it, so it contains the reading from the hour after the half-hour it labels. Treat it as interpolated, not as a separate measurement (experiment 104). Applies to experiments. Confidence: high, because the mean absolute difference from the neighbours' average is zero.

Do not read the PV capacity of a pooled demand model as a measurement, and do not expect a prior to hold it near the vintages. In the pooled differentiable-physics model, the inferred capacity of a substation changed by up to 20 points of capacity with another start or with the network off (D5 50 or 30, D9 12 or 23, in season-year 2023), and a prior centred on the vintage with scale 5 changed nothing, because the prior is a few nats against about 340,000 rows of data. A swap of the fitted capacity paths among substations still worsened the summer-midday error at 6 of 6 (experiment 105). Applies to experiments that fit capacity inside a demand model. Confidence: medium. A capacity profile shows the free fit's loss is 4,563 nats above a fit with the capacities pinned at the convex model's, so the optimiser is the weak point; why it is slow is not tested.

Skip the solar-offset arms at D18, which has no capacity vintage before 2025-07-01. Its first usable data begin in February 2025, so an origin on or before the cut does not exist (experiment 105). Applies to experiments. Confidence: high.

Rebuild a new substation's effective capacity from its own rows before a model pools it in points, and fit its solar capacity from the same rows. A power series is divided by its effective capacity, the 99th percentile of its absolute power over its history, and a substation with 4 weeks of history has only that window to take the percentile from. In experiment 109 the whole-history capacity was 1.29 to 2.04 times the capacity rebuilt from June 4-week windows, 1.09 to 1.66 times the one rebuilt from April-to-June 3-month windows, and 0.91 to 0.98 times the one rebuilt from January 4-week windows, so a model that pools coefficients in points sees a June substation as larger than it is. A vintage capacity that is fitted after the cut holds the future, so a model that reads it for a short window leaks it. The same applies to a pooled substation that holds only part of its window (D18 in experiment 109): its scale is rebuilt from the rows it holds. Applies to experiments that pool a substation with a short history, and to onboarding in production. Evidence: experiment 109 (scored year, six held-out Primaries; provisional: one experiment, gate not passed under its pre-registered definition). The rule is motivated by leakage. Pooling D18 on its whole-history scale instead moves three contrasts by 0.03 to 0.05 points.

Do not pool a capacity read from a vintage fitted long after the cut. In a joint fit such a capacity moves the fleet mean, and so every other substation's forecast. Give the substation a capacity fitted from its own rows before the cut instead (D9 at the 2024-07-01 cut and D18 at the 2025-07-01 cut, experiment 109; provisional: not measured, and the experiment's gate did not pass under its pre-registered definition).

Do not rely on the farm series behind a disaggregated Primary's reading. For D8 (Marsh Lane), the metadata table names two farms whose output was added back, and the raw power table holds 1 reading for one farm and 4,643 for the other (441 above zero, none after 2026-01-26). The notes in the information field are a July 2026 snapshot, so the files carry no history of when an analogue failed (experiment 182).

Clip the solar term at D5 at 60% of the held capacity (medium confidence, provisional). D5 is the one substation with the export-clip flag in the series table, and its sunny-daylight forecast error against BG2 falls from +0.202 MW to +0.069 MW when the solar output the GAM subtracts from demand is capped at 60% of the capacity held after the cut. The same clip at D10 and D16, which show no plateau in clear-sky net power, leaves their sunny error unchanged and raises their error over all half-hours by 0.005 to 0.006 MW, so apply it only where the limit exists.
