A ceiling of 100% clips nothing. The evidence is one substation and one scored year, with the ceiling chosen on the tuning months (experiment 180; applies to experiments and production).

docs.title: Switching and the switching log
docs.text:
Mask switching with the 66 hand-filtered real transfers, and with nothing else. The transfers run from January 2022, and the raw log holds many events too small to matter (experiment 101, filtering the labelled set of experiment 41). Applies to experiments, and to production once a detector runs there.

Do not rely on a training mask for switching transfers to improve the convex GAM. Training the 24-month convex GAM with no mask worsened the score by 0.002 points on clean rows and 0.003 points after a logged transfer, and 476 simulated transfers worsened it by 0.009 points, because the hand mask is at most 7% of the training half-hours (experiment 212). Applies to experiments and production at D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16. Confidence: moderate, with a provisional status until the experiment's review is merged.

Expect D10 to carry unlabelled jumps of 15 to 20 points. D10's night-time floor rose from 25 to 45 points on 8 November 2024 and stayed high to about 1 December, and its residuals rose by 15 to 20 points from 17 November to 14 December 2025. Neither window is in the hand-filtered labels, and both are probably unlabelled switching. Dropping the 2025 window lowered D10's scores by 0.09 to 0.53 points and moved the five-site contrasts by under 0.08 points (experiment 104, Correction). Masking both windows in the quarterly refits of experiment 107 moved the quantile score contrast of all years with drift minus all years without drift from -0.451 to -0.512 points (a larger drift gain) and left every label unchanged. Applies to experiments scoring D10. Confidence: medium, because the cause is not confirmed.

Do not conclude that a logged closure moved no load because no detector flagged the closure. Of 381,830 logged half-hours on 16 series, 80.5% lie in closures over 60 days that no label covers, and only 2.6% lie inside labelled transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load (experiment 101). Applies to experiments and production.

Treat a logged closure of 2 to 6 hours as unconfirmed, and treat unexplained alarms as an upper bound on false alarms. An unexplained alarm is a detector alarm with no logged closure near it. Nine one-sided confirmations of 2 to 6 hour closures appeared against about 6 on shifted logs, while longer closures gave 28 against 0.4 (experiment 37). The log misses real steps, so an alarm with no logged cause is not necessarily false. Applies to experiments.

Add the substation pair 14-25 to the interconnection list before attributing closures to the pair. The detector of experiment 37 could not attribute those closures. Applies to experiments and production.

Treat the labelled set as reliable only for transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load that last over 1 day. Only that band reached labeller recall of 0.80 in experiment 41, so mark smaller, shorter, and unmetered-receiver cases as not scored. Applies to experiments.

Recompute moved_share_of_receiver from the events, and never read the stored column. The stored value is missing for 62 of the 81 visible events that touch a Primary series, because the labeller wrote some series identifiers as strings and 20 events name no metered receiver (experiment 44). Applies to experiments.

Report the 21 of 66 real transfers that have no metered receiver separately. Their receiving-load share is blank, and their megawatts are the labeller's estimate (experiment 101). Applies to experiments, and to production once a detector runs there.

Do not read the lower recall at injected transfers without a metered receiver as a property of the detector alone. The gap comes mostly from small injected steps: 211 of 274 such transfers step by less than the alarm threshold (experiment 58, experiment 55). Applies to experiments that inject transfers.

Restore the missing residual readings at series 12 and 13, or count the affected events as unobserved, before scoring on real transfers. Of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, 6 (11.5 MW) have no readings in the stored residual panel (experiment 101). Series 12 and 13 have residuals only from 2026-02 (experiment 37). Applies to experiments.

Do not mask with the labels of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC). RO-NC marks 9% to 16% of half-hours per year from 2022, and masking on the labels raised the error (experiment 89). The detector labels were also not shown to help on rows outside switching in experiment 86. Applies to experiments and production.

Do not set lagged power inside an ARA to missing. Masking those lags raised the error by 0.409 points of capacity (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517) on the rows with such a lag (experiment 89). Applies to experiments, for the Primary demand model.

Do not remove the detected intervals from the history of the error correction. The threshold-weighted error rose 57% on half-hours outside logged switching (experiment 38). Applies to production, with the caveat that the detector of that experiment is an early version.

Count overlapping detected intervals once when summing the megawatts, and end each interval when the transfer ends. Of the cases where the detector marked a transfer, 21% held two or more overlapping intervals, whose megawatts were added together, and the detector kept reporting megawatts for a median of 48 hours (90th percentile 96 hours) after a transfer ended, because it alarmed the return step as a new transfer of opposite sign (experiment 88). Applies to experiments and production.

Expect the end of a found transfer to be known 19 to 24 hours late, and expect the detector's score to separate poorly in the first 24 hours after an onset. The 24-hour blocks delay the end (experiment 43). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is 0.60 in the first 24 hours (experiment 91). Applies to production.

Do not suppress detector alarms near the monthly refit of the residual model. Suppression lost about 5% of the moved megawatts, all in the 13% of headline-band transfers that start or end within 24 hours of a refit (experiment 71). The headline band is the injected transfers that move 25% to 40% of the receiving load for over 1 day. Applies to experiments and production.

Treat D8's multi-day drops as events, and do not read them as transfers to its metered neighbours or expect RO-NC to find them. D8 has 29 runs of 2 days or longer in which its power sits about 2.7 MW (range 1.2 to 5.4) below the convex demand model, 28 of them since July 2023. A metered neighbour steps up with them at a rate not clearly above random times (8 of 29 against 0.21), and 10 of the 52 RO-NC alarms on D8 fall within 6 hours of a drop's start or end (experiment 159). Applies to experiments and to production, for D8. The scope is one series and one residual model, the cause is unknown, the count depends on the threshold (15 to 48 for -2.5 to -1.0 MW), and the entry is provisional until NGED has said what moved.

Mask the rows of every known load transfer out of the training data of a forecast that uses no recent power. The evidence is provisional and the confidence medium, and masking itself was not tested. A generalised additive model (GAM) with a 24-month training window, refitted every month, learned injected transfers of 25% of a substation's power lasting 7, 30, and 90 days as 8.5%, 19%, and 32% of their size in the 48 hours after each transfer ended, and learned a permanent step to one half after about 12 months (experiment 274; 10 Primary substations, 4 onset dates, the ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather). No tested duration kept the bias under 0.1 points of effective capacity (1 point is 1% of the substation's capacity). Applies to experiments and production.

Treat the Kalman filter's correction as undefined, not zero, before a series' first reading. The filter's correction of a series is exactly zero until its first reading, so the difference between the forecast with recent power and the forecast without it is zero there too. Series 13 has no reading for 67% of the grid and series 7 for 37%; their standard deviation of that difference was zero until those rows were set to missing (experiment 308; 15 Primary series). Applies to experiments and to production, for any score built on the filter's correction. Provisional until the experiment's reviews are merged.

Give every detector alarm a closing rule that works when no end is known, and mask the alarm to that close. Applies to: experiments and any pipeline that masks detected load shifts. An alarm with no close masks the series to its end, so a rule such as a 14-day cap has to close the alarm. With the cap closing the alarm, a label-free detect-and-mask pipeline scores 0.016 points of capacity better than no mask on ordinary rows, on the 95% pinball loss (experiment 327). Confidence: provisional, 15 Primaries, one record.

docs.title: Forecast tails and curtailment cost
docs.text:
Count the half-hours beyond a limit before ranking forecasts on curtailment cost. Two bulk supply points have only 19 half-hours beyond a limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export, which cannot rank forecasts (experiment 84). Applies to experiments.

Label every curtailment cost "calibration to history, not a saving". The experiment's headline cost, £571,823 at a scaled limit of 0.9 times the maximum, is a calibration to history and not a saving (experiment 84). Applies to experiments.

Read tail coverage month by month, and expect the coverage to swing. The q95 tail coverage of the stored best-guess quantiles at Primaries swung from 0.88 to 0.97 across months, and a recalibration fitted on earlier months did not move coverage by more than its own interval (experiment 97). Applies to experiments, for the 12 to 36 hour lead band.

Re-fit a residual detector's noise for D8 before and after 2025-03, and label D8's engine only up to 2025-02 (provisional). Applies to: experiments. D8's residual noise (the median absolute step-to-step error of the residual) is 0.17 to 0.27 MW in clean months and 0.35 to 0.75 MW from 2024-05, rising most after 8.91 MW of 11 kV solar was connected on 2025-03-24. A detector with its noise fitted on 2022 to 2023 flags 40% to 45% of D8's half-hours from 2025-03 onward, even in April to June 2026, when 2% of half-hours are below -2.5 MW (experiment 196). The flags are not solar noise alone: the same detector flags 29% to 36% of D8's night half-hours from 2025-03, and neither night-only evidence, an edge test, nor a price gate removes them (experiment 199). The scope is one Primary; the confidence is moderate, and the entry is provisional until the experiment has had its reviews.

Sort the stored quantiles of a farm forecast before reading its median (provisional). Applies to: experiments, and production if a stored quantile set is ever read column by column. In the stored solar-farm forecasts that experiment 255 read from experiments 224 and 243, 26,344 of 77,897 rows (34%) had quantile columns that were not in increasing order, in every forecast arm, so q50 is not always the middle value of the forecast's own quantiles. Scoring the curtailment cost with the quantiles sorted per row moved the avoidable cost of the forecast arms by up to 3.7% and left every contrast's sign and 95% interval verdict unchanged (experiment 268). studies.node_curtailment sorts each row by default and counts the rows that crossed. The scope is the six trial solar farms (labelled A to F) in experiments 224 and 243; the confidence is high for the count and moderate for the size of the effect.

Do not read a metered solar farm's coverage at the 0.01 quantile as calibration without checking for exact zeros (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. Coverage at the 0.01 quantile is the share of half-hours with output at or below that quantile. Farm D's metered output is exactly zero in 11.7% of the half-hours scored in 2025-09 to 2026-08 (7% in September, 24% to 26% in October and November, 44% in December, 49% in January, 0% from April), so the 0.01 quantile of every arm tested sits at about zero and its coverage equals the zero share. The pinball loss on those rows is about zero for every arm, so they add nothing to any contrast but dilute the percentage differences; report 0.01 contrasts with and without farm D. The cause of the zeros (outage, curtailment, or an export limit) is not established. Evidence: experiment 284, farm D, 2025-09 to 2026-08.

Take climatology and the manual heuristic from experiment 87's stored references when a scorer needs eleven quantiles (provisional). Applies to: experiments. The stored climatology and manual-heuristic forecasts of experiment 48 hold nine quantiles (q05 to q95), so code that pads the missing q01 and q99 fills them with either the capacity or a copy of q05 and q95, and the padded tails are wrong. The versions in experiment 87's ref_climatology and ref_manual_heuristic hold all eleven. Both experiments store power as a fraction of capacity, not in percentage points of capacity (experiment 277). The scope is the six Primary substations (which step 33 kV down to 11 kV) and the two bulk supply points D13 and D17 (which step 132 kV down to 33 kV); the confidence is high, because we read the stored files.

Report a tail's coverage as the share strictly below the quantile, beside the share at or below it and the share of exact zeros, wherever the actual output can sit on a point mass. For the six metered solar farms, 3.0% of daylight half-hours read exactly zero. The share at or below the 0.01 quantile is 3.3% to 3.5% for Metered solar farms research default 1, and the share strictly below it is 1.2% to 1.4%, so the "at or below" figure overstates the lower-tail miss by the zeros (experiment 321). Applies to experiments, for the 12 to 252 hour lead range. Confidence: provisional, six farms, one scored year.

docs.title: Privacy and anonymisation
docs.text:
Never publish the name, the identifier, or the time series of an NGED metered generator, and label each generator (for example "Solar farm A"). Substations are not covered by this rule. Public data, such as the settled output of Balancing Mechanism Units in Elexon's published data, may be named. Applies to experiments, studies, and production reports.

Give a bulk supply point's relation its own coefficients before using it. Applies to: experiments. A bulk supply point (BSP) reading is import-positive, the generator series are export-positive, and the Primaries' apparent-power series are positive. At the one BSP that closes, the reading equals 1.01 to 1.16 times the MW Primaries plus 1.03 to 1.10 times the MVA Primaries minus 0.85 to 0.90 times the metered generation, plus unmetered solar and a level (the closure audit of experiment 124). The scope is two BSPs, of which one closed; the confidence is moderate, and the entry is provisional until the experiment has had its reviews.

Average several network seed sets before scoring a small contrast. Applies to: experiments. Experiment 201's median-correction network, retrained with 6 different seed sets, moves the pooled score at 0.5 to 168 hours between 2.5787 and 2.6038, so one seed set carries 0.01 to 0.02 points of noise (experiment 325). Confidence: provisional, one family, one scored year.

docs.title: Glossary of terms used in the experiment pages
docs.text: This page defines each term that the experiment pages and the theme Summary pages use without redefining. Every definition gives its source: the experiment that introduced the term, or the code or contract that fixes its meaning. Terms appear in alphabetical order. The data-processing page has its own short list of terms for the processing steps it describes.

docs.title: 14-day correction
docs.text: The 14-day correction adds the mean error of the last 14 days to every forecast quantile. The error is the observed power minus the forecast median, taken over the half-hours whose power was already observed when the forecast was issued, and the correction is zero when fewer than 3 days of errors exist (experiment 19 and its scoring script).

docs.title: Abnormal running arrangement (ARA) and normal running arrangement (NRA)
docs.text: The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the electricity network as it is when no load transfer is on, and an abnormal running arrangement (ARA) is the period while an operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation carries load that belongs to a neighbour. An "NRA forecast" predicts the demand that the substation would have drawn under the NRA (experiment 88, experiment 89).

docs.title: Base margin
docs.text: A base margin is a starting prediction that an XGBoost model receives for each row, in place of the single base score that XGBoost otherwise estimates from the training labels. The wind models use the power that the turbine power curve gives at the forecast wind speed. The solar offset of the Primary models uses the forecast output of the unmetered solar panels behind the substation (experiment 80, experiment 87).

docs.title: Best guess
docs.text: The best guess is the forecasting recipe assembled in experiment 33. For Primary substation demand it is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15, which is the stack without its half-life (experiment 19's stack_minus_h arm, rebuilt in experiment 33 as n1_cs). For bulk and grid supply points it is N1 alone. For solar and wind farms it is a mixture, over the 51 ENS members, of XGBoost models trained on ERA5 weather, with a spread factor and, for wind, a power-curve base margin.

docs.title: BG2
docs.text: BG2 is the second best-guess recipe, assembled in experiment 87 from the best earlier ideas. For Primary substations it is a quantile blend of five members, with a solar offset at the five Primaries that have a clean solar capacity estimate. The members are a weekly-refitted XGBoost model, a monthly-refitted XGBoost model, an analogue model (the experiment's summary does not state its type), a model pooled by substation type, and the stack. For bulk and grid supply points it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no correction. Experiment 97 recalibrates only the stored weekly-refitted forecast and calls it BG2. Production does not run BG2: it serves xgboost_baseline, which scored 10.536 points on the Primary quantile score in experiment 87, against 5.260 for BG2.

docs.title: Bulk supply point and grid supply point
docs.text: A grid supply point (GSP) is a substation where the transmission network feeds NGED's distribution network, and a bulk supply point (BSP) is a substation one step further down. NGED's GSPs step voltage from 400 kV or 275 kV to 132 kV, and its BSPs step from 132 kV to 33 kV or 66 kV (NGED's network and its data). A Primary substation sits below a BSP. The trial area holds two GSPs and two BSPs, and the experiments report them together as "supply points" or "BSP and GSP". The data-processing page says not to treat them as clean demand.

docs.title: Capacity and points of capacity
docs.text: Capacity in the experiment scores is the effective capacity of a series: the 99th percentile of the absolute power over the series' whole observed history, in the series' own unit (MW or MVA). The EffectiveCapacity contract fixes this definition for version 0.1 (packages/contracts/src/contracts/power_schemas.py), and the experiment scripts divide power and forecast by effective_capacity_mw. A point of capacity is 1% of that value, so a score of 5.26 points on a series of 20 MW capacity is an error of about 1.05 MW. A lower score is better.

docs.title: Climatology
docs.text: climatology is a baseline forecaster that predicts each half-hour from past power in the same calendar cell. A cell is a series, a local month, a local half-hour of the day, and a weekday-or-weekend flag, smoothed over the neighbouring months and half-hours. The forecaster stores 51 equiprobable quantiles per cell and consumes no weather (packages/baseline_forecasters/src/baseline_forecasters/climatology.py).

docs.title: Control member
docs.text: The control member is the one ENS run that starts from ECMWF's unperturbed analysis of the current weather. The other 50 of the 51 ENS members start from perturbed analyses (ENS horizons). N1 is trained on the control member and then applied to all 51 members, and the 51 sets of quantiles are pooled (experiment 13).

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text: The coverage of a forecast quantile is the share of observed values at or below it. A correct q05 covers 0.05 and a correct q95 covers 0.95. The coverage of the 5% to 95% range is the share of observed values between q05 and q95, which is 90% for a correct forecast (experiment 19 reports it as "5% to 95% coverage").

docs.title: CRPS
docs.text: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) scores a whole forecast distribution against the observed value, and the experiments approximate it from the forecast quantiles. The approximation is twice the probability-mass-weighted sum of the pinball losses, which is the quantile score (studies.cross_validation.crps). Experiments 2, 16, and 20 report it under the name CRPS, and experiments 13 and 33 say that the quantile score is its estimate.

docs.title: D codes
docs.text: A D code (D1 to D22) is the anonymised label of one of the 22 demand-side series in fold A: 16 Primary substations, 4 bulk or grid supply points, and a battery and a biofuel generator. The labels are defined in experiment 3 and are used with the same meaning in the pages checked (experiments 5, 27, 46, 51, 53, 64, and 74 and the data-processing page), for example D1 is a grid supply point and D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five Primaries with a clean solar capacity estimate. A D code and a substation name are different labels. D codes are not the same as the detector names D0, D0M, D1, and D2 (see Detectors D0, D0M, D1, and D2), nor the labels P12 and P13 of experiment 101. Generators carry separate anonymous labels such as "Solar farm A", assigned by studies.anonymise.

docs.title: Detectors D0, D0M, D1, and D2
docs.text: In the switching experiments, D0, D0M, D1, and D2 are names of detectors, not series. D0 is the single-series detector. D0 raises an alarm when the average residual over a window steps by more than a threshold. D0M is D0 with its threshold chosen by the same search that sets D2's threshold and with no veto; at the 24-hour window it uses 4.0 noise units and ends each alarm interval with a level tracker that stops after 60 days. D0 at the thresholds of experiment 43 (6.0 noise units at the 4-hour window and 4.0 at the 24-hour window) is a separate arm, although the search returned those same thresholds. D1 is the neighbour-balance detector of experiment 37, which also requires a neighbouring substation to step the opposite way (thresholds 3.75 at the 4-hour window and 2.5 at the 24-hour window). D2 is D0M plus a neighbour veto (experiment 37, experiment 43, experiment 55, experiment 58, experiment 66). Experiment 49 also uses D0 as the label of a spread-factor contrast, and experiment 87 uses D1 and D4 as labels of decisions.

docs.title: ENS, ERA5, and CAMS
docs.text: ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast with 51 members, and ERA5 and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance are estimates of past weather. ENS is a forecast issued before the weather happens, and the live forecast is given ENS. ERA5, the fifth-generation ECMWF reanalysis, arrives about 5 days late (experiment 10), so a result that uses ERA5 as a forecast input is a ceiling and not a usable product. CAMS is a satellite-based estimate of sunlight (experiment 7). An XGBoost model trained on ERA5 or CAMS learns from weather that was not forecast.

docs.title: Frozen XGBoost model
docs.text: A frozen XGBoost model is trained once, on data up to the start of the validation year, and is not refitted during that year. In experiment 87, the frozen forecast without the 14-day correction scores 6.927 for Primary substations (S1), and the frozen forecast with the correction is the stack (S2, 5.543).

docs.title: Half-life
docs.text: A half-life of 0.5 years gives a training row a weight of 0.5 raised to the power of the row's age in years divided by 0.5. The weight therefore halves for every 0.5 years of age (ml-experiments/00017-training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand/e00017_fit.py, experiment 17).

docs.title: Injected and real load transfers
docs.text: A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor) onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. An injected transfer is a synthetic transfer that the experiment adds to the real power readings, so its start, end, and size are known. A real transfer is one of the 66 hand-labelled operations of experiment 41, of which 35 last over 1 day. A transfer is "large" when it moves at least 25% of the receiving substations' load.

docs.title: Interval-level convention
docs.text: Each interval states its level, and the level depends on how many contrasts the experiment planned. An experiment that plans one contrast reports a 95% interval. An experiment that plans N contrasts divides the 5% error rate across them with a Bonferroni correction, so nine contrasts give a 99.44% interval (1 minus 0.05 divided by 9). Intervals resample whole calendar months (.claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md, experiment 19).

docs.title: manual_heuristic
docs.text: manual_heuristic is a baseline forecaster that predicts each half-hour as an ensemble of the power observed at the same weekday and time of day in earlier weeks and years. Under its configuration the 13 ensemble members are the same time in each of the last 6 weeks and the same time 49 to 55 weeks earlier; a lag that would not yet have been observed at the forecast origin is absent. The forecaster consumes no weather (packages/baseline_forecasters/src/baseline_forecasters/manual_heuristic.py).

docs.title: MW and MVA
docs.text: A series is metered in MW (signed active power, which can be negative when the substation exports) or in MVA (apparent power, which is never negative). The unit is the units column of the metadata table. Eight of the 16 trial Primaries are metered only in MVA, so solar output behind such a Primary appears as demand in daylight. See the data-processing page and experiments 56 and 79.

docs.title: N1
docs.text: N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model, one per series, that is trained on the ENS control member with recent power as inputs. It receives power lags measured from the forecast origin and weather columns from the ENS member, and its output quantiles are pooled across the 51 ENS members (experiment 13).

docs.title: Noise unit
docs.text: One noise unit is 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of a substation's 24-hour residual step on odd-numbered months. A step of 4.0 noise units is therefore four times the usual size (experiment 66).

docs.title: NWP
docs.text: NWP is numerical weather prediction: a physical weather model run forward from the current state of the atmosphere. ENS is the NWP product that the live forecast consumes. Other NWP products in the experiments include the Met Office UKV and NOAA's GEFS.

docs.title: PF14
docs.text: PF14 is the benchmark end rule of the switching experiments, written after seeing results. It ends each alarm interval at the first opposite step that is at least half the onset step (and at least 1.5 noise units) within 14 days, takes the largest step back within one window after that, and keeps the tracked end when no step qualifies (experiment 66, experiment 69).

docs.title: Pooled mixture
docs.text: A pooled mixture applies the XGBoost quantile model to each of the 51 ENS members and pools the resulting quantiles as equal-weight points. The forecast quantiles are the weighted quantiles of the pooled values (experiment 13, experiment 2).

docs.title: Pre-registration, decision rule, and verdict words
docs.text: An experiment pre-registers its hypothesis, prediction, and decision rule in a result.md that is committed with status planned before any code runs. The decision rule states which interval and threshold make each verdict, so the verdict follows from the numbers and not from the author's reading. The verdicts are supported, partly supported, small gain (the interval excludes zero in the predicted direction but misses the threshold), not supported, refuted, inconclusive, invalid, and failed. See How an experiment is recorded and .claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md. A write-up marks a verdict that its decision rule does not cover as not pre-registered, as experiment 13 does.

docs.title: Primary substation
docs.text: A Primary substation steps voltage down from 33 kV or 66 kV to 11 kV. NGED operates 1,161 Primary substations (NGED's network and its data), and 16 of the 32 trial series are Primaries. A Primary is fed from a bulk supply point, which is a higher-voltage substation (see Bulk supply point and grid supply point).

docs.title: Quantile score and pinball loss
docs.text: The quantile score is twice the probability-mass-weighted mean of the pinball losses over the forecast quantile levels, in points of capacity. The pinball loss of a quantile at level τ is τ times the shortfall of the forecast below the observation, or (1 − τ) times the excess of the forecast above it. Each level's weight is the probability mass between the mid-points to its neighbouring levels, so the score is not a plain mean over the levels. Experiments 33, 34, and 48 use nine levels (0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.75, 0.90, and 0.95), and experiment 87 and later use 11 levels (those nine plus 0.01 and 0.99) (pinball_quantile_score in ml-experiments/00087-bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations/e00087_common.py). Scores from experiments with different levels, row sets, or series cannot be compared.

docs.title: Recall (MW-weighted)
docs.text: MW-weighted recall is the share of the moved megawatts that sit in found transfers. A detector finds a transfer when it raises an alarm starting within 2 hours of the transfer's start and places the end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the transfer's duration (experiment 66, experiment 101).

docs.title: Refit and rolling refit
docs.text: A refit retrains the XGBoost model on newer data at a scheduled interval, such as weekly or monthly. A rolling refit (P-roll) retrains monthly on a rolling 12-month window with 150 boosting rounds (experiment 34). Weekly refits are the cadence of BG2.

docs.title: Research default
docs.text: A research default is the fixed forecast of one target family, against which every change experiment is measured. Each version has a name made of the family, the words "research default", and a number, such as "Primary demand research default 1" (the GAM stack A+H+S). An adopted change makes the next version. A research default is not what production serves: production serves xgboost_baseline, and "champion" and "promote" are production words (rule, log).

docs.title: Residual
docs.text: In the switching experiments, the residual is the measured power minus the forecast of an XGBoost demand model trained on ERA5 weather that uses no past power. The detectors look for steps in the residual (experiment 66).

docs.title: RO-NC
docs.text: RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector. RO-NC is PF14 with two changes. The step is taken from whichever of two residual models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours. The candidates are scored by a logistic regression that includes the count of neighbours stepping the same way as the alarming substation (experiment 82, experiment 101). X is the refit-offset detector alone. The experiment scripts under ml-experiments/ still name RO-NC XL in code, for example in the arm names lagmw_xl and mask_xl of experiment 86, so a search of the code for XL finds the RO-NC detector.

docs.title: Season-year
docs.text: A season-year is a 12-month period, and its start month depends on the series of work. In the solar-disaggregation experiments it runs from September to August, such as 2019/20 (experiment 39). In the differentiable-physics series it runs from July to June (FIRST_SEASON_MONTH in packages/studies/src/studies/dp_calendar.py).

docs.title: Skill
docs.text: Skill is 100 times (1 minus the best guess's quantile score divided by manual_heuristic's quantile score), pooled over the series being compared. A positive skill means the best guess beats manual_heuristic (experiment 56).

docs.title: Spread factor
docs.text: The spread factor scales each forecast quantile's distance from the median. A quantile q becomes the median plus the factor times (q minus the median), so a factor of 1.15 widens the band by 15% and a factor below 1 narrows it (experiment 19). For solar and wind farms the factor is fitted on earlier cases to bring the 5% to 95% coverage near its target (experiment 33).

docs.title: Stack
docs.text: The stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15, and the experiments differ on the half-life. The stack of experiment 19 weights older training rows with a half-life of 0.5 years. The stacks of experiments 33, 34, and 48 use a half-life of 2 years, and are trained once. The experiment 87 scripts use the same 2-year weighting for its stack, which its write-up does not state, and there the stack is the frozen forecast plus the 14-day correction.

docs.title: Stages 0, 1a, and 2
docs.text: Stage 1a is an XGBoost quantile model per series, trained on analysis weather (ERA5 and CAMS), with no power lags and no lead time. Stage 0 maps ENS weather toward the weather that stage 1a trained on (a quantile mapping in experiments 16 and 20). Stage 2 is a calibrator, a second XGBoost model that corrects the stage 1a quantiles and can use lagged power (staged probabilistic forecast).

docs.title: Tail coverage
docs.text: Tail coverage is the coverage of a quantile in the tails: the share of observed values below the 0.01 and 0.05 quantiles or above the 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles. A correct forecast has a tail coverage equal to the quantile's level on the lower tail, and equal to one minus the level on the upper tail. Experiment 87 reports it at those four levels beside the pinball loss there (experiment 87).

docs.title: xgboost_baseline
docs.text: xgboost_baseline is the production-style forecast: the stored forecast of the XGBoost model that the project's production recipe produced. The experiments read it from the power_forecasts Delta table for the fold mid_2025_to_mid_2026. Experiment 87 did not confirm whether the local Dagster cross-validation assets or S3 wrote that table, so none of the experiments we read confirms that the stored forecast matches the deployed one (experiment 13, experiment 87).

docs.title: Log of research default versions
docs.text: This log lists every version of each family's research default, newest first. The rule page defines the families, the adoption conditions, and the eight items in each row. The pull request of the adopting experiment adds the row, and a row is never edited afterwards except to change its status.

docs.title: Metered solar farms
docs.text:
Version Change Adopting experiment Scored-year gain Replicate gain Absolute headline score Benchmarks (manual_heuristic, climatology, XGBoost reference) Stored forecasts Code commit Status Metered solar farms research default 1 The spread-binned plant P2 with an additive band, a mixture-density neural network (five seeds averaged), and XGBoost, blended per quantile with sorted quantiles 300 First version First version Blend 5.27 points of capacity with each farm's own history and 5.45 with none (zero history) 8.69, 8.64, and 5.45 (own history) and 5.56 (zero history) The predictions of experiment 300, written once under its id d59e93445 First version, set by the rule

Single-family scores of Metered solar farms research default 1 (quantile score in points of capacity, own history then zero history): the mixture-density neural network alone 5.34 and 5.55, the additive model alone 5.43 and 5.59, and plant-fed XGBoost (XGBoost on the plant forecast, its ensemble spread, the unit mean, and the availability ratio) 5.45 and 5.56. The first production update uses one model family, so these rows show what each family scores without the blend.

The scored lead range of this row is 12 to 36 hours, and NGED's range is 1 to 10 days. Experiment 310 scores the row from 1 to 10 days. The frozen XGBoost reference is the XGBoost forecast of experiment 243 with the floors of experiment 224.

docs.title: Wind farms
docs.text: No version exists. The family accepts no adoption until its first default is named.

docs.title: Bulk and grid supply points
docs.text: No version exists. The family accepts no adoption until its first default is named.

docs.title: The research default and the rule for adopting a change
docs.text:
Each target family has one fixed research default forecast, one fixed test for adding a change to it, and a log of versions. An experiment of kind change asks whether the research default plus change x beats the research default. A win produces the next version of the research default. The rule exists so that the experiments build one forecast in order, and so that a gain is always measured against the current forecast and never against a stale or partial one.

Adopting a change into the research default does not put the change into production. The release-model skill governs production changes. This page says "research default" and "adopt" because production deployment already uses "champion" and "promote" for the deployed XGBoost model. Every version has a name made of the family, the words "research default", and a number N that counts up within the family from 1, for example "Primary demand research default 1" for the GAM stack A+H+S. "C1" and "C2" already name the planned contrasts on every result page, so a bare "default 3" or "v3" is never used. Every result.md and pull-request body cites the version by name, for example "default plus x versus Primary demand research default 1". The two arms of a change experiment are called "default" and "default plus x".

The research default is not what runs in production. Production serves a much weaker XGBoost model, stored as xgboost_baseline. Experiment 87 scored it at 10.536 points on the Primary quantile score, against 5.260 for BG2. A page that names BG2 as a benchmark says that production does not run BG2.

docs.title: Families
docs.text:
Each family has its own research default, row set, headline metric, protected groups, benchmarks, retraining cadence, and version line. The family definition below fixes these values once, and an experiment's plan never sets or changes them. A per-plan choice would let an experiment pick the metric on which its change wins. The metrics used across the experiments so far include the quantile score, the mean absolute error of the median, tail-weighted continuous ranked probability score (twCRPS), a single quantile's pinball loss, and avoidable curtailment cost.

Family Rows and period Lead range First version of the research default Retraining cadence Primary demand (six Primaries) fold_a_daily_gap_v1, scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, replicate year 2024-25, rows outside hand-filtered events 0.5 to 168 hours (7 days) Primary demand research default 1: the GAM stack A+H+S of experiments 220 and 251 Monthly for the GAM stack; weekly for its XGBoost benchmark BG2 Metered solar farms A to F Daylight half-hours, scored year 2025-09 to 2026-08, 6-month replicate 12 to 36 hours Metered solar farms research default 1: the blend assembled by experiment 300 A single fit or monthly, as the family's first version states Wind farms W1 to W3 and the public wind farms of experiment 288 fold_a_tuesdays_v1, 53 Tuesday runs To be named with the first default Wind farms research default 1: to be named when the first default is chosen. No adoption until then To be named with the first default Bulk and grid supply points fold_a_daily_gap_v1 To be named with the first default Bulk and grid supply points research default 1: to be named when the first default is chosen. No adoption until then Weekly

NGED care about the 1 day to 10 day horizon, so each family states its lead range, and a lead range shorter than that is a limit on every result. The Primary-demand range stops at 7 days and the metered-farm range stops at 36 hours. A change result for such a family repeats its lead range in its headline caveat, for example "scored at 12 to 36 hour leads only".

The headline metric for all four families is the quantile score over 11 levels, in points of effective capacity. A point is 1% of a series' capacity.

A family with few series and few runs will rarely pass the gain test, and the rule does not lower the bar for it. Three wind farms on 53 runs give wide intervals, so a wind change will seldom satisfy condition 1. A change that cannot reach the bar stays a candidate, and the maintainer may judge it by a descriptive report instead.

The Primary-demand family fixes the following tolerances, in points unless stated. A tolerance is the harm a protected group may suffer before an adoption fails.

Protected group Tolerance Pooled six-Primary headline 0.02 0.01 and 0.99 pinball tails (the worse end is scored, with coverage reported beside it) 0.05 Cold winter nights 0.05 Sunny daylight half-hours 0.05 twCRPS 2% relative

The other three families use a headline tolerance of 0.02 and the same tail tolerance of 0.05. Their other protected groups are set when each family's first version is written.

The minimum gain depends on the complexity of the change. The point estimate of the gain must reach the value for the change's tier.

Tier Minimum gain A changed setting, an added column, or a changed loss 0 A new fitted step, a new input, or a new data source 0.02 points A new head 0.03 points

Experiment 278 anchors the values: it used 0.02 points for the convex model's cadence and 0.03 for the head.

Two further lists are part of each family's definition. The reported groups have no pass or fail: each Primary on its own, and the rows near a load shift (seven logged transfers are too few for an interval, per experiment 277). The admissible subgroups for a targeted gain are a short list set in advance (cold nights, the Economy 7 step, sunny daylight), and a targeted adoption on a subgroup also needs no harm on the family headline.

The cumulative harm budget is 2 times the group's tolerance, measured against the family's first version. The no-harm condition compares each adoption only with the previous version, so n adoptions that each cost up to the tolerance could cost n times the tolerance in total. At each adoption, the current research default must also stay within the budget against the first version, using the first version's stored forecasts.

docs.title: The three fixed benchmarks
docs.text:
Each family keeps three benchmarks whose recipes never change: manual_heuristic, climatology, and one frozen XGBoost-based reference. The rows grow as months arrive, and the benchmarks are extended with the same recipe and never retuned. Every change page reports the research default's absolute score against the three benchmarks, with intervals, because a chain of small contrasts can hide a drift in absolute skill. Diagnostic pages need not report them.

For Primary demand the frozen reference is BG2. BG2 is the stored arm p_s6_bg2 of experiment 87. BG2 is a quantile blend of five forecasts, with an explicit solar offset at the 5 of 16 Primaries that have a clean solar capacity estimate. The five forecasts are a weekly-refitted XGBoost model, a monthly-refitted XGBoost model, an analogue model (the experiment 87 page does not state its type), an XGBoost model pooled by substation type, and the frozen stack of experiment 48. For the bulk and grid supply points, BG2 is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model alone (b_weekly). The metered-farm pages compare with the XGBoost forecast of experiment 243 and the floors of experiment 224, and the frozen reference for the farm and wind families is named when each family's first version is written.

The GAM stack trails BG2 on sunny April-to-June half-hours. Experiment 251 found the stack worse than BG2 in April, May, and June (+0.162, +0.220, and +0.054 points), and at D5 on sunny half-hours. Every Primary-demand change page reports this finding until a version of the research default closes the gap.

docs.title: Reusing the research default's code and forecasts
docs.text:
A change experiment starts from the stored forecasts of the research default and, when the change acts inside a fitted stage, from the default's code. The change is one of two kinds, and the experiment's page says which.

  • Tier 1 changes act on stored forecasts. A clip, a band-widening rule, a blend, a recalibration, or a quantile interpolation needs only the research default's stored forecasts. The D8 as-of widening, the lead-band interpolation, the D5 clip, and the blend of experiment 287 are all of this kind.
  • Tier 2 changes act inside a fitted stage. A change to the convex model, the head, the solar summary, or the features needs the research default's code. The experiment imports that code directly from the folder of the experiment that holds it, with that folder on PYTHONPATH, as the ml-experiment skill describes. The code moves into packages/studies in a reviewed pull request only when several experiment folders need it or when production might one day need it.

The research default's definition holds four items. These are the code (a script in an experiment folder and its commit, a module and commit in packages/studies, or "stored forecasts only"), a configuration file naming every setting and the seed policy, the stored forecasts for every scored, replicate, and holdout period, and the scores. The seed policy matters: averaging three seeds of the correction network scored 0.123 points below arm D, against 0.104 for the mean single seed (experiments 201 and 220), so "more seeds" would otherwise adopt as a change.

Each version's stored forecasts are written once and never overwritten. Several worktrees share one data/ folder,, and a re-run by one session would replace the evidence of another. Experiments in flight read Primary demand research default N while Primary demand research default N+1 is being built. Each version is written once with experiment_store.write_predictions under the adopting experiment's id and a fixed name. Where a refit is needed to reproduce the default, the reproduction uses the default's cadence exactly, because refit cadence is itself a contrast (experiment 278).

docs.title: What an experiment must contain to be eligible
docs.text:
An experiment is eligible for adoption only when its front matter says kind: change and its plan, committed before any score is read, states five items. Diagnostics, audits, data checks, and detection or decision studies are kind: other and never adopt. The five items are the following.

  • The family and the research default version the experiment starts from.
  • The arms: the default, and the default plus x. The default's arm reads the stored forecasts of that version, with a reproduction gate when the experiment refits the default, as experiment 278 did.
  • The tier of the change (tier 1 or tier 2) and its complexity tier from the minimum-gain table.
  • The pre-registered default-plus-x arm or arms.
  • The controls that apply: a known-answer test, a placebo, a leakage check.

An experiment that evaluates a blend reports each constituent model family alone beside the blend. The single-family table comes first, and the page states the blend's added value over the best single family, with an interval. The first production update is a relatively simple model implemented as one model family, for example XGBoost only, while blends stay of interest. A blend is adopted into the research default only with that table present.

The default plus x is produced on the research default's full row set. Its stored forecasts then serve as the next version without a separate regeneration job.

docs.title: The adoption rule
docs.text:
A change is adopted only when all five conditions hold.

  1. Gain. The 99% month-block interval of (default plus x, minus default) on the family headline lies wholly on the better side of zero, and the point estimate is at least the minimum gain for the change's tier. With k pre-registered arms the interval is read at the level 1 − 0.01/k.
  2. No harm. Each protected group is gated by a one-sided 95% non-inferiority bound: the upper bound of the harm must not exceed the group's tolerance. The six Primaries are pooled for this gate, and the per-Primary results are reported. A Primary whose point estimate is worse than the tolerance triggers a look, not a failure. Because every group must pass, the gate is an intersection test and needs no multiplicity correction. A neutral change passes a group with probability Φ(τ/SE − 1.645), where τ is the group's tolerance and SE is its standard error, so a tolerance of 2 standard errors passes a neutral change 64% of the time and a tolerance of 3 standard errors passes it 91% of the time. A change that truly harms a group by exactly the tolerance passes that group 5% of the time.
  3. Replication. The gain has the same sign in a second period, and the replicate estimate is at least half of the smaller of the main estimate and the minimum gain. Where the minimum gain is zero, the condition reduces to the same sign. Leave-one-series-out is a check for changes tuned on one series and does not stand in for a second period: a change with no second period stays a candidate. A change that fails condition 3 is not retried on the same replicate period with a tweaked x unless the tweak is pre-registered as a new experiment and the failed attempt is counted.
  4. Controls. The experiment's own controls passed, and none of the audit triggers in the ml-experiment skill is unresolved. The audit's findings are triaged in the pull request before the adoption. A change that meets condition 3 satisfies audit trigger 7, and a candidate that fails condition 3 never becomes a base for later work.
  5. Serving. The change uses only inputs available at forecast time. If the change would need a serving-path change to port, the page says so.

A change that wins on condition 1 but fails conditions 2 to 5 is recorded as a candidate, not adopted. Candidates are retested when the missing evidence arrives, or when a rebase run is available.

The nominal 99% interval covers less than 99% on short periods. A percentile bootstrap that resampled independent normal months with a nominal 99% interval covered 96.5% of the time at 12 months, 92.0% at 6 months, and 83.7% at 4 months (1,500 trials of 2,000 resamples each). The real procedure also resamples seeds and has autocorrelated months, so the figures are indicative. For periods under 12 months, add a t test on the monthly paired differences or use a studentised bootstrap. Adoption contrasts use 99% whatever the number of arms, as a stated exception to the interval-level convention, and a change page says "the 99% interval lies wholly on the better side of zero" in place of the study skill's "statistically significant at the 5% level".

The recorded gain of each version is an upper bound. Winners are selected on the scored year, so the recorded estimate overstates the true gain. In a simulation, a true gain of 2 standard errors was recorded on average as 2.7. The log therefore also reports the cumulative gain on the replicate period, which carries no selection bias, beside the scored-year sum.

docs.title: The holdout
docs.text:
The frozen period is the existing holdout: valid times on or after 2026-07-01. No experiment scores those valid times, which are kept for a finalist. The release-model skill scores the holdout once per release, on the sign of the effect only, and a month may confirm one release only.

The holdout holds under four months and no winter on 2026-10-23. It covers July to October 2026, and the months from November to February arrive by about March 2027. Until then, a change that acts in winter (the heating curve, cold nights, the Economy 7 step) is adopted on the replicate year alone, and its log entry reads "winter-unconfirmed". The holdout confirms its sign in March 2027 or later.

The metered-farm family has already scored part of the holdout. Experiments 224, 243, 257, 270, 272, 275, 284, 287, and 293 state a scored year of 2025-09 to 2026-08, so July and August 2026 are no longer untouched for metered solar farms. That family's holdout starts at 2026-09-01 at the earliest.

The same-months shrinkage check pauses a family's adoptions only on evidence of shrinkage. The check compares the holdout months with the same calendar months of the scored year (July to October 2025 for the current holdout). Adoptions in the family pause when the one-sided 90% upper bound of the holdout months' cumulative gain lies below half of the cumulative gain on those same scored-year months. A month read for a decision, or for a pause investigation, joins the scored months, and the holdout rolls forward as new months arrive. In a simulation of a 12-month scored year and a 4-month holdout, the check paused the family after 29% of false adoptions, 7% of adoptions with a true gain of 2 standard errors, and 3% of adoptions with a true gain of 3 standard errors. The check understates the chance of a pause for a change whose effect is seasonal.

docs.title: Several arms, post hoc arms, and experiments planned before the rule
docs.text:
An experiment may hold several default-plus-x arms, and at most one of them is adopted. Each arm is read at the level 1 − 0.01/k, and the others become candidates that rebase on the new version. A bundle of two components is adopted as one change only when it was pre-registered as one change and its leave-one-out arms show neither component harmful.

Only a pre-registered arm can be adopted. A post hoc arm becomes a candidate that needs a fresh experiment. When an experiment tests k variants of one change (tilt 20 and tilt 27, for example), the best variant needs replication on its own after the Bonferroni read.

Experiments planned before the rule are grandfathered, and their winners reach the research default only through a rebase run. Their front matter has no kind, and experiment_tables.py --check accepts its absence for an experiment whose id is below the cut-off id of 320. A proposal with no plan commit yet is re-planned as kind: change where it tests a change.

docs.title: The rebase rule for stale results
docs.text:
A result measured against an older version stays valid as an estimate of x on that version, but it answers a stale question. The estimate (Primary demand research default 3 plus x, minus Primary demand research default 3) is still correct for Primary demand research default 3. The estimate does not apply to x on Primary demand research default 4. Adoption one change at a time is path-dependent: a change that failed against one version may pass against a later one, and two changes that act on the same error can both win alone while only the first to merge adopts. The two gains of experiment 220 added to a stacking ratio of 0.99, while the drift term improved the bare GAM-K by 0.40 points and worsened arm D by 0.03.

  1. A result that passes against a version that is no longer current becomes a candidate with the status "candidate (stale)".
  2. A short rebase run scores (current default plus x, minus current default) against the stored forecasts of the current version, under the same five conditions and with no new plan.
  3. A rebase is needed unless every adoption since the experiment's version belongs to a different family.
  4. Where two candidates change the same component (two widening rules, for example), the rebase scores them head to head.
  5. Adoptions go in merge order. The second of two overlapping changes gets a rebase run against the new version.
  6. Changes rejected against the last few versions stay on a retest list that the periodic ablation revisits.

After every fifth adoption in a family, an ablation experiment removes each adopted component in turn. The ablation is an experiment with its own id and a planned result.md. A component is dropped only when the interval of its removal lies wholly on the better side, or when its removal is non-inferior within the tolerance and the component sits in a higher complexity tier.

docs.title: Who adopts, and what the log holds
docs.text:
The experiment's own pull request carries the adoption. Its front matter holds promoted_to (the name of the new version, for example "Primary demand research default 2") and the scores against the three benchmarks, and the same pull request adds a row to the log. The reviewing session checks the five conditions before merging and assigns the version number. Versions are serial within a family.

Each log row holds eight items. These are the change, the adopting experiment, the scored-year and replicate gains with intervals, the absolute headline score, the three benchmarks' scores on the family's rows, the stored-forecast name, the commit of the code, and the status "scored-year gain is an upper bound". A result against an old version keeps its verdict with the status "candidate (stale)" until a rebase runs. A component that a later ablation removes sets production_status: superseded on its experiment.

Adoption needs the maintainer's approval in four cases. These are a new data source, a cost above £30 or a recurring cost in production, a change that would need a serving-path change to port, and a change whose code must enter packages/studies. Other adoptions run autonomously under the merge rules in the ml-experiment skill.

A model release is a separate step. The Primary-demand research default is a GAM stack, and a model release is a numbered, trained XGBoost model, so most demand adoptions are not release candidates until the GAM stack has a production design. The release-model skill starts from the log of versions since the last release.

docs.title: Retraining cadence
docs.text:
The cadence is part of the research default, so each family's definition states one, and a change of cadence is a change experiment. The evidence differs by family.

Family Evidence on cadence Cadence Primary demand, XGBoost benchmark BG2 Weekly beats monthly by 0.123 (experiment 87) to 0.13 (experiment 48) points Weekly, with a 12-month-window monthly refit as a research proxy (experiment 85) Primary demand, GAM stack Weekly minus monthly +0.001, quarterly minus monthly +0.010 (experiment 278) Monthly Bulk and grid supply points Weekly beats monthly by 0.160 points (0.066 to 0.247, experiment 87) Weekly Metered solar and wind farms Monthly minus frozen -0.044 for solar and +0.007 for wind (experiment 48), inside a ±0.05 band A single fit, or monthly, as the family's first version states

Quarterly refits are not used for the XGBoost-based families. Experiment 85 found that quarterly refits scored 0.38 points above weekly refits on the same 12-month window, and advised against using them to compare arms that differ in cadence or in how fast they adapt. For the GAM stack, quarterly refits save about 19 seconds per arm-year and add a loss of 0.010 points (99% interval -0.014 to +0.032), concentrated in winter, so they are not shown adequate. Their effect on the power of a default-plus-x contrast has not been measured.

docs.title: Does an ERA5-trained weather-to-power model beat the same model trained on ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether a model that turns weather into solar or wind farm output works better when it is trained on estimates of past weather than when it is trained on archived weather forecasts. We trained one model each way for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, gave both the same 51 weather forecasts for the days ahead, and compared their errors over 53 weekly forecast runs in one held-out year. Training on estimates of past weather gave the smaller error for forecasts up to 6 days ahead, and the benefit was not shown beyond that.

Verdict: supported up to day 6, not supported beyond. Stage 1a (one XGBoost model per series, trained on ERA5 (a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) and CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite estimate of sunlight), no calendar and no power-history columns) applied to the 51 members of ENS (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast) and averaged has a smaller error than the same columns trained on ENS weather, for lead bands up to 6 days, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, in one held-out year (fold A, 53 weekly runs). The planned contrasts were revised after two scientific reviews, so they are not pre-registered. The full write-up is the study README in studies/stage1_pilot/README.md.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
Every arm except c0 gets the same columns, and none is a calendar column or a power lag. Solar zenith and azimuth carry the time of day and the time of year.

  • Solar farms (9 columns): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth.
  • Wind farms (6 columns): wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, wind_dir_sin_10m, wind_dir_cos_10m, wind_dir_sin_100m, wind_dir_cos_100m. The wind farms' ERA5 cells have no temperature or pressure on disk.
  • ens_trained_plus_s1 adds one column, stage1a_prediction.
  • The *_calendar arms (the first run) add hour_sin, hour_cos, doy_sin, and doy_cos (solar 13 columns, wind 10).
  • c0, the production control, has 24 columns: categorical_precipitation_type_surface, dew_point_temperature_2m, downward_short_wave_radiation_flux_surface, geopotential_height_500hpa, local_day_of_week, local_day_of_week_cos, local_day_of_week_sin, local_time_of_day_cos, local_time_of_day_sin, local_time_of_year_cos, local_time_of_year_sin, local_utc_offset_minutes, power_lag_24h, power_lag_48h, power_lag_168h, power_lag_336h, pressure_reduced_to_mean_sea_level, pressure_surface, temperature_2m, windchill, wind_direction_10m, wind_direction_100m, wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m.

docs.title: Absolute scores, all leads
docs.text:
Mean absolute error, points of capacity, with 95% intervals that resample whole validation months.

arm solar wind ens_trained (reference) 8.25 (6.18 to 10.72) 17.09 (15.32 to 18.67) s1_memberavg (ERA5-trained, 51 members averaged) 7.67 (5.74 to 10.04) 15.39 (13.26 to 17.21) climatology 8.62 (6.49 to 11.14) 19.16 (16.49 to 21.50) c0 (production control, 24 production columns) 8.74 (6.51 to 11.37) 19.08 (17.25 to 20.71) era5_ceiling (given ERA5 weather, not a forecast) 5.98 (4.32 to 8.05) 7.90 (7.14 to 8.70)

docs.title: Planned contrasts (revised)
docs.text:
• P1 (s1_memberavg minus ens_trained) is material up to day 6 for both technologies. Wind -3.18, -4.04, and -2.37 points at 0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 days, and 3 to 6 days; solar -1.23, -1.41, and -0.73. At 7 to 10 and 11 to 15 days neither passes.
  • P2 (adding stage 1a's prediction as a column to ens_trained) is not material anywhere. Solar -0.06 (-0.12 to -0.01), wind +0.02 (+0.01 to +0.03) over all leads.
  • Beyond day 6 stage 1a is within about 1 point of climatology.

docs.title: What else the study found
docs.text:
• Averaging the 51 members is associated with a much larger drop in error for the ERA5-trained model (-0.70 solar, -2.23 wind) than for the ENS-trained model (-0.15, -0.22). With the control member alone, ERA5 training is associated with lower error at 0 to 2 days and higher error at 7 to 15 days.
  • Removing hour and day-of-year columns lowered the ENS-trained error by 1.13 (solar) and 3.40 (wind) points and the ERA5-trained error by 0.23 (solar) and 0 (wind). The first run's control, with 24 production columns, looked like it memorised calendar position.

docs.title: Effect of the feature lists (post hoc)
docs.text:
Removing the hour and day-of-year columns helped the ENS-trained model a lot and the ERA5-trained model little. The first run gave every arm those four calendar columns, and the production control also had 24 production columns including power lags. The table gives each change in mean absolute error over all leads, in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals. Every row is post hoc. The first run's arms are the *_calendar arms, scored on the same cases.

change solar wind ERA5-trained, calendar columns removed (F1) -0.23 (-0.47 to -0.08) +0.03 (-0.08 to +0.15) ENS-trained, calendar columns removed (F2) -1.13 (-1.71 to -0.65) -3.40 (-4.81 to -1.97) ENS-trained, 24 production columns replaced by the common columns (E13) -0.49 (-0.70 to -0.29) -1.99 (-2.73 to -1.31)
  • The ENS-trained model with calendar columns is the one that does worse. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, once per lead, so a model given the calendar position can learn the weather of that day rather than a weather-to-power relation.
  • The first run's headline against the production control was largely this effect. The common feature list, with no calendar column, is used in every arm of the revised contrasts.

docs.title: Gains in the tails (exploratory)
docs.text:
For wind, the gain from ERA5 training is much larger on the largest outputs; for solar it is larger in points at short leads but uncertain. The tail is the cases where observed power exceeds the series' 90th percentile of cleaned power in stage 1a's training window (20,020 solar and 9,747 wind cases per seed). The table gives s1_memberavg minus ens_trained in points of capacity, with 95% month-resampled intervals, against the same contrast on all cases.

lead band wind, top decile wind, all cases solar, top decile solar, all cases 0 to 24 h -16.54 (-18.82 to -12.81) -3.18 -2.99 (-7.73 to +0.23) -1.23 1 to 2 days -17.56 (-20.63 to -13.17) -4.04 -3.52 (-6.24 to -0.89) -1.41 3 to 6 days -8.46 (-11.47 to -5.18) -2.37 -1.76 (-4.52 to +0.78) -0.73 7 to 10 days -1.22 (-2.46 to -0.08) -0.45 -0.19 (-3.60 to +2.91) -0.30 11 to 15 days +0.12 (-1.17 to +1.56) -0.61 +0.58 (-2.70 to +3.73) -0.12 all leads -6.14 (-7.66 to -4.33) -1.70 -1.05 (-3.93 to +1.25) -0.57
  • Relative to each arm's own error, the wind gain is about 12% in the tail and 10% overall. The top-decile error of ens_trained is 53.22 points and of s1_memberavg 47.08, against 17.09 and 15.39 over all cases. At 0 to 24 h the tail gain is 42% of the error against 27% overall.
  • For solar the relative gain is smaller in the tail (4% against 7% over all leads), and every solar tail interval over all leads and at 0 to 24 h and 3 to 6 days spans zero.
  • Tail errors are large for every forecast, and the weather input is associated with most of them. era5_ceiling has a top-decile error of 13.16 (wind) and 18.43 (solar) points. Without a second model, both ERA5-trained and ENS-trained forecasts miss most of the largest wind outputs.
  • The control member alone gives the same tail result for wind (-6.95, -8.39 to -5.23), so averaging the members is not needed for the tail gain, unlike the all-cases gain.
  • Selecting on the observed value truncates the outcome, so slopes on this subset are not comparable across studies; only paired differences are reported. Tail pinball loss, exceedance Brier scores, and reliability for the probabilistic forecasts are in the stage 2 experiment.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• The first run compared against a control that memorised calendar position, and the headline was revised after two Opus reviews. The revised contrasts were chosen after seeing the first run.
  • One held-out year, nine generators in two weather regions, fold A only, 24 decisions without a multiple-comparison correction.
  • ENS is biased against ERA5 (10 m wind 13% to 15% slower, shortwave 7% brighter). Mapping ENS onto ERA5 before stage 1a is untested.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Give every arm the same feature columns, and add a control without calendar columns whenever the training rows repeat a valid time.
  • Report the benchmark's absolute score and a climatology row beside every contrast.
  • Predictions: the per-member predictions of every arm are under data/studies/per_study/stage1_pilot/ (stage1a/, ens_trained/, scores/). They have not been written into data/ml-experiments/00001-era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained/predictions/ with a manifest, because the experiment_store module of PR #1187 does not exist yet.

docs.title: Does a stage 2 calibrator beat the pooled stage 1a mixture?
docs.text:
We asked whether a second model, which corrects the spread of the forecast (its 5% to 95% band) produced by a first weather-to-power model, makes solar and wind farm forecasts better than simply pooling the first model's output over the 51 weather forecasts. We compared both with a model trained directly on archived weather forecasts, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms over 53 weekly forecast runs in one held-out year. Pooling the first model's output beat the model trained on archived forecasts. The second model gave no improvement over pooling, and made the solar forecasts worse.

Verdict: the pooled ERA5-trained mixture beats the ENS-trained quantile model, and the stage 2 calibrator and learned blend did not improve on it, and were worse for solar. Study 2b ran in one held-out year (fold A, 53 weekly runs) for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. The full write-up is the Results section of studies/stage1_pilot/README_stage2.md. ERA5 is a reanalysis, an estimate of past weather. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members. The stage 2 calibrator is a second model that corrects the forecast quantiles that stage 1a produces.

docs.title: Input columns
docs.text:
The columns are those of experiment 00001, with no calendar column and no power lag.

  • Solar farms (9 columns): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, solar_zenith, solar_azimuth.
  • Wind farms (6 columns): wind_speed_10m, wind_speed_100m, wind_dir_sin_10m, wind_dir_cos_10m, wind_dir_sin_100m, wind_dir_cos_100m.
  • The calibrator takes the stage 1a quantiles for one ensemble member plus the same columns.

docs.text:
• Q1 (stage 2 minus the mixture) is not material. Solar +0.40 (+0.26 to +0.61), wind +0.26 (-0.17 to +0.64).
  • Q2 (stage 2 minus the ENS-trained quantile arm) is material for wind only. Wind -0.36 (-0.59 to -0.12), solar +0.17 (-0.03 to +0.50).
