We compared several variants on 4 such series and on 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), over 73 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The 14-day additive correction stayed the best variant. It did not lower the error at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, but it lowered the Primary error by the same amount as in experiment 00019.

Verdict: inconclusive for bulk supply points (BSP) and grid supply points (GSP), and the 14-day additive correction stays the best variant. N1 is the single-stage quantile model trained on the control member of the ensemble weather forecast (ENS) of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. The correction does not lower the BSP and GSP quantile score: C1 is +0.36 points of capacity (99.375% interval -0.19 to +0.98) on 4 series. It does lower the Primary score with power 2 days old: C3 is -0.99 (-1.82 to -0.18), the same size as the -0.99 that experiment 00019 found with power 3.5 hours old. Against manual_heuristic the corrected forecast scores -0.68 on BSP and GSP (C2, -1.57 to +0.26; mean absolute error of the median -1.47, -2.36 to -0.63). No variant beat the 14-day additive correction. A point is 1% of the series' effective capacity. Scores are on 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days, from July 2025 to June 2026, with ENS weather. The generators are not named. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better. manual_heuristic is a stored baseline that forecasts from the power at the same time of day in earlier weeks and years.

docs.title: What the arms score
docs.text:
Quantile score over all leads (mean signed error of the median in brackets; negative means the forecast is too low).

Arm Primary (16) BSP (2) GSP (2) climatology 7.46 (-2.87) 9.29 (+1.16) 21.18 (-9.67) manual_heuristic 5.89 (-1.34) 8.86 (+0.76) 20.81 (-4.80) N1 6.33 (-2.60) 8.06 (+0.01) 19.52 (-5.17) N1 plus 14-day correction 5.34 (-0.52) 8.22 (+0.08) 20.08 (-1.93)

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• A bias correction cannot help where N1 has no bias. N1's two BSP series have a mean error of +0.01 points, so the correction only adds noise to those series (E2, +0.16, -0.09 to +0.39). The two GSP series are biased low by 5.2 points, the correction removes 3.2 of that, and the quantile score still rises (E3, +0.56, -0.29 to +1.45). The 4 series leave intervals too wide to separate the two types.
  • Over all leads, a delay of 2 days costs nothing. The correction with 3.5-hour-old power scores the same as with 2-day-old power for Primary (E4, -0.0003, -0.018 to +0.019) and for BSP and GSP (E5, +0.02, -0.10 to +0.14). Up to 48 hours, fresher power helps a little (E4 -0.07, -0.11 to -0.03; E5 -0.19, -0.35 to -0.05).
  • A 7-day window is worse (C4, +0.19, +0.11 to +0.28) and a 28-day window is level or slightly better (C5, -0.07, -0.15 to +0.01). No window qualifies to replace 14 days under the decision rule. A longer window is worth testing with monthly retraining in place.
  • The multiplicative form is much worse (C6, +2.28, +0.50 to +5.46). Its mean error of the median is -3.4 points against -0.5 for the additive form.
  • A per-half-hour shift (C7, +0.02, -0.04 to +0.06) and recency weights (C8, +0.04, -0.00 to +0.09) change nothing.
  • The corrected forecast beats climatology on BSP and GSP (E11, -1.09, -1.70 to -0.42), and N1 alone is level with manual_heuristic on Primary substations over all leads (E10, +0.44, -0.10 to +0.93), but worse at leads of 3 days or more (+0.57, 0.00 to +1.10).

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Missed: the correction was predicted to lower the BSP and GSP score by at least 0.5 points; it raised it by 0.36 (C1).
  • Met: the Primary gain was predicted at 0.6 to 0.9 points; it was 0.99 (C3).
  • Partly missed: the 28-day window and the per-half-hour form were predicted to lose; each was level with the 14-day form, and the 28-day window was nominally the best variant.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• BSP and GSP have 2 series each. The 99.375% interval on C1 is 1.2 points wide, wider than any gain the correction could plausibly give.
  • Errors are measured at short lead and applied at long lead. Each past half-hour's error uses the forecast of the run current at that time, at a lead of 0 to 5 days, and the correction is applied up to 15 days ahead.
  • Runs with under 3 days of history get no correction. That is 44 of 1,460 runs per seed for the 14-day variants (73 runs times 20 series); the 7-day and 28-day windows and the 3.5-hour delay differ by a few runs.
  • The rows are runs every 5 days, not daily. Experiment 19's limit on daily forecasts applies.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets only, under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched. A run with under 3 days of history gets no correction.
  • Defensible designs: more than one. The variants are the question; each is fixed below.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00019's corrections_for and scoring, which the author could name without searching.

Selection. C4 to C8 test five variants at threshold 0, so replacing A14 by the best qualifying variant carries a selection effect that only the Bonferroni correction covers.

Size: medium. No model is fitted, because every arm post-processes the stored predictions of N1 from experiment 00013, which covers all 20 series. One Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code (leakage and the delay), and one of the write-up.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
All arms are scored on the cases of fold_a_every5d_v1 that every arm holds, with an observed value and a valid time before 2026-07-01. The corrected arms apply to N1's three seeds. A correction shifts or scales all 9 quantiles of a run and re-sorts them. No spread factor is applied, so that the correction is isolated.

The correction. For each run with origin T, the window is the W days that end 2 days before T. For each half-hour in the window, the forecast is the median of the latest earlier run that began before it (the rule of 00019, which checks that no forecast comes from a run that began after its half-hour). The error is the observed power over capacity minus that median. A run with under 3 days of paired history gets no correction.

  • A14: add the mean error over a 14-day window to every quantile (00019's correction, with the delay changed from 3.5 hours to 2 days).
  • A7, A28: the same with a 7-day and a 28-day window.
  • M14 (Primary substations only, where power stays positive): multiply every quantile by the ratio of the window's mean observed power to its mean forecast median, clipped to 0.5 to 2.0; no correction when the mean median is under 0.01 of capacity.
  • H14: add, to each valid time, the mean error of the window's half-hours with the same Europe/London half-hour of day; a cell with fewer than 3 pairs gets the window's overall mean error.
  • R14: the 14-day mean error with weights 0.5 ** (age_days / 3.5), age counted back from the window's end, so the newest days weigh most.
  • A14-fast: A14 with 00019's 3.5-hour delay, to measure what the 2-day delay costs (exploratory).
  • References: N1, manual_heuristic, climatology, all uncorrected. A stored arm has no seed, so it is repeated once per seed.

Delay. A run at origin T uses only power stamped at or before T minus 2 days and a half-hour (97 half-hours), so the correction needs power that is 2 days old. The run's code asserts this bound. The delay is much longer than the 3.5 hours of 00013's lags.

Lead mismatch. Each past half-hour's error is measured against the forecast of the run with the latest origin at or before that half-hour, so the correction measures errors at leads of 0 to 5 days, and applies the result at leads up to 15 days. A bias that grows with lead is under-corrected.

Bias is the mean signed error of the median, reported by arm and by group (Primary, BSP, GSP), beside the quantile score and the mean absolute error of the median.

Groups. BSP and GSP have 2 series each. The planned contrasts pool the 4 and the tables also show each type. A resolved interval for either type alone is not expected.

docs.title: Plan: past weather
docs.text: No past weather is used; the correction reads observed power only, and N1's weather is ENS in training and scoring.

docs.title: Experiment 22: how much would Primary demand gain from ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather?
docs.text:
We asked how much better the demand forecast for Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) would be if its weather input were an estimate of past weather instead of a weather forecast. The answer is an upper limit on what better weather products could bring, because estimates of past weather arrive about 5 days late and cannot be used live. We swapped the weather in the best demand forecast and scored 16 Primary substations over 73 forecast runs. The estimates of past weather lowered the error by only 0.10 points of capacity, so the 0.3-point gain we had predicted is ruled out.

Refuted: ERA5 weather lowered the quantile score by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the decision rule asked for is ruled out. The rows are the 16 Primary substations and 73 forecast runs of experiment 00019, scored with its full stack (N1 with a half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day correction, the spread factor of 1.15). The ENS arm scores 5.32 and the all-variable ERA5 arm scores 5.22, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity). manual_heuristic scores 5.89 on the same rows. The ENS arm matches experiment 19's stored stack to within 0.0003 points. ERA5 reaches us about 5 days late, so no serving system could use it: the arm is a ceiling for a weather product as accurate as ERA5. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better. manual_heuristic is a stored baseline that forecasts from the power at the same time of day in earlier weeks and years.

Weather column from ERA5 Quantile score minus ENS arm (99.38% interval) All seven columns -0.100 (-0.162 to -0.044) Shortwave radiation -0.084 (-0.130 to -0.043) Longwave radiation -0.016 (-0.028 to -0.008) Temperature at 2 m -0.013 (-0.039 to +0.011) Dew point at 2 m -0.003 (-0.010 to +0.002) Surface pressure +0.008 (-0.007 to +0.025) Precipitation -0.006 (-0.012 to -0.0002) Wind speed at 10 m -0.001 (-0.008 to +0.005)

Shortwave radiation carries nearly all of the gain. The seven single-column gains sum to -0.115 against -0.100 for all columns together. Temperature, which the plan expected to lead, gave -0.013 with an interval that includes zero. Precipitation is near zero in both sources, so its interval excluding zero is not a finding.

The all-variable ERA5 arm helps only from 3 days ahead. The gain by lead band is -0.075 at 3 to 6 days (95% interval -0.112 to -0.039), -0.130 at 7 to 10 days (-0.192 to -0.070) and -0.147 at 11 to 15 days (-0.216 to -0.078). It is +0.028 at 0 to 24 hours (+0.005 to +0.047) and +0.002 at 1 to 2 days (-0.036 to +0.038), so ERA5 is not better than ENS inside 2 days. The ENS arm scores 4.50 at 0 to 24 hours and 5.75 at 11 to 15 days. The band intervals are not corrected for five bands.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The N1 XGBoost model was trained on ENS control-member weather and not on ERA5. ERA5 differs from ENS in bias (for example, its mean shortwave is 132.6 against 139.1 W/m² over the validation year), so a model trained on ERA5 might gain more.
  • The 5% to 95% band covers 86% with ERA5 against 85% with ENS, and the 10% to 90% band covers 74% against 76%. The spread factor was fitted for ENS and was not refitted.
  • Each arm's correction history comes from that arm's own forecasts. An ERA5 arm has therefore also had its past errors corrected with ERA5 weather.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
docs.text:
• Model. Each series' N1 model with the half-life of 0.5 years is refitted as in experiment 19, on the ENS control member up to 2025-06-30, because that experiment stored no fitted models. The 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor are applied as in experiment 19.
  • Arms. The ENS arm feeds the 51 ENS members as in experiment 19. The all-variable ERA5 arm replaces the seven weather columns (shortwave, longwave, temperature, dew point, surface pressure, precipitation, wind speed at 10 m) with ERA5 at the valid time; the same value enters every member, so the 51 members collapse to one. Seven single-variable arms replace one column and keep the ENS members for the other six. The correction history of each arm comes from that arm's own past forecasts.
  • Weather source and availability. ERA5 reaches us about 5 days late, so it does not exist at forecast time. The arms therefore give a ceiling for a weather product with ERA5's accuracy, and no deployable system could reach it.
  • Training and serving mismatch. The model is trained on ENS control-member weather. ERA5 differs from ENS in bias (for example radiation), so the ERA5 arms may understate the gain from a model trained on ERA5; retraining on ERA5 is not tested.
  • Rows. The 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 and valid times before 2026-07-01, as in 00019. Leads are banded 0-24 h, 1-2 d, 3-6 d, 7-10 d, 11-15 d, reported exploratorily.
  • Leakage checks. The fit stops at 2025-06-30 23:30; lags and the correction use observations at least 3.5 hours before the origin; the ERA5 values are those of the valid time only.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets only.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: one; it is a permutation of the serving weather.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00019's helpers.

Size: simple, with one Sonnet review of the code and one of the write-up.

docs.title: Earlier advice
docs.text: Followed: test the correction on the winning recipe (00019); read the ENS control in the same way as 00013. No departure.

docs.title: Does recent observed power help solar and wind forecasts?
docs.text:
We asked whether recent measured power helps forecasts of solar and wind farm output, as it helps forecasts of demand. We gave the second step of the forecast the power from earlier times and summaries of it, and separately applied a correction based on the previous 14 days of errors, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. Recent power changed the accuracy by less than about 0.1 points of capacity, and the 14-day correction made the forecast about 0.4 points worse.

Verdict: inconclusive, with no sign of a benefit. Lagged power and summaries of recent power left the stage 2 calibrator's continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) unchanged for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, to within the resolution of about 0.1 points of capacity. The pre-registered 14-day correction raised the CRPS of the pooled mixture by about 0.4 points for both technologies. This is proposal P18 of the research plan, with the 14-day correction of experiment 00017 and experiment 00019 added. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble. The stage 2 calibrator is a second model that corrects the forecast quantiles that stage 1a produces.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: private prediction sets only. No schema in packages/contracts/ changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes (the form of the calibrator and of the correction), and the plan fixes one of each by copying experiments 00005 and 00019.
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no.

The size is medium: one Sonnet review of the code, which found no leakage and no index error, and one of this write-up.

docs.title: Which earlier advice this plan follows
docs.text:
• Followed: compare lagged arms against a calibrated arm without lags (00005); keep the raw lags and add summaries beside them (00008); pool the members before scoring and report the pooled mixture beside every stage 2 arm (00002); use only forecast-time inputs at lag times, namely observed power at least 3.5 hours old and the earlier forecasts' own errors.
  • Departs from: none.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Rows. The 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms of fold_a_tuesdays_v1: 53 Tuesday runs with valid times from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30, three seeds.

Weather source at forecast time. ENS members only, through the ERA5-trained stage 1a quantile models of experiment 00002. ERA5 is a reanalysis of past weather that arrives about 5 days late, and no arm reads it at a lag time. Recent observed power is usable once it is 3 hours old plus the half-hour it spans, as in experiment 00019.

Calibrators. One multi-quantile XGBoost model (9 levels, depth 4, 300 rounds, the settings of experiment 00005) per technology, seed, and arm, trained on the ENS control member's rows with out-of-fold stage 1a quantiles from 2024-07 to 2025-06 (the calibration table of experiment 00002), with the observed power over effective capacity as the target. The calibrator takes the member's 9 stage 1a quantiles, the lead in hours, and the recent-power columns of its arm. The calibrator has no calendar column. The calibrator is applied to each of the 51 members, and the calibrated quantiles are pooled into a mixture as in experiment 00020.

Recent-power columns. Lagged power is the newest usable value, the value at the valid time's half-hour on the latest earlier usable day, and the same on the latest earlier usable week (experiment 00019's three lags). Summaries are the minimum, mean, and maximum of the 48 half-hours ending at the newest usable value, and of the latest earlier usable day on the target's weekday (experiment 00008); a window needs at least 24 observed half-hours.

14-day correction. For the run at time t, the correction is the mean of observed power minus the mixture's median over earlier runs' non-trivial cases (95% quantile above 1% of capacity) with a valid time in [t - 14 d, t - 2 d], taking for each series and valid time the latest earlier run's forecast. Fewer than 500 such cases means no shift. The run's non-trivial quantiles are shifted by the correction, clipped to 0 to 1, and sorted.

Arm What it is mixture the pooled ERA5-trained mixture (the production recipe) cal0 calibrator with no recent-power column cal_lags calibrator + lagged power cal_sums calibrator + summaries cal_both calibrator + lagged power + summaries mix_c14 mixture + 14-day correction (mean error) cal_both_c14 cal_both + 14-day correction (mean error) mix_c14_median post hoc: mixture + 14-day correction using the median of the errors

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute CRPS, all leads (points of capacity). Solar: mixture 5.03, cal0 5.30, cal_lags 5.29, cal_sums 5.32, cal_both 5.30, mix_c14 5.46, cal_both_c14 5.89, climatology 5.63. Wind: mixture 11.11, cal0 11.41, cal_lags 11.43, cal_sums 11.53, cal_both 11.52, mix_c14 11.52, cal_both_c14 12.34, climatology 13.03. The seed spread is at most 0.005. The mixture reproduces experiment 00002 (solar 5.03 against 5.05, wind 11.11 against 11.11).
  • C1, lagged power in the calibrator (decides). Solar -0.012 (-0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146): inconclusive, because the interval cannot rule out a gain of 0.05 or a loss of 0.1. By lead band the point estimate is positive (worse) in the first two lead bands, under 3 days, for both technologies, so the lags did not help at the short leads where recent power should matter most.
  • C2 and C3, summaries. Summaries alone: solar +0.023 (-0.122 to +0.143), wind +0.115 (-0.051 to +0.307). Adding them to the lagged calibrator: solar +0.015 (-0.057 to +0.063), wind +0.098 (+0.009 to +0.213), so for wind they made the calibrator worse.
  • C4, the calibrator against the recipe. Solar +0.276 (+0.152 to +0.417), wind +0.417 (-0.095 to +0.971). The calibrators are worse than the pooled mixture before lags are added: cal0 scores 0.27 (solar) and 0.31 (wind) points above mixture.
  • C5, the 14-day correction on the mixture (decides). Solar +0.437 (+0.215 to +0.664), wind +0.413 (-0.003 to +0.924): refuted by the decision rule for both technologies, since the lower bound is above -0.05 and the interval is not wholly below zero. C6, the correction on the calibrator, is worse again: solar +0.590, wind +0.814.
  • Prediction against result. The predicted wind gain from lagged power (-0.10) and solar gain (-0.05) did not appear. The correction was predicted to move the CRPS by under 0.05, and moved it by +0.44 and +0.41.
  • Coverage. The mixture covers 94.3% to 95.3% (solar) and 89.5% to 95.3% (wind). The mean-error correction cuts coverage to 53% to 68% (solar, mix_c14 and cal_both_c14) and 67% to 77% (wind).
  • Why the correction hurts (post hoc). Observed power minus the median is positive on average for a right-skewed, zero-bounded target even when the quantiles are calibrated, so the mean error is a bias that the correction then adds to every quantile. Using the median of the errors instead (mix_c14_median, P1, read at 95%) gives solar +0.010 (-0.005 to +0.037) and wind -0.064 (-0.198 to +0.082) with coverage of 90% to 92% (solar) and 78% to 86% (wind): no gain, but no loss. This was run after seeing the C5 result; it leaves the pre-registered contrasts and verdict unchanged.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• A resolution limit. With 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, the C1 intervals are 0.21 (solar) and 0.24 (wind) points wide, so a lag effect under about 0.1 points is not resolved.
  • The calibrator is trained on 12 months of the ENS control member only. The control-trained calibrator applied to each member is worse than no calibrator, so C1 measures lags in a weaker baseline than the recipe. A calibrator trained on pooled members was not tested.
  • The 14-day correction has validation runs only (one a week), so its window holds at most two runs. A daily history, as in experiment 00019, was not available.
  • The 14-day correction on the calibrated arms uses the mean error only. Only the mixture was corrected with the median error.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• Weather explains these farms' output well enough that recent power adds nothing detectable at leads from 0 to 15 days, unlike Primary substation demand in experiment 00005.
  • A correction built from the mean error assumes a symmetric error. The assumption held for Primary demand in experiments 00017 and 00019 and does not hold for a farm's output.

docs.title: Experiment 24: which groupings of substations can share one XGBoost model?
docs.text:
We asked how many separate XGBoost models are needed to forecast demand: one per substation, one per group of similar substations, or a single model for all. We compared groupings by substation type and by size, with one model per series as the reference, on 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) and 4 bulk and grid supply points over 73 forecast runs. Sharing one model across a group raised the error by 0.15 points of capacity, and one model for all series raised it by 0.29.

Supported: pooling the series into 3 or 4 models raised the error by 0.15 points of capacity against one model per series, and one model across all series raised it by 0.29. Scores are the quantile score over all leads, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' effective capacity), after the 14-day error correction and the spread factor of 1.15 (the stack of experiment 00019), with ENS weather, on 73 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. On the 16 Primary substations, one model per substation type with the series identifier (4 models) scores 5.47 against 5.32 for 20 per-series models, and C1 is +0.15 (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin. One model per size band (3 models) scores the same (C3, +0.15, +0.05 to +0.26). One model across all series (1 model) does not meet the margin (C2, +0.29, +0.19 to +0.42). By the pre-registered rule the winner is the size bands, because it has the fewest models among the arms inside the margin, but the size-band and by-type pools score the same to two decimal places. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' ensemble forecast, which has 51 members. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better.

Arm Models Primary (16) BSP and GSP (4) Saved size (MB) One model per series 20 5.32 13.94 435 Per size band, with ID 3 5.47 14.23 73 Per substation type, with ID 4 5.47 13.96 94 Per random group of 5, with ID 4 5.47 14.25 95 All series, with ID 1 5.61 14.49 26 Per substation type, no ID 4 6.29 14.84 88 All series, no ID 1 6.11 16.71 22 manual_heuristic 5.89 14.70 climatology 7.46 15.11

The series identifier is essential. Dropping it raises the score by 0.82 for the by-type pools (C7, +0.46 to +1.23) and by 0.85 for the all-series pool (C8, +0.72 to +1.00). Without the identifier the by-type pools score worse than manual_heuristic on Primary substations (+0.41, +0.15 to +0.69, exploratory, 95%).

On the Primary substations, which series share a model hardly matters. A random partition into 4 groups of 5 of all 20 series scores 5.47 on the 16 Primary substations, the same as the by-type pools (5.47). On all 20 series the by-type pools beat the random partition by 0.06 (C9, -0.13 to -0.01), and on the 4 BSP and GSP series by 0.29 (13.96 against 14.25, exploratory). Size bands (3 models), by-type pools (4), and random groups (4) all lose 0.15 on Primary, so the data show a step between 1 model and 3 or 4 models, not an effect of the grouping.

The error correction helps pooled models less. Without the correction, by-type pools beat per-series models by 0.30 on Primary (exploratory, -0.56 to -0.03, 95%): 6.04 against 6.34. The correction lowers per-series models by 1.0 points (6.34 to 5.32) and by-type pools by 0.6 (6.04 to 5.47), so the corrected pools lose 0.15. The difference between the two reductions has no interval, so this finding is exploratory.

All-series pooling costs most on the BSP series. By-type pools are worse than per-series models on 15 of the 20 series (largest loss 0.57, largest gain 0.68). The all-series pool is worse on 18, and the BSP series lose 0.80 (0.64 to 1.00, exploratory, 95%). The 4 BSP and GSP series cannot separate the by-type pools from per-series models (+0.03, -0.15 to +0.15).

The pooled stacks still beat manual_heuristic on Primary substations. By-type pools: -0.42 (-0.68 to -0.19). All-series pool: -0.27 (-0.56 to -0.03). Per-series models: -0.56 (-0.82 to -0.33).

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Arm Models Fit seconds, one seed Rows per model One model per series 20 465 one series Per size band 3 432 6 to 7 series Per substation type 4 184 2 to 8 series Per random group 4 550 5 series All series 1 161 20 series

The fit seconds are not comparable between arms. Other sessions loaded the machine during the size band and random group fits (the by-type and random fits train 4 models on similar row counts and took 184 and 550 seconds), so only the model counts and the saved sizes are reliable. The saved size falls from 435 MB to 22 to 95 MB with pooling.

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Met: by-type pools were predicted within plus or minus 0.3 points of per-series (+0.15), and the all-series pool 0.2 to 1.0 worse (+0.29, at the low end). The prediction that the loss falls mostly on BSP and GSP was not confirmed: the Primary-only contrast is +0.29, and the BSP and GSP contrast is +0.55 with an interval from -0.00 to +0.95 (exploratory).
  • Met: dropping the identifier raised the all-series score by 0.2 to 1.0 (+0.85).
  • Missed: dropping the identifier was predicted to raise the by-type score by at most 0.2; it raised it by 0.82.
  • Met: size-band pools fell between the by-type and all-series pools (level with by-type).
  • Met, barely: the random partition scored worse than by type on all 20 series (by 0.06), and level with it on the 16 Primary series.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only 20 series. BSP and GSP have 2 each, so their per-type pools are tiny and their intervals are wide. The verdict rests on the 16 Primary series, and an extrapolation to 2,500 series is not tested.
  • The intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so they say nothing about new series.
  • Pooled models have a fixed 500 rounds and depth 6, so their capacity per series falls as the pool grows. The experiment did not scale the rounds, so the all-series loss may be partly a capacity effect.
  • The correction history comes from runs 5 days apart (experiment 19's limit), and 26 of 1,460 series-runs had no history and got no correction.
  • Effective capacity is one fixed number per series, shared by every arm, so it cannot explain a difference between arms.
  • The plan had one Sonnet review and the code had one; the project's credit setting kept Opus for other work.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets only, under data/ml-experiments/.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • Defensible designs: more than one; the groupings, the pooled models' columns, and the per-series reference are fixed below before any fit.
  • Callers: the scripts copy 00019's fit and 00021's scoring, which the author could name without searching.

Size: complex, because more than one design tests the hypothesis. One Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code (leakage, the fit stopping at 2025-06-30, the correction's history bound), and one of the write-up. Opus is kept for work that is truly vital.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
Recipe. Every model is 00019's single-stage quantile model: the 9-level quantile loss on the ENS control member, 00006's columns, the lead in hours, and the three power lags measured from the forecast origin (00013's 3.5-hour telemetry delay). The recency half-life is 0.5 years (00017), the training data are daily runs from 2024-04-01 with valid times up to 2025-06-30 23:30, and the model is frozen there. Targets and lags are power over effective capacity, so series of different sizes share one scale. Predictions pool the 51 ENS members into the 9-quantile mixture. The 14-day additive error correction and the spread factor of 1.15 (00019's stack, correction history measured with 00019's 3.5-hour delay) are then applied per series to each arm's quantiles.

Series. The 20 demand series of 00013 and 00021: 8 Primary substations that meter in MW, 8 Primary substations that meter in MVA, 2 BSP, and 2 GSP.

Groupings. The models differ only in which series a model trains on.

Arm Models Rows per model own: one model per series 20 one series type_id: one per substation type (BSP, GSP, Primary-MW, Primary-MVA), with the identifier 4 2, 2, 8, 8 series type_noid: the same without the identifier 4 as above all_id: one model across all series, with the identifier 1 20 series all_noid: the same without the identifier 1 20 series size_id: one per capacity band (terciles of effective capacity, 7, 7, and 6 series), with the identifier 3 7, 7, 6 series random_id: one per group of a random partition of the 20 series into 4 groups of 5 (seed 24, drawn before any fit), with the identifier 4 5 series each

The identifier is the series' integer code (0 to 19, fixed by site order) as a categorical column (enable_categorical, XGBoost's default max_cat_to_onehot); every code is in the range of every model, and a code the model never saw goes to the default direction. own has no identifier because each model sees one series. The size bands use only each series' effective capacity, a fixed property of the series, and the random partition is the control that separates "similar series share a model" from "fewer models". Primary substations' units (MW or MVA) come from the metadata table. Each arm is fitted for seeds 0, 1 and 2. References: manual_heuristic and climatology stored by 00013.

Cost. For each arm the experiment records the number of models and the wall-clock fit seconds (training only, GPU, after checking the CPU load), summed over models for one seed, and the size of the saved models.

docs.title: Plan: leakage and scoring checks
docs.text:
• The scoring script asserts the correction's history bounds as 00019's and 00021's do: every observation in a correction is at or before the origin minus 7 half-hours, and the forecast for a past half-hour comes from a run that began at or before it.
  • Training rows end at 2025-06-30 23:30 and only the control member is used; the scripts assert both.
  • The validation rows are fold_a_every5d_v1 (73 runs, every 5 days, valid times before 2026-07-01), with ENS weather. Past weather is not used at lag times.
  • A check compares own with 00019's N1H (same recipe): the two should agree within the seed spread of 00019's N1H on the 16 Primary series.
  • No calendar control is added: the calendar columns of 00006's set are in every arm, so the contrasts compare groupings, not the value of the calendar.

docs.title: Plan: earlier advice
docs.text: Followed: 00006's columns, 00017's half-life of 0.5 years, 00019's 14-day correction and spread factor of 1.15 (stack, not tested separately here), 00021's finding that the correction is unproven for BSP and GSP (reported per type, not assumed to help), and a climatology row. Departure: the half-life is tested on a frozen model, which 00019 found neutral.

docs.title: Plan: limits stated in advance
docs.text:
• BSP and GSP have 2 series each, so their per-type intervals are wide and the by-type pools for them are tiny pools of 2 series; the verdict is driven by the 16 Primary series.
  • Only 20 series, so conclusions about 2,500 series are an extrapolation, and the intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so they say nothing about new series.
  • Capacity per series falls as a pool grows. Every model has 500 rounds and depth 6 whatever its row count, so a pool of 20 series gets less capacity per series than a per-series model; the experiment does not scale the rounds.
  • The 14-day correction removes level bias, which is the main error of a badly pooled model, so the stack can hide pooling effects; the uncorrected contrasts are exploratory.
  • Effective capacity is a fixed property of each series (as in every earlier demand experiment), and the targets and lags are scaled by it.
  • Review: the plan is sized complex but had a Sonnet review only, as the project's credit setting asks.
  • The correction's history comes from 5-day-spaced runs (00019's limit).

docs.title: Does the change in the intra-day price help a stage 1 demand model explain power?
docs.text:
We asked whether the change in the electricity price during the day helps a demand model, beyond the price level alone. We added several price inputs to a weather-to-power model, and compared each with the base model and with controls that used shuffled prices, on Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network) in a selection year and a confirmation year. Price changes beat the price level in both years, but by only 0.04 to 0.05 points of capacity, below the 0.1 points we had set as worth using.

Verdict: small gain, and too small to use. On Primary substations, price changes beat the price level alone and beat other-week changes in both years, with intervals wholly below zero, but by 0.04 to 0.05 points of capacity against the pre-registered 0.1. The system price gained 0.05 to 0.08 over the level. National demand and wind, with no price, scored 0.22 and 0.40 points below the price change arm. Follows experiment 00015.

Absolute scores, Primary substations (mean absolute error of the median, points of capacity, 3 seeds, 13 series in the selection year and 14 in the confirmation year):

Arm Selection Confirmation BASE 6.933 6.616 PRICE_LEVEL 6.905 6.715 PRICE_CHANGE 6.868 6.665 PRICE_SHAPE 6.866 6.648 SHUFFLED_CHANGE 6.907 6.712 SHUFFLED_SHAPE 6.934 6.719 NATIONAL 6.652 6.268 SYSTEM 6.828 6.669 CLIMATOLOGY 8.527 8.928

docs.title: What the contrasts say
docs.text:
• C1, changes against level only (verdict): -0.037 (-0.056 to -0.018) in the selection year and -0.050 (-0.083 to -0.018) in the confirmation year. 11 of 12 months are below zero in each year.
  • C2, changes against other-week changes (verdict): -0.039 (-0.070 to -0.015) and -0.047 (-0.086 to -0.006). Both estimates miss the -0.1 threshold, and both intervals lie wholly above -0.1, so a gain of 0.1 points is ruled out. The rule's "refuted" and "small gain" clauses both apply and it states no precedence. The verdict is small gain, because the skill reserves that label for an interval that excludes zero in the predicted direction below the threshold. Both pre-registered predictions missed: the gain of 0.15 to 0.4 points did not appear, and PRICE_CHANGE did worse than NATIONAL.
  • C3, changes against national demand and wind: +0.216 (+0.020 to +0.468) and +0.397 (+0.167 to +0.633). National demand and wind are better in both years.
  • C4, shape against changes: -0.002 (-0.043 to +0.040) and -0.017 (-0.063 to +0.024). The extra shape columns add nothing to the changes. Shape against other-week shape is -0.068 (-0.125 to -0.009) and -0.071 (-0.138 to -0.024).
  • C5, level against no price: -0.028 (-0.159 to +0.112) and +0.099 (-0.047 to +0.248). Both intervals include zero, so the level alone shows no help. In the confirmation year PRICE_CHANGE (6.665) is still above BASE (6.616).
  • C6, system price against level only: -0.077 (-0.105 to -0.048) and -0.046 (-0.078 to -0.018), as large as or larger than the price change gain.
  • C7, by time of day: in the selection year there is no gain from 00:00 to 08:00, and the 16:00 to 20:00 block (-0.031, interval -0.069 to +0.009) is smaller than the 08:00 to 16:00 and 20:00 to 24:00 blocks (-0.056 to -0.064). The prediction of a peak at 16:00 to 20:00 did not hold. On the days with the top 5% largest half-hourly price move, C1 is +0.100 (-0.046 to +0.312) in the selection year and -0.251 (-0.332 to -0.189) in the confirmation year, so the day-level result did not repeat.
  • BSP and GSP, four series, each read alone: no consistent sign. C1 in the confirmation year is -0.114 (-0.214 to -0.025) at B2 and +0.938 (+0.141 to +1.902) at G1, and the other two intervals include zero. NATIONAL beats PRICE_CHANGE at all four series in the confirmation year.

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• Some series have too little history, so 13 of the 16 Primary series were fitted in the selection year and 14 in the confirmation year. All 2 BSP and 2 GSP series were fitted in both years.
  • Nine days of system price are missing at the source (47 of 48 periods); the experiment treats them as missing. Market Index Data holds exact duplicate rows, which are harmless.
  • The shuffle shifts in UTC, so the weekday and half-hour match is off by one local hour in the weeks around a clock change.
  • Market Index Data is a proxy for the intra-day price. The tick-by-tick intraday price that jumps after an interconnector trip is paid for and was not tested, so this result does not rule out an effect of that price.
  • The model uses the price at the target half-hour, so no score is a forecast skill.
  • Reviews: Sonnet plan and code reviews, triaged on the pull request. No Opus review was run.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Stage 1 here is an explanatory model, not a forecaster. It maps the ERA5 weather, the clock, and information about the price at time t or earlier to power at time t. Every column uses only values at or before the target half-hour. The price at t is published only after the half-hour, so no score is a forecast skill.

The base is experiment 00006's Primary input set with the 0.5-year recency half-life of experiment 00017. Folds, purge, XGBoost settings (no column subsampling), the 20 series (16 Primary, 2 BSP, 2 GSP), the seeds (0, 1, 2), and the minimum training history are those of experiment 00015. The 14-day error correction and the rest of experiment 00019's stack are stage 2 steps and are not part of stage 1, so they are left out.

Arm Adds to BASE BASE nothing PRICE_LEVEL price_now: Market Index Data (APXMIDP) at the target half-hour PRICE_CHANGE price_now, and d1, d2, d4, d12: price(t) minus price(t-k half-hours) PRICE_SHAPE price_now, price minus its trailing 24-hour mean, rank within the trailing 24 hours, half-hours since the last spike (price above the trailing-24-hour mean plus 2 standard deviations, capped at 48), and the 6-hour range SHUFFLED_CHANGE the real price_now, and d1, d2, d4, d12 read at another week's same weekday and half-hour SHUFFLED_SHAPE the real price_now, and PRICE_SHAPE's other four columns read at another week's same weekday and half-hour NATIONAL GB demand and wind at t, their d1, and demand's d4 (5 columns) SYSTEM (descriptive) price_now, the system price, the net imbalance volume, and the one-half-hour changes of both CLIMATOLOGY not a fit: month-by-half-hour median of the fold's training window

Rolling columns use only the past. The rolling mean, standard deviation, rank, and range are trailing windows that end at t. check_no_lookahead in e00025_inputs.py removes the future rows of the series and fails if any added column changes. The report prints the share of rows with each added column missing, for every arm, because the real and shuffled columns have different gaps and XGBoost can learn from a gap. No row is dropped for a missing column. The join uses the half-hour's start, valid_time minus 30 minutes, and the script asserts that valid_time is the period end.

A shuffled arm keeps the real price level and takes the changes from another week. The shift is 1 to 4 weeks either way, drawn per week and per seed, so the arm keeps the week's price level and the calendar structure and loses the match between the changes and the target half-hour. Keeping the real price_now makes C2 isolate the change columns. A training row whose shifted time would fall after the training end shifts backwards instead, so no price from the purge or validation weeks enters training; a row with no source on either side gets missing values.

Prices. Market Index Data is the experiment 10 pull, 2019 to 2026, with a zero volume treated as missing. The system price (single price since 2015) and the net imbalance volume come from Elexon DISEBSP, fetched free for 2019-09-01 to 2025-08-31 with studies/market_downloads/fetch_gb_prices.py and joined to the 2025-09 to 2026-09 pull already on disk. Market Index Data is a proxy for the intra-day price: it is an index of short-term trading, published after the period, and it is not the tick-by-tick intraday price in which an interconnector trip shows. The tick price is paid for and is not used. Weather is ERA5, which arrives about 5 days late, so no arm can run at forecast time. The system price is a second, free signal of fault stress. A SYSTEM gain is not causal, because the system price partly reflects the demand that the substations carry.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
All are differences in mean absolute error in points of capacity, over the selection year (2024-07 to 2025-06) and then, once, the confirmation year (2025-07 to 2026-06), with month-resampled intervals, pooled over the series of one substation type and the 3 seeds. The types are scored separately and never pooled.

  • C1 (verdict, Primary): PRICE_CHANGE - PRICE_LEVEL.
  • C2 (verdict, Primary): PRICE_CHANGE - SHUFFLED_CHANGE.
  • C3: PRICE_CHANGE - NATIONAL.
  • C4: PRICE_SHAPE - PRICE_CHANGE, and PRICE_SHAPE - SHUFFLED_SHAPE.
  • C5: PRICE_LEVEL - BASE (the experiment 00015 check).
  • C6: SYSTEM - PRICE_LEVEL.
  • C7: C1 by 4-hour block of local time, in the 16:00 to 20:00 peak, and on the days with the top 5% absolute half-hourly price change.
  • BSP and GSP: C1 to C6 for each of the 4 series separately, with no type-level interval, because each type has two series. The page makes no claim comparing these types with Primary.

docs.title: Sizing
docs.text:
• Stores: private predictions and a private download of system prices; nothing is committed.
  • Serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes (which price columns, which controls), fixed above.
  • Code whose callers could not be named without searching: no, the code copies experiment 00015's.

This is complex because it adds a data source and more than one defensible design. Reviews: one Sonnet plan review, one Sonnet code review, one Sonnet write-up review. Opus is not used, by the manager's instruction on credits.

Resources. Slot A: 12 cores, one process per fit with one thread, no GPU.

Earlier advice. Follows 00015's advice to keep an other-week price control and to try national demand and wind, and 00017's advice to use a 0.5-year half-life. Departs from 00019's stack because this is stage 1 only.

docs.title: Does a recent effective-capacity feature lower the solar and wind forecast error?
docs.text:
We asked whether telling a solar or wind forecast each farm's recent effective capacity lowers its error. We added a feature stating that capacity to the forecast and compared the error with and without it, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. The feature moved the error by -0.018 points of capacity (1% of a farm's effective capacity, roughly its usual maximum output) for solar and +0.013 for wind. The data could not tell either change from no effect, and could not rule out the 0.03-point gain that would justify using the feature.

Verdict: inconclusive. A feature stating each farm's recent effective capacity moved the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by -0.018 points of capacity for solar and +0.013 for wind, and the intervals include both no effect and the 0.03-point threshold. The experiment is proposal P30 of the research plan. The farms are 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. ENS is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble, ERA5 its reanalysis of past weather, and CAMS the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite irradiance estimate.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: private prediction sets and tables only. No schema in packages/contracts/ changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched. A port would add a daily table of capacity features.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The statistic, the window, the weather variable that ranks the steps, and how training rows get a forecast origin all admit alternatives. This page fixes one of each.
  • Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no. The scripts copy the patterns of experiments 00020 and 00023.

The size is complex. One Sonnet reviewer reviewed the plan, and its findings (a season-preserving shuffle, a matched shuffled copy of the single feature, a Bonferroni family of the 4 decisive contrasts, a threshold of 0.03, and a training lead drawn from the validation leads) are applied. The reviewer's rescaling design was rejected, because it tests a correction and not a feature. One Sonnet reviewer reviews the code and one the write-up (Sonnet in place of Opus, as the credit budget requires).

docs.title: Which earlier advice this plan follows
docs.text:
• Followed: test solar changes with a control that shares the column count (00020); keep colsample_bytree at 1.0 in every arm, because column subsampling gives a wider arm a free win; use the power-curve base margin for wind (00020); train on ERA5 from 2019-09 with no calendar column (00012); report absolute scores beside contrasts and the climatology row.
  • Departs from: none. Experiment 00023 found recent power useless as a calibrator input, but it gave the calibrator the newest lags, not a capacity statistic, and the calibrator was weaker than the recipe.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Rows and series. The 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms of fold_a_tuesdays_v1: 53 Tuesday runs with valid times from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30, three seeds. Only anonymised labels appear.

Stage 1a quantile model. The experiment 00020 recipe: one XGBoost model per series and seed with the 9-level multi-quantile objective (500 rounds, eta 0.05, depth 6, colsample_bytree 1.0), trained on cleaned power at valid times from 2019-09 to before 2025-06-17, applied to the 51 ENS members and pooled into a mixture. Inputs: the 9 solar or 6 wind columns of experiment 00020, plus the arm's capacity features. No calendar column and no lag column.

The cutoff. Every capacity feature is a function of a series and a cutoff day: the UTC day that contains the forecast origin minus 5 days. The windows are whole trailing UTC days that end before the cutoff day starts. The 5 days are ERA5's delay; CAMS is assumed no faster. Power is cleaned power over effective capacity, so a feature is a fraction of capacity. One function computes the daily table of features for a series, and a unit test truncates all inputs after the cutoff and asserts that the features do not change.

Training rows have no forecast origin. The ERA5-trained model sees one row per valid time. Each training row gets a lead drawn at random (seeded) from the leads of the validation frames, its origin is the valid time minus that lead (the validation origin is power_fcst_init_time), and its features are the daily table's row for that origin's cutoff day. A serving row uses its real origin, so the feature is as stale in training as in serving. The effective capacity used to normalise power is the whole-record 99th percentile that every arm already uses, so it is the same in all arms.

Weather that ranks the steps. CAMS shortwave at the farm for solar, and ERA5 100 m wind speed for wind. Both are past weather read at a cutoff 5 days old, so training and serving read the same product and nothing is late at forecast time.

Features. A top-decile feature is null when its window has fewer than 100 usable steps or its top decile holds fewer than 10. A ratio feature is null under 10 usable steps. A percentile of all power is null when under half the window's steps are observed. XGBoost handles nulls, and the write-up reports each feature's null share by month.

Name Technology Definition top_decile_28d solar 99th percentile of power over daylight steps (solar zenith under 85 degrees) in the top 10% of CAMS shortwave within the window, 28 days top_decile_7d, top_decile_90d solar the same over 7 and 90 days power_to_cams_q90_28d solar 90th percentile of power divided by CAMS shortwave in kW per square metre, over steps with CAMS above 200 W per square metre, 28 days top_decile_last_year solar top_decile_28d for the 28-day window centred 365 days before the cutoff day top_decile_28d wind 99th percentile of power at the steps in the top 10% of ERA5 100 m wind speed, 28 days p995_28d, p995_90d wind 99.5th percentile of all usable power, 28 and 90 days power_to_wind3_q75_28d wind 75th percentile of power divided by the cube of speed, over steps with speed from 3 to 8 m/s, 28 days p995_last_year wind p995_28d for the window centred 365 days before the cutoff day

A feature that needs a window before 2019-09 is null, so the 90-day and last-year features are null for the first 90 and 365 days of training and never null at serving; the model sees nulls only early in training.

A static capacity control is not included. The design brief proposed one, but each series has its own model, so a per-series constant column carries no information.

Arms. Equal column counts are not possible, so each shuffled control carries the columns of the arm it matches.

Arm Extra columns A0 none (benchmark) A2 top_decile_28d A3 top_decile_28d, top_decile_7d, top_decile_90d (solar); top_decile_28d, p995_28d, p995_90d (wind) A4 A2 + power_to_cams_q90_28d (solar) or power_to_wind3_q75_28d (wind) A5 A2 + the last-year feature A6 A3's columns, from the shuffled table A7 A2's column, from the shuffled table

The shuffle permutes, within each series, whole calendar months among the same calendar month of other years before 2025-06 (every June among Junes), and a day takes its month's replacement day by day of month. The seasonal marginal remains, so a control that gains must be gaining from season and not from capacity. Months from 2025-06 on take a random same-calendar-month source before 2025-06, so no validation power enters a training row.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text:
Each contrast is the arm named first minus the arm named second, per technology (12 in all).

Id Contrast What it tests C1 A2 - A0 (decides) does a trailing capacity feature help C2 A2 - A7 (gates C1) does the feature beat a season-preserving shuffle of itself C3 A3 - A6 do several windows beat the same number of shuffled columns C4 A3 - A2 do several windows help C5 A4 - A2 does a second kind of statistic add (exploratory: it differs in kind from the top-decile feature) C6 A5 - A2 does the same window a year earlier add (exploratory: a seasonal reference)

The write-up reports each arm's absolute CRPS, the climatology row, a per-farm breakdown (gains are expected to concentrate in the few months with a loss of capacity).

docs.title: Limits stated in advance
docs.text:
• The pre-registered estimate was that the sample resolves about 0.1 points for solar. Experiment 00020's solar paired intervals were 0.19 to 0.30 points wide, so the threshold of 0.03 is below what 6 farms resolve unless a feature effect is concentrated.
  • The intervals resample initialisation months, not farms, so the true uncertainty is larger than reported.
  • The cutoff of 5 days applies to power as well as weather, a deliberate simplification that dilutes a signal about a recent loss.
  • The prior study found few real losses of capacity, so little can be learned from most months.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute CRPS, all leads (points of capacity). Solar: A0 5.026, A2 5.008, A3 5.012, A4 4.990, A5 4.991, A6 5.057, A7 5.049, climatology 5.629. Wind: A0 11.053, A2 11.066, A3 11.015, A4 11.005, A5 11.091, A6 11.072, A7 11.056, climatology 13.029. The seed spread is at most 0.034. A0 reproduces experiment 00020 (solar 5.03, wind 11.05).
  • C1, the single feature minus no feature (decides). Solar -0.018 (-0.162 to +0.096), wind +0.013 (-0.054 to +0.101): inconclusive for both, because each interval holds zero and a gain of 0.03.
  • C2, the single feature minus its shuffled copy (gates C1). Solar -0.041 (-0.324 to +0.131), wind +0.010 (-0.099 to +0.137). The shuffled solar copy A7 is 0.023 worse than A0, so the shuffle hurt a little, but no interval excludes zero.
  • C3 to C6 (descriptive). Three features minus their shuffled copies: solar -0.045 (-0.314 to +0.134), wind -0.057 (-0.195 to +0.066). Three features minus one: solar +0.005, wind -0.052 (-0.110 to +0.004). Shape feature added to the single feature: solar -0.017 (-0.188 to +0.085), wind -0.061 (-0.107 to -0.025), the only interval wholly below zero. Last-year feature added: solar -0.016, wind +0.024.
  • Per farm. The single feature changed the CRPS of solar farm E by -0.235 points and of wind farm W1 by -0.044, and raised it for solar farm A by +0.085 and wind farm W3 by +0.113. The shuffled copy changed farm E by -0.034. The per-farm figures have no intervals, and farm E is one farm of six.
  • Coverage. The 5% to 95% band of every feature arm covers up to 2.7 points less than A0's (solar 92.2% to 95.0%, wind 87.4% to 92.6%, against 94.3% to 95.3% and 89.4% to 93.7%).
  • Null shares over the validation year. The solar 7-day feature is null on average 24% of days (44% at the worst farm); every other feature is null under 2% of days.
  • Prediction against result. The solar single-feature effect (-0.02) matched the estimate. The wind effect (-0.03, within its stated range) came out at +0.01. The shuffled copy was predicted to move the CRPS by under 0.02 and moved solar by +0.023. Extra windows, a shape feature, and a last-year feature were predicted to move the CRPS by under 0.03 beyond the single feature, and for wind two of them moved it by more (C4 -0.052, C5 -0.061).

docs.title: Failures and limits
docs.text:
• The observed interval widths show the sample resolves about 0.15 points for solar and 0.1 for wind. The decisive intervals are 0.26 (solar) and 0.16 (wind) points wide, so a gain of the predicted size is not resolved.
  • Intervals resample months, not farms. The per-farm figure shows the spread between farms is larger than the contrast.
  • The wind shape feature's gain is exploratory. C5 is one of 12 contrasts and sits outside the 4 that set the interval level.
  • No post hoc tweak was run.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• A trailing capacity feature is not worth its serving step on this evidence. The two decisive contrasts straddle zero, and the farm that gained most is one of six.
  • The cubic power-to-speed feature is worth a separate test for wind. The cubic power-to-speed feature is the only feature with an interval wholly below zero among the descriptive contrasts (C5 is one of 12), and it needs no weather product beyond the wind speed already used.

docs.title: Does PV_Live at the lag times help the stage 2 forecast of GSP demand?
docs.text:
We asked whether Sheffield Solar's estimate of solar generation at the earlier times used as inputs (the lag times, such as 24 and 48 hours before the forecast origin) helps the second step of a demand forecast at two grid supply points. We gave the second step that estimate and compared its error with the same step without it, over 73 forecast runs. The estimate lowered the error by at most 0.08 points of capacity, and every interval included zero, so a gain of 0.3 points or more is ruled out for these two series.

Verdict: refuted for the two grid supply points (GSPs), Walpole and Bicker Fen. Giving the stage 2 calibrator Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate at the lag times lowered the quantile score by at most 0.08 points of capacity, and every interval includes zero. The best planned contrast, C1 (PV_Live level minus no PV_Live, all leads), is -0.08 (98.33% interval -0.26 to +0.08). The three intervals all lie above -0.30, so a gain of 0.3 points or more (the decision threshold) is excluded at 98.33% for these two series, and the intervals say nothing about other GSPs. Scores are on 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days, July 2025 to June 2026, with ENS weather, in points of capacity (1% of the series' effective capacity). Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0. The stage 2 calibrator is a second model that corrects the forecast quantiles that stage 1a produces. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Arm Quantile score, all leads Up to 48 h C, all leads (98.33%) A0, no PV_Live 19.04 15.21 A1, PV_Live level 18.97 15.24 C1 -0.08 (-0.26 to +0.08) A2, PV_Live share 18.98 15.28 C2 -0.06 (-0.22 to +0.09) A3, delta plus PV_Live 19.01 15.21 C3 -0.03 (-0.13 to +0.09) A3m, delta minus PV_Live (post hoc) 18.99 15.19 -0.05 (-0.17 to +0.03, 95%) Day-type climatology 24.40 24.51
  • A0 reproduces experiment 00005's l3 arm for these 2 GSPs exactly (difference 0.000).
  • No series or lead band has an interval wholly below zero. The season and hour split below has no intervals. The largest nominal gain is at midday in March to May and September to November (A3 minus A0, -0.44 over 31,365 rows; exploratory, no interval), and December to February is nominally worse (+0.08 to +0.09).
  • The sign check failed. On summer middays the delta correlates with PV_Live at +0.45 at Bicker Fen and -0.26 at Walpole, and the delta plus PV_Live correlates at +0.85 and +0.20. Adding PV_Live did not remove the solar part of the delta, so A3 did not separate solar from other demand as the plan assumed. The post hoc arm A3m (subtracting PV_Live) scored the same as A0 (-0.05, -0.17 to +0.03), so the sign does not explain the null result.
  • PV_Live was usable for most positions. The 24-hour lag is never usable under the 1-day settling delay, the 48-hour lag only for leads under 1 day, and the 168-hour lag up to 6 days. The same-time-of-day and same-time-of-week positions are always usable.

docs.title: S1: stage 1a with PV_Live at the valid time (exploratory)
docs.text: Adding PV_Live's level at the valid time lowered stage 1a's mean absolute error at observed ERA5 weather at Bicker Fen, by 1.28 points over all valid times (95% interval -1.90 to -0.67) and 2.57 points in daylight (-3.58 to -1.31), and not at Walpole (-0.03, -0.27 to +0.23; daylight +0.04, -0.41 to +0.53). The valid-time value is not known at the forecast origin, so this does not show a gain for the forecast.

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Missed: the plan predicted a 0.5-point gain from the adjusted delta; C3 was -0.03.
  • Missed: the plan expected intervals too wide to resolve 0.3 points; the 98.33% intervals are 0.22 to 0.34 points wide, and each excludes -0.30.
  • Partly missed: gains were predicted mostly at midday in summer; the nominal gain is -0.14 at midday in June to August and -0.44 in the other months of spring and autumn, with no intervals.
  • Missed: A1 and A2 were predicted to gain 0.2 points; they gained 0.08 and 0.06.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Availability shares count a present PV_Live level over all validation cases of seed 0, so A3 has slightly fewer usable values where the delta is missing.
  • Two series. The intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so the result describes Walpole and Bicker Fen only.
  • PV_Live is fully revised. The download holds the latest estimate, and its updated_at column is the bulk download time. The 1-day settling delay is an assumption, so every arm is a ceiling for PV_Live as well as for ERA5 at the lag times.
  • The delta uses ERA5 weather at the lag times, which arrives about 5 days late. The comparison across arms is unaffected, because every arm shares the delta.
  • The calibrator is fitted on 15 months of runs every third day, which may be too little for it to learn a subtraction (A1 and A2) from raw columns.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets only, under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched. A missing PV_Live value is a missing input of the calibrator.
  • Defensible designs: more than one (which PV_Live transform to give the calibrator). The transforms are the arms, fixed below.
  • Callers: the scripts reuse experiment 00005's calibrator, which the author could name without searching.

Size: medium. One Sonnet review of the plan and one of the code.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
Series: Walpole (series D6) and Bicker Fen (series D1), the two GSPs of the 20 demand series, matched to PV_Live's WALP_B and BICF_1. The calibrator is experiment 00005's l3 arm for the primary training window (from 2023-09): stage 2 XGBoost models, one per series and seed, on the stage 1a member statistics, the lead, and the recent-origin inputs, with 00005's hyperparameters. The stage 1a statistics, the out-of-fold ERA5 predictions, and the observed-power lags are read from experiment 00005's stored work folder, so no stage 1a is refitted for the calibrator arms.

  • A0: the l3 inputs, no PV_Live.
  • A1, PV_Live level: l3 plus PV_Live's generation_mw divided by the series' effective capacity at six positions: the lags of 24, 48, 168, and 336 hours, and the same time of day and the same time of week as the target, at the newest usable day and week.
  • A2, PV_Live share: l3 plus generation_percent_of_capacity divided by 100 at the same six positions. The share is of PV_Live's own installed capacity, so it stays comparable as capacity grows.
  • A3, PV_Live-adjusted delta: l3 plus, at the same six positions, the delta of that position (the observed power minus the stage 1a prediction at ERA5 weather, over capacity) plus A1's PV_Live level. The sum separates solar from other demand at the lag time.
  • S1, stage 1 variant (exploratory, no verdict): the final stage 1a model of each GSP and seed refitted with PV_Live's level at the valid time as one more input, against the same model without it. Both are scored by the mean absolute error of the point prediction at observed ERA5 weather over the validation year (July 2025 to June 2026). The observed PV_Live value at the valid time is not known at the forecast origin, so S1 says only whether stage 1a understands the GSP's solar better, and not what a forecast gains.

Known at the forecast origin. A lag position counts only when it is a past half-hour that the PV_Live estimate had time to settle. PV_Live revises each half-hour's estimate as more data arrive, and the download keeps only the latest estimate, so the experiment uses a conservative delay: a PV_Live value is usable at origin T only when its half-hour ended at least 1 day before T. Power and the stage 1a delta at the lag positions keep experiment 00005's rule (before T), so A1 to A3 use PV_Live values 1 day older than the newest delta. The script asserts the bound.

Positions and missing values. Each PV_Live position is chosen by the PV_Live rule alone (the half-hour ended at least a day before the origin), so a PV_Live column can be present where the experiment 00005 lag is missing, and the reverse. A3 pairs each PV_Live value with the delta at the same position, computed from the observed power and stage 1a whether or not experiment 00005's own lag rule allows it. The write-up reports the share of cases with a usable value per lead band. The 24-hour lag position is never usable. The updated_at column of the download is the time of the bulk download and not the time of each revision, so the settling delay cannot be checked from the data. PV_Live revises its estimates, so validation inputs are fully revised values, and every arm is a ceiling for PV_Live as well as for ERA5.

Sign check. The write-up checks, on summer middays, that the adjusted delta is less correlated with PV_Live than the plain delta is. An hour-of-day and season split of A3 minus A0 is exploratory.

Past weather. The delta uses stage 1a's prediction at ERA5 weather at the lag times, as in experiment 00005. ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, so every arm is a ceiling for the delta; PV_Live is a measurement and has no such gap. The comparison across arms is unaffected, because every arm shares the same delta.

Rows and seeds. The 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1, valid times before 2026-07-01, 3 seeds that A0 to A3 share. Calibration runs are experiment 00005's (every third day from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30), and no model is fitted on PV_Live values after 2025-06-30.

Resolution. Two series give two independent clusters. Intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so a result describes these two GSPs and may not carry to other GSPs. The plan expected the interval to resolve gains of roughly 1 point of capacity, not 0.3.

docs.title: Plan: references
docs.text:
Day-type climatology (r2) and A0, both from experiment 00005 or refitted identically.

Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Does a forecast of the GSP's PV_Live solar generation help the stage 2 demand forecast?
docs.text:
We asked whether a forecast of the solar generation feeding a grid supply point helps the demand forecast for that point. We gave the second step of the demand forecast a forecast of Sheffield Solar's PV_Live solar generation and, as an upper limit, the true PV_Live value (an oracle, which a live forecast would not have), and compared the errors at two grid supply points over 73 forecast runs. The solar forecast lowered the error by 0.14 points of capacity, short of the 0.30 points we required, and the interval included zero. The true value would have lowered it by 0.50.

Verdict: inconclusive. Giving the stage 2 calibrator a forecast of the grid supply point's (GSP's) solar generation lowered the quantile score by 0.14 points of capacity, short of the 0.30-point bar, and the interval includes zero. C1 (solar forecast minus no solar forecast, all leads) is -0.14 (95% interval -0.34 to +0.04), and up to 48 hours it is +0.04 (-0.32 to +0.31). The true PV_Live value at the target time, an oracle, lowered the score by 0.50 (C2, -0.91 to -0.12), and most of the gain is at leads of 7 to 15 days (-0.71), with 3 to 6 days at -0.31 (-0.71 to +0.07). Scores are in points of capacity (1% of the series' effective capacity) on 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days, July 2025 to June 2026, with ENS weather, for Walpole and Bicker Fen. Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0. The stage 2 calibrator is a second model that corrects the forecast quantiles that stage 1a produces. The quantile score measures how well the forecast quantiles fit what happened, and smaller is better.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Arm Quantile score, all leads Up to 48 h 7 to 15 d vs B0 (95%) B0, no solar column 19.04 15.21 B1, solar forecast 18.91 15.25 -0.21 (-0.40 to -0.05, exploratory) B2, true PV_Live (oracle) 18.54 15.22 -0.71 (-1.14 to -0.30, exploratory)
  • B1 is worse than the oracle B2 by +0.36 over all leads (+0.12 to +0.61, exploratory), and the difference is at 7 to 15 days (+0.50, +0.22 to +0.79).
  • The gain from the solar forecast is at Walpole. Each GSP alone, exploratory: C1 at Walpole is -0.28 (-0.54 to -0.04) and at Bicker Fen +0.02 (-0.16 to +0.16). The plan guessed the larger gain would be at Bicker Fen.
  • Cases scored: 50,498 per seed at Walpole and 46,178 at Bicker Fen, those with a PV_Live value at the target time.

docs.title: The solar forecast's own score
docs.text: On daytime half-hours of the validation runs, the member mean's mean absolute error was 4.95 to 5.24 points of PV_Live capacity in the first 24 hours, 5.9 to 6.0 at 1 to 2 days, 6.8 to 7.0 at 3 to 6 days, and 9.0 to 9.2 at 7 to 15 days. The month-by-half-hour climatology scored 8.8 to 9.5 in every band, so the forecast beats it up to day 6 and ties it after. The member mean was too high by +1.75 to +3.01 points in every band and both GSPs, so the ERA5-trained model is biased on ENS weather. The calibration-period error by chain quarter ran from 7.1 to 9.2 points, with the latest quarter lowest at 7.1 to 7.4 and the other quarters from 8.4 to 9.2.

docs.title: Predictions against outcomes
docs.text:
• Met: C1 was predicted at -0.15 (plausible 0 to -0.5) and was -0.14.
  • Met: C2 was predicted at -0.5 (-0.1 to -1.5) and was -0.50.
  • Missed: a larger gain at Bicker Fen; the solar forecast helped at Walpole only (exploratory).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Two series. The intervals resample months and seeds, not series, so the result describes Walpole and Bicker Fen only.
  • The oracle gain is at long leads, where the target value is far from the origin, and B2 has one added column against two for B1, so B1 minus B2 is not a clean comparison.
  • The solar forecast's daytime mask uses the observed PV_Live value (above 1% of capacity), which conditions on the outcome. A mask on the sun's position moved the mean bias by less than 0.15 points and the mean absolute error by less than 0.2.
  • PV_Live is fully revised, and the scores are against revised values.
  • The delta at lag times uses ERA5 weather, so every arm is a ceiling for the lagged inputs.

docs.title: Plan, written before any code ran
Plan: sizing
docs.text:
• Stored data: prediction sets and the solar forecast's statistics, under data/ml-experiments/; no production table changes.
  • Production serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched. A missing solar forecast would be a missing input.
  • Defensible designs: more than one (the solar model's inputs and the summary given to stage 2). Both are fixed below.
  • Callers: the scripts copy experiment 00005's archive reader and calibrator and experiment 00027's PV_Live loader, which the author could name without searching.

Size: medium. One Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code, and one of the write-up.

docs.title: Plan: the solar forecast
docs.text:
Target: the latest revision of PV_Live's generation_percent_of_capacity divided by 100 (the share of PV_Live's own capacity), because the share stays comparable as capacity grows. The chain's 15-day gap exceeds any settling time, and the scores below are against the revised values. Model: one XGBoost model per GSP and seed, with experiment 00005's stage 1a hyperparameters, trained on ERA5 weather at the valid time. Inputs (weather only): shortwave, longwave, temperature_2m, dew_point_temperature_2m, pressure_surface, precipitation, wind_speed_10m, and the solar zenith and azimuth, which are geometry and not weather. No calendar column and no power lag. Training window: 2019-09-01, the start of the ERA5 and PV_Live grid, to before 2025-06-17 for the final model (the cut-off of experiment 00005's stage 1a). The solar model starts earlier than the demand model's 2023-09 because its relationship is physical and has no demand drift, and a window from 2023-09 would leave the first chain models without a summer. Calibration runs use a forward chain: the model for each quarter from 2024-04 is trained on valid times that end 15 days before the quarter starts, so no calibration case sees a model trained on its own period.

Applied to ENS as in experiment 00012: each of the 51 members is run through the model at the valid time, on the same half-hourly resampling that experiment 00005's statistics use. The summary given to stage 2 is the member mean and standard deviation of the forecast share at the target time; two columns keep the stage 2 inputs few. The forecast is known at the forecast origin, because it uses ENS weather only.

The solar forecast's own score, before any demand effect, on the validation runs: the mean absolute error of the ensemble mean and the quantile score of the 51 member quantiles, in points of PV_Live's capacity, by lead band, against a month-by-half-hour climatology of PV_Live's share trained on the same window. The report adds the member mean's bias against PV_Live by lead band and its error by chain quarter, to show the ERA5-trained model's behaviour on ENS weather.

docs.title: Plan: arms
docs.text:
Series, calibrator, rows, seeds, and hyperparameters are those of experiment 00027's A0.

  • B0: stage 2 without PV_Live.
  • B1: B0 plus the solar forecast's mean and standard deviation at the target time.
  • B2 (oracle): B0 plus the true PV_Live share at the target time, which is not known at the forecast origin. B2 has one added column and B1 has two, so B2 need not score below B1.

Past weather. The delta at lag times uses ERA5 weather as in experiments 00005 and 00027, so every arm is a ceiling for the lagged inputs; the solar forecast uses ENS weather only, and the PV_Live training target is a measurement that exists at training time.

Rows. Every arm is scored on the cases that have a PV_Live value at the target time and a solar forecast, and the report states the number of cases per GSP.

Resolution. Two series, so the intervals describe these two GSPs. Experiment 00027's intervals were 0.2 to 0.35 points wide at 98.33%, and the same width is expected here.

Attribution: Sheffield Solar PV_Live, CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Does a differentiable physics stage 1 beat the XGBoost stage 1 for solar farms?
docs.text:
We asked whether a solar forecasting model built from the physics of a solar panel, with its parameters fitted by gradient descent, beats an XGBoost model for solar farms. We fitted the physics model and combinations of it with XGBoost for 6 solar farms, and compared their forecast accuracy. No combination beat XGBoost, and the physics model alone was worse by 0.079 points of capacity.

Verdict: refuted. No physics arm lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the XGBoost stage 1, and the PyTorch physics stage 1 alone scored 0.079 points of capacity worse (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135).

This page is proposal P31 in the research plan. ENS is the ECMWF ensemble, ERA5 is the ECMWF reanalysis, and CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite irradiance estimate. Farms appear only under anonymous labels A to F.

docs.title: Survey of the earlier PV fits (step 1)
docs.text: The best fitted PV model in the earlier studies was a five-parameter physical model with free orientation, and it still trailed XGBoost. The beam-diffuse study fitted tilt, azimuth, capacity, an inverter limit, and a temperature coefficient per farm with a Powell optimiser. On CAMS irradiance it scored 6.28% of P99 output against 5.24% for XGBoost, and an XGBoost calibration that saw the weather closed most of the gap. The solar BMU study found that a free orientation held out better than a fixed or tracking plant, and recovered simulated plants' tilt with a +9.6 degree bias. Chosen: the SciPy free-orientation fit (studies.pv_fit) as the scipy arm, and for the PyTorch PV model the ideas the differentiable-physics page proposes: priors on tilt, azimuth, DC capacity, and the AC-to-DC ratio, a smooth clip, and a posterior for intervals. The SciPy model is the best fit in the two earlier studies we read, so it is the comparison for the new PyTorch PV model.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute CRPS, all leads (points of capacity): XGBoost stage 1 5.026 (95% interval 3.729 to 6.494), hybrid 5.026, PyTorch physics 5.105, SciPy physics 5.110, climatology 5.629. Seed spread is at most 0.001.
  • C1 PyTorch physics minus XGBoost: +0.079 (+0.029 to +0.135). C2 hybrid minus XGBoost: -0.000 (-0.015 to +0.018). C3 PyTorch minus SciPy: -0.005 (-0.020 to +0.010). C4 SciPy minus XGBoost: +0.084 (+0.029 to +0.148). The rule refutes the hypothesis when the lower bounds of C1 and C2 are both above -0.05, and they are (+0.029 and -0.015).
  • Stage 1 alone: the member-average physics power has a mean absolute error of 7.44 points (SciPy) and 7.53 (PyTorch), against 7.64 for experiment 00012's XGBoost stage 1a on the same rows. This comparison is descriptive: experiment 00012's CAMS-trained arm scored 7.50, level with the PyTorch physics, and the rows may differ. The cause of the CRPS gap was not isolated; a possible cause is the spread that the XGBoost layer builds from one physics column.
  • Coverage of the 5% to 95% band: SciPy 96.6%, PyTorch 96.5%, hybrid 94.8%, XGBoost 94.7%.
  • Fitted parameters: the table below gives every fitted parameter. Five of the six PyTorch tilts fall in the beam-diffuse study's 14 to 27 degrees, and farm E is higher; every azimuth is within 5 degrees of south, as in that study. SciPy values are within 3 degrees of tilt of the PyTorch values for five farms, and within 0.07 of capacity.
