The next experiment on the switching detector should therefore change what happens after the alarm, with paired-step intervals that find the onset and the return step together (SW2-6 in the research plan), or a combination of the 4-hour and 24-hour windows (SW2-13), not the residual that the alarm reads. A lag-48 filter, or a coefficient per series, was not run, and would shrink the step less, but the lag-48 correlation of 0.54 is only half the lag-1 correlation of 0.91, so we do not expect it to change the verdict.

docs.title: Post hoc and limits
docs.text:
• Post hoc: the filter-effect table, the signal-to-noise ratio, and the big-step table were added after the plan and do not enter the verdict.
  • The coefficients are not cleaned. They were fitted from odd-month residuals without masking logged closures or labelled transfers, so a persistent real step can raise a coefficient towards the clip. The median share of coefficients at the clip is 0.14, and 0.50 for the worst substation.
  • The alarm counts differ, as the section "What the matching of alarms did" says.
  • The transfers are injected into a residual that a fixed lagless weather model produced. The residual does not reflect an XGBoost model refitted on the injected period, as in experiments 43, 55, 58, and 60.

docs.title: Experiment 63: does a linear joint fit of baseline, solar, and transfers beat the Flexpectation v1 baseline?
docs.text:
We asked whether one small fit can explain the power a Primary substation draws as three separate parts: ordinary weather-driven demand, the output of solar panels behind the meter, and load moved onto the substation from a neighbour during a switching job. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV substation. We built the fit for the 5 of the 8 Primaries metered in MW that have enough data, because 2 are excluded for the quality of their solar-capacity estimate and 1 has under a year of usable data. Flexpectation v1 is NGED's production forecast, built on one XGBoost model that forecasts the metered total. We compared the fit's median forecast with the Flexpectation v1 forecast outside switching, in hindsight. "In hindsight" means the weather and sunshine inputs are estimates of the past that do not exist at forecast time, so the gain we measure is a ceiling.

The error measure is the mean absolute error of the median forecast, in points. One point is 1% of a Primary's capacity. The Flexpectation v1 baseline scores 5.807 points, and 0.35 points is the smallest gain we judged worth adding the fit to the serving path. The sunshine shape is the unit solar output estimated from CAMS (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service). The solar part of the fit lowered the error by 0.32 points. We then added known amounts of solar-farm output and of transferred load to the metered power and checked how much of each the fit found again. Those checks could not be passed, and the reason lay in how the checks were designed.

We learned that, in hindsight, the solar part of the fit lowers the error by about a third of a point, close to the 0.35-point threshold. We did not learn whether the fit recovers the true size of each part, because the injection checks failed for reasons of test design: CAMS sunshine matches a real solar farm's output with a slope of only 0.76, and a share of 0.10 cannot be pinned down in windows of 6 to 12 hours at small donors; the transfer terms were barely exercised, with 2 pairs of event and Primary fitted. The next experiment should keep the fit's own regressor shape as a positive control, scale the share gate by donor size, use intervals of 24 hours or longer, allow events in unobserved weeks, and cover all 8 Primaries.

Verdict: inconclusive. The pre-registered rule tests refuted first: C1, the paired error difference above, is not wholly above zero. The rule then tests the gates: S1 and S2 both failed, and C1 is not wholly above zero, so the verdict is inconclusive. C1 is -0.322 points (-0.437 to -0.207) over 48,795 half-hours at 5 Primaries, in 112 series-months. C1's 95% interval lies wholly below zero but not wholly below -0.35, so with both gates passed the rule would have given small gain. Every number below comes from work/report.txt, work/charts_report.txt, and the sensitivity reports printed by the committed scripts. Items marked "post hoc" were added after the first run, and never change the verdict.

Prediction against outcome. C1 was predicted at -0.2 points (-0.6 to 0.0) and came out at -0.322, inside the range. S1 was predicted to recover 0.80 to 0.95 of an injected capacity and recovered 0.759, below the range. S2 was predicted to have a median absolute share error of 0.02 to 0.06 and had 0.055, inside the range. The placebo share was not predicted.

docs.title: The raw series
docs.text: The fitted solar term moves with the baseline's residual by day, and explains only part of it. The figure shows Trusthorpe over the April to September week with the largest mean absolute solar term, which starts at the end of April 2026. The residual is metered power minus the baseline without radiation inputs. The fitted solar term is the joint fit's addition to that baseline. The third line is what the radiation inputs add to the frozen Flexpectation v1 baseline.

docs.title: C1 and the descriptive contrasts
docs.text:
C1 is -0.322 points (-0.437 to -0.207), and the solar term does most of its work from October to March. The paired contrasts below are all in points of capacity; a negative difference means the first arm has the smaller error.

Contrast All daylight April to September October to March C1: c1 minus the Flexpectation v1 baseline (decides the verdict) -0.322 (-0.437 to -0.207) -0.251 (-0.383 to -0.118) -0.530 (-0.731 to -0.306) control minus the Flexpectation v1 baseline (radiation removed, no solar term) +0.855 (+0.711 to +1.007) +0.718 (+0.557 to +0.888) +1.257 (+1.017 to +1.499) c1 minus control (what the solar term buys) -1.177 (-1.375 to -0.986) -0.970 (-1.181 to -0.761) -1.787 (-2.125 to -1.441) C2: c2 minus c1 (scale fixed at 1 minus fitted scale) +1.356 (+1.196 to +1.508) +1.382 (+1.185 to +1.569) +1.278 (+1.077 to +1.486) C3: c3 minus c1 (weekly capacity minus season-year constant) -0.006 (-0.025 to +0.011) -0.013 (-0.037 to +0.009) +0.013 (-0.005 to +0.030) C4: c4 minus c1 (without transfer terms minus with them) +0.000 (-0.000 to +0.000) +0.000 (-0.000 to +0.000) +0.000 (-0.000 to +0.000) C5: c5 minus c1 (previous season-year's capacity minus in-sample), 41,477 half-hours +0.003 (-0.008 to +0.016) +0.003 (-0.010 to +0.020) +0.002 (-0.012 to +0.017)
  • The solar term is worth more than the radiation inputs it replaces. Removing the radiation inputs alone costs 0.855 points, and the solar term then recovers 1.177 points.
  • The fitted scale is about 0.5, not 1. Its median over the 112 held-out months is 0.497 (10th to 90th percentile 0.471 to 0.517), and it is positive in every month. Fixing it at 1 costs 1.356 points (C2). One untested conjecture is that the scale falls below 1 because CAMS sunshine and the sun over the substation differ (the slope of a real farm's anomaly on the CAMS anomaly is 0.65 to 0.87), and because the baseline without radiation still holds temperature, dew point, solar zenith, and hour, which carry some of the solar dip.
  • The capacity leak is small. The previous season-year's constant, which the held-out months never helped set, gives C1 -0.357 (-0.480 to -0.231) on the same 41,477 half-hours where in-sample capacity gives -0.360 (-0.480 to -0.239) (C5).
  • C4 is exactly 0 by construction. The transfer terms are zero outside switching, and the scored half-hours lie outside switching, so C4 cannot measure the transfer terms. S2 and R1 are the only tests of the transfer terms in this experiment.
  • A weekly capacity changes nothing. C3 is -0.006 (-0.025 to +0.011).
  • The pinball loss at the 10th and 90th quantiles agrees. The joint fit lowers it by 0.086 (-0.124 to -0.049) at q10 and 0.062 (-0.102 to -0.025) at q90 against the Flexpectation v1 baseline.

The 28 calendar months are drawn jointly in 50,000 resamples, so the weather that every Primary shared in a month stays together. The all-daylight interval is -0.470 to -0.177, April to September is -0.251 (-0.384 to -0.112), and October to March is -0.530 (-0.834 to -0.124).

docs.title: S1: the injected solar capacity was recovered at 0.76, and the gate was out of reach
docs.text:
The fit recovered 0.759 of an injected solar farm's capacity (10th to 90th percentile 0.675 to 0.840), so the gate of 0.15 on the miss failed (median miss 0.241). The injection added the output of each of 6 real solar farms, labelled A to F as in experiment 00045, at 10%, 25%, and 50% of a substation's capacity, at 6 substations (108 injections). The ratio is 0.761 in April to September and 0.752 in October to March. Post hoc, it is the same at every injection size (0.759 at each).

The ratio is the agreement between a real farm and the CAMS sunshine shape, and no fit that uses the CAMS anomaly as its regressor can do better. Post hoc, the least-squares slope of each farm's anomaly (its output minus its mean at the same month and half-hour of the day) on the CAMS anomaly is 0.65 to 0.87 across farms and substations, with correlations of 0.64 to 0.89. The median slope is 0.765 over all farms and substations, and it matches the S1 ratio farm by farm (farm A 0.703 against 0.691, farm B 0.791 against 0.805, farm C 0.766 against 0.770, farm D 0.806 against 0.804, farm E 0.724 against 0.705, farm F 0.772 against 0.810). The median miss of 0.241 fails the gate, and the farm slopes (0.65 to 0.87) show that agreement with CAMS sunshine, not the fit, sets the ceiling.

The positive control passes exactly. Post hoc, the fit's own regressor shape (capacity times the CAMS anomaly) was injected at 10%, 25%, and 50% at the same 6 substations, in all three season subsets (54 injections). The recovered share divided by the injected share lies between 0.999999999999996 and 1.000000000000004 in every injection (largest miss 4.22e-15), so the fitting code recovers what it should.

docs.title: S2: the placebo spread of a transfer share is set by the donor's size
docs.text:
Injected transfers were recovered with a median absolute share error of 0.055 against a gate of 0.05, and the 95th percentile of the placebo share was 0.304 against 0.10, so both S2 gates failed. The test added a donor's real power, times a share of 0.1, 0.25, or 0.5, to a substation over 6, 12, 24, or 72 hours, 240 intervals in all, and 240 placebo intervals with a true share of zero, at 6 substations. The error is 0.071 from April to September and 0.052 from October to March. Post hoc, by share it is 0.051 at 0.1, 0.055 at 0.25, and 0.077 at 0.5, and the breakdown by duration is in work/report.txt.

Post hoc, the placebo share is large for small donors and short intervals. A donor of 1.2 MW mean absolute power (Wrangle T1) gives a median absolute placebo share of 0.176, and donors of 7.0 and 7.1 MW (Mount Bridge Boston and Horncastle) give 0.025 and 0.047. The 95th percentile falls from 0.582 for donors under 3 MW to 0.158 for donors of 3 to 5 MW and 0.137 for donors over 5 MW, and the 95th percentile of the placebo share by interval length is 0.407 at 6 hours, 0.289 at 12 hours, 0.312 at 24 hours, and 0.159 at 72 hours. No cell of donor size and interval length reaches 0.10: the lowest is 0.118 (donors of 3 to 5 MW, 24 to 72 hours).

Donor size (mean absolute power) Interval length Placebo intervals Median absolute share 95th percentile Under 3 MW 6 to 12 hours 38 0.159 0.631 Under 3 MW 24 to 72 hours 40 0.091 0.481 3 to 5 MW 6 to 12 hours 36 0.064 0.180 3 to 5 MW 24 to 72 hours 35 0.021 0.118 Over 5 MW 6 to 12 hours 46 0.047 0.141 Over 5 MW 24 to 72 hours 45 0.037 0.132

The 0.10 gate cannot be met at 6 to 12 hours with small donors. The injected transfers show the same pattern: the median absolute share error is 0.179 for donors under 3 MW at 6 to 12 hours and 0.031 for donors over 5 MW at 6 to 12 hours.

docs.title: R1: only 2 event-Primary pairs could be fitted
docs.text: R1 fitted 2 event-Primary pairs, so it says nothing about the transfer terms. An event-Primary pair is one Primary's side of one labelled event. Of 73 real labelled events, 37 had a side that is not one of the 8 Primaries metered in MW, 14 named no donor, and the status filter and the observed-weeks filter removed most of the rest. At the 2 pairs fitted, the share of the residual's variance explained inside the event has a median of 0.027, against a median of 0.158 on 22 placebo windows of equal length (20 for one pair and 2 for the other, because the plan shifts each event by whole weeks into periods outside every logged closure and only 2 windows were found for the second pair; the report prints no further reason) and a 95th percentile of 0.538. Neither pair exceeds its own placebo 95th percentile (0 of 2, against a chance of 0.1), and the mean rank of the event among its placebos is 0.150, where 0.5 means no effect.

docs.title: Sensitivity runs (post hoc)
docs.text:
Allowing events in unobserved weeks raises the number of fitted pairs from 2 to 7, and 2 of the 7 exceed their placebo 95th percentile, against 0.4 expected by chance. C1 is unchanged. The mean rank of the event among its placebos is 0.401, the median share is +0.009, and 5 of the 7 shares are positive. The 2 pairs that exceed their placebo are a 6-half-hour event with a share of 1.015 and a variance explained of 0.978, and a 13-half-hour event with a share of -0.718, the wrong sign.

Keeping all four capacity statuses, not only clean and low-power, moves C1 to -0.226 (-0.352 to -0.105) over 66,587 half-hours at 7 Primaries. Wrangle T1 (not-clean) gives C1 -0.759 and Kirton (range-only) gives +0.381. With events in any week as well, 15 event-Primary pairs fit and 4 of the 15 exceed their placebo 95th percentile, against 0.8 expected by chance. The verdict stays inconclusive in all four runs.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
• The series scored are 5, not 8. Experiment 00045's status of Wrangle T1 is not-clean and of Kirton is range-only, so the plan's rule of clean or low-power statuses removes both. Mount Bridge Boston has under one year of observed data once its first 104 weeks are skipped, so no half-hour has a second year in the same calendar month to give an anomaly mean, and none of its rows is scored. It still takes part in S1 and S2 as a substation that receives injections.
  • The unobserved-weeks filter removes most event rows. A week is unobserved when closure padding leaves fewer than 3 usable days, and the plan's filter applied it to event half-hours as well, which left 2 event-Primary pairs for R1 and for the fit. The sensitivity run above lifts it.
  • The R1 window starts in 2022-01, not in September 2023. The plan set no window for R1, so the events are read from the first month of the baseline files.
  • The events are the real labelled events of experiment 00041 with kind starting real_, visibility conserved or one-sided, and both an onset and an end: 73 events.
  • The injected output is subtracted, not added. Embedded solar lowers the net power, so the farm's output is subtracted from the metered power.
  • Seeds. The XGBoost baseline uses seed 0 and 1 thread. The S2 interval draws are seeded by the Primary's identifier times 1,000 plus 63. The bootstrap uses the shared seed in studies.bootstrap. One seed only, so no interval here covers fitting-seed variation.
  • The baseline for each training month was fitted by a model that saw the held-out month. The baseline for month m is fitted without month m, but the residuals of the other months, on which the scale is fitted, come from models that included month m. The effect is tiny, and the Flexpectation v1 arm has the same property.
  • The month bootstrap re-draws months within each Primary. The plan pooled the Primaries after resampling within each. The post hoc shared-month bootstrap above draws the same months for all Primaries.
  • No climatology row and no leaderboard post. The rows are hindsight rows that use the weather at the valid time, so the experiment has no forecast rows to post, and its arms are all fits of one hindsight baseline.
  • The anomaly mean excludes the held-out month in the C scoring, and uses all months in S1 and S2. The injection harness refits on all months with no month held out.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
• The solar term is worth keeping in the next test, as a ceiling. The 0.32-point gain uses the CAMS sunshine of the valid time and a capacity fitted on the same power, and experiment 00046 found that served ensemble sunshine kept almost none of an oracle's gain.
  • The injection tests need their own known answers. A positive control (the fit's own shape), a gate expressed against the real farm's agreement with CAMS, and a share gate scaled by donor size would have let the injections pass or fail on the fit and not on the test.
  • The transfer terms are untested. Two event-Primary pairs, and a placebo spread that swamps shares of 0.1 at small donors, leave no evidence on whether the labelled transfers help.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should answer whether Flexpectation v2's split into baseline, solar, and transfers costs accuracy once the test can tell a working fit from a broken one. It keeps the fit's own regressor shape as a positive control and judges a real farm's recovery against its agreement with CAMS. It scales the share gate by donor size, and injects on donors of 5 MW or more and on intervals of 24 hours or longer. It allows the rows of labelled events in unobserved weeks, which raised the fitted pairs from 2 to 7, and it covers all 8 Primaries, which needs a full year of data at Mount Bridge Boston and a decision on the statuses of Wrangle T1 and Kirton.

docs.title: The pre-registered plan
docs.text: Plan, written before any fit. We ask whether one small linear fit per substation can explain a substation's metered demand as three separate parts: ordinary weather-driven demand, the output of solar panels behind the meter, and load lent by a neighbouring substation during a switching job. Flexpectation v1 forecasts the metered total with one XGBoost model. Flexpectation v2 is meant to forecast the three parts separately, so that NGED can read each one. This experiment is v2 in miniature, with the switching times given, to learn whether the split costs accuracy and whether the parts come out at the right size.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
• What gets stored: private predictions and tables under data/ml-experiments/; nothing in the repository except the page and scripts.
  • Production serving path: not touched; the experiment reads stored hindsight baselines.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes. The capacity can be an input or a fitted value, and the baseline can include or exclude radiation. This plan fixes the capacity (the brief's primary), fits a scale on it, and excludes radiation from the joint fit's baseline.
  • Code whose callers could not be named without searching: no; the scripts copy patterns from experiments 00041 and 00045, which no other code imports.

This is medium: a plan, one Sonnet plan reviewer, Sonnet implementation, one Sonnet code review, and a Sonnet write-up review. Opus is not used because no verdict depends on a judgement that a Sonnet reviewer could not check against the printed report.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Series. The 8 Primaries metered in MW with a capacity in capacity_weekly.parquet of experiment 00045: Trusthorpe, Horncastle, Spilsby, Wrangle T1, Wrangle T2, Mount Bridge Boston, Kirton, and Donington. Mount Bridge Boston from 2023-09-04 to 2025-08-25 is skipped, because its constant capacity is about 0 MW over 104 unobserved weeks. Rows use status clean or low-power and unobserved false.
  • Capacity. The primary is the season_year_constant variant (recommended = true). The weekly recommended series (post hoc a=2, r=10) is a sensitivity (C3). The vintages file holds no season-year-constant rows, so this experiment is a hindsight decomposition and does not claim a real-time capacity.
  • Weather and the caveat. Every weather input is ERA5 at the valid time, and the PV shape is the CAMS unit PV shape at the valid time (u in experiment 00045's half-hourly inputs). Neither exists at forecast time: ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, and CAMS is a past estimate. The experiment therefore bounds what a v2 decomposition could do with perfect sunshine. Experiment 00046 showed that served ENS sunshine keeps almost none of that gain.
  • Why an anomaly. Both baselines keep the solar zenith, solar azimuth and hour columns, so they have already learned the average solar dip in metered demand. Subtracting the full shape would count that mean twice, and the experiment 00041 baseline's residual slope on u changes sign by month. The fit therefore regresses on the anomaly, as experiment 00046 did.
  • Capacity leak. Experiment 00045 fitted the season-year constants to the same 2023-2026 power, so the held-out months helped set the capacity and C1 is optimistic. The page calls C1 "with in-sample capacity" and adds a sensitivity (C5) that uses the previous season-year's constant.
  • Baseline. Experiment 00041's leave-one-month-out XGBoost (13 columns, logged closures padded by 24 hours excluded from training) is the frozen v1 baseline, read from its stored files. The joint fit's baseline is the same procedure refitted without shortwave and longwave, one file per series, on 4 cores. Every baseline prediction for a month comes from a model that never saw that month, so the joint fit's residuals are not shrunk by overfitting.
  • The joint fit. For Primary p, with residual r_t = y_t - b_t, an ordinary least-squares fit of r_t = -k x C_w(t) x a_t + sum_j beta_j x x_j,t x 1[t in I_j] + e_t, where k is a scale on the capacity C_w(t) of the week, a_t the anomaly of the CAMS unit PV shape u_t (u_t minus its mean at the same calendar month and half-hour of the day, over the training months of the fold), I_j the labelled interval of transfer j, x_j,t the donor's net power in MW (receiver gains when the donor is switched onto it), and beta_j its share. Rows are daylight half-hours (for k) plus all half-hours inside labelled intervals, with rows in logged closures that carry no label dropped. The labelled intervals are experiment 00041's real visible events, conserved or one-sided, with onset_utc and end_utc.
  • Held-out scoring (C1). Leave one calendar month out. Fit k on the other months, predict b_t - k x C x u_t for the held-out month, and score the median. Transfer terms are zero outside switching, so C1 is a test of the solar term only; the transfer terms are tested by S2 and R1. The v1 arm is b_t with radiation, and the control arm is b_t without radiation, so the page can say what the solar term buys over simply removing radiation.
  • Injection harness S1. The baseline stays frozen (a refit on every injection would need about 1,300 more XGBoost fits), so the fit sees only the anomaly of the injected output, and the page says so. For each Primary, add the half-hourly AC output of a real solar farm from farm_half_hourly.parquet (experiment 00045's farms) normalised by its 99th percentile and scaled to 10%, 25% and 50% of the Primary's capacity, to the Primary's metered power in the scored period, and refit. The recovered added capacity is the change in k*C. The injected path is the truth.
  • Injection harness S2. Pick 40 intervals per Primary at random starts outside labelled and logged switching, durations 6, 12, 24 and 72 hours, add beta times a donor's real net power (donor drawn from the other MW-metered series with data, so the donor's own solar is included; MVA-only series are excluded because their power has no sign), beta in {0.1, 0.25, 0.5}, plus 40 placebo intervals with beta 0. Half the intervals fall in April to September and half in October to March. The recovered beta is compared with the injected one, with the interval given to the fit.
  • R1, real events. For each real visible event with a named donor that names one of the 8 Primaries as donor or receiver (events with a null donor are counted and skipped; when a Primary is the donor its own power falls, so the regressor is the receiver's net power and the share is read with the opposite sign), fit beta in sample and report the variance explained, against 20 shifted placebo intervals. This is descriptive, because there is one parameter per event.
  • Rows per series. The write-up reports the scored rows per series (closures remove 12% to 47% of rows) with a per-series table.
  • Compute. The XGBoost refits (about 400 quick fits) run in 4 workers of 1 thread each in slot E; the linear fits are negligible. Each fit writes its own file atomically.

docs.title: Departures planned
docs.text: The page will say plainly that C1 uses oracle sunshine, that the fit is in hindsight, and that the only test of the transfer terms outside the injection harness is the descriptive R1.

docs.title: Advice followed
docs.text:
• Experiment 00045: the season-year constant is the primary capacity, because the weekly series did not beat it on injected changes.
  • Experiment 00046: oracle sunshine is worth about 1 point, served sunshine about nothing; this plan labels its gain as a ceiling for that reason.
  • Experiment 00041: labelled events are scored as given, with the don't-care bands for transfers under 25% of the receiving load named in the write-up.

docs.title: Experiment 64: does demand minus forecast solar match the best guess? (PVDIS-5)
docs.text:
Take-home message: giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset (a fixed amount added to every tree prediction), with its weight fitted on the training window, beat d0, the best-guess recipe of experiment 33, by 0.15 points of capacity. Training the XGBoost model on gross demand (metered power plus the solar panels' output) and then subtracting the forecast solar output was not shown to score within 0.10 points of d0. The starting-offset forecast has a separate solar term, was no worse than d0 over all leads, and scored lower than d0 at leads under 10 days. The open questions are whether the gain survives a capacity table that is current for the validation year, and why the starting offset also scores better at 10 days and beyond, where the weight on the solar term is set to zero.

We asked whether a forecast of the power that a Primary substation draws can be split into ordinary demand and the output of the solar panels behind the substation without losing accuracy. A Primary substation is a 33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substation in the electricity distribution network. The substation's meter reads demand minus the panels' output. We built four forecasts that each carry an explicit solar term, which is the panels' capacity times a forecast of how much sunnier or cloudier the day will be than usual. We scored them on five Primary substations over daylight half-hours of April to September. We compared each with d0, and with the same forecast given the solar term of another date. The score is the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity. Three of the four forecasts scored 0.06 to 0.15 points lower than d0. The fourth was not shown to score within 0.10 points of d0.

The verdict is supported. The decision rule is in the front matter and was committed before any code ran. Contrast N is an arm's quantile score minus the quantile score of d0. A negative value favours the arm. Contrast T is an arm's quantile score minus that of its placebo twin, the same arm given the forecast solar shape of another date, so T measures what the forecast of the sunshine adds. An arm passes when two conditions hold. The upper end of N is below +0.10 points, so the arm is within the margin of d0. The upper end of T is below 0, so the arm beats its placebo twin. Arms sf, a, and am pass; b beats its twin but is not shown to be within the margin of d0. A gain is reported where the upper end of N at leads under 48 hours is below -0.10, which holds for a and am.

Arm N: score minus d0, all leads T: score minus placebo twin Gain: score minus d0, leads under 48 hours sf -0.063 (-0.126 to -0.008) -0.293 (-0.418 to -0.180) -0.168 (-0.357 to -0.002) a -0.059 (-0.103 to -0.016) -0.164 (-0.236 to -0.089) -0.212 (-0.317 to -0.112) am -0.152 (-0.199 to -0.111) -0.300 (-0.407 to -0.198) -0.272 (-0.420 to -0.145) b +0.105 (-0.090 to +0.292) -1.068 (-1.361 to -0.790) -0.338 (-0.661 to -0.040)

The values are differences in quantile score, in points of capacity, with 98.75% intervals (a 95% interval split across the four arms by a Bonferroni correction) from 50,000 resamples of whole ISO weeks of forecast start and of seeds. The 68,903 scored rows per seed are half-hourly forecasts from 29 ISO weeks of forecast start, with 3 seeds, at five Primary substations anonymised as D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (as in experiment 46). Every other read on this page is exploratory, at 95%.

docs.title: The four arms
docs.text:
Every arm uses experiment 46's d1l inputs and recipe (experiment 33's XGBoost quantile model, trained on the ENS control member, without radiation inputs) and adds the solar term s: the capacity times the calibrated anomaly of the ensemble-mean ENS sunshine forecast, in power over capacity. The weight w on s is fitted per series, lead band, and season.

  • sf adds w * s to the stored d1l quantiles after the fit. No XGBoost model is refitted.
  • a adds the capacity times the calibrated ENS solar shape as one extra input column.
  • am gives XGBoost the base margin w * s, so the trees fit only the remainder.
  • b trains on gross demand (the metered power plus the capacity times the CAMS solar shape), with lagged inputs converted to gross demand the same way, and subtracts the capacity times the forecast solar shape from each ensemble member's quantiles at inference.

Each arm has a placebo twin (sf_twin, a_twin, am_twin, b_twin) that replaces the forecast solar shape with that of another forecast run in the same series, local month, half-hour, and lead band. The reference rows are d0, d1l, climatology, and manual_heuristic (experiment 33).

docs.title: Arm am is the best arm, and b is the only arm not shown to match d0
docs.text:
The scores are close together, and the paired contrasts are what separate the arms. The 95% intervals of the absolute scores overlap because every arm's error rises and falls with the weather from week to week, which pairing removes. Absolute scores, in points of capacity, with 95% intervals:

Arm Quantile score Placebo twin d0 4.620 (4.294 to 4.946) d1l 4.724 (4.382 to 5.058) sf 4.557 (4.239 to 4.878) 4.850 (4.497 to 5.217) a 4.561 (4.240 to 4.890) 4.724 (4.384 to 5.060) am 4.467 (4.143 to 4.785) 4.767 (4.407 to 5.133) b 4.724 (4.365 to 5.113) 5.792 (5.343 to 6.258) climatology 5.272 manual_heuristic 4.952

climatology and manual_heuristic are experiment 33's stored forecasts, scored on 68,863 rows because 40 of the 68,903 rows are missing from them. Neither enters the paired intervals.

The twin of b scores 1.07 points worse than b. One candidate explanation is that b subtracts the shape with a weight of 1 built in, so a wrong-dated shape does more harm there than in the arms with a fitted weight; no arm tests this. The size of T for b is not evidence that b uses the forecast sunshine better than the other arms.

docs.title: The gain sits mostly within 6 days of the forecast start
docs.text:
The gain of a is clear up to 6 days and the gain of sf from 1 to 6 days, and both are gone beyond, and am stays below d0 at every lead. At 10 days and beyond, am is -0.082 points (-0.126 to -0.038) from d0 although its weight there is zero, a is +0.036 (+0.006 to +0.065), and sf is +0.013 (-0.019 to +0.051). The weight is zero in that band because the calibrated ENS anomaly has a correlation of 0.03 with the CAMS anomaly there on the training rows (0.80, 0.76, 0.58, and 0.27 in the four shorter bands), and the fitted slope ranged from -8.2 to +6.2 across series and seasons. The 10-plus-day gain of am is unexplained. One candidate is the starting point: am starts from its margin alone, while d1l and a start from XGBoost's estimated base score.

Arm b is worse than d0 at 6 days and beyond. Its N is +0.249 points (0.035 to 0.479) at 6 to 10 days and +0.296 (0.132 to 0.462) at 10 days and beyond, where the ENS forecast of the subtracted term has little or no skill (its correlation with the CAMS anomaly is 0.27 at 6 to 10 days and 0.03 beyond). This experiment does not test that as the cause.

docs.title: The fitted weights are below 1, and lagged power does not explain why
docs.text:
The fitted weight on the ENS shift is -0.60 to -0.29 at leads under 10 days, well short of the -1 that a perfect shift of the right size would take. These are the means over the five series of the slope of the out-of-fold residual (actual minus median forecast) on the shift that sf applies, fitted per lead band and season on the training window. The slope on the oracle shift (the CAMS anomaly) is -0.80 to -0.47, to compare with experiment 51's -0.69 to -0.42. The effective weights of the arms, measured as the slope of each arm's median minus d1l's median on minus the shift, are 0.49 for sf, 0.41 for a, 0.31 for am (on top of its fitted margin), and 0.64 for b, against the constant 1 built into b.

Lagged power absorbs none of the sunshine anomaly, cloud proxies absorb about 0.15 at leads under 2 days, and about -0.73 remains with neither. Experiment 51 left open whether the slope below 1 comes from the XGBoost model already absorbing part of the anomaly through its inputs, or from error in the CAMS sunshine estimate. Four cross-fitted variants of d1l (seed 0) give the median oracle slope below, over five series and two seasons.

Variant 0-24 h 1-2 d 2-6 d 6-10 d 10+ d All inputs -0.570 -0.578 -0.669 -0.741 -0.774 Without the 3 lagged-power columns -0.551 -0.564 -0.658 -0.741 -0.776 Without the 3 cloud-proxy columns -0.726 -0.730 -0.740 -0.764 -0.770 Without either -0.726 -0.728 -0.738 -0.766 -0.778

The remaining slope of about -0.73 with neither group of columns points to noise in the CAMS estimate of the fleet's sunshine (which pulls a regression slope towards zero) or to a mismatch between the CAMS shape and the panels' real output. The diagnostic does not separate the two.

docs.title: Arms sf and am beat d0 in every valid month
docs.text: sf and am are below d0 in all six months, a in five (+0.005 in July), and b loses from April to July and wins in August and September. The mean of b's N is +0.460 in April and +0.416 in July, and -0.173 in August and -0.327 in September. These are the sign of a mean, not an interval.

docs.title: Other reads (exploratory, 95%)
docs.text:
• Per series: am is below d0 at all five series, from -0.113 (-0.165 to -0.058) at D9 to -0.236 (-0.298 to -0.174) at D10.
  • Sunniest decile of rows by clear-sky index: sf is -0.296 (-0.437 to -0.168), a -0.216 (-0.283 to -0.147), am -0.283 (-0.350 to -0.216), and b -0.017 (-0.363 to +0.305). Arm am beats a by 0.093 points (0.057 to 0.129) over all rows and by 0.067 (-0.019 to +0.150) on the sunniest decile, so the trees' inability to extrapolate past the capacities seen in training is not shown to matter more on the sunniest rows.
  • Against the fixed-coefficient shift of experiment 46: d1l plus that shift scores 4.667, which is 0.056 below d1l. The arm sf is 0.111 points (0.023 to 0.196) below it, and am lowers d1l by 0.256 (0.205 to 0.306).
  • Per-member against ensemble-mean shift: sf_member minus sf is -0.004 (-0.010 to +0.001), so the member spread adds nothing for sf. b_member minus b is -0.145 (-0.206 to -0.094), so b needs the member spread.
  • Temperature derating: sf_temp minus sf is +0.0003 (-0.0016 to +0.0022), so a derating of 0.4% per kelvin removes nothing. On sunny rows the quantile score rises 0.070 points per kelvin of cell temperature for d1l and 0.036 for sf, and sf_temp leaves that slope at 0.037.
  • Coverage: the table gives the share of actuals below the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles, where the targets are 0.05 and 0.95. Sunny rows have a clear-sky index of 0.7 or more and cloudy rows under 0.3. The lower quantile is too high on sunny rows in every arm, and b has the worst upper-quantile coverage on cloudy rows.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
The experiment departed from its plan in the 11 ways below, all decided before any arm was scored. None changes the hypothesis, the prediction, or the decision rule.

  1. The weight is zero in the 10-plus-day band. The ENS anomaly has a correlation of 0.03 with the CAMS anomaly there, and the fitted slope ranged from -8.2 to +6.2. The rule was fixed from the weights table, which uses training rows only, before any arm was scored.
  2. The capacity is divided by experiment 45's recovery ratio. The refitted season-year constant for 2024/25 is divided by experiment 45's stored recovery ratio (0.71 to 0.79, from an injection test on tuning farms), as experiment 45 defines capacity. The capacities used, in MW, are D9 2.751, D10 2.356, D11 3.457, D14 3.705, and D16 3.578. D14 uses experiment 40's 2023/24 constant, because the experiment 64 refit has no 2024/25 constant for it (all of its weeks are unobserved).
  3. The no-cloud-proxy variant drops 3 columns, dew_point_temperature_2m, precipitation, and pressure_surface, because d1l has no precipitation_type or pressure_msl column.
  4. The placebo is a seeded cyclic shift, not a random permutation. It moves each row's shape by between a quarter and three quarters of its group (series, local month, half-hour, and lead band). A random permutation paired runs that forecast the same valid time, so the permuted anomaly stayed correlated with the real one. After the change, the correlation of the twin's anomaly with the real anomaly is -0.012 on the 256,230 validation rows.
  5. Arm b drops training rows whose lag has no shape. At inference the gross lag is missing (NaN) there, on 2.8% of validation rows for the lag of the same time the day before and 8.6% for the week before. No sensitivity read of this exists. The climatology fallback was not needed.
  6. Two small confounds remain. The reference temperature of sf_temp uses the control member's temperature. Arm am starts from the margin alone, while d1l and a start from XGBoost's base score, a small confound in the a against am contrast.
  7. climatology and manual_heuristic lack 40 of the 68,903 rows, so they are scored on shared rows, outside the paired bootstrap.
  8. The plan's refit count was wrong. The experiment ran 75 refits (5 arms, 3 seeds, 5 series), not "about 90 plus 60".
  9. The weights rest on little data. The training window holds two April-to-June periods and one July-to-September period (2024). The 4 time-block folds of the cross-fit group months by month index modulo 4, so adjacent months train each other.
  10. The held capacity is stale. The held value is 5% to 19% below experiment 45's 2025/26 constants at the five series (D9 5%, D10 17%, D11 15%, D14 13%, D16 19%). D14 holds the 2023/24 constant of experiment 40. A capacity that is too low plausibly weakens the solar term and so works against the placebo contrast, which would make the gains conservative; no run tests this.
  11. The sunniest-decile read and the a against am contrasts are exploratory (95%), not corrected across the four arms.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The evidence supports am as a candidate for a model release, and the decision to port belongs to the maintainer and the roadmap. The next experiment should answer four questions that remain open:

  • Does the gain survive a current capacity? Refit sf and am with capacities that follow the validation year (experiment 45's 2025/26 constants are 6% to 23% higher), because the capacity held here is stale.
  • Do the weights hold with more training data? The July-to-September weights rest on one summer, so a window with a second summer would show whether the weights move.
  • Why does am also beat d0 at 10 days and beyond? The weight is zero there, so the base score, the margin in training rows at shorter leads, and the trees are the candidates.
  • Can the live service supply am's inputs? The live service cannot use am as built: it needs the capacity table, the table of weights, and the ENS calibration slopes at predict time, and am sets a base margin on each prediction matrix. Whether the serving path can do so is a question for the roadmap.

Arm b stays untested in two respects. Its gross lags are missing on 2.8% and 8.6% of validation rows with no sensitivity read, and its loss to d0 at 6 days and beyond could come from the ENS forecast of the subtracted term, which has no skill there. A variant that subtracts the shape only inside 6 days would separate the two.

docs.title: Experiment 65: does one score from a substation's own step and its neighbours' opposite steps find more of the moved load?
docs.text:
Adding the neighbouring substations' opposite-sign steps to a substation's own step did not find clearly more of the moved load than the own step alone. In a post hoc variant, adding the count of neighbours that stepped the same way raised the share found. The neighbour veto of experiment 55 already uses that count. Whether one score that combines the own step, the opposite neighbour step, and the same-sign count beats the own step alone is untested.

We asked whether load transfers are found more often when one alarm score adds a substation's own step to the largest opposite step among its neighbours. A load transfer moves power off a donor Primary substation and onto receiver substations. The step of a substation is the change in the average of its residual (measured minus predicted power) from the 24 hours before a half-hour to the 24 hours after it, in noise units (multiples of the usual size of that step on a quiet day). We injected 620 known load transfers into the measured power of 16 Primary substations and counted the share of the moved megawatts (MW) found. A transfer counts as found when an alarm starts within 2 hours of its start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration. Every detector was held to 80 alarms on odd months that match no closure in the NGED switching log. The single-series detector D0M finds 0.646 of the moved MW (0.354 missed). The logistic-regression score (LOGIT) finds 0.665, which is +0.019 more (99.17% interval, from resampling whole calendar months, -0.011 to +0.062). The likelihood-ratio score (LR) finds 0.651, which is +0.005 more (-0.010 to +0.014).

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
The experiment is inconclusive, because the better score's interval against D0M includes zero. The likelihood-ratio score (LR) is refuted, because the upper end of its interval against D0M is below +0.02. The logistic-regression score (LOGIT) is inconclusive, because its interval against D0M includes zero and its upper end is above +0.02. The experiment takes the more favourable verdict of the two scores, and that choice is not covered by the correction for six planned contrasts (a Bonferroni correction). All intervals are 99.17%, from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar months, over the 620 injected transfers that move 25% to 40% of the receiving load for over 1 day and start in even months, pooled with equal weight over the constant-MW, receiver-profile, and fitted-mix shapes (none of which the scores assume). Interval ends come from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days, the end rule of experiment 61. That rule needs up to 14 days of hindsight, so detectors built on it serve training-time masks and the NGED event table, not live forecast inputs.

Contrast (gain in MW-weighted recall) LR LOGIT Against D0M, the 24-hour single-series detector +0.005 (-0.010 to +0.014) +0.019 (-0.011 to +0.062) Against D1, the neighbour gate +0.101 (+0.043 to +0.176) +0.116 (+0.050 to +0.231) Against D2, the neighbour veto of experiment 55 -0.007 (-0.036 to +0.008) +0.008 (-0.028 to +0.042)

Both scores beat the neighbour gate D1 clearly, but D1 is the weakest detector. At 80 unexplained alarms D1 finds 0.550 of the moved MW against D0M's 0.646. D2 finds 0.658. The pre-registered rule needed an interval above zero against D0M as well, and neither score has one.

docs.title: Recall by arm
docs.text:
The best arms still miss about a third of the moved MW. The table gives MW-weighted recall under each end rule, pooled over the three shapes.

Arm Tracked end Strongest-opposite-step end (PE) MW missed under PE D0M 0.455 0.646 0.354 D1 0.389 0.550 0.450 D2 0.459 0.658 0.342 LR 0.460 0.651 0.349 LOGIT 0.466 0.665 0.335 LOGIT + same-sign count (post hoc) 0.479 0.681 0.319 D2 at veto 1.0 (post hoc) 0.466 0.666 0.334

The same contrasts under the tracked end have the same signs and sizes (LR +0.005, LOGIT +0.011). Even-month unexplained-alarm counts on the real residual were 80 for D0M, 78 for LR, 54 for LOGIT, 72 for D2, and 49 for D1, so no combined score bought its recall with extra alarms. The odd-month counts are all 80 or 79.

docs.title: Where the gain sits
docs.text: The scores gain where the donor step is 2.5 to 6 noise units, mostly for transfers with a metered receiver. A noise unit is the usual size of the 24-hour step statistic on a quiet day. With a metered receiver (a receiver whose own power is measured) the share of transfers found at a donor step of 2.5 to 4 rises from 0.58 for D0M to 0.71 for LOGIT with the same-sign count. Without a metered receiver the gain spans 2.5 to 6 noise units and is larger at 4 to 6 (0.37 for D0M, 0.55 for that arm). Donor steps below 2.5 noise units are found for 5 of 40 transfers at most. A donor step above 6 gains nothing, because D0M already finds those transfers.

docs.title: Labelled real transfers
docs.text: On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day, the scores find 6 to 8 against D0M's 7 under PE, so the real data cannot separate them. With the tracked end the scores find 5 and D0M finds 2. Alarms at the right start are found for 14 (LR), 12 (LOGIT), and 11 (D0M) of the 35. The count is too small to rank the scores. Of the 35, 20 start in even months and 15 in odd months.

docs.title: Fitted scores
docs.text: The fitted LR lookup tables rise with both statistics, and LOGIT weights the neighbour step about as much as the own step. The standardised logistic coefficients are 2.59 on the own step, 2.95 on the largest opposite neighbour step, and -1.11 on the number of neighbours. The coefficient on the MVA-neighbour flag is zero, because every one of the 16 series has an MVA-only neighbour, so the flag is constant. The post hoc same-sign count has a coefficient of -0.85, which means a same-sign neighbour step lowers the score, as the veto does.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Training data come from the same injection generator as the test transfers. Training uses odd months and scoring uses even months, but both draw donors and receivers the same way, so the scores may do worse on real transfers.
  • The candidate floor of 2.5 noise units caps recall. The 507 negative examples are alarm candidates from the real odd-month residual.
  • Weights and shrinkage. Every shape weights a transfer by its MW moved under the donor-profile shape, so the three shapes share one set of weights. The logistic regression's penalty of 1.0 is weak against about 2,700 training candidates, so it shrinks the coefficients very little.
  • Alarm counts. LR and both logistic scores land on exactly 80 unexplained odd-month alarms. D0M, D1, and D2 reach at most 80 on a 0.05 grid of thresholds (D0M 80, D1 80, D2 80, veto 1.0 at 79).
  • The post hoc arms were chosen after reading the pre-registered result, so their intervals overstate the evidence. Their contrasts use the same level as the planned ones.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does one pre-registered score that uses the largest opposite neighbour step, the count of same-sign neighbour steps, and the own step together beat D0M by at least +0.02? The post hoc arm suggests it does (+0.034, +0.013 to +0.091). A pre-registered run would also say whether the gain holds on the labelled real transfers, where this experiment could not tell the arms apart.

docs.title: Experiment 66 (SW2-16, part of the LSC series): which window and cap should the end rule use?
docs.text:
Ending each alarm's interval at the first opposite step that is at least half the size of the step that raised the alarm finds more of the moved power than searching 14 days for the strongest opposite step, and a 24-hour averaging window beat a 4-hour window. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for some hours or days. A Primary substation is the 11 kV or 6.6 kV substation that feeds local distribution circuits. D0M is the single-series detector of this series. It raises an alarm (the onset step) when the 24-hour average of a substation's residual steps away from the previous 24-hour average by 4.0 noise units or more. The residual is the measured power minus an XGBoost forecast that uses weather forecasts and no past power. One noise unit is 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of that 24-hour step on odd months, for that substation, so 4.0 noise units is a step four times the usual size. An alarm interval runs from the onset step to the opposite step (the return step) that ends the transfer. D0M's own tracker finds that end by following the residual's level. Experiment 61 ended each alarm interval at the strongest opposite step within a cap of 14 days after the onset, and that end rule finds 0.19 more of the moved power than the tracker. All scores below are shares of the moved power (in MW), from 0 to 1.

We added known load transfers to the power history and asked what share of the moved power each end rule finds. A transfer counts as found when an alarm interval starts within 2 hours of the true start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the true duration. The score is called MW-weighted recall: the share of the moved MW that sits in found transfers. Two sets of injected transfers carry the scores: experiment 58's 620 transfers (25% to 40% of the receiving load, lasting over 1 day), and a new long set of 215 transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. On the long set, a 30-day cap finds 0.547 of the moved power and the 14-day cap finds 0.013. On the 620 transfers, the 30-day cap finds 0.045 less than the 14-day cap, because the 30-day cap picks a later, wrong step for some short transfers. The 4-hour window, with a 14-day cap, finds 0.147 less than the 24-hour window on the 620 transfers. A rule written after seeing the results (post hoc) ends the interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step, and otherwise keeps the tracked end. The post hoc rule finds more than the 14-day cap on both sets, although on the long set it finds less than the 30-day cap. The pre-registered decision rule (fixed before any result was read) gives the verdict inconclusive, because the gain on long transfers and the loss on short ones appear together.

docs.title: What we tested
docs.text:
Twelve variants of the end rule (arms) plus three post hoc arms, all scored on the same transfers, with D0M's alarms in every arm. The arms differ in the window of the step statistic and in where the interval ends. D0M and the end rules at one alarm setting therefore raise the same alarms, so their unexplained-alarm counts match by construction.

  • D0M ends each interval with a level tracker that stops after 60 days.
  • PE14, PE30, and PE60 (labels for the end rule with a cap of 14, 30, or 60 days) end the interval at the stamp between 24 hours and 14, 30, or 60 days after the onset where the step back is largest, when it is at least 1.5 noise units (experiment 61's rule). Otherwise the tracked end stays.
  • Three alarm settings. The 24-hour window at 4.0 noise units gives 80 unexplained alarms on odd months. The 4-hour window at 6.0 gives 120 (experiment 43's setting). The 4-hour window at 6.35 gives 78, the threshold that matches the 24-hour window's alarm rate, and C5 uses it.
  • PF14, PF30, and PF60 (labels for the first-return rule with a cap of 14, 30, or 60 days; post hoc, 24-hour window only) take the first stamp where the step back reaches half the onset step (and at least 1.5 noise units), end at the largest step back within one window after that stamp, and keep the tracked end when no stamp qualifies.

The 620 transfers are experiment 58's headline band (25% to 40% of the receiving load, lasting over 1 day) that start in even months. Only 17 of its 1,160 headline transfers (all months) last over 14 days, so the 620 cannot separate the caps. The long set is 400 new injected transfers that last 15.6 to 60 days, of which 215 start in even months and form the scored set. Each takes its duration and its pair of substations from one of the 25 labelled real operations that last that long, and 57 of the 215 scored (26.5%) last over 30 days. Five shapes of moved power (a share of the donor's profile, a constant MW, a share of each receiver's profile, a mix fitted to real transfers, and the donor's profile shifted by 12 hours; S1 to S5, from experiment 60) carry the moved power. The headline pools S2, S3, and S4, the shapes that none of this series' detectors assumes. Intervals are 99% (Bonferroni across the five planned contrasts), from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar months.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
inconclusive: C1 and C2 pass the rule's tests on the long set, and C3 and C4 fail its guard on the 620 transfers. C5 shows that the window should not change from 24 hours (tested with the 14-day cap, on the 620 transfers). The rule changes the cap only when the long-set gain is at least +0.01 and the point change on the 620 transfers is no lower than -0.01. The benchmark stays the 24-hour window with a 14-day cap, and no planned contrast supports a change.

Contrast (24-hour window unless stated) Change in MW-weighted recall Reading C1, 30-day cap, long set +0.534 (+0.131 to +0.780) Large gain on transfers over 15.6 days C2, 60-day cap, long set +0.535 (+0.122 to +0.781) Same gain as the 30-day cap C3, 30-day cap, 620 transfers -0.045 (-0.070 to -0.011) Fails the guard of -0.01 C4, 60-day cap, 620 transfers -0.080 (-0.113 to -0.035) Fails the guard C5, 4-hour window (78 alarms), 620 transfers -0.147 (-0.248 to -0.054) The window stays at 24 hours 60-day cap minus 30-day cap, long set (descriptive) +0.001 (-0.035 to +0.042) No gain from 60 days

Absolute MW-weighted recall (S2, S3, and S4 pooled, even months) is in the next table. The missed share is one minus the recall. For PE14 on the 620 transfers, 0.281 of the moved MW sits in transfers with no alarm at the start and 0.073 in transfers whose start was found and whose end was wrong. On the long set the 14-day cap misses 0.599 as wrong ends.
