On odd months, which were not used to rank the pre-registered arms (see Limits for their dependence on the even-month draw), the 620-transfer recall is 0.372 for D0M, 0.491 for PE14, and 0.521 for PF14. Unweighted recall for PE14 on the 620 transfers is 0.478.

docs.title: The cap trades short transfers for long ones
docs.text:
A longer cap repairs transfers over 15.6 days and breaks some shorter ones. The strongest opposite step in 30 days is probably sometimes a later step that belongs to another event, and the 60-day cap probably picks such a step more often. The printed report shows only the number of wrong ends: the mean number of transfers per shape on the 620 set whose start was found and whose end was wrong is 49 at 14 days, 75 at 30 days, and 101 at 60 days. The interval of C1 runs from +0.131 to +0.780, which is wide, probably because few calendar months contribute.

The first-return rule is better than the 14-day cap on both sets of transfers, and the cap barely matters for it. The post hoc arm PF14 is +0.042 (+0.013 to +0.066) over PE14 on the 620 transfers and +0.412 (+0.067 to +0.621) on the long set. On odd months the gains are +0.030 (+0.011 to +0.047) and +0.371 (+0.018 to +0.595). PF30 and PF60 differ from PF14 by 0.009 and 0.018 on the 620 transfers. A return step has to reach half the onset step to end an interval. When no such step exists, the rule keeps the tracked end. PF30 and PF60 find no more than PF14 on the long set (0.422 and 0.429 against 0.425), and PF14 stays below PE30 there (0.425 against 0.547), with 0.187 of the long-set MW lost as wrong ends against 0.065 for PE30. The arm was written after seeing the results, so PF14 needs a confirmation on a fresh draw before the series adopts it. Suppose transfers over 15.6 days were as common as in the labelled operations (25 of the 151 labelled operations over 1 day, 17%, which is a larger set than the 35 transfers scored below). Mixing the long-set and 620-transfer point gains at that share (post hoc, with no interval) gives +0.051 for PE30, +0.022 for PE60, and +0.103 for PF14 over PE14.

docs.title: Recall by donor step
docs.text:
Recall rises with the size of the donor step, and is low for steps below 2 noise units and for small steps with no metered receiver. The table counts transfers found out of transfers, summed over S2, S3, and S4, on the 620 transfers. Steps are in 24-hour noise units.

Donor step Receiver Transfers D0M PE14 PE30 PE60 PF14 2 to 4 metered 126 49 67 61 46 86 4 to 6 metered 175 85 106 99 82 122 6 to 10 metered 295 174 240 217 205 254 10 or more metered 343 202 304 289 284 319 2 to 4 unmetered 563 73 98 77 57 107 4 to 6 unmetered 179 45 67 63 55 74

The printed report also gives the 4-hour arms, the steps below 2, and the 6-to-10 unmetered row.

docs.title: Labelled real transfers
docs.text: On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day, the caps make little difference. D0M finds 2, PE14 finds 7, PE30 finds 6, PE60 finds 5, and PF14 finds 8 (the same 8 for PF30 and PF60). Only 11 of the 35 have any alarm at the start, so the onset still limits the real transfers. Of the 5 labelled transfers over 14 days, PE14 finds none, and PE30, PE60, and PF14 find 1 each. The counts are too small for an interval.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Held: C1 +0.534 (predicted +0.30 to +0.55, near its upper edge) and C2 +0.535 (predicted +0.40 to +0.65, mid-range).
  • Held at its lower edge: 60 days over 30 days, +0.001 (predicted +0.00 to +0.20), although about 27% of the long set lasts over 30 days.
  • Mechanism: the 60-day cap's extra gain on transfers of 30 to 60 days (0.139 against 0.000) is cancelled by its extra wrong ends on shorter transfers.
  • Not held: C3 -0.045 and C4 -0.080, against predicted -0.01 to +0.01 and -0.03 to +0.01.
  • Held: C5 -0.147, against a predicted -0.15 to 0.00, at its lower edge.
  • The expected winner, the 24-hour window with a 30-day cap, did not pass the guard.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The end rule needs up to the cap's worth of hindsight, so detectors built on it serve training-time masks (SW2-12) and the event table for National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), not live forecast inputs.
  • The long set was redrawn once. The first draw used experiment 58's quietness rule over the whole transfer, which left transfers in 9 months only. The redraw applies the rule to the 7 days around the onset and the end, requires 90% of the power to be present there, and allows at most 16 transfers starting in one month. The first run's contrasts had been printed before the redraw. The redraw changed no arm, contrast, or decision rule.
  • Injected transfers are clean boxcars, so a return step is easier to find than a real transfer's.
  • The end rule is applied to every substation of a transfer, and a longer cap more often picks a noise step on a receiver with a small step. A transfer counts as found when any of its substations matches.
  • Odd and even months are assigned by the month in which the transfer starts. A long transfer that starts in an even month ends in later months, so the odd-month check is not independent of the even-month draw.
  • The donor-step table uses 24-hour noise units for the 4-hour arms too, because the transfer's step is defined once.
  • The long set and the real transfers share their durations and substation pairs, so they are not independent evidence.
  • PF's half-step share and the 1.5 noise-unit floor are the first values tried and were not tuned.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Plan review (Sonnet agent): accepted an explicit rule for every outcome, the cap taken from the 24-hour contrasts only, a guard that does not enter the refuted test, the 15.6-day lower limit, the odd-month recall of the chosen setting, a split of the missed MW, and a list of the code that changes. Rejected a one-sided 99% level (the intervals are two-sided at 1 minus 0.05 over 5) and the claim that no real operation lasts over 30 days (5 of the 25 do).
  • Code review (Sonnet agent): found no leakage and no off-by-one. Accepted asserting the population counts, dropping a tautological alarm count, labelling the donor-step units, printing the count of wrong ends, and checking that every shape covers the same months. The inherited behaviour of applying the end rule to every substation of a transfer is recorded in Limits.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The first step of SW2-17 confirms the first-return rule on a fresh draw, and the result of that step picks the benchmark for the rest of SW2-17. The step is pre-registered here. It draws new injections with a new seed on both sets of transfers (the 620-style transfers and the long set), scores even months only, and reads PF14 minus PE14 in MW-weighted recall at the same alarm rate. If the interval lies above zero on both sets, PF14 is the SW2-17 benchmark. If not, PE14 stays the benchmark. SW2-17 (the missed onsets of the end rule) then classifies by cause the 24 of 35 labelled real transfers with no alarm at the start, and tests an onset rule that a later return step confirms.

Code: ml-experiments/00066-sw2-16-end-rule-as-baseline/, with every number printed by e00066_report.py.

docs.title: Experiment 67: does one convex fit of load flows across all boundaries find more load?
docs.text:
Fitting one flow of power across every pair of neighbouring Primary substations at once, in a single optimisation, found far less of the moved load than a detector that looks at each substation alone, and the cause is how the estimator scales hourly residuals by their noise, not the conservation of power. We inserted 620 artificial load transfers (power moved from a donor substation to its neighbours for over 1 day) into the measured power of 16 Primary substations, and counted the share of the moved megawatts (MW) that each method found. The single-series detector, which flags a step in one substation's residual (measured minus predicted power) over 24 hours, found 0.646 of the moved MW. The joint estimator found 0.108, with both methods tuned to raise about 80 alarms that no recorded outage explains, counted over the odd-numbered calendar months (the months used for tuning). A change we made afterwards to the threshold of the estimator's Huber loss (quadratic for small residuals, linear for large ones) lifted that to 0.527, still 0.120 lower. The estimator matched the single-series detector only on transfers that drop the donor's load by 10 or more standard deviations of its usual noise and have a receiving substation metered in MW. It found almost nothing where no receiver is metered. The verdict is refuted: the estimator's gain over the single-series detector has an interval wholly below the +0.02 bound set in the plan.

We asked whether fitting every boundary at once finds switched load more reliably than looking at each substation alone. The estimator explains the residual of all 16 Primary substations as a flow across each of the 30 pairs of neighbouring substations (a boundary), plus a slack term per substation for load moved to a neighbour that is not metered. A flow is zero almost always and flat when it is not. The benchmark is D0M, the 24-hour single-series step detector with the strongest-opposite-step end rule of experiment 61.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
The joint edge-flow estimator (EF) is refuted: it finds 0.538 less of the moved MW than D0M, with an interval wholly below the +0.02 bound. MW-weighted recall is the share of the moved MW that sits in found transfers. A transfer is found when an alarm interval on one of its series starts within 2 hours of the true start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration. The table gives recall pooled with equal weight over three injection shapes that the estimator does not assume (S2, a constant MW; S3, a share of the receiver's profile; and S4, a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers). The 620 scored transfers move 25% to 40% of the receiving substation's load for over 1 day and start in even months, and each is scored under all three shapes. Weights are the transfers' moved MW under the donor-profile shape, as in experiment 65.

Arm MW-weighted recall MW missed Unweighted recall Unexplained alarms, odd / even months D0M, 24-hour step, strongest-opposite-step end (PE) 0.646 0.354 0.478 80 / 80 LOGIT + same-sign count (post hoc benchmark, experiment 65) 0.681 0.319 0.527 not counted EF, pre-registered (Huber threshold 3) 0.108 0.892 0.082 77 / 88 EF, Huber threshold 10 (post hoc) 0.527 0.473 0.334 71 / 82

In the table, LOGIT + same-sign count is experiment 65's logistic score that adds the count of neighbours stepping the same way as the alarming substation.

The contrasts, read at 97.5% (Bonferroni across two) from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar year- months:

  • C1, EF minus D0M: -0.538 (-0.605 to -0.421).
  • C2, EF minus LOGIT + same-sign count (no verdict): -0.573 (-0.631 to -0.474).
  • Post hoc, Huber 10 minus D0M: -0.120 (-0.190 to -0.084), and minus LOGIT + same-sign: -0.154 (-0.262 to -0.103).

docs.title: Where the estimator loses
docs.text:
The post hoc estimator (Huber threshold 10) matches D0M only for large transfers with a metered receiver, and both estimators find almost nothing when no receiver is metered. The table gives the unweighted share of transfers found, pooled over the three shapes and counted once per shape.

| Donor step (noise units) | Metered receiver: EF / EF Huber 10 / D0M / LOGIT + same-sign | No metered receiver: the same four | |---|---|---| | 2.5 to 4 | 0.11 / 0.14 / 0.58 / 0.71 | 0.02 / 0.03 / 0.20 / 0.26 | | 4 to 6 | 0.14 / 0.37 / 0.61 / 0.62 | 0.09 / 0.07 / 0.37 / 0.55 | | 6 to 10 | 0.18 / 0.66 / 0.81 / 0.81 | 4 of 7 transfers for every arm | | 10 or more | 0.09 / 0.92 / 0.89 / 0.90 | no transfers |

Below 2.5 noise units no method finds more than 5 of the 39 to 41 transfers with a metered receiver in any shape.

In one transfer that EF missed, the donor, a Primary substation metered only in MVA (apparent power, with no direction), had a residual 8.8 hourly noise standard deviations below its baseline, and the fit placed no slack run on it. The gradient of a Huber loss with threshold M is at most 2M per noise unit of residual. At M = 3 the slack penalty that holds the alarms to 80 (1.5 times 3.7, or 5.6) is close to the maximum gradient of 6, so a slack of a few noise units per hour is switched off. At M = 10 the maximum gradient is 20. The pre-registered tuning shows the same limit: the penalty that gave 0 alarms was only 2.5 times the one that gave about 80.

docs.title: Labelled real transfers
docs.text: On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day, EF finds 4, D0M 7, and LOGIT + same-sign 6. Both EF runs find the same 4. Of the 20 transfers that start in even months, EF finds 4, D0M 6, and LOGIT + same-sign 5. EF finds none of the 15 that start in odd months, D0M finds 1, and LOGIT + same-sign finds 1. The counts are too small to rank D0M and LOGIT + same-sign.

docs.title: Method and what was fixed in advance
docs.text:
• Fit. Hourly residuals, divided by each series' noise scale, in windows of 70 days. A Huber (threshold 3), a level penalty lambda on flows and slacks (the slack penalty multiplied by m), and a fused penalty rho * lambda on the hourly change of each flow and slack, solved with CVXPY and Clarabel. The 8 Primaries metered only in MVA enter as slack-only nodes. - Tuning on odd months. For each of 6 cells (rho of 1, 3, or 10; m of 1.5 or 3), lambda was matched to at matched to at most 80 unexplained odd-month alarms, then the cell was scored on 300 odd-month transfers. Recall was 0.064 to 0.086 in every cell, and the cell with rho of 10 and m of 1.5 won (lambda 3.72, 77 alarms). - Post hoc variant. A Huber threshold of 10 with the range of lambda scaled to match, tuned over 2 cells (rho of 3 or 10, m of 1.5): recall on the tuning transfers was 0.296 and 0.332, and the second cell won (lambda 4.07, 71 alarms). It was chosen after reading the pre-registered result and does not change the verdict.
  • Alarms. Each run counts as two alarms per series metered in MW, at its onset and at its end, as D0M alarms on both the onset step and the return step. An alarm is explained when a logged closure touches its series within 24 hours of its own stamp. A run that starts within 24 hours of a monthly refit of the baseline power model that produces the residual is dropped.
  • Checks. A planted flow and a planted slack were recovered at the right onset and end, and the injection reproduced experiment 65's moved MW. All 3,720 scored fits of the two runs were optimal.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A simpler fused penalty than the roadmap's. The group version that ties the changes at one Primary together solved 25 times slower (55 s against 2.2 s on a 28-day window), so each flow changes on its own. The result does not test the group version.
  • An edge to an MVA-only neighbour is a cheaper slack. The flow is seen at the metered end only, so for those neighbours the fit gains no conservation check. All 16 Primaries have an MVA-only neighbour.
  • More context than the benchmark. Each fit sees 21 to 49 days of residual on each side of a run (35 days around a scored transfer), against 14 days for the strongest-opposite-step end. Scored transfers sit 35 days from the window edges and the tuning windows have 21 to 49 days of context, so the tuning alarm counts are slightly pessimistic for EF.
  • The benchmark is experiment 65's detector. EF was not scored against the end rule of experiment 66, because the plan fixed D0M with the strongest-opposite-step end rule as the verdict arm.
  • A coarse grid. Six cells for the pre-registered run and two for the variant; the Huber threshold, the read-out threshold of 0.1 noise standard deviations, and the 24-hour minimum run were not tuned.
  • Tuning odd months and scoring even months share residual context in windows that cross months, as the benchmark's 24-hour windows do.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Does a joint fit to the 24-hour step statistics, in noise units, find more of the moved MW than D0M? The step statistic already carries a noise scale calibrated on odd months, and the conservation constraint and slack could be applied to it. The experiment would also say whether conservation across the 8 MW-metered Primaries helps once the noise model is fixed.

Reproduce with uv run --with cvxpy python ml-experiments/00067-sw2-15-joint-edge-flow-estimator/e00067_run.py check tune score real, and the same with --huber 10 --out <data folder>/huber10. Then run e00067_report.py and e00067_charts.py.

docs.title: Experiment 68 (SW2-5, part of the LSC series): does refitting the forecast without the load transfers the detector found help the detector?
docs.text:
Refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the load transfers that the detector found barely changed what the detector finds, or the forecast error. In these 16 series, with this XGBoost configuration, the limit on the detector is therefore not that the forecast has learned the transfers. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for some hours or days. A Primary substation is the 11 kV or 6.6 kV substation that feeds local distribution circuits. SW2 is the series of experiments on detecting these transfers from the telemetry alone.

The detector reads the residual, which is the measured power minus the forecast of the lagless XGBoost model. The model uses weather forecasts and calendar inputs and no past power. The detector raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of a substation's residual steps away from the average of the previous 24 hours by 4.0 noise units or more, where one noise unit is the typical size of that step on odd calendar months. We asked whether the model, trained through a transfer, partly learns the transfer. If it does, the transfer's step shrinks in the residual and the forecast is biased.

We ran a loop of three rounds. Round 0 is the refit with no mask. In each later round the model was refitted with zero weight on the half-hours inside the intervals that the detector had found on the previous round's residual (the mask), and the detector was then run again. To test the loop, we added 130 synthetic load transfers to the measured power before the model trained. The detector found 0.522 of the megawatts (MW) that those transfers moved at round 0 and 0.532 at round 3 (+0.011, 97.5% interval +0.000 to +0.034). This share of the moved MW is called MW-weighted recall. We also measured the forecast's mean absolute error on half-hours more than 24 hours from every logged closure and every labelled real transfer. It changed by -0.175% (-1.145% to +0.603%) from round 0 to round 3. A mask of about equal volume at random times did as well as the real mask, so the small changes are no evidence that the detected intervals matter.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
Inconclusive by the decision rule, and the loop is not worth adding at this size. The rule asked for two things. Recall had to gain at least +0.02 with an interval above zero. The forecast error had to fall by at least 1% with an interval below zero. Neither condition holds. refuted needed the upper end of the recall interval below +0.02 and the lower end of the error interval above -1.0%, and both ends lie just outside (+0.034 and -1.145%). The rule gave small gain no opening either, because the recall interval's lower end is 0.000, not above zero, and the error interval's upper end is +0.603%. The even-month count of unexplained alarms in world A (defined in "What we tested") was also 15% below round 0's in rounds 1 and 3, outside the 10% that the rule allows, so supported and partly supported were closed as well.

In the table, C1 and C2 are the two contrasts the rule reads, and C3 compares round 1 with a mask of about equal volume placed at random times.

Contrast Change Reading C1, recall, round 3 minus round 0 (world B) +0.011 (+0.000 to +0.034) Under the +0.02 bar C2, forecast error, round 3 minus round 0 (world A) -0.175% (-1.145% to +0.603%) Under the 1% bar C3, round 1 minus random mask, error -0.052% (-0.422% to +0.340%) The mask does no better than random C3, round 1 minus random mask, recall (world A) +0.004 (-0.003 to +0.016) The same

docs.title: What each round found
docs.text:
Absolute recall barely moves between rounds, and a third to a half of the moved power is missed. Recall is the share of the MW moved by the injected transfers that sits in transfers the detector found, pooled with equal weight over three transfer shapes (S2, S3, and S4, none of which the detector assumes). The two worlds hold different transfers, so their levels are not comparable.

Round World B recall World A recall World A error (points of capacity) Labelled real transfers found (of 35) 0 0.522 0.663 8.936 7 1 0.530 0.659 8.909 6 2 0.532 0.659 8.917 7 3 0.532 0.664 8.920 6 Random mask, round 1 not run 0.655 8.914 5

In world B the missed share of the moved MW is 0.478, 0.470, 0.468, and 0.468. In world A it is 0.337, 0.341, 0.341, and 0.336. The donor step is the size of the step that a transfer makes in the substation it takes load from, in noise units. A metered receiver is a neighbouring substation whose power is in the data. In world B, transfers with a metered receiver are found at 16 of 20 with a donor step of 10 noise units or more, and at 13 of 22 with 6 to 10. None of the 22 transfers below 2 noise units is found in world B, and 3 of 166 are found in world A. Every bin is in the output of e00068_report.py.

A detail in world A: transfers over 7 days gain +0.018 (+0.000 to +0.037) from round 0 to round 3, over 93 transfers, and transfers of 7 days or less gain 0.000. World B has 2 transfers over 7 days, so it cannot test this. The gain is post hoc and its interval touches zero.

docs.title: What we tested
docs.text:
The lagless XGBoost model. The model is the H0.5 arm of experiment 17: 13 inputs (weather, clock, calendar), refitted monthly on rows that end 7 days before the month, recency weights with a half-life of 0.5 years, 16 Primary substation series. The round-0 refit reproduced experiment 17's stored predictions with a largest difference of 0.

The loop. Round k refits with zero weight on the half-hours inside the intervals found on round k-1's residual. The detector raises its alarms at the 24-hour window and takes the end of each interval from the strongest opposite step within 14 days (the detectors D0M and PE of experiment 61). The mask for the refit of a month uses only intervals that end at least 15 days before the refit's training end. In every round the threshold was lowered from a high value to the lowest that leaves at most 80 unexplained alarms on odd months. An alarm is unexplained when it lies more than 24 hours from every logged closure on its series, and odd months set the threshold so that even months are left to score. The detections and the thresholds use the whole span, so the loop uses information that a live refit would not have (a research set-up).

Two worlds. World A is the real data. World B adds 130 injected transfers to the measured power before the model trains (a fresh draw of headline-band transfers from experiment 58's generator, onsets in even months, no two on one series within 1 day, none crossing into an odd month, in the shapes S2, S3, and S4 in turn). World A also scores 620 injected transfers added to the residual only, as experiment 61 did. Intervals are 97.5% (Bonferroni across C1 and C2), from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar months.

Round Threshold (noise units) Median noise scale over the 16 series (MW) Unexplained alarms, odd months Unexplained alarms, even months (world A) Detected intervals, all series 0 4.0 0.2343 80 80 297 1 4.1 0.2342 75 68 274 2 4.05 0.2345 78 73 288 3 4.1 0.2338 78 68 276 Random mask, round 1 4.1 0.2354 77 73 278

At round 0's threshold, rounds 1 to 3 have 87, 85, and 87 odd-month unexplained alarms, so the matched threshold rose by 0.05 to 0.1. Recall at round 0's threshold in world A is 0.664, 0.663, and 0.668, the same as the matched-alarm figures. The masks hold 84,817 half-hours in round 0's intervals, about 7% of the grid's half-hours across the 16 series.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Held: the predicted recall gain of +0.00 to +0.03 (C1). The gain was +0.011.
  • Held: the predicted change in error of -1.0% to 0.0% (C2). The change was -0.175%.
  • Held: neither a recall gain of +0.02 nor a fall of 1% in error was expected, and neither occurred.
  • Not held: the likeliest verdicts, refuted and small gain. The verdict was inconclusive.
  • Not tested in world B: the larger gain on transfers that last over 7 days. World B has 2 such transfers. The post hoc split in world A shows +0.018 for transfers over 7 days and 0.000 for the rest, with an interval that touches zero.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• A transfer that starts in month M has never been in the training data of the refit that forecasts month M. The mask can raise that transfer's recall only through earlier transfers the model learned from, or through a transfer that runs past a month boundary. A null result does not show that the mechanism is absent.
  • World B has 130 transfers, and only 2 last over 7 days.
  • Zero weight is not the same as removing rows, because XGBoost's histogram bins, row sampling, and leaf values depend on the rows present.
  • The random-mask control could not move 72 of its 297 intervals so the control is looser than "equal volume" suggests. Those intervals are the longest, which fill their calendar month, and the ones where all 100 random draws overlapped a detected interval. It places 79,018 half-hours against round 1's 78,318.
  • The 35 labelled real transfers are in the training data and the mask, so the counts found (7, 6, 7, 6) are descriptive.
  • The round-0 check on the stored residuals gave an MW-weighted recall of 0.653 to 0.671, against experiment 61's 0.63 to 0.65. The harness here injects only the 620 transfers of the headline band, so its random draws differ from experiment 61's, and the weights here are each shape's own moved MW rather than experiment 61's shape-S1 weights.
  • The MW-weighted recall of both worlds is read at a matched count of 80 odd-month unexplained alarms, which the threshold grid met at 75 to 80, not exactly.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Plan review (Sonnet): accepted a mask rule that requires each interval to end 15 days before the training end, a second world in which the injected transfers are in the training data, a verdict order with refuted covering harm, world A's alarm count in the rule, per-round noise scale and threshold, recall at round 0's threshold, and a note that a null result does not disprove the mechanism. Rejected an oracle mask (optional, and the refit costs 20 minutes per round) and a random-mask control for every round (one round has the control, as stated).
  • Code review (Sonnet): accepted dropping world-B transfers that cross into an odd month, one capacity median for the injected target and the panel, a stable left join, a guard on negative stamps, per-world reference thresholds, and counting the intervals the random mask could not move. Rejected nothing; it found no leakage in the mask and no difference from experiment 17's refit other than the mask.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The results point to the onset step, not the forecast, as the place to look next. Recall in world A sits at 0.66 whatever the round, and 24 of the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 24 hours raise no alarm at their start (experiment 61). Experiment 69 tried weak alarms. They recovered some of the missed onsets but needed a higher threshold for the strong alarms, so the net gain was +0.007 (experiment 69). The candidates are a better onset statistic or the joint edge-flow fit of experiment 67 (SW2-15). This loop is not a candidate.

Code: ml-experiments/00068-sw2-5-train-detect-retrain-loop/, with every number printed by e00068_report.py and the figures drawn by e00068_charts.py.

docs.title: Experiment 69 (SW2-17, part of the LSC series): why do real transfers raise no alarm at their start?
docs.text:
Half of the 24 real load transfers with no alarm at their start are not a threshold problem. Accepting weaker alarms that a step back confirms did not help either, because the stricter threshold needed to hold the alarm count lost as much as the weak alarms gained. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand to neighbouring substations for some hours or days. A Primary substation is the 11 kV or 6.6 kV substation that feeds local distribution circuits. The single-step detector D0M raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of a substation's residual (measured power minus an XGBoost forecast that uses no past power) steps by 4.0 noise units or more. One noise unit is the usual size of that 24-hour step on a substation's odd-numbered months, so 4.0 noise units is a step four times the usual size. An unexplained alarm is an alarm more than 24 hours from any closure in NGED's switching log, and the detector's threshold is set so that it raises 80 unexplained alarms on odd-numbered months. Of the 35 labelled real transfers lasting more than 1 day, 24 have no D0M alarm within 2 hours of the start. We sorted those 24 by cause: 6 lie in gaps in the data, 3 where the monthly refit of the XGBoost forecast suppresses the alarm, 3 have an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start, 8 have a sharp step of 2 to 4 noise units, 2 have a step that is spread out or late, and 2 show no step. We then added known transfers to the power history and tested a paired low-threshold onset rule (PP) that also raises a weaker alarm when an opposite step of a matching size follows within 14 days. With the strong threshold tuned so that PP and D0M each raise 80 unexplained alarms on odd-numbered months, PP found 0.675 of the moved power on transfers that start in even-numbered months, against 0.668 for the benchmark, a difference of +0.007 (98.75% interval -0.014 to +0.040). The benchmark is D0M's alarms with the better of two ways to end each alarm interval, and we confirmed on newly drawn transfers that the better way is PF14: end at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step. The alternative, PE14, ends at the strongest opposite step within 14 days.

PF14, PE14, and PP use up to 14 days of hindsight, so they serve training-time masks (the SW2-12 experiment) and the event table for National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), not live forecast inputs.

docs.title: What we tested
docs.text:
Three steps, all scored on injected transfers or on the labelled real transfers, never on forecasts. All scores are shares of the moved power in MW (MW-weighted recall): a transfer counts as found when an alarm interval starts within 2 hours of the true start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration.

  • Step 1, confirm PF14. New injected transfers: 1,160 in the headline band (25% to 40% of the receiving load, lasting over 1 day; 625 start in even months) and 400 lasting 15.6 to 60 days (206 start in even months), under five injection shapes. The headline pools the three shapes (S2, S3, and S4) that no detector in this series assumes: a constant MW, a share of each receiver's profile, and a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers. PE14 ends each interval at the strongest opposite step within 14 days, and PF14 at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step.
  • Step 2, sort the 24 unalarmed real transfers into seven classes by the first test that applies, using the 24-hour step statistic in noise units and D0M's alarms, with control windows (windows in odd months with no logged closure nearby) that show how large the largest step is by chance.
  • Step 3, PP. PP raises every D0M alarm at a strong threshold, and also a weak alarm at half that threshold when a later opposite step of the same size (0.5 to 2.0 times) follows within 14 days. The strong threshold is tuned on odd months so that PP and D0M both raise 80 unexplained alarms, and the contrasts are read on even months with 98.75% intervals from resampling whole calendar months. The arm S raises only the strong alarms of PP.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
inconclusive for PP by the rule fixed in the plan: the lower end of C1 is below zero and its upper end is above +0.02. The interval does not exclude a gain of +0.04. The point values say that PP is no better than the benchmark: C1 is +0.007 on the headline-band transfers and C2 is -0.006 on the long transfers. The benchmark end rule is PF14, because the lower ends of A1 and A2 both lie above zero.

Contrast (even months, S2, S3, and S4 pooled) Change in MW-weighted recall Reading A1, PF14 minus PE14, 625 fresh headline-band transfers +0.038 (+0.016 to +0.077) PF14 confirmed A2, PF14 minus PE14, 206 fresh long transfers +0.416 (+0.059 to +0.595) PF14 confirmed C1, PP minus PF14, headline band +0.007 (-0.014 to +0.040) No gain C2, PP minus PF14, long transfers -0.006 (-0.063 to +0.018) No gain

Recall rises by +0.146 with the weak alarms and falls by 0.140 with the stronger threshold. The control arm S raises only the strong alarms of PP, at the threshold of 6.55 (S itself raises only 4 unexplained alarms on odd months, so it is not at the same alarm count as PP). S finds 0.528 of the moved MW on the headline-band transfers (0.345 to 0.625), a difference of -0.140 from PF14 (-0.221 to -0.089), and PP finds 0.146 more than S (+0.091 to +0.253). The version of PP with the weak threshold at three quarters of the strong one, tuned separately to a strong threshold of 4.65, differs from PF14 by +0.008 (-0.004 to +0.027).

For PF14 on the headline band, 0.298 of the moved MW sits in transfers with no alarm at the start and 0.034 in transfers whose start was found and whose end was wrong. For PP the two shares are 0.304 and 0.021.

Most of the extra unexplained alarms are weak ones. At D0M's threshold of 4.0, PP would raise 673 odd-month unexplained alarms, of which 593 are weak. Only a strong threshold of 6.55 brings the count to 77, of which 73 are weak (figure 4). No threshold below 6.55 on the grid from 4.0 to 9.0 brought the count down to 80. On even months, which were not used to tune the threshold, PP raises 56 unexplained alarms and D0M 80, so PP raises fewer alarms than D0M there and the comparison does not favour PP.

The table counts transfers found out of transfers, summed over S2, S3, and S4, on the fresh headline-band transfers that start in even months, in 24-hour noise units. docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Held: A1 (+0.038, predicted +0.02 to +0.06), C1 (+0.007, predicted -0.15 to +0.03), and C2 (-0.006, predicted -0.15 to 0.00). The lowest strong threshold that keeps 80 alarms, 6.55, was known before any transfer was scored.
  • Just outside: A2 at +0.416, against a predicted +0.10 to +0.40 and a predicted size smaller than experiment 66's +0.412.
  • Not held: PE14 was expected to stay the benchmark, and PF14 became it. The classification was predicted to put at least 12 of 24 in classes under the threshold, and put 10 there. The first plan commit also predicted at most 4 in the data gap class (6 are) and 2 to 6 more real transfers found by PP than the benchmark's 8 (PP finds 2 fewer).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The end rule and PP need up to 14 days of hindsight, so they serve training-time masks and the event table, not live inputs.
  • A fresh draw is new in the placement of transfers and in the injection noise only. It uses the same table of residuals, series, months, and set of 25 long operations as experiment 66, so the confirmation cannot detect a rule that fits quirks of that panel. On odd months the gain of PF14 over PE14 is smaller: +0.010 (-0.005 to +0.031) on the headline band and +0.333 (0.000 to +0.560) on the long set.
  • PP and the benchmark are scored on the same fresh draws that chose PF14 as the benchmark.
  • Injected transfers are exact rectangular steps up and then down, so a matching step back always exists, which favours PP. PP gained nothing even so.
  • Weak alarms can chain: a weak alarm can itself be the step back of an earlier weak alarm.
  • Alarms within 24 hours of a logged closure count as explained, for both arms.
  • The weak threshold of half the strong one and the ratio range of 0.5 to 2.0 are the first values tried and were not tuned; the version at three quarters is the only other value tried.
  • The 35 real transfers are too few for an interval, and the class counts rest on a log whose start times may be late or early by hours.
  • The control windows draw an independent stamp for each series of a transfer, so they are a fair test of the largest step but not of a step shared across series at one stamp.

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
• Plan review (Sonnet agent): accepted control windows for the classification, an exhaustive verdict rule, a full-grid tuning scan, a control arm of strong alarms only, a check that PP with the weak alarms disabled equals D0M, named seeds and ids, and a note on boxcar favouritism. Accepted a prediction about the benchmark end rule. Rejected a second-series consistency requirement for the pair and a minimum duration, because the plan tests the simplest rule first.

  • Code review (Sonnet agent): found no leakage. Accepted a NaN-safe quantile, a clamp on slice starts, a stricter refit test, and a hand-built test of the pairing rule's boundaries. Rejected extending the harness check to PP (the control arm S already isolates it) and excluding refit windows from the controls (the effect is conservative).

  • Fact check against the printed report (Sonnet agent): every number matched. Accepted replacing "most" with "half" for the transfers that are not a threshold problem, deleting an unsupported comparison with a lower threshold, softening two causal claims, saying that the control arm S is not at the same alarm count as PP, and renaming the classes-table column. Rejected nothing.

  • Prose review (Sonnet agent): accepted defining D0M, PP, PF14, PE14, noise units, unexplained alarms, and the benchmark in the opening, stating that the threshold is tuned on odd months and scored on even months, splitting the bold lead, describing the pooled shapes, defining control windows at first use, renumbering the figures, and renaming the closing section so that it commits the project to nothing. Rejected rewriting the pre-registered front matter (the plan commit fixes it), apart from the arithmetic restatement "2% of the moved MW".

docs.title: Two untested options
docs.text:
Two options could recover onsets that a lower threshold cannot reach, and neither has been tested. Of the 24 unalarmed real transfers, 3 have a largest step above the control windows that the monthly refit suppresses, and 3 have an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start. A detector that survives a refit, or a scorer that allows 12 hours at the start, could add up to 6 more onsets among the 35 (their ends were not tested), and the 6 in data gaps are unobservable. A second series that must confirm each weak pair is a possible way to cut the 593 weak alarms that a single series raises at 4.0.

Code: ml-experiments/00069-sw2-17-missed-onsets-of-the-end-rule/, with every number printed by e00069_report.py.

docs.title: Experiment 70 (SW2-19, an LSC experiment): does counting the neighbours that step the same way find more moved load?
docs.text:
Counting how many neighbouring substations step in the same direction as the alarming substation finds more of the moved load on injected transfers, so the count is worth testing again on more real transfers. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain. The planned contrast is supported.

We asked whether a detector for load transfers finds more of them when its alarm score uses the count of neighbouring substations that step the same way as the alarming substation. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor) onto neighbouring substations (the receivers) for some hours or days. A Primary substation is the 11 kV or 6.6 kV substation that feeds local distribution circuits.

The benchmark detector is PF14. It raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of a substation's residual (measured power minus an XGBoost forecast that uses no past power) steps by 4.0 noise units or more. One noise unit is the usual size of that 24-hour step on odd-numbered months. PF14 then ends the alarm at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step, the first-return end rule of experiment 69. LOGIT is a logistic score on a candidate alarm's own step, the largest opposite-sign step among its neighbours, and its number of neighbours. LOGIT_SAME adds the number of neighbours that step the same way.

We added known transfers to the power history of 16 Primary substations and counted the share of the moved megawatts (MW) that each detector found. A transfer counts as found when an alarm starts within 2 hours of its start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration. Each detector was held to 80 unexplained alarms on odd months, meaning alarms more than 24 hours from any closure in the switching log of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED).

On 615 fresh transfers per injection shape, all starting in even months, LOGIT_SAME found 0.712 of the moved MW against PF14's 0.665. The difference is +0.048 (97.5% interval +0.021 to +0.096, from resampling whole calendar months). The share of moved MW missed falls from 0.335 to 0.288. The injection shapes are three ways of spreading the moved power over the receivers; the Verdict section names them.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
The hypothesis is supported. C1, LOGIT_SAME minus PF14 on the fresh headline-band draw, has its lower end above zero (+0.021) and a point value above the threshold of +0.02. C2, the same contrast on the fresh long draw, is 0.000 (0.000 to 0.000), above the guard of -0.02. All intervals are 97.5% intervals, wide enough that the two planned contrasts together keep a 5% error rate (a Bonferroni correction), from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar months. The headline band is transfers that move 25% or more of the receiving load for over 1 day. The long draw is transfers of 15.6 to 60 days.

The injection shapes pool S2 (a constant MW), S3 (a share of the receiver's profile), and S4 (a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers), from experiment 60. None of the three is assumed by the scores, and they are pooled with equal weight.

The alarm ends use up to 14 days of hindsight, so the detector serves training-time masks and the NGED event table, not live forecast inputs.

Arm (even months, 80 odd-month unexplained alarms) Headline-band recall Share of MW missed Long-set recall PF14 (benchmark) 0.665 (0.555 to 0.745) 0.335 0.400 (0.092 to 0.562) LOGIT (no same-sign count) 0.688 (0.597 to 0.760) 0.312 0.402 (0.095 to 0.563) LOGIT_SAME 0.712 (0.621 to 0.793) 0.288 0.400 (0.092 to 0.562)

The same-sign count roughly doubles the gain of the logistic score. LOGIT minus PF14 is +0.024 (-0.004 to +0.061), and LOGIT_SAME minus LOGIT is +0.024 (+0.007 to +0.053). Both descriptive contrasts use the same 97.5% level and carry no verdict. On odd months, which the scores were fitted on, LOGIT_SAME minus PF14 is +0.050 (+0.017 to +0.096).

The gain did not come from raising more alarms. Even-month unexplained alarms were 80 for PF14, 54 for LOGIT, and 61 for LOGIT_SAME, against exactly 80 on the odd months for all three.

docs.title: Where the gain sits
docs.text:
The gain sits in transfers with no metered receiver, where the donor step is 2 to 6 noise units. A metered receiver is a receiver whose own power is measured. Counts here are transfers summed over S2, S3, and S4. Without a metered receiver, PF14 finds 68 of 537 such transfers, LOGIT finds 118, and LOGIT_SAME finds 167. With a metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4 noise units, LOGIT_SAME finds 84 of 135 against PF14's 85, so it gains nothing there. Without a metered receiver and with a step of 4 to 6, LOGIT_SAME finds 146 of 257 against PF14's 125 of the same 257. The experiment does not test why the gain is confined to transfers with no metered receiver.

By injection shape the contrast is similar. LOGIT_SAME minus PF14 is +0.046 for S2, +0.050 for S3, and +0.047 for S4. It is +0.049 for S1 (the donor's own profile) and +0.039 for S5 (that profile shifted by 12 hours). All five have their lower end above zero.

docs.title: Long transfers and labelled real transfers
docs.text:
Long transfers gain nothing. The long-set recall of PF14 and LOGIT_SAME is 0.400 for both, and C2 is 0.000. The share of MW with no alarm at the start falls from 0.365 to 0.326, and the share with a wrong end rises from 0.235 to 0.275, so the extra onsets do not become found transfers. The experiment does not test why.

On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day, LOGIT_SAME found 7 and PF14 found 8. An alarm started within 2 hours of the labelled start for 12 with LOGIT_SAME and 11 with PF14. The 35 transfers are too few to rank the arms, so the real data do not confirm the injected result.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The scores are fitted on transfers drawn by the same code that draws the test transfers. Training uses odd months of the draw of experiment 58 and scoring uses even months of a draw with new seeds, but both draws choose donors and receivers the same way. Real transfers may look different, and the 7 of 35 does not confirm the gain.
  • The fitted weights are shrunk very little. The standardised logistic coefficients are 2.66 on the own step, 2.44 on the largest opposite neighbour step, -1.02 on the number of neighbours, and -0.85 on the same-sign count, from 2,230 positive and 507 negative candidates. The neighbour count may be a stand-in for how well a substation is connected.
  • The return-step threshold is looser for the scores' alarms. The first-return end rule needs a return step of half the onset step. The scores raise alarms with onset steps of 2.5 to 4 noise units, so their return threshold is lower than PF14's, a second effect on top of the better alarm ranking.
  • The candidate floor of 2.5 noise units caps recall. Steps below it cannot be found.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does the same-sign count survive a labelled set of real transfers large enough to separate the arms? The injected transfers show a gain of about +0.05, and the 35 real transfers cannot confirm or refute it. The detector series could next test the score on the transfers labelled in a later period, or combine it with the refit and gap fixes of SW2-18.

docs.title: Experiment 71 (SW2-18, part of the LSC series): does ignoring alarms near a refit make the detector miss load transfers?
docs.text:
The detector ignored every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its forecasting model. Lifting that rule recovers about 5% of the moved power, and the second model that we added to replace the ignored alarms adds nothing to the recovery on injected transfers. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the 11 kV or 6.6 kV substation feeding local distribution circuits) to neighbouring substations for some hours or days. The single-step detector D0M subtracts an XGBoost forecast that uses no past power from the measured power, averages that residual over 24 hours, and raises an alarm when the average steps by 4.0 noise units or more. One noise unit is the usual size of that 24-hour step on a substation's odd-numbered months. The benchmark PF14 is D0M with a rule that ends each alarm interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step. A transfer counts as found when an alarm starts within 2 hours of its start and its end falls within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration. We score each detector by MW-weighted recall, the share of the moved power in megawatts (MW) that sits in found transfers.

Three changes to the detector were tested on injected transfers: synthetic transfers added to the substations' real power history. The XGBoost model is refitted on the 1st of every month, and PF14 ignores every alarm within 24 hours of a refit, so a transfer that starts there is never found. Arm X adds a second residual model refitted on the 16th. At each stamp the step statistic comes from the first model, except within 24 hours of the first model's refit, where it comes from the second model. Arm G makes the step statistic bridge data gaps of a day or longer. Arm XG makes both changes. Each arm's alarm threshold is set so that it raises at most 80 unexplained alarms (alarms more than 24 hours from any closure in the logbook of National Grid Electricity Distribution, NGED) on odd-numbered months, and all contrasts are read on transfers that start in even-numbered months. Arm X found 0.715 of the moved power against 0.665 for PF14, a gain of +0.050 (98.33% interval +0.012 to +0.107; 98.33% is 95% corrected for three planned contrasts). The whole gain lies in the transfers that start or end within 24 hours of a refit. Of the 3 real transfers that start at a refit, arm X found all 3, where PF14 found none.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
supported by the rule fixed in the plan: the lower end of C1 lies above zero and its point value is at least +0.01.

PF14 misses 0.335 of the moved MW and X misses 0.285, mostly in transfers with no alarm at the start. The missed share is one minus the recall. For PF14, 0.301 of the moved MW sits in transfers with no alarm at the start and 0.035 in transfers whose start was found and whose end was wrong. For X the two shares are 0.265 and 0.019. Each arm's threshold is the lowest on a 0.05 grid whose odd-month count of unexplained alarms is at most 80. The injected shapes S2, S3, and S4 are a constant MW moved, a share of each receiver's own profile, and a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers. The headline band is the injected transfers moving 25% to 40% of the receiving load for over 1 day, and the long set is the transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days.

docs.title: The gain sits in the refit zones
docs.text:
The gain comes from transfers that start or end within 24 hours of a refit, and the 13% of transfers in that zone carry all of it. A zone is the 24 hours either side of a refit of the model refitted on the 1st. Of the 615 headline-band transfers per shape that start in even months, 81 per shape start or end in a zone. PF14 finds 0.177 of the moved MW there and X gains +0.431 (+0.182 to +0.696). Outside the zones X is slightly worse, -0.005 (-0.011 to -0.001), because the alarm threshold rises from 4.0 to 4.1 to hold the alarm count. We also drew 300 further transfers with onsets forced into a zone, of which 149 start in even months. On those 149, PF14 finds 0.000 and X finds 0.689, a gain of +0.689 (+0.420 to +0.845), which shows the mechanism cleanly.

The second model does not improve on lifting the suppression for injected transfers. The control L only stops ignoring alarms near a refit and keeps the first model throughout. L finds 0.720 and X 0.715. L raises 84 unexplained alarms on even months where X raises 80. A real alarm is an alarm on the real residual, with no transfer injected. Of L's 311 real alarms, 73 lie within 24 hours of a refit of either model, against 66 of X's 297 and 46 of PF14's 297. The refit jump therefore produces a few extra alarms in L, and those extra alarms are too few to lower L's recall.

docs.title: Gaps, and the real transfers
docs.text:
Gap bridging changes no outcome, because the panel has nothing to bridge. The residual panel holds 188 gaps inside its 16 series. Only 7 last 13 half-hours or longer, and only 3 last a day or longer. G differs from PF14 in the outcome of 0 of 1,860 injected transfers (the 1,160 headline-band, 400 long, and 300 zone-drawn transfers, under one shape). The 6 real transfers that experiment 69 called "data gap" all lie on series 12 and 13, whose residual panel holds no rows before March 2026 (series 12) and February 2026 (series 13), so there is no data on either side of those transfers to bridge.

X finds 10 of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, against 8 for PF14. Its MW-weighted recall is 0.350 against 0.156. The 3 real transfers that start at a refit are 3.9, 2.5, and 2.0 MW; X raises an onset alarm for all 3, and L for 2 of them. X also finds one further transfer of 1.0 MW whose onset PF14 found but whose end PF14 placed wrongly. X loses two small transfers (0.6 and 0.5 MW) when the alarm threshold rises to 4.1, so the 8 found by PF14 become 8 + 4 - 2 = 10. The other 21 of the 24 transfers with no PF14 alarm at the start are unchanged under every arm: 6 in "data gap", 3 with an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the start, 8 with a sharp step of 2 to 4 noise units, 2 with a spread or late step, and 2 with no visible step. | Class of the 24 transfers with no PF14 alarm | Transfers | Onset alarm under X | Found under X | |---|---|---|---| | Monthly refit | 3 | 3 | 3 | | Data gap | 6 | 0 | 0 | | Alarm outside the 2-hour tolerance | 3 | 0 | 0 | | Sharp step of 2 to 4 noise units | 8 | 0 | 0 | | Spread or late step of 2 to 4 noise units | 2 | 0 | 0 | | No step visible | 2 | 0 | 0 |

docs.text:
X finds more of the steps of 6 or more noise units with a metered receiver and more of the 4 to 6 unit steps with no metered receiver, and one fewer at 4 to 6 units with a metered receiver. The donor is the substation that loses load and a receiver is a substation that gains it; a receiver is metered when its power is in the telemetry. The table counts transfers found out of transfers, summed over S2, S3, and S4, on the headline-band transfers that start in even months, by the donor's step in 24-hour noise units. The table omits donor steps under 2 noise units (143 transfers with a metered receiver, of which each arm finds 8, and 66 with none, of which each arm finds none) and the 13 transfers with an unmetered receiver and a step of 6 to 10 (PF14 finds 7 and X 10). The printed report also gives G, XG, and L.
