  • am_sy, am_sy_twin, am_wk: experiment 64's fitted am and am_twin models, predicted with the capacity of the season-year vintage (am_sy, am_sy_twin) or the weekly vintage (am_wk). Nothing is refitted, so the weights and the capacity in the training margin stay experiment 64's.
  • d1l_r, d0_r, d0_m0: d1l and d0 refitted here with experiment 64's recipe and seeds, and d0 refitted with a zero base margin.

The season-year vintage re-fits experiment 45's season-year constant before each forecast run. The fit uses the usable half-hours of the weeks up to two weeks before the Monday of the run's week, and divides by experiment 45's recovery ratio. The recovery ratio is experiment 45's measured fraction of injected solar capacity that the fit recovers, and a usable half-hour is one with an observed power and a CAMS solar estimate. A run takes the capacity from the first of three steps that applies. Step 1 is the vintage's constant for the run's season-year (September to August), once that season-year has 8 observed weeks. Step 2 is the previous season-year's constant. Step 3 is experiment 64's held capacity. Step 1 supplied 84% of runs at D9, D10, and D16, 47% at D11, and 29% at D14. D14's weeks from 2023-09-04 to 2025-08-25 are unobserved, so step 3 supplies the other 71% of its runs. The weekly vintage averages the 4 latest observed weeks of experiment 45's frozen weekly fit (a free capacity per week with a fixed penalty on changes), from the vintage with the latest origin up to a week before the run.

docs.title: The estimated capacity rose 13% to 31% above the held value by May 2026
docs.text: The vintages move away from the held capacity in November 2025 and sit 13% to 31% above it in May 2026. D9's vintage falls 14% below the held value in November, and D10's and D16's rise 9% and 10% above it. The season-year vintage in June 2026 is 3.0 MW at D9 (held 2.751 MW), 2.9 at D10 (2.356), 4.3 at D11 (3.457), 4.8 at D14 (3.705), and 4.6 at D16 (3.578), against experiment 45's final 2025/26 constants of 2.9, 2.9, 4.1, 4.2, and 4.4. The weekly vintage is higher and noisier. In November 2025 the new season-year's own constant takes over at D9, which is why the vintage there falls (2.37 MW against 2.75). Experiment 45 found that the latest weeks of a real-time fit are the least accurate.

docs.title: The gain is small and sits mostly in May 2026
docs.text:
The point estimate is negative at every lead, but only the 2-to-6-day and 10-days-and-beyond intervals exclude zero. The effect is almost zero at 10 days and beyond. The point estimates of am_sy minus am are -0.039 (-0.097 to +0.014) at 0 to 24 hours, -0.027 (-0.061 to +0.003) at 1 to 2 days, -0.029 (-0.053 to -0.009) at 2 to 6 days, -0.013 (-0.032 to +0.003) at 6 to 10 days, and -0.006 (-0.012 to -0.001) at 10 days and beyond. By valid month, the read is about zero from July to September 2025 (the vintage is within 4% of the held capacity there), -0.035 (-0.097 to +0.002) in April 2026, -0.058 (-0.100 to -0.028) in May, and -0.008 (-0.021 to +0.015) in June. At D16 the read is -0.045 (-0.073 to -0.020), at D14 -0.022 (-0.044 to -0.002), at D10 -0.018 (-0.034 to -0.003), at D11 -0.012 (-0.032 to +0.005), and at D9 +0.006 (-0.003 to +0.018). These reads are exploratory, at 95%.

The weekly vintage does no better than the season-year vintage. am_wk minus am_sy is -0.005 (-0.013 to +0.003), and am_wk minus am is -0.023 (-0.042 to -0.007) over all leads and -0.054 (-0.116 to +0.004) under 48 hours. A weekly refresh would lower the score by a further 0.005 points at most, which the intervals do not separate from zero. Restricted to runs where step 1 supplied the capacity, am_sy minus am is -0.022 (-0.037 to -0.008), so the fallback to the held value dilutes the effect slightly.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Mean quantile score in points of capacity, after the 14-day correction and the 1.15 spread factor.

Arm All leads Under 48 hours 10 days and beyond am_wk 4.444 3.717 4.896 am_sy 4.449 3.739 4.898 am 4.467 3.772 4.904 d0_m0 4.550 3.966 4.916 d0 4.620 4.044 4.986 d0_r 4.620 4.044 4.987 am0 4.640 4.237 4.939 d1l_r 4.723 4.342 5.025 d1l 4.724 4.343 5.025 am_twin 4.767 4.478 4.975 am_sy_twin 4.807 4.570 4.982

The climatology scores 5.272 on the 68,863 rows it holds (a month-by-half-hour mean, experiment 64). The wrong-date twin gets worse when the capacity grows: am_sy_twin minus am_twin is +0.040 (+0.022 to +0.058), as expected for a solar term that carries no timing information.

docs.title: XGBoost's estimated starting point raises the score by 0.07 to 0.10 points
docs.text:
A refit of d1l in this pipeline scores the same as experiment 46's stored d1l, so the gap that experiment 76 saw is not a difference between pipelines. d1l_r minus d1l is -0.0004 (-0.0020 to +0.0013), and d0_r minus d0 is +0.0004 (-0.0018 to +0.0025).

Contrast Difference 98.33% interval D1: d1l_r minus am0, 10 days and beyond, no 14-day correction +0.102 +0.035 to +0.169 D2: d0_r minus d0_m0, 10 days and beyond, no 14-day correction +0.089 +0.028 to +0.153 D3: d1l_r minus am0, all leads +0.084 +0.053 to +0.121

The pre-registered rule reads D1 as a real starting-point effect: the lower end of D1 is above zero and its point estimate is above 0.05. D2 gives the same reading for d0. Over all leads, d0_m0 minus d0_r is -0.071 (-0.099 to -0.047, exploratory), and under 48 hours -0.078 (-0.118 to -0.036).

XGBoost estimates one base score per quantile level, and the score rises with the level. For d0_r at D9 it runs from 0.403 at the 0.05 level to 0.899 at the 0.95 level (power over capacity), and it is identical across seeds and for d1l_r. The recipe trains a fixed 500 rounds at a learning rate of 0.05, with no early stopping, so no interaction with early stopping exists. The reason a start at zero scores better is not tested here.

The solar term survives the correction for the starting point. am_sy is 0.100 points (-0.142 to -0.061) below d0_m0 over all leads and 0.227 (-0.361 to -0.103) under 48 hours (post hoc, exploratory), against 0.171 and 0.305 below d0. Experiment 64's gain of am over d0, 0.152, is 0.082 (-0.113 to -0.052) over d0_m0.

docs.title: Which predictions held
docs.text: Prediction made in the plan Result C1 at -0.02 (-0.04 to 0.00) Held: -0.018 (-0.036 to -0.004) C2 at -0.04 (-0.09 to 0.00) Held in size: -0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012) am_wk the same as am_sy or 0.00 to 0.05 higher Held for "the same": -0.005 (-0.013 to +0.003) d1l_r 0.00 to 0.10 above am0 at 10 days and beyond, uncorrected Just above the range: +0.102 (+0.035 to +0.169) Verdict small gain or inconclusive small gain

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
1. The weekly vintage drops weeks older than 8 weeks before the run's Monday. The code review found that D14's weekly vintage would otherwise average weeks from 2023, from before the gap in its record. The change was made before any arm was scored.
  2. The first run of the statistics script grouped the bootstrap by month, not by week. A column name was wrong, so the intervals rested on 7 blocks. The corrected run uses 29 weeks. The verdict changed from refuted to small gain, so every number on this page comes from the corrected run.
  3. Six exploratory reads were added after the results were seen, and are labelled post hoc: d0_m0 against d0_r under 48 hours, am_sy and am against d0_m0 (each over all leads and under 48 hours), and am0 against d0_m0. The reads against d0_m0 carry the claim that the solar term survives a zero start.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The training margin keeps the held capacity. The weights, and the capacity inside every training row, are experiment 64's, so the contrast measures the capacity at prediction only. A refit with a vintage capacity in the training rows is a larger design that this experiment does not test.
  • The recovery ratio is the full-record value. Each vintage divides by one number per series, from experiment 45's injection test on the full record, so the vintages carry a small look-ahead that am and the vintage arms share.
  • One validation year and 29 weeks of forecast start. July to September 2025 and April to June 2026 are two seasons of one year, and the 2026 months hold the gain.
  • D14 keeps its held capacity for 71% of runs. The vintage for D14 matters only from March 2026.
  • The reason a zero start helps is not tested. The experiment shows the size, not the mechanism.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does a zero base margin help every XGBoost model in the production recipe, and at which leads? The effect is 0.07 to 0.10 points on the Primary demand models of this experiment, larger than the effect of the capacity, and it costs nothing in production. A test across the series and model types that the best guess d0 covers (BSP and GSP demand, solar, and wind) would settle whether the base score belongs to the production recipe. If the capacity matters for a later model release, the evidence here is consistent with refreshing the capacity table once a season-year.

docs.title: Reproducing the figures
docs.text:
uv run python ml-experiments/00078-pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages/e00078_capacity.py
bash ml-experiments/00078-pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages/e00078_run.sh
uv run python ml-experiments/00078-pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages/e00078_stats.py
uv run python ml-experiments/00078-pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages/e00078_charts.py
npx svgo@4 --multipass --precision=1 --final-newline figure_*.svg

The code is in ml-experiments/00078-pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages/.

docs.title: Experiment 79: can the direction of flow be recovered at Primaries metered only in MVA?
docs.text:
Hiding the sign of a Primary's power and recovering it works for the solar capacity, and finds the direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78 (0.5 is a guess), but the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA show almost no reverse flow to recover, and the one that might (Stickney) cannot be checked. A Primary is a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. At 7 of the 8 Primaries metered only in megavolt-amperes (MVA), the MVA reading can stand in for megawatts (MW) from April to September, so no fit is needed there. Stickney is the exception, and the next step is a few weeks of signed power from NGED for Stickney. The verdict is partly supported: the capacity part passed the pre-registered rule and the direction part did not.

We asked whether the direction of the power flowing through a Primary, and the capacity of the solar panels behind it, can be found from a meter that records only the size of the flow, not its direction. First we tested the method where the answer is known. We took the 8 Primaries whose meters record signed power in MW. We subtracted the recorded output of a real solar farm, scaled to the Primary's typical midday power (level 1.0) or to 1.5 times that (level 1.5), so that the flow reversed on sunny middays. Then we threw the sign away and asked the fit to recover the capacity and the direction. Last, we ran the same fit on the real readings of the 8 other Primaries, which are metered only in MVA. The median error of the fitted capacity was 0.09 to 0.11 of the capacity found by fitting the unhidden signed power. A fit that treated the magnitude as if it were signed (the naive fit) had median errors of 0.29 to 1.00. The fit gave the right direction of flow with a balanced accuracy of 0.78 to 0.81 (the mean of the share of reverse-flow half-hours and the share of forward-flow half-hours labelled correctly), or 0.82 to 0.86 after leaving out one Primary where reverse flow is the usual state. The balanced accuracy fell to 0.67 when the reading also held reactive power equal to 20% of midday power, which the fit does not know about. At 7 of the 8 real Primaries metered only in MVA, the fit found no reverse flow.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Capacity is identified, and direction is not, by the rule fixed before the run. In this rule, capacity needed a median relative error of at most 0.25 and an upper interval end below zero for the difference from the naive fit (contrast C1). Direction needed a balanced accuracy of at least 0.80 and a lower interval end of at least 0.25 above the all-positive guess of 0.5 (contrast C2). A window is one Primary in one April-to-September season, and the years run from September to August as in experiment 00073. Intervals are 99% from a bootstrap that resamples Primaries and then windows. The unfolding fit is the method under test: it alternates between choosing a sign for each half-hour and fitting the signed model to the signed series.

Injected solar Capacity error, unfolding fit Capacity error, naive fit C1: unfolding minus naive Balanced accuracy C2: accuracy minus 0.5 Level 1.0 (227 windows) 0.092 0.290 -0.198 (-0.409 to -0.068) 0.779 +0.279 (+0.157 to +0.337) Level 1.5 (227 windows) 0.113 1.000 -0.887 (-0.920 to -0.754) 0.811 +0.311 (+0.184 to +0.372)

Median relative capacity error against the signed fit, and balanced accuracy of the fitted flow direction, 8 MW Primaries and 6 farms. Four windows at level 1.0 and one at level 1.5 had too few reverse-flow half-hours to score for sign.

Against the capacity of the injected farm alone, the median error is 0.151 at level 1.0 and 0.073 at level 1.5, where against the signed fit it is 0.092 and 0.113, so the signed fit's own error is part of every figure in the table. Level 0.5 has little reverse flow at 7 of the 8 Primaries and is a no-signal check. The median relative capacity error is 0.004 for the unfolding fit and 0.001 for the naive fit, and the median fitted negative share is 0 (single windows reach 0.21). On the 30 windows of the 5 Primaries that almost never go negative, with no injection, the median fitted negative share is 0.0000, so the fit does not invent reverse flow. The no-injection check passes trivially for a fit that never finds reverse flow.

A reactive-power floor the fit cannot see lowers both parts quickly. The reading was sqrt(power² + q²) with q equal to 10%, 20%, or 40% of midday power (level 1.0). The unfolding fit's capacity error is 0.130, 0.309, and 0.529 against the naive fit's 0.331, 0.404, and 0.539, and its balanced accuracy is 0.756, 0.666, and 0.561. At 20%, three Primaries (Horncastle, Trusthorpe, and Donington) fall to a recall of reverse flow of 0.01 to 0.23. The reactive-power result is descriptive and did not change the verdict. A power factor of 1 is therefore a strong assumption for the direction, and nothing in this experiment measures the real reactive power at any Primary.

docs.title: Post hoc: Wrangle T1 and Stickney
docs.text:
One MW Primary, Wrangle T1, drags the direction score below its limit, and the same weakness may hide Stickney. Wrangle T1 is net generation on 59% to 94% of April-to-September daylight half-hours in its two seasons. With level 1.0 injected, the fit returns capacity 0 and no negative flow there, against a signed capacity of 1.73 MW, so its balanced accuracy is 0.5. Without it, the balanced accuracy is 0.819 (0.791 to 0.843) at level 1.0 and 0.856 (0.831 to 0.874) at level 1.5, with 0.69 and 0.77 of reverse-flow half-hours found and 0.95 and 0.94 of forward-flow half-hours kept. The split between Wrangle T1 and the other Primaries was chosen after seeing the result and does not change the verdict.

Stickney's reading rises on sunny middays, which is what reverse flow would look like, and the registered fit does not find reverse flow there. Stickney's median midday reading is about 2.4 times its typical reading on sunny days and about 0.8 times on cloudy days (figure 1). Ingoldmells is flat, and the other six MVA-only Primaries fall on sunny days by 1% to 38% of their typical reading. Experiment 00039 found a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. With extra starting sign patterns that flip every half-hour above a solar-output threshold (a post hoc change, not tried on the known answers) the fit reaches a capacity of 1.3 to 7.2 MW with a negative flow in 75% to 87% of daylight half-hours from 2021, and lowers the loss by 9% to 18% in 4 of 5 windows. Because the same fit fails at Wrangle T1, where the answer is known, the Stickney capacity from the post hoc starts is not evidence.

docs.title: The real series
docs.text: At 7 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries the fit finds no reverse flow, and its capacity equals the naive fit's (figure 4). The median fitted negative share is 0.0% at all of them except Stickney, where the registered fit gives 0.7% and a capacity of 0. The fitted capacities are 6.0 MW at Warth Lane Skegness, 2.5 at Sleaford Road Boston, 1.4 at Langrick, 1.1 at Alford, Chapel St Leonards, and Marsh Lane, and 0.7 at Ingoldmells. These capacities come from a fit that cannot be checked against signed power, and a load that tracks sunshine would give the same numbers. The 95th percentile of the negative share over resampled weeks is 0.095 at Ingoldmells, 0.054 at Stickney, and under 0.001 at the others. The 5th to 95th percentile of the fitted capacity runs from 0 to 3.4 MW at Ingoldmells and from 0 to 2.4 MW at Marsh Lane. The lowest midday readings are 0.017 MW at Stickney, 0.026 MW at Marsh Lane, and 0.099 MW at Langrick; the other five stay above 0.87 MW.

docs.title: Failures and caveats
docs.text:
• All 6 solar farms (A to F) are used for the injection, because the fit has no tuning parameter that could be chosen to favour a farm. The 8 MW Primaries are 8 independent clusters in the bootstrap, so every conclusion about direction rests on 8 Primaries, one of them an outlier.
  • The capacity truth is the signed fit, so a capacity error here measures the unfolding step and not the real solar capacity. Real capacity at the MVA-only Primaries has no truth.
  • Natural reverse flow, with no injection, gave only 5 eligible windows (Spilsby in three season-years and Wrangle T1 in two), so known answer (4) of the plan says little. Spilsby's recall of reverse flow is 0.35.
  • The unfolding fit's starting sign patterns are sized from the magnitude reading alone, and not from the scale that sizes the injection, so the fit never begins at the answer.
  • The fit's capacity at the MVA-only Primaries uses the fleet shape (0.2 east, 0.6 south, 0.2 west at a DC:AC ratio of 1.15) and the nuisance terms of experiment 00073. The capacity is not corrected for the 0.77 recovery that experiment 00039 found.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text: The sign can be recovered where reverse flow is sometimes present, and the capacity follows, but the fit has no validated answer for a Primary that exports power on most sunny days. Wrangle T1 is the known answer where the fit fails, and Stickney is the real Primary that looks like Wrangle T1. The registered starts and the post hoc starts both need a known answer in that regime before any Stickney value is quoted.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Does a starting pattern that flips every daylight half-hour of the clearest days recover the capacity and direction at Wrangle T1, and, if so, does the pattern give a consistent answer at Stickney? The threshold-flip starts of the post hoc section already return capacity 0 at Wrangle T1 in both seasons. The test should use injection at levels where reverse flow is the usual state (level 2.0 and above), keep the 50-row sign rule, and add the post hoc starts to the self-tests. The test should also check that the other seven MVA-only Primaries, which show no reverse flow, still return the naive fit. Signed power from NGED for Stickney on even a few days would settle the question without a fit.

docs.title: The plan as registered
docs.text:
Question. Eight of the 16 trial-area Primaries have a meter that records only the magnitude of apparent power (MVA). When embedded solar pushes net flow through zero, that reading bounces off zero and shows no direction. NGED cannot supply real and reactive power at these 8, so the only route to MW is the model. The fit assumes a power factor of 1.

Method. Each window's model is as in experiment 00073: power equals a calendar cell (month, half-hour, day type) plus heating degree-days and cloud terms, minus a capacity c >= 0 times a solar shape (the fleet orientation mix of 0.2 east, 0.6 south, and 0.2 west at 25° tilt, clipped at a DC:AC ratio of 1.15). The unfolding fit sees only |power|. It starts from a set of sign patterns (all positive, and the patterns implied by capacities of 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 times the window's median absolute midday power), alternates between fitting the model to sign x |power| and resetting each sign to the sign of the fitted value, and keeps the start with the lowest squared error. The naive fit is the first pass of the all-positive start.

Known answers. (1) Injected: the output of each metered solar farm (A to F, normalised to a 99th percentile of 1) is scaled and subtracted from each of the 8 MW Primaries' power, at levels 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 times the window's median absolute midday power, then the sign is hidden. The truth is the signed fit to the same series. (2) Reactive floor: the same at level 1.0, with sqrt(power^2 + q^2) taken as the reading, where q is 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4 times the window's median absolute midday power, unknown to the fit. Only 0.2 enters a contrast (C3). (3) No injection: the sign of the five MW Primaries that almost never go negative is hidden, and the share of half-hours where the fitted flow is negative counts false reverse flow. (4) Natural reverse flow: Wrangle T1 and T2 and Spilsby go negative in the real data; the sign is hidden and recovered with no injection, where a window has at least 20 reverse-flow half-hours.

Self-tests. On a synthetic series with a known capacity and no noise, the fit recovers it to 1%. On series with capacity 0 and a small capacity that never nears zero, the unfolding fit returns an all-positive sign pattern. A start that flips the signs wins only if it lowers the loss by more than 0.5% of the all-positive start's loss. The run records, per window, the number of distinct capacities the starts reach and the loss gap between the best and second-best start. Before any fit runs, a script tabulates the reverse-flow rows per window and level, and the midday minimum of the magnitude at each MVA-only Primary, to show whether level 1.0 resembles the real series.

Size. Medium. What gets stored: private tables only. Serving path: untouched. Degradation rule: untouched. More than one defensible design: yes (alternating signs, a grid over capacity, or a mixture fit), so the plan is reviewed once. Callers: the experiment copies experiment 00073's fitting code, and nothing imports it.

Earlier advice followed. Experiments 00039 and 00056: leave the MVA Primaries out of a signed capacity estimate (here they are fitted with the unfolding fit and reported apart), and report the share of near-zero half-hours. Experiment 00039: injection into a linear fit tests the shape only; the magnitude link is non-linear, so injection tests the fit here. Experiment 00045: use the season-year constant capacity, which this experiment does. No earlier advice item is departed from.

docs.title: Experiment 80: does a zero starting value lower the error of the production XGBoost models? (BM0)
docs.text:
Take-home message: starting an XGBoost model from zero instead of from its own estimate does not lower the error of the forecasts that serve, so the zero start is not worth porting. The gain of 0.071 points that experiment 78 found for its reference model did not appear for Primary substation demand, bulk and grid supply point demand, or solar farms, where every difference was under 0.04 points of capacity with an interval that includes zero. For wind XGBoost models without a power-curve margin a zero start was worse by 0.049 points. Four times as many boosting rounds did not help either start. The verdict is inconclusive, which here means that no gain could be shown.

XGBoost's quantile model begins from a starting prediction (the base score) that it estimates from the training labels, one value for each of the nine quantile levels. We refitted XGBoost models for four classes of series with a starting prediction of zero, and compared them with the stored models of experiment 48, which use the estimated start, on the same 292 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The classes are Primary substations (the 33 kV or 66 kV to 11 kV transformers) and bulk and grid supply points (the larger sites above them), all retrained weekly, plus solar farms and wind farms, retrained monthly. We also asked whether more boosting rounds (500 are used now), or early stopping, make the estimated start catch up. The score is the quantile score, an error measure in which lower is better, and 1 point is 1% of a series' capacity.

Each dot is the difference in mean quantile score; negative means the zero start is better.

The zero-start gap does not close with more rounds; the early-stopping dots compare the two starts at different stopping rounds.

The zero start begins far behind and approaches the estimated start by about 250 rounds.

  • Arms: the estimated start (experiment 48's stored predictions) against a zero start (base_score 0, the same XGBoost model as a zero base margin), refitted here with the same rows, weights, seed 0, and spread factor 1.15, and for C3 the 14-day correction. Arm scores below use every run of the arm; the differences use only the runs both arms share.
  • Row set: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 292 daily runs; intervals resample whole origin months.
  • C1, Primary substations, weekly refits: 5.104 against 5.119 points; difference -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054). Per series the difference ranges from -0.107 to +0.151.
  • C2, bulk and grid supply points, weekly refits: the 2 bulk supply series score 9.417 against 9.409 and the 2 grid supply series 17.258 against 17.223; difference +0.006 (-0.091 to +0.092).
  • C3, Primary substations, frozen XGBoost model with the 14-day correction: 5.302 against 5.339; difference -0.033 (-0.084 to +0.031).
  • C4, solar farms, monthly refits: 4.961 against 4.971; difference -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028).
  • Wind (exploratory, 95%): experiment 48's wind XGBoost model supplies a power-curve base margin, which makes XGBoost ignore its starting value, so a zero start changes nothing there. On wind XGBoost models without the margin the zero start scores 11.100 against 11.051 (+0.049, +0.032 to +0.065), and the model with the margin scores 10.989.
  • Held-out loss by round: on the 90 days before the training end, the mean pinball loss at Primary substations is 0.122 for the zero start against 0.045 for the estimated start at round 10, 0.0288 against 0.0283 at round 250, and 0.0246 against 0.0214 at round 500.
  • Rounds (exploratory, 95%): at 8 Primary substations the zero-start gap is +0.015 (-0.067 to +0.101) at 500 rounds, +0.112 (+0.031 to +0.204) at 1,000, and +0.150 (+0.071 to +0.243) at 2,000. The gap is not detectable at 500 rounds and grows with more rounds, so the rule "removed by more rounds" is not met for any class. With the estimated start, 2,000 rounds scored 0.211 points worse than 500 (+0.100 to +0.352) at Primary substations.
  • Early stopping (exploratory): on the last 90 days before the training end, the stopping round ranged from 90 to 1,292 at the demand series. Against its own matched 500-round prefix, early stopping with the estimated start gained -0.011 (-0.032 to +0.008) at Primary substations and -0.035 (-0.070 to -0.003) at solar farms. The comparison of the two starts at each start's own stopping round (+0.431 at Primary substations) mostly reflects different stopping rounds.
  • Noise floor: GPU fits are not bit-reproducible. A repeat fit of the estimated-start frozen XGBoost model scored +0.004 (Primary substations) and -0.007 (grid supply points) points from experiment 48's stored predictions, above the planned tolerance of 0.001 and well below the intervals. In the weekly repeat fits, single quantiles moved by up to 0.06 of capacity.
  • Deviations, made before any result was read: weekly zero-start refits cover every second weekly refit (26 of 52), because all 52 would have taken about 35 hours on the shared GPU. The differences therefore use half the runs (1.7 million of 3.2 million Primary-substation cases, 417,000 of 785,000 supply-point cases). The rounds family covers every second Primary substation (8 of 16) and all 4 bulk and grid supply series, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms. The reproduction check covers 2 weekly refits, not 4, and the planned tolerance was exceeded.
  • Caveats: one seed, so intervals reflect months only; with 4 bulk and grid supply series, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms the intervals are wide; the early-stopping held-out block is not purged of runs that began before the cut.
  • Next: at the Primary substations, the median best round on the held-out block is 373, so fewer than 500 rounds may be enough; the number of rounds, not the starting value, is the open question.

docs.title: Experiment 81: do the weekly-retraining findings hold on a second set of forecast runs, July 2023 to March 2024?
docs.text:
Take-home: refitting the XGBoost demand model every week, with no error correction, scored better than the stack again, on forecast runs from a different period, by 0.24 points of capacity (experiment 48 found 0.20), so the case for porting weekly retraining now rests on two periods. The stack is an XGBoost model fitted once, with a 14-day correction built from its recent errors. The gain is concentrated: without three substations (D8, D12, and D5, which carried experiment 48), it is 0.09 points (95% interval -0.19 to -0.01). Weekly retraining beat monthly retraining by 0.04 points. The four-model blend gained a further 0.04 points, short of the 0.05 needed to justify serving it. The verdict is supported.

We scored the Primary demand forecasts of 13 substations (the 16 of experiments 48 and 49 less three with no data in the period) on 274 daily runs from 2023-07 to 2024-03. For those runs the project holds only the control member of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS), so every number is a control-only number and no absolute score is comparable with experiments 48 or 49. The error is the quantile score in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a substation's capacity); smaller is better. The weather product changed from 18 km to 9 km resolution on 2023-06-27, which matters below.

  • Arms: the stack; weekly, monthly, and rolling-12-month refits (half-life 0.5 years, which halves the weight of data every half year; no correction); rolling without the Christmas column (the input counting days to 25 December); rolling with a 2-year half-life; a blend of weekly, monthly, rolling, and stack. Baselines: manual_heuristic and climatology. Every arm uses a spread factor of 1.15 that widens its quantiles.
  • Rows: fold B is control_fold_b_daily_v1 (274 runs, 2023-07-01 to 2024-03-31, 9 km). Fold C is control_fold_c_daily_v1 (273 runs, 2022-07-01 to 2023-03-31, 18 km, 15 months of training history). Seed 0. Intervals use 4-week blocks of forecast start (10 blocks).
  • Absolute scores, fold B: blend 4.457, weekly 4.494, monthly 4.533, rolling 4.681, stack 4.734, manual_heuristic 5.211, climatology 5.700 (95% intervals plus or minus 0.3 to 0.5). Fold C: weekly 4.020, monthly 4.054, rolling 4.073, stack 4.100, manual_heuristic 4.845, climatology 6.099.
  • C1, weekly minus the stack: fold B -0.240 (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145; 95% t-interval over months -0.359 to -0.121). Fold C -0.080 (-0.187 to +0.051). Without D8, D12, and D5 (the series with data in each fold), fold B is -0.093 (95% -0.189 to -0.014) and fold C -0.084 (-0.170 to +0.018). D8 alone gains 2.05 (95% -2.60 to -1.44).
  • C2, monthly minus the stack (descriptive): fold B -0.201 (-0.324 to -0.105); fold C -0.045 (-0.162 to +0.082). Most of C1 is therefore retraining against the stack, not weekly against monthly.
  • C3, weekly minus monthly: fold B -0.039 (-0.064 to -0.012; the t-interval, -0.078 to -0.000, only just excludes zero). Fold C -0.035 (-0.085 to +0.014).
  • C4, rolling without the Christmas column minus with it: fold B +0.011 (-0.115 to +0.188), fold C +0.041 (-0.054 to +0.252), unresolved. Inside 2023-12-18 to 2024-01-04, dropping the column raised the score by 1.20 points, against -0.07 outside the window; the winter before, +1.79 against -0.08. January alone favoured dropping it (-0.099, -0.184 to -0.020). Pooled over three winters with experiment 49's, the contrast is -0.013 (-0.037 to +0.010), dominated by experiment 49's narrow interval. We keep the column.
  • C5, half-life 2 years minus 0.5 years: fold B -0.019 (-0.060 to +0.040), fold C +0.014 (-0.027 to +0.058), unresolved.
  • C6, blend minus weekly: -0.038 (-0.070 to -0.007), a small gain that misses the -0.05 threshold. The blend has four members; experiment 49's had five.
  • Correction and spread: the 14-day correction did not help the frozen model (+0.091, -0.005 to +0.187, a worse score whose interval includes zero). The exceedance rate of the 0.95 quantile (nominal 0.05) is 0.052 for weekly with the spread factor and 0.073 without it. Re-choosing the factor on the first three months (1.10) changed later scores by +0.002.
  • 9 km check (descriptive): the frozen model beat manual_heuristic by 9.1% on runs before 2023-06-27 (18 km) and by 6.3% after, but the monthly figure swings from 11.6% (April) to 1.2% (June) to 8.8% (August), so the drop is within the seasonal swing. We predicted that weekly retraining's gain over the stack would grow late in the fold as 9 km data accumulates; C1 by month went the other way (-0.552 in December, -0.381 in January, -0.147 in February, -0.137 in March). The experiment found no evidence of adaptation to the 9 km product and could not rule it out.
  • Caveats: neither fold can separate retraining from adaptation to a weather product, and fold C also confounds the all-18 km period with a short history. The effective capacities, which scale the scores and the inputs, come from the stage 1 pilot's table built from all data, not fitted before each fold. The spread check chose its factor on cases whose targets reach 14.6 days into the first scored month. The pooled read (R-b) treats two periods as independent although both score the same 13 substations, which exclude series 7, 13, and 12 (no data in the period).
  • More history or the full ensemble? More history would narrow C4 and C5, whose intervals include zero in both folds, and a longer run on one weather product would test the 9 km confound. This experiment did not test whether full-ensemble features (spread, CRPS) change any contrast, because only the control member exists for these runs.
  • Next: the solar and analogue contrasts of experiments 64, 78, and 74 need April-to-September rows with a control-only sunshine anomaly. Fold B has 92 such days and no April to June, so this experiment did not run them.

docs.title: Experiment 82: do two improvements to the load-transfer detector add up?
docs.text:
Yes: the two improvements find different missed load transfers, so using both finds about twice as much extra moved power as either alone. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor's) onto neighbouring substations (the receivers) for hours or days. A Primary substation steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. On injected transfers, the combined detector (RO-NC) found a share of 0.770 of the megawatts (MW) moved, and the benchmark detector (PF14) found 0.656. The misses that remain are mostly (by count) transfers with a small donor step and no metered receiver, so the next experiment could test a stronger detection signal for those transfers. The verdict is supported.

We asked whether two earlier improvements to a detector for load transfers combine. The detector subtracts an XGBoost forecast, which uses no past power, from a substation's measured power, and raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of that residual steps by 4.0 noise units or more. One noise unit is the usual size of that step on odd-numbered months. The XGBoost model is refitted on the 1st of every month, and PF14 ignores every alarm within 24 hours of a refit. Experiment 71 removed that blind spot by adding a second XGBoost model refitted on the 16th (the refit offset). Experiment 70 scored each alarm candidate partly by the number of neighbouring substations stepping the same way as the donor (the same-sign neighbour count).

We added synthetic transfers to the real power history of 16 Primary substations, combined the two improvements, and counted the share of the moved MW that each detector found. Each detector was held to 80 alarms on odd months that no closure in the switching log (the log of real switching operations) explains. Odd months set the thresholds and fitted the scores. Recall was read on transfers that start in even months.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. PF14: alarm when the 24-hour residual step reaches 4.0 noise units, end at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step. X: PF14 with the step taken from whichever of two residual models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours. LOGIT_SAME: PF14's candidates scored by a logistic regression that includes the same-sign neighbour count. RO-NC: the same logistic score fitted on X's candidates.
  • Row set. 611 fresh headline-band transfers per injection shape (25% or more of the receiving load, over 1 day) starting in even months, shapes S2, S3, and S4 pooled (S2 a constant MW, S3 a share of the receiver's profile, S4 a mix fitted to the labelled real transfers); 214 long transfers (15.6 to 60 days). Fresh seeds, not those of experiments 69 to 71.
  • MW-weighted recall (98.33% interval, resampling whole calendar months): PF14 0.656 (0.530 to 0.727); X 0.713 (0.596 to 0.803); LOGIT_SAME 0.706 (0.591 to 0.776); RO-NC 0.770 (0.665 to 0.857). The sanity arms X and LOGIT_SAME reproduce their experiments' gains: +0.056 and +0.050 over PF14.
  • Planned contrasts: C1 RO-NC minus PF14 +0.114 (+0.074 to +0.182); C2 RO-NC minus X +0.058 (+0.034 to +0.096); C3 RO-NC minus LOGIT_SAME +0.064 (+0.028 to +0.127). All three lower ends are above zero, C1 is above the threshold of +0.02. The sum of the single gains (+0.106) is slightly below C1, so the gains add and do not overlap; C1, C2, and C3 all landed above the ranges predicted in the plan, which expected a combined gain smaller than the sum.
  • Share of the moved MW missed: PF14 0.344, X 0.287, LOGIT_SAME 0.294, RO-NC 0.230. For RO-NC, 0.195 is transfers with no alarm at the start and 0.035 is transfers with a wrong end.
  • Shapes: RO-NC minus PF14 is +0.107 to +0.116 for S1, S2, S3, and S4, and +0.096 for S5; all lower ends are above zero.
  • By donor step, transfers found (S2 to S4 summed): with a metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4 noise units, RO-NC 109 of 151, PF14 81. With no metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4, RO-NC 149 of 550, PF14 42. With no metered receiver and a step of 4 to 6, RO-NC 175 of 255, PF14 131.
  • Long transfers (descriptive): RO-NC minus PF14 +0.000 (-0.026 to +0.026).
  • Labelled real transfers of more than 1 day (35): found RO-NC 12, X 10, PF14 8, LOGIT_SAME 7; an alarm started within 2 hours of the labelled start for RO-NC 15, X 12, LOGIT_SAME 12, PF14 11. The 35 are too few to rank the arms; MW-weighted recall on them is RO-NC 0.357, X 0.350, PF14 0.156, and LOGIT_SAME 0.144, so X alone nearly matches RO-NC there.
  • Alarms: unexplained alarms on even months were PF14 80, X 80, LOGIT_SAME 61, RO-NC 67, against at most 80 on odd months for all arms (X 75, at its grid threshold of 4.1).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The alarm ends use up to 14 days of hindsight, so the detector serves training-time masks and the NGED event table, not live forecast inputs.
  • The logistic score is fitted on odd-month injections, so the odd-month contrast (+0.141) is in-sample and decides nothing.
  • A check on experiment 71's draw (850 rows per arm) reproduced the found flags of PF14, X, and LOGIT_SAME exactly; there is no earlier reference for RO-NC.
  • The 35 real transfers give a weak signal only (12 against 8 found).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: By count, 401 of the 725 transfers RO-NC misses have a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units and no metered receiver (149 of 550 found). Options to test include a longer averaging window and a check that the receivers' combined step balances the donor's.

docs.title: Experiment 83: tail calibration, on experiment 48
docs.text: Every stored forecast of experiment 48 is too narrow in both tails, and weekly retraining has the lowest pinball loss at both levels. We built a tail-calibration table for the studies code and ran it on the stored demand forecasts of experiment 48. The stack is the demand model fitted once, with a correction from its own recent errors. This experiment first also built a single-series curtailment-cost metric. We withdrew that metric, because curtailment binds at a substation, so a metric that scores each meter alone against its own history does not measure it.

docs.title: Results (exploratory, 20 demand series pooled, every lead and run from 2025-07-02)
docs.text:
• Coverage: coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927, so every forecast is too narrow in both tails. The target coverage is the level itself.
  • Pinball loss: weekly retraining has the lowest pinball loss at both levels.
  • Levels not delivered: the 0.01 and 0.99 rows read "not delivered", because the stored sets hold nine quantiles from 0.05 to 0.95.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Not scored: experiment 64's stored sets carry no actual column, so they were not scored here.
  • Next: write the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles in new experiments.

Reproduce with uv run python ml-experiments/00083-*/e00083_report.py. The printed report is in data/ml-experiments/00083-curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-worked-example/report.md.

docs.title: Experiment 84: the substation-limit curtailment metric on the pilot, a worked example
docs.text:
Two substations hold too few half-hours beyond a limit to rank forecasts: at 0.9 times each substation's earlier maximum export there are 19. We asked what it would have cost if the electricity network operator had capped nearby generators whenever a forecast said a substation would export more than a limit. We scored the stored demand and generator forecasts of experiment 48 (an earlier experiment that stored them) for Boston and Skegness, two bulk supply points (132 kV to 33 kV substations), over the year to 30 June 2026.

Most of the cost is breach, not unneeded cuts. For the best guess at 0.9 times the maximum, 81% of the avoidable cost is breach: export that stayed over the limit because the forecast did not order enough cuts. The next step is the January 2027 delivery of about 2,500 series, which the same code can score unchanged.

Verdict: inconclusive (no registered contrast). Every cost below is a calibration to history, not a saving. The best guess has the lowest avoidable cost at all three limits, but at 0.9 the order of the arms cannot be separated statistically: no difference is significant at the 5% level. The published thermal limits are NGED's, Supported by NGED Open Data. Questions for NGED are collected in issue #1318 (Questions to ask NGED about curtailment).

docs.title: Which limit, and why a scaled one
docs.text: The published thermal limit is a ceiling, and the maintainer understands that NGED does not operate to it. The understanding, unconfirmed, is that NGED curtails early so that one more fault still leaves headroom. Boston's metered export reached its published limit once, so the ceiling is not unreachable. The limit we score against therefore stands in for operating headroom: 0.9, 0.75, or 0.5 times each substation's maximum export before 2025-07-02 (the scaled limit). Boston's earlier maximum is about 39 MW, so 0.9 times it is 35.2 MW. History's maximum can be exceeded in the scored year: the highest export in all history, 45.08 MW at Boston, came inside it.

docs.title: The event census comes first
docs.text:
The counts are too small to rank forecasts at the headline limit. Counts below are half-hours of metered flow beyond the limit in the scored year, from cleaned unflagged power. The published thermal limits (NGED's, Supported by NGED Open Data) are the smaller of each substation's two transformer limits. A Technical Limit is the single figure NGED publishes for a grid supply point.

Node Published thermal limit (reference) 0.9 x maximum 0.75 x maximum 0.5 x maximum Boston 1 (45.0 MW) 17 36 215 Skegness 0 (29.8 MW) 2 10 108 Bicker Fen (sign unconfirmed, not scored) 0 0 84 734
  • Scored nodes: Boston and Skegness together have 19 half-hours at 0.9 times the maximum, 46 at 0.75, and 323 at 0.5. Only at 0.5, half the observed peak, are there more than 100 per node.
  • Scoring coverage: the census counts all 34,942 metered half-hours of the two nodes. Scoring uses the 27,936 that have a stored forecast in the 12 to 36 hour lead window. All 19 events at 0.9 are scored, 41 of 46 at 0.75, and 268 of 323 at 0.5. The unscored half-hours hold 4% of the excess energy at 0.75 and 14% at 0.5.
  • Import: the scaled import counts are in figure 1. No published import limit is used, and curtailing generators cannot relieve an import limit, so import is counted and not priced.
  • Signs: Boston and Skegness are -1 (a positive reading is import), inferred from the sign of the metered net flow in our power table. Bicker Fen is +1 and unconfirmed. Walpole's sign is unknown, so the metric excludes it.
  • Seasons: each limit is the same in all four NGED seasons (Winter December to February, Intermediate Cool March, April and November, Intermediate Warm May, September and October, Summer June to August).

docs.title: Does the code reproduce a hand-worked answer?
docs.text: Yes: all eight quantities agree exactly. The example is made up (a 45.0 MW limit and two generators of 10 MW and 20 MW). One generator's share is cut to its own forecast energy, and some export is left over as breach. e00084_known_answer.py fails if the code and the hand answer disagree.

docs.title: What the cost contains
docs.text:
Each arm forecasts a substation's export and its generators' output, and the cost counts cuts and breach. An arm is one pair of forecasts. When an arm's 95th-percentile forecast of export (tau 0.95) exceeds the limit, the metric orders the generators beneath the substation to cut that excess, sharing it by capacity. The energy proxy is the price times (MWh of generator output cut + 20 x MWh still over the limit after the cuts). The 20 is the breach ratio, so a MWh left over costs 20 times a MWh cut. Curtailment Limit 0 means no hours of curtailment are free. The six arms are:

  • Best guess (weekly retrained): the substation forecast retrained every week, with each generator's forecast retrained monthly.
  • Best-guess stack: the substation forecast fitted once, corrected from its own recent errors, with a generator forecast fitted once.
  • Climatology: the typical value for that month, half-hour and weekday or weekend.
  • NGED baseline (unconfirmed): the manual heuristic's substation forecast, with every generator assumed to run at full capacity. This is the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of NGED's practice, and the name always means that.
  • Best-guess nodes with actual generation: the best guess's substation forecast, with each generator's metered output known exactly (a diagnostic).
  • Perfect forecast: every quantile equal to the metered value, so the arm is charged only what cannot be avoided.

For the best guess at 0.9 times the maximum, the avoidable cost of GBP 571,823 splits into three parts. Avoidable cost is the arm's cost minus the perfect forecast's GBP 87,460.

Part GBP Unneeded cuts: output cut in half-hours where metered export was within the limit 114,496 Energy lost on the 19 event half-hours, more than the perfect forecast loses -7,791 Breach: MWh still over the limit on event half-hours, at 20 times the price 465,118

The forecast ordered 13.6 MWh of cuts on event half-hours against 35.1 MWh needed, so most of the excess was left as breach. Climatology orders no cuts at 0.9, so its whole avoidable cost is breach. The perfect forecast still costs GBP 87,460 because it cuts a little more than needed: some generators produce more than their estimated capacity, and the cap removes that extra output.

At the published thermal limit, both figures are absolute costs. The one scored half-hour is 0.038 MWh over the limit. Every arm except the perfect forecast costs GBP 1,540 (0.038 MWh x 20 x GBP 2,000, because none ordered a cut) and the perfect forecast costs GBP 1,225. The avoidable cost is GBP 315.

docs.title: Cost per arm
docs.text:
Absolute cost of the perfect forecast, and avoidable cost of each other arm, in GBP over the scored year at GBP 2,000 per MWh, Curtailment Limit 0. All figures are a calibration to history, not a saving.

Arm Avoidable GBP at 0.9 x maximum at 0.75 x at 0.5 x Perfect forecast (absolute cost) 87,460 252,428 1,341,908 Best guess (weekly retrained) 571,823 2,449,203 9,385,270 Best-guess stack 1,572,512 4,889,923 13,161,772 Climatology 1,318,078 4,638,378 20,187,791 NGED baseline (unconfirmed) 1,323,425 4,136,392 18,073,166 Best-guess nodes with actual generation 779,645 2,718,739 11,574,478

Figure 4 also shows the avoidable cost at three other prices, GBP 100, 380 and 11,100 per MWh. The last three are the ends and the geometric middle of a GBP 380 to 11,100 range reconstructed from April 2025 contracts, and GBP 100 is an illustrative balancing price. The energy proxy scales with price, so the order of the arms does not change. The DCUSA form follows the payment rule of the Distribution Connection and Use of System Agreement (Metric 2 of the cost-savings roadmap). It charges each instructed generator its whole headroom, so it ranks arms differently. Its avoidable cost is negative for climatology because the perfect forecast instructs generators and is charged for their headroom, while climatology instructs none.

  • 0.9 times the maximum: no difference is statistically significant at the 5% level. The best guess minus the NGED baseline is -GBP 751,603 (95% interval -2,293,480 to +14,988), and minus climatology is -GBP 746,255 (-2,288,392 to +30,815). The stack minus the best guess is +GBP 1,000,690 (0 to 2,865,606).
  • 0.75 times the maximum: the stack costs GBP 2,440,720 more than the best guess (96,371 to 6,686,043), which is significant. The best guess minus climatology is -GBP 2,189,175 (-6,255,250 to 0) and minus the NGED baseline is -GBP 1,687,189 (-5,138,390 to +38,991), neither significant.
  • 0.5 times the maximum: the best guess is GBP 10,802,520 cheaper than climatology (-20,880,964 to -3,342,553), which is significant. Against the NGED baseline it is GBP 8,687,896 cheaper (-26,251,726 to +2,339,946), not significant. We have no evidence that NGED operates at this limit, so it is a rehearsal.

docs.title: What to watch
docs.text:
• Generators without a forecast: summed over the six arms, 100,632 of 754,272 generator-half-hours (13%) on the scored rows had no finite forecast. Those generators were not capped, gave no relief, and so add to the breach. None had a forecast with no metered output.
  • Forecast capped at capacity: a generator forecast above its effective capacity is capped at the capacity, as node_curtailment requires. All arms are capped alike.
  • Thermal limits: Boston's highest export in all history, 45.08 MW, sits on the published 45.0 MW limit, so 45.0 MW may be an operating ceiling or a clipped meter.
  • Anonymisation: no generator appears singly. Every generator figure is a sum over at least 4 generators, in GBP or MWh, and the table joining generators to substations stays in the private data folder.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Whether a ranking appears once the January 2027 delivery gives about 2,500 series. The same function scores any number of nodes from longer tables.

Reproduce with uv run python ml-experiments/00084-*/e00084_report.py, then e00084_split.py, e00084_known_answer.py and e00084_charts.py. The printed reports are in data/ml-experiments/00084-substation-limit-curtailment-cost-worked-example/.

docs.title: Experiment 85: do cheaper retraining schedules rank arms the way weekly retraining does? (SPD1)
docs.text:
Refitting the XGBoost demand-forecasting model monthly on the latest 12 months of data (150 boosting rounds), or weekly on the whole history with 150 rounds at a higher learning rate, gives a gap between monthly and weekly retraining within 0.01 points of the gap that full weekly retraining gives, at 0.03 to 0.31 of its fit time. Refitting only quarterly scores much worse. The effect of starting the XGBoost model from zero, not from XGBoost's estimated value, is too small on these rows to rank any schedule, so the agreement on that contrast says nothing.

We asked whether research experiments can use a cheaper retraining schedule instead of weekly retraining. For the 16 Primary substations (which step 33 kV down to 11 kV) we refitted the XGBoost demand model (N1: one XGBoost model per substation, trained on the ECMWF ensemble control forecast) under six cheaper schedules. We then compared the gaps in the quantile score between arms under each schedule with the gaps stored weekly retraining gives, on 158 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The quantile score estimates the continuous ranked probability score from nine quantile levels, in percentage points of the substation's capacity (lower is better). The verdict is partly supported. By the rule fixed in advance every schedule passes. The pass on the starting-value contrast is empty, so only the cadence contrast supports the claim. The experiment leaves out the am-against-d0 contrast of experiment 64 (a demand model given a solar forecast, against the best guess) and the five-model blend of experiment 49, because experiment 64 has no weekly reference and the blend mixes schedules.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Terms: the cadence gap is the monthly arm's score minus the weekly arm's. The starting-value gap is the score of a model whose boosting starts from zero minus that of a model that starts from XGBoost's estimate from the training labels. A 12-month window means each refit trains on the latest 12 months only (150 rounds, learning rate 0.15). The full setting trains on the whole history (500 rounds, learning rate 0.05).
  • Rows: 16 Primary substations, 158 runs, N1 model with the spread factor 1.15 (a fixed widening of the quantiles) and no 14-day correction. Every weekly arm refits at the 28 weekly dates that experiment 80's stored zero-start arm holds, and every contrast keeps the runs those refits serve.
  • Noise floor: 0.01 points, the minimum the plan sets. The measured differences between repeats are 0.0004 to 0.0013. A repeat of the 12-month-window monthly fit scored 5.563 against 5.563, and its zero-start repeat 5.547 against 5.546. The tolerance is 0.05.
  • Cadence gap: the full-setting reference is +0.125 (95% interval +0.036 to +0.229). The 12-month window gives +0.118 and the 150-round whole-history recipe +0.125, so both agree with the reference. Quarterly minus weekly refits on the 12-month window, descriptive because no full-quarterly reference exists, is +0.381 (+0.207 to +0.565).
  • Starting-value gap: the reference is -0.017 (-0.062 to +0.037), smaller than the -0.07 the plan predicted. Every schedule gives between -0.003 and -0.020, so each agrees under the rule for an unresolved reference (an estimate within 0.05 of zero). Any estimate within 0.05 of zero passes, so the agreement is weak evidence.
  • Pass table: monthly 12-month window 2 of 2 contrasts, weekly 150 rounds 2 of 2, weekly 12-month window 1 of 1, quarterly 1 of 1, full monthly 1 of 1 (the last three on starting value only). The plan also predicted that quarterly refits would score 0.10 to 0.20 above monthly and that the monthly gap would lie within 0.05 of the reference. Quarterly scored 0.263 above monthly, and the monthly gap was within 0.01 of the reference.
Arm Score 95% interval Coverage of q05 to q95 Pinball at q05 Pinball at q95 Weekly, full setting 5.405 5.111 to 5.716 0.889 0.910 1.236 Weekly, 150 rounds 5.408 5.119 to 5.711 0.897 0.908 1.233 Weekly, 12-month window 5.445 5.157 to 5.749 0.889 0.912 1.245 Monthly, full setting 5.530 5.179 to 5.912 0.888 0.907 1.294 Monthly, 150 rounds 5.533 5.185 to 5.913 0.896 0.911 1.288 Monthly, 12-month window 5.563 5.219 to 5.939 0.889 0.920 1.288 Quarterly, 12-month window 5.826 5.446 to 6.252 0.883 0.946 1.372

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
• Fit time of one refit (one series, 2 threads): 114 s at the full setting, 33 to 36 s for the 150-round whole-history recipe, and 13 to 51 s for the 12-month window. Other jobs shared the machine, so the same recipe varied by up to 4 times.
  • A year for 16 series: full weekly about 1,590 compute minutes (the full monthly fit time times 52, not measured separately), full monthly 366, weekly 150 rounds 460 to 500, monthly 12-month window 42 to 164, quarterly 54.
  • Against the one-third rule: monthly 12-month window (0.03 to 0.10 of full weekly's fit time) and weekly 150 rounds (0.29 to 0.31) pass. Weekly on the 12-month window (0.31 to 0.35) is borderline.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Departure from the written rule: by the pre-registered rule every schedule passes, and quarterly (0.034 of full weekly's cost) would become the default for the starting-value contrast. We do not adopt that default. The rule is vacuous for a gap of 0.017. The descriptive quarterly gap of 0.38 is also large.
  • Starting value is untested: the stored weekly zero-start arm covers half of the weeks, and the gap on those runs is within the noise. A later experiment should test schedules on a contrast of 0.1 points or more that has a stored weekly reference.
  • One series class, one seed: the experiment covers the cadence and starting-value contrasts for Primary N1 demand only. Tail scores stop at q05 and q95, because the stored quantile models have nine levels from 0.05 to 0.95.
  • Cost is noisy: the plan priced a schedule by the mean fit time of its recipe. Identical recipes ran up to 4 times apart because other jobs shared the machine, so we give a range, and each cost is accurate only to within a factor of about 4.

docs.title: Recommended R&D defaults
docs.text:
• Feature and recipe contrasts of 0.05 points or more: use monthly refits on a 12-month window with 150 rounds and learning rate 0.15. The schedule reproduced the cadence gap to within 0.01 and repeated to within 0.001. A weekly year costs about 1,590 compute minutes and this schedule saves 1,420 to 1,545 of them (90 to 97%). Only the cadence contrast was tested, so a feature contrast is assumed to carry over.
  • Contrasts about cadence, retraining rules, or how fast an XGBoost model adapts: use the weekly refit on the whole history with 150 rounds and learning rate 0.15. The schedule scored within 0.003 of full weekly and saves about 1,090 minutes (69%). Experiment 34 found that the gain from adding weekly-analogue inputs (0.05 on a frozen model) shrank to 0.01 under monthly retraining, so a conclusion about recent-data features, the 14-day correction, the training window, or the half-life can change with the schedule. Check that conclusion on the weekly 150-round refit.
  • Absolute scores and tail scores: quote them from weekly retraining at the full setting. Monthly refits on a 12-month window score 0.16 points above that (5.563 against 5.405) and 0.05 above at the q95 pinball loss, so an XGBoost model reads worse under any cheaper schedule than under weekly retraining.
  • Quarterly refits: do not use quarterly refits. They score 0.26 above monthly refits, and the experiment cannot show that they rank any contrast correctly.
  • Contrasts under 0.05 points: the experiment cannot say which schedule keeps such contrasts, because the only one tested, the zero-start gap, was -0.017.

docs.title: Experiment 86: do the detector's load-shift labels give the same gain as NGED's logs?
docs.text:
Take-home message: correcting each past power reading (a lag) for switching did not lower the error of the XGBoost demand forecast for Primary substations with either source of labels, and the detector's labels raised the error slightly on all rows outside switching. Here "oracle labels" are the switching events in NGED's logs, and "detector labels" are the events found by a detector that reads no log. On the half-hours whose lag falls inside a logged event, the oracle labels changed the quantile score by -0.29 points of capacity (98.33% interval -2.06 to +0.68), and the detector labels by +0.48 (-0.06 to +1.72). On all half-hours outside switching, the detector labels changed the score by +0.056 (+0.016 to +0.126). The detector marks 8.1 times as many half-hours as the logs and marks only 15% of the half-hours the logs mark. These data cannot show whether the detector or the logs is wrong where they disagree. Eight months of in-event half-hours are too few to show a gain even for the logs. One option for a next experiment is to inject switching events of known size and test whether the corrected-lag forecast recovers the true normal running arrangement. The verdict is inconclusive.

An electricity network operator sometimes closes a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) carries load that belongs to a neighbour. A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) matters most for two cases: half-hours whose lags were measured during such a switch, and forecasts made while a substation is in an abnormal arrangement. We asked whether subtracting the moved MW from each lag, and giving the moved MW to XGBoost as three more columns, lowers the error. We tried it with the events in NGED's switching logs (oracle labels) and with the events found by the RO-NC load-transfer detector of experiment 82. The detector reads no log.

We refitted the XGBoost demand model monthly on a rolling 12-month window (experiment 49's cheap schedule) for 16 Primary substations, and scored 292 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity, where smaller is better.

  • Arms (experiment 75's inputs, seed 0). plain: all rows, no label input. lagmw_oracle: lags minus the signed MW plus three MW columns, oracle labels, trained on all rows. lagmw_xl: the same inputs with the detector's (RO-NC) labels. mask_xl: training rows inside an RO-NC event dropped (descriptive).
  • Rows. 3,199,243 cases, of which 2,928,842 lie outside switching (oracle events and logged closures). The headline rows are the 37,394 of those (1.3% of the 2,928,842, in 8 months) with a lag inside an oracle event.
  • Score on the headline rows (plain / oracle / RO-NC / mask_xl): 10.778 / 10.488 / 11.260 / 10.736. manual_heuristic scores 8.975 and climatology 13.231 on the same rows.
  • Score on all rows outside switching: 5.408 / 5.417 / 5.464 / 5.412. manual_heuristic 6.121 and climatology 7.479 (on slightly fewer rows).
  • Contrasts (98.33% intervals). C1 +0.48 (-0.06 to +1.72). C2 -0.29 (-2.06 to +0.68). C3, the skill lost without NGED's logs, +0.77 (+0.13 to +2.34). The share of the oracle gain recovered is not defined, because C2 is not a gain. N1, C1 on all rows outside switching, +0.056 (+0.016 to +0.126): its upper end exceeds the +0.02 margin.
  • Descriptive contrasts (95%). lagmw_xl minus plain on the 296,878 rows with a lag inside an RO-NC event only: +0.47 (+0.24 to +0.84), which is the harm from detector labels the logs do not confirm. lagmw_oracle minus plain on all rows outside switching: +0.009 (-0.006 to +0.022). mask_xl minus plain outside switching: +0.004 (-0.017 to +0.026); on the headline rows -0.042 (-0.084 to -0.008).
  • Tails (coverage of the 5%-to-95% band, nominally 90%; pinball loss at 0.05 and 0.95, in points). Outside switching, plain 0.893, 0.914, 1.162; oracle 0.892, 0.913, 1.161; RO-NC 0.885, 0.929, 1.181. On the headline rows, plain 0.784, 1.506, 3.386; oracle 0.750, 1.498, 3.385; RO-NC 0.721, 1.808, 3.424. The 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles are not stored (nine levels).
  • Label coverage. Rows outside switching with a lag inside an event: 37,394 by the logs, 302,619 by the detector, 5,741 by both. The detector may be marking real transfers that NGED did not log, which these data cannot tell apart from false alarms.
  • Caveats. Both label sources use hindsight: an event's end is known up to 14 days later. C3 therefore compares like with like, but the absolute gain is not what a live service would get. The headline rows are few and fall in 8 months, so the intervals are wide. There is one seed. The detector's signed MW is the substation's own 24-hour residual step, not a logged MW. Where both sources label a half-hour, the correlation is weak (0.19 at the only substation where it could be computed).
  • Models kept. All 768 boosters (4 arms, 12 monthly refits, 16 substations) are saved under data/ml-experiments/00086-sw2-12-detector-labels-for-nra-forecast/work/boosters/<arm>/ for the follow-up that injects switching events.
  • What the next experiment should answer. Whether the corrected-lag forecast recovers the true normal running arrangement when switching events of known size are injected into the lags, so that the in-event rows are numerous enough to measure.

docs.title: Experiment 87: BG2, the best guess so far and what each part contributes
docs.text:
Take-home message: weekly refitting and a blend of five models lower the forecast error at Primary substations and at bulk and grid supply points, while the solar and wind farm forecasts are still too close to call. A Primary substation steps 33 kV or 66 kV down to 11 kV. A bulk or grid supply point is a substation where the transmission network feeds the distribution network. BG2 is the second "best guess" recipe, assembled from the ideas that scored best in earlier experiments. The score is the quantile score, which is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of capacity; one point is 1% of a series' capacity, and a lower score is better. At the 16 Primary substations BG2 scores 5.260, against 5.543 for the previous best, the stack: an XGBoost model trained once, with a correction from the last 14 days of errors. At the 4 supply points BG2 scores 12.925, against 13.559 for the stack. The solar offset (the forecast output of the unmetered solar panels behind the substation, experiments 64 and 78) lowers the score by 0.114 points (0.075 to 0.164) on the rows it can touch: daylight from April to September at the 5 Primaries that carry an offset, 8.5% of the Primary rows. The point value is inside the prediction of 0.10 to 0.15. Averaged over all rows of all 16 Primaries the gain dilutes to 0.010. For the solar and wind farms, training on the archived ECMWF ensemble forecasts scored 0.050 and 0.228 points worse than experiment 33's mixture trained on ERA5 weather. With 6 solar and 3 wind farms the experiment cannot tell whether the loss is under the 0.10 (solar) or 0.30 (wind) points we would accept. The verdict is partly supported.

We asked whether the ideas that scored best in earlier experiments still work when they are combined in one forecast, and which idea gives which part of the gain. We refitted each XGBoost model weekly or monthly, as its idea requires, forecast 292 daily runs from July 2025 to June 2026, and scored each target class against its previous best forecast and against NGED's manual_heuristic. Each drop-one ablation removes one idea at a time from the best guess and scores the result again. Solar and wind farms are anonymised in every figure.

The other figures are in this folder: the stages and ablations as lines (figure_2_*), error by lead band, hour, month, season, and sunshine (figure_5_*), error by series (figure_6_by_series), tail calibration (figure_7*), and the side panels of experiments 81 and 54 (figure_9_side_panels). In the figures and below, S1 to S6 are the stages of the Primary staircase (frozen, stack, monthly, weekly, blend, and blend plus offset). A2 to A7 are drop-one ablations of BG2: no blend, monthly in the weekly slot, the correction on every member, no spread factor, capacity held at its value before the validation year, and three members. The spread factor widens or narrows the quantiles about the median. Experiment 81 (R11) is a replication on other forecast runs.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity on the 292 runs, with 95% intervals from resampling whole months. Negative differences mean BG2 scores lower, which is better.

  • BG2 beats the stack at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points. BG2 scores 5.260 (4.987 to 5.534). The verdict contrast is -0.283 (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146), supported. Against manual_heuristic the difference is -0.920 (-1.078 to -0.767). The mean absolute error of the median is 7.432 (7.063 to 7.814), against 8.695 for manual_heuristic.
  • BG2 beats the stack at the 4 supply points by 0.634 points. BG2 scores 12.925 (11.569 to 14.177). The contrast is -0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279), supported. The stack is the frozen XGBoost model with the 14-day correction. Against manual_heuristic the difference is -1.578 (-1.951 to -1.251). The mean absolute error is 18.666 (16.484 to 20.682), against 20.876.
  • The solar farm forecast is 0.050 points worse than the ERA5-trained mixture, but the interval includes no change. BG2 scores 5.012 (3.788 to 6.392) against 4.962; the contrast is +0.050 (-0.125 to +0.168). The upper end exceeds the +0.10 margin, so non-inferiority is not shown. Against manual_heuristic the difference is -0.703 (-0.966 to -0.474). The mean absolute error is 7.444 (5.610 to 9.510), against 8.533.
  • The wind farm forecast is 0.228 points worse, with a wide interval. BG2 scores 11.032 (9.641 to 12.303) against 10.804; the contrast is +0.228 (-0.178 to +0.653), and non-inferiority within 0.30 is not shown. Against manual_heuristic the difference is -2.871 (-3.568 to -2.234). The mean absolute error is 15.915 (13.745 to 17.895), against 19.607. The power-curve margin lowers the wind score by 0.057 (0.024 to 0.098) against BG2, and the fitted spread factor lowers it by 0.016 (0.009 to 0.025).
  • Weekly refitting and the blend produce the Primary gain. The staircase scores are: frozen 6.927; the stack lowers the score by 1.384 (0.943 to 1.785); monthly refitting by 0.065 (-0.117 to 0.244); weekly refitting by 0.123 (0.051 to 0.202); the blend by 0.086 (0.038 to 0.135); the offset by 0.010 (0.000 to 0.019), which is the all-row dilution of 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on the rows the offset can touch. The ablation that removes the blend from the final blend raises the score by 0.091 (0.048 to 0.138), which differs from the staircase step because the two remove the blend from different forecasts.
  • Other ablations. At the supply points, adding the 14-day correction raises the score by 0.305 (0.060 to 0.594) and moving from weekly to monthly refitting by 0.160 (0.066 to 0.247). At Primaries, monthly in the weekly slot raises it by 0.028 (0.003 to 0.058), the correction on every member by 0.067 (-0.039 to 0.160), no spread factor by 0.017 (0.003 to 0.033), and capacity held by 0.001 (0.000 to 0.002). The three-member blend is 0.002 below BG2 (-0.006 to 0.000), so the experiment found no difference between three and five members.
  • Solar and wind ablations. Refitting monthly instead of freezing the ensemble-trained model lowers the score by 0.030 (-0.015 to 0.077) at solar farms and 0.098 (0.027 to 0.171) at wind farms. Swapping in the ERA5-trained mixture changes the score by -0.050 (-0.148 to +0.085) at solar farms and -0.228 (-0.560 to +0.095) at wind farms.
  • The noise floor is 0.001 points. A repeat fit of the monthly Primary model at 4 Primaries moved the score by -0.001 (-0.003 to +0.001).
  • The check on the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1 is not independent. The blend and the offset were chosen on those runs. BG2 minus the previous best is -0.285 (-0.402 to -0.171) at Primaries, -0.652 (-1.057 to -0.332) at supply points, +0.037 (-0.093 to +0.149) at solar farms, and +0.323 (-0.042 to +0.736) at wind farms.

  • The Primary tails match their nominal levels, and the other classes' tails are mostly too wide. At Primaries every interval includes its nominal level. At supply points the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles cover 0.004 and 0.995 of the actuals, and at wind farms the 0.01 quantile covers 0.003, so those bands are slightly wide. At solar farms the 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles cover 0.028, 0.973, and 0.997, so the bands are too wide.
  • Curtailment cost is a calibration to history, not a saving. Curtailment cost is the cost in GBP per MW of generator capacity per day under node limits set at 0.9 times the highest export seen before the scored year. The 3 scored supply points saw 19 export half-hours beyond that limit out of 40,714 scored half-hours, too few to rank forecasts. A fourth supply point (Walpole) is excluded because the sign of its flow is unknown. NGED's method is the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of it: every generator assumed to run at capacity. The assumed risk level is a breach ratio r of 20 (planning to the 0.95 quantile).
    • Headline, f = 0.9 and r = 20: BG2 minus NGED's method is -32.85 GBP per MW per day (-99.24 to +0.00), or -11,989 GBP per MW per year pro-rated from 292 days, not statistically significant at the 5% level. The previous best is +6.64 and the perfect forecast -57.39.
    • Risk level: r = 4, 10, and 100 give -0.81, -13.87, and -166.89 GBP per MW per day.
    • Limit: f = 0.75 gives -87.03 (-298.28 to +34.62) with 118 events, and f = 0.5 gives -418.99 (-1242.54 to +129.46) with 853 events. The published thermal limit has 1 event and is a reference only.
    • Primaries (node only): 0 events at f = 0.9 and 0.75, and 12 at f = 0.5, among 104,141 half-hours of the 6 scored series.

docs.title: Deviations, caveats, and next steps
docs.text:
• The generator rows refit monthly. The planned weekly refits of each of the 9 farm models did not fit the 16 GPU-hour budget, which the manager raised to 20. The arms g_ens_weekly and g_a_weekly_to_frozen in the stored predictions are monthly refits. The hypothesis above described weekly refits at the farms. The noise-floor repeat used the monthly schedule too. Total GPU use was 14.4 hours of wall time.
  • Schedule for the rest: the full production recipe, with 500 rounds, a learning rate of 0.05, and a half-life of 0.5 years. Primary and supply-point models refit weekly.
  • The offset follows experiment 74's mechanism, not the design's. The weights come from experiment 64's fit before the validation year, where the design says to refit them. The capacity per run comes from experiment 78's vintages, and the offset models start from the median of the training labels plus the offset. Ablation A6 holds the capacity at experiment 64's value, which was estimated before July 2025. The offset lowers the score by 0.114 on its daylight April-to-September rows at the 5 offset Primaries (0.010 over all rows of all 16 Primaries). Nothing dilutes or cancels the effect: the base margin, blend weights, gate, and member twins are the same in training and prediction. Using the held capacity at prediction instead of the vintage capacity gives 0.105 (ablation A6), so the vintage capacity helps slightly. The spread factor is a fixed 1.15 around the median and the 14-day correction uses the stack member's own errors, so neither carries a replica-year bias into the offset.
  • The pooled member refits monthly on the full history with 500 rounds, not under P-roll (the rolling-window schedule of experiment 49).
  • References: climatology and manual_heuristic are recomputed at 11 levels. The production-style row is the stored xgboost_baseline from the local data/power_forecasts table. Whether the local Dagster cross-validation assets wrote it, and not S3, was not confirmed. Its band is too narrow, so its tail scores are noise.
  • Ablation A3 replaces the weekly member with the monthly one, so the blend holds a duplicate. Ablation A7 (three members) is exploratory and not in the best guess.
  • Selection bias: the spread factor 1.15, the blend scheme, the offset gate, and the half-life were chosen or scored on this validation year, so the Primary and supply-point gains are optimistic.
  • Not run: corrected lags, analogues on top of the offset, pooling by type on cleaned targets, and any UKV, ICON-EU, or IFS blend. The side panels of figure 9 repeat numbers from experiments 81 and 54, labelled control-only and "ceiling, not available live".
  • Next: a second validation year for the offset, and more farms or a second year to rank the farm models. The solar bands need recalibration, because the tail check shows them too wide; the other classes' tails need no tail-specific spread factor on this evidence.

docs.title: Experiment 88: does the full NRA forecast recover the normal arrangement during a switch?
docs.text:
Take-home message: a demand forecast that corrects its inputs for a switching transfer recovers the power the substation would have drawn only when the megawatts (MW) moved are known, and the detector we have does not yet supply them well enough. A switching transfer is load that the network operator NGED moves from one Primary substation to its neighbours for hours or days. The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the network as it is when no transfer is on. With the true MW, correcting the earlier half-hours of power that the forecast reads (the lags) closed about half of the extra error that a transfer causes, and an XGBoost model trained on NGED's logged transfers closed 83%. With the MW from the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), run only on data from before the forecast, the gain was 16% and could not be told from zero. The detector's MW over all marked cases had a weighted median of 1.07 times the true MW from day 2, and cases with a single interval had a median of 1.00. The loss comes from the 21% of marked cases in which the detector reports two or more overlapping time intervals for one transfer, and their MW is added together. The detector also kept reporting MW for days after a transfer had ended, because it alarms the return step as a new transfer of opposite sign and holds it for a median of 48 hours (90th percentile 96 hours). Counting overlapping intervals once, a choice made after seeing the results, closed 43% during a transfer but still raised the error after it ended. Dropping the transfer's half-hours from the training data added nothing. The verdict is inconclusive.

The headline numbers cover only forecast origins inside an injected transfer, 13% of the year's forecast origins. The forecasts are issued at 09:00 UTC each day from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30 (292 daily runs) for 16 Primary substations, which is 4,672 pairs of a substation and a forecast origin. We injected known transfers into the recorded power of those substations, under five shapes (ways of spreading the moved MW over time, listed in the method bullet below). A case is one transfer under one shape at one substation and one origin.
