The 613 cases per shape that fall inside a transfer come from 172 transfers and 233 distinct substation-origin pairs (5% of the 4,672), and give 292,575 forecast half-hours, 13% of the year's roughly 2.24 million half-hours at leads up to 10 days. The four pooled shapes give 2,452 cases. The transfers start in four of the even-numbered months (October 2025, February, April, and June 2026), and those four months are the blocks that the intervals resample. August and December hold no 15-day window with no logged closure or detector alarm on a substation, so they are not scored. Every forecast is scored against the true, unmodified power, never against the metered power, which is abnormal while a real switch is on.

We asked whether the NRA booster of experiments 75 and 86 forecasts the power a substation would have drawn had the switch not happened, while the switch is on (family A) or after it has ended (family B). Five arms were scored. Arm 1 is the plain booster on the contaminated lags. Arm 2 corrects the lags with the MW. Arm 3 is the NRA booster trained on NGED's logged transfers, and arm 4 the NRA booster trained on RO-NC transfers, both with corrected lags and the MW as columns, and with the transfers' half-hours removed from the training targets. Arm 5, the ceiling, is the plain booster on lags the transfer never touched. Arms 2 to 4 were run with the MW from the injection and with the MW from RO-NC. The gap is arm 1 minus arm 5, and a share of the gap closed is the fall in error from arm 1 divided by that gap.

  • Method: injected transfers. We injected 839 transfers over 10 months, using experiment 82's sampler, which places each transfer where no logged closure or detector alarm lies within 7 days. Each transfer is injected under five shapes. S1 takes a share of the donor substation's own daily profile, S2 moves a constant MW, S3 takes a share of each receiver's profile, S4 mixes constant and profile (the mix fitted to the labelled real transfers), and S6 uses the donor's profile reversed in time. The headline pools S2, S3, S4, and S6, the shapes that do not match how the sampler builds S1. Shape S5 of experiment 82 (the profile shifted by 12 hours) is not scored.
  • Method: boosters and scoring. Arms 1, 2, and 5 are experiment 86's plain and lagmw_xl boosters. Arms 3 and 4 are two new boosters, nra_oracle and nra_xl. (The xl in lagmw_xl and nra_xl names the RO-NC detector's labels.) All are refitted monthly on a rolling 365-day window (150 rounds, eta 0.15, seed 0), because the contrasts are about lags and not retraining cadence. Each forecast uses 11 of the 51 ensemble members and leads to 10 days. The error is the mean absolute error of the median forecast, in percentage points of the substation's capacity, weighted by the transfer's mean MW.
  • Absolute error in family A (points of capacity, 95% interval). Plain 5.409 (4.785 to 6.049). Ceiling 4.455 (3.913 to 4.976). Lag correction, injected MW 4.923; RO-NC MW 5.190. Oracle-trained NRA, injected MW 4.619; RO-NC MW 5.069. RO-NC-trained NRA, injected MW 4.929; RO-NC MW as built 5.261; largest-step MW (post hoc) 5.003. The plain-to-ceiling gap is 0.95 (0.70 to 1.44) points, and it persists at every lead: plain minus ceiling is 0.74, 0.78, 1.05, and 0.96 at leads of 0 to 24 h, 1 to 2 d, 2 to 6 d, and 6 to 10 d.
  • Planned contrasts (98.75%, which is 95% adjusted for four contrasts; shapes pooled). C1 is arm 4 with RO-NC MW minus arm 1, C2 is arm 3 with injected MW minus arm 1, C3 is arm 4 minus arm 2 (both with RO-NC MW), and C4 is arm 2 with RO-NC MW minus arm 1. C1 -0.149 (-1.174 to +0.148), 2 of 4 months negative. C2 -0.790 (-1.397 to -0.412), 4 of 4. C3 +0.070 (-0.015 to +0.171). C4 -0.219 (-1.159 to +0.095). Per shape (95%), C1 is -0.06 to -0.25 with every interval containing zero, and C2 is -0.69 to -0.84 with none containing zero.
  • Share of the gap closed (95%). Injected MW: lag correction 51% (9% to 74%), RO-NC-trained NRA 50% (12% to 73%), oracle-trained NRA 83% (70% to 91%). RO-NC MW as built: lag correction 23% (-10% to 66%), RO-NC-trained NRA 16% (-17% to 67%), and oracle-trained NRA 36% (-2% to 74%). Largest-step MW (post hoc): lag correction 48% (18% to 71%), NRA 43% (17% to 71%). By time since onset the gap is 0.42, 0.93, and 1.95 points (0 to 24 h, 1 to 3 d, over 3 d), and RO-NC-trained NRA with the as-built MW closes 17%, 8%, and 23%, none separable from zero.
  • What the detector reports. At the newest lag the forecast may use (3.5 hours before the origin), it had marked 32%, 73%, and 70% of the moved MW (by time since onset), with the right sign in all but 2% of cases. The median ratio of its MW to the injected median was 0.66, 1.07, and 1.09 (weighted median, right-sign cases). Split after the fact by the ratio of the detector's MW to the injected MW, the as-built RO-NC-trained NRA booster changed the error against plain by -0.73 points where the detector's MW was at most 1.5 times the true MW (735 of 2,452 cases), +1.45 where it was more than 1.5 times (291 cases), and -0.06 where the detector marked nothing (1,426 cases). The as-built loss comes entirely from cases with two or more overlapping intervals (219 cases, among them early fire plus a later re-alarm on the same series, and an alarm plus a partner interval one or two stamps apart); single-interval cases already recover 59% of the gain the injected MW gives. The causal detector's de-duplication matches only an identical onset, so it misses these.
  • Is the MW the wrong scale? No. Arm 4 was trained on hindsight labels that sum overlapping intervals in the same way, so training and scoring use the same MW definition. Dividing the MW by 1.5 would cut the gain of the single-interval cases, whose median ratio is 1.00.
  • Stability of the planned contrasts (point values). C2 is robust: it ranges from -0.62 to -0.92 when October 2025, February 2026, April 2026, or June 2026 is left out. C1 is fragile: without February 2026 it is +0.09, and without the single event 89073 (a February event) it is -0.06. The as-built result rests on February 2026; the largest-step contrast keeps its sign without it (-0.20).
  • Known fault in the report script. The report script takes the detector's MW from the first pass for some arms and the second pass for others, so its printed MW ratios mix stale and fresh values. The MW ratios on this page come from an audit that re-ran the causal detector on every case and reproduced every headline number (C1, C2, the largest-step contrast, and the shares of the gap closed), because those numbers come from the second-pass forecasts only.
  • After a transfer ends (family B, descriptive). Plain 4.93, 4.77, and 4.90 points at 0 to 24 h, 1 to 3 d, and 3 to 7 d after the end. RO-NC-trained NRA with as-built MW is higher than plain by 0.36 (0.07 to 0.55), 0.46 (0.23 to 0.73), and 0.35 (0.12 to 0.50). The same booster with injected MW is lower than plain by 0.31, 0.16, and 0.11. The detector still marked 43%, 36%, and 13% of cases after the end.
  • Tails (family A, shapes pooled). Pinball loss at the 0.05 quantile, pinball loss at the 0.95 quantile, and 90% interval coverage, in that order: plain 0.794, 0.792, 0.878; oracle-trained NRA with injected MW 0.609, 0.675, 0.913; RO-NC-trained NRA as built 0.798, 0.736, 0.882; ceiling 0.587, 0.667, 0.923. The stored boosters hold nine quantile levels, so the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles and the curtailment-cost metric are not scored.
  • Odd months (descriptive; the detector was tuned there). C1 -0.165 (-0.590 to +0.060), post hoc largest-step MW -0.204 (-0.592 to just below zero), oracle -0.328 (-1.102 to +0.034), 95% intervals.
  • False-alarm check. On 401 distinct (series, origin) pairs with no transfer, the detector marked none at the newest lag, so no false alarm arose. Running the NRA boosters with zero MW raised the error over the ceiling by +0.004 (RO-NC-trained), +0.015 (lag correction), and +0.041 (oracle-trained) points.
  • Real-event check: not scored. Three conserved real transfers of the validation year (load that left one substation and arrived at others) have both sides at most half missing. They last 12.0, 5.0, and 13.5 hours, and no daily 09:00 origin falls inside any of them. The longer conserved transfers have one side mostly missing.
  • Caveats. Four month blocks give a coarse interval, and intervals read as ranges. Injected transfers add a known MW to recorded power with the stored residual model unchanged (the fast path of experiment 43). The causal detector may fire up to a day before the true onset with the step understated, which the code reproduces from experiment 82. Experiment 86's RO-NC labels sum overlapping intervals, as the as-built arm does. The oracle-trained arm 3 uses NGED's logged events at training, and the RO-NC-trained arm 4 uses hindsight labels, so neither is a live service.
  • Deviations from the plan. Months, draw size, and shapes are in the plan section "Changes made before any scoring" below. After the first scoring pass, the causal detector's overlapping alarm and partner intervals at one onset were summed twice (the experiment 82 label export keeps one); the double-counting was fixed and the causal variants re-run before any number above was written. The largest-step variants are post hoc.
  • What to try next. De-duplicate overlapping same-sign intervals of one series, keeping the largest step. Suppress an opposite-sign alarm inside an earlier interval or within 48 half-hours after its end, and let the MW decay in the days after the end. Then repeat the family A and B contrasts and report the result without February 2026 beside the full result. Score real transfers with several forecast origins a day.

docs.title: Plan (written before any code ran)
docs.text:
• Question. Experiment 75 could not tell whether a forecast trained without switching half-hours, with corrected lags, helps, because the metered target is abnormal during a switch and only 1.3% of scored half-hours had a lag inside an event. Injection makes the unmodified power known, so the forecast can be scored on what it is for.
  • Sizing (the five plan-issue triggers). What gets stored: two new sets of boosters (arms 3 and 4), per-case forecast tables, and the injected-event tables, all private under data/; no table the production code reads. Production serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one defensible design: yes (how a detector run causally reports an open event, and which shapes form the headline), so the plan fixes both. Code whose callers cannot be named without searching: no, the scripts copy the experiment 82 injection and detector code and the experiment 86 forecasting code. The experiment is complex because it has a new method (the causal detector and the injected-lag forecasting) and more than one defensible design. Per the brief, all plan and code reviews are Sonnet.
  • Earlier advice followed. Experiment 75: test corrected lags with the MW columns (arm 2), judge a refit arm against a same-code repeat of the plain arm (arm 1 and arm 5 use experiment 86's stored boosters, so no repeat is needed), and score on rows with a lag inside an event (every injected case has one by construction). Experiment 82: score a detector on shapes it does not assume (S6 is new), and report by donor step in noise units. Experiment 58 and 43: injected events are in quiet periods (no logged closure within 7 days, no alarm within 2 days).

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Injection. Experiment 82's harness: draw_events with the 600-event stratification (160 in the headline band, 55 in each of the other eight bands of size and duration), onsets restricted to the six even months of the validation year (2025-08, 2025-10, 2025-12, 2026-02, 2026-04, 2026-06), each quiet on every series it touches. inject_shaped injects each event under five shapes: S1 donor profile, S2 constant MW, S3 receiver profile, S4 fitted mix (the profile shares fitted to the labelled real transfers), and S6, the donor's profile in time-reversed order across the interval (new; replaces experiment 82's S5, the profile shifted 12 hours, which is also reported). The headline pools S2, S3, S4, and S6. Each shape rescales its MW to S1's mean, as in experiment 82. The pilot sets the number of events: if forecasting all of them would take over 4 hours, the draw is halved to 300 before any scoring, and the number is recorded in the write-up.
  • Cases. The 292 daily runs of fold_a_daily_gap_v1 (origin 09:00 UTC; the runs that experiment 86's boosters forecast, so the 73 every-fifth-day runs are not used). Family A: the origins with onset at or before the origin minus 3.5 hours (so the newest usable lag is inside the interval), up to 7 days after the onset and before the end. Family B: the origins from 3.5 hours after the end up to 7 days after the end (the lag window; a lag at least 7 days and 3.5 hours before the origin cannot touch the interval). A case is an (event, series, origin, valid time), for the donor and each metered receiver, with lead up to 10 days. The donor, the metered receivers, and the unmodified power are read from the dense half-hourly grid of experiment 86; the injected power adds the injected MW to it, and the lags are rebuilt from the injected power. Cases whose true power is missing, or inside a logged closure or an oracle-labelled event, are dropped. Experiment 82's stamps start on 2022-01-01 and experiment 86's grid on 2019-09-01, an offset of 40,896 half-hours. The injected MW is divided by each series' effective_capacity_mw, and a printed check asserts that the panel's observed power over that capacity equals the dense grid wherever both exist.
  • Truth. The unmodified observed power over effective capacity. Weights: the case's event's mean injected donor MW, so a large transfer counts for more (the MW-weighted rule of experiments 37 and 82); unweighted means are secondary.
  • Bins. Family A by time since onset at the origin: 0-24 h, 1-3 d, over 3 d. Also by lead band (0-24 h, 1-2 d, 2-6 d, 6-10 d), step in noise units (donor step over experiment 82's noise scale, bins 2-4, 4-6, 6+), shape, duration band, and metered receiver or not.
  • Boosters. Arms 1, 2, and 5 re-use experiment 86's boosters (work/boosters/<arm>/<site>_s0_<refit>.ubj, monthly refits from 2025-07-01, N1 recipe, 150 rounds, learning rate 0.15, seed 0): plain and lagmw_xl. Arms 3 and 4 are new boosters on the same schedule and recipe as experiment 86: nra_oracle and nra_xl drop the training rows whose valid time lies inside an oracle (arm 3) or RO-NC (arm 4) event, replace each lag by the lag minus the signed MW, and add the signed MW as three columns. Labels are the hindsight labels of experiment 86 (oracle: experiment 41; RO-NC: experiment 82's xl_intervals.parquet). Arm 2 uses lagmw_xl so that arms 2 and 4 differ only in the training-target mask.
  • Forecast-time MW. Two sources for arms 2 to 4. (i) Injected: the event's median injected MW on each series (negative on the donor), constant over the interval, as the oracle labels are; used for a lag whose valid time lies in the interval. (ii) Causal RO-NC: experiment 82's RO-NC detector (refit-offset step statistic, logistic score models.pkl, threshold from thresholds.json), run on the injected residuals (fast path of experiment 43: the stored residual plus the injected MW) with every value at or after the cut stamp (the origin minus 3.5 hours) set to missing, and with only the 45 days before the cut visible. The functions are those that built experiment 82's xl_intervals.parquet, with four causal rules added. The step statistic exists only where its 48-half-hour after-window is complete, and a candidate is a local peak among those stamps. A rising step can therefore fire up to 24 hours before its true onset, with the step understated; this is what the same code does when run live, so it is kept, and the write-up reports the onset error and the detected step over the injected median MW by hours since onset. A return step or level failure ends an interval only when it lies at least 48 half-hours before the cut, and the first-return search stops at the cut. Any other interval is open and runs to the cut. Partners follow the rule that built xl_intervals.parquet (an opposite-sign neighbour step above 2.0 noise units whose level holds at least half the step for 24 hours). The signed MW of an interval is its series' 24-hour step at the onset over capacity. Known mild leaks, stated rather than removed: the noise scales, the logistic score and its threshold were fitted on odd months of the whole record, including months after an origin, and the injected power does not enter the monthly residual-model refits (the fast path). A property test perturbs every residual value at or after the cut over many (event, origin) pairs and asserts that the detector output is unchanged.
  • Contrasts and bootstrap. As in the decision rule. Family B is reported by hours since the end of the transfer. The share of the arm 1-to-ceiling gap that arms 2, 3, and 4 close is reported overall and by time since onset, lead band, step size, shape, and duration, with 95% intervals by the same resampling. The quantile score and the pinball loss at the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles are reported beside the MAE. The stored boosters have 9 quantile levels, so the 0.01 and 0.99 tails cannot be scored.
  • False-alarm check (descriptive). For 500 (series, origin) pairs drawn at random outside every injected interval and outside logged closures, arm 4 and arm 2 with causal RO-NC MW minus arm 5. This is how much the NRA boosters raise the error when the causal detector raises an alarm that is not a transfer.
  • Second check: real events. The conserved two-sided events of experiment 41 in the validation year with both sides at most half missing (about 22). For each side the NRA estimate is the metered power minus the labelled signed MW of the other side of the event (the donor's estimate adds the receiver's step, and vice versa); inside the event the target is this estimate and outside it the metered power. Arm 1 and arm 4 (causal RO-NC MW, with the oracle MW beside it) are scored on family A origins with the same MAE. This truth is itself an estimate.
  • Schedule. The cheap monthly P-roll schedule of experiment 49: a refit on the 1st of each month, 365-day window, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, recency half-life 0.5 years, seed 0. The contrast is not about retraining cadence, so a weekly schedule is not used. The two new booster arms need 12 refits x 16 Primaries x 2 arms = 384 fits, on the slot's GPU share (12 GB) and 8 cores.
  • Compute. The causal detector runs once per (batch of events, shape, origin), on arrays restricted to the 45 days before the cut. The pilot measures seconds per detector run and per booster prediction (about 480 valid times by 51 members per case and arm) and the plan's event count is fixed from them before scoring. Worker count times threads per worker stays within 8 cores. Each worker handles one batch of events (disjoint series within 7 days) and writes its output to its own file. Scoring waits until experiment 86 has written all its boosters.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
1. Sonnet writes this plan; one Sonnet reviewer reads it; findings are triaged below.
  2. Sonnet implements. One Sonnet code reviewer checks for leakage (nothing at or after the origin minus 3.5 hours reaches the causal detector or the lags; the booster for a case is the latest refit at or before its origin; training masks use hindsight labels, which is allowed).
  3. Sonnet runs and writes up. A Sonnet reviewer checks the write-up against the printed report, and a second Sonnet reviewer runs the prose review.
  4. The PR merges under the skill's "Merging" rules.

docs.title: Plan review
docs.text:
A Sonnet reviewer found these, all accepted unless noted.

  • Rising-step peaks fire early on a partial window: kept as live behaviour, with onset error and step ratio reported by hours since onset.
  • "Open interval" was undefined on truncated data: fixed by the explicit end rule above.
  • The first-return search could fix an end early: ends are accepted only 48 half-hours before the cut.
  • Family B is hurt for about a day after the end: predicted, and reported by hours since the end.
  • Fitted constants are a mild leak: stated. Partner rule: made explicit. Grid and capacity offsets: stated and asserted.
  • Six month blocks: per-month signs are now part of the verdict. Bonferroni now covers four contrasts, adding the lag correction alone (C4).
  • The 20% threshold is also reported for the 1-3 d bin. A share of the gap is reported only where the gap's interval excludes zero.
  • Compute estimate and a pilot are added; the 73 every-fifth-day runs are dropped.
  • Rejected: none.

docs.title: Changes made before any scoring
docs.text:
The event draw and a timing pilot ran before any forecast was scored. They changed the plan as follows.

  • Scored months. August and December 2025 hold no 15-day window that is quiet on any series, so the draw returned none. The scored months are the four even months that do: October 2025 (76 events), February 2026 (72), April 2026 (99), and June 2026 (99). The decision rule's resampling therefore uses four month blocks, and C1 must be negative in 3 of them. Events starting in the odd months (July, September, January, March, May) are drawn too and reported separately as a descriptive check, because the detector's score and threshold were fitted on odd months and so favour it there.
  • Quiet rule. Experiment 37's switching log ends in March 2026, so the quiet rule also excludes 7 days around every closure in experiment 41's labelled set, which runs to June 2026.
  • Draw. 839 events in total, 27 headline-band and 9 per other band requested per month, those drawn over a data gap removed. Shape S5 (profile shifted 12 hours) is not scored.
  • Compute. The pilot forecast 40 cases with all 8 variants in 9 s, so all events and 5 shapes are scored. Each forecast uses 11 of the 51 ENS members (the control member and every fifth), leads up to 10 days, and the spread factor of 1.15 of experiment 33 on the quantiles.

docs.title: Experiment 89: does the longest history, with load shifts masked, improve the NRA forecast?
docs.text:
Take-home message: hiding the past power readings (lags) that were measured while the electricity network was switched away from its normal arrangement made the demand forecast for Primary substations (the substations that step down to the local distribution network) worse, and training on all history since March 2021 instead of the last 12 months changed nothing. Removing the switched half-hours from the training targets therefore did not make the longer history help, so the labelled switching we have does not explain why a long history fails to help demand forecasts. The masking raised the error by 0.409 points of capacity (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517) on the half-hours whose lags were measured during switching. The longest history scored 0.009 points worse than the 12-month window (-0.052 to +0.069). The next step is to test whether a label that marks fewer half-hours lets masking help, using injected events of known size. The verdict is refuted: the plan called a masking interval wholly above zero a refutation.

An electricity network operator sometimes moves load between substations by closing a normally open switch. We call the period while the network is switched away from its normal arrangement an abnormal running arrangement (ARA). NGED, the network operator, supplied the data, and NRA means normal running arrangement. We asked two questions of an XGBoost demand model for 16 Primary substations. First, with ARA half-hours removed from the training targets, does training on all history since March 2021 beat training on the last 12 months? Second, does setting to missing every past power reading (lag) that was measured inside an ARA lower the error on forecasts that use such a lag? We refitted the model monthly and scored 292 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026 on half-hours outside every ARA. The ARA is the union of the intervals of the refit-offset neighbour-count (RO-NC) detector, NGED's logged events, and NGED's logged closures. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity (smaller is better).

  • Arms. R: last 365 days, recency half-life 0.5 years, lags unmasked. M: R with lags in an ARA set to missing. L: all rows since 2021-03, half-life 2 years, lags unmasked. LM: L with masked lags. L_ens and LM_ens: L and LM using only runs from 2024-04-01. Every arm drops training rows whose target is inside an ARA. Monthly refits, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, control member only, seed 0.
  • Rows. 3,199,243 forecast cases (one substation, one forecast run, one lead time); 2,704,935 outside every ARA (the scored rows), of which 352,765 (13.0%) have a lag inside an ARA (the headline rows) and 30,950 have a lag inside a logged event. Row set fold_a_daily_gap_v1.
  • Planned contrasts (98.33%). C1, LM minus L, rows with a lag in an ARA: +0.409 (+0.281 to +0.517). C2, L minus R, all rows outside switching: +0.009 (-0.052 to +0.069). C3, LM minus R, rows with a lag in an ARA: +0.436 (+0.301 to +0.603). No-harm check, LM minus L, all rows outside switching: +0.054 (+0.024 to +0.086), above the +0.02 margin.
  • Absolute scores, all rows outside switching. R 5.468, L 5.478, L_ens 5.485, LM 5.531, LM_ens 5.546, M 5.554; manual_heuristic 6.184; climatology 7.616.
  • Absolute scores, rows with a lag in an ARA. R 5.591, L 5.618, L_ens 5.633, LM 6.027, LM_ens 6.090, M 6.095; manual_heuristic 5.990; climatology 6.785. Masking pushed the XGBoost model behind manual_heuristic on these rows.
  • Descriptive contrasts (95%). M minus R: +0.504 (+0.407 to +0.611) on rows with a lag in an ARA, +0.086 (+0.056 to +0.117) elsewhere. LM_ens minus L_ens: +0.456 (+0.332 to +0.566) and +0.061 (+0.038 to +0.087). L_ens minus R: +0.017 (-0.018 to +0.053). L minus L_ens: -0.007 (-0.028 to +0.010). LM minus L on the 30,950 rows with a lag in a logged event: -0.038 (-0.652 to +1.927).
  • Tails, all rows outside switching (share of actuals below the 0.05 quantile and above the 0.95 quantile, nominal 0.05): R 0.044 and 0.078; L 0.036 and 0.064; LM 0.037 and 0.066; M 0.047 and 0.080. Pinball loss at 0.05 and 0.95: R 0.912 and 1.202; L 0.899 and 1.185. The longer history crossed the 0.95 quantile less often and scored a little better in the tails, though the quantile score did not move. The nine quantile levels have no 0.01 or 0.99.
  • Labelled switching per year (share of half-hours inside an ARA, all 16 series): 2021 0.2%, 2022 8.9%, 2023 11.8%, 2024 16.2%, 2025 13.1%, 2026 (January to June) 15.6%. None of the three sources labels most of 2021, so the first 10 months of training history keep their switching in the targets.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits, which the 12-month and longest-history arms share. A weekly schedule was not run, and the history contrast could depend on it.
  • Weather. The forecast's own control-member weather at forecast time; nothing from ERA5. The control member is 18 km before 2023-06-27 and 9 km after, and the archive from 2024-04-01 is a different product. L_ens and LM_ens (runs from 2024-04-01) scored within 0.02 of L and LM outside switching, so the seam did not decide the contrasts.
  • Curtailment cost. Not scored: this experiment forecasts Primary demand only and has no generator forecasts for the node metric.
  • Caveats. Masks use hindsight labels, so C1 and C3 are the best masking could do for an event known only afterwards. L differs from R in window and half-life together, and L_ens separates them only partly. Possible reasons for the harm (not tested): the union marks 9 to 16% of half-hours per year from 2022, so masking discards a good lag on many rows, and a missing lag leaves the model with no recent anchor.
  • What to try next. Test masking with a tighter label (logged events only, 30,950 rows), or replace a masked lag with a forecast of the normal arrangement, both on injected switches whose truth is known (experiment 88 injects them).

docs.title: Experiment 90: does telling the model how unusual each lag is improve the forecast?
docs.text:
Take-home message: telling the XGBoost demand model how unusual each of its lags is made the forecast worse, not better. In this experiment the extra inputs added no useful signal beyond what the lag values and the calendar already give. The three lags are the newest reading, the reading at the same time yesterday, and the reading at the same time last week. The unusualness of a lag is the share of that series' ordinary readings, at the same time of day, kind of day, and month, that were lower than the lag. On the half-hours whose lag lies inside a logged switching event, the extra inputs did not make the XGBoost model widen its quantiles either. A switching event is a period when the electricity network operator closes a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) carries a neighbour's load. The next approach to test is an explicit widening rule (SW2-27, a planned experiment). Do not retry the unusualness inputs in this form. The verdict is refuted.

We asked two questions with the same model fits. First, does the unusualness of each lag improve the forecast on all half-hours outside switching? Second, on the half-hours whose lag lies inside a logged switching event, does the model learn to give wider quantiles? We refitted the XGBoost demand model monthly for 16 Primary substations, with and without the three unusualness inputs, and scored 292 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. Both versions train only on half-hours outside every switching event. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity (smaller is better), over 11 quantile levels from q01 to q99.

  • Arms (seed 0, one refit a month on a rolling 12-month window, 150 rounds, eta 0.15; the cheap schedule of experiment 49). plain: the inputs of experiment 86 with raw lags. clim_pit: the same plus the three lag PITs (the probability integral transform: the share of reference values below the lag, ties counted as half). The reference is the series' readings outside switching in the refit's training window, in cells of local month, weekday or weekend, and half-hour of day, each pooled with the two half-hours either side.
  • Training rows. Both arms drop half-hours inside an oracle event, a logged closure, or an event of the RO-NC detector. This is a lab shortcut: these are hindsight labels, and the weather inputs are ERA5 at lag times, which a live service would not have.
  • Rows scored. 2,928,842 half-hours outside switching (the general headline). 37,394 of them have a lag inside a logged event (the switching headline, 1.3%, spread over 8 of the 12 months). The spread factor of 1.15 is applied to both arms, as in the production recipe.
  • Planned contrasts (clim_pit minus plain, 97.5% interval, whole months re-drawn). C1, all rows outside switching: +0.355 (+0.209 to +0.513), refuted. C2, rows with a lag inside a logged event: +0.795 (-0.325 to +2.787), inconclusive. The supported bar was an upper end below -0.02.
  • Absolute scores (plain / clim_pit). Outside switching 5.349 / 5.703; with a lag inside a logged event 10.506 / 11.301. By lead band on all rows outside switching, the difference runs from +0.30 (10 days and beyond, 95% interval +0.14 to +0.46) to +0.41 (2 to 6 days, +0.29 to +0.53).
  • Descriptive contrasts (95%). All half-hours: +0.334 (+0.203 to +0.471). Rows with a lag inside a detector event: +0.097 (+0.002 to +0.243); inside a detector event only: +0.083 (-0.013 to +0.234).
  • Tail calibration (plain / clim_pit; coverage nominal 0.98, 0.90, 0.80; pinball loss in points).
Rows Coverage q01-q99 Coverage q05-q95 Coverage q10-q90 Pinball q01 q05 q95 q99 Outside switching 0.985 / 0.985 0.888 / 0.874 0.789 / 0.759 0.298 / 0.300 0.918 / 0.969 1.172 / 1.203 0.390 / 0.391 Lag inside a logged event 0.971 / 0.972 0.770 / 0.740 0.668 / 0.612 0.482 / 0.491 1.494 / 1.530 3.629 / 3.573 0.665 / 0.678
  • What it rules out. The unusualness inputs did not make the XGBoost model widen its band: on rows with a lag inside a logged event the band covers 0.740 instead of 0.770 with the inputs. Only the upper tail on those rows improved (pinball at q95 3.573 against 3.629), and the 97.5% interval of C2 contains zero.
  • Caveats. The training PITs are in sample (a lag usually lies inside the climatology window that defines its PIT), while forecast-time PITs for lags after the refit are out of sample. A cell's pooling also crosses midnight, so the first and last half-hours of a day borrow values from the neighbouring day type and month. The in-sample training PITs and the midnight pooling may each add to the harm. This experiment tested neither. The result uses one seed and the monthly schedule: this experiment did not test a weekly refit. Only the climatology reference was run. The lag-free-booster PIT and neighbour arms of SW2-28 need the booster of SW2-27, which does not exist yet, and experiment 88's injected cases were not rescored. The curtailment metric was not scored.
  • Open question for the next experiment. Whether an explicit rule that widens the quantiles from the probability that a lag is inside an abnormal arrangement (SW2-26 feeding SW2-27) fixes the 0.77 coverage that the inputs tested here did not fix.

docs.title: Experiment 91: a probability that a past half-hour lies inside a load-shift period
docs.text:
Take-home message: a probability built from the causal switching detector is not reliably better than the detector's yes-or-no flag, and against NGED's switching logs it has almost no skill. The detector is called RO-NC here (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector) and is "causal" because it sees only data before the forecast origin. A rule that widened the forecast's uncertainty bands whenever the probability is high would widen them for only about 8% of the half-hours that NGED's logs mark as switching. The probability beats the flag only for injected transfers large enough for the detector to see. One option for a later experiment is a warning signal that needs no switching label, such as how unusual the recent power readings are.

An abnormal running arrangement (ARA) is a period when a network operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) carries load that belongs to a neighbour. A forecast made at an origin time takes as inputs the power readings (lags) of the 7 days before the origin, the lag window. The forecast is misled when one of those readings was taken during an ARA. We asked whether the detector can give each half-hour of the lag window a probability of lying inside an ARA.

We added a known amount of load (a transfer) to the recorded power of 16 Primary substations, 839 times, using the draw of experiment 88. A second draw added 183 longer transfers, lasting 1 to 60 days, so the two draws hold 1,022 transfers. The probability was fitted on transfers that start in odd calendar months and scored on transfers that start in even months.

The verdict is inconclusive. The calibrated score of the latest candidate (arm 2, defined below) has a Brier score (the mean squared error of a probability; smaller is better) 3.3% below the recalibrated yes-or-no flag (arm 1), with a 97.5% interval from -7.6% to +1.6%. The interval includes zero, so the experiment can neither support nor refute a gain, and the pre-registered prediction required at least 20%. The 20% threshold is the smallest gain judged worth carrying the extra detector output to the serving path. In a post hoc subset (chosen after seeing the results) that drops transfers whose donor substation steps by under 4 noise units (the size of the substation's usual half-hour-to-half-hour variation), the gain is 11.2% (-20.3% to -2.0%). Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.5 means no skill, 1.0 means perfect separation of half-hours inside a transfer from half-hours outside) is 0.53 against NGED's logs.

Arm 2's gain over the flag is small and its interval includes zero on the pre-registered rows.

The probability separates well for transfers under 14 days and poorly beyond.

Probabilities above 0.5 are too high.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
A candidate is an interval that the detector proposes, with a score, an onset, a size in noise units, and, once it has ended, a return step.

  • Arm 1: the flag. A half-hour is flagged when it lies inside a candidate whose score reaches the detector's threshold. Each flag value is replaced by the share of odd-month half-hours with that value that lay inside a transfer, so the flag is calibrated too.
  • Arm 2: for the most recent candidate whose switching has not been reversed, a logistic regression on its score, its age, the time from its onset to the half-hour, and any return step, then isotonic regression (a monotone calibration curve). A half-hour with no such candidate gets the odd-month rate.
  • Arm 3: arm 2 plus the candidate's size in noise units.
  • Post hoc arm: arm 2 with the highest-scoring candidate instead of the most recent.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Pre-registered rows. The even-month test set holds 3,358,215 half-hours with 85,650 inside a transfer, for the five shapes S1 to S6 that the injection uses (a shape is how the moved MW varies through the day). The four shapes S2, S3, S4, and S6 are pooled for the contrasts. Brier scores: arm 1 0.02321, arm 2 0.02243, arm 3 0.02229, post hoc arm 0.02239. Area under the curve: 0.710, 0.728, 0.729, and 0.718.
  • Contrasts (change in Brier score against arm 1, 97.5% intervals from resampling the 83 injection batches, each a set of about 10 transfers injected together). C1, arm 2: -3.3% (-7.6% to +1.6%). C2, arm 3: -4.0% (-8.2% to +0.8%). Arm 3 against arm 2: -0.7% (-1.9% to +0.9%). In 3 of the 4 even months that contain half-hours inside a transfer, arm 2 has the lower Brier score.
  • Calibration. The prediction's reliability condition (no probability bin holding at least 5% of half-hours misses the diagonal by more than 0.1) is met. It is met only because 97% of half-hours fall in the lowest bin, so the condition tests almost nothing. In the bins covering probabilities 0.55 to 0.77, only 0.29 to 0.35 of the half-hours lie inside a transfer.
  • Post hoc rows. Dropping the half-hours that the same detector already flags on the uninjected power (which holds unlabelled real switching) changes arm 2 to -1.6% (-6.1% to +2.9%). Also dropping transfers whose donor step is under 4 noise units gives the table below.
Arm Brier score Change against arm 1 (97.5% interval) Area under the curve 1: flag 0.00902 - 0.871 2: latest candidate 0.00801 -11.2% (-20.3% to -2.0%) 0.880 3: with size 0.00798 -11.6% (-20.7% to -2.2%) 0.880 Post hoc: highest-scoring candidate 0.00780 -13.5% (-23.6% to -3.5%) 0.879
  • By duration of the newest injected transfer (post hoc subset, both draws, half-hours at origins whose newest transfer has that duration):
Duration Half-hours inside a transfer Area under the curve: flag arm 2 post hoc arm Flag marks (inside / outside a transfer) Under 24 hours 5,752 0.813 0.826 0.829 64% / 1.1% 1 to 3 days 20,878 0.835 0.855 0.861 70% / 2.8% 3 to 14 days 44,008 0.827 0.828 0.837 68% / 2.9% Over 14 days 75,132 0.675 0.670 0.682 37% / 2.4%
  • Real half-hours. The 292 forecast origins (one per daily run) have lag windows holding 130,816 half-hours, of which 19,099 lie inside a closure in NGED's logs or a labelled event. Area under the curve: flag 0.521, arm 2 0.532, arm 3 0.528, post hoc arm 0.531. The flag marks 6,271 half-hours, of which 1,607 (26%) lie inside the logs, and misses 17,492 of the 19,099 logged half-hours. NGED's logs are incomplete, so some flagged half-hours counted as wrong may be real switching, and 26% is a lower bound on the share of flagged half-hours that are real.

docs.title: Laboratory shortcuts and caveats
docs.text:
• A live probability would need a different weather input. The detector's expected-power model uses ERA5 weather estimates, which arrive about 5 days late. A live version would use ENS (ECMWF ensemble) forecasts, and this experiment does not test one.
  • Some fitted constants saw months after the origin. The noise scales, the logistic score, and its threshold were fitted on odd months of the whole record, including months after an origin.
  • The injected power skips the monthly refits. The expected-power model is not refitted on the injected power, and its expected power is floored at 10% of its whole-record median.
  • Rows are sampled and split by month. The lag window contributes every sixth hour. A half-hour inside a transfer takes the calendar month the transfer starts in, and any other half-hour takes the month of its timestamp. Half-hours at one origin can therefore fall on both sides of the odd-even split.
  • The longer draw is smaller than planned. We planned 384 longer transfers and placed 183, because the requirement that a transfer start in a quiet period left few windows long enough.
  • The calibration curve and the regression share training rows. The isotonic regression is fitted on the logistic regression's own odd-month training rows. All scores use even months, so this does not touch the results above.
  • Arm 3 adds little at the receiving substation. A receiving substation's candidates inherit the score and size of the donor substation's alarm, so the size gives arm 3 almost no extra information there.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: One option is an input that measures how unusual the recent lag power is, which needs no switching label (the question of experiment 90, SW2-28). Another is a detector that sees the real switching that the logs hold, since this detector flags only 8% of the half-hours that NGED's logs mark as switching.

docs.title: Experiment 92: how has Primary demand drifted since 2022? (LV0)
docs.text:
The demand of Primary substations has drifted since 2022, differently in each substation, but a plain level shift does not explain why longer training history or pooled XGBoost models score worse. In this page, "drift" means the trend over time of the residual: observed power minus the forecast of a model that was frozen in 2022. The experiment is LV0, the first of three planned on a slower per-series level term: LV1 is the level-normalised long-history experiment, and AGE1 asks whether an old training year still hurts once its level is removed. The result narrows the plan for LV1. An explicit solar term, such as the am solar offset, is the likeliest carrier of the drift. AGE1 should run first. The pre-registered prediction was not met on one of its two measures, so the verdict is inconclusive.

We took the stored forecasts of six earlier experiments (17, 24, 48, 78, 82, and 89), which hold each Primary substation's forecast beside its observed power. We measured the residual by hour of day, by season, and by month, in percentage points of the substation's effective capacity ("points" below). We then asked whether the drift in that residual explains three results of those experiments: longer training history scoring worse (D4), pooled models scoring worse than per-series models (D5), and weekly refits scoring a little better than monthly refits (D6). D1 to D3 describe the drift itself. No model was fitted.

Figure 1 (headline): the drift by hour band and season, in points a year.

Figure 2: each series' monthly residual, with the persistent steps found.

Figure 3: the persistent steps, by what each matches.

Figure 4: the loss from extra history against each series' level change.

Figure 5: the pooled models' extra bias against each series' monthly level.

Figure 6: the gain from weekly over monthly refits, by drift flag.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• Predictions and schedules used. The residual is observed power minus experiment 17's XGBoost model frozen at its first forecast origin and fed ERA5 weather, in points of capacity. D4 also reads experiment 17's all-history and 12-month-window arms (monthly refits) and experiment 89's reference and longest-history arms (monthly refits). D5 reads experiment 24's per-series and pooled models. D6 reads experiment 48's weekly and monthly refits at the full setting. Experiment 78 supplies the solar capacity flag for 5 series only. Experiment 82 supplies the switching alarms. Experiment 81 was not used because it has no weekly arm, and experiment 87 because its predictions have no observed-power column.
  • Series. Experiment 17 holds 16 series. Three have under 24 months of data (4, 5, and 22 months) and are dropped, leaving 13.
  • D1, drift by hour band. The pooled all-hours slope is +0.04 points a year (-0.90 to +0.89), because the series drift in both directions. In 12 of 13 series some band moves by at least 1 point a year, and in 5 of 13 the all-hours slope does. April-to-September midday is -1.30 (-2.32 to -0.92), evening is -0.88 (-1.57 to -0.24), and night is +0.69 (+0.15 to +1.36). The October-to-March bands span zero. The midday fall may reflect growing embedded solar output; this is untested.
  • D1, share of drift that is a common level. By a straight-line fit, the all-hours component holds over half of the trend variance in 6 of 13 series (95% interval 6 to 11). By a 12-month rolling mean, which also captures steps, it holds over half in 12 of 13. The prediction of at least 10 of 16 holds on the second measure and fails on the first, so the experiment cannot say the prediction held. The threshold of 10 was set for 16 series, and 13 remain.
  • D2, step census. A step is a change of at least 2 points in the weekly mean residual lasting at least 8 weeks. The search finds 63 steps over all hours (33 with no other event nearby, 20 with an opposite step at another series within 4 weeks, 10 within 2 weeks of an alarm of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector, "RO-NC"). The penalty was set so that shuffled weekly values gave 0.39 steps per 5 years. Caveat: the frozen model's seasonal misfit also produces persistent changes, so 63 is an upper bound, and the median step is 14 points. At night only, where solar does not enter, the search finds 77 steps (23 untagged).
  • D3, common against own drift. The first principal component of the monthly level holds 39% of the variance (95% interval 34% to 48%), and the median correlation between two series is 0.25 (0.15 to 0.34). Drift is mostly specific to each series. That is consistent with pooled models struggling without a per-series level, but D5 finds the pooling gap does not follow level.
  • D4, loss from extra history. In experiment 17, all history scored 0.86 points worse than a 12-month window. The loss tracks each series' level change at r = 0.70 (interval -0.34 to +0.98), but one series with a 30-point level change carries the correlation: without it r = -0.03 and the rank correlation is 0.27. Experiment 89's longest-history arm scored 0.07 points better on average, and its correlation with level change is 0.91 with that series and 0.08 without. No link is detectable in the other 12 series (n = 12, no interval computed), and the removed series has both the largest level change and the largest loss.
  • D5, pooling gap. Experiment 24's XGBoost model pooled over all series, with the series identifier as a feature, scored 0.40 points worse than per-series models (0.51 after the 14-day correction). The pooled models' extra monthly bias correlates with the series' monthly level at r = 0.13 (-0.04 to +0.33), so no link to level is detected, though a correlation up to 0.33 is not excluded.
  • D6, cadence gap. Weekly refits scored 0.017 points of capacity better than monthly refits over the 156 series-months, in mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels. The gap is larger in the 3 series with the steepest all-hours slope (+0.033, 0.012 to 0.057 more than elsewhere), and not larger in months with a step (-0.008, -0.025 to +0.003) or a switching alarm (-0.001). The capacity-growth flag cannot be tested, because all 5 series with a capacity record grew by over 5%. Any flag holds 83% of the gap in 60% of the series-months, so the prediction's "over half" is met, but the excess comes entirely from the 3 series chosen by slope: the step, alarm, and capacity flags hold no more of the gap than their share of series-months.
  • Tails, weekly and monthly refits on the same 13 series. The table is the stored forecasts of experiment 48. The stored forecasts stop at q05 and q95, so q01 and q99 are not available. Both tails are too narrow: q05 covers 0.07 of the actuals against 0.05 nominal, and q95 covers 0.91 against 0.95. A curtailment-cost score does not apply because no new forecast was made.
Refit q05 coverage q05 pinball q95 coverage q95 pinball Weekly 0.071 0.834 0.913 1.025 Monthly 0.070 0.834 0.912 1.038

docs.title: Lessons and next experiment
docs.text:
• Verdict. Inconclusive: the two measures of the common-level share disagree, and the D6 prediction is met only against a high base rate.
  • LV1. The decision rule to proceed to LV1 is met by D1 (5 of 13 series at 1 point a year or more overall), but D4 and D5 do not support level removal as the mechanism, so AGE1 should run first.
  • AGE1 should run first. AGE1 tests directly whether an old year still hurts after its level is removed.
  • Intervals. Every interval re-draws whole months with the series held fixed, so the intervals leave out the uncertainty between series, which is large with 13 series, and are too narrow. The threshold of 10 of 16 series scales to about 8 of 13; the straight-line count (6, interval 6 to 11) lies at the bottom of its interval.
  • Caveat on every diagnostic. The residual comes from a frozen model on ERA5 weather, so the results describe drift in a lab setting, not in the live service.
  • What the next experiment should answer. Whether a frozen model's seasonal misfit hides real steps. A later experiment on steps could first remove the seasonal pattern before searching for them.

docs.title: Experiment 93: does an old training year still hurt once the level is removed? (AGE1)
docs.text:
Taking each substation's average demand level out of the training data removes under half of the extra forecast error that an old training year causes, and removes none of it for 12 of the 13 substations. The old training year differs from the recent one in more than its average level. The weather data also changed between the years (18 km grid spacing in the old years, 9 km in the recent year), and this experiment could not separate that change from age, so the next experiment should test the change of weather product. The prediction is refuted: the extra error reached the size predicted, but level removal took off 42% of it, not the half predicted.

We trained one XGBoost quantile model per substation on one year of forecasts from the unperturbed run ("control member") of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble, for 13 primary substations (33 kV to 11 kV substations, the "Primary" type in NGED's data). Each model was trained once and not retrained. We scored every model on 365 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026, with the quantile score: the average pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, in percentage points of the substation's effective capacity ("points"; smaller is better). Four planned models trained on 2021-07 to 2022-06 or on 2024-07 to 2025-06. For each year, one model used the demand as measured and one had the substation's trailing 365-day average demand (its "level") subtracted from the target and from the power lags (demand at earlier times), then added back to the forecast. Four post hoc models repeat the design with other training years and a half-hourly level.

Names used below. The "raw penalty" is the 2021-07 model's score minus the 2024-07 model's score, both raw (planned contrast C1). The "level-removed penalty" is the same difference with the level removed (C2). C3 is the raw penalty minus the level-removed penalty.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Penalty. The raw penalty is 1.57 points (98.3% interval 1.14 to 2.00); the level-removed penalty is 0.91 (0.69 to 1.20). The difference C3 is 0.65 (0.04 to 1.23), which is 42% of the raw penalty. The 98.3% level is the Bonferroni level for three planned contrasts. The prediction needed a raw penalty of at least 0.5 and a removed share of at least 50%, so its second half failed.
  • Without the substation with the largest raw penalty (post hoc, 95%). The raw penalty is 0.61 (0.41 to 0.81) and the level-removed penalty is 0.68 (0.47 to 0.94), so level removal raised the penalty slightly. One substation has a raw penalty of 13.1 points; the other 12 range from 0.0 to 2.2.
  • Repeat with 2022-07 to 2023-06 (post hoc, 95%). The raw penalty is 1.28 (1.04 to 1.55) and the level-removed penalty is 0.86 (0.60 to 1.17), so level removal takes off 33%.
  • Half-hourly level (post hoc, 95%). Subtracting a level for each half-hour of the day gives a penalty of 0.75 (0.47 to 1.09) for the 2021-07 year, close to the 0.91 from the level averaged over all hours.
  • Rows in the normal switching arrangement only (95%). These are the rows where the substation's part of the electricity network was not in a labelled abnormal arrangement. The raw penalty is 1.65 (0.85 to 2.03) and the level-removed penalty is 0.72 (0.56 to 1.00).
  • Level removal does not help the model trained on the recent year. Its score is 4.78 raw and 4.84 with the level removed.
  • Quantile score of each model (points, 95% interval). 2024-07 raw 4.78 (4.45 to 5.14); 2024-07 level removed 4.84 (4.49 to 5.22); 2021-07 raw 6.34 (6.01 to 6.69); 2021-07 level removed 5.75 (5.29 to 6.32); 2022-07 raw 6.05 (5.60 to 6.62); 2022-07 level removed 5.70 (5.18 to 6.34).
  • Level removal more than halves the old year's miss at the 0.01 quantile, and widens its miss at the upper quantiles. The table gives the share of actual values at or below each quantile.
Model 0.01 0.05 0.95 0.99 Ideal share 0.01 0.05 0.95 0.99 2024-07 raw 0.015 0.077 0.913 0.984 2024-07 level removed 0.012 0.071 0.903 0.981 2021-07 raw 0.091 0.196 0.924 0.984 2021-07 level removed 0.041 0.109 0.838 0.958

The pinball loss at the 0.01 quantile is 1.30 for 2021-07 raw and 0.27 for 2024-07 raw.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Schedule. Frozen fits of 150 boosting rounds at learning rate 0.15, seed 0, one fit per substation and arm. The comparison is between frozen models, so the retraining schedule does not enter.
  • Weather data. The old years use the 18 km control member and the recent year uses the 9 km control member, so age and weather resolution cannot be separated here.
  • Switching labels. Labels that mark when a substation was in an abnormal switching arrangement exist only from 2022-01, so the rows of the first half of the 2021-07 training year could not be excluded. The 2022-07 repeat is fully labelled and gives a raw penalty of 1.28 and a level-removed penalty of 0.86.
  • Intervals. The intervals resample 12 whole calendar months with replacement, so they rest on only 12 blocks and are coarse.
  • Not scored. The climatology and manual_heuristic benchmark rows and the curtailment-cost metric were not computed, because the question is a contrast between training years of one model.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: Most of the penalty is not explained by the level. For the 12 substations without the large outlier, the old year is about 0.6 points worse with or without the level. A candidate next experiment separates age from the change of weather product, for example by training the recent year on the 18 km control member. After that, the heating-demand and solar-generation terms remain to be checked. The planned experiment LV1 (training on a long history with the level subtracted) is not supported by this result.

docs.title: Experiment 94: does an explicit heating term lower the cold-hour error? (HT1)
docs.text:
Giving the XGBoost demand model an explicit heating term lowered its error in cold weather by a little, and did not fix the cold-weather tail. We asked whether telling the model about heating explicitly helps when it is cold. XGBoost is a forecasting method built from decision trees, and a tree predicts a constant for temperatures colder than any hour it was trained on. For each of 16 Primary substations (which step 33 kV down to 11 kV) and each hour of the day, we fitted by least squares how much a substation's demand, as a fraction of its capacity, rises per degree Celsius below 15.5 °C, using the training rows only. We then gave XGBoost the product of that slope and the degrees below 15.5 °C as a base margin (a fixed starting prediction supplied for each row). We compared the result with the same XGBoost model without the term on 365 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026.

The quantile score is an error measure for a probabilistic forecast, in points of a substation's capacity (lower is better). In cold hours (ensemble-mean forecast temperature below 3 °C from the ECMWF ensemble, ENS) at leads up to 48 hours, the heating term lowered the score by 0.143 points. The threshold fixed in advance for a worthwhile gain was 0.3 points, so the verdict is small gain. The q95 forecast should be exceeded by 5% of observations. In those hours it was exceeded by 16.7% of observations without the term and 16.2% with it. A decreasing monotone constraint on temperature gained about half as much as the heating term. This experiment did not locate the remaining cold-hour error. One untested candidate is the ENS temperature forecast, so the next experiment could compare the forecast temperature with the observed temperature in cold hours by lead.

A second comparison, block B, adds the heating term to experiment 64's solar term. It covers only the 5 Primaries that have a solar term and the 73 forecast runs of fold_a_every5d_v1, and it lowered the all-rows score by 0.050 points. The 16-substation arms have no solar term, so the two blocks do not share rows.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms: ref is the stored zero-start monthly P-roll arm pm0 of experiment 85 (no solar term). ht adds b_h * H to the base margin, where H is the degrees the ensemble temperature is below 15.5 C and b_h is a per-series coefficient for each local hour of day, fitted on the refit's training rows with a month-by-hour intercept and floored at zero. mono is ref with a decreasing monotone constraint on temperature_2m.
  • Schedule: monthly refits on the latest 12 months, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, seed 0, no 14-day correction, spread factor 1.15. The schedule is the research default of experiment 85, so absolute scores and the bias of about +2.4 points over all rows are those of this cheap schedule and would be smaller under weekly refits. The contrasts may depend on the schedule.
  • Rows: 4,004,653 cases (16 series, 365 runs, all valid times); cold means the ensemble-mean ENS 2 m temperature of the case is below 3 C (215,476 cases, 5.4%; 28,344 at leads up to 48 hours). The temperature is available at forecast time; ERA5 enters only in a check.
  • Pre-registered contrasts (98.75% intervals from 20,000 resamples of whole ISO weeks), quantile score, arm minus ref:
    • C1, ht in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours: -0.143 (-0.203 to -0.034).
    • C2, ht over all rows: -0.022 (-0.042 to +0.000).
    • C3, mono in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours: -0.074 (-0.111 to -0.020).
    • C4, mono over all rows: -0.011 (-0.024 to +0.003).
  • Absolute quantile scores (ref, ht, mono): all rows 5.564, 5.542, 5.553; cold up to 48 hours 5.841, 5.698, 5.767; cold over 48 hours 5.957, 5.893, 5.931; mild winter hours 5.491, 5.488, 5.498.
  • Tail calibration (share of observations above q95, target 0.05; below q05, target 0.05; pinball loss at q95 in points of capacity):
Slice Arm Above q95 Below q05 Pinball at q95 Cold, up to 48 h ref 0.167 0.042 1.460 Cold, up to 48 h ht 0.162 0.045 1.381 Cold, up to 48 h mono 0.161 0.040 1.405 Cold, over 48 h ref 0.173 0.040 1.618 Cold, over 48 h ht 0.163 0.046 1.564 Cold, over 48 h mono 0.165 0.040 1.597 Mild winter ref 0.122 0.030 1.240 Mild winter ht 0.122 0.033 1.214 Mild winter mono 0.120 0.030 1.240
  • Bias (observed minus median, points of capacity) in cold hours: over 48 hours 2.90, 2.70, 2.81; at leads up to 24 hours 1.80 (ref), 1.73 (ht), 1.61 (mono); at 6 to 10 days 3.31, 3.14, 3.27; beyond 10 days 2.89, 2.57, 2.78. The bias is positive at every lead, so the forecast is too low in the cold.
  • Exploratory contrasts (95%): ht in cold hours at all leads -0.074 (-0.138 to +0.007), over 48 hours -0.064 (-0.132 to +0.030), with cold hours defined by ERA5 temperature at leads up to 48 hours -0.118 (-0.163 to -0.048), in mild winter hours -0.003 (-0.054 to +0.053), and in June to August +0.002 (-0.006 to +0.009). ht minus mono in cold hours up to 48 hours is -0.069 (-0.104 to +0.005).
  • Block B (5 series, 73 runs, 3 seeds, experiment 64's frozen recipe, 14-day correction, 95% intervals): amh (the solar margin plus the heating margin) minus am: all rows -0.050 (-0.065 to -0.036), cold hours -0.160 (-0.234 to -0.067), cold up to 48 hours -0.198 (-0.375 to -0.035), mild winter hours -0.075 (-0.111 to -0.038), April to September -0.024 (-0.034 to -0.014). Absolute scores am 3.940 and amh 3.890 over all rows. The heating term therefore lowers the score of the solar model further, by more than in block A in every slice. Block B differs from block A in series, runs, seeds, refits, and the 14-day correction, so the sizes are not comparable. No arm with the heating term alone ran on the block B rows, so additivity is not tested. In cold hours up to 48 hours the bias of amh is -0.425 against -0.155 for am (more over-forecast), and the q95 exceedance is unchanged (0.136 against 0.136).
  • Explainability: the last figure shows the fitted term for one substation over 3 to 9 January 2026. The term follows the temperature and the daily shape, and sits at about 5% to 15% of the substation's capacity when the demand is 55% to 105%.
  • Deviations from the plan: the solar offset is not in the 16-substation arms (it acts only in April to September at 5 series, and its inputs exist only for the 73 runs and to June 2025), so block B tests the heating term on top of the solar term. The plan said "member temperature" for the cold slice; the scoring uses the ensemble mean, one value per case. The curtailment-cost metric and q01 and q99 tail reads are not reported, because the nine-level model stops at q95. The optional arm scaled by Low Carbon Technology heat-pump counts was skipped, because the data needs a portal account.
  • Caveats: in block B the heating coefficients are fitted on net power without removing the solar margin first, so the heating coefficient may absorb part of the demand reduction that the solar margin already models. Block A used one seed. Experiment 85 found that repeat fits change the score by 0.000 to 0.001. Three ISO weeks (2025-W47, 2026-W01, and 2026-W02) hold 66% of the 28,344 cold cases at leads up to 48 hours, and the C1 and C3 intervals rest on 21 weeks of one winter. The other intervals rest on 53 weeks (C2, C4), 23 weeks (cold, all leads), 13 weeks (mild winter), and 15 weeks (June to August).
  • Predictions against results: a cold-hour fall of at least 0.3 failed (0.143). A q95 exceedance fall of at least 0.03 failed (0.005, from 0.167, not the 0.18 predicted). An all-rows change of at most +0.01 passed (-0.022). A long-lead bias fall of under half passed (5% to 11%). A mono gain of at most a third of the offset's failed (0.074 against 0.143, 52%).
  • What the result shows: in this winter's data, the heating degree-hour term did not repair the cold-hour tail. The heating term leaves the exceedance of q95 at 16% to 17% of cold hours.
  • What to try next: compare the forecast temperature with the observed temperature in cold hours by lead; test the monotone constraint inside the production recipe, since it adds no serving column; a second winter is needed before any decision to port the heating term.

docs.title: Experiment 95: does an old training year score worse because of the weather product, or its age? (AGE2)
docs.text:
A model trained on demand from July 2021 to June 2022 forecasts demand in 2025-26 worse than a model trained on 2024-25 demand, and the coarser weather forecast of the old years is not the main reason. The extra error ("gap") was 1.71 points of capacity when both models were trained and scored on ERA5, the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) estimate of past weather, against 1.57 points with the ECMWF ensemble forecast's unperturbed run ("control member"). Here "points of capacity" are percentage points of a substation's effective capacity on the quantile score, where smaller is better. The gap also grew with each year older. Experiment 93 found that a difference in the average demand level between the years does not explain the gap. The cause is therefore probably a change in how the substations' demand depends on weather and time of day, such as growing embedded solar output or heating, or a change to the electricity network. Explicit solar and heating terms are the candidate explanations the next experiment could test.

The prediction was refuted on both counts. The ERA5 gap was 109% of the control-member gap, not under half. The model trained on July 2023 to June 2024 was 0.50 points behind the 2024-25 one, not under 0.3.

We trained one XGBoost quantile model per Primary substation (13 substations, each named in the figures by an anonymised code such as D8) on one year of demand and weather. "The 2021-07 year" means the year of data from 2021-07 to 2022-06, and likewise for the other years. Experiment 93 had shown that the 2021-07 year scores 1.57 points worse than the 2024-07 year, and that its years also used a coarser weather forecast (18 km grid spacing, against 9 km from July 2023). Here each arm (one training year with one weather product) was trained once, not retrained, and scored on the 365 daily forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The ERA5 arms used ERA5 weather at the valid time. The control-member arms used the control member's forecast. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels from 0.01 to 0.99, weighted by the probability each level represents, in percentage points of capacity.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• The ERA5 gap is no smaller than the control-member gap (99% intervals, the Bonferroni level for five planned contrasts). C1, the 2021-07 year minus the 2024-07 year on the control member, is 1.57 (1.12 to 2.03). C2, the same on ERA5, is 1.71 (1.15 to 2.29). C3, C1 minus C2, is -0.15 (-0.32 to -0.002), so the ERA5 gap is slightly larger; C2 is 109% of C1 (1.00 to 1.18). C4, the 2023-07 year minus the 2024-07 year on the 9 km control member, is 0.50 (0.28 to 0.76). C5, the 2021-07 year minus the 2022-07 year on the 18 km control member, is 0.29 (-0.35 to 0.85), which cannot separate one year of age from zero.
  • The gap grows with each year of age on ERA5 (95%). Against the 2024-07 year the 2022-07 year is 1.26 points behind (1.10 to 1.44) and the 2023-07 year is 0.46 behind (0.36 to 0.57). On the control member the 2022-07 year is 1.28 behind (1.04 to 1.55).
  • Absolute quantile score (points, 95% interval).
    • ERA5: 2021-07 6.22 (5.82 to 6.60); 2022-07 5.77 (5.37 to 6.27); 2023-07 4.97 (4.58 to 5.43); 2024-07 4.51 (4.18 to 4.89).
    • Control member: 2021-07 6.34 (6.01 to 6.69); 2022-07 6.05 (5.60 to 6.62); 2023-07 5.28 (4.84 to 5.77); 2024-07 4.78 (4.45 to 5.14).
  • Without D8, the substation that carries most of the penalty (post hoc, 95%). C1 is 0.61 (0.41 to 0.81), C2 is 0.78 (0.53 to 1.04), C4 is 0.35 (0.19 to 0.53), and C5 is -0.05 (-0.52 to 0.37). The ERA5 gap is larger than the control-member gap here: C3 is -0.18 (-0.28 to -0.08) and C2 is 129% of C1 (116% to 144%), so D8 dilutes the ratio with all 13 series. D8's own gap is 13.1 points on the control member and 12.9 on ERA5.
  • D8's demand fell smoothly; the checks found no step change or stuck meter. Its monthly mean demand fell from 0.82 of capacity in 2021-07 to 0.34 in 2026-06, with no month under 99.3% observed half-hours and under 0.6% of half-hours repeating the previous value. The largest change in the 60-day mean demand over 60 days is 0.22 of capacity, a rise ending 2024-08-25. Summer demand fell faster than winter demand (August 0.77 in 2021 and 0.31 in 2025; January 0.76 in 2022 and 0.48 in 2026), which fits growing embedded solar output, but this experiment did not test whether embedded solar output grew.
  • Rows in the normal switching arrangement only (95%). C1 is 1.65 (0.84 to 2.03) and C2 is 1.81 (0.79 to 2.26), so labelled switching events are not the main explanation, though the intervals are wide. The switching-event labels start in 2022-01, so the first half of the 2021-07 year is not masked.
  • Weather product within one year (post hoc, 95%). ERA5 gives a quantile score 0.31 points lower (better) than the control member for the 2023-07 year (0.16 to 0.46) and 0.27 lower for the 2024-07 year (0.13 to 0.42).
  • Tail calibration (share of actual values at or below the quantile; ideal 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99).
Model 0.01 0.05 0.95 0.99 2021-07, control member 0.091 0.196 0.924 0.984 2021-07, ERA5 0.098 0.233 0.917 0.983 2024-07, control member 0.015 0.077 0.913 0.984 2024-07, ERA5 0.019 0.096 0.893 0.980

The pinball loss at the 0.01 quantile is 1.30 (control member) and 1.35 (ERA5) for the 2021-07 year, and 0.27 and 0.28 for the 2024-07 year, in points of capacity.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Schedule. Frozen fits of 150 boosting rounds at learning rate 0.15, seed 0, one fit per substation and arm. Weekly or monthly refits would give an old year's model newer data, so the contrasts describe how old a frozen model's training data is, not a retraining schedule.
  • ERA5 arms are diagnostic. ERA5 arrives about 5 days after the weather, so no live service could use it at forecast time. The ERA5 arms score the same runs and valid times as the control member arms, with a single weather value per time and no ensemble spread. Absolute scores and tail calibration are therefore not like for like across the two products, and C3 compares two contrasts, each computed within one weather product.
  • The 2023-07 year. Its rows come from experiment 81's daily frames up to 2024-03-31 and from the stage 1 pilot's training file from 2024-04-01. The 2024-01-03 run is missing, so the year has one run fewer. The 18 km to 9 km change took place in June 2023, so the 2023-07 year is 9 km.
  • Intervals. They resample 12 whole calendar months, so they are coarse. The share C2 over C1 is a ratio of two means and its interval is only informative because C1's interval excludes zero.
  • Not scored. The curtailment-cost metric and the manual_heuristic and climatology rows, as in experiment 93.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: The age penalty is about 0.5 to 0.8 points for each year older on ERA5 and 0.3 to 0.8 on the control member, and a level shift does not explain it. Two experiments could test what does: an explicit heating offset (the subject of the reserved experiment 94) and an explicit embedded-solar term, with the old years re-scored. If either term shrinks the gap across the four years, the result would support trying a longer training history. If neither does, the data give no reason to move away from the newest year or two.

docs.title: Experiment 96: do synthetic load shifts in the training data make the NRA forecast recover the normal arrangement better?
docs.text:
Take-home message: adding about three times as many synthetic switching transfers to the training data did not improve the forecast of the power a substation would have drawn without the transfer, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the limit is the estimate of the MW moved, not the amount of training data. A switching transfer is load that the network operator NGED moves from one Primary substation (the donor) to its neighbours (the receivers) for hours or days. A synthetic transfer is one made by adding a known MW to the recorded power of a donor and its receivers. The forecast error rose by 0.03 to 0.08 points of capacity (percentage points of the substation's capacity, in mean absolute error) when synthetic transfers were added, and no 98.75% interval excluded zero. Given the true MW, the XGBoost model trained on real transfers alone already closes 83% of the gap between the error of a plain model (no correction) and the error of the same model reading unmodified lags (the ceiling). A lag is an earlier power reading. Given the detector's MW, the same model closes 32% to 53% of the gap, and training on exact MW did not change that. A likely reason is that a lag corrected by the exact MW equals the lag with no transfer, so a synthetic transfer looks like a row with no transfer. The next test of synthetic transfers should train with a MW that carries the detector's errors.

The experiment asked whether more switching examples in training help the model that recovers the normal running arrangement (NRA). The NRA forecast subtracts the MW moved from each earlier power reading it uses. Experiment 88 trained that XGBoost model on the 56 real transfer intervals (one per series and transfer) of its training windows. In this experiment a second XGBoost model was trained on those 56 intervals plus 169 synthetic ones (from 94 synthetic transfers, 3.0 times the real count). Both models were scored on experiment 88's held-out synthetic transfers, with the MW at forecast time taken from the injection, from the causal refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), or from the largest overlapping detector step.

  • Arms. Arm 1: booster trained on the real transfers only (experiment 88's nra_oracle recipe, refitted at 11 quantile levels). Arms 2 to 4: one booster trained on the real and the synthetic transfers, scored with the injected MW (2), the RO-NC MW as built (3), or the largest-step MW (4). Each synthetic arm is compared with arm 1 scored with the same MW source.
  • Training recipe. Monthly rolling refits (P-roll: 365-day window, 150 rounds, learning rate 0.15, recency half-life 0.5 years, seed 0). The ensemble-control rows inside a real or synthetic transfer are dropped as targets. Each lag is replaced by the lag minus the signed MW at the lag time, and the signed MW at the three lags is a column. A synthetic transfer's signed MW is its median injected MW, constant over the transfer. The correction is the one experiment 88 used, with no other.
  • Rows. Experiment 88's 2,452 injected cases in even onset months (October 2025, February, April, and June 2026), shapes S2, S3, S4, and S6, forecast origins inside the transfer (family A). The synthetic training transfers start only in odd months (2024-07 to 2026-05); one of the 94 ends in an even month.
  • Absolute error, family A (points of capacity, 95% interval). Plain 5.409 (4.785 to 6.049); ceiling 4.455 (3.913 to 4.976). Injected MW: arm 1 4.620 (4.116 to 5.176), arm 2 4.698 (4.150 to 5.325). RO-NC MW: 5.068 (4.332 to 5.782) and 5.101 (4.322 to 5.843). Largest-step MW: 4.905 (4.227 to 5.644) and 4.943 (4.219 to 5.690).
  • Planned contrasts (98.75%). C1 +0.079 (-0.031 to +0.153). C2 +0.032 (-0.019 to +0.067). C3 +0.038 (-0.008 to +0.053). C4 -0.466 (-1.283 to -0.004). C1 to C3 were negative in 1 of 4 onset months. The decision rule gives inconclusive: no interval of C1 to C3 excludes zero in either direction.
  • Share of the plain-to-ceiling gap closed (95%). Injected MW: arm 1 83% (71% to 90%), arm 2 75% (54% to 87%). RO-NC MW: 36% (-3% to 73%) and 32% (-10% to 73%). Largest-step MW: 53% (14% to 79%) and 49% (9% to 76%).
  • By time since onset (95%). Synthetic minus real-trained error grows with the age of the transfer: with the injected MW +0.044 (-0.002 to +0.078) in the first 24 hours, +0.085 (-0.015 to +0.173) from 1 to 3 days, and +0.128 (-0.034 to +0.211) after 3 days. With the largest-step MW -0.006, +0.059, and +0.075; every interval includes zero.
  • After a transfer ends (family B, descriptive). Every contrast lies within +/-0.03 points and every interval includes zero. All arms with the RO-NC MW have an error about 0.4 points of capacity higher than the plain model's (5.31 against 4.86), as in experiment 88.
  • Tails (family A). Nominal values are 0.01 for the share of actuals below q01 and above q99, and 0.05 for the share above q95. Real-trained and synthetic-trained arms with the injected MW: below q01 0.0136 and 0.0134; above q95 0.0133 and 0.0139; above q99 0.0004 and 0.0003; pinball loss at q01 0.212 and 0.212, at q99 0.329 and 0.330; coverage of q01 to q99 0.986 and 0.986. With the largest-step MW: below q01 0.0145 and 0.0144; above q99 0.0004 for both. Synthetic training did not widen the quantiles. The lower tail is slightly under-covered and the upper tail over-covered in every arm. The plain booster has 9 quantile levels, so its tails are not scored. The curtailment-cost metric was not scored, because the injected cases are single series and not a node with its generators.
  • Reproduction check. Arm 1's error minus experiment 88's stored nine-level scores is +0.000 (-0.008 to +0.007) with the injected MW and -0.000 (-0.009 to +0.008) with the RO-NC MW.
  • Schedule and lab conditions. Monthly P-roll refits; the contrast is about training data, not cadence, and could depend on it only through the number of synthetic transfers in each window. Training uses hindsight labels and the injected MW, and the detector's residual uses ERA5, so no arm is a live service. The median-MW correction uses power after a refit when a synthetic transfer straddles one, which is the same hindsight convention as the real labels.
  • Caveats. Only 4 onset months, so intervals are coarse. The training transfers needed a looser quiet rule than experiment 88's (see below). Arms 2 to 4 share boosters, so they are not three independent trainings.
  • Reviews. One Sonnet code review found no leakage. It flagged that one training transfer ends in an even month (accepted as immaterial: 1 of 94, stated above), that the median MW uses hindsight (stated above), and that the reproduction guard might trip on 11-level pooling (it did not). Findings on the unused power argument and on memory were not acted on. A numbers review and a prose review followed; their valid findings (four rounding slips, one mislabelled range, and an opening that used undefined terms) were applied.
  • What to try next. Train the booster with a MW that carries the detector's errors (overlapping intervals summed, a return step held for a median of 48 hours) in the synthetic transfers, and score it with the detector's MW. A better MW estimate at forecast time is the other route.

docs.title: Plan (written before any code ran)
docs.text:
• Question. Experiment 88 showed that a booster trained on the real logged transfers recovers the normal arrangement during an injected transfer only when the MW is known (83% of the gap closed), because the real record holds about 56 transfer intervals in the training window. Does adding about three times as many synthetic transfers to the training history help, and does the help survive the detector's MW?
