  • Sizing (the five plan-issue triggers). What is stored: two sets of boosters (arms 1 and 2), a table of the synthetic training events, and per-case scores, all private under data/. Production serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one defensible design: yes (how many events, which shapes, which months, which MW the booster is trained with), so the plan fixes them below. Code whose callers could not be named without searching: no, the scripts copy experiment 88's harness. Size: complex (new method and several designs), with Sonnet reviewers only, as the brief says.
  • Training injection. Experiment 88's harness (draw_events, inject_shaped) draws synthetic transfers in the odd calendar months from 2024-07 to 2026-05, quiet on every series they touch (no logged closure within 1 day, no alarm within 2 days; see "Changes made before any fit"). The shapes S2, S3, S4, and S6 are assigned in turn. The number of series-intervals injected is 3 times the number of real labelled transfer intervals (experiment 41's labels) that start in the 365-day windows of the refits, counted per series; the script prints both counts. Test transfers (experiment 88's 839) start in even months only, so no training transfer shares a calendar month with a test transfer.
  • What the booster sees in training. The booster's rows are experiment 88's: the ENS control member, a 365-day window, monthly refits (P-roll, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, half-life 0.5 years, seed 0), no calendar columns beyond the existing derived set. The power the lags are read from is the recorded power plus the injected MW. Rows whose valid time lies inside a real (experiment 41) or injected transfer are dropped as training targets (the ARA, abnormal running arrangement, is masked). Each lag is replaced by the lag minus the signed MW at the lag time, and the signed MW at the three lag times is added as three columns. The signed MW is each event's median injected MW, constant over the event, summed over events, plus the real oracle MW. No other lag correction is used. This is experiment 88's nra_oracle recipe with the injected events added.
  • Arms. Arm 1: nra_oracle, real transfers only, refitted at 11 quantile levels (q01, q05 to q95, q99) with the injected MW, the RO-NC MW, and the largest-step MW at forecast time. Arm 2: synthetic-trained, injected MW (oracle). Arm 3: the same boosters, RO-NC MW from the causal detector as built. Arm 4: the same boosters, largest-step MW (post hoc in experiment 88; a planned arm here). Arms 2 to 4 share boosters, so the training cost is two booster sets.
  • Scoring. Experiment 88's script copied: the same 839 test transfers, shapes, origins, causal detector, and truth. Plain and ceiling come from experiment 88's stored cells. A check that arm 1's q05 to q95 reproduce the stored 9-level nra_oracle scores to 0.01 points guards the copy. Families A and B, bins by time since onset and lead band, the quantile score, and tail calibration (coverage and pinball at q01, q05, q95, q99) are reported.
  • Labels and lab conditions. Training labels use hindsight (oracle events and injected MW), the detector's residual model uses ERA5, and the MW at forecast time in arm 2 is the injected truth. Nothing here runs live. The forecast needs the weather the lags are corrected with only through the lags themselves, so no ERA5 enters the booster.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits on a rolling 365-day window, because the contrasts are about training data and not retraining cadence. The contrast could depend on the schedule only through the number of injected events inside each window, which the write-up reports.
  • Compute. 2 arms x 12 refits x 16 Primaries = 384 fits at about 25 s, at most 4 GPU hours; scoring about 3 CPU hours. If the pilot shows over 4 GPU hours, arm 1's refit at 11 levels is dropped (stored 9-level scores are used and the tails are reported for arm 2 only) and the manager is told.
  • Earlier advice followed. Experiment 88: use the largest-step MW and not the sum (arm 4); test with the true MW first (arm 2); do not expect target masking to add (arm 1 is masked already). Experiment 89: lag masking is worse and the longest history no better, so the window is 365 days. Departures: none.

docs.title: Changes made before any fit
docs.text: • Quiet rule for training transfers. With experiment 88's rule (no logged closure within 7 days), only 33% of the odd-month half-hours are quiet and the draw yielded 74 series-intervals, 1.3 times the 56 real ones. The training transfers therefore keep only 1 day clear of a logged or labelled closure and 2 days clear of a detector alarm, which yields 94 transfers and 169 series-intervals (3.0 times the real count). A nearby real transfer does no harm in training because it is corrected with its labelled MW. The test transfers keep experiment 88's 7-day rule.

docs.title: Experiment 97: which post-hoc recalibration of the best guess fixes its tails
docs.text:
Take-home: the best guess's stored tails are already close to nominal, and a calibration table fitted on earlier months does not reliably improve them. A quantile forecast at level 0.05 (q05) should have 5% of measurements at or below it; that share is the quantile's coverage, and 0.05 is its nominal level. At 12 to 36 hours lead for Primary substations, the stored q05 has a coverage of 0.035 and the stored q95 has 0.938 (nominal 0.95), so the lower quantile sits too far out and the upper quantile slightly too close in. No recalibration of arms 1 to 7b moved the Primary q05 or q95 coverage by more than 0.013, which is less than the plus or minus 0.02 interval that 9 months of data give. Two larger faults show in the results: the coverage of q95 swung between 0.88 and 0.97 from month to month, and the stored median has a coverage of only 0.45 for Primary substations, so those forecasts sit slightly low. A static table cannot correct either fault.

We asked whether the 11 stored quantiles of the weekly-retrained best-guess forecast (BG2, experiment 87) can be recalibrated after the fact. For each month from October 2025 to June 2026 we fitted eight recalibrations (arms 1 to 7b) on every earlier measurement, compared each with the stored forecast (arm 0), and scored them on the forecast runs of that month, for 16 Primary substations and 4 bulk or grid supply points. Verdict: refuted by the pre-registered rule, but inconclusive about recalibration in general. No arm brought the coverage of q01, q05, q95, and q99 within 0.01 of nominal in both classes and kept its centre score within 1% of the stored forecast's. Nine months of data are too few to tell a real improvement from noise.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Stored sets: p_s4_weekly (Primary) and b_weekly (supply points) of experiment 87, 292 daily runs from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, weekly retraining, 3,984,540 rows after dropping rows with no measurement. Scored months October 2025 to June 2026, calibration window expanding from July 2025. The experiment reads no weather data; it uses only the stored quantile forecasts.
  • Arms: 0 as stored; 1 global factor 1.15; 2 scale per level; 3 scale per level, lead band, and class; 4 isotonic level remapping; 5 split-conformal shift; 6 stored q10 to q90 plus Pareto tails; 7a Student-t; 7b skew-normal. Arms 8 and 9 are post hoc: arms 3 and 5 refitted on the last 90 days only. Levels 0.5%, 99.5%, 0.1%, and 99.9% are extrapolated (arms 0 to 5) or fitted (arms 6 and 7). Arm 6 can widen a tail and cannot narrow one: a level whose stored tail is already too wide keeps its stored value.
  • Leakage guard: the script asserts, before any number prints, that every calibration row's valid time precedes the first scored run of its month. A fitted scale factor was clipped to the allowed range of 0.5 to 5 in 44 of 1,440 fits.
  • Classes: the supply-point class pools 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points. The BG2 sets that existed when the experiment ran held no solar or wind series, so neither class is covered.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Stored forecast, Primary, 12 to 36 hours: coverage of q01, q05, q95, q99, and q99.5 is 0.0037, 0.0346, 0.9383, 0.9905, and 0.9934.
  • Stored forecast, supply points, 12 to 36 hours: coverage of q01, q05, q95, and q99 is 0.0039, 0.0362, 0.9323, and 0.9939, from 44 to 347 days with an exceedance.
  • Primary tail coverage after recalibration: arm 3 gives Primary coverage of 0.0100, 0.0478, 0.9397, and 0.9855, but supply-point q95 coverage of 0.9248, which is 0.025 from nominal.
  • Tail test: all 9 arms fail at least one of the 8 decision cells (4 levels, 2 classes). Every cell has at least 30 days with an exceedance except the supply-point q01 and q99 cells of arm 1.
  • Centre test: arms 0 and 6 pass; arms 1 to 5, 7a, and 7b fail it on the all-leads centre score (upper bound above 1% of the stored centre score). At 12 to 36 hours the Primary centre changes by at most 0.0003 for arms 1 to 6.
  • Quantile score, Primary, 12 to 36 hours (minus arm 0, points of capacity): arm 1 +0.00032 (+0.00021 to +0.00043), arm 3 -0.00002 (-0.00011 to +0.00009), arm 5 -0.00002, arm 6 -0.00009 (-0.00015 to -0.00001), arm 7a +0.00055 (+0.00044 to +0.00066), arm 7b +0.00135 (+0.00104 to +0.00167). The stored forecast's score is 0.01882.
  • Beyond q99: arm 6 gives Primary coverage of 0.9949 at 99.5% (stored 0.9934, arm 5 0.9912) and 0.0064 at 0.5% (stored 0.0024, arm 5 0.0044; nominal 0.005). Arm 6 is closer to nominal than the stored forecast at both levels, and closer than arm 5 at 99.5% only. The intervals of all three arms overlap. Supply-point q99 coverage falls from 0.9939 to 0.9772 under arm 6.
  • Median bias: the stored q50 has a coverage of 0.452 (Primary) and 0.427 (supply points) at 12 to 36 hours. Among arms 0 to 7b, arm 5 is the only arm that moves the median's coverage, to 0.487 and 0.442; the post hoc arm 9 gives 0.501 and 0.479.
  • Drift: stored Primary q95 coverage by month ranges from 0.880 (January 2026) to 0.974 (April 2026), and q05 coverage from 0.018 (March 2026) to 0.063 (April 2026).
  • Post hoc arms 8 and 9: the last-90-days window does not beat the expanding window: Primary q05 coverage 0.051 for both, q95 0.945 and 0.943, quantile score +0.00009 and -0.00002 against arm 0.
  • Curtailment at the scaled limit of 0.9 (node-only, two bulk supply points, GBP 2,000 per MWh, a retrospective calculation, not a saving): 17 half-hours of export beyond the limit, all at one node. Avoidable cost is GBP 618,171 for the stored forecast and GBP 629,684 to 668,866 for arms 1 to 5, with every interval from 0 upwards, so the arms are not separable. Arms 7a and 7b have avoidable costs of GBP 2.36 million and GBP 3.12 million because they plan 911 and 1,364 MWh of curtailment against 57.5 MWh for the stored forecast and 33.7 MWh needed.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Few months: 9 scored months give coarse intervals, so a pass or fail at 0.01 is partly noise.
  • Classes missing: solar and wind sets did not exist, and the supply-point class holds 4 series.
  • Exploratory: only the 12 to 36 hour cells are decision cells; every other number is exploratory, and arms 8 and 9 are post hoc.
  • Extrapolation: arms 0 to 5 read levels beyond q01 and q99 off a normal extrapolation, so differences between those arms at those levels reflect the extrapolation rule.

docs.title: What the results point to
docs.text:
• Median bias: the median's coverage is the largest fault in the central levels, and only a shift of the median (arms 5 and 9) changes it.
  • Drift: the month-to-month swing in tail coverage is larger than any arm's correction, so a test of an update that tracks recent level and spread needs at least 2 years of scored runs.
  • Solar and wind: the Pareto tails of arm 6 are untested on those classes.

docs.title: Experiment 98: do the best guess's solar and heating offsets sharpen the LSC?
docs.text:
Giving the demand forecast behind the switching detector two explicit corrections, one for solar output and one for heating, did not detectably raise the share of moved power the detector finds, although the solar correction made the forecast error in summer middays 12% smaller. So removing the solar and heating part of the forecast's weather error does not reach the misses that remain. They are mostly small load transfers from substations whose neighbours are unmetered. The verdict is inconclusive: the interval for the solar and heating arm (+0.034 at its upper end) cannot rule out a gain of the +0.02 that we set as worth porting, and the two solar-only arms show no gain.

A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (the donor's) onto neighbouring substations (the receivers) for hours or days. A Primary substation steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC, defined in experiment 82) subtracts an XGBoost forecast of demand, H0.5, from the measured power and raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of the difference, the residual, steps by a set number of noise units. The best guess is the project's current forecasting recipe, which gives its XGBoost model a solar term and a heating term as a base margin (a fixed starting prediction for each row). We gave H0.5 the same terms, using irradiance from ERA5 or from CAMS (two estimates of past weather), and re-ran experiment 82's detector on the same synthetic transfers. Each arm, meaning each variant of the forecast model, is held to 80 alarms on odd months that no logged closure explains. We compared the share of the moved megawatts (MW) found, on transfers starting in even months.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. h05_stored is experiment 82's own result, reproduced (0.770). ctrl is H0.5 refitted here with a constant starting margin. era5_solar and cams_solar add a base margin of minus the capacity over effective capacity times the anomaly of a unit PV shape, at the 5 series that have a capacity (experiment 64's D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), with the margin's weight fixed at -1. heat adds experiment 94's heating term at all 16 series to the CAMS solar arm, which had the smaller summer midday residual on odd months (5.29 points of capacity, against 5.73 for ERA5 and 5.41 for ctrl).
  • Row set. The row set is the 611 headline-band transfers per shape of experiment 82, with the same seeds, shapes S2, S3, and S4 pooled, starting in even months, on 16 Primary substations. The S4 profile shares are fitted once on the stored panel and reused in every arm. There are no forecast rows, so no tail-calibration or curtailment-cost table applies.
  • RO-NC MW-weighted recall (98.75% interval): h05_stored 0.770 (0.659 to 0.860); ctrl 0.766 (0.654 to 0.855); era5_solar 0.764 (0.647 to 0.853); cams_solar 0.769 (0.651 to 0.857); heat 0.776 (0.670 to 0.861). PF14 stays at 0.656 to 0.663 in the first four arms and 0.685 in heat.
  • Planned contrasts: C1 era5_solar minus ctrl -0.002 (-0.019 to +0.012); C2 cams_solar minus ctrl +0.003 (-0.014 to +0.011); C3 heat minus ctrl +0.010 (-0.012 to +0.034); C4 heat minus cams_solar +0.007 (-0.011 to +0.036). The rule calls refuted only when the upper ends of C1, C2, and C3 are all under +0.02, and C3's is +0.034. ctrl minus h05_stored is -0.004 (-0.014 to +0.003), so the cheaper refit schedule moved the detector by less than the width of the interval.
  • Residual noise. The median absolute residual of the 5 solar series at 10:00 to 14:00 UTC, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a substation's effective capacity). In June to August: ctrl 5.26, era5_solar 5.27, cams_solar 4.63, heat 4.63. In March to May: ctrl 5.44, era5_solar 6.26, cams_solar 5.51, heat 5.45. At 14:00 to 18:00 UTC in June to August: ctrl 4.63, era5_solar 4.78, cams_solar 4.00, heat 3.99. On odd months from April to September, the slice that chose the parent arm, the CAMS gain is 2% (5.41 to 5.29). The mean absolute error of H0.5 over all 16 series and all hours, row-weighted, in points of capacity: ctrl 6.72, era5_solar 6.75, cams_solar 6.70, heat 6.68.
  • By donor (exploratory, same interval level). When the donor is one of the 5 solar series (325 transfers per shape) RO-NC finds 0.512 (ctrl), 0.518 (cams_solar), and 0.537 (heat); heat minus ctrl is +0.025 (-0.030 to +0.062). When the donor is one of the other 11 (286 transfers) it finds 0.940 in ctrl and 0.938 to 0.941 in every arm.
  • By donor step (S2 to S4 summed, each arm in its own noise units). With no metered receiver and a step of 2 to 4 noise units, transfers found out of transfers in the bin: ctrl 139 of 545, cams_solar 105 of 490, heat 95 of 456. A quieter residual turns the same MW step into more noise units, so the larger steps move to the 4 to 6 bin (ctrl 174 of 256, cams_solar 206 of 308, heat 221 of 333), and the counts of the two bins are not comparable between arms.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Lab shortcuts. The experiment takes three. It uses ERA5 weather in the XGBoost demand model, where a live service would use the ECMWF ensemble. It uses the 24-hour hindsight end rules of experiment 82. It uses solar capacities fitted partly on data after some scored dates (experiment 64's held value before July 2025, experiment 78's season-year value after).
  • Schedule. H0.5 is refitted on the 1st and on the 16th of each month, 150 rounds at eta 0.15, against experiment 17's 500 rounds at eta 0.05. ctrl matches the stored fit's mean absolute error for series 7 to three decimals, so the contrasts should not depend on the schedule.
  • Only 5 of 16 series have a solar term, so the pooled recall cannot move much by construction. The donor split shows no detectable change among transfers from those 5 series either (cams_solar minus ctrl +0.007, -0.029 to +0.028; heat minus ctrl +0.025, -0.030 to +0.062).
  • The margin's weight of -1 was fixed before the run. Experiment 64's fitted weights of -0.3 to -0.6 were for noisy forecast anomalies, and no other weight was tried. The capacity is used as experiment 64 used it, and its unit (AC or DC) was not re-checked. The ERA5 arm raised the spring midday residual, which may mean the margin is mis-scaled; the run does not test that.
  • CAMS has no value for about 10% of daylight half-hours (dawn, dusk, and gaps), where the anomaly counts as zero. ERA5 shortwave is taken as the half-hour ending at its timestamp.
  • Not run. The blend arm (4) was not run because ERA5 and CAMS recall did not differ, and the bank-holiday arm (6) because experiment 47 found it leaves recall unchanged.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Of the 725 transfers that experiment 82's stored fit missed out of 1,833, 401 had a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units and no metered receiver, and another 66 had a step under 2 and no metered receiver. Recall there needs a different detection signal. Experiment 82 lists two candidates: a longer averaging window for the 24-hour step, and a check that the receivers' combined step balances the donor's.

docs.title: Experiment 99: does training on the CRPS of the pooled ensemble forecast beat the pinball loss? (CRPS1 pilot)
docs.text:
Take-home message: training on several ensemble members at once, with a loss that scores their pooled forecast, recovers only about half of the harm that extra members do to the usual loss, so a run on all 51 members is not worth its cost for Primary substations on this evidence. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) loss beat the pinball loss, the usual quantile-regression loss, on the same rows by 0.039 points of capacity. One point is 1% of a substation's capacity, and a lower score is better.

Giving the pinball loss 6 ensemble members per run, instead of the control member alone, made it 0.052 points worse. The control member is the ensemble's unperturbed forecast. The CRPS arm is therefore 0.036 points (95% interval, resampling whole months, -0.022 to +0.111) from the current recipe, which trains the pinball loss on the control member only. The interval includes zero, so the pilot cannot say whether the CRPS arm is better or worse than the current recipe. The CRPS arm's tails are not within 0.01 of nominal at 12 to 36 hours. The gain from a CRPS-type loss sits in the median, and the tails need a different fix. The pre-registered verdict, which covers only the contrast between the CRPS and pinball losses, is small gain.

We asked whether a substation forecast improves when the XGBoost quantile model learns from the ensemble's members jointly. Each daily run gave the control member and 5 drawn members as separate rows. The CRPS arm scores the pooled forecast, which combines the 6 rows' predicted quantiles into one distribution, and the pinball arms score each row alone. All arms refit monthly on a rolling 12-month window with 150 rounds and learning rate 0.15 (a cheap schedule, called P-roll in earlier experiments). They forecast the 292 daily runs of July 2025 to June 2026 at 16 Primary substations, pooling all 51 ensemble members at prediction time.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• The CRPS loss beat the pinball loss by 0.039 points of capacity (C1, c1 minus p3, the verdict): -0.039 (95% interval -0.057 to -0.018), small gain. The pre-registered threshold needed the interval's upper end below -0.05. With the best guess's spread factor of 1.15 (widening the quantiles about the median by 15%) on both arms: -0.051 (-0.069 to -0.032).
  • C5, c1 minus p3m: -0.064 (-0.083 to -0.042), where p3m is arm p3's trained XGBoost models pooled with the CRPS atom masses. C5 is larger than C1 because pooling arm p3's pinball atoms with the CRPS masses scores 0.025 points worse.
  • Six members as separate rows made the pinball loss worse (C2, p2 minus p1): +0.052 points of capacity (0.029 to 0.074).
  • C3, p3 minus p2: +0.023 (-0.046 to +0.111). On the quantile score, the custom optimiser and the built-in one cannot be told apart.
  • The CRPS loss on 6 members does not beat control-member pinball training (C4, c1 minus p1): +0.036 (-0.022 to +0.111).
  • Reference: c1 is 0.227 (0.148 to 0.317) and p1 is 0.190 (0.131 to 0.251) worse than the best guess, which refits weekly with 500 rounds; the schedule (weekly refit, 500 rounds) differs, which probably accounts for this gap. c1 beats the manual_heuristic by 0.598 (0.396 to 0.796).
  • Absolute scores, all leads (95% interval): p1 5.547 (5.216 to 5.890); p2 5.599 (5.278 to 5.932); p3 5.622 (5.280 to 5.987); c1 5.583 (5.243 to 5.946); best guess 5.356 (5.072 to 5.653); manual_heuristic 6.182 (5.850 to 6.544).
  • Other scores for C1: the mean absolute error of the median falls by 0.109 (0.066 to 0.149); the threshold-weighted CRPS (which scores only errors beyond a threshold) at the 95th percentile of history rises by 0.008 (0.002 to 0.014); at the 99th and 5th percentiles the change is within noise.
Tail check, 12 to 36 h Quantile c1 p3 p1 Best guess Share of actuals below the quantile 0.01 0.012 0.010 0.009 0.004 0.05 0.061 0.051 0.058 0.036 0.95 0.924 0.938 0.919 0.945 0.99 0.987 0.989 0.986 0.992 Pinball loss at 0.95 (points of capacity, 100 times the script's printed fraction) 0.95 1.32 1.28 1.18 1.09

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Schedule: monthly P-roll with 150 rounds, not the weekly production recipe, so the absolute scores cannot be compared with the best guess's. The contrasts C1, C2, C3, and C5 hold the schedule fixed; whether they depend on it is untested.
  • Pilot limits: 6 members per run at training (51 at prediction), every third daily run, and 16 Primary substations. A run on all 51 members could behave differently, and the pilot cannot say how.
  • Tuning: the constant Hessian (10, the constant second-derivative value that the custom objectives hand to XGBoost) was chosen on four substations and January to March 2025, inside the training period. Both custom arms share it; its best value for each loss may differ. The level weights of the CRPS gradient are divided by twice the atom mass, so c1 is a preconditioned CRPS gradient with the same fixed point.
  • Not scored: the curtailment-cost metric covers supply points with generators behind them, and this pilot trains Primary substations only. Climatology is left out because its rows stop short of the longest leads, so including it would drop 5% of the rows from every arm.
  • Rows: all arms and the stored best guess share 3,197,611 forecast rows.
  • Interval width: the intervals resample 12 origin months, so they may be a little narrow. The upper end of C1's interval, -0.018, is far from the -0.05 threshold, so the verdict does not depend on it.
  • Compute: 1.55 GPU hours of wall-clock time, up to 10 worker processes of one thread each.
  • Options for later: a tail-specific spread factor on the best guess, or pooled-member spread statistics as input columns, because this pilot moved the centre of the distribution and left the tails where they were.

docs.title: Tuning the constant Hessian (training period only)
docs.text:
Each custom arm was fitted at a refit on 2025-01-01 at four Primary substations and scored on the 6-member rows of runs from 2025-01-02 to 2025-03-31 that the fit had not seen. The table gives the mean quantile score (points of capacity, pooled over 6 members) and the coverage of the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles. Arms p3 and c1 share one Hessian, 10, the lowest score for both. The built-in pinball arm p2 scored 3.640 on the same rows. These numbers are not results of the experiment.

docs.title: Experiment 100: does random lag dropout make the demand forecast widen its band when a lag is missing?
docs.text:
Take-home message: training the XGBoost demand forecast with its earlier power readings (lags) hidden at random did not make its forecast interval wider where a lag is missing. On the 37,394 real half-hours for which a lag is set to missing, the forecast's 5% to 95% interval contained 0.799 of the actual demand readings for the plain model (plain11, which never masks a lag) and 0.802 for the model trained with lags hidden in 10% of its training rows (drop10). A well-calibrated interval contains 0.90. The change was +0.003 (98.75% interval -0.093 to +0.101; the level is 98.75% because four contrasts were planned). Dropout did fix a different problem. On synthetic switching transfers of known size (from experiment 88), masking lags without dropout raised the quantile score by 1.36 points of capacity against the plain model. Dropout in 30% of training rows brought that difference to -0.02 (95% interval -0.35 to +0.38), which is no detectable difference. A forecast that must run with missing lags can therefore be trained to do so. An input column that flags a missing lag is one untested way to get the widening. The verdict is inconclusive: the planned coverage contrasts did not exclude zero, and the quantile score on rows without a masked lag rose by up to 0.046 points, above the 0.02-point limit set in the plan.

An electricity network operator sometimes closes a normally open switch, so that a Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) carries a neighbour's load for hours or days. We asked whether an XGBoost demand forecast for 16 Primary substations, trained with some lags set to missing, would learn that a missing lag means more uncertainty. Four XGBoost models were refitted each month on the preceding 12 months of data. plain11 masks nothing and has 11 quantile levels. mask drops the training rows whose target lies inside a labelled switching event or logged closure (9% of rows) and sets to missing every lag inside a labelled event. drop10 and drop30 add lags set to missing inside random intervals during training, in 10% and 30% of training rows. Real rows were scored on 292 daily forecast runs (July 2025 to June 2026). The synthetic transfers supplied rows where the true unmodified series is known. The quantile score is the mean pinball loss over the quantile levels, in points of capacity, and smaller is better.

  • Rows with valid truth. Real rows whose target lies outside every labelled event and logged closure (2,928,842). Of these, 37,394 have a lag inside a labelled event (masked rows, 81% from 3 substations, 89% in 5 months) and 2,891,448 do not (unmasked rows). Real rows with the target inside an event or closure have no valid normal-arrangement truth and are never scored. Point accuracy during a real abnormal arrangement is not a metric.
  • Injected rows. 3,000 family A cases (forecast origin inside the transfer; shapes S2, S3, S4, and S6 pooled with equal weight), from every second batch of experiment 88's events, in 10 onset months. Truth is the unmodified series. The lag mask is the injected interval plus the labelled real events (oracle masking).
  • Arms. All at seed 0, 150 rounds, learning rate 0.15, half-life 0.5 years, 11 quantile levels, spread factor 1.15, mixture of 51 members (injected cases: 11). plain11: all rows, no masking. mask: 9% of rows dropped as targets; lags inside a labelled event set to missing in training and test. drop10 and drop30: mask plus pseudo-event intervals (durations drawn from the 82 labelled events) inside which lags are also set to missing in training only, covering 9.3% to 10.1% and 29.3% to 30.1% of each series' training rows. At test time every arm masks only the lags inside a labelled event. The rows and weights of mask, drop10, and drop30 are identical (the script checks the row counts).
  • Reproduction. Experiment 86's stored plain had nine quantile levels and covered 0.784 on the masked rows; plain11 has 11 levels and covers 0.799. plain11 minus experiment 86's stored plain on 2,928,842 shared rows: +0.0000 points of quantile score (stored mean 5.408). The masked rows number 37,394, as in experiment 86.
  • Absolute scores, real masked rows (plain11 / mask / drop10 / drop30). Quantile score 10.726 / 11.820 / 11.718 / 10.291. Coverage of the 5% to 95% band 0.799 / 0.769 / 0.802 / 0.836. Mean width of that band 44.9 / 46.6 / 46.0 / 44.4 points of capacity.
  • Absolute scores, real unmasked rows. Quantile score 5.339 / 5.381 / 5.356 / 5.374. Coverage 0.906 / 0.894 / 0.893 / 0.892. Width 31.2 / 30.0 / 29.8 / 29.9.
  • Absolute scores, injected family A (plain11 on contaminated lags / ceiling / mask / drop10 / drop30). Quantile score 3.790 / 3.435 / 5.149 / 4.046 / 3.770. Coverage 0.906 / 0.938 / 0.815 / 0.923 / 0.936. Width 23.6 / 23.2 / 25.7 / 25.0 / 24.3. The plain model with its lags masked (never trained with a missing lag) scored 5.453, covered 0.867, and was 27.6 wide.
  • Planned contrasts, drop10 minus plain11 (98.75%). P1, coverage on real masked rows: +0.003 (-0.093 to +0.101). P2, coverage on injected cases: +0.017 (-0.013 to +0.055). G1, quantile score on injected cases: +0.256 (-0.148 to +0.847). G2, quantile score on real unmasked rows: +0.017 (-0.013 to +0.046); its upper end exceeds the +0.02 guard. Width on real unmasked rows: ratio 0.956 (0.940 to 0.969), so the guard of at most 1.03 holds, because the band narrowed.
  • Descriptive contrasts (95%). On real masked rows drop30 minus drop10: coverage +0.034 (+0.000 to +0.069), quantile score -1.43 (-2.67 to -0.28). drop10 minus mask: coverage +0.033 (+0.011 to +0.062), quantile score -0.10 (-0.74 to +0.39). On injected cases drop10 minus mask quantile score -1.10 (-1.66 to -0.44), coverage +0.108 (+0.039 to +0.168); drop30 minus drop10 -0.28 (-0.41 to -0.17). Injected cases with the target inside the transfer give the same signs (drop10 minus plain11: coverage +0.012, quantile score +0.267). Family B (after the transfer ends): drop10 minus plain11 quantile score -0.033 (-0.121 to +0.013).
  • Tails on real masked rows (plain11 / mask / drop10 / drop30). Coverage of the 1% to 99% band 0.983 / 0.977 / 0.975 / 0.979 (nominal 0.98). Share of actuals above q99 0.0166 / 0.0234 / 0.0249 / 0.0208 (nominal 0.01). Pinball loss at q01 0.503 / 0.508 / 0.508 / 0.510 and at q99 0.654 / 0.629 / 0.692 / 0.680. Quantiles crossed before sorting in no member forecast, in any arm.
  • Why the verdict is inconclusive. The planned rule needs P1 and P2 to exclude zero for supported, P2 to exclude zero for small gain, and P2's upper end below zero or G1's lower end above +0.02 for refuted. P2's interval contains zero and G1's lower end is -0.148, so none applies. G1's upper end (+0.847) and G2's upper end (+0.046) both exceed the +0.02 guard. The plan sets not-for-production when G2 fails, which is a production status and not a verdict word, so the verdict word stays inconclusive and production_status is not-for-production.
  • A confound the plan did not isolate. mask alone lowered the coverage of the 5% to 95% band on unmasked rows from 0.906 to 0.894 and narrowed it by 4%. The cause is probably the 9% of training rows (event and closure half-hours) dropped as targets. Dropping them leaves the XGBoost model fitted to quieter data. A control that drops the same rows but leaves every lag unmasked would separate the effect of dropping rows from the effect of masking lags. The plan did not include that control.
  • Schedule, weather, and lab shortcuts. The models are refitted each month on a rolling 12-month window (the P-roll schedule). The dropout contrasts could depend on that schedule only through which refits contain pseudo-event intervals. Weather is the control (unperturbed) member of the ECMWF ensemble forecast, available at forecast time. Labels are hindsight labels at training and test, and the injected mask is the true interval, so no arm is a live service. Causal-detector masks and the curtailment-cost metric were not scored (see the changes below).
  • Caveats. The real masked rows come from an estimated 15 to 20 events, mostly at three substations, in 10 months, so P1's interval is wide (nearly +/-0.1). The injected cases are 3,000 cases from 10 onset months. Coverage is not a proper score: a wider band reaches 0.90 without being better, so every coverage read is beside the quantile score.
  • Changes made after the plan. (1) The first fit run failed at one substation, whose 30% pseudo share overshot (0.345), because the bisection over a prefix of intervals jumped over the target. The pseudo-event masks were rebuilt by accepting intervals greedily until the share is within 1.5 points, and both dropout arms were refitted (plain11 and mask were kept). (2) The injected scoring ran on shapes S2, S3, S4, and S6 and on every second batch of events, because the full run would have taken more than 12 hours; the planned causal-detector (RO-NC) masks were dropped for the same reason. (3) The manual_heuristic and climatology reference rows were not scored. (4) The plain model with masked lags was added as a descriptive variant.
  • Reviews. One Sonnet code review found no leakage and no bug. The pseudo-event share is measured on each series' whole training history and not on each refit's window (accepted: the per-series shares are printed). The same-rows check compares row counts only (accepted: the three arms share one filter). An Opus design review preceded the fits. A Sonnet numbers review found two wrong figures (the 30% pseudo share range and a width range in lessons), both corrected, and asked that the verdict follow the plan's order of rules (rejected, because not-for-production is a production status and not a verdict word; the page now says so). A Sonnet prose review's findings on undefined terms in the opening, bare "model", numerals, and the claim that the widening "has to" come from elsewhere were applied.
  • Options for a next experiment. Add one missingness-indicator column for each lag, so that a tree can give a masked lag its own leaf. Alternatively, fit a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread on rows with a masked lag. Dropout rates above 30% are a third option, because the 30% arm had the higher coverage and the lower quantile score than the 10% arm on both the real masked rows and the injected cases. A control that drops the event and closure rows but leaves every lag unmasked would separate the effect of dropping rows from the effect of masking lags.

docs.title: Plan (written before any code ran)
docs.text:
• Question. Experiment 89 set lags inside a union of detector and logged events to missing and made the forecast worse. Experiment 86 showed that on the 37,394 rows with valid truth and a lag inside a logged event, the 5% to 95% band covers only 0.784 of actuals. We ask whether training with lags missing at random intervals teaches the model to widen its band when a lag is missing, instead of treating a missing lag as an extreme value.
  • Design. An Opus design review is committed beside this file as opus_design.md (in ml-experiments/00100-drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals/). It departs from the maintainer's brief in two ways, both accepted: lags are set to missing in place (not by adding masked copies), so every dropout arm has the same rows and weights as mask; and the dropout masks whole pseudo-event intervals with durations drawn from the 82 labelled events (not each lag independently), so the missing-lag patterns match real events. The fourth arm is a 30% dose check rather than a group-dropout arm, because intervals already mask lags in groups.
  • Arms (seed 0, 12-month rolling window, monthly refits, 150 rounds, eta 0.15, 11 quantile levels, spread factor 1.15). plain11: all rows, no masking. mask: targets inside a labelled event or logged closure dropped, lags inside a labelled event missing in training and test. drop10: mask plus pseudo-event dropout touching 10% of training rows. drop30: the same at 30%, whose pseudo events include those of drop10.
  • Rows with valid truth. Real rows whose target lies outside every labelled event and logged closure. Of these, the 37,394 with a lag inside a labelled event are the masked rows (headline); the rest are the unmasked rows. Real rows whose target lies inside an event or closure have no valid normal-arrangement truth and are never scored. Experiment 88's family A injected cases (truth: the unmodified series) cover the cases real data cannot validate, including a target inside the transfer. Point accuracy during a real abnormal arrangement is not a metric.
  • Interval behaviour is the primary read: coverage and width of the 5% to 95% and 1% to 99% bands on masked and unmasked rows, the widening ratio against plain11 on the same rows, and the quantile score as the proper score beside them.
  • Sizing (the five plan-issue triggers). Stored: private boosters and predictions only. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one defensible design: yes, so the design review fixed it. Callers not nameable without searching: no. Size: complex, with Sonnet reviewers only (the brief), and the Opus design review above.
  • Earlier advice followed. Judge lag treatments on injected events of known size (experiments 88 and 89); report tails at q01 to q99; do not mask on an over-marking detector label (experiment 89). Departure: none.
  • Schedule. Monthly P-roll refits; the contrast is about training-time exposure, and could depend on the schedule only through the number of refits in which pseudo events fall.
  • Lab conditions. Hindsight event labels at training and test, oracle masking on injected cases. Causal RO-NC masks on injected cases are descriptive.

docs.title: Experiment 101: the 66 labelled real transfers, event by event
Experiment 101: how well does the refit-offset neighbour-count detector find real load shifts?
docs.text:
The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) finds about a third of the real load transfers lasting over 1 day (12 of 35) and none of the 31 shorter ones. On injected transfers (synthetic transfers that experiment 82 added to the real power readings) it finds 0.770 of the megawatts (MW) moved. Part of the gap comes from the real transfers: 6 of the 35 sit where the detector's residual panel holds no readings, and 12 have a step under 4 noise units. A noise unit is the usual size of the detector's 24-hour step on odd-numbered months, a period used to set the detector's thresholds. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. A detector finds a transfer when it raises an alarm within 2 hours of the transfer's start and places the end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration.

The 66 real transfers are those that a language model (Sonnet), checked by a second run and by Opus on disagreements, judged visible in the power readings of 16 Primary substations since January 2022 (experiment 41). Of the 66, 35 last over 1 day, and 14 of those 35 move 25% or more of the receiving substations' load, the kind the injected transfers represent. We scored five detectors from experiments 43 to 82. D0 is the original single-series detector. PF14 is D0 with a better end rule. X takes the step from two XGBoost residual models refitted half a month apart. LOGIT_SAME scores PF14's alarms by the count of neighbouring substations that step the same way. RO-NC combines X and LOGIT_SAME. We refitted nothing: the alarms come from the stored XGBoost models and thresholds of experiment 82. Of the 17 real transfers over 1 day with readings and a step of 4 noise units or more, RO-NC finds 10, where injected transfers of the same step size, found at the rates measured in experiment 82, predict about 14. The verdict is partly supported: the 14-transfer band is consistent with the injected recall, but the expected number found across all 35 is not. Thirty-five events are few, so every interval below is wide.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Found, by detector (events found, with a 95% Wilson interval; MW-weighted recall with a 95% interval from resampling whole events). The 14-event band is transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load lasting over 1 day, the band the injected recall of 0.770 describes.
Detector All 66 found Over 1 day, 35 found Over 1 day, MW-weighted Band of 14, MW-weighted D0 2 (0.03; 0.01 to 0.10) 2 (0.06; 0.02 to 0.19) 0.054 (0.000 to 0.144) 0.045 (0.000 to 0.167) PF14 8 (0.12; 0.06 to 0.22) 8 (0.23; 0.12 to 0.39) 0.156 (0.058 to 0.289) 0.226 (0.060 to 0.496) X 10 (0.15; 0.08 to 0.26) 10 (0.29; 0.16 to 0.45) 0.350 (0.156 to 0.543) 0.672 (0.343 to 0.877) LOGIT_SAME 7 (0.11; 0.05 to 0.20) 7 (0.20; 0.10 to 0.36) 0.144 (0.048 to 0.276) 0.198 (0.038 to 0.455) RO-NC 12 (0.18; 0.11 to 0.29) 12 (0.34; 0.21 to 0.51) 0.357 (0.169 to 0.553) 0.559 (0.203 to 0.816)
  • The ordering of the detectors matches experiment 82, but the intervals overlap. RO-NC and X find the most. RO-NC finds all but one of PF14's eight events (E04) and five more. On the band of 14 events X (0.672) is above RO-NC (0.559), and the two intervals overlap almost completely. The 35 events cannot rank the two detectors.
  • The MW-weighted recall is 0.357 on the 35 real events over 1 day and 0.770 on injected ones. On the 14 real events that match the injected band, RO-NC's 0.559 has an interval (0.203 to 0.816) that includes 0.770, so that band alone cannot show a gap. The expected number found, if each real event were found as often as an injected transfer of the same step size and metering, is 10.5 of 14 and 18.8 of 35; the detector found 6 and 12.
  • By size. Over 1 day, RO-NC finds 6 of 14 events of 25% or more of the receiving load, 4 of 11 under 25%, and 2 of 10 with no metered receiver. The other four detectors find none of the 10 with no metered receiver (figure 2).
  • By duration, all 66. Every detector finds 0 of 16 events of 2 to 6 hours and 0 of 15 of 6 to 24 hours. RO-NC finds 4 of 17 events of 1 to 3 days (0.24; 0.10 to 0.47) and 8 of 18 over 3 days (0.44; 0.25 to 0.66). Every detector needs the 24 hours after a step, so events under 1 day are outside what any of these detectors can find.
  • Time to detection. Among the events with an alarm at the start, the median error of the alarm's start is 0.0 hours, and every detector needs the following 24 hours to confirm the step, so the detection lag is 24 hours by construction. The end of an interval is known only after the first opposite step.
  • Half-hours flagged. Of the 9,332 half-hours of the 35 events, RO-NC flags 5,042 (0.54), PF14 3,497 (0.37), and D0 3,832 (0.41). Within the events a detector finds, it flags 0.99 or more. A half-hour counts as flagged if any alarm interval on the event's series covers it.
  • Unexplained alarms. Over the whole history (2022-01 to 2026-06), at experiment 82's thresholds, RO-NC raised 286 alarms: 50 inside a labelled event, 89 within 24 hours of another logged closure, and 147 with no logged explanation. D0 and PF14 raised 297 (31, 106, and 160), X 297 (37, 105, and 155), and LOGIT_SAME 267 (40, 86, and 141). The thresholds were set at 80 unexplained alarms on odd months, so these counts are not matched on all months.

docs.title: Why the real recall is lower than the injected recall
docs.text:
• Six events have no readings in the detector's data. The residual panel holds no readings on P12 or P13 during the six events E44, E49, E50, E52, E54, and E59, which hold 11.5 of the 42.7 MW. No detector can find them. Experiment 82's count of 12 found of 35 includes them as misses.
  • Twelve events have a step under 4 noise units. The step is the largest 24-hour step in the stored residual within 2 hours of the labelled start, in noise units (the usual size of that step on odd-numbered months). These 12 hold 10.6 MW, 4 have no metered receiver, and RO-NC finds 2 of them. On injected transfers, recall at 2 to 4 noise units is 0.651 with a metered receiver and 0.209 without, so injected transfers of these steps predict 4.4 found, against 2.
  • RO-NC finds 10 of the other 17 events. Injected transfers of the same step size and metering predict about 14. Of the 7 missed, 3 have an alarm at the start but a wrong end (E13, E23, and E47) and 4 have no alarm at the start (E02, E04, E30, and E45). X finds E02.
  • Real events differ from injected ones in more than step size. The injected transfers add a clean shape to a quiet window, and their labelled start and end are exact. Real starts and ends were placed by a labeller, who put the start within 1 hour in 77 of 78 injected cases but may be further off on real events.
  • The sample is small. The expected count over the 35 events has a standard error of 2.0 events if each event were found independently at its predicted rate, so 12 against 18.8 is a gap of about 3.4 standard errors, and the 14-event band alone (6 against 10.5) is not enough to show it.

docs.title: What share of NGED's logged switching half-hours lie inside labelled transfers
docs.text:
A small share: 2.6% of logged half-hours lie inside labelled transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, and 4.4% inside any labelled transfer. Most logged half-hours are in closures that the labels do not cover, so the reading that most logged closures move little load is supported only for closures of 2 hours to 60 days.

  • Experiment 91's 19,099 logged half-hours (rows in the lag windows of its 292 origins, July 2025 to June 2026; 3,443 distinct half-hours): 42 (0.2%) lie inside a labelled transfer of 25% or more of the receiving load, and 1,950 (10.2%) inside any of the 66 labelled transfers.
  • Whole history, 16 series, 381,830 logged half-hours: 9,868 (2.6%) lie inside a labelled transfer of 25% or more of the receiving load, 7,045 (1.8%) inside another labelled transfer, 307,266 (80.5%) in closures over 60 days, 1,254 (0.3%) in closures under 2 hours, and 56,397 (14.8%) in 2-hour-to-60-day closures where no transfer was seen.
  • Closures of 2 hours to 60 days only (69,792 logged half-hours): 9,063 (13.0%) lie inside a transfer of 25% or more of the receiving load, and 13,395 (19.2%) inside any labelled transfer. The other 80.8% show no transfer the labeller could see, which means no large transfer: the labeller finds transfers under 25% of the receiving load or under 24 hours with a recall under 0.80 (experiment 41).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The 66 labels come from a language model. A transfer the labeller missed is not here, so the recall above is a recall against visible, hand-filtered transfers only.
  • The residual panel is the stored one of experiment 37. It holds no readings on P12 and P13 in the six events above. Why the labeller saw a transfer there is not checked here.
  • The share of the receiving load is blank for 21 events with no metered receiver, 10 of them over 1 day, and the labelled MW comes from the labeller's median estimate.
  • The step sizes are two different quantities. The real step is the largest measured 24-hour step within 2 hours of the labelled start, over all series of the event, so noise can inflate it. The injected step is the exact size of the added transfer. Real events may therefore sit in a higher step band than injected events of the same true size, which raises the expected count.
  • The expected counts pool two injected sets. The rates are from experiment 82's headline-band and long transfers together (metered, 2 to 4 noise units: 0.651). Its headline-band transfers alone give 0.722, and an expected 20.2 of 35 found, a slightly larger gap.
  • Lab shortcuts. The residual uses ERA5 weather and hindsight ends of up to 14 days, so the numbers describe the detector as a training-time tool, as in experiment 82.

docs.title: What a next experiment could test
docs.text:
One option is to test whether a detector can find the 12 events with a step under 4 noise units, which hold 10.6 MW. Experiment 82 suggested a longer averaging window and a check that the receivers' combined step balances the donor's. Another option is to restore the readings of P12 and P13 in the residual panel, so that the 6 events there can be scored. The research plan owns the choice.

The event-by-event table is on the events page. Code: ml-experiments/00101-ro-nc-detector-on-real-hand-filtered-switching-events/; every number above is printed by e00101_real.py and e00101_report.py.

docs.title: Experiment 102: SIMP1, which parts of the BG2 best guess can be removed before production
docs.text:
Take-home message: the three recent-power inputs are the one part of BG2's XGBoost models that cannot be removed at Primary substations and supply points, but the pre-registered cost of removing them was inflated by one substation's uncut commissioning months. A Primary substation steps 33 kV or 66 kV down to 11 kV, and a supply point is a bulk supply point (BSP) or grid supply point (GSP), where the transmission network feeds the distribution network. BG2 is the best-guess forecast of experiment 87. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity, where one point is 1% of a series' capacity and lower is better. The simplest Primary forecast (a single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the power inputs, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend) scores 6.066 against BG2's 5.260. That pre-registered contrast, C1, is +0.806 points (99% interval 0.367 to 1.569), about 15% of BG2's score. C1 removes four parts at once. Removing the power inputs alone costs 0.710 points (95% interval 0.360 to 1.233). The lag result is driven by two of the 16 Primaries: Primary M (whose first months are uncut, a defect) and Primary K (whose demand level fell in March 2026). With Primary M's commissioning months cut, the lags alone cost 0.361 points (0.198 to 0.546) and the simplest candidate loses 0.448 (0.261 to 0.652) against BG2, still above the 0.15 limit. The verdict is partly supported: 2 of the 5 pre-registered contrasts hold.

We asked which parts of BG2 earn their place in production. We removed each part in turn from the best guess (the blend of five models, the three recent-power inputs, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, the spread factor of 1.15), scored each result against BG2 on the same 292 daily forecast runs, and also scored the solar offset on midday summer rows. The blend, offset, correction, and spread factor each cost 0.1 points or less when removed, and a blend of weekly, analogue, and frozen models matches BG2's five models. At the wind farms the lags make no measurable difference (-0.059 points); at the solar farms the change is within noise (+0.010), but the interval misses the 0.10 limit by 0.010.

Example forecasts. Each figure shows BG2, the simplifications, and manual_heuristic for one series, in the week with the highest mean power in summer (which at a series with embedded solar panels need not be a sunny week), the week with the highest mean power in winter, and the week with the largest error. Each day shows the 15 to 39 hour lead window of the run that started that morning. The series are Primary G, Supply point A, Solar farm A, and Wind farm A.

The five blend members. Each figure shows the median forecast of the weekly, monthly, analogue, pooled-by-type, and frozen-with-correction members, with the blend and the actual, at one Primary substation. The same three weeks are drawn for Primary G and Primary K in this folder (figure_5_members_g_* and figure_5_members_k_*).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Architecture and arms. Every arm is BG2 (experiment 87) with one part removed. The removal arms are the five blend members alone, every blend of two or three members, BG2 with the frozen member uncorrected, BG2 without the offset, BG2 without the spread factor (the last two stored in experiment 87), and the single XGBoost model without the three power inputs. The weekly model without lags is the Primary and supply point simplest candidate; the monthly model without lags is the farm candidate and the monthly contrast at Primaries. Every no-lag model is BG2's model with the three lag columns removed (same rows, weights, 500 rounds, seed 0). A lag-free model with a level term, or with fewer rounds, was not tested.
  • Row set and schedule. The 292 runs of fold_a_daily_gap_v1. Primary and supply point contrasts C1 and C2 use weekly refits, as BG2 does. The farm contrasts and the monthly lag contrast use monthly refits, as BG2's farm arms do. The lag cost has the same sign and a similar size under both schedules (0.903 points monthly and 0.710 weekly, at Primaries). GPU use was 14.2 hours of wall time, including the D18 refits.
  • The lags are observed power. The lag columns hold the observed power of the series, not weather, and every lag is at least 3.5 hours older than the forecast origin.
  • The five verdict contrasts, each at 99%. Primary C1: +0.806 (0.367 to 1.569), not safe against 0.15. Supply points C2: +0.278 (0.040 to 0.720), not shown safe against 0.30. Solar farms C3: +0.010 (-0.107 to +0.110), not shown safe against 0.10, because the upper end exceeds the limit by 0.010. Wind farms C4: -0.059 (-0.184 to +0.058), safe against 0.30. Solar offset C5, midday in summer at the 5 offset Primaries: -0.184 (-0.297 to -0.103), the offset helps. The C1 interval is skewed (0.37 to 1.57 around 0.81) because one month at Primary M, December 2025, adds about 46 points to that substation's cost.
  • Why the Primary lag cost is large: a data defect at Primary M and a level change at Primary K. Weekly refits, no-lag minus with-lag, per substation: Primary M +5.69, Primary K +3.94; Primary I +0.63, Primary P +0.52, Primary E +0.51; the other 11 range from -0.09 to +0.22. Primary M's training history starts in December 2024 at zero output while the site was being commissioned, and docs/ml-experiments/data-processing.md says to cut those months. A lag-free model trained on them forecasts 20% of capacity in December 2025, against an actual of 75%, and only the lagged models see the true level. After the refits with D18's first 2.6 months cut (training from 2025-03-01), Primary M's lag cost is -0.030 (weekly) and +0.024 (monthly). Primary K's cost is real: its net export fell by about 20 points of capacity from March 2026, and the lag-free model keeps forecasting the old level.
  • The lag-only cost with Primary M cut, at 16 Primaries. Weekly +0.361 (0.198 to 0.546), monthly +0.510 (0.319 to 0.722), both 95%. Leaving out Primary K as well, weekly +0.125 (99% interval 0.042 to 0.213) and monthly +0.213 (0.149 to 0.279). Without Primary K and Primary M (uncut M), the lag cost is +0.136 (99% interval 0.055 to 0.232) weekly. The simplest candidate against BG2 is +0.448 (0.261 to 0.652) with Primary M cut, and +0.173 (0.081 to 0.295) without Primary K and Primary M, which still fails the 0.15 limit. The leave-two-out result removes about four-fifths of C1.
  • Where each simplification lands, Primary. Differences from BG2 (5.260), 95% intervals: weekly model with lags +0.095 (0.050 to 0.140); blend of weekly, analogue, and frozen -0.002 (-0.006 to 0.000); analogue and frozen pair +0.016 (-0.005 to +0.041); without the 14-day correction +0.060 (0.021 to 0.094); without the spread factor +0.017 (0.003 to 0.033); without the offset +0.010 (-0.000 to 0.019); each member alone +0.091 (weekly), +0.154 (analogue), +0.210 (monthly), +0.270 (frozen), +0.336 (pooled). Against the stack (5.543) the simplest candidate is +0.523 (0.124 to 1.071) worse; against manual_heuristic it is -0.115 (-0.433 to +0.430), no difference. With Primary M cut the simplest candidate scores 5.708, against 5.346 for the weekly model with lags.
  • Supply points. Weekly without lags 13.203, monthly without lags 13.379, against BG2 12.925. The loss is mostly one of the 4 supply points: without it, the C2 interval spans zero (-0.038 to +0.358, 99%). The simplest candidate beats manual_heuristic by 1.300 points (0.784 to 1.803) and the stack by 0.356 (0.118 to 0.677).
  • Farms. Solar farms: BG2 5.012, without lags 5.022; manual_heuristic 5.718; the fitted spread factor changes the score by +0.002 (-0.005 to +0.013). Wind farms: BG2 11.032, without lags 10.973; the power-curve margin changes the score by -0.057 (-0.098 to -0.024) and the fitted spread factor by -0.016 (-0.024 to -0.009), both statistically significant at the 5% level; manual_heuristic 13.906. The no-lag farm forecasts beat manual_heuristic by 0.693 (solar) and 2.930 (wind) points. Wind without lags scores lower than wind with lags at all three farms (-0.098, -0.073, and -0.007), inside the interval; a fixed 500 rounds can overfit to the three extra inputs. At solar farms the cost sits at one farm: without solar farm E, C3 is -0.003 (99%: -0.024 to +0.018), and E's cost comes from rows that read zero output, which may be outages.
  • Farms by time of day. Midday in summer: C3 +0.010 (99% interval -0.532 to +0.414) and C4 -0.094 (-0.146 to -0.014); night: C3 +0.0005 (0.0004 to 0.0007), because solar output is zero, and C4 -0.007 (-0.148 to +0.125). The lags do not help the farms in daylight.
  • Midday in summer, night, and other hours (offset effect, BG2 minus BG2 without the offset, 99% intervals). At the 5 offset Primaries: midday in summer -0.184 (-0.297 to -0.103), night -0.014 (-0.044 to +0.019), other hours -0.017 (-0.056 to +0.021), all rows -0.031 (-0.071 to +0.011). At all 16 Primaries: midday in summer -0.058 (-0.093 to -0.032), all rows -0.010 (-0.022 to +0.003). The score at the 5 offset Primaries at midday in summer is 5.319 with the offset and 5.503 without it. Midday in summer is the half-hours that start from 10:00 to 13:30 UK time in April to September, and night is the half-hours that start from 23:00 to 03:30.
  • Lead time. The simplest Primary candidate (C1) loses at every lead band, and the loss shrinks with lead: +1.085 at 0 to 24 hours, +0.993 at 1 to 2 days, +0.906 at 2 to 6 days, +0.743 at 6 to 10 days, and +0.670 at 10 days and beyond (all 99% intervals exclude zero).
  • Blend weights. After the first month (equal weights), the blend gives the monthly and the pooled-by-type members zero weight in every month. The weekly member takes 0.25 to 0.50, the analogue member 0.25 in every month, and the frozen member with correction 0.25 to 0.50. The best three-model blend (weekly, analogue, frozen) is therefore the same blend with the zero-weight members removed, and its -0.002 comes from July's equal-weight start. The best pair and triple were chosen on the 73 runs of fold_a_every5d_v1, which do not overlap the 292 scored runs but interleave with them in time.
