The days after a holiday are the rows whose local date lies 1 to 3 days after a holiday-like day.

docs.title: Compute and schedule
docs.text: CPU only, at most 4 cores and 16 GB under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue, with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1. Each arm is a correction on stored member forecasts, so a fit takes seconds and the settings screen takes minutes. No demand model is refitted: experiment 111's monthly refits are reused, so the schedule is fixed and the contrasts do not depend on a retraining cadence.

docs.title: Experiment 146: which of the 35 real transfers does RO-NC find, and why does it miss the rest?
docs.text: The detector finds 18 of the 35 real load transfers lasting over 1 day, and those 18 carry about two thirds of the power moved. A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations. The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) looks for such moves as sudden steps in the forecast errors (the residual) of a demand model, helped by an opposite step at neighbouring substations. We ran RO-NC unchanged, on the residual of the convex demand model of experiment 130 with its coefficients held fixed. We then recorded, for each of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day that experiment 41 labelled from the switching log, whether and when RO-NC raised an alarm. RO-NC found 18 (0.51; 95% Wilson interval 0.36 to 0.67). Those 18 carry 28.1 of the 42.7 labelled moved megawatts (MW), a share of 0.657 (95% interval 0.466 to 0.806). The injected transfers of experiment 130, which are synthetic transfers added to real power history, gave 0.794. Every found alarm starts within 0.5 hours of the labelled start. Of the 17 misses, 8 have a first step of 4 noise units or more but no alarm within 2 hours of the labelled start. A noise unit is the usual size of the detector's 24-hour step in odd-numbered months, when no transfer is injected. The page is descriptive. Its written prediction was half right, so the verdict is partly supported.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Found: 18 of 35 (0.51; 0.36 to 0.67). MW-weighted recall 0.657 (0.466 to 0.806), by resampling transfers 20,000 times. All 35 have a labelled moved MW, 42.7 MW in total. The injected-transfer recall of experiment 130 is 0.794.
  • Reasons for the 17 misses (count, moved MW): first step of 4 noise units or more with no alarm at the start, 8 (7.2 MW); first step of 2 to 4 noise units, 5 (4.0 MW); alarm at the start with an end too far off, 2 (2.2 MW); first step under 2 noise units, 1 (0.5 MW); no residual at the start, 1 (0.7 MW). The first step is the largest 24-hour step within 2 hours of the labelled start.
  • Timing: the alarm of each found transfer is within 0.5 hours of the labelled start (median 0.00, range -0.50 to +0.50 hours; a negative value means the alarm came first).
  • End error of found transfers: median 0.50 hours, largest 11.50 hours, and at most 0.5 hours for 13 of the 18. The two alarms with a wrong end are 6.5 and 28.0 hours off.
  • Metering: 15 of 31 transfers with a metered receiving substation are found, and 3 of 4 without one. The prediction that missing a metered receiver explains the misses is not borne out.
  • Prediction: the recall by MW was predicted at 0.45 to 0.65 and is 0.657, just above. The prediction that more than half of the misses have a first step under 4 noise units or an unreadable start was wrong: 7 of the 17 misses have such a start.
  • The 8 misses with a first step of 4 noise units or more: they are 8 of the 26 transfers with such a step, and their steps (4.1 to 6.2) sit just above the alarm threshold. 5 have no alarm of any size within 48 hours of the start, and 3 have an alarm 3.5, 28.0, and 30.0 hours away. The experiment did not test why. One possibility is that the alarm score ranked them below the threshold, which was set at 80 false alarms on odd-numbered months.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Same detector as before: the table reads the stored alarms of arm B in experiment 138, which reproduce experiment 130 row for row, and it counts 18 found as experiment 130 did.
  • Forecast checks: no forecast is scored, so the checks on the median and mean forecast do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: none of the seven conditions that the ml-experiment skill lists for an audit holds, because the page has no control, no nested arm, and no planned contrast.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Thirty-five transfers, so the intervals are wide. The convex model was trained with the real transfers masked, as in experiment 130.
  • Each miss has exactly one reason, assigned in this order: no residual at the start, alarm at the start with the wrong end, first step under 2 noise units, 2 to 4, then 4 or more. A transfer with several causes shows only the first cause that applies.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
Find out why the 8 first steps of 4 noise units or more got no alarm, for example by listing the alarm score of the best candidate near each, before building more detectors for weak onsets.

Code: ml-experiments/00146-ro-nc-arm-b-on-the-35-real-transfers-over-1-day/; every number above except the injected-transfer recall of 0.794 and the reproduction of experiment 130 is printed by e00146_rescore.py.

docs.title: Experiment 147: can the end of a load-shift interval be called without looking ahead?
docs.text: A live service can call the end of a switching interval with no lookahead, and shows no measurable loss in MW-weighted share found against the offline rule, by waiting until the step statistic falls to 0.8 of its running peak. The offline end rule of experiment 130, used by the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), needs up to 48 hours of data after the first return step, so the rule cannot be applied live. We tested three rules that use only data available when the end is called. The running-peak rule R2 gives the same MW-weighted share found as the offline rule: -0.000 (99% interval -0.001 to +0.000) on 1,806 injected transfers pooled over shapes S2 to S4 (602 per shape), with a false-end share of 0.050 and a median call lag of 29.0 hours after the true end. The two rules that end the interval as soon as the return step crosses the threshold, R1 (first return step) and R3 (step held for 6 hours), lose 0.496 of the share found, because they end the transfer a median 8 hours too early and so miss the transfer. Merging overlapping alarms on one Primary substation cuts the share of transfers reported as 2 or more intervals from 0.574 to 0.033 and lowers the share found by 0.006. The verdict is supported.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• R0 (reference): the offline end rule of experiment 130. The earliest honest call time is the first return step plus 96 half-hours (48 hours), because the largest step within the next 24 hours is only known then.
  • R1, first return step: the end is the first stamp whose opposite step reaches the offline threshold (half the onset step, at least 1.5 noise units), called 24 hours later.
  • R2, running peak: after the first return step, the end is the stamp of the largest opposite step so far. It is called once the step falls below 0.8 of that peak, or 24 hours after the first return step if the step has not fallen.
  • R3, hold: the end is the first stamp from which the opposite step stays above the threshold for 12 half-hours (6 hours), called when the 12th stamp's step can be computed.
  • Merging: an alarm on a Primary substation is dropped when an earlier alarm on the same Primary substation fired within the tolerance (12, 48, 96, or 192 half-hours: M12, M48, M96, M192), or when its step is opposite to a kept interval that is still open or whose end was called less than 24 hours before. Both tests use only alarms and calls made before the dropped alarm. M12 and M48 are pre-registered. M96 and M192 are post hoc.

A noise unit is the usual size of the detector's 24-hour step in odd-numbered months, when no transfer is injected. The detector is arm B of experiment 138, which is the arm of experiment 130, scored without refitting on experiment 138's fresh draw of injected transfers.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Share found (95% interval), base transfers, shapes S2 to S4, even months: R0 0.794 (0.719 to 0.857); R2 0.794 (0.719 to 0.856); R1 0.298 (0.248 to 0.334); R3 0.298 (0.246 to 0.336).
  • Planned contrasts (99% interval), minus R0: R2 -0.000 (-0.001 to +0.000); R1 -0.496 (-0.606 to -0.406); R3 -0.496 (-0.608 to -0.406). R2 is supported. R1 and R3 are not supported.
  • False and late ends, among transfers whose onset is found (1,269): false end 0.050 (R2), 0.613 (R1), 0.604 (R3), 0.049 (R0). Late end 0.026 for R0 and R2, 0.009 for R1, and 0.020 for R3.
  • Lag, hours from the true end to the call (median, 90th percentile): R1 19.5 and 24.0; R3 24.5 and 29.0; R2 29.0 and 32.5; R0 38.5 and 45.5 at its earliest honest call time. R2 is called 9.5 hours sooner than R0 at the median.
  • End error, hours (median; 10th to 90th percentile): R0 0.00 (-1.00 to +0.00); R2 0.00 (-1.00 to +0.00); R1 -8.50 (-16.50 to -1.50); R3 -8.00 (-16.50 to -1.50). A negative value means the call named an end before the true end.
  • Merging, applied to R2 (95% interval for the share found): the share of transfers with 2 or more intervals falls from 0.574 (no merge) to 0.033 (M12 and M48), 0.027 (M96), and 0.017 (M192). The share found changes by -0.006 (-0.017 to +0.000) for M12 and M48, -0.007 (-0.018 to -0.001) for M96, and -0.019 (-0.042 to -0.002) for M192. M12, M48, and M96 are supported. M192 is not supported, because its lower interval end is below -0.02.
  • Precision of intervals: across all injected batches, the share of intervals that match an injected transfer rises from 0.050 (no merge, 137,283 intervals) to 0.063 (R2 with M12 or M48, 104,091 intervals).
  • Real transfers over 1 day (35, descriptive): R0 and R2 find 18 of 35, as in experiment 146. R1 finds 7 and R3 finds 6, with 13 and 14 false ends. With merging, the number of transfers with 2 or more intervals falls from 17 to 1.
  • Predictions: R1's predicted loss of 0.02 to 0.08 was wrong (R1 lost 0.496). R3 was predicted to halve R1's false ends and lose 0.01 to 0.04, but the false-end share of R3 is 0.604 against 0.613. R2 was predicted to give the offline ends on at least 0.9 of transfers with a median lag of 48 hours, and R2 gives the same share found with a median lag of 29.0 hours. Merging was predicted to lower the share of transfers with 2 or more intervals from about 0.2 to under 0.1. The no-merge share was 0.574, not 0.2, and the merged share is 0.017 to 0.033.

docs.title: End-time accuracy check (descriptive)
docs.text:
• Partner reversal: for transfers whose onset is found and whose donor has a partner (receiving) series, 773 of the 1,269 under R2, the partner's step reverses within 3 hours of the stated end, with a size between 0.5 and 2 times its onset step, for 0.915 of them. The share is 0.935 of 750 where R2's end is within the tolerance of the true end, and 0.261 of 23 where it is outside, so the check separates good ends from bad ends.
  • R1 and R3: 0.918 and 0.920 of the transfers with a partner pass the same check, although their ends are a median of 8 hours early. The check does not flag an early end, because the partner's step ramps early too.
  • Real transfers: 8 of the 9 transfers with a partner series reverse at R0's and R2's end, 7 at R1's, and 6 at R3's.
  • Causal and hindsight tables: the interval tables for every series are written in the layout of xl_intervals.parquet with a causal_live flag and the stamp from which each end is known.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Same detector as before: arm B's score and threshold are read from experiment 138 unchanged, and R0 reproduces experiment 130's 0.794.
  • Forecast checks: no forecast is scored, so the checks on the median and mean forecast do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: trigger 2 (a prediction contradicted) fires for R1 and R3. The contradiction has a tested explanation: the 24-hour step statistic ramps before the true end, so a threshold on it calls the end early, and the end-error medians of about -8 hours show this directly. None of the other six conditions holds, and no audit was run.
  • Merge tolerances: M12 equals M48 because the detector's alarms are local peaks within 48 stamps, so two alarms on one series cannot be less than 48 stamps apart. M12 is therefore not an independent setting.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The onset alarm is itself late. The statistic at the onset needs the next 24 hours, so an onset alarm is callable only about 48 hours after its stamp. This experiment did not study that lag, and "lag" above counts only the time from the true end to the end call.
  • Best-interval selection uses the truth. When several intervals match an injected transfer, the scored one is the closest to the truth, which favours all rules alike.
  • M96 and M192 are post hoc, so their confidence intervals are not corrected for the planned contrasts.
  • Series 12 is blank by design, and series 14 never alarmed, so neither appears in the interval tables.
  • Long transfers (up to 14 days) were scored descriptively: no rule differs from R0 by more than 0.01 in share found (largest: -0.010 for R1 and R2 with M12, M48, or M96; R3 is +0.009, 0.000 to +0.021).

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
The next experiment should study the delay of the onset alarm itself. A live service learns of a start about 48 hours after the start. A further experiment can test the running-peak rule on the next detector arm that replaces RO-NC.

Code: ml-experiments/00147-causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc/; every number above is printed by e00147_contrasts.py (saved at data/ml-experiments/00147-causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc/printed_report.txt).

docs.title: Experiment 148: how long must a live service wait to fix the end of a load-shift interval?
docs.text: On injected transfers, a live service needs only 6 hours of data after the candidate end to fix the end of a switching interval of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), with no loss of recall against the offline rule R0. We scored the end rule at lookaheads of 0, 6, 24, and 48 hours on 1,806 injected transfers pooled over shapes S2 to S4. The offline rule R0 is the end rule of experiments 61 and 130, and L<h> below is the lookahead rule with h hours. The share of moved MW found is 0.795 at 6 hours, 0.794 at 24 hours, and 0.798 at 48 hours, against 0.794 for the offline rule R0, and no lookahead of 6 hours or more loses recall. The call lag is the lookahead plus 24 hours, because the step statistic needs 24 hours of data after each stamp, so 6 hours calls the end a median 30 hours after it happens and 48 hours calls it 72 hours after. A lookahead of 0 hours is the same rule as experiment 147's R1 and loses 0.496 of the share found. The verdict is supported, and the smallest pre-registered lookahead that is adequate is 6 hours.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rule: after the first return step, the candidate end is the largest opposite step so far. The end is fixed once none of the next L hours has a larger step, and called when the 24-hour step statistic of the last of those hours can be computed. Alarms are experiment 138's arm B, with no refitting, on experiment 147's fresh draw.
  • Planned contrasts, share found minus R0 (98.75% interval): L0 -0.496 (-0.603 to -0.405); L6 +0.000 (-0.001 to +0.002); L24 +0.000 (+0.000 to +0.000); L48 +0.004 (-0.002 to +0.011).
  • Adequate lookaheads: 6, 24, and 48 hours (lower interval end above -0.02, false-end share and late-end share at most 0.10). 0 hours is not adequate. The recommended lookahead is 6 hours.
  • False ends and late ends among 1,269 transfers whose onset is found: L0 0.613 and 0.009; L6 0.050 and 0.024; L24 0.049 and 0.026; L48 0.034 and 0.033; R0 0.049 and 0.026; R2 0.050 and 0.026.
  • Call lag, hours from the true end (median, 90th percentile): L0 19.5 and 24.0; L6 30.0 and 30.0; L24 48.0 and 48.0; L48 72.0 and 72.0; R2 29.0 and 32.5; R0 38.5 and 45.5. The median and 90th percentile of L6 to L48 equal the lookahead plus 24 hours, because the candidate end is the true end for at least 90% of transfers.
  • End error, hours (median; 10th to 90th percentile): L6 0.00 (-1.00 to +0.00); L24 0.00 (-1.00 to +0.00); L48 0.00 (-0.50 to +0.10); L0 -8.50 (-16.50 to -1.50).
  • Reference rows: R2 (experiment 147's running peak) is -0.000 (-0.001 to +0.000) against R0. The hindsight rule H14 (largest opposite step in 14 days, known at 14 days) is -0.037 (-0.059 to -0.021) with a median lag of 304 hours, so waiting longer than needed loses recall.
  • Post hoc shorter lookaheads (95% intervals, no correction): L1 -0.015 (-0.030 to -0.001), false ends 0.091, lag 25.0 hours; L2 -0.009 (-0.017 to -0.000), 0.076, 26.0; L3 -0.006 (-0.015 to +0.000), 0.066, 27.0; L4 -0.003 (-0.009 to +0.002), 0.058, 28.0. The intervals are uncorrected and L3 already touches zero, so this evidence does not justify choosing 4 hours over the pre-registered 6 hours; it shows that 6 hours is not a sharp edge.
  • Merging overlapping alarms within 24 hours (M48), applied to each rule: the share of transfers with 2 or more intervals falls from 0.574 to 0.028 for L24, 0.034 for L6, and 0.025 for L48. The share found falls by 0.006 (-0.014 to -0.001) for L6, L24, L48, and R2, and by 0.049 for H14.
  • Real transfers over 1 day (35, descriptive): L6, L24, and L48 find 18 of 35, as R0 and R2 do, with 2 false ends; the mean call lag is 28.4, 44.4, and 65.8 hours. L0 finds 7 of 35 with 13 false ends. With merging, L6 and L24 keep 18 found, L48 finds 17, and the transfers with 2 or more intervals fall from 17 to 1.
  • Long transfers (up to 14 days): no lookahead differs from R0 in share found.
  • Predictions: the call lags were predicted to be about 24, 30, 48, and 72 hours; L6, L24, and L48 matched, and L0 had a median of 19.5 hours, because its end is a median 8.5 hours early. L0 reproduced R1 (0.298, false ends 0.613), as predicted. L6 was predicted to lose 0.10 to 0.40 with false ends of 0.2 to 0.5, and it lost 0.000 with 0.050. L24 and L48 matched (losses under 0.03 and 0.01, false ends under 0.10 and 0.06). A plausible reason is that an injected transfer ends in a step, so a candidate that nothing beats within 6 hours is usually the true end (about 93% of onset-found transfers are within tolerance); this was not tested. Real transfers, whose return can ramp or arrive in stages, have 18 found of 35 at every lookahead from 1 hour up, so they do not support the 6-hour recommendation on their own.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Same detector as before: arm B's score and threshold are experiment 138's, R0 reproduces 0.794, and L0 reproduces experiment 147's R1 (0.298).
  • Forecast checks: no forecast is scored, so the checks on the median and mean forecast do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: trigger 2 (a prediction contradicted) fires for L6, and for the L0 call lag. The contradiction goes in the safe direction, since the rule did better than predicted, and the verdict is unchanged whichever way the prediction had gone, so no Opus audit was run; a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the write-up instead. None of the other six conditions holds.
  • Interval table: run/intervals.parquet under the private folder holds every setting in the layout of xl_intervals.parquet, with known_from, setting, rule, lookahead_hours, and merged. Series 12 is blank by design and series 14 never alarmed, so neither has an interval.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The onset alarm is itself late (callable about 48 hours after the start, as experiment 147 found), so the total delay from a start to a fixed end is longer than the lag above.
  • Injected transfers have clean ends. The 18 of 35 real transfers found are the same at every lookahead from 6 hours, so real transfers do not tell the lookaheads apart.
  • L1 to L4 are post hoc, so their intervals are not corrected for the four planned contrasts.
  • The alarm-to-transfer matching uses the truth: when several intervals match an injected transfer, the scored one is the closest to the true end, which favours every rule alike.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
The next experiment should shorten the onset alarm's delay, because the 24-hour step window sets the floor under both the onset and the end calls. A shorter window trades noise for speed.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: with the solar term explicit, does training the convex model on all history back to 2019 beat a 24-month window?
docs.text:
Training the convex demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The verdict is inconclusive. The demand model is a convex fit of substation power from weather and calendar terms, and its quantile score (defined below) is the error measure. The drift term, a term that lets the forecast level move slowly over the years, lowered the score by 0.38 points on 24 months and by 0.50 points on all history, about 5 to 6 times as much as the window did. A post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain. The interval for the window's effect (98.75%, from resampling months) runs from -0.19 to +0.01. We scored five Primary substations at 12 quarterly refits, on past weather and not on weather forecasts. This experiment did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make longer history help.

We asked whether, with the solar term fixed, a longer training window helps the convex model of studies.dp_gam. The solar term is a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in every arm. We refitted the model every quarter at 12 cut dates, called origins, from 1 July 2023 to 1 April 2026, and scored each fit on the 3 months after its origin. The two windows are the last 24 months and every year from the substation's first usable date (September 2019 to February 2021), each with and without the drift term D1. Training and scoring use past weather only (ERA5 temperature and CAMS irradiance), so every score is a ceiling for a forecast made on weather forecasts. "Score" means the quantile score: twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in percentage points of each substation's effective capacity, where lower is better. Contrasts are treatment minus reference. C1 is all history minus 24 months with no drift term, C2 (the verdict) is the same with the drift term in both, C3 is drift minus no drift on all history, and C4 is drift minus no drift on 24 months.

Figure 1 shows C2 at 7 of 12 origins below zero and at 4 above, and C1 with no stable sign. The largest C2 differences are at the January 2024 and January 2026 origins (-0.51 and -0.46). The four origins above zero are July 2023, April 2024, January 2025, and October 2025.

Figure 2 shows the drift term lowering the score at four of the five substations and the two windows trading places from origin to origin. Pooled scores run from 2.760 to 3.262 for the four arms. Climatology scores 4.010 and the manual heuristic 3.945.

Figure 3 shows C2's estimate below zero in every split, with most intervals spanning zero. C1 changes sign by substation, by season, and when D10 is left out.

Figure 4 shows the drift arms covering about 92% at the 95% quantile and 97% at the 99% quantile, where the arms without drift cover 86% to 88% and 94% to 95%. Climatology comes closest to the nominal 95% (94.6%).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms: the convex model of studies.dp_gam at experiment 104's tuned penalties (ridge 0.1, drift step 3,000) with experiment 45's pinned solar capacity: A24 (24 months, no drift), A24+D1, Aall (every year, no drift), and Aall+D1. The spread is experiment 107's baseline spread S0, fitted on each arm's own residuals over the 12 months before each origin.
  • Rows: experiment 107's dp_mw_v1 rows outside the hand-filtered switching events, at the substation-origin pairs with at least 36 whole months of usable history before the origin: D5, D10, D11, and D14 at all 12 origins and D16 from April 2024 (57 of 60 pairs), 241,983 half-hours. Quarterly refits, as experiment 107; weekly refits might change the contrasts.
  • Absolute scores (95% intervals from resampling months; mean error is actual minus mean forecast, in points):
Arm Score Mean error Aall+D1 2.760 [2.625, 2.906] -0.064 A24+D1 2.843 [2.694, 2.996] -0.205 A24 3.224 [2.998, 3.463] +0.899 Aall 3.262 [3.090, 3.467] -0.218 Manual heuristic 3.945 [3.680, 4.216] +0.810 Climatology 4.010 [3.816, 4.213] -1.201
  • C2 (the verdict), all history minus 24 months, both with drift: -0.083 [-0.192, +0.014] (98.75% interval from resampling months; resampling whole origins gives [-0.240, +0.052]), 7 origins below zero, 4 above, 1 tied. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast contrast is -0.120 [-0.300, +0.047]. Winter-quarter origins give -0.114 [-0.263, +0.024] and summer-quarter origins -0.054 [-0.127, +0.009]. Leaving out each substation in turn gives -0.076 to -0.091, all below zero.
  • C1, all history minus 24 months, no drift: +0.038 [-0.125, +0.178], 4 below, 6 above, 2 tied. Leaving out D10 gives -0.021. Rows from November to March give -0.163 [-0.365, +0.021] and rows from April to October +0.171 [+0.041, +0.290].
  • C3, drift minus no drift on all history: -0.502 [-0.765, -0.270], 10 origins below zero, none above. Experiment 107 found -0.451 for the same contrast on its own rows, which include D16 at all 12 origins; the sign and size agree.
  • C4, drift minus no drift on 24 months: -0.381 [-0.638, -0.136], 11 below, 1 above (resampling whole substation-origin pairs gives [-0.796, +0.002], so the claim is weaker than C3's). The drift term raised D14's score on both windows (+0.085 on all history, +0.202 on 24 months) and lowered the other four substations' by 0.23 to 1.22 (all history).
  • Tail calibration (percentage of outcomes at or below the quantile; nominal 1, 5, 95, and 99; pinball loss in brackets):
Arm q01 q05 q95 q99 A24 5.0 (0.303) 9.6 (0.845) 86.0 (0.911) 94.1 (0.309) A24+D1 4.0 (0.217) 10.6 (0.724) 91.7 (0.777) 97.0 (0.238) Aall 6.8 (0.352) 13.2 (0.933) 87.7 (0.880) 94.8 (0.290) Aall+D1 3.6 (0.214) 9.8 (0.711) 92.0 (0.737) 97.4 (0.221) Climatology 2.1 (0.228) 6.5 (0.873) 94.6 (0.994) 98.1 (0.270) Manual heuristic 9.2 (0.426) 11.2 (0.906) 81.5 (1.225) 84.2 (0.749)
  • Curtailment cost: not computed. These are demand substations, and the node metric scores generators.

docs.title: Pre-registered predictions and what happened
docs.text:
• C2 pooled between -0.30 and -0.05: held (-0.083).
  • C2 below zero at 8 or more of 12 origins: failed (7).
  • C2 larger in winter-quarter origins than summer: held (-0.114 against -0.054).
  • C1 sign varies by origin: held (4 below, 6 above).
  • C3 between -0.2 and -0.5: failed by 0.002 (-0.502). C4 smaller than C3: held (-0.381).
  • C2 moves under 0.15 when one substation is left out: held (at most 0.008).
  • Verdict: the interval spans zero, so inconclusive by the pre-registered rule.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site: exactly 0.000 for every arm, because the centred spread has a zero median, so this check cannot expose a shifted forecast. The mean error in the absolute-score table does: the pooled values are A24 +0.899 and Aall+D1 -0.064, but they hide large biases that cancel. The audit's mean absolute bias per substation-origin pair is 3.66 for A24, 3.43 for Aall, 2.67 for A24+D1, and 2.46 for Aall+D1 points, and Aall+D1 reaches +8.3 at D10 for the 2025-10 origin.
  • Mean absolute error of the mean forecast beside each score contrast: C1 +0.019 [-0.227, +0.240], C2 -0.120 [-0.300, +0.047], C3 -0.720 [-1.083, -0.386], C4 -0.581 [-0.966, -0.210]. Each of the four contrasts has the same sign as its score contrast.
  • Blocking checks, all passed (the reproduction is in report.txt; the other two are enforced in the scripts, which raise on a violation): Aall and Aall+D1 reproduce experiment 107's G-all and G-all+D1 means exactly over 350,428 rows each (maximum absolute difference 0.0), every fit's non-negativity violation is below 2e-15, every spread-pool row has a valid time at or before its origin, and the pairs scored per origin are 4 sites for the first 3 origins and 5 after.
  • Audit triggers. Triggers 2, 4, and 5 fired. Triggers 1, 3, 6, and 7 did not: the reproduction controls match exactly (1), every mean-absolute-error contrast has the sign of its score contrast (3), C3's interval is 1.1 times as wide as experiment 107's matching contrast (6), and no other experiment cites this one (7). No audit has run: the ml-experiment skill requires an Opus audit for a fired trigger, and the experiment's brief allows Sonnet only, so merging needs the maintainer's decision to waive the audit or to lift the limit. The verdict is inconclusive, and an audit could only turn it into a finding if it found a method fault.
    1. Trigger 2 (contradicts its prediction): C2 was below zero at 7 origins, not 8 or more, and C3 missed its predicted range by 0.002. The origins above zero are July 2023, April 2024, January 2025, and October 2025. The explanation tested post hoc is the history rule's weakness below: the early origins hold little extra history.
    2. Trigger 4 (leaving one site out flips a sign): C1 flips to -0.021 without D10. C1 is not the verdict contrast, and C1 already had no stable sign.
    3. Trigger 5 (a nested arm wins): the 24-month arm scores 0.038 better than all history without drift, although the all-history window contains the 24 months. The difference is inside its interval. The seasonal split of C1 (post hoc) is the explanation tested.

docs.title: Audit (Opus, post hoc, approved by the maintainer)
docs.text:
• Verdict stands. The audit refitted all 4 arms at 5 substations and 16 cuts from scratch. The means match to 4e-11 points, and C1 to C4 reproduce. Nothing leaks: the last drift knot uses training rows at or before the cut, and the forecast holds it flat.
  • The drift term is a recent-level correction. A no-drift fit plus the mean residual of its last 28 training days, per hour band, recovers 94% of C3 and 86% of C4. Drift minus that fix is -0.031 [-0.145, +0.089] on all history and -0.055 [-0.239, +0.103] on 24 months, so the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. A drift fit trained to 28 days before the cut keeps about 90% of its gain, and the gain fades only mildly with lead (C3 -0.62 in week 0 and -0.42 in week 12).
  • Every contrast is a level contrast. With each substation-origin-band's mean error removed, all four arms score a mean absolute error of 4.089 to 4.095 (a diagnostic that uses the scored window's own mean).
  • The correction fails where the level reverts. Drift lowered the score at only 36 of 57 substation-origin pairs, and raised D10's by +0.52 [+0.11, +0.94] (95%) from the 2024-10 origin on.
  • C2's sign pattern is consistent with chance. The origin-level sign test gives p = 0.55, C2 is below zero at 28 of 57 pairs, and C2 does not grow with extra history (Spearman 0.02; -0.054 [-0.193, +0.063] with at least 12 extra months). With levels removed, all history is better by 0.046 on November to March rows and worse by 0.027 on April to October rows. D16 has only 8.4 extra months at the April 2024 origin.
  • The earlier sign flips look like level effects. Without drift, C1 per pair correlates 0.82 with the difference in held-level bias, and C1 is about zero once levels are removed. So whether more years help depends on where each substation's next level sits relative to the window average. This experiment does not test the annual frozen fits of experiments 104 and 106 (up to 12 months of stale level, against 3 here), the best form of level correction, weather forecasts, or a replication of experiment 106's design.
  • The month-block interval is narrow for this design, because the 3 months of an origin share one fit's level error. The page's intervals use months, as experiment 107 did; the origin-block and pair-block intervals are given above for C2 and C4.
  • Triage: all findings accepted. The full report is in the private briefs/ folder (e149_audit_report.md).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Past weather (ERA5 and CAMS) at forecast time is a ceiling, as in experiment 107.
  • Five Primaries are scored, with D16 entering at April 2024, so the first three origins hold four substations.
  • The 36-month rule does not guarantee 12 extra months of training data. The rule counts calendar months from each substation's first usable date, but training skips the COVID-lockdown window and the switching masks. At the July 2023 origin the all-history window holds only 1.7 extra months at D5, 3.7 at D10, and 6.2 at D11, and none at D14, so C2 compares two identical fits there. Extra history reaches 12 months from the April 2024 origin for D10, D11, D14, and D16, and from July 2024 for D5. Post hoc, over the 8 origins from July 2024 on, C2 is -0.066 [-0.201, +0.052] and C1 is +0.031 [-0.186, +0.228] (98.75%), so the conclusion does not change.
  • Quarterly refits and one drift step (3,000, tuned on 2024-07 to 2025-06) are used. Experiment 85 found quarterly refits score worse than weekly refits, so the contrast could change with the schedule.
  • The pinned solar capacity of experiment 45 uses a hindsight growth prior at the four burn-in cuts, and the July 2023 cut uses a vintage dated 37 days after it. The burn-in residuals form the spread pools of the first four scored origins. Both arms of every contrast get the same capacity, so the leak is not differential. The as-of capacity of experiment 139 is not used.
  • D10's two unlabelled jump windows stay in training, spread pools, and scoring, as in the base variant of experiment 107. Without D10, C2 is -0.076 [-0.173, +0.010].
  • The 36-month rule is a choice made before the fits; it leaves out D16's first three origins.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Settle the level-correction question: score a de-levelled error as the primary metric, apply a common causal level correction (the 28-day mean residual) to both window arms, and run both the quarterly and the annual-refit designs over two or more years.
  • Rerun C2 with weekly refits and ensemble weather forecasts only if a use needs full history, because the pooled improvement is 3% and the interval spans zero.
  • Test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms make long history lower the score. The window alone did not, at these five substations.

docs.title: Differentiable physics, N0: rerunning experiment 109's known-answer gate with a fair oracle and five seeds
docs.text:
We tested a forecasting method on made-up data whose right answer we know, and the test did not settle whether the method shrinks each substation's own coefficients towards the fleet's correctly. The method is a convex demand model of experiment 109 that gives each substation the fleet's shared coefficients plus a penalised deviation of its own ("partial pooling"). We built 8 synthetic substations from real calendar and weather data with injected coefficients, fitted the method to a substation that held only 4 weeks of data, and compared the fit with a reference estimator (the "oracle") that is told the fleet mean, the true spreads, and the noise variance. We repeated this on 5 random draws of the injected coefficients ("seeds"). A control that keeps no deviation at all (complete pooling) passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when the 4 weeks were in June, because a substation's heating signal is weak then, so the line could not tell a good fit from a bad one. The verdict by the pre-registered rule is inconclusive.

Other results were mixed. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 substations on every seed. The tuning rule chose a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds. The pooled fit's heating-slope error was smaller than the oracle's on 5 of 5 seeds. The line that checks full-history coefficients passed on 2 of 5 seeds, and the fleet-mean line on 4 of 5. A gate that scored the heating-slope error against the injected truth on winter weeks would settle the shrinkage question; a post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks showed that the controls then fail.

Experiment 109's gate was unfair in two ways, and this rerun removes both. The oracle was given each substation's true capacity, which the pooled fit had to estimate from the same 4 weeks, and the tuning rule was checked on one seed per definition. Here the oracle estimates every coefficient, capacity included, and the gate runs 5 seeds under one definition fixed in advance. The gate code is copied from e00109_gate.py.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every number below is printed in report.txt.

Line (pre-registered) Seeds passed Detail (a) fleet mean 4 of 5 Seed 1 missed by 0.02 points (profile 0.518 against 0.5). (b) shrinkage against the fair oracle 2 of 5 Passes on seeds 4 and 5, where the oracle's slope is near 0. controls for (b) both fail 3 of 5 Complete pooling passed on seeds 4 and 5; no pooling never passed. (c) full history keeps its own coefficients 2 of 5 Slopes 0.82 to 0.94 against the 0.85 bar. (d) tuning within one grid step 5 of 5 Exactly the best penalty on 3 of 5 seeds. (e) capacity from a short window 5 of 5 8 of 8 within 25% at 4 weeks and at 3 months on every seed.
  • Verdict rule as pre-registered. The gate is not passed: line (b) passed on 2 of 5 seeds, line (c) on 2, and the controls failed line (b) on 3, each below the 4 needed. The tuning rule is stable. Complete pooling passed line (b) on 2 seeds, so the rule's inconclusive clause, checked first, applies. - The oracle is the worse heating estimator in June and in January (post hoc). The oracle's heating error was 2.35 to 3.45 against 2.01 to 2.38 for the pooled fit in June, and 2.30 to 4.06 against 1.87 to 2.46 in January. One untested explanation: the oracle treats the noise as independent, while the noise keeps multi-day persistence, so the oracle trusts 4 weeks of evidence too much. Another is that capacity and heating are hard to separate over 4 weeks. This experiment does not isolate either. - Line (b) fails by design in June. The slope half asks the pooled fit to match the oracle's slope. The oracle's slope was 0.35, 0.43, 0.42, -0.10, and 0.08 on the 5 seeds, so a fit that keeps nothing (slope 0) is within 0.15 of the oracle on seeds 4 and 5. - Capacity is estimated well. The fair oracle's fitted capacity was 0.90 to 1.20 of the truth (report section "Fair oracle capacity ratios"). - Tuning. The rule picked 1,000 rows on 4 seeds and 300 on seed 4. The best penalty on the noise-free truth was 1,000, 300, 1,000, 100, and 1,000.

docs.title: Post hoc: line (b) with 4 January weeks
docs.text:
This rerun is labelled post hoc and changes no pre-registered verdict. The rerun holds the 4 weeks before 2025-02-01 on the same 5 fleets, with the penalty tuned on June (not retuned for January).

  • The controls failed on 5 of 5 seeds, so with winter weeks line (b) can detect both no pooling (error 4.3 to 8.4) and complete pooling (error 2.1 to 2.6). - The pooled fit failed line (b) on 5 of 5 seeds, on the slope half only. Its slope was 0.20 to 0.50 against the oracle's 0.63 to 1.06, while its error (1.87 to 2.46) was below the oracle's (2.30 to 4.06). The pooled fit shrinks harder than the oracle and is more accurate, consistent with the oracle's independent-noise assumption being wrong, which this experiment does not test.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site. This check does not apply, because the gate scores coefficients and noise-free truth, not forecast spreads.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each contrast. The tuning check scores the mean forecast against the noise-free truth (line (d)); the quantile-score rule gave the same penalty as the truth-based rule on 3 of 5 seeds. Tuning on the median's absolute error instead picked 1,000, 300, 300, 300, and 1,000, which agrees with the quantile-score rule on 3 of 5 seeds.
  • Audit triggers that fired. Trigger 1 (a known-answer test fails), trigger 2 (the result contradicts the prediction that line (b) passes on 4 or 5 seeds; explained above), and trigger 7 (the pooled experiments listed in the theme's plan depend on this gate). Triggers 3 to 6 do not apply, because the gate has no per-site forecast contrast. One Sonnet reviewer re-derived every number from the stored runs and read the prose; no Opus audit ran.

docs.title: Pre-registered lines
docs.text: • Synthetic fleet. As in experiment 109: 8 synthetic substations on the real calendar and weather of the MW Primaries, a known fleet mean and known deviations, noise taken as whole weeks of residuals from a different substation. Each of seeds 20261101 to 20261105 builds a new fleet. - (a) Fleet mean. The fitted heating slopes (summed over the four smoothing windows) are within 10% of the true fleet mean in every hour band, and the centred profile is within 0.5 points root mean square. Line (a) is the same as in experiment 109. - (b) Shrinkage on 4 June weeks, against the fair oracle. The fair oracle is the posterior mean of the Gaussian model with the realised fleet mean, the true spread of each family, and the true noise variance, and a flat prior on the capacity. It estimates every coefficient jointly from the held-out substation's 4 weeks. Line (b) passes when both hold: the slope of the pooled fit's deviation on the true deviation, measured on the heating contribution to the prediction, is within 0.15 of the oracle's slope, and the heating root mean square error across the eight substations is at most 1.2 times the oracle's. - Controls for (b). The same line, with the pooled fit's penalty set to 0 rows (no pooling) and to 1,000,000 rows (complete pooling). Both must fail line (b); if either passes, the line cannot detect a bad fit. - (c) Full history keeps its own coefficients. With 2 years of rows the slope of the fitted deviation on the true deviation is at least 0.85. Line (c) is the same as in experiment 109. - (d) Tuning rule picks the best penalty within one grid step. The rule is experiment 109's (the penalty minimising the mean of the 4-week and 3-month score ratios against no pooling, subject to the all-rows score within 0.02 points). The best penalty is found by applying the same rule to the root mean square error of the mean forecast against the noise-free injected truth, on the same rows. Line (d) passes when the rule's penalty is within one step of the best on common.LAMBDA_GRID (nine values from 0 to 1,000,000). Experiment 109's line (d), which multiplied every spread by 10 or by 0.1, is dropped, and the two extra fleets that it needed are not built. - (e) Capacity from a short window. As in experiment 109, the 4-week and 3-month pooled fits recover the held-out substation's capacity within 25% at 6 or more of 8 substations. - Reported, not blocking: the fair oracle's capacity ratio.

docs.title: Predictions against outcome
docs.text: • Predicted: line (b) passes on 4 or 5 of 5 seeds. Line (b) passed on 2. The prediction assumed the oracle's capacity advantage was the only fault; the oracle's independent-noise assumption was a second one. - Predicted: the tuning rule within one grid step on 3 or 4 of 5 seeds. The tuning rule was within one step on 5 of 5.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The pooled fit is given the true capacity of the seven full-history substations, because the synthetic vintages equal the truth (inherited from experiment 109). Lines (a), (c), and the tuning feasibility rule run with capacity known; lines (b) and (e) estimate the held-out substation's capacity.
  • The oracle's prior mean is the mean of all 8 true coefficient vectors, including the held-out substation's own, which slightly flatters the oracle and biases against passing line (b).
  • The 5 fleets share the real calendar, weather, and noise weeks, and differ only in the injected coefficients, so they are not independent replicates of the noise.
  • Schedule. One refit per fit at the 2025-07-01 cut (2025-02-01 for the post hoc rerun), so the contrasts do not depend on a retraining schedule.
  • Torch. e00150_tune.py imports torch inside its worker function and is on the ty torch override list.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: Replace line (b) by the error of the pooled fit against the injected truth, held on 4 winter weeks, with the complete- and no-pooling errors as controls. The pooled fit's heating error (1.87 to 2.46) beat complete pooling (2.1 to 2.6) on 4 of 5 seeds and no pooling (4.3 to 8.4) on 5 of 5 in January, which such a line would test directly.

docs.title: NRA forecast rescored against the true NRA series, with the merged RO-NC intervals
docs.text:
Take-home message. Once the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) has raised its alarm that a load transfer is under way, taking the transfer out of the forecast's recent power closes most of the gap in forecast error between a filter that ignores transfers and a filter fed the true normal running arrangement (NRA) series. Ignoring recent power altogether closes nearly as much, and masking the readings closes more than subtracting the detected megawatts (MW). Counting the transfers the detector missed and the first 2 days before its alarm, the forecasts that use detected transfers gain little (subtracting: nothing; masking: 21% of the gap), and on real days with no logged transfer they make the forecast worse.

We tested the correction on simulated load transfers added to recorded power, so the true NRA series is known. We asked whether a forecast of the power a substation would draw with no load transfer (the NRA) improves when the forecast's recent-power input is corrected for the transfers that RO-NC finds. The simulation uses the 44 worlds of experiment 141 (a world is one simulated copy of the recorded power series), six substations, and 475 pairs of a transfer and a Primary substation. The true NRA series is the recorded power without the simulated transfers. We scored every forecast against that true series, which experiment 141 did not: it scored against the observed power, which rewards a filter for following a transfer. The filter is the Kalman filter of GAM-K (the weather-driven demand forecast of earlier experiments). The detector's intervals come from experiment 147 and experiment 148. The share of the gap closed is the measure used in experiment 88, where the detector closed 16% of the gap.

By the pre-registered rule the verdict is partly supported, and the headline is fragile. The pre-registered arm (SUB-DET) closed 71% of the gap on forecasts issued after the alarm, with a 99% interval of 25% to 85%. The pre-registered rule calls the result supported only if the lower end is at least 40%; here it is 25%. Two further checks change the reading: with each transfer weighted equally the share is -31%, and without substation D11 it is 33%. The detector-driven arms also do worse than no correction before the alarm, and on real rows outside logged transfers.

Figure 1 draws 95% intervals; the verdict uses the 99% interval of 25% to 85%.

  • Arms. All arms are GAM-K's member forecasts plus a correction from a Kalman filter run on a stream (the power series the filter reads), with experiment 141's spread. The gap is K0's score minus CLEAN's. K0 (no correction) reads the stream with the transfers in it. CLEAN reads the stream without them (the ceiling, 100%). SUB-DET subtracts the detected MW (the stored step of the detector, a constant per interval) over every interval known at the forecast origin. MASK treats the readings inside known intervals as missing. GAM-only ignores recent power. SUB-DET-LAG96 knows the end 96 half-hours after it (the 90th percentile of the 6-hour rule's lag) instead of 60. SUB-TRUE-LAG subtracts the true shaped MW, and SUB-TRUE-CONST a constant at the event's mean MW (an oracle, because the mean uses the whole transfer). S-KF and S-ORACLE are experiment 141's two-regime filter fed detected and true intervals. SUB-PLACEBO shifts the detected intervals by whole weeks. SUB-FALSE subtracts only the detected intervals that match one of the 148 unexplained real alarms that match no logged transfer.
  • Intervals. The injected worlds store the offline-end intervals (R0_M48), so those are used, with the onset known 96 half-hours after the step and the end known at the later of the stored known_from and 60 half-hours after the end. Experiment 148's 6-hour rule has the same onset and the same end for most intervals (median difference 0 stamps). The stored known_from of the R0_M48 intervals is a median of 76 half-hours after the end (10th percentile 48, 90th percentile 94).
  • Rows. 214,992 forecast rows (six substations, 44 worlds, leads 0.5 to 168 h, the replicate months and the scored year) with a target inside a transfer or in the 48 hours after its true end. The rows are the same for every arm. The C1 rows are the 24,716 whose forecast origin is after the alarm is known (11 calendar months); 188,817 rows have the origin between the onset and the alarm, and the detector found 36.4% of the 475 transfer-and-substation pairs (45% of the larger ones; the 475 pairs come from 145 distinct transfers). The median ratio of the detected step to the true mean MW is 1.03.
  • Headline, C1 (the share of the gap SUB-DET closes after the alarm). SUB-DET closes 71% (99% interval 25% to 85%) of the K0-to-CLEAN gap of 2.872 points of capacity (95% interval 1.490 to 3.481). Inside the transfer it closes 84% (78% to 97%) and in the 48 hours after the end 62% (29% to 78%). On the absolute error of the median forecast it closes 69% (43% to 82%).
  • Other arms on the C1 rows (95%). MASK 84% (61% to 95%). GAM-only 78% (67% to 82%). SUB-DET-LAG96 69% (37% to 82%). SUB-TRUE-LAG 83% (64% to 88%) and SUB-TRUE-CONST 82% (70% to 87%). S-KF -10% (-13% to -4%) and S-ORACLE -27% (-42% to -24%): the two-regime filters follow the transfer, as predicted. SUB-PLACEBO -6% (-15% to 13%) and SUB-FALSE -9% (-20% to 4%).
  • Robustness of SUB-DET. With each of the 145 distinct transfers weighted equally: -31% (-107% to 17%). With each substation weighted equally: 65%. Without D11, which supplies 12,203 of the 24,716 rows and 61% of the gap: 33% (-66% to 73%). By substation: D10 55%, D11 94%, D14 105%, D16 -23%, D5 81%, D9 77%. By duration of the transfer: 1 to 3 days -72% (-625% to 17%), 3 to 7 days 69% (41% to 88%), over 7 days 89% (85% to 99%). MASK with each transfer weighted equally is 65% (37% to 82%), and without D11 62% (-8% to 93%). Shares by the shape of the injected profile are not available, because the shape is not stored in experiment 141's worlds.
  • Before the alarm and on all rows. On the 188,817 rows whose origin is after the onset and before the alarm: SUB-DET -28% (-111% to 15%), MASK -3% (-35% to 25%), GAM-only 35% (18% to 55%), SUB-TRUE-LAG 57% (9% to 63%). On all 213,533 rows after the onset, including the missed transfers: SUB-DET -1% (-51% to 35%), MASK 21% (-3% to 47%), GAM-only 47% (35% to 62%), SUB-TRUE-LAG 64% (32% to 69%). SUB-DET differs from K0 on 86% of the rows before the alarm, because real-stream alarms (false or true) are subtracted too.
  • Absolute scores (mean quantile score, points of capacity), after the alarm. K0 5.108, CLEAN 2.236, MASK 2.687, SUB-TRUE-LAG 2.728, SUB-TRUE-CONST 2.751, GAM-only 2.859, SUB-DET 3.079, SUB-DET-LAG96 3.120, S-KF 5.406, S-ORACLE 5.885. Before the alarm: K0 3.422, CLEAN 2.431, GAM-only 3.078, MASK 3.448, SUB-DET 3.702.
  • Real stream, descriptive. Part A: 9 combinations of a logged real transfer and a substation have forecasts issued inside the transfer with targets in the week after its logged end (the observed power is then the NRA). Row-weighted mean quantile score: K0 9.843, SUB-DET 4.992, MASK 5.018, GAM-only 4.713. Part B, no harm: on 877,540 real rows outside logged transfers, K0 scores 2.712, SUB-DET 2.929 (+0.217, 95% interval +0.114 to +0.328), MASK 2.929 (+0.217, +0.082 to +0.376), GAM-only 3.001 (+0.289, +0.202 to +0.380); positive is worse.
  • Tail calibration after the alarm (share of actuals at or below the quantile; the pinball loss). K0: q01 0.040 (0.401), q05 0.068 (1.130), q95 0.650 (1.962), q99 0.788 (0.999). MASK: 0.037 (0.306), 0.088 (0.777), 0.971 (0.625), 0.994 (0.163). SUB-DET: 0.054 (0.396), 0.129 (0.943), 0.970 (0.709), 0.991 (0.201). GAM-only: 0.002 (0.174), 0.014 (0.653), 0.839 (0.761), 0.931 (0.251). CLEAN: 0.009 (0.150), 0.043 (0.533), 0.974 (0.579), 0.996 (0.153). The spread is experiment 141's K0 spread for every arm, so the tail contrasts are contrasts in location.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast is -0.030 points of capacity over all rows and identical for every arm, because the spread is shared. By substation: D5 -0.329, D10 -0.091, D9 -0.107, D11 -0.038, D16 +0.031, D14 +0.106.
  • Mean-forecast contrasts point the same way as the quantile score. The error of the median forecast gives SUB-DET 69%, MASK 83%, and GAM-only 74%.
  • Triggers. Three fired: SUB-DET above its predicted band, a sign flip under per-transfer weighting, and dependence on D11. SUB-DET (71%) is above its predicted 30% to 60%. Weighting by transfer flips SUB-DET's sign, and leaving out D11 lowers the share to 33%, but the verdict stays partly supported when D11 is left out. Re-deriving the headline from the stored scores reproduces 71%. Three D11 transfers hold 45% of the gap.
  • Overlapping windows. SUB-TRUE-CONST is labelled an oracle. At one substation the 48-hour window after a transfer overlaps the next transfer in 271 of 906 consecutive pairs, and a row takes the latest transfer that has begun; the overlap is not corrected.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• C1 conditions on detection. The detector missed 64% of the transfers; the share on all rows after the onset is the figure that includes them.
  • Intervals come from the offline end rule with a 30-hour call lag, not from rerunning the 6-hour rule on each world.
  • The scored months are few. The C1 rows fall in 11 calendar months, with 29 to 8,791 rows each, so the month-block intervals are wide.
  • Real transfers inside the stream are not removed from CLEAN. Subtracting a real-stream alarm that is a true transfer is scored against observed power, which still contains it.
  • Retraining schedule. The experiment refits nothing: it reuses experiment 141's cached GAM-K forecasts.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Whether a forecast that masks the readings inside a suspected transfer, and uses a detector that alarms within hours instead of about 2 days, beats the weather model alone on all rows, including the rows before the alarm and the normal rows where the weather model alone scores 0.289 points worse.

docs.title: Changes made after the first run
docs.text:
The decision rule, the prediction, and the arms of the plan were committed before any run. The first run gave a SUB-DET share of 71% (99% interval 25% to 85%) on the post-alarm rows, which this page still reports as C1. The reviews that followed changed the experiment, and each change is post hoc:

  • Added arms (the ML experiment manager's request): GAM-only, MASK, SUB-DET-LAG96, and SUB-FALSE (a placebo of real alarms). The week-shifted placebo stays.
  • Added strata and robustness (the audit): shares by transfer duration, with each transfer weighted equally, by substation, and without D11.
  • Corrections (the code review): SUB-TRUE-LAG used the true end before it was known; it now holds the amount it had when the interval became known until the end is known, which lowered its share from 94% to 83%.
  • Real-stream check redesigned (the manager's request): the first design added the labelled MW to observed power, which is circular with the detector's step.
  • Not applied: shares by the shape of the injected profile, because the shape is not stored in experiment 141's worlds.

docs.title: Experiment 152: does modelling the fold help the forecast at the Primaries metered in MVA?
docs.text:
At Stickney (D12), the one MVA-only Primary with clear reverse flow, folding the forecast quantiles at zero lowered the score on sunny middays, did no harm at the other seven Primaries, and did not clear the pre-registered bar for the whole year. Against the same meter fit with symmetric quantiles, arm F scored 0.40 points better on D12's sunny middays (98.75% interval -0.65 to -0.07; replicate year -0.26, -0.51 to -0.02), which passes R2. Against reading the apparent power as signed power (arm N), arm F scored 0.39 points better over all of D12's rows in the scored year, but the interval (-0.95 to +0.16) includes zero, so R1 failed there. In the replicate year the gain was 0.53 points (-0.86 to -0.27). Pooled over the other seven Primaries, F minus N was -0.02 (-0.11 to +0.06), so R3 passed. The known-answer test on five Primaries with a hidden solar farm passed on the sign of the flow at the larger injection (balanced accuracy 0.81 to 0.87) and failed at the smaller one (0.51 to 0.81) and on the upper-tail coverage (11.5% of readings above q95 at the larger injection). The verdict is inconclusive: all of R1 and R2 rests on one substation, and the sign of its flow could be checked only indirectly.

In this page, arm N reads the apparent power as signed power. Arm A fits the demand model through the meter and uses symmetric quantiles. Arm F is arm A with quantiles folded at zero. R1 to R3 are the pre-registered contrasts in the front matter, and the Terms paragraph below defines the other abbreviations.

docs.title: Step 0: only D12 has clear reverse flow
docs.text:
Only D12 has predicted reverse flow on most sunny middays, so all of R1 and R2 rests on one substation. The table uses experiment 110's fit through the meter (past weather, the scored year; the replicate year agrees within 0.2 MW and 3 percentage points). Sunny middays are April to September half-hours starting 10:00 to 13:30 UTC with CAMS irradiance at least 70% of the Haurwitz clear-sky value, outside switching masks. "Sure" is the share of those half-hours with a fitted reverse-flow probability above 0.9 under a normal residual.

Site NGED reverse flow? PV capacity (MW) Sunny-midday half-hours with reverse flow Sure (probability above 0.9) Largest reverse flow (MW) Lowest reading (MVA) D12 Maybe 5.9 100% 100% 5.3 0.87 D22 Maybe 1.6 3.7% (replicate 0.7%) 0% 0.14 0.21 D8 Yes 4.6 0% 0% 0 0.14 D2 No 6.9 0% 0% 0 5.4 D3 No 3.5 0% 0% 0 4.9 D4 No 1.3 0% 0% 0 4.9 D19 No 1.6 0% 0% 0 0.92 D21 No 1.4 0% 0% 0 1.6
  • D8's zero is weak evidence. NGED's monitoring file marks D8 "Yes", but the series changes meaning in April 2025, so the fit rests on little data and is scored from 2025-04-01 only.
  • D22's sign is unsure. The fit puts the flow near zero (mean reverse-flow probability 0.09), so its sign cannot be called.
  • The sign at D12 can be checked only indirectly. D12 has no MW meter, so signed MW does not exist. The bulk-supply-point closure (F1) put a coefficient of 1.02 on D12's signed flow, where an exact closure gives 1, but the variance of the closure error fell by only 0.7% (interval including zero), so the check neither contradicts nor firmly supports the sign. No reactive-power series exists for these Primaries.

docs.title: Headline result
docs.text:
Terms. The eight MVA-only Primaries are D2 (Warth Lane Skegness), D3 (Sleaford Road Boston), D4 (Ingoldmells), D8 (Marsh Lane), D12 (Stickney), D19 (Chapel St Leonards), D21 (Alford), and D22 (Langrick). GAM-K is the convex additive demand model with a Kalman filter of experiments 111 and 136, driven by the mean of the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) forecast. BG2 is the production-style best guess of experiment 87. CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance. Effective capacity is the series' reference power (4.68 MW at D12), the unit of every "point". Arm N reads |S| as signed power; arm A fits through the meter (experiment 110's L0) with the filter correcting |S|; arm F fits through the meter, filters the signed flow, and folds its quantiles. A bulk supply point (BSP) is the substation above a group of Primaries.

Eight of the 16 trial Primaries report only the magnitude of apparent power (MVA), and the reading rises again once embedded solar pushes the net flow below zero, because it is the absolute value of the flow. This experiment asks whether a forecast that models that bounce explicitly beats one that treats the reading as signed power. Experiment 110 already fitted the bounce for day-ahead forecasts on past weather and found it helps at Stickney (D12) alone. This experiment tests the same idea on the ensemble-driven forecast, to seven days ahead, with a filter and quantiles that also know about the fold.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rows. The scored year is 292 daily ensemble runs from 2025-07-01, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events: 97,046 half-hourly rows at D12 and 679,066 over the other seven sites (D8 from 2025-04-01, and only in the scored year because its replicate months precede its first usable fit). The replicate year is the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06. The tuning months, odd months of the same span, fit the spread and the folded-quantile pools. D8 has no tuning months of its own, so it borrows the other six sites' tuning forecasts for its spread.
  • R1, F minus N at D12, all rows. Scored year -0.39 points (98.75% interval -0.95 to +0.16); replicate -0.53 (-0.86 to -0.27). The point estimate is below the bar of -0.30 in both years, but the scored-year interval includes zero, so R1 fails as pre-registered.
  • R2, F minus A at D12, sunny middays. Scored year -0.40 (-0.65 to -0.07; 3,692 rows, 6 months); replicate -0.26 (-0.51 to -0.02; 2,799 rows). R2 passes in both years. On all rows the same contrast is -0.12 (-0.22 to -0.02) and -0.05 (-0.25 to +0.11).
  • R3, F minus N pooled over D2, D3, D4, D8, D19, D21, D22. Scored year -0.017 (-0.113 to +0.056); replicate -0.025 (-0.089 to +0.005), without D8. Both are below the +0.03 bar. Dropping any one of D2, D3, D4, D19, D21, or D22 moves the scored-year estimate between -0.019 and -0.027.
  • R4, F minus BG2 at D12. Not computed: experiment 87 stored BG2 only for the MW Primaries, and none exists for D12. The reference arms climatology and the manual heuristic are likewise not available for the MVA series.
  • A minus N at D12. Fitting through the meter without folding the quantiles already helps in the replicate year (-0.48, -0.77 to -0.25) and not clearly in the scored year (-0.27, -0.88 to +0.33): absolute quantile score at D12 is 7.56 (N), 7.29 (A), and 7.17 (F) in the scored year, and 7.33, 6.85, and 6.80 in the replicate year.
  • By site, F minus N, scored year. D2 +0.011, D3 +0.015, D4 -0.009, D8 -0.189, D12 -0.391, D19 -0.009, D21 +0.017, D22 +0.042. Only D3 and D21 have an interval wholly above zero (D3 +0.005 to +0.027; D21 +0.009 to +0.024), by under 0.03 points.

docs.title: Stage 1: the known-answer test
docs.text:
Five MW Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16) had a metered solar farm's output subtracted from the signed power at 1.0 and 2.0 times the Primary's midday median absolute reading in the year before the scored year. Each Primary receives a different metered farm. The series was then folded to |P| (zero reactive power) or to sqrt(P² + (0.2506 D)²) (power factor 0.97, with the pre-injection reading as the demand D, which is simpler than the plan's as-of-capacity demand estimate). The scored year only.

Check Rule Result Passed? K1, sign balanced accuracy, level 2.0 at least 0.80 at 4 of 5 sites 0.81 to 0.87 at 5 of 5, both reactive-power settings yes K1, sign balanced accuracy, level 1.0 at least 0.80 at 4 of 5 sites with zero reactive power 0.70 to 0.81, at 1 of 5 sites; with power factor 0.97 0.51 to 0.79, at 0 of 5 sites no K2, F minus N, level 2.0 at most -0.10, interval wholly below zero -0.71 (-1.02 to -0.44) zero reactive power, -0.56 (-0.84 to -0.31) power factor 0.97 yes K2, F minus N, natural level at most +0.03 -0.016 (-0.041 to +0.010) yes K3, mean absolute error of the signed median on reverse-flow rows, level 2.0 F at most 1.5 times S, N at least 2 times S F 1.04 times S, N 2.99 times S yes K4, fitted-capacity rise over injected capacity, level 1.0 0.75 to 1.25 at 4 of 5 sites 0.84, 0.79, 0.88, 0.87 at four sites, -0.05 at D5 yes K5, coverage on sunny middays, level 2.0 within 3 points of 5% below q05 and above q95 2.5% below q05, 11.5% above q95 no

The signed ceiling S scored 5.4 to 6.8 points at level 2.0, against 2.2 to 4.0 at the natural level, so the injected farm makes the signed series harder to forecast. Stop rule S1 (balanced accuracy under 0.80 at 3 or more sites at level 2.0) did not fire.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean, D12 (points, scored year, all rows and sunny middays). F -0.23 and +1.81; A +0.01 and 0.00; N 0.00 and 0.00. Folding makes the median differ from the mean on sunny middays by 1.8 points, which is the mechanism of the gain.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the contrasts, D12. F and A share one fit and filter, so their mean forecasts are identical (all rows -0.09, sunny middays -12.6 points). N's is +0.04 over all rows and -22.9 on sunny middays. Every quantile gain of F over A therefore comes from the quantiles. A's gain over N on sunny middays comes with a mean forecast error that is 10 points smaller.
  • Tail calibration at D12, scored year. Share of readings below q01, q05, above q95, above q99, all rows: F 3.7%, 7.9%, 7.5%, 3.0%; A 3.5%, 8.8%, 6.5%, 2.1%; N 4.2%, 9.9%, 5.6%, 1.9%. On sunny middays: F 0.9%, 2.7%, 15.1%, 6.9%; A 0.6%, 1.9%, 15.8%, 7.3%; N 0.0%, 0.2%, 18.1%, 7.6%. All three arms leave 15% to 18% of readings above q95 on sunny middays, because the forecast reading is too low there.
  • Audit triggers that fired. R1 failed in the scored year while the replicate year passed, so R1's point estimate agrees across the two years, and the scored-year interval is too wide to exclude zero. The known-answer test failed K1 at level 1.0 and K5. One site decides R1 and R2. The pre-registered verdict is inconclusive, and no audit was run, because the brief allows no Opus review and none of the findings would change the verdict.
  • Predictions against outcomes. F minus N at D12 was predicted at -0.5 to -1.0 and came out at -0.39 (scored) and -0.53 (replicate). F minus A on sunny middays was predicted at -0.05 to -0.25 and came out at -0.40 and -0.26, larger than predicted. F minus N pooled over the other seven was predicted within +-0.02 and came out at -0.02 and -0.03. Coverage below q05 on D12's sunny-midday rows was predicted at 9 to 11% for N, 6 to 8% for A, and near 5% for F, and came out at 0.2%, 1.9%, and 2.7%. The sunny-midday forecast is too low in all arms, which leaves almost no readings below q05 and explains the miss for N and A.
  • Folding helps more in Stage 2 than the Stage 0 replay predicted. The replay of folded quantiles on experiment 110's day-ahead predictions with past weather moved D12's sunny-midday score by +0.03 and +0.04 points. Stage 2 uses ensemble-driven forecasts at leads 0.5 to 168 hours. One possible reason is the longer leads, but the experiment did not test the difference separately.
  • Not computed. BG2, climatology, and manual heuristic at the MVA Primaries (no stored predictions), the curtailment-style cost (the folded series has no signed export), and a learned reactive-power arm.

docs.title: Deviations from the plan
docs.text:
• The latent filter was dropped by stop rule S0, so arm F is arm A plus folded quantiles.
  • Plain GAM-K with experiment 133's shared filter settings (POOL), not T-all. The plan's engine copy omitted the heating split.
  • Arm S uses the fitted capacity and the known-answer demand is the pre-injection reading.
  • D8 borrows the other six Primaries' tuning forecasts for its spread because its tuning months precede its first usable fit.
  • Stage 1 uses the scored year only, one farm per Primary, and the sign check's floor is 5% of the Primary's 99th-percentile reading.

docs.title: Decisions made at the start of the run
docs.text:
• Run now. Experiment 139 is not awaited: no as-of capacity can be built at an MVA Primary, so the capacity is fitted through the meter in every monthly refit.
  • Step 0 comes first. Step 0 measures how much reverse flow each MVA-only Primary has, and its table heads the finished page.
  • Falsifier F3 is dropped. Stickney has no MW meter, so its signed MW cannot exist. Only F1 and F2 remain, and the page says the sign at D12 can be checked only indirectly.
  • Marsh Lane (D8) is scored only from 2025-04-01, the month its series changed meaning. Its replicate months before April 2025 are empty, so R3's replicate rests on six sites.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Stage 0 (CPU minutes). F1: the bulk-supply-point (BSP) closure of experiment 124 for the BSP above D12, run on summer-midday rows with D12's |S| in the sum and again with D12's fitted signed flow, each with a free term for the BSP's unmetered solar. A clear gain in residual variance from the signed version supports the sign, no gain fails it. The free solar term is partly collinear with D12's reverse flow, so a pass is weak evidence and a clear fail is strong. F2: replay the filter on experiment 110's stored D12 predictions, additive on |S| against the latent filter with gating, plus folded quantiles, day-ahead. Neither falsifier needs new fits. No reactive-power series exists for these Primaries (experiment 79: NGED cannot supply P and Q), so there is no reactive check. Time one multi-start meter refit, confirm that the hand-filtered switching list covers the MVA Primaries, and confirm D8's cut date from its monthly profile.

Stop rules. S0: if F2 moves D12's sunny-midday score by less than 0.05 points in either direction, drop the latent filter and run only N, A, and folded quantiles (A plus folded quantiles becomes arm F). If F1 contradicts the sign at D12, stop and report that the sign cannot be established from the data we hold. S1: if arm F's balanced accuracy in the known-answer test is under 0.80 at level 2.0 with Q = 0 at 3 or more of the 5 sites, stop. S2: after the replicate months, if F minus N at D12 has an interval wholly above zero, stop and diagnose. S3: if D12's fitted reverse-flow share jumps by more than 20 percentage points between consecutive monthly refits, flag it, and stop if it happens in 3 or more refits. S4: if one multi-start meter refit takes longer than 5 minutes on one core, cut stage 2 to D12, D22, and D8.

Stage 1, the known-answer test. Fold the five MW decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16), where the signed truth is known, by injecting farm output (levels none, 1.0, 2.0 as in experiment 79) and taking |P| with Q = 0 or a power factor of 0.97; run arm F, arm N, and a signed ceiling arm S (GAM-K on the unfolded signed series) through the same ENS GAM-K configuration, on the scored year only, with the injected farms' output used in training and scored rows alike and never as a forecast input. A power factor of 0.97 uses a demand estimate built from experiment 129's as-of capacity, fitted before each cut. Pass thresholds, fixed now: K1, balanced accuracy of the forecast flow's sign at least 0.80 at 4 of 5 sites at levels 1.0 and 2.0, under Q = 0 and under a power factor of 0.97, on rows with |P_true| of at least 5% of effective capacity (rows nearer zero have a sign with no effect on the reading); K2, F minus N on the quantile score of the folded series, pooled over the 5 sites and leads 0.5 to 168 hours, at most -0.10 at level 2.0 with the interval wholly below zero, and at most +0.03 at the natural level; K4, the fitted capacity rises by the injected farm's capacity within a ratio of 0.75 to 1.25 at 4 of 5 sites at level 1.0; K5, coverage below q05 and above q95 within 3 points of nominal on sunny-midday rows at level 2.0, pooled. K1, K2, K4, and K5 block. K3 blocks only a claim about the signed flow: on rows with P_true below zero at level 2.0, pooled, F's mean absolute error of the signed median is at most 1.5 times S's while N's is at least 2 times S's.

Stage 2, the real test. Arms N, A, F on the 8 MVA-only Primaries, driven by the calibrated ensemble mean over experiment 136's 292 daily runs, monthly refits on a 24-month window ending at each cut (capacity is fitted through the meter on data before the cut only), all 11 quantiles. A and F share the meter fits and differ in the filter and the quantiles. F's filter has the signed-flow state, an observation row H = (P_hat + l + z) / y_hat, and skips the update where the flow's sign is ambiguous. F's quantiles fold 200 samples of the signed flow. A two-branch update is added as arm F2 only if F fails K1 near crossings. A learned-Q arm at D12 is exploratory. D8's fits start at 2025-04-01 and are flagged.

Compute. CPU only, at most 4 cores, every thread cap at 1, run under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue: about 10 to 20 core-hours.

docs.title: Stage 0 results (written before stage 1 ran)
docs.text:
F1 does not contradict the sign at D12, and gives only weak support for it. On 1,185 sunny-midday half-hours of 2024-07 to 2026-06, the BSP regression put a coefficient of 1.02 on D12's signed flow (the coefficient of an exact closure is 1) and 0.00 on D12's unsigned reading. The signed version lowered the residual standard deviation by 0.7% (6.97 to 6.92 MW), and the month-block interval of the variance drop (-0.29 to 1.98 MW squared) includes zero. Under the rule written above, "no gain fails it" would stop the experiment, but a clear contradiction would be the signed version fitting worse, and it fits slightly better. The experiment goes on, and the page reports the sign at D12 as unestablished.

F2 triggers stop rule S0 in the scored year, so the latent filter is dropped. Replaying the filters on experiment 110's stored D12 predictions (day-ahead, past weather), the gated signed-flow filter minus the additive filter was +0.02 points (95% interval -0.24 to +0.30) on scored-year sunny-midday rows, under the 0.05-point threshold, and -0.37 (-0.91 to -0.03) in the replicate year, so the sign differs between the years. On all rows it was worse in both years (+1.57 and +0.80 points). Folded quantiles on the additive filter's corrected reading moved the sunny-midday score by +0.03 and +0.04 points. Following S0, arm F becomes arm A plus folded quantiles, and R2 compares those two. The replay reproduced experiment 110's stored filtered mean. The replicate-year residual pool came from the scored year and the scored-year pool from the replicate year; the convention is for screening only.

docs.title: Size triggers
docs.text:
• What gets stored: private files under the experiment's data folder only.
  • Serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes, for the latent filter; the cheapest is planned and the others are named fall-backs.
  • Callers whose names need a search: none; the scripts copy experiments 110 and 136.

docs.title: Earlier advice followed
docs.text: Experiment 39's advice to leave MVA Primaries out of signed capacity fits is followed by fitting capacity only through the meter. Experiment 56's advice to test the near-zero half-hours on more series is followed by the near-zero slice. Experiment 79's standing advice to ask NGED for signed MW at Stickney is dropped, because Stickney has no MW meter.

docs.title: A latent normal-running-arrangement state inside the GAM-K filter
docs.text:
Adding a separate state for a load transfer (demand switched from one substation to another) to the Kalman filter that corrects the forecast from recent power readings did not forecast the normal running arrangement (NRA) any better than two simpler filters. The NRA is the power a substation would have drawn had no transfer been switched in. One simpler filter ignores recent power altogether (GAM-ONLY). The other drops the half-hourly readings recorded while the transfer detector's alarm is open (MASK).

We added the recorded power of real transfers to the metered power of two Primary substations (D11 and D16), so that the NRA series is known. We then scored each filter's forecast against that series with the quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles; smaller is better). The gap is the quantile-score difference between the plain filter (K0) and the new filter given the true transfer intervals (NEW-ORACLE). The new filter with detected intervals (NEW-DET) closed 78% of that gap. GAM-ONLY closed 79% and MASK closed 81%.

Verdict: partly supported. The pre-registered rule needs a 99% lower bound of at least 40%, and the lower bound is 5%, so the new filter's gain is not established. The real-alarm placebo also failed, although the audit found that the placebo's pass rule cannot be met on real alarms.

docs.title: Question
docs.text: Does a Kalman filter that carries the normal running arrangement (NRA) as a latent state, and routes a detected load transfer into a separate offset state, give a better forecast of the NRA than the filters we have? The maintainer wants the switching detector for two purposes: reading recent power observations better, and producing an NRA forecast. Experiment 141 (PR 1453, not merged when this page was written) scored observed power, which rewards following a transfer. Experiment 151 (not merged when this page was written) re-scores the existing filters against the true NRA. This experiment changes the filter: none of the earlier designs in this project ties the Kalman state to a latent NRA. The edge-flow design of experiment 116 treats the NRA as the frozen GAM, and 141's regime S is a variance switch on the same level state. The filter is a standard linear-Gaussian state-space model with a switched process noise, in the family of Harvey (1989) intervention models. We re-implement it and do not claim it as new.

docs.title: The filter
docs.text:
Per hour band, as in GAM-K, the filter reads the residual r of observed power minus the frozen GAM forecast. State: the NRA level n (a random walk with GAM-K's fitted process noise, so it moves as slowly as GAM-K's level), GAM-K's decaying anomaly z, and a transfer offset x. Observation: r = n + z + x + noise. The offset x has zero mean. While an alarm interval is open its process noise is a large multiple (four settings pre-registered, see below) of n's; after the interval's end is called it decays to zero by a factor of 0.5 per reading and has no process noise. The NRA forecast is n plus the decayed anomaly, with x not carried forward.

GAM-K's level and the NRA level are the same state: two random-walk levels observed only through their sum cannot be told apart, so a separate fourth state would add nothing. This differs from the brief's wording ("two extra states") on that point only.

Intervals come from the merged causal RO-NC alarm with experiment 147's R2 rule (the onset is known 96 half-hours after the step, the end is known 60 half-hours after the true end, the 6-hour lookahead of experiment 148). When an alarm becomes known at a forecast origin, the filter is re-run from the interval's onset with x switched on over [onset, now], so the step is not left in n.
