  • Known answer. Experiment 154 is the known-answer gate of the same fit, on synthetic fleets. It is not repeated here.
  • Bookends. K0 (no pooling) and tied (complete pooling) bracket PH and PS. A pooled arm that scores worse than tied at 24 months on all rows fails the check that shrinkage is working.

Five triggers (size). Stored: private files only. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one design defensible: yes, pre-registered above. Callers not nameable without searching: no, the scripts copy experiment 136's and call one reviewed fit.

Audit triggers to watch. Trigger 1 (the bookend check), trigger 2 (a result against its prediction, likely at full history), and trigger 5 (a nested arm beating the arm that contains it: PS against PH).

Resources. CPU only, at most 8 cores with one thread per worker, each job under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue. No GPU. A joint fit across 27 monthly cuts takes under a minute and one substation's forecast takes seconds.

Advice followed and departures. From experiment 154: share the heating curve, keep every offset and level per substation, and do not claim a substation's own heating offset is learned from short windows (the 3-month arms are scored on forecast skill, not on the offset). From experiment 150: treat the penalty as tuned on the tuning months, not carried over. From experiment 149: no drift term is used. Departure: K0 is experiment 136's A0 and not experiment 155's arm, because experiment 155 has not run.

docs.title: Experiment 159: what are D8's multi-day drops, do they recur, and do they look like transfers?
docs.text:
D8's multi-day drops are 29 episodes in which its power runs about 2.7 megawatts (MW) below what a demand regression model expects, for 2 to 19 days. Its three connected neighbours step up with the drops at a rate not clearly above their rate at times chosen at random. D8 is a Primary substation, and D3, D14, and D5 are its connected neighbours with metered power. An earlier analysis found that the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), which flags a possible switching event (an operator moving load between substations) when the regression model's errors shift together, raised alarms on D8 that match no logged switching. That analysis also found that D8's power falls for days at a time while the demand forecast does not follow. We listed every such drop in the residual (metered power minus the power the regression model expects) of experiment 130. We then described when the drops happen. Finally, we checked whether a neighbour steps up by a similar amount at the same time, which would make a drop a load transfer (an operator moving some of D8's customers onto a neighbouring substation).

A neighbour steps up by half the depth at 8 of the 29 drops (0.28; 95% Wilson interval 0.15 to 0.46), against 0.21 at random times of the same time of day. Among the explanations we did not test, the drops could be a change in what D8's own customers draw, an outage, or a move of load to an unmetered substation. The drops show no detectable weekday, hour of day, bank-holiday, or seasonal pattern. Of the 29 drops, 23 have a logged closure of D8 within 24 hours, against 0.45 for random windows of the same lengths. Switching may therefore be involved, although closures within 24 hours are common (see Caveats). The alarms of RO-NC are mostly elsewhere: 10 of its 52 alarms on D8 fall within 6 hours of a drop's start or end, which is about 10 times the 1.0 expected by chance but leaves 42 of 52 away from the drops. We wrote predictions before looking at the data. Two held (the count of drops and the lack of a detectable weekday or hour pattern), one narrowly missed (the neighbour rate), and one failed (the alarms), so the verdict is partly supported. The page is descriptive, and the substations are labelled D3, D5, D8, and D14.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Drops: 29 runs of 2 days or longer in which the 24-hour median of the residual is below -1.5 MW. Gaps under 12 hours are merged. The drops cover 148 of the 1,642 days of history (a share of 0.090). Of the 29 drops, 28 start on or after 2023-07-01. By start year, 1 drop starts in 2022, 3 in 2023, 7 in 2024, 15 in 2025, and 3 in 2026. The number of drops depends strongly on the threshold: -1.0 MW gives 48 drops, -2.0 MW gives 24, and -2.5 MW gives 15.
  • Depth and duration: median depth 2.71 MW (range 1.19 to 5.36) and median duration 3.6 days (range 2.0 to 19.2). Inside drops the median metered power is 3.43 MW against an expected 6.20 MW. Of the half-hours inside drops, 0.435 are below 3 MW, against 0.158 of the half-hours outside drops after the first drop. The Spearman correlation of depth with start time is -0.40 (p = 0.032). The correlation arises because the four drops from October 2023 to January 2024 are the deepest (4.9 to 5.4 MW).
  • What the power does inside a drop: the metered power alternates between the expected level and 0 to 3 MW within each day, as in drop 20, which lasts 19 days. A drop is a run in which the periods at 0 to 3 MW dominate, not a steady 3 MW shift.
  • Recurrence: the 29 drops show no detectable weekday, hour, or interval pattern. Drop starts per weekday, Monday to Sunday, are 3, 5, 7, 3, 1, 5, and 5 (chi-squared p = 0.48). Drop starts per 6-hour block of the day (00:00 to 06:00, 06:00 to 12:00, 12:00 to 18:00, and 18:00 to 24:00) are 11, 3, 5, and 10 (p = 0.10). The spacing between starts has a median of 16.4 days (quartiles 10.3 and 42.3). Of the 29 starts, 1 falls within 1 day of a bank holiday (0.03; 0.01 to 0.17), against a share of 0.069 of all days. Drop starts per calendar month, January to December, are 5, 0, 0, 0, 3, 6, 2, 4, 2, 3, 1, and 3 (p = 0.12). The mean temperature during a drop is 0.55 degrees Celsius below the month's mean (95% interval -1.61 to +0.49).
  • Neighbour check: the largest step-up in any one of D3, D14, and D5, in the 6 hours after a drop's start, is at least 0.25, 0.50, and 0.75 times the depth for 11 of the 29 drops (0.38; 0.23 to 0.56), 8 (0.28; 0.15 to 0.46), and 5 (0.17; 0.08 to 0.35). At 5,000 randomly chosen times from July 2023, away from any drop and at the time of day of a drawn drop start, the rates are 0.34, 0.21, and 0.12. Every interval of the drops contains the rate at random times, but the drops' rates are above it at all three thresholds. A neighbour steps down by at least half the depth at the end of 13 of the 29 drops (0.45; 0.28 to 0.62). That step-down is the one sign of a shared cause in these checks. No comparison with random times was run for the step-down.
  • Logged closures: of the 29 drops, 23 (0.79; 0.62 to 0.90) have a logged closure of D8 within 24 hours, against 0.449 for 2,000 random windows of the same lengths that start in July 2023 or later and overlap no drop. A closure is a switching outage in NGED's switching log. Of the 29 drops, 14 (0.48; 0.31 to 0.66) still have a closure when one long-running switching job (reference 21D5583, a closure between D8 and D14 that overlaps 12 of the 18 drops that start in 2025 or later) is set aside. Six drops have no closure in the log.
  • What the alarms did: RO-NC raised 52 alarms on D8, of which 28 match no logged closure. Of those 28, 27 (0.96; 0.82 to 0.99) have a half-hour jump of at least 0.3 times the capacity (3.11 MW) within 24 hours, against 0.644 of all half-hours, and 16 step down while 12 step up. Of the 28, 5 (0.18; 0.08 to 0.36) fall inside a drop, 0 within 6 hours of a drop's start, and 2 within 6 hours of its end. Of all 52 alarms, 10 fall within 6 hours of a drop's start or end, against 1.0 expected by chance (0.018 of half-hours lie that close to an edge), and 4 of the 29 drops have an alarm within 6 hours of their start. The alarms track D8's within-day jumps more than chance and are mostly away from the drops, although the 10 near an edge are above chance. Within-day jumps occur in 2,642 of the 78,736 half-hours in the history. Of the 28 alarms, 26 fall between August 2023 and September 2024, while 18 of the 29 drops start in 2025 or later.
  • Prediction: the count (20 to 40 drops, nearly all after mid-2023) and the lack of a weekday or hour pattern held. The neighbour prediction (a step-up of half the depth at fewer than a quarter of the drops) narrowly missed, at 0.28, and the comparison with random times matters more. The alarm prediction (at least 20 of 28 within 6 hours) failed, at 2 of 28. The neighbour prediction said a step-up within 2 hours of the start, and the check uses 6-hour medians around the start, so the two are not the same test.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Same inputs as before: the 28 unexplained alarms, the 27 of 28 with a jump, and the 78 logged closures touching D8 reproduce the false-alarm analysis.
  • Forecast checks: no forecast is scored, so the checks on the median and mean forecast, the tail coverage, and the curtailment cost do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: one of the seven audit triggers in the ml-experiment skill fires, because the result contradicts the written prediction for the alarms (2 of 28 against at least 20). The page tests an explanation. 26 of the 28 alarms fall between August 2023 and September 2024, while 18 of the 29 drops start in 2025 or later (figure 7), and 27 of the 28 alarms have a jump (0.644 of all half-hours do). The other six triggers do not apply, because the page has no control, no nested arm, no planned contrast, and no earlier experiment on the same rows to compare an interval with.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The definition of a drop is ours. The count changes from 15 to 48 as the threshold moves from -2.5 to -1.0 MW. A drop's start and end can be off by up to 12 hours, because of the 24-hour smoothing.
  • The residual is the lab residual. The residual comes from the frozen convex regression model of experiment 130, as the false-alarm analysis stored it, with estimates of past weather from ERA5 and the real transfers left out of training. A drop that the regression model partly follows is under-counted.
  • The neighbour check is crude. The check compares 6-hour medians, so a transfer spread over a day would not show. The random-time comparison matches the time of day of the drop starts, which controls for the daily rise of the neighbours' demand. D5 has a median power of 2.96 MW, so D5 can absorb only part of a 5 MW drop.
  • A logged closure within 24 hours does not show that the closure caused a drop. NGED's log holds 78 closures touching D8 in 4.5 years, and the random-window rate of 0.449 shows that a closure within 24 hours is common.
  • The random-time comparisons are limited. The window and time-of-day matching use July 2023 onwards only, with 29 drops, so an interval contains several rates. The calendar tests have little power at 29 drops, and the month test uses expected counts below 5.
  • Not done: National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) has not confirmed any drop, and no cause was tested beyond the neighbours, the closures, and the calendar.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: Ask NGED which load D8 moves and which customers it serves. Start with the six drops that have no logged closure. The answer from NGED decides whether a drop should be left out of the regression model's training data, or shown to NGED's operators as an event.

docs.title: Experiment 160: a smooth spread table removes the band-width staircase
docs.text:
The 90% prediction interval of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, and reading its stored spread table by interpolation removes the equal days at a cost of 0.002 points of quantile score. Lead day 0 is up to 24 hours ahead, so day 2 is 48 to 72 hours ahead. The interval runs from the 5% quantile (q05) to the 95% quantile (q95). The forecast is arm D of experiment 155 with the spread table of its arm A. Arm D is the stage 1 demand forecast of experiment 136 plus two corrections: a night offset in winter, and recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour of the day.

The spread table holds the quantile offsets from the mean forecast, for each hour band, calendar quarter, and one of four lead bands (up to 24, 48, 144, and 168 hours). Each row reads the offsets of its own lead band, so within one hour band and quarter every row between 48 and 144 hours has the same width. Experiment 136 found the resulting steps.

We changed only how the stored table is read along the lead, never the mean forecast, and scored the result at five Primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in percentage points of effective capacity (lower is better). The reference scores 2.7507. Arm I (interpolated) scores 2.7529 (+0.0022 against the reference, worse; 95% interval from resampling calendar months -0.0011 to +0.0061). Arm IM (interpolated and non-decreasing) scores 2.7523 (+0.0017, -0.0026 to +0.0062). Arm M (non-decreasing only) scores 2.7498 (-0.0009, -0.0029 to +0.0012) and leaves the equal days. The replicate months give upper bounds of +0.0036 (I), +0.0025 (M), and +0.0070 (IM). The pre-registered rule asks for an upper bound under +0.01 and no equal days, so arms I and IM pass and arm M fails. Arm I wins, because arm IM is within 0.002 points of it and arm I comes first in the pre-registered order.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. Reference: experiment 155's d_spread_a as stored. I: offsets interpolated linearly in lead between the band centres (12, 36, 96, and 156 hours), flat outside. M: upper offsets replaced by their running maximum over the four lead bands and lower offsets by their running minimum. IM: I applied to M's table. The table is recovered from the stored tuning rows (each cell holds one value) and nothing is fitted on the scored year. No weather model is run: every input is experiment 155's stored forecast, which already respects the forecast-time availability of its own weather.
  • Rows. fold_a_daily_gap_v1: one row is one substation, forecast time, and valid time. The scored year is the 292 daily runs from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29 (D9 is scored beside the five decision substations and enters no contrast). Scored year (561,172 rows at the 6 substations, 464,228 at the 5 decision substations in the common set with BG2, climatology, and the manual heuristic), outside the hand-filtered switching events. The replicate months (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06) give the second period. Schedule: experiment 155's monthly refits, so no contrast here depends on retraining cadence; the fix acts after the forecast.
  • Staircase measured on the reference. The year-median q05 to q95 width is identical on lead days 2, 3, 4, and 5 at every decision substation (three equal pairs of adjacent days at each), for example 25.0 points at D5 and 14.1 at D16, with steps at 24, 48, and 144 hours. Arm I leaves no equal pair at any substation, arm IM leaves one at D11, and arm M leaves three at every substation. The replicate months give the same counts for arms I and M, and arm IM leaves one pair at each of D11, D14, and D16. The largest one-day step, as a share of the substation's median width, falls from 0.105 (median over substations) to 0.056 (I) and 0.063 (IM), and rises to 0.142 for M.
  • Coverage by lead day (reference, mean over substations). The share of actuals inside the 90% band is 0.88 over all leads (0.80 to 0.95 across substations and lead days), against 0.90 nominal. The q95 covers 0.948 of rows, and the q05 is crossed by 0.065 (nominal 0.05). The pooled q05 and q95 figures of I, M, and IM stay within 0.01 of the reference; per substation and lead day the inside-band share differs by up to 0.017 (M) and 0.031 (IM).
  • Quantile score, all leads (points; lower is better). Reference 2.7507, I 2.7529, M 2.7498, IM 2.7523, BG2 2.7804, manual heuristic 3.4968, climatology 3.8038. At 12 to 36 hours: reference 2.4028, I 2.4047, M 2.3982, IM 2.4027, BG2 2.5178.
  • Score by lead band, I minus reference. Under 24 hours +0.0024 (+0.0008 to +0.0043, worse), 24 to 72 hours -0.0071 (-0.0123 to -0.0021, better), 72 to 168 hours +0.0069 (+0.0008 to +0.0141, worse). Interpolation narrows the early part of each stepped band and widens the late part, so it helps at 24 to 72 hours and hurts at the shortest and longest leads.
  • Substations. I minus reference by substation: D10 +0.0088, D5 +0.0037, D16 +0.0008, D11 -0.0001, D14 -0.0018. D10 is the only substation that loses by more than 0.004 (IM +0.0113 there, above the 0.01 limit, which the pre-registered rule applies to the pooled score only). Without D10, C1 is about +0.0007. Months: C1 is negative in 5 of 12, C2 in 7 of 12, and C3 in 6 of 12.
  • Tail calibration, scored year, all rows. Coverage is the share of actuals at or below the quantile; loss is the pinball loss in points (lower is better).
Arm q01 cover q01 loss q05 cover q05 loss q95 cover q95 loss q99 cover q99 loss Reference 0.022 0.214 0.065 0.711 0.948 0.748 0.982 0.231 I 0.022 0.216 0.065 0.713 0.947 0.746 0.981 0.232 M 0.020 0.212 0.061 0.711 0.949 0.748 0.984 0.227 IM 0.020 0.213 0.061 0.713 0.949 0.747 0.983 0.228 BG2 0.010 0.220 0.040 0.643 0.944 0.778 0.982 0.268

Contrasts on the q99 loss: I +0.0014 (0.0000 to +0.0029), M -0.0039 (-0.0080 to -0.0007), IM at -0.0030 (-0.0075 to +0.0007); on the q01 loss: M -0.0025 (-0.0045 to -0.0006).

  • Cold nights (winter nights, day mean temperature below 2 °C; 5,395 rows). The q95 coverage is 0.848 for the reference, 0.846 for I (-0.002, -0.005 to +0.001), and 0.852 for M and IM (+0.004, +0.001 to +0.011). The q99 coverage is 0.940 (reference), 0.933 (I), 0.954 (M), and 0.953 (IM). The score on those rows moves by +0.021 for I (+0.002 to +0.053, worse), -0.028 for M (-0.068 to -0.001), and -0.015 for IM (-0.045 to -0.001). On all winter nights M is worse by +0.0035 (+0.0006 to +0.0074) and IM by +0.0079 (+0.0010 to +0.0166). BG2 covers 0.756 at the q95.
  • Width smoothness. The mean absolute change in median width between adjacent lead days is within 0.15 points of the reference at every substation for I, and larger for IM at D14 and D16 (0.59 and 0.50 against 0.21 and 0.39) because the monotone table widens those substations' late days. Arm I has one falling step, at D14 (the reference has none).
  • Curtailment-cost proxy. The node-only rule of studies.node_curtailment run on each substation's own demand, with the limit set at 0.9 times its maximum before the scored year, at GBP 2,000 per MWh over leads 12 to 36 hours. Avoidable cost against the perfect forecast, in GBP per MW of capacity per day over the 292 daily runs (42.7 MW in total): reference 106.3, I 105.9, M 106.5, IM 106.2, BG2 150.8, manual heuristic 267.1. The reference saves 160.8 GBP per MW per day against the stored manual-heuristic forecast. The intervals are wide (the reference's avoidable cost is 0.11 to 3.3 million GBP in total for the 5 substations) and the variants differ from the reference by under 0.5 GBP per MW per day at the limit of 0.9, so the proxy cannot rank them. With the limit at 0.5 of the maximum the order of the four variants reverses (M lowest, I highest) and M differs from the reference by about 19 GBP per MW per day, so the order is not stable. A Primary substation has no published export limit here, and a demand series is treated as the flow that can breach, so the figures show the arithmetic and are not a curtailment forecast.
  • Caveats. The staircase test uses lead-day medians pooled over a year and over the hour bands, so a staircase that survives inside one hour band by quarter cell would not show. The score and coverage hold over 5 substations and 12 months, so the intervals are wide; the contrast against the reference is better resolved than any absolute figure. The spread table is the stored one of arm A, whose lead bands are coarse, and a table fitted on finer lead bands would be a refit and is not tested here. Arm C (recipe R alone) was experiment 155's pre-registered winner; the fix acts on the spread, so the result is expected, but not shown, to carry over to arm C.
  • What follows from this result. A smooth reading of the table is a free change (no fitted term and no stored state); a smoother spread does not move the cold-night upper tail (q95 coverage 0.85 in every variant), so the mean forecast on those nights is one place a later experiment could look. A refit of the spread on 12-hour lead bands and a test of M's table on tail scores are the two follow-ups.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site, at 12 to 36 hours. Exactly 0.000 for every arm at every substation (the spread table has median zero and the variants share the reference's mean).
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast is identical across arms (contrast 0.0000 for C1, C2, and C3), because the mean is unchanged. No contrast of the quantile score and of the mean error can point in different directions.
  • Reproduction control. The reference rescored from experiment 155's stored forecasts scores 2.7507, the same as experiment 155's d_spread_a. The plan's rule capped the verdict at inconclusive if the reference differed from the "printed arm D score" by more than 0.001. That wording was wrong, because arm D with its own refitted spread scores 2.756 and the reference is d_spread_a. The control applied is against d_spread_a, and it was met. The run script prints the reproduction gap of the recovered table (under 2e-5 points). In the plan, "days 3 to 6" counts from one and names the same days as "lead days 2 to 5" here.
  • Audit triggers. None fired. The score changes (within ±0.005) and the equal-pair counts (at most 1 for I and IM) matched the predictions. The prediction that the cold-night q95 coverage stays near 83% missed in level: it was 0.846 to 0.852 (the 83% came from experiment 155's arms on a slightly different definition of cold nights). D10 loses 0.009 under I. The unweighted mean of the other four substations' differences is +0.0007, so C1's sign is unchanged without D10 (not recomputed from rows), and the verdict does not depend on it. No audit ran.

docs.title: Experiment 161: a bulk supply point is forecast no better from its children than on its own
docs.text:
Take-home: building a bulk supply point (BSP) forecast from its children's forecasts did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series, at either BSP. In the scored year, the bottom-up arm scored 4.387 points at D13 against 4.361 for top-down (C1, bottom-up minus top-down: +0.026, 97.5% interval -0.033 to +0.102), and 7.706 at D17 against 7.672 (+0.035, -0.012 to +0.094). The bottom-up arm is 0.6% and 0.5% worse, within the noise.

The likely reason is the share of the BSP that the sum can reach. Only three children per BSP report real power and have a long history, so they cover 42% (D13) and 56% (D17) of the BSP's effective capacity, and most of the BSP's forecast error is in the load they do not cover (figure 3). With the children's readings known exactly (the oracle), the score improves by only 12% and 7%. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high (see Checks), though the verdict does not depend on it.

This experiment compares two ways of forecasting a BSP, which sits above several Primary substations in the electricity network. The top-down arm gives the BSP's own half-hourly reading to the best-guess generalised additive model chain (GAM-K; experiment 155's arm D). The bottom-up arm forecasts each covered child Primary with the same chain, weights the forecasts by learned weights, and adds the chain's forecast of the remainder, the BSP's reading minus the weighted children's readings. Quantile scores are in points: percentages of the BSP's effective capacity, lower is better. Scored rows are the 291 daily runs of 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside switching events.

Scope. Two BSPs have child Primaries with usable data: D13 (seven children) and D17 (nine children). Only the children that report real power and have a long history enter the sum (D9, D10, and D11 under D13; D5, D14, and D16 under D17). The other children report apparent power (4 of 7 and 4 of 9), or have under 5 months of readings (D15 and D18), so they stay in the remainder. The test is therefore a partial bottom-up. NGED's hierarchy for the other BSPs is not yet known, so no other BSP is in scope.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Bottom-up scored the same as top-down, within the noise. Figure 1 shows the four bottom-up variants and the oracle against zero. The fixed-sum variant (every weight 1) scored the same as the learned weights (C3, learned minus fixed-sum: -0.003 at D13, +0.003 at D17, both intervals including zero). Giving the bottom-up arm the top-down arm's spread table moved the score by -0.016 at D13 and +0.002 at D17 (C5, bottom-up with the top-down table minus top-down), so the two means tie. The positive sign of C1 comes from the spread table: bottom-up refits its table on the corrected errors, which narrows its band and under-covers the tails, while top-down keeps the table fitted before the corrections.

No lead band favoured bottom-up with confidence. The prediction said the gain would be largest below 24 hours (C4, C1 by lead band). At D13 the difference is -0.031 (-0.065 to +0.007) below 24 hours, +0.006 between 24 and 72 hours, and +0.050 (-0.015 to +0.140) beyond 72 hours. This is the pattern the prediction named, but every interval includes zero. At D17 the difference is +0.040, +0.010, and +0.046, with the wrong sign in every band.

Most of the BSP's error is in the remainder. At D13 the remainder's error has a standard deviation of 9.4 points and the weighted children's summed error 2.3 points; at D17 the figures are 16.6 and 3.5. The bottom-up error (10.9 at D13 and 18.2 at D17) is about the same as the top-down error, because the remainder dominates it. The two parts' errors also correlate positively (0.56 and 0.39), so correcting the children cannot remove the remainder's error. Even the oracle, which removes the children's error, only gets from 4.361 to 3.838 points at D13 and from 7.672 to 7.108 at D17 (C7, oracle minus top-down).

Arm (scored year) D13 score D17 score Top-down 4.361 7.672 Bottom-up, learned weights 4.387 7.706 Bottom-up, weights fixed at 1 4.389 7.703 Bottom-up, unbounded weights 4.388 7.728 Bottom-up, learned weights, top-down spread table 4.345 7.674 Oracle (observed children) 3.838 7.108 Manual heuristic 5.466 8.424 Climatology 5.905 8.953

Rows are the shared rows: 96,324 at D13 and 82,137 at D17. Top-down on all of its own rows scores 4.355 at D13 (97,046 rows). The replicate months (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06) agree: C1 is -0.014 (-0.067 to +0.031) at D13 and +0.036 (-0.010 to +0.084) at D17.

The weights cannot be estimated reliably. The bounded fit (0.8 to 1.2) puts all six weights on the upper bound, 1.2. The unbounded fit gives D13 weights of 3.3, 4.3, and 1.4 (D9, D10, D11) and D17 weights of 5.0, 0.2, and 1.1 (D5, D14, D16). Both fits use the winter window 2023-10 to 2024-03. The children probably stand in for their unmetered siblings, so the weight on a child is not that child's transformer ratio. The weighted sum of the children does not reproduce the BSP's reading: the in-sample residual has a standard deviation of 6.3 MW (47% of the BSP's variance) at D13 and 8.8 MW (70%) at D17.

docs.title: Tail calibration (scored year)
docs.text:
BSP, arm Coverage at 0.01 0.05 0.95 0.99 D13 top-down 0.018 0.067 0.921 0.969 D13 bottom-up 0.025 0.080 0.915 0.961 D17 top-down 0.020 0.077 0.906 0.964 D17 bottom-up 0.022 0.086 0.906 0.963

Both arms are too narrow in the tails, and bottom-up is slightly more so. The nominal values are 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99. Bottom-up's pinball loss at the four tail quantiles is higher than top-down's at both BSPs (C6: +0.012 to +0.042 at D13, +0.012 to +0.040 at D17), with every interval including zero except the 0.05 quantile in the replicate months at D17. The top-down spread table brings bottom-up's coverage back to top-down's (D13 0.017, 0.066, 0.921, 0.969).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per BSP: 0.000 for every arm at both BSPs, because the residual table is centred, so this check exposes nothing here.
  • Mean forecast's error beside each contrast (mean absolute error): C1 -0.030 at D13 and +0.002 at D17; C2 -0.026 and -0.003; C5 -0.030 and +0.002; C7 -0.975 and -1.037. At D13 the mean of the bottom-up forecast is slightly better than top-down's while its quantile score is slightly worse, so the spread table, not the mean, costs the score there (C5 confirms).
  • Controls. Reproduction: the copied chain rescored at D10 reproduces experiment 136's and experiment 155's stored scores exactly (passed). Leakage: the weight window ends on 2024-03-31, before the first run, and the chain's assert_no_lookahead holds (passed). Weather frames built for the BSP cells match the stored frame of 2025-07-02 bit for bit (passed). The decomposition BSP = remainder + weighted children holds exactly in the observed readings (passed).
  • Oracle control: failed. The oracle gained 0.523 points at D13 and 0.563 at D17, against thresholds of 0.918 and 2.140 (half of the covered capacity share times the top-down score). The threshold assumed the oracle's error would fall in proportion to the covered load. In fact the oracle's error equals the remainder's error, so the gain depends on how large the remainder's error is. The independent audit found the two equal to within 1e-5 on every scored row. The ratio of standard deviations in figure 3 predicts gains of 13.7% (D13) and 8.9% (D17) against the observed 12.0% and 7.3%. The failure therefore reflects the mis-specified threshold and not a plumbing fault. The cap on the verdict does not bind, because both C1 intervals include zero and the decision rule gives inconclusive anyway. In the replicate months the D17 oracle gain is -0.361 (-0.652 to +0.070), which includes zero.
  • Audit triggers fired (defined in the ml-experiment skill). Trigger 1 (the oracle control failed). Trigger 2 (the prediction missed: C1 predicted -2% to -8% and found +0.6% and +0.5%; the oracle predicted -15% to -40% and found -12% and -7%; the error decomposition above explains the miss). Trigger 3 (C1 and C2 point in different directions on the mean absolute error and the quantile score at D13; C5 explains it as spread). Triggers 4 to 7 did not fire: no site-level ablation applies to two BSPs, no nested arm beat its container, no sister experiment on BSPs exists to compare interval widths with, and no later experiment depends on the headline.

docs.title: Audit and triage
docs.text: An independent Opus audit re-derived C1 and C7 from the stored predictions, matched both to four decimals, and found six issues, all accepted and reflected in the text above: the spread table carries C1's sign, the oracle threshold was wrong before the run, one sentence named the wrong arm, the scored year holds 291 runs, the weight bounds were set after the first unbounded fit and before any score was read, and the replicate-month D17 oracle gain includes zero.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Two BSPs, three covered children each. The sum reaches 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, so the result says little about a BSP whose children are all metered in real power.
  • The weights come from one winter (2023-10 to 2024-03), and the unbounded weights are not stable. A fit on all year or a hierarchical estimate may behave differently.
  • The covered children and the BSP get different solar-capacity inputs. The covered children use a photovoltaic (PV) capacity fixed from a dated record, while the BSP and its remainder fit their PV capacity. The variant that fits the children's capacity (C8) was not run, because with no bottom-up gain there was nothing to split.
  • The weight-refit variant (C9) was replaced by the unbounded-weights variant, which tests whether bounding the weights matters. Whether refitting the weights on later data helps is untested.
  • The curtailment metric was not scored, because this experiment did not build the generator inputs it needs for these BSPs.
  • Weather is past-weather ensemble means calibrated as in experiment 136, which every arm uses, so the comparison is fair and the absolute scores are not production scores.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Forecast the apparent-power children's demand (night-time rows only, where the sign of the flow is not hidden by solar output, as experiment 124 does) and put them into the sum, so the covered share rises from about half toward all of the BSP.
  • Estimate the weights jointly with the remainder on a full year, with a ridge penalty or the 1.2 bound, so the weights stop standing in for unmetered siblings.
  • Wait for NGED's hierarchy for the other BSPs before adding BSPs beyond D13 and D17.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
Departures from this plan. The scored year holds 291 runs, not 292. The weights are bounded (0.8 to 1.2), because the first unbounded fit was unstable; the bounds were set before any score was read. The unbounded fit is the free variant, which replaces BU-w2 (C9). BU-fc (C8) was not run. The oracle threshold was too high and the prediction missed, as the Checks list says.

Question. Experiment 36 summed the Primaries' forecasts and fed the sum to a BSP's XGBoost model, and the sum added nothing. Experiment 124 showed that a BSP reading does not close exactly over the Primaries beneath it. The maintainer's hierarchy aims treat the topology as a soft hint and not a hard sum. This experiment asks the question again with the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) on both sides: is the BSP forecast better when it is built from its children's forecasts plus a learned remainder than when the BSP is forecast as a stand-alone series?

Scope: two BSPs (seven and nine children), and the children that report real power. NGED's hierarchy file places 16 Primaries under two BSPs, D13 (seven children) and D17 (nine children). Four of D13's children (D2, D4, D19, D21) and four of D17's (D3, D8, D12, D22) report apparent power in megavolt-amperes, which hides the sign of the flow in daylight (see the data-processing page, "Use a Primary metered in MVA for demand only on dark rows"). No observed net-power remainder can be formed from such a child, and arm D has no forecast for it. The MVA children stay inside the remainder. The covered children are the Primaries that report real power and have a long history and an arm D forecast: D9, D10, and D11 under D13 (23.3 of 55.3 MW of effective capacity), and D5, D14, and D16 under D17 (26.5 of 47.6 MW). D15 and D18 under D17 (the two transformers of one Primary substation) report real power but have under 5 months of readings before the scored year, so they stay in D17's remainder too. The scope is therefore a partial bottom-up, and the write-up says so in its first paragraph. A bottom-up arm that also forecasts the MVA children (demand terms only, on dark rows, as experiment 124's joint fit does) is the obvious follow-up and is not tested here.

Arms. All arms use arm D's recipe: the ensemble-mean weather, T-all, the shared filter noise (POOL), monthly refits, the winter night offset, recipe R, and arm A's spread table.

Arm Forecast of the BSP TD (top-down) Arm D's chain on the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series BU (bottom-up) The sum over covered children of weight times the child's arm D mean, plus arm D's mean for the remainder series; quantiles from a spread table fitted on the sum's own tuning-month residuals BU1 (fixed-sum) The same, with every weight 1 (reference) BU-oracle (diagnostic) The same as BU, with the children's observed readings in place of their forecasts; no verdict

The remainder series. For each BSP the remainder is r(t) = BSP(t) - sum_i w_i * y_i(t), where y_i is the covered child's observed reading in MW. The chain forecasts r as it forecasts any series, with the BSP's location for the weather and calibration, a PV capacity fitted and not pinned (no capacity vintage exists for a BSP, and the remainder holds the unmetered and the MVA children's embedded solar), the same filter, and arm D's two corrections applied to the remainder's own errors. The BU forecast of the BSP is sum_i w_i * mean_i + mean_r, because the decomposition is exact in the observed readings. BU1 runs its own remainder chain on BSP - sum_i y_i.

A confound the design names. The covered children's arm D forecasts use the pinned PV capacity of experiment 139. No capacity vintage exists for a BSP, so TD and the remainder fit the PV capacity. Part of any BU gain may therefore come from the children's pinned capacity and not from the bottom-up structure. A pinned capacity is information that bottom-up legitimately has and top-down lacks, so C1 stays the headline. Variant BU-fc replaces the children's forecasts with arm D chains that fit the capacity (C8, BU-fc minus BU), which splits the gain into the two parts. Arm D also corrects the children and the remainder separately, so a shared error is corrected twice in BU; this is part of the design.

Feasibility steps. (1) Build a feature cache that adds D13 and D17 to experiment 103's 16 Primaries, from experiment 103's panel.parquet, with experiment 103's rows rule (present and unflagged, outside the fixed lockdown window and the hand-filtered switching events), and add each remainder series as a further site that copies the BSP's weather and replaces the reading. (2) Build the ensemble weather arrays and the weather calibration for the two BSP locations; the remainders reuse them. (3) Copy experiment 136's T-all fit and prediction with a fitted-capacity option, because predict_tall asserts a pinned capacity. This is code inside this folder only. (4) Experiment 155's stored forecasts hold the runs that experiment 155 scored, which are not the every-fifth-day stride runs; the TD and remainder chains are built on the same runs so that recipe R sees the same error stream, and every score uses the runs the arms share.

The weights. Non-negative least squares of the BSP's reading on the covered children's readings, with no intercept, on the half-hours in 2023-10-01 to 2024-03-31 where the BSP and the children are present, unflagged, and outside the hand-filtered switching events. The window ends on the day before the first run (2024-04-01) and starts at the first usable day of the youngest child (D9, 2023-10-01 at D13). The weights are fixed for the whole experiment, so no weight uses a reading after any cut. The weights are 15 to 27 months old in the scored year, and the remainder series before 2024-04 is in-sample for the weights; no scored row is affected. Variant BU-w2 refits the weights on data to 2025-06-30 and is scored on the scored year only. The window is winter only at D13, so the weights say little about summer; the write-up shows the fitted weights beside experiment 124's multipliers.

Spread. Each arm's quantiles are its mean plus a residual table (hour band by calendar quarter by lead band) fitted on that arm's own tuning-month forecasts (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), every factor 1, as experiments 136 and 155 do. TD uses arm D's own rule (arm A's table). BU uses a table fitted on the sum's residuals. A variant gives BU TD's table (BU-spreadTD), which isolates the mean.

Rows and periods. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, 09:00 UTC power_fcst_init_time, the 292 runs of the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads 0.5 to 168 hours. A row is scored when the BSP and its three covered children have a reading and sit outside the hand-filtered switching events, so every arm is scored on the same rows. Tuning months and replicate months are experiment 136's. Series are D-labels. No generator series enters.

Weather and what exists at forecast time. The weather is the calibrated ensemble mean of experiment 136 for the BSP's grid cell, and the filter's analysis proxy is built from earlier runs. The children's arm D forecasts are the stored forecasts of experiment 155, made at the same origin. Every input exists at forecast time.

Scoring. Beside the headline: lead bands, the tail table (coverage and pinball loss at 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99), the mean absolute error of the mean forecast beside every quantile-score contrast, absolute scores for climatology and the manual heuristic, and the node curtailment metric of studies.node_curtailment at the scaled limit (f = 0.9, with 0.75 and 0.5), if the BSP's generators-beneath inputs it needs exist for these two BSPs. Where it cannot be scored, the write-up says so.

Planned contrasts. C1 BU minus TD (headline, at D13 and at D17), with TD also reported on all of its own rows beside the shared rows. C2 BU1 minus TD. C3 BU minus BU1 (do learned weights help). C4 C1 by lead band. C5 BU-spreadTD minus TD (the mean alone). C6 BU minus TD at the tail quantiles. C7 BU-oracle minus TD (diagnostic). C8 BU-fc minus BU. C9 BU-w2 minus BU. Each is read through studies.bootstrap.

Controls, run before any contrast is read.

  • Reproduction. Arm D rescored from experiment 155's stored forecasts at the covered children on the common rows matches experiment 155's stored per-site scores within 0.001. - Oracle (positive control). BU-oracle scores below TD at both BSPs by at least half the share of effective capacity that the covered children make up (42% at D13, 56% at D17) times TD's score. The decomposition is exact in observed readings, so a smaller gain means a plumbing fault in the remainder, the weights, or the join. Experiment 36's oracle gained 3.4 to 5.6 points. - Leakage. The weight window ends before the first run, and an assertion checks that no remainder fit trains on a reading after its cut (the chain's assert_no_lookahead). - Closure check. Print the in-sample residual of the weight fit in MW and its share of the BSP's variance, to compare with experiment 124's audit (1.2 to 1.8 MW at the BSP that closes, 11 points at the other).

Five triggers (size). Stored: private files only. Serving path: not touched. Degradation rule: not touched. More than one design defensible: yes, three, each pre-registered above. Callers not nameable without searching: no, the scripts copy experiments 111, 136, and 155.

Audit triggers to watch. Trigger 1 (a control fails: the oracle), trigger 2 (the result contradicts experiment 36's null, or this plan's prediction), and trigger 6 (an interval more than twice as wide as experiment 155's per-site intervals) are the likely ones. The write-up lists which fired and tells the manager if any did.

Resources. CPU only, at most 6 cores with one thread per worker, each job under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue. No GPU. New work: the ensemble frames for the two BSP locations for the 456 early runs (the scored year's frames already hold both), the weather calibration, and six chains (TD, the BU remainder, and the fixed-sum remainder at each BSP).

Outputs. Predictions for every arm in the dp_preds layout under data/ml-experiments/00161-dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up/work/dp_preds/.

Advice followed and departures. From experiment 36: do not expect the children's median forecasts to help an XGBoost BSP model, and do not read the oracle's gain as headroom; this experiment uses a different model and reports the oracle only as a control. From experiment 124: the BSP reading is not an exact sum, so the weights and the remainder are estimated. From experiment 155: use arm D (the instruction for this experiment), apply recipe R at every lead, and read the tails.

docs.title: Do load transfers follow the donor's demand and solar shapes, and does a constant-MW injection flatter the LSC detectors?
docs.text:
Take-home message. A load transfer is an operator moving demand from one substation to a neighbour by switching. If a transfer removed a daytime load that follows the donor substation's solar output, or removed solar output itself, the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) would find about half of the transfers instead of 91%, and the live end rule would cover 22% of the true interval instead of 62%. The pair alarm of experiment 156 loses much less once a step may start at first light. The 25 logged real transfers cannot say whether they move solar output: a daily shape fits them no better than it fits quiet stretches. If real transfers do move solar output, earlier RO-NC recall and end-rule coverage results are optimistic by about 0.40 to 0.46. A realistic mix of houses and small solar sites is nearer the share-of-net-power injection of earlier experiments, which both detectors find as easily as a constant transfer.

We asked whether the power a transfer moves follows the donor's demand and solar shapes, and whether injecting a constant number of megawatts flatters the detectors. The idea comes from the roadmap's magnitude-only mixture model: a switch moves houses, factories, and solar sites, not a constant. Part 1 split the convex model of experiment 130 (a generalised additive model, GAM) into its demand term and its solar term, and fitted each logged transfer's effect on the donor's residual as a constant, as a daily shape, and as both, scoring on held-out days. Part 2 re-injected the 1,160 transfers of experiment 141 with five rules of the same mean megawatts at the donor (constant, demand-shaped, two solar shapes, half demand and half daytime load), beside the original share-of-net-power rule, and re-ran the detectors, the end rule, and the mask forecast of experiment 156. Experiment 60 had already found that a detector weighted by the donor's profile finds the same share of moved power on five shapes; the solar-only shapes are new here.

The verdict is partly supported, but the pre-registered rule did not cover this outcome. The rule defined partly supported only when P1 (the held-out fit of a daily shape) held and fewer than two part-2 contrasts did. Here P1 did not hold, while RO-NC recall and end-rule coverage fell with intervals excluding zero. The verdict was set after the results.

  • Arms. Six injections with the same mean megawatts at the donor (0.865 to 0.872 MW across arms): constant (CONST, the reference), share of net power (SHARE, exactly the injection of experiments 141 and 156), demand-shaped (DEMAND), a daytime load that leaves the donor (SOLAR, proportional to the donor's solar output, subtracted from the donor), half demand and half daytime load (MIX), and solar output that leaves the donor, so the donor's net power rises at midday (PVOUT). Shaped arms divide the donor's term by its mean over the transfer. Detectors, thresholds, and scoring code are those of experiment 156 (4-hour pair-alarm window, k = 3.75); SHARE reproduces experiment 156's event table exactly and its mask scores to three decimals. Convex-model terms come from monthly refits, and solar plus demand equals experiment 130's stored forecast to 5e-15 MW on six series. Series 12 has no terms; series 13 has terms from 2025-07 to 2026-06 only. 37 DEMAND events and 57 SOLAR, MIX, and PVOUT events have a donor without terms, or no daylight, and use the donor's net-power shape instead.
  • Weather. ERA5 at lag times, as in experiments 130 and 156, so every number is a lab ceiling: ERA5 arrives about 5 days late and is not available at forecast time. - A daily shape fits the logged transfers no better than it fits quiet stretches of the same length. Part 1, logged transfers over 1 day (35; 25 have a fitted series; 37 series fits; 13 logged donors). P1, constant plus shape against constant on held-out days: median +0.067 (95% -0.033 to +0.126; 99.4% -0.110 to +0.160), not supported. Shape alone +0.069 (99.4% -0.111 to +0.138). The placebo median is +0.004 over all stretches; a placebo matched to the transfers' lengths has a median of +0.052, and 39% of such placebos reach +0.067. The demand share is beyond the placebo's 2.5th percentile at 5 of 13 logged donors (0.38; exact 95% 0.14 to 0.68), the solar share beyond the 97.5th percentile at 0 of 13; neither is above one half (P2). Median fitted shares: 0.130 demand and 0.140 solar. The 181 intervals RO-NC detected over a day (experiment 147): median +0.005; these intervals are chosen because a step was found, so they are not evidence about transfers. - Receivers (12 receiver fits).** The donor's terms fit the receiver's opposite step better than the receiver's own terms in 8 of 12 (held-out reduction +0.091 against -0.004). The direction matches what a transfer predicts, but rests on 12 fits.
  • P3, injected known answers (182 per scenario, the same stretches in each). The injected shares are recovered without bias (demand 0.158 for 0.15, solar 0.349 for 0.35), as the fit contains the injected shape, so the identification rates below are best cases. With the placebo-calibrated rule, the demand share is identified in 0.10 of transfers of 1 to 3 days, 0.75 of 3 to 7 days, and 0.96 of over 7 days. The solar share is identified in 0.07, 0.08, and 0.29. The under-1-day band reads 0.52 for demand from 33 short stretches and is not trustworthy.
  • Solar-shaped injections cut RO-NC recall and live end-rule coverage by about 0.40, and the pair alarm's recall by 0.44 as drawn. P4 to P7, even-month transfers (611), minus constant, 99.4% interval, onset as drawn. Pair-alarm recall: SOLAR -0.437 (-0.633 to -0.300), PVOUT -0.463 (-0.663 to -0.368), MIX -0.279 (-0.417 to -0.180), DEMAND -0.019 (-0.089 to +0.017), SHARE -0.037 (-0.085 to -0.011). RO-NC recall: SOLAR -0.398 (-0.601 to -0.269), PVOUT -0.405 (-0.629 to -0.231), MIX -0.042 (-0.107 to -0.011), DEMAND -0.004, SHARE -0.006. Absolute recall (pair alarm, RO-NC): CONST 0.786 and 0.907; SOLAR 0.349 and 0.509; PVOUT 0.324 and 0.503. P6, the lag from step to alarm, is 6 hours for every arm, because the window fixes it. P7, share of the true interval the live end rule covers (missed transfers count 0): CONST 0.620, SOLAR 0.217, PVOUT 0.201, MIX 0.496; SOLAR minus CONST -0.403 (-0.552 to -0.280).
  • Scored from first light, the pair alarm's loss falls to about 0.07, but RO-NC and the end rule lose as much as before (post hoc). A solar-shaped step cannot start before sunrise, so a drawn onset at night is not a fair target for an alarm. Scoring each alarm from the donor's first light changes the pair alarm to SOLAR -0.072 (-0.130 to -0.013) and PVOUT -0.100 (-0.166 to -0.020), but RO-NC stays at SOLAR -0.406 and PVOUT -0.460. The end rule, scored on the covered share of the interval, loses about 0.40 under either scoring. Most of the pair alarm's loss in the as-drawn score is therefore a scoring effect, and the RO-NC and end-rule losses are real.
  • P8 and P9, mask forecast on all 277,056 rows after an onset (SOLAR 274,294 paired rows), minus constant. MASK-UNION: SOLAR +0.149 points of capacity (99.4% -0.085 to +0.490), PVOUT +0.464 (-0.008 to +0.923), DEMAND +0.066 (-0.028 to +0.158), MIX -0.008 (-0.080 to +0.118), SHARE +0.196 (-0.115 to +0.322); none is supported at the corrected level. Scores of no correction, weather model only, mask from RO-NC, mask from either alarm, true series: CONST 3.576, 3.025, 3.160, 3.023, 2.416; SHARE 3.549, 3.025, 3.338, 3.219, 2.416; DEMAND 3.473, 3.025, 3.187, 3.089, 2.416; MIX 3.487, 3.025, 3.281, 3.015, 2.416; SOLAR 3.805, 3.019, 3.505, 3.169, 2.407; PVOUT 4.218, 3.019, 3.791, 3.484, 2.407.
  • The mask forecast loses little on solar-shaped transfers although recall falls, because the mask still helps on rows the recall metric counts as missed. The audit found an improvement over no correction of 0.72 points on those rows of the SOLAR arm, because the mask covers a window that includes part of the transfer. The recall metric therefore understates what the mask achieves on solar-shaped transfers.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast by site, points of capacity: D10 -0.076, D11 -0.044, D14 +0.084, D16 +0.040, D5 -0.347, D9 -0.091, the same for every arm.
  • Mean-forecast contrast has the quantile score's sign everywhere: SOLAR minus CONST +0.210 (99.4% -0.102 to +0.661) in the error of the mean forecast and +0.149 in the quantile score. - Checks that flagged a problem. A control failed: the 95% bootstrap intervals of the fitted shares flag 16% (demand) and 14% (solar) of placebos, so part 1 uses a placebo-calibrated rule. A headline interval is more than twice as wide as the same contrast's in experiment 156 (P8 for SOLAR is 0.58 points wide, experiment 156's C4 was 0.22). A Sonnet code review found the bootstrap intervals too narrow, P2 chosen by the fit, a biased energy-share measure, contaminated placebos, and P7 dropping missed transfers; each was fixed before the numbers above. An Opus audit then found a wrong sign on the solar arm (fixed by relabelling it a daytime load and adding PVOUT), onset scoring, inherited weights, and the by-construction recovery in P3. The findings and their triage are in the audit report, kept in the private data store.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• P1 and P2 rest on few transfers. Part 1 uses 25 logged transfers, 13 of them with a logged donor, and placebos of 33 to 73 stretches per length band. A shape effect of the size the controls inject (15% of demand) would be found in about three quarters of transfers longer than 3 days; the real transfers show less, but few are that long.
  • Real transfers may move solar output in a way the donor's fitted solar term does not describe, for example because the donor's solar capacity changed during a transfer.
  • The solar arms are extreme cases. The realistic mix of houses and small solar sites is nearer the SHARE arm (RO-NC -0.006, pair alarm -0.037) than the SOLAR or PVOUT arms, which move no demand.
  • Missing terms. Series 12 has no terms, which cuts the real transfers from 35 to 25, and the donor's net-power shape stands in for 37 to 57 injected events.
  • Mean-matching a solar shape raises its midday power to several times the mean, so the solar arms also differ from the others in peak size.
  • Lab conditions as in experiment 156: ERA5 residuals, balanced steps, hindsight end rule in the RO-NC intervals that the live end rule replaces only in P7. Recall weights are inherited from the constant arm's megawatts.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test whether real transfers move solar output. The cheapest test uses the 35 logged transfers with their metered receivers: fit the receiver's opposite step and the donor's step jointly, so that the two together identify the solar share from a sum constrained to be zero. A second test replays RO-NC and the end rule on the solar arms with a daylight-only step test, to see how much recall that recovers.

docs.title: Changes to the pre-registered plan
docs.text:
• Prior art (added after the plan). Experiment 60 had already compared constant and profile injections for a profile-weighted detector.
  • Interval method (after the code review). Bootstrap intervals over whole days flagged 14% to 16% of placebo stretches, so the P2 and P3 tests use the placebo-calibrated rule, and the bootstrap intervals are reported beside them. The pre-registered statement that the solar share "b is identified (95% interval excluding zero) only at transfers of 3 days or more" rested on the bootstrap intervals.
  • P2 donors are the logged donors, not the series with the largest fitted effect; P3's share of moved energy was dropped for a bias towards the demand term, and recovered shares are reported instead; P7 counts missed transfers as 0; controls and placebos avoid RO-NC's detected intervals and use the same stretches in each scenario.
  • P3 used 182 injections per scenario, not 200, and P2 and P3 take no Bonferroni level, so seven or eight contrasts share the 99.4% level, not nine.
  • After the audit: the SOLAR arm is a daytime load leaving the donor, and the PVOUT arm was added for solar output leaving the donor; first-light scoring, the daylight-only sensitivity, and the receiver check are post hoc.

docs.title: Real logged load transfers: the XGBoost-free stack with a load-shift mask against best guess 2
docs.text:
After a real load transfer ends, a forecast that sets the power readings of the transfer period missing, or that ignores recent power, has an error score about 40% lower than best guess 2 and about 54% lower than the same forecast with no mask. The scores are 6.32 for the pair-alarm mask, 10.09 for best guess 2 (an XGBoost forecast that uses recent power), and 13.69 for the unmasked forecast, in points of a substation's effective capacity (lower is better). The effect rests on 7 logged transfers at four of the six decision Primary substations in the scored year. Three transfer-substation pairs, from two long December-to-January transfers, carry 31.1 of the 39.3 points of gap, the intervals are wide, and the pair alarm found 5 of the 7 pairs whose gap exceeds 0.25 points. Over the year, the masked forecast and best guess 2 are indistinguishable on ordinary days. The next experiment needs more logged transfers, or a forecast that drops recent power whenever the pair alarm or the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) is active.

We asked how two forecasts cope with real transfers of load between substations that the network operator logged. The stack is a weather-driven generalised additive model (GAM) with a Kalman filter on its recent errors, and it sets the readings missing from the moment an alarm is known. The alarm is the pair alarm of experiment 156 (two metered substations step in opposite directions within hours), with the end rule of experiment 148. Best guess 2 (BG2) is the XGBoost forecast of experiment 87, which takes recent power as an input. The stack and BG2 were both scored on the same rows, in points of a substation's effective capacity (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles; smaller is better).

By the pre-registered rule the verdict is partly supported. The gap test (C3) passes: the share of the gap to the logged-interval mask (the oracle mask) that the pair-alarm mask closes is 100% on the pooled rows, above the 40% required. The no-harm test (C4) fails by 0.005 points: the pair-alarm mask minus the unmasked stack on ordinary rows is +0.033 points, and the upper end of its 95% interval, +0.105, is above the required +0.10. The pre-registered rule did not say whether the 40% applies to the point estimate or to the lower interval end. The lower end, 12%, is under 40%, so the pass rests on the point estimate. The comparison with BG2 carried no threshold.

  • Arms. STACK-K0 (the stack, no mask), STACK-NEW (mask from the pair alarm), STACK-UNION (mask from either the pair alarm or the refit-offset neighbour-count detector, RO-NC), STACK-RONC (mask from RO-NC alone), GAM-ONLY (no correction from recent power), ORACLE (the logged interval masked from its logged onset, its end known at once), BG2, experiment 155's arm C (the unmasked stack with recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the error of the last 14 days by half-hour of day, on the base of experiment 136), the manual heuristic, and climatology. The stack arms share the K0 spread of experiment 115 (the forecast's width, fitted once), so they differ in location only. Arm C is not masked, because the masked filter is the experiment 156 stack, which has no recipe R.
  • Rows. The scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30), six decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16, D9), rows with a reading that the stack and BG2 share: 572,541. The no-harm rows are 556,930 of them, outside the logged transfers and their 72 hours after and outside the hand-filtered switching events. The scored year holds 7 logged transfers that involve a decision Primary (13 transfer-substation pairs with rows after the logged end, counting the replicate months, the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06). Weather in the filter's residual is the analysis proxy, as in experiments 141 and 156; the member forecasts are the ensemble of experiment 111.
  • Row sets, fixed before any score. By target time, with the forecast origin at or after the logged onset: BEFORE (until either alarm is known), INSIDE (alarm to logged end), AFTER (72 hours after the logged end). Only AFTER is scored against a series free of the transfer. BEFORE has 11 shared rows at 1 transfer, so it cannot be read; INSIDE has 3 transfers.
  • AFTER, absolute scores (7 transfers, 3,675 rows; winter 5 transfers, 3,255 rows). STACK-K0 13.69, GAM-ONLY 6.94, STACK-NEW 6.32, STACK-UNION 6.31, STACK-RONC 7.41, ORACLE 6.35, BG2 10.09, arm C 12.44, manual heuristic 7.65, climatology 7.49. Winter: K0 15.02, STACK-NEW 6.77, BG2 11.00. Other months (2 transfers, 420 rows): K0 3.37, STACK-NEW 2.88, BG2 3.07, climatology 2.42.
  • C1 and C2, minus BG2 on AFTER (95%, resampling the 7 transfers). STACK-NEW -3.77 (-6.01 to +0.02); STACK-UNION -3.79 (-6.01 to +0.00); STACK-K0 +3.59 (-0.08 to +5.70); GAM-ONLY -3.16 (-4.76 to +0.10); arm C +2.35 (-0.28 to +4.53). Leaving out one substation: D5 out -1.85 (-3.07 to +0.19), D14 out -4.57 (-6.76 to -0.15), the sign holds at every substation.
  • C3, share of the gap from STACK-K0 to ORACLE closed on AFTER (9 transfer-substation pairs). STACK-NEW 100% (95% 12% to 101%), STACK-UNION 101% (17% to 101.5%), STACK-RONC 86% (-21% to 126%), GAM-ONLY 92% (-5% to 112%), BG2 50% (21% to 84%), arm C 17% (15% to 78%). Per pair (7 pairs with a gap over 0.25 points, two of them from replicate months, for which BG2 has no rows): STACK-NEW median 89%, range -61% to 103%; STACK-UNION median 98%; STACK-RONC median 0%; BG2 median 72% over its 5 pairs. The three December-to-January pairs, from two transfers, carry the pooled shares.
  • Alarms. Of the 7 transfer-substation pairs whose gap exceeds 0.25 points (two from replicate months), the pair alarm found 5 and RO-NC found 4. An alarm that matches no logged transfer still masks, as in a live service.
  • INSIDE (3 transfers, 12,168 rows), against observed power that contains the transfer. STACK-K0 5.94, BG2 7.38, STACK-NEW 10.69, GAM-ONLY 12.33. A forecast of the normal running arrangement is expected to miss the moved power, so this row set cannot rank the arms.
  • C4 and C5, no harm on 556,930 ordinary rows (95%, resampling calendar months). Scores: STACK-K0 2.725, STACK-NEW 2.759, STACK-UNION 2.827, STACK-RONC 2.986, GAM-ONLY 3.030, BG2 2.693, arm C 2.666, manual heuristic 3.391, climatology 3.654. STACK-NEW minus STACK-K0 +0.033 (-0.043 to +0.105); STACK-UNION +0.102 (-0.013 to +0.207); STACK-RONC +0.261 (+0.093 to +0.484); GAM-ONLY +0.304 (+0.192 to +0.431). STACK-NEW minus BG2 +0.066 (-0.109 to +0.245); STACK-K0 minus BG2 +0.033 (-0.112 to +0.185). Winter: STACK-NEW minus BG2 -0.208 (-0.370 to -0.019); other months +0.248 (+0.083 to +0.426).
  • Tail calibration (share of readings at or below the quantile; pinball loss in points), ordinary rows. STACK-NEW: q01 0.0145 (0.188), q05 0.052 (0.685), q95 0.956 (0.712), q99 0.988 (0.203). BG2: 0.0097 (0.208), 0.041 (0.617), 0.945 (0.739), 0.983 (0.249). After a transfer ends (7 transfers), STACK-NEW covers 0.175, 0.231, 0.835, and 0.898 at the four quantiles, and BG2 0.0035, 0.323, 0.745, and 0.842, so both forecasts are far too confident in the days after a transfer. The node-plus-generators curtailment metric is not scored here, because the experiment forecasts six Primaries alone.
  • Predictions against outcome. The unmasked stack and BG2 were predicted to score 4 to 12 on AFTER; the stack scored 13.69 (above the range), BG2 10.09. The pair-alarm mask was predicted to close 20% to 60% of the gap and the union 40% to 75%; both closed about 100% pooled (89% and 98% per-transfer median), above the ranges. BG2 was predicted to close 0% to 50%: 50%. The predicted agreement of all arms before the alarm could not be tested (1 transfer). No harm on ordinary rows was predicted within 0.10: +0.033 for STACK-NEW.

The mask does not clearly beat ignoring recent power. The comparison is with GAM-ONLY: STACK-NEW minus GAM-ONLY on AFTER is -0.62 (95% -1.28 to +0.40) and STACK-UNION minus GAM-ONLY is -0.63 (-1.28 to +0.38). GAM-ONLY closes 92% of the gap to ORACLE with no alarm, so most of the "gap closed" is the gain from not reading the contaminated power, and the alarm adds a little on top. The mask's gain over GAM-ONLY cannot be told from zero here.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast by substation, identical for every stack arm: D10 -0.064, D11 -0.027, D14 +0.034, D16 +0.014, D5 -0.136, D9 -0.021 points of capacity.
  • Error of the median forecast beside the quantile contrast, AFTER, shared rows: STACK-K0 18.23, GAM-ONLY 10.73, STACK-NEW 9.64, STACK-UNION 9.62, BG2 15.47 points, the same order as the quantile score.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 fired: the pooled gap shares (about 100%) sit above the predicted ranges. The tested explanation is concentration: the three December-to-January pairs hold 31.1 of the 39.3 points of gap, and the per-transfer median share is 89% with a range of -61% to 103%, so the pooled figure is not typical. Trigger 5 fired: GAM-ONLY or a mask beats ORACLE at 6 of 7 pairs, so the logged interval is not a ceiling; the logged onset is later than the step in the telemetry at the first December transfer (the pair alarm's step in experiment 156's alarm table is 13 hours before the logged onset). Trigger 4 (leaving one substation out flips a contrast) did not fire: the sign of the pair-alarm contrast with BG2 holds when each substation is left out. Triggers 1 (a failed control), 3 (quantile score and error of the median forecast disagree), 6 (interval width against a sister experiment), and 7 (a later design depends on this result) did not fire.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Four substations, not six. D9 and D11 hold no logged transfer in the scored year, so the comparison with BG2 rests on D5, D10, D14, and D16. Leaving D5 out shrinks C1 from -3.77 to -1.85.
  • Row sets include rows issued before the alarm was usable. INSIDE and AFTER rows need only a forecast origin at or after the logged onset, so for some rows the mask is not yet on while ORACLE is, which dilutes the share of the gap closed. The 4 transfers of the replicate months (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06) appear only in stack-only numbers, which no verdict uses, and BG2 has no rows there.
  • Seven transfers. The scored year holds 7 logged transfers at the decision Primaries, and BG2 exists only there; BG2 comparisons rest on those 7. The stack-only rows add 4 transfers from the replicate months and move no conclusion.
  • Lab conditions for the stack. The filter's residual uses the analysis proxy (a stand-in for the weather at the forecast origin, built from the weather model's analysis fields), but the alarm tables are experiment 156's, tuned on odd months of the real stream.
  • The logged interval is imperfect. The share closed can exceed 100%, and the ORACLE arm is not a floor.
  • Past weather. The proxy is built from past weather available at the origin; no future weather enters the filter.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next question is whether a forecast that drops recent power while the pair alarm or RO-NC is active (the GAM-ONLY arm switched on by an alarm), and otherwise uses it, beats both the stack and BG2 across all rows. GAM-ONLY scored 6.94 after a transfer and 3.03 on ordinary days (K0 2.73), so the alarm decides between the two. More logged transfers would also let the BG2 comparison rank the forecasts.

docs.title: Experiment 164: a one-sided widening lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 0.896, short of 0.90
docs.text:
On cold nights, the 95% quantile (q95) of the best forecast of experiment 155 is exceeded on 15% of readings, and the cause is mostly a prediction interval that is too narrow when it is cold. A cold night is a winter night (November to March, evening or night hours) whose daily mean temperature, from the ERA5 weather reanalysis, is below 2 °C. Coverage is the share of readings at or below the quantile, so a calibrated q95 has coverage 0.95. We asked whether the shortfall comes from a narrow interval or from a mean forecast that is too low. We then tested three fixes, called T, S, and O, that widen the interval on days the ensemble weather forecast calls cold. Each fix was fitted on one set of months (the tuning months) and scored on a later year (the scored year) and on other months of the earlier year (the replicate months), with the mean forecast unchanged. Fix O, which widens only the upper quantiles, lifts cold-night q95 coverage from 0.846 to 0.896. That misses the 0.90 we set before running the experiment, so the verdict is refuted by our decision rule. The gap of 0.004 is small against the uncertainty of the figure, which rests on 10 cold days. All scores are in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand).

The forecast is arm I of experiment 160: arm D of experiment 155 with its table of quantile offsets (the spread table) read by interpolation along the lead. The cold gate is the mean temperature of the 51-member ensemble of experiment 111, averaged over about 24 hours centred on the valid time, so the gate exists at forecast time. The three fixes are T (one multiplier per temperature class at q01, q05, q10, q90, q95, and q99), S (all offsets scaled by one plus 0.1 times the ensemble temperature standard deviation, below 2 °C only), and O (multipliers 1.65, 1.36, 1.26, and 1.16 on q75, q90, q95, and q99 below 2 °C only).

  • Row set and schedule. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the five decision substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 beside), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, rows outside the hand-filtered switching events. The mean forecasts come from experiment 155's stored runs (monthly refits on a rolling window, whatever schedule 155 used); no refit happens here. The tuning months are the odd months and the replicate months the even months of the year before the scored year. The scored year is 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29: 5,395 cold-night rows (1,583 each at D10, D11, and D14, and 323 each at D5 and D16) of 464,228 rows at the five decision substations.
  • Diagnosis (scored year, reference). The cold-night residual (actual minus mean forecast) has mean +1.24 points and standard deviation 7.45 (0.17 of the standard deviation, under the pre-registered 0.3 line). By hour band, the residual standard deviation on cold days (any month, 9,265 rows) is 1.70, 1.22, 1.04, and 1.29 times that of other winter days. The 1.2 to 1.6 prediction held in 2 of 4 bands. At an ensemble-mean temperature of 0 °C or below the mean residual is +3.12 points (0.47 of the standard deviation, 3,201 rows) and q95 coverage is 0.821. No post hoc shift arm was run, because the pooled bias is under 0.3.
  • Cold-night q95 coverage, scored year (pooled). Reference 0.846, T 0.895, S 0.865, O 0.896. Replicate months: 0.876, 0.912, 0.897, and 0.913. Pass rule (0.90 or more and all-row upper bound under +0.01): O passes in the replicate months only, so no fix passes in both periods.
  • Contrasts, all rows, scored year (98.33% month-resampled intervals). C1 T minus reference +0.0031 (-0.0057 to +0.0121); C2 S minus reference -0.0005 (-0.0014 to +0.0001); C3 O minus reference -0.0010 (-0.0037 to +0.0012). Replicate months: +0.0035, -0.0002, and +0.0002. Absolute all-row scores in the scored year: reference 2.7529, T 2.7560, S 2.7525, O 2.7519, BG2 2.7804, manual heuristic 3.4968, climatology 3.8038.
  • Contrasts, cold nights, scored year. C1 -0.038 (-0.082 to +0.013); C2 -0.031 (-0.043 to -0.016); C3 -0.096 (-0.143 to -0.048).
  • Tail calibration, scored year, all rows (coverage / pinball loss). Reference: q01 0.022 / 0.216, q05 0.065 / 0.713, q95 0.947 / 0.746, q99 0.981 / 0.232. O: q95 0.948 / 0.745, q99 0.982 / 0.232 (O leaves the lower tail unchanged). T: q95 0.954 / 0.754, q99 0.987 / 0.230.
  • Tail calibration, scored year, cold nights. Reference: q01 0.045 / 0.391, q05 0.090 / 0.950, q95 0.846 / 0.934, q99 0.933 / 0.328. O: q95 0.896 / 0.819, q99 0.959 / 0.282. T: q95 0.895 / 0.830, q99 0.960 / 0.281. S: q95 0.865 / 0.887, q99 0.949 / 0.300. The lower tail is under-covered at q05 on cold nights (readings fall below it on 0.090 against 0.05) in every fix.
  • Width by lead day. O changes the median q05 to q95 width by at most 0.1 points on any lead day, because the fix acts on the upper quantiles on cold days only; T widens it by 0.2 to 0.6 points on lead days 0 to 6 (reference 15.9 to 19.2, T 16.3 to 19.8).
  • Curtailment-cost proxy (the node-only rule of studies.node_curtailment on each substation's own demand, scaled limit 0.9 times the maximum before the scored year, GBP 2,000 per MWh, leads 12 to 36 hours). Avoidable cost against the perfect forecast, summed over the five substations: reference GBP 1.32 million, O 1.27 million, T 1.26 million, S 1.31 million, BG2 1.88 million, manual heuristic 3.33 million. The 95% month-resampled intervals overlap (reference 0.11 to 3.3 million), and the order of the fixes changes at the limit 0.5, so the proxy cannot rank the fixes. A Primary substation has no published export limit here and a demand series is treated as the flow that can breach, so the figures show the arithmetic and are not a curtailment forecast.
  • Caveats. The scored cold rows come from 10 valid dates in 5 spells (20 to 21 November, 31 December, 2 to 6 January, 8 January, and 10 January), and D5 and D16 contribute only on 20 to 21 November. The day-block 95% interval of pooled cold-night q95 coverage is 0.774 to 0.918 for the reference and 0.844 to 0.948 for O, and 0.90 lies inside the second. The reference's cold-night coverage is below 0.90 with probability 0.93, and O's is at or above 0.90 with probability 0.45. The tuning and replicate months share cold days (four of the seven replicate cold dates are also tuning cold dates), so the replicate months are not an independent check. The gate misses 23% of the scored cold-night rows, which O never widens. The multipliers pool five substations and one winter, so a substation-specific difference (D10 and D11 sit at 0.87 and 0.85 under O) is not fitted.
  • What to try next. (1) A bias correction of the mean forecast at ensemble-mean temperatures of 0 °C or below, where the mean is 0.47 standard deviations low. (2) Fit and score over at least two winters, so the cold days are not 10. (3) A gate that also fires on a short run of cold days before the target.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site, at 12 to 36 hours. Exactly 0.000 for the reference and for O at every substation (the spread table has median zero, and fixes S and O leave the median offset at zero; T leaves it unchanged).
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast is identical across arms (contrast 0.0000 for C1, C2, and C3), because the mean is unchanged, so no pair of contrasts can point in opposite directions.
  • Reproduction control. The reference rescored from experiment 160's stored forecasts scores 2.7529, a gap of 7e-6 from experiment 160's printed 2.7529.
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 4 fired: leaving out D10 or D11 lifts O's pooled cold-night q95 coverage from 0.896 to 0.909 or 0.917. A fresh Opus audit re-derived the coverages and contrasts from the stored forecasts with its own code and agreed with every number. Its findings and triage: (F1, F2) the arm files on disk had been built before the fit script's final edits, and the committed fix O did not apply its q75 multiplier, so the fit, report, and charts were rerun with the corrected code, which moved only C1 (from +0.0089 to +0.0031); (F5b) the replicate months share cold days with the tuning months, recorded above; (F6) the day-block intervals above; (F7) the gate catches 77% of cold-night rows, recorded above. F5a, F5c, F5d, F5e, and F8 were confirmed harmless. The audit report is private (data/ml-experiments/briefs/e164_audit_report.md). Triggers 1 to 3 and 5 to 7 did not fire.

docs.title: A forecast that ignores recent power whenever an LSC alarm is active, scored on every real row
docs.text:
Ignoring recent power while a switching alarm is active helps only in the days after a logged transfer ends, and the mask from either alarm fails the pre-registered limit on rows outside transfers. The stack scores 6.31 points of a substation's effective capacity in the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends, against 13.69 with no mask and 10.09 for best guess 2 (BG2). On the 559,137 real rows outside logged transfers, the mask scores 0.102 points worse than no mask (95% interval from resampling calendar months, -0.013 to +0.205). The extra error is largest while an alarm is active on rows that match no logged transfer, and in months outside winter (November to March). The next step is a mask gated on how reliable the alarm is, or used in winter only.

We asked whether the filter on recent errors should be switched off while a switching alarm is active. The forecast, called the stack here, is a frozen generalised additive model (GAM) with a Kalman filter that corrects each forecast using its recent errors, as in experiment 163. The mask sets the filter's readings missing from the moment an alarm is known until the end rule of experiment 147 and experiment 148 fires (the rule that decides a switching event has ended), and the filter then restarts. The alarms are the pair alarm of experiment 156 (two metered substations step in opposite directions within hours) and the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC). Experiment 163 scored the mask on logged transfers and on ordinary rows that left out the hand-filtered switching events. This experiment scores every real row at the six decision Primary substations, in the scored year July 2025 to June 2026, and splits the rows by logged transfer and by the alarm active at the forecast origin. Scores are twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles (the standard loss for quantile forecasts), in points of effective capacity; lower is better.

By the pre-registered rule the verdict is not supported. The gain test passes: the mask from either alarm scores 7.38 points lower than no mask after a transfer ends on the 7 transfers BG2 also forecasts, and 4.95 points lower on all 11 transfers, with intervals that end just below zero. The no-harm test fails: the upper end of the interval for the mask from either alarm on the real rows outside logged transfers is +0.205, against a required +0.01. The mask from the pair alarm alone also fails, with an upper end of +0.105. The test while a transfer runs fails as predicted, because the observed power then contains the moved load.

  • Arms. K0 (the stack with no mask), MASK_NEW (mask from the pair alarm), MASK_UNION (mask from either alarm, the headline), MASK_RONC and GAM_ONLY (the generalised additive model alone, with no recent power) as references, ORACLE (the logged interval masked from its logged onset, on logged-transfer rows only), BG2 (experiment 87), experiment 155's arm C, the manual heuristic, and climatology. The stack arms share the K0 spread of experiment 115, so they differ in location only. The GAM and the filter are frozen, so no refit schedule applies.
  • Rows. The scored year holds 586,232 rows with a reading at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (anonymised substation labels), and 581,078 of them are shared with BG2.
