  • Cold nights. The pre-registered ratio is the cold nights' share of the row-level excess over their share of all rows. It is 2.88 with a 95% interval of -0.42 to 5.81, so the interval is too wide to say that the loss sits on cold nights. Post hoc, two stabler ratios agree on the direction. Cold days (day mean ERA5 temperature below 2 C) carry 2.6 times their share of the day excess (95% interval 1.9 to 3.6), and the mean night score on cold days is 1.7 times that on other winter days (1.2 to 2.0). The cold days are only 28 of 1,392 days and carry 5.3% of the excess. At 3 C and 5 C the day ratios fall to 1.7 and 1.4.
  • Controls. The best of 1,000 random draws of the same number of days carried 8.5% of the excess (mean 3.1%), so the real share of 41.7% is not an accident of the ranking. The pre-registered injected control adds 5 points to 10 random days per substation (the plan first said 18 days, and was corrected to 10 before any score was read, because 18 exceeds the 14 to 15 slots of the worst 5%). It put 89.2% of the injected days in the worst 5%, below the required 90%. By substation it recovered 94% (D5), 100% (D10, D11, D14), and 52% (D16). D16 has the heaviest tail, so its worst-5% slots are already taken by real days with more than 5 points of excess. Post hoc, 10 injected points recovered 100% at every substation.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site: 0.0 points at all six substations, and the largest absolute difference at any row is 0.0. Arm D's median forecast equals its mean forecast, so a quantile spread that shifts the median away from the mean cannot explain the loss.
  • Mean forecast's error beside the quantile score: ranking days by the mean forecast's mean absolute error gives a worst-5% share of 36.7% (41.7% for the quantile score), and 76 of the 87 worst pinball days (six substations) are among the worst mean-error days. Both measures point the same way.
  • Audit triggers: trigger 1 (a control fails) fired, because of the injected control. An Opus audit ran, and the "Audit" section below gives its findings and their triage. Trigger 2 was also considered, because the labelled fraction (48.6%) came in just under the predicted half: the sensitivity with the switching rows kept (62.7%) tests the explanation that the scored rows hide switching days. Dropping one substation moves the share by at most 3.6 points.

docs.title: Sensitivities (post hoc)
docs.text:
• Switching rows kept: the share rises to 45.6% and 62.7% of the worst days are labelled.
  • All leads (0 to 168 hours) instead of the D+1 band: the share is 44.9% and 47.8% of the worst days are labelled.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
An Opus agent re-derived the numbers from the stored forecasts with its own code. Its report is private (data/ml-experiments/briefs/e172_audit_report.md). No headline conclusion changed.

  • Reproduced: the worst-5% share (41.73%), the per-site shares, the leave-one-out range, and the month bootstrap interval match. The audit's day table matches ours on every day, and its labels for switching, cold snap, holiday, flagged reading, and any label agree on all 1,392 days. Economy 7 was not re-derived.
  • The share is robust: 39.6% to 42.5% across 18 day definitions (local or UTC days, start or end dating, 1 to 48 minimum rows). Dropping January 2026 gives 38.0%.
  • The labelled fraction sits on the 50% bar: a one-day pad around switching intervals, or UTC dating, gives 52.8%. Padding both switching and holiday days gives 56.9%. RO-NC intervals alone give 45.8%. A different window would therefore read as supported where ours reads partly supported, so "about half" is the finding.
  • The switching label is not an artefact: shifting the switching days by 7 to 28 days labels 2 to 6 of the worst days, against 29 for the real label. One D10 interval runs 60 days (2025-12-12 to 2026-02-10) and covers 17% of D10's days.
  • The control failure is explained: D16 has 9 days with more than 5 points of excess, and 14 worst-day slots, so a 5-point injection must beat the fifth-largest real excess (6.6 points) and about half of the injected days land. Ranking by excess cannot misorder days, so the control tests the size of D16's tail and not the method. The pre-registered cap stays.
  • Fixed: the detector stamps mark the end of a half-hour and were dated as starts. Correcting them changed no day and no number. The flagged-reading day is dated by the reading's own timestamp and was not changed.

docs.title: Method and caveats
docs.text:
• Row set: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the scored year of experiment 155, arm D, d_scored_* forecasts. Days with fewer than 24 rows in the D+1 band are dropped, which removes about 13% of D5's days (252 of 287 remain) because many of its switching rows are excluded, and ranks D5's tail on fewer days. No forecasting model was fitted. The run used one CPU core and about a minute.
  • Dating: a row's day is the local date of the half-hour's start, as in the holiday flag of studies.dp_calendar.
  • Switching label: the day overlaps an interval of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC, setting R0, experiment 147) or a pair alarm (experiment 156, window 8) on the substation's series. The intervals use hindsight end rules, as in a lab test. The alarm table may cover only part of the year. The earlier detectors of experiment 141 are not used. The D8 drops of experiment 159 do not apply, because D8 is not among the six substations.
  • Flagged reading: the cleaned power table flags a reading on the day, or the day has fewer than 42 of 48 readings. Only D9 has such a day among the worst days; none of the decision substations does.
  • Cold snap: the day's mean ERA5 temperature (the ECMWF reanalysis of past weather) is below 2 C. ERA5 labels days after the fact and is not a forecast input.
  • Economy 7 step: a winter day on which the four half-hours starting 00:00 to 01:30 UTC carry at least 35% of the day's loss above the median. The 35% is an assumption fixed before any score was read, and fits 0.9% of days. A different definition could label more days.
  • Holiday: a holiday period of studies.dp_calendar.
  • One year: the scored year has one winter, and 19 of the 72 worst days fall in January 2026. The shares describe that year.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Look for a label for the 37 unlabelled worst days, starting with the D16 days of January 2026.
  • Test a cold-night term on a winter with more cold days, since this year cannot rank it.

docs.title: Does the convex demand forecast with the Kalman filter and recipe R stay within 1.3 times its ordinary-weekday error over every Christmas back to 2019-20, at all 16 Primary substations?
docs.text: The prediction failed, but only fits with little or no winter in their training data failed; on fits with a winter, every Christmas scored under 1.3 times an ordinary weekday. We asked how much worse a demand forecast gets over Christmas. We fitted a demand model at up to 16 Primary substations (the stations that step 33 kV down to 11 kV; 7 to 15 had enough data in each Christmas) before each Christmas back to 2019-20, forecast the next 168 hours every day, and compared the quantile score (a probabilistic error measure; lower is better) on 24 December to 2 January with the score on ordinary weekdays at the same times of day. A ratio of 1.0 means Christmas is no harder than a weekday. We wrote down, before reading any score, that the ratio would stay under 1.3, the level at which a Christmas-specific term would begin to be worth adding. It did not: the ratio was 1.91, 1.38, 1.22, and 1.50 for 2020-21 to 2023-24, and 0.98 and 0.97 for 2024-25 and 2025-26. The lockdown window (23 March 2020 to 19 July 2021) is left out of training, so the fits for the first two Christmases saw little winter. Keeping only fits with at least 180 days of training rows, a choice made after the scores were read, gives 1.22, 1.12, 0.98, and 0.97 for 2022-23 to 2025-26. The demand model is that of experiment 107, fitted by convex optimisation, with a Kalman filter (a running correction from recent errors) and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days, held to 0.75 of its size), as experiment 170 scored over two Christmases at five substations. Observed weather drives every forecast, because ensemble forecasts exist only from 2024, so the ratios exclude the error a real weather forecast would add.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. m12 (pre-registered): convex model on 12 months of history, fitted solar capacity, no drift term, cut on 1 November (16 December for Christmas 2019-20), Kalman filter with the single noise setting shared by all substations from experiment 133, recipe R, and no night offset (a correction to winter nights). all (post hoc): the same with all years of history.
  • Rows. 24 December to 2 January (local dates), daily 09:00 UTC runs of 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events. Reference: Monday to Friday from 8 December to 31 January, outside bank holidays and the Christmas window. Substations with a fitted model: 7, 9, 13, 13, 14, 14, 15 in the seven seasons; D15 has a model only for 2025-26.
  • P1 fails on the pre-registered rows. Pooled quantile-score ratio (95% interval from resampling days): 1.91 (1.47 to 2.40) in 2020-21, 1.38 (1.21 to 1.56), 1.22 (1.04 to 1.46), 1.50 (1.20 to 1.87), 0.98 (0.84 to 1.17), 0.97 (0.84 to 1.12). Christmas 2019-20 has no spread, so only the absolute error of the mean exists: 1.70 (1.19 to 2.32). By its own decision rule the pre-registered result is refuted (a pooled ratio of 1.4 or more in 2020-21 and 2023-24, and 7 substations at 1.3 or more); the verdict is inconclusive only because of the control cap below.
  • P2 fails on the pre-registered rows. Pooled over Christmases, 7 of 15 substations have a ratio of 1.3 or more (D2, D3, D5, D9, D10, D11, D14). With all years of history (arm all), 5 of 15 reach it on the pre-registered rows, and the pooled ratios by Christmas are 1.88, 1.27, 1.11, 1.50, 0.96, 0.89 for 2020-21 to 2025-26.
  • P3 fails on the pre-registered rows. Bias on 25 and 26 December as a share of measured power (positive: demand above the forecast): +47%, +12%, -13%, +2.5%, +3.1%, -3.0%, +2.5% for the seven Christmases. In 2021-22 the ordinary weekdays are also 10% too high, so that bias is not specific to Christmas.
  • Post hoc subset: fits with at least 180 days of training rows. Ratio 1.22 (1.04 to 1.46), 1.12 (1.00 to 1.26), 0.98 (0.84 to 1.17), 0.97 (0.84 to 1.12) for 2022-23 to 2025-26, 1.06 (0.97 to 1.15) pooled. Three of 15 substations reach 1.3 (D2, D3, D10). The bias on 25 and 26 December is +2.5%, -5.0% (on the limit, with D9 removed from 2023-24), -3.0%, +2.5%. Thresholds of 90 and 270 days give the same picture for 2022-23 to 2025-26; 90 days keeps Christmas 2020-21 and 2021-22 (1.43 and 1.38). Under this rule the prediction holds, but the subset was chosen after the scores were read.
  • Day groups (quantile-score ratio, all Christmases pooled, pre-registered rows): 24 to 25 December 1.48, 26 December 1.39, 27 to 31 December 1.23, 1 to 2 January 1.29. The last two Christmases are 0.82 to 1.23 in every group.
  • Absolute quantile scores (points of effective capacity, quantile score, m12, Christmas window): 5.92, 10.14, 2.81, 4.34, 3.20, 3.29 for 2020-21 to 2025-26.
  • Tail coverage (m12, pre-registered rows, all Christmases pooled). Coverage of the 95% quantile: 0.886 over the Christmas window (0.834 on 24 to 25 December, 0.915 on 27 to 31 December) against 0.916 on ordinary weekdays. Coverage of the 5% quantile: 0.174 against 0.124. Pinball losses are in report_m12.json.
  • Leave-one-out. Removing one substation moves the 2020-21 ratio to 1.49 to 2.07 and 2023-24 to 1.12 (without D9) to 1.68. D9's own 2023-24 ratio is 5.6.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Positive control, pre-registered: failed. The pooled ratio at the five decision substations in the last two Christmases was 1.07 (experiment 170: 1.13), within the allowed 0.15. The ordinary-weekday score was 3.09 points against experiment 170's 2.756, above the allowed value, on unlike rows (a year-round score against a December and January weekday score). The verdict is capped at inconclusive for this reason.
  • Matched-rows control, post hoc. On the 106,924 half-hours of November 2025 to January 2026 that this experiment and experiment 155's arm D both forecast (decision substations, scored runs, paired on substation, origin, and valid time), this pipeline scores 2.941 against 3.046, but on ordinary weekdays 3.372 against 3.356. The pipeline is roughly level with arm D, not clearly better, which is the expected size of the observed-weather gain minus the missing night offset.
  • Median minus mean forecast. Zero at every substation by construction, because the spread is centred on the corrected mean; the check does not expose a shifted forecast here.
  • Error of the mean beside the quantile score. The absolute-error ratios agree with the quantile-score ratios in direction in every Christmas (figure 1).
  • Triggers fired. Two review triggers fired: the positive control failed, and leaving one substation (D9) out moves a pooled ratio (2023-24) from 1.50 to 1.12. A fresh Opus audit re-derived every headline ratio and bias exactly from the stored forecasts and found no leakage in the mean forecast: the fit's training rows end at the cut, the filter reads only data ending 3.5 hours before each origin, and recipe R's newest input ends 9 hours before. Triage of its findings:
    • Fits with too little training data: accepted. The lockdown window (23 March 2020 to 19 July 2021) is left out of training, so Christmas 2020-21 fits used 51 to 143 days, every substation in Christmas 2021-22 used the same 104 summer days, and D9 in 2023-24 used 31 days. The plan applied its 90-day minimum only to 2019-20. This experiment now reports the 180-day subset beside the pre-registered rows, and does not change the verdict.
    • Matched control double counted rows: accepted. The file pattern matched six file families of experiment 155; the control now uses the scored rows only, deduplicated, and reads roughly level as above.
    • The spread sees part of the reference: accepted as minor. With a 3 to 31 January reference, 2023-24 moves from 1.50 to 1.43 and 2021-22 from 1.38 to 1.35.
    • Reference choice: noted. A 15 to 31 January reference raises 2021-22 to 1.46 and 2022-23 to 1.36; 2020-21 stays at 1.9 or more under all four references tried (15 to 31 January only, 8 to 23 December only, Tuesday to Thursday only, and weekends included).
    • Plan names the 2.756 benchmark inconsistently (experiment 170 or 155): accepted, both are the same arm D score.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Spread. The spread is fitted on 16 November to 22 December of the same season and is poorly calibrated in some seasons (coverage of the 5% quantile 0.37 on ordinary weekdays in 2021-22), so the quantile-score ratio there is unreliable. The absolute error of the mean does not use it.
  • Observed weather. The weather at forecast time is not available live, so these ratios are a ceiling for the ensemble-driven forecast, and the Christmas weather is not an error source.
  • Post hoc subset. The 180-day rule was chosen after the audit showed which fits were short, and only four Christmases pass it, so the result rests on four Christmases, each with 10 days.
  • Not arm D. The winter night offset, the pinned solar capacity, the 24-month window, and the ensemble weather of experiment 170's arm D are left out.
  • COVID. Christmases 2020-21 and 2021-22 were under tier restrictions and the omicron wave; the model has no term for either.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Do not add a Christmas term. The four Christmases with at least 180 days of training rows score 0.97 to 1.22 times a weekday.
  • Add a minimum-history flag. A forecast from a fit with under 180 days of usable training rows should carry a degradation flag and wider bands, as the inherent-stability rules ask.
  • Re-score the ensemble-driven forecast over the next Christmas with the day-group table above as the baseline, because the ratio here excludes weather error.

docs.title: Is the loss on the forecast's unlabelled worst days weather error, a day shared with other substations, or an error at one substation only?
docs.text:
Replacing the weather forecast with estimates of past weather removes only about a third of the loss on the worst days that experiment 172 could not explain, so most of that loss is not weather error. Experiment 172 ranked each day of five Primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16) by its excess loss, the day's quantile score above the substation's median day. It labelled the worst 5% of days that overlap a switching event, a holiday, a cold snap, a flagged reading, or an Economy 7 step. Of its 72 worst days, 37 carry no label. We re-ran the forecast that experiment 172 scored (experiment 155's arm D) for those days with past weather in place of the forecast weather. The past weather is ERA5 (the ECMWF reanalysis) temperature and Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) solar irradiance, and the forecast weather is the mean of the ECMWF ensemble forecast. We also counted how many of the other Primaries of experiment 87 were in their own worst 5% of days on the same day. Past weather removes 31.5% of the unlabelled days' excess loss. The other 68.5% splits into 38.9% on days that another Primary also has and 29.5% on days that no other Primary has, so the three shares add to 100% of the excess loss. Other Primaries share these days about as often as random shifting of their days gives, so the remaining loss could come from events at one substation.

The pre-registered verdict is partly supported. The weather condition failed: 31.5% against the required 50% (95% interval 21.9% to 39.8%). The shared condition passed its stated threshold: 48.6% of the unlabelled days coincide with another Primary's worst-5% day, against one third required. The shifting control shows that this condition carries little information. Shifting each other Primary's days separately gives 46.6% on average. Shifting all of them together, which keeps their own worst days on the same days, gives 35.5%, and 7.8% of those draws reach 48.6%. ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, so the past-weather forecast cannot be issued in practice. ERA5 and CAMS are themselves estimates, so 31.5% is a lower bound for the weather share.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Weather share W (headline): 0.315 of the 37 unlabelled days' excess loss (total 108.1 points of day score), 95% interval 0.219 to 0.398 from resampling the 11 calendar months that hold an unlabelled day. By substation: D5 0.60, D14 0.45, D10 0.28, D11 0.20, D16 0.16. Leaving one substation out gives 0.28 to 0.35.
  • Labelled comparison set: the 35 labelled worst days (total excess 188.0) lose 0.063 of their excess to past weather.
  • Weather share sensitivities: 0.319 with the ensemble arm's quantile-band widths kept (the quantiles shift only), 0.340 with the Kalman filter also run on the ERA5-driven residuals, 0.367 with the ensemble arm's median day as the reference, and 0.292 on the mean forecast's absolute error. All sit under 0.5.
  • Shared share S: 0.486 (95% interval 0.279 to 0.704) of the unlabelled days have at least one other Primary in its own worst 5% (mean 0.84 others). The labelled days give 0.657 (mean 1.26). Leaving one substation out gives 0.42 to 0.56. The 16 series of experiment 87 sit on 15 Primaries (two series share one Primary), and a series on the target's own Primary does not count.
  • Chance control: each other Primary's worst-day series is moved by a random whole number of days, 1,000 times. Moved separately, the share averages 0.466 (95% interval 0.297 to 0.649) and 47.5% of draws reach 0.486. Moved together by one amount per draw, it averages 0.355 (0.189 to 0.568) and 7.8% of draws reach 0.486. Interconnected neighbours (25 interconnected pairs among the 15 Primaries) share 16.2% of the unlabelled days, against 15.6% when moved separately.
  • Split of the unlabelled days' excess: weather 31.5%, shared 38.9% (interval 20.6% to 56.9%), neither 29.5% (15.9% to 48.4%). The shared part is the excess that stays with past weather on a day another Primary also has. Chance alone would give a share of days about this large.
  • Known-answer controls: 10 points added to 10 random days per substation. The pre-registered bar was 90% of the 50 days recovered. Added to the observed demand of both arms, 100% of the days keep their excess (weather share under 0.5; mean share 0.03). Added to the ensemble arm's forecast only, 92% of the days lose it (share at least 0.5; mean 0.89). Both pass, so the controls do not cap the verdict.
  • Unlabelled days by month: every month but February 2026 holds at least one; November 2025 and May 2026 hold 6 each. The four January 2026 days (all at D16) lose 3.0 of their 18.4 points of excess to weather (16%), and all four coincide with another Primary.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site: 0.0 points at all six substations in the past- weather arm, as in experiment 172.
  • Mean forecast's error beside the quantile score: the share computed on the mean forecast's absolute error is 0.292, against 0.315 on the quantile score, so both point the same way.
  • Audit triggers: the plan listed seven audit triggers (ml-experiment skill, "Audit before merge"). The reproduction control matches: the ensemble arm's day table equals experiment 172's, with a maximum score difference of 0.0. The trigger for a result outside its predicted range fired, because W came in below the predicted 40% to 70%. The explanations tested are in the sensitivities above: the filter's state carried over from the ensemble-driven runs (0.340 when rerun on ERA5), the spread (0.319), and the reference median (0.367). None reaches 0.5, so no audit was requested. The other six triggers did not fire.

docs.title: Method and caveats
docs.text:
• Row set: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the scored year of experiment 155, arm D, D+1 band (lead 15 to 39 hours), hand-filtered switching rows excluded, days of at least 24 rows, as in experiment 172.
  • Arm D: experiment 136's monthly T-all fits (a convex demand model) driven by the calibrated ensemble mean, plus a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 155's winter night offset, and its 14-day mean-error profile.
  • Past-weather arm: the fits and the stored Kalman level and anomaly stay. The temperature, irradiance, and PV shape come from the feature cache's ERA5 and CAMS columns at each valid time. Experiment 155's offset and profile and the spread are rebuilt from the new forecast's own errors. The stored Kalman state came from ensemble-driven residuals and may partly absorb ensemble-weather error, which would understate W; the 0.340 sensitivity reruns the filter on ERA5 residuals.
  • Other Primaries: experiment 87's BG2 forecasts (the production-style XGBoost blend) cover 16 series of 15 Primaries, including the five decision substations and D9. BG2 has no switching mask, so the hand-filtered switching rows stay in its scores. Topology is the interconnection table NGED supplied; only D-labels appear here.
  • Controls: the injected controls act on the day table and do not rebuild experiment 155's correction. The weather-side control adds error to the ensemble arm only, so it tests the day-level split and not the ERA5 pipeline.
  • One year: the scored year has one winter, and shares are approximate. The bootstrap resamples the 11 months that hold an unlabelled day.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Read the 13 unlabelled days that keep more than 1.5 points of excess with past weather and have no other Primary in its worst 5% against the substation's own readings and NGED's switching logs, to find a further label.
  • Test whether weather matters more at D5 and D14 (W 0.60 and 0.45) than at D11 and D16 (0.20 and 0.16), which would point to site-specific weather sensitivity.

docs.title: What shape does the forecast's error take on the unlabelled worst days: a sharp-edged block, a smooth offset, a ramp, or a spike?
docs.text:
The forecast's worst unlabelled days are about half sharp-edged blocks and 40% smooth offsets, and interconnected neighbours do not explain the blocks. Experiment 172 ranked every day of five Primary substations (the substations that step transmission voltage down to distribution voltage) by its forecast loss, and labelled the worst days that overlap a logged switching event, a holiday, a cold snap, a flagged reading, or an Economy 7 step. Experiment 174 took the 37 worst days that carry no label, and found that most of their loss is not weather error and is not shared with other Primaries. We took the forecast's error on each of those 37 days (observed minus forecast power at each half-hour, for the forecast of experiment 155's arm D: a convex demand model with a Kalman filter, driven by the ensemble weather forecast). We then sorted each day into one of four shapes with rules fixed before any day was looked at: (a) a sharp-edged block, where the error jumps and stays shifted for hours, as a switching event would; (b) a smooth offset, with the same sign most of the day; (c) a ramp or midday-only error; or (d) a spike of 1 to 3 half-hours. For each block day we asked whether a Primary joined to the first by an interconnection shows a step of opposite sign within 2 hours (a load transfer between the two), and whether the switching detectors of earlier experiments fired.

The pre-registered verdict is refuted. Class (a) holds 17 of the 37 days, and half of 37 rounded up is 19. A neighbour's opposite step on the block days (52.9%) is below what rolling the neighbours' residuals by whole days gives (71.2%), so the second half of the prediction failed the rule that the observed rate must exceed chance by 10 points. The shape rules recover only about 60% of injected blocks, so 17 against 19 does not exclude a majority of blocks, and the block-share half is unresolved at that recovery rate. The block share is higher than on ordinary days (45.9% against 27.5%, with intervals that just overlap). The offset share is the stronger contrast (40.5% against 16.0%). Experiment 172's known-answer control recovered 89.2% of injected days against a 90% bar, so every share here is approximate.

Figures 3 to 6 show every one of the 37 days, one panel each, grouped by substation:

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Shape counts (37 days): sharp-edged block 17 (45.9%, 95% Wilson interval 31.0% to 61.6%), smooth offset 15 (40.5%, 26.3% to 56.5%), ramp or midday-only 4 (10.8%), none of the four 1, spike
  • All 4 ramp days put at least half their squared residual in 10:00 to 16:00, so the midday part of class (c) is not separated from the ramp part.
  • By substation: D10 6 blocks and 2 offsets; D11 0 blocks, 8 offsets, and 2 ramps; D14 6 blocks, 3 offsets, 1 ramp, 1 none; D16 2 blocks and 2 offsets; D5 3 blocks and 1 ramp.
  • Ordinary days (200 days, 40 per substation from the middle half by excess loss): block 27.5% (21.8% to 34.1%), offset 16.0%, ramp or midday-only 31.0%, none of the four 25.5%.
  • Neighbour step on the block days: all 17 block days have at least one neighbour with a BG2 forecast. Of these, 9 show an opposite-signed step within 2 hours (52.9%, 31.0% to 73.8%). Rolling each neighbour's residuals by 1 to 90 whole days (1,000 draws) gives a mean of 71.2% (95% range 52.9% to 88.2%). The 55 ordinary-day blocks give 49.1% (36.4% to 61.9%). The neighbour test is lenient (2 spreads, 8 candidate times, a noisy neighbour forecast), so chance is high.
  • Detectors on the 17 block days: the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC; experiments 141 and 147) fired within 3 hours of the edge on 0 with either the causal-live end rule (R2) or the hindsight end rule (R0), and the pair alarm of experiment 156 on 0. The five substations have 2 to 26 RO-NC onsets over the whole stored history, and the base rate over all 200 ordinary days (an onset within 3 hours of any part of the day) is 0 of 200 for RO-NC with either end rule and 3 of 200 for the pair alarm.
  • Return and persistence: 4 of the 17 blocks return within the local day. The step persists over the following 7 days on 1 of 17 and reverts on 14 (2 unknown), but the Kalman filter inside arm D adapts to a level shift, so persistence of the real step is understated. Ordinary-day blocks persist on 1 of 55.
  • Known-answer control (a shape added to 40 ordinary days each): intended class recovered on 24 of 40 injected blocks, 24 of 40 offsets, 1 of 40 ramps, and 3 of 40 spikes. Blocks and offsets are found about 60% of the time. A ramp to 4 spreads usually passes the offset test first, so offsets absorb ramps, and a spike of 3 readings usually fails the half-of-the-deviation test. The ramp and spike counts are therefore lower bounds, and every count is approximate. Injected blocks sit exactly on the 3-spread edge threshold, which also lowers their recovery.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site: 0.0 points at every substation, as in experiments 172 and 174 (the arm D quantile forecast has its median equal to its mean).
  • Audit triggers: trigger 2 (a result contradicting its own prediction) fired on five predictions: class (a) 17 days against 19 to 28; class (b) 15 against 5 to 10; chance rate of a neighbour step 71.2% against 10% to 25%; detector firing 0 of 17 against 25% to 50%; persistence 1 of 17 against 15% to 35%. The explanations tested are the known-answer control (about 60% recovery of blocks, which covers the 2-day shortfall in class (a) and may move days between classes (a) and (b)), the ordinary-day rates (block 27.5% and offset 16.0%), and the neighbour test's leniency (49.1% on ordinary-day blocks, 71.2% on rolled neighbours). The pre-registered rule gives refuted on both halves, and no later experiment depends on this result's sign yet. The manager ran no audit, because the experiment is descriptive and fits no model.

docs.title: Method and caveats
docs.text:
• Row set: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, experiment 155's arm D (a convex demand model with a Kalman filter, driven by the ensemble-mean weather forecast), D+1 band (lead 15 to 39 hours), hand-filtered switching rows left out, 2025-07-03 to 2026-06-30. Weather at forecast time is the ensemble forecast, so nothing here uses weather that arrives late.
  • Rules: fixed in the plan commit of this pull request before any day was looked at, and coded in e00175_classify.py. A day is a block when its residual has a jump of more than 3 day-before spreads within 1 hour that lasts 4 hours. The classes are tested in the order block, spike, offset, ramp or midday-only.
  • Neighbours: Primaries joined to the substation's Primary by NGED's interconnection table that have a BG2 forecast (experiment 87, 16 series). BG2's residual is observed minus its median forecast, in the same points of effective capacity as arm D, and it has no switching mask.
  • Small departures from the plan: the spread floor is the 10th percentile of daily spreads over 2025-06-01 to 2026-07-31, a month wider than the scored year on each side, and edges that qualify within 1 hour of each other merge into the strongest one, chained from the last kept edge.
  • Block edge at the day boundary: a block that starts before the day's first half-hour is not found, and the 8-reading windows need at least 4 valid readings on each side.
  • One year, five substations: the denominators are small (17 block days), and the 95% intervals are wide (about 30 points for the shape shares and 43 for the neighbour-step share).

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Read the 17 block days against NGED's switching logs (Switching Logs.xlsx in the hierarchy folder), to see which blocks are logged switching that the detectors missed and which are unlogged.
  • Test a faster level adaptation in the Kalman filter on the 15 offset days. Offset days are 2.5 times as common as on ordinary days and concentrated at D11 (8 of 10 days).

docs.title: Experiment 176: does the band width need to be smoother in lead?
docs.text:
D5's forecast band already widens with lead time on the rows we score. The dips seen on D5 are therefore not a property of the spread table, and smoothing the table does not remove them. The spread table holds one quantile offset for each cell, a combination of hour band, calendar quarter, and lead band. D5 is one of six anonymised substations (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16). The five decision substations are all of them except D9. The forecast is arm A of experiment 169. Arm A reads the interpolated spread table of experiment 160 and widens the upper quantiles on forecast-cold days, as experiment 164 did (fix O). Arm A's band is the interval from its q05 to its q95, the 5th and 95th percentile forecasts, and its width is the q95 minus the q05, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of a substation's rated demand). Lead day 0 is the first 24 hours ahead. A request from the experiment manager reported that D5's median width by lead day peaks on day 3, dips, and jumps on day 7, and asked whether three fixes remove that shape. Fix P is a growth in lead that is non-decreasing and piecewise linear. Fix S shrinks sparse cells of the stored table towards the table pooled across the six substations (the mean of the substations' tables, each scaled by its substation's mean width). Fix PS combines the two. We fitted every fix on the tuning months (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06) and scored each fix on the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29) and on the replicate months (the even months). The score is the quantile score: twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points, where lower is better. A row is one forecast of one substation from one forecast run (one issue time) for one valid time. The scored rows are the rows outside the hand-filtered switching events, which every experiment in this series scores. The mean forecast is unchanged. Fix P leaves the score unchanged and leaves the dip. Fix S lowers the score at D10 and D14 and raises it at D5.

  • Diagnosis. On the rows the experiments score (outside the hand-filtered switching events), arm A's D5 median width by lead day is 19.7, 20.8, 23.9, 24.6, 25.4, 26.6, and 27.8 points, which never falls. On all rows it is 19.7, 17.6, 23.9, 19.6, 20.6, 21.5, and 22.3. The row sets differ by 3.2 to 5.5 points on five of the seven days. The median of D5's cells may sit between a group of narrower cells (hour bands 0 and 3, widths 6 to 28 points in the stored table) and a group of wider ones (hour bands 1 and 2, 20 to 51 points), so that a small change in the row mix moves it. That mechanism is a hypothesis: we did not test it, and did not identify which cells the switching rows sit in. The brief's "day 7" holds the 282 rows at a lead of exactly 168.0 hours, all in hour band 1 with a median width of 37.6, because floor(lead / 24) puts them in an eighth day. Binning by ceil(lead / 24) - 1 removes day 7. The brief's eight widths mix a scored-row value (24.6 on day 3) with an all-rows value (20.6 on day 4), so no single row set reproduces them. The other five substations have no fall larger than 3% from one lead day to the next on either row set (figure 2).
  • Arms. A: the reference. P: offset = scale(substation, hour band, quarter) times a growth curve per hour band and quarter, pooled over substations, non-decreasing in lead with a knot every 24 hours, fitted on the pinball loss by linear programme (the open-source HiGHS solver) at the eight levels q01, q05, q10, q25, q75, q90, q95, and q99. PB: the growth curve per hour band only. U: a growth curve per substation, hour band, and quarter (no pooling). S: each cell of the stored table shrunk towards the pooled table (the pool includes D9), with weight runs / (runs + k), where runs counts the forecast runs of the cell in the tuning months and k = 80. PS: P with its cell scales shrunk the same way. All fitted residuals are centred on the median of their cell, as the stored table is. Every arm keeps the mean, the offsets at q40, q50, and q60, and experiment 164's fix-O multipliers (1.65, 1.36, 1.26, and 1.16 at q75, q90, q95, and q99 on forecast-cold days). Contrasts: C1 is P minus A, C2 is S minus A, C3 is PS minus A.
  • Shrinkage constant. Three-fold cross-validation across alternate tuning months gave held-out pinball losses of 19.91, 19.58, 19.40, 19.32, 19.32, and 19.33 for k = 0, 5, 20, 80, 320, and
  • The curve is flat from 80 upwards, so 80 is weakly identified. The grid runs from 0 to 1280. The same k = 80 is reused for PS, whose cells hold about four times as many runs, so PS shrinks less than S.
  • Row set and schedule. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the five decision substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 is scored beside them, is in the pool of fix S, and is in the per-substation limit of rule 2 but not in any pooled contrast), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, rows outside the switching events, 464,363 rows over the five substations in the scored year. The mean forecasts are experiment 155's monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. We rebuilt arm A from experiment 169's reference arm and the fix-O multipliers. It scores 2.7521 over the five substations against the printed 2.7519, inside the 0.001 cap.
  • Pre-registered rule, scored year. The plan's "all-row" score means the rows outside the switching events. Rule 1 (D5's median width non-decreasing to within 3% on both row sets): A passes on the scored rows and fails on all rows (day 3 is 0.82 of day 2); P fails on all rows (0.75); PS fails (0.95); S passes both (lowest ratio 0.995). Rule 2 (every substation's upper bound at or under +0.005): no arm passes (largest upper bound P +0.0192, S +0.0358, PS +0.0194). Rule 3 (cold-night q95 coverage at or above 0.89): A 0.896, P 0.897, S 0.888, and PS 0.886, so S and PS miss by 0.002 and 0.004. A cold night is a winter night (November to March, night or evening hours) with an ERA5 day-mean temperature below 2 °C, over 5,395 rows at the five substations.
  • Pooled contrasts against A, five substations. Scored year / replicate months. C1 (P): -0.0017 (-0.0076 to +0.0050) / +0.0005 (-0.0080 to +0.0094). C2 (S): -0.0196 (-0.0343 to -0.0069) / -0.0169 (-0.0366 to -0.0004). C3 (PS): -0.0217 (-0.0391 to -0.0067) / -0.0177 (-0.0425 to +0.0027). PB: -0.0017 / -0.0008. U: +0.0014 / +0.0039. Absolute scores, scored year: A 2.7521, PB 2.7504, P 2.7503, U 2.7534, S 2.7325, PS 2.7304; replicate months: A 2.6821, PB 2.6812, P 2.6826, U 2.6859, S 2.6651, PS 2.6644.
  • Per substation, scored year. P: D5 +0.0056 (-0.0070 to +0.0192), D16 -0.0071, the other four within 0.004. S: D10 -0.0884 (-0.1719 to -0.0178), D14 -0.0100 (-0.0166 to -0.0036), D5 +0.0095 (-0.0214 to +0.0358), D11 -0.0024, D16 -0.0019, D9 +0.0001. PS: D10 -0.0943 (-0.1791 to -0.0240), D14 -0.0113 (-0.0215 to -0.0021), D5 +0.0019. Replicate months, S: D10 -0.0848 (-0.2021 to -0.0089), D14 -0.0139 (-0.0253 to -0.0068), D5 +0.0205 (+0.0045 to +0.0403).
  • Leaving one substation out, pooled contrast. Without D10, S is -0.0015 (-0.0108 to +0.0060) in the scored year and -0.0006 (-0.0100 to +0.0087) in the replicate months, and PS is -0.0027 (-0.0107 to +0.0056) and -0.0015 (-0.0158 to +0.0144). Leaving out any other substation keeps S at -0.022 to -0.026 in the scored year. D10's quarter-3 cells come from November 2024 alone (about 30 runs each, a shrinkage weight of 0.27). The month has q05 offsets down to -31.5 points. Shrinkage therefore pulls those cells strongly towards the pool. The audit found the same D10 gain in October 2024 and in October to December 2025.
  • Tail pinball loss, scored year, five substations (q01, q05, q95, q99). A: 0.216, 0.714, 0.745, 0.232. P: 0.210, 0.710, 0.746, 0.228. S: 0.217, 0.705, 0.732, 0.223. PS: 0.213, 0.704, 0.733, 0.220. Cold-night q05 coverage: A 0.090, P 0.093, S 0.083, PS 0.086.
  • q95 coverage by lead day, scored year. A: 0.946, 0.948, 0.951, 0.951, 0.952, 0.946, 0.943. S: 0.951, 0.953, 0.955, 0.954, 0.956, 0.949, 0.947. PS: 0.949, 0.954, 0.958, 0.955, 0.957, 0.952, 0.951.
  • Caveats. The tuning months are six alternate months, so a cell holds about 45 forecast runs. The shrinkage cross-validation holds out whole months, so a held-out November or May is scored against cells built from a few runs in the same quarter. That set-up makes heavy shrinkage score well. Month-end runs forecast seven days into the next month, so 18% of the replicate months' valid times are also targets of tuning runs (the scored year has no overlap). No arm can meet rule 2 unless its effect is near zero. Month-resampled intervals over 12 months have half-widths of 0.004 to 0.10, and rule 2 requires an upper bound of +0.005 at every substation. S's drop in cold-night coverage comes mostly from D11 (0.846 to 0.810), not D5. The cold-night rows are dominated by D10, D11, and D14 (1,583 rows each) over D5 and D16 (323 each).
  • Candidate follow-ups. (1) Show the substation cards' band width by lead day on the scored rows, per hour band. (2) Test shrinking stored cells on more substations. (3) A small neural component that learns the offsets as a smooth function of lead, hour band, and season, pooled over substations and fitted to residuals from a longer history, is a candidate, with the convex growth as the comparison arm. The prediction that could fail: its pooled score stays within ±0.005 of arm A's, because the convex growth already scores within that range. The neural component can then gain only by improving a substation that shrinkage improves (D10 or D14).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site. Exactly 0.000 for every arm and decision substation.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast is 4.7096 in the scored year and 4.6207 in the replicate months for every arm, because the mean is unchanged.
  • Reproduction control. Arm A rebuilt from the stored reference and fix-O multipliers differs from experiment 169's stored arm A by at most 1.5e-5 points in any quantile.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 of the ml-experiment skill (a result contradicts its prediction) fired: fix S moved the pooled score by -0.0196 against a prediction of under 0.003, and D10 moved by -0.0884. The leave-one-out and the audit explain the D10 move and the fix-S move (D10's November cells). Trigger 4 (leaving one site out changes a contrast's verdict) fired: S's and PS's pooled gains lose significance without D10, and S's replicate-month gain does without D14. The experiment's verdict does not depend on either, because every arm fails rule 2 with or without them.
  • Audit (fresh Opus agent; report private, data/ml-experiments/briefs/e176_audit_report.md). The stored table is centred on each cell's median, so every fit here uses residuals centred the same way (audit finding F1). Fitting raw residuals instead carried each cell's bias into the band and gave P +0.0052 in the scored year and +0.0644 in the replicate months (D10 +0.1695). The shrinkage cross-validation builds centred tables too (F3), and k stayed 80. Fix S matches an independent rebuild with a gap of 0, and D10's gain is real but comes from one substation's one-month cells, as described under "Leaving one substation out" (F2). The pool includes D9 (F4). The audit found no leakage; the 18% overlap is in the caveats (F5).
  • Code review (Sonnet). The reviewer found no leakage and no bug that changes a result in the scripts it read. The cross-validation's confound with season and the reuse of k for PS are in the caveats. The 0.001 reproduction cap is applied by hand (gap 0.00016).

docs.title: Can data we already hold, other than power and weather, explain the 37 unlabelled worst days of the best-guess forecast?
docs.text:
None of the six sources we tested explains the 37 worst unlabelled days, so the hypothesis that data we already hold explains them is refuted. Each day here is one substation on one local date. The best-guess forecast is arm D of experiment 155, a convex demand model with a Kalman filter, driven by the ensemble weather forecast. Experiment 172 ranked every substation-day of five Primary substations (the substations that step transmission voltage down to distribution voltage) by the forecast's loss, and set aside the worst days that overlap a logged switching event, a holiday, a cold snap, a flagged reading, or an Economy 7 step. The 37 worst days left over are the "unlabelled" days. Experiment 174 found that better weather inputs explain under a third of their forecast error, and experiment 175 found that about half show an error that steps up or down for several hours. We asked whether other data marks those days: NGED's (National Grid Electricity Distribution's) logged switching operations, faults in the substation's own readings, the substation's own bad weekdays, and public Demand Flexibility Service (DFS) events and national system prices from NESO (the National Energy System Operator) and Elexon (the Balancing and Settlement Code company). Each source gives one yes-or-no indicator per day. We counted the days each indicator covers among the 37, and among 1,000 random sets of 37 ordinary days, which are days outside the worst 5% at the same substations and in the same calendar months.

The decision rule asked for a source that covers at least 15 percentage points more of the 37 days than ordinary days do (5.6 days), and none did. The closest is a high national system price, which covers 18 days against a mean of 14.9 over the 1,000 ordinary-day draws, 3.1 days more. In the table, "covers" means the indicator is true on the day, and p is the share of the 1,000 draws that cover at least as many days as the 37 worst days do.

Source (indicator) 37 worst days Ordinary days (mean, 95% range) p Share of all scored days S1 logged switching: a confirmed open or close on the substation's switching-log sheet 0 0.3 (0 to 1) 1.0 0.7% S3 reading quality: 6 or more missing half-hours, or 8 or more identical readings in a row 0 0.0 (0 to 0) 1.0 0.4% S4 own history: 2 other worst days on the same weekday within 8 weeks 5 5.1 (2 to 8) 0.62 12.4% Union of S1, S3, and S4 5 5.4 (2 to 9) 0.69 13.4% P1 DFS event scheduled on the day 9 8.5 (6 to 11) 0.49 25.9% P2 a settlement-period system price in the top 5% of the scored year 18 14.9 (11 to 18) 0.075 39.9% S2 metered-generator step on the same or an interconnected Primary not testable not testable n/a 0%
  • The prediction missed. The plan predicted that the raw switching log would cover 8 to 15 days. It covers none.
  • Raw NGED files. In the three files read, one for each of three decision Primaries, each reading holds only startTime, endTime, and value. The top-level fields are the ones the metadata table already stores. No voltage, current, power factor, or tap position was available.
  • S2 could not be tested. The 13 metered generators have their own substation numbers, so none shares a number with a Primary or an interconnected Primary. A step test needs a location join that this experiment did not build.
  • The selection of the 37 days weakens S1 and S3. Experiment 172 set aside every day that overlaps a hand-filtered switching event or a flagged reading, so none of the 37 days carries either. The ordinary-day pool still holds such days (25 of its 200), so the ordinary-day means for S1 and S3 are not matched on that label. S1 and S3 were close to certain to cover none of the 37 days.
  • Looser indicators cover too many days to be informative. Switching-log rows of any state and action cover 15 of 37 days (ordinary 11.2, p = 0.035), but the indicator is true on 39.5% of all scored days. A step in any generator in the area covers 26 of 37 (ordinary 20.5, p = 0.019, 14.9 percentage points above ordinary, just under the bar), but is true on 62.6% of all days and uses a step test that departs from the plan (below).
  • Coverage gaps. The switching log ends on 2026-03-25, and the DFS archive on 2026-03-27, so about 3 of the 12 scored months have no record to test. That includes 14 of the 37 days for DFS. The DFS archive holds live events only, and no test events.
  • Matching. One of the 37 days has no ordinary day from the same month at its substation, so each draw falls back to the substation's other months for that day.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
• S4's second branch was not run. The plan also counted a repeat of the date a year earlier. The scored period starts on 2025-07-03, so no earlier year is available.
  • The step test for S2 differs from the plan. The code compares the day-on-day change in power (a lag of 48 readings) averaged over the 8 readings after each half-hour with the 8 before. A step is a shift above the larger of 3 times the standard deviation of that shift over the previous 28 days and 5% of the series' 99th percentile. This feeds only the any-generator sensitivity.
  • "Evening before" for S1 means 18:00 or later, and the switching log's Manual Time is read as local time. The log's own time zone is not stated.
  • Neighbours for S1 and S2 are the Primaries joined to the substation by NGED's interconnection table that have a series in experiment 87's forecast (16 series). Neighbours outside that set are not searched.
  • The switching-log actions are the four the plan named (Telecontrol OPEN, Telecontrol CLOSE, Open from Earth, Confirm Opened). Plain OPEN and CLOSE rows, Confirm Closed, and the parallel-switching actions are not counted. An operation that opens on one day and closes days later flags only its opening day.
  • The price threshold is the 95th percentile of all settlement periods in 2025-07-03 to 2026-06-30, 143.5 pounds per megawatt-hour.
  • Power readings come from studies.power.scan_power, which drops flagged readings. A first run on the raw table gave the same counts for every indicator.
  • Unreported sensitivities. The top 0.5% price indicator covers 1 of 37 days (ordinary 2.7). The union of P1 and P2 covers 24 (ordinary 21.6, p = 0.18).

docs.title: What was looked at
docs.text:
• Public data checks. The 365 cached days of system prices (2025-07-02 to 2026-07-01) hold 17,520 settlement periods: 363 days of 48 periods, one of 50, and one of 46 at the clock changes. There are no duplicate keys and no nulls. Prices run from -97.92 to 800.00 pounds per megawatt-hour, and the monthly mean runs from 64.5 to 103.1 pounds per megawatt-hour. The sell and buy prices are identical in every period.
  • The NGED Connected Data Portal publishes 92 datasets. Of those we looked at, none gives events at the five Primaries for 2025-07 to 2026-06. Live Power Cuts is a live snapshot with no history. Substation Loading (MW and MVAr per bus on an intact-topology basis, with outliers and outages imputed) covers calendar 2024 for the Bicker Fen and Walpole grid supply points. Flexibility trade results deliver from 2026-04 and are mostly small low-voltage zones. The datasets marked Shared hide their download links, and need an access key.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The median forecast minus the mean forecast, and the error of the mean or median forecast beside each quantile-score contrast: not applicable, because the experiment fits no forecasting model and scores no forecast.
  • Which audit triggers fired: none. The audit triggers of the ml-experiment skill concern controls, score contrasts, and nested arms, and this experiment has none of them.

docs.title: Sources not yet tested
docs.text:
Sources we have not tested include local outage notices, local events, and a location join of the metered generators to the Primaries. Planned and unplanned outage notices would test whether a network event, not a change in demand, shaped a block day. School terms and local events would test a change in demand. A location join would let a step in a nearby generator be tested. Experiment 175 found that about half the days show an error that steps for several hours at one substation, and that interconnected neighbours do not mirror the step more often than chance.

An archive request to NGED would need these items: Primary-level MVAr or 5-minute readings, and power-cut and switching records, for 2025-07 to 2026-06 at the five decision Primaries. The request would be a few hundred megabytes and one access key for the Shared portal datasets. NGED has not been asked.

docs.title: Pre-registration
docs.text:
The sections below are the pre-registration, written before any result was read.

  • Raw NGED telemetry fields. The parser keeps only endTime and value from each file's readings, and the stored Delta table has only power, time, and time_series_id. The raw JSON files sit on S3, not on disk.
  • S1, raw switching log (Switching Logs.xlsx, one sheet per time-series pair, "Unknown" for Primaries outside the trial area). Indicator: the substation's own sheet or a sheet of an interconnected Primary holds a row with state Confirmed or Field Confirmed and action Telecontrol OPEN, Telecontrol CLOSE, Open from Earth, or Confirm Opened whose Manual Time falls on the local date or the evening before. Sensitivity: any state; a window of plus or minus 1 day.
  • S2, metered generators. Indicator: a metered generator with the same substation_number as the Primary, or on an interconnected Primary, has a step in its half-hourly power on the local date: a jump of more than 3 times the spread of its day-before changes, lasting at least 4 hours. Sensitivity: any generator in the trial area.
  • S3, reading quality of the substation's own series. Indicator: the local date holds at least 6 missing half-hours, or a run of at least 8 identical consecutive readings, or a reading-count shortfall against the substation's usual 48.
  • S4, own history. Indicator: the same substation has at least two other worst-5% days on the same weekday within 8 weeks, or within plus or minus 3 days of the same date a year earlier. Only dates before the day count for the second branch.
  • Deferred to a later stage: Elexon and NESO public data (demand turn-up, balancing actions, Demand Flexibility Service events), Distribution Future Energy Scenarios (to test local new load), published outage lists, school terms, and local events.
  • Weather the ensemble mean misses (local convective cloud, fog, snow, wind-chill) is a separate cause, and experiment 174 already put an upper bound on that share.
  • Pre-registered checks. The count and rate of each indicator on the 37 days, on each ordinary-day draw (mean and 95% range), and the union; and each indicator's coverage of the whole year, so that an indicator true on most days is reported as uninformative.

Stage 2 addendum, fixed before any public data was read. The raw NGED file check came first: three files, one per decision Primary, carry only startTime, endTime, and value in each reading. Stage 2 reads public data under the same decision rule and the same 1,000 matched ordinary-day draws.

  • P1, DFS events. Source: the NESO DFS service-requirement archive for 2025/2026. Indicator: a live or test DFS event is scheduled on the local date.
  • P2, system price spikes. Source: Elexon settlement system prices for each day. Indicator: the highest system sell price or system buy price in any settlement period of the local date lies in the top 5% of all settlement periods in 2025-07-03 to 2026-06-30.
  • Reading the result. A national indicator can only explain a single-substation block through a mechanism, such as a demand-turn-down event moving load. A rate near the ordinary-day rate is reported as no explanation, however many days the indicator covers.

docs.title: Where does the best GAM lose to the XGBoost model of BG2 on sunny daylight half-hours: which hours, clear-sky bands, leads, or substations?
docs.text:
On sunny daylight half-hours, the best generalised additive model (GAM) has a mean absolute error 0.05 MW higher than BG2. One substation, D5, holds most of that gap. A sunny daylight half-hour is one in the top third of its substation's daylight half-hours, ranked by the output per megawatt of capacity of a fixed south-facing solar fleet driven by CAMS irradiance. BG2 is the second best-guess XGBoost forecast, built in experiment 87. We asked which hour of day, clear-sky band (the ensemble-mean forecast irradiance as a fraction of clear-sky irradiance), lead band (hours between the forecast run and the half-hour), or substation holds the gap. We joined both models' stored forecasts for the scored year on the same substation, daily forecast run, and half-hour, and cut the gap four ways. Without D5, the gap falls to 0.02 MW and its 95% interval, resampled by month, includes zero.

An earlier plot of errors by weather condition gave a gap of 0.13 MW, and we could not reproduce it. The plot's code is not in the repository, so the rows above are our reconstruction. Under this definition the gap is 0.05 MW over all leads, and we do not know whether the plot used different rows. The definition gives 90,143 half-hours over all leads and 13,198 at 12 to 36 hours, against 12,125 in the plot.

The GAM is experiment 164's fix O. It is a convex model fitted by experiment 155 and calibrated by experiments 160 and 164, the same forecast as arm A of experiment 169. Its median forecast equals that of experiment 155's arm D on these rows. BG2 is experiment 87's p_s6_bg2. The ranking uses the unit solar shape of experiment 106's feature cache, the definition experiment 139 uses for its sunniest third.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rows and scope: six substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16, D9), the 291 daily runs of fold_a_daily_gap_v1 that both models forecast, from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, on rows outside the hand-filtered switching events. The plan did not fix the lead range, so the headline uses all leads to 168 hours (chosen after seeing the data). The 12 to 36 hour range, nearest to the plot's row count, is beside it. The "five decision substations" are D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, the substations of the differentiable-physics series' contrasts; D9 is reported beside them.
  • Absolute errors (MW), sunny daylight, all leads: mean absolute error 0.590 for the GAM against 0.541 for BG2; pinball loss 0.166 against 0.152.
  • Gap (GAM minus BG2 mean absolute error, MW), with month-resampled 95% intervals from 12 monthly blocks:
Scope Rows Gap Interval Pinball gap All leads, six substations 90,143 +0.050 +0.014 to +0.079 +0.0143 All leads, five decision substations 74,728 +0.044 +0.006 to +0.071 +0.0123 12 to 36 h, six substations 13,198 +0.031 -0.017 to +0.065 +0.0083 12 to 36 h, five decision substations 10,952 +0.027 -0.018 to +0.059 +0.0072 All leads, D5 only 14,045 +0.202 +0.111 to +0.273 +0.0519 All leads, without D5 76,098 +0.022 -0.009 to +0.046 +0.0073
  • Verdict against the pre-registered rule: partly supported. On the headline definition and all leads the rule is met: D5 holds 63% of the gap with 16% of the rows, and the total gap's interval excludes zero. The rule is not met for the 12 to 36 hour range, whose interval includes zero, or when sunny half-hours are ranked by realised clear-sky index (next bullet). The stated prediction also failed: the shoulder hours did not hold 60% to 70% of the gap.
  • The size of the gap depends on how sunny is defined; D5's loss does not. The audit of this experiment ranked each substation's daylight half-hours three ways (all leads, top third per substation):
Ranking measure Half-hours Total gap D5 only Without D5 Unit solar shape (headline) 87,690 +0.049 (+0.013 to +0.080) +0.206 +0.020 Realised irradiance (CAMS) 87,701 +0.055 (+0.018 to +0.083) +0.219 +0.024 Realised clear-sky index 87,684 +0.015 (-0.024 to +0.049) +0.118 -0.004

The three rows drop half-hours where the clear-sky irradiance is under 20 W per square metre, so the headline row differs slightly from the 90,143 half-hours above. D5 is worse than BG2 under all three, and the other five substations together are level under the third.

  • Cuts (all leads; rule: at least 60% of the gap in a level holding under 40% of the rows):
    • Substation: D5 holds 63% of the gap with 16% of the rows. The rule is met.
    • Clear-sky band: the 0.4 to 0.7 band holds 83% of the gap with 32% of the rows. The rule is met. In this band the GAM's error is 0.749 MW against BG2's 0.622 MW. In the 0.9 and above band, the GAM's error at the five substations other than D5 is 0.438 MW against BG2's 0.499 MW.
    • Hour of day: no 2-hour bin holds more than 32% of the gap (10:00 to 12:00 UK local time), and the two busiest bins hold 26% and 29% of the rows. The rule is not met. The 16:00 to 18:00 bin holds 16% of the gap with 10% of the rows. Without D5, that bin holds 35% of the remaining gap with 10% of the remaining rows.
    • Lead band: 72 to 168 hours holds 77% of the gap and 58% of the rows. The rule is not met.
  • D5 loses in every band: at every hour from 08:00 to 18:00; in all four lead bands (0 to 12 h 0.572 against 0.387 MW, 12 to 36 h 0.581 against 0.393, 36 to 72 h 0.610 against 0.411, 72 to 168 h 0.704 against 0.494); and in every clear-sky band with more than 100 half-hours (0.873 against 0.590 MW at 0.4 to 0.7, 0.523 against 0.412 at 0.7 to 0.9, 0.602 against 0.304 at 0.9 and above). The gap at 0.9 and above (0.298 MW) is about as large as at 0.4 to 0.7 (0.283 MW), so at D5 the loss is not confined to half-hours with a lower clear-sky index.
  • D9 is a second loss site: it holds 27% of the gap with 17% of the rows (0.497 against 0.418 MW), and its loss grows with lead.
  • Solar share: D5 has the largest relative fall from the night mean to the sunny-daylight mean (3.44 to 1.14 MW, 67%), which we use as a proxy for its solar share because the fitted capacities can only be read in the GPU environment, which this session does not have. D10 has the next largest relative fall (2.42 to 1.26 MW, 48%) and the GAM beats BG2 at D10 (-0.009 MW), so solar share alone does not explain D5. D9's sunny-daylight mean is not lower than its night mean.
  • Ensemble clear-sky index on the sunny rows: the median is 0.77, and the 5th to 95th percentile range is 0.52 to 0.98.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Mean versus median forecast: not computable for BG2, which stores no mean. The GAM's stored mean equals its median in the files of experiment 164, so the median is used for both models.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score: the mean absolute error of the median forecast and the pinball loss point the same way in every row of the results table and in every hour bin.
  • Audit conditions met: two of the ml-experiment skill's audit conditions apply. Leaving out one substation changes a verdict: without D5, the all-leads gap's interval includes zero. The result also contradicts the experiment's own prediction, because the shoulder hours did not hold 60% to 70% of the gap. One Opus audit re-derived the conversion, the join, and the gaps from the stored files and reproduced every number. It found that the size of the gap depends on the ranking measure, which the page now reports and which lowered the verdict from supported.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The row set is our reconstruction. The plot's mean absolute error (0.58 against 0.45 MW) is not reproduced: the same definition gives 0.59 against 0.54 over all leads and 0.52 against 0.49 at 12 to 36 hours. An exploratory check that defined sunny days by the realised daily clear-sky index (top third of days) also gave almost no gap (0.44 against 0.45 MW at five substations, 12 to 36 hours, 11,670 half-hours). That daily check is not in the script.
  • Level shares are descriptive. Only the totals carry month-resampled intervals, and 12 monthly blocks make those intervals coarse.
  • The plot's 12,125 half-hours are close to our 13,198 at 12 to 36 hours, and not to our 90,143 over all leads. At 12 to 36 hours the total gap's interval includes zero.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Check the solar shape of D5 and D9 (orientation, tilt, and fitted capacity) against D10, where the GAM does well.
  • Ask for the by-condition plot's row definition and the models it scored, so the 0.13 MW gap can be reproduced before another experiment is built on it.
  • A small neural component looks worth testing, after the cheap shape check above. D5 loses to BG2 in every hour, lead band, and clear-sky band, which points at the fixed south-facing solar shape more than at the irradiance forecast. A learned smooth response from irradiance and solar elevation to solar output, fitted per substation inside the GAM, could replace that shape. The convex GAM stays as the comparison arm. The prediction that can fail: the learned response cuts D5's all-lead gap to BG2 from +0.20 MW to +0.10 MW or less, and raises the error at D10 and D16 (where the GAM already beats BG2) by less than 0.02 MW. If D5's gap stays above +0.15 MW, the cause is not the solar shape.

docs.title: Do the six metered solar farms show an AC clipping plateau, step drops, or slow drift, and is their cleaned series fit to reuse?
docs.text:
Four of the six metered solar farms (C, D, E, and F) flatten at about 1.05 times their capacity at high clear-sky irradiance. The pre-registered test found only two farms, and the flat top may be an export cap rather than AC clipping. We asked whether the six metered solar farms of the trial area (labelled A to F, which anonymises them) show alternating-current (AC) clipping, step drops (outages), or slow drift (soiling or degradation). AC clipping is output flattening at the inverters' alternating-current limit, below the direct-current (DC) capacity of the panels. We plotted each farm's half-hourly power over capacity against clear-sky irradiance from the Ineichen clear-sky irradiance model in the pvlib solar library. We then ran the data-validation checklist, which looks for gaps, duplicates, stuck readings, spurious zeros, and timestamp errors, and wrote a cleaned series in the private data folder, in which flagged half-hours stay in place with a reason. No statistical or forecasting model was fitted.

Under the pre-registered rule, two of six farms (C and E) show clipping, against a prediction of at least four, so the stop rule fires. The stop rule says that follow-up 4 (DC versus AC loss) is dropped when fewer than three farms show clipping. It is therefore dropped for the other four farms.

The rule required the 99th percentile of power within 2% of the 95th at the three highest clear-sky irradiance bins, where each bin is one twentieth of the farm's clear-sky irradiance range. The 99th percentile is above that limit at four farms (A, B, D, and F), which noise or cloud-enhancement events (brief output above clear-sky level) could cause; this was not tested. A rule chosen after seeing Figure 1 (post hoc) asks only that, over the top three bins, the 95th-percentile power rises at under 25% of the rate at which it rises over the lower-middle bins. The pre-registered rule is applied to the binned median, as written; a variant on the 95th percentile finds only E. The post hoc rule finds clipping at farms C, D, E, and F. The maintainer decides whether the stop rule stands.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Clipping tests (clipping_tests.csv), per farm A to F: the ratio of the 99th to the 95th percentile over the top three bins is 1.08, 1.05, 1.02, 1.04, 1.02, and 1.02. The ratio of the binned-median slope over the top three bins to its slope over the lower-middle bins (the pre-registered test, limit 0.10) is 0.14, 0.47, −0.28, −0.04, −0.82, and 0.22, so C and E pass both tests. The same slope ratio on the 95th percentile (post hoc rule, limit 0.25) is 0.85, 0.46, 0.15, −0.09, 0.06, and 0.07.
  • Other causes of a flat top: power was compared with clear-sky irradiance on a horizontal plane, not on the panel plane, so panel tilt and azimuth, and summer heat derating, can flatten power at high sun without any clipping. The highest bins hold only midsummer midday half-hours, so season and irradiance are confounded. Farm C's 95th percentile is still rising in the top bin.
  • Plateau level: the 95th percentile peaks at 1.10, 1.08, 1.05, 1.04, 1.05, and 1.04 times effective capacity for farms A to F. If effective capacity is itself estimated from the observed output, a plateau near 1.0 is partly by construction; this was not checked.
  • Export cap confound: an export cap produces the same flat top, and studies.export_cap was not applied. Clipping and curtailment are not separated.
  • Timestamp convention: each timestamp marks the end of its half-hour. Power correlates best with clear-sky irradiance at lag 0 for all six farms, which is consistent with that convention.
  • Gaps: 7.6% (B) to 27.6% (E) of half-hours are missing, and 22.4% at D. There are no duplicate timestamps.
  • Zeros in clear sun: 134 to 1,291 half-hours per farm read zero or less when clear-sky irradiance exceeds 500 W/m², flagged zero_in_clear_sky (outage or curtailment). These are the counts in the cleaned series; the raw count in validation_checks.csv is 250 to 1,291 and includes E's commissioning period.
  • Stuck runs: 3 half-hours at D only (six or more identical positive daylight readings).
  • Negative readings: 0 to 24 half-hours per farm. Night-time readings above 2% of capacity: 0 to 30 half-hours per farm.
  • Commissioning: 9,226 half-hours at E before 2024-10-06 are flagged, as studies.commissioning already does.
  • Step drops: the test finds total outages only, so a partial outage or missing data goes unseen. Four runs of three or more April-to-September days with peak under 5% of capacity (candidate_outages.csv; a run may span a data gap): B from 2022-08-09 (3 days), D from 2022-08-10 (5 days) and 2022-08-27 (3 days), and E from 2025-09-20 (4 days).
  • Slow drift (trend of the monthly yield index after removing month means, drift.csv, 90% interval from resampling months), farms A to F, in percent per year: −0.55 (−1.5 to +0.4), +0.93 (+0.2 to +1.7), −0.53 (−0.9 to −0.1), −0.08 (−0.9 to +0.6), −1.8 (−4.8 to +1.6, 18 months only), and −0.21 (−0.6 to +0.2). One month at D (February 2020, a partial outage) is left out of the fit. Drift is not detected at A, D, E, or F, with wide uncertainty. B and C have intervals that exclude zero but are small, and the fit includes months with 20 to 25% partial outages.
  • Replication status: the count of farms with clipping is unreplicated, and the post hoc rule is exploratory; no other experiment or data set has confirmed either.
  • Audit triggers: the audit trigger for a result that contradicts its own prediction fires in form. The explanation, a too-strict rule, was tested by the post hoc rule above. The trigger for a later design that depends on an unreplicated result applies, because follow-up 4 depends on the count. This experiment has no control, nested arm, or leave-one-out check. No audit was run; the manager decides whether one is needed.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does each farm's flat top coincide with export-cap hours (studies.export_cap)?
  • What is each farm's DC capacity from an independent source, so that the AC limit can be separated from it?
  • Does a small learned clipping response (a smooth saturation of power against irradiance) fit farms C, D, E, and F better than a hard cap at 1.05 times capacity? The prediction that could fail is that it fits no better.

docs.title: Can a per-substation solar term close the best GAM's sunny-daylight loss to BG2 at D5, without harming the other substations?
docs.text: D5's net power flattens like an export limit, and a 60% ceiling on the solar term removes most of the substation's loss to BG2. We asked whether the best generalised additive model (GAM) loses to BG2 on sunny daylight half-hours at one substation, D5, because the GAM subtracts the wrong solar shape from demand. BG2 is the best-guess forecast of experiment 87, and the gap is the GAM's mean absolute error minus BG2's. Experiment 178 had found that D5 holds 63% of the six-substation gap. We re-ran the GAM of experiment 155 with two alternative solar terms beside the control and scored the same half-hours. Choosing each substation's panel tilt and azimuth did not help. Capping the solar term at 60% of the solar capacity pinned for D5 at each monthly refit, using the smooth clip that experiments 103 and 110 had flagged at D5, cut the gap from +0.202 MW to +0.069 MW. A learned response from irradiance to solar output was not run, because the clip already met the target.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rows and scope: experiment 178's rows, the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads to 168 hours, outside the switching events. A sunny daylight half-hour is in the top third of its substation's daylight half-hours ranked by the fixed fleet shape. D5 has 14,045 such half-hours. The control re-run reproduces experiment 178's D5 gap of +0.202 MW and arm D's forecasts exactly.
  • Absolute scores at D5, sunny daylight (MW): the control's mean absolute error is 0.655, arm P's is 0.637, arm K's is 0.523, and BG2's is 0.453. Pinball loss (average over 11 quantiles) is 0.185 for the control, 0.181 for P, and 0.154 for K.
  • Headline (arm K minus control, mean absolute error, 98.75% interval): -0.133 MW (-0.214 to -0.033). The gap to BG2 falls to +0.069 MW (98.75% interval +0.023 to +0.094). Over all D5 half-hours, arm K's gap to BG2 is -0.011 MW (-0.040 to +0.009), against +0.007 MW for the control.
  • Placebos: arm K moves D10 by +0.004 MW (-0.025 to +0.037) and D16 by -0.004 MW (-0.051 to +0.049), inside the 0.02 MW margin. Over all half-hours the clip raises D10's error by +0.005 MW (+0.001 to +0.011) and D16's by +0.006 MW (-0.000 to +0.014), and the audit found rises of +0.012 to +0.020 MW on daylight half-hours outside the sunny third at D5, D10, and D16. A clip belongs only where the export limit exists. Arm K was not run at D9, D11, or D14.
  • Arm P (tilt and azimuth): the selection kept the fleet shape at D11 and D9. It chose a tilt of 15 degrees at D5, 55 at D10, and 15 at D14 and D16. The sunny-daylight change against the control is -0.018 MW at D5 (-0.031 to +0.007), +0.007 at D10 (-0.001 to +0.014), -0.008 at D14, and -0.008 at D16, none with an interval excluding zero. The 25-cell selection surface per substation is in the private work/select.json.
  • A fixed ceiling in points gives the same gain. D5's held capacity swings from 62 to 81 points across the cuts, so a ceiling of 60% of it moves with the capacity. A post hoc arm with a fixed ceiling of 39 points (60% of the held capacity's typical value before the scored year) gives -0.130 MW (-0.225 to -0.021) on the scored year and -0.088 and -0.119 MW on the tuning and replicate months, so the gain does not come from the capacity's swings.
  • Six-substation total: with arm K at D5 and the control elsewhere, the total sunny-daylight gap to BG2 is about +0.029 MW, against +0.050 MW (computed from the per-substation means, without an interval).
  • By-condition slices at D5 (mean absolute error, MW; control, K): all half-hours 0.344 and 0.325; winter 0.365 and 0.367; winter nights 0.225 and 0.226; cold nights (834 half-hours) 0.197 and 0.201; Economy 7 step hours 0.156 and 0.155; bank holidays (1,900 half-hours) 0.328 and 0.291. Arm K changes none of the winter slices by an interval excluding zero. Over all D5 half-hours it lowers the error by 0.018 MW (-0.041 to -0.000). Christmas has too few half-hours to score.
  • Decision rule: supported. The best arm's D5 gap is +0.069 MW against a target of +0.10 MW, its interval against the control lies wholly below zero, and both placebos move by under 0.02 MW. The other four substations are unchanged by construction for arm K.
  • Not run: the learned response (arm L), the neural network (arm N), the farm-learned response (arm F), and known-answer gates 1 and 2. The plan ran them only if the target stayed out of reach (arm N) or after the gates (arms L and F), and arm K met the target. Gate 1 was not run, so the cap at inconclusive does not apply.
  • Post hoc: the clip ceiling. The plan fixed 100% of held capacity, which clips nothing, so the planned arm K gave an exact null (-0.000 MW). We then scored ceilings of 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, and 90%, and chose 60% on the tuning months alone. The replicate months agreed (figure 3). The scored year was read for arm K at 60% after that choice. The scored year had also been read earlier for arm K at 80%, the first post hoc guess, before the sweep. The other ceilings were scored on the tuning and replicate months only. The scores of every ceiling and of the null arm are in the private work/scores_*.json files.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast: zero at all six substations in arm D's stored forecasts (the mean equals the median), so no spread shifts the forecast.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score: the pinball loss and the mean absolute error point the same way at D5, D10, and D16 for arm K. At the placebos both are indistinguishable from the control.
  • Tail calibration at D5, sunny rows (coverage; pinball loss in MW): for the control, q01 0.051 and 0.025, q05 0.168 and 0.097, q95 0.967 and 0.081, q99 0.993 and 0.022. For arm K, q01 0.056 and 0.023, q05 0.176 and 0.085, q95 0.996 and 0.076, q99 0.999 and 0.021. Arm K lowers the pinball loss at all four quantiles, but the lower tail stays under-covered (q05 coverage 0.18 against 0.05 nominal).
  • Triggers fired: a result that contradicts its own prediction (the plan expected no arm to reach +0.10 MW). The explanation, tested before the audit, is figure 4: D5's solar output per unit of shape falls towards midday while the other four substations stay flat. The Opus audit reproduced the headline (-0.133 MW, 98.75% interval -0.223 to -0.036) and found no leakage. The Sonnet code review found that arm P's fits had been trained on the fleet shape; we fixed that, refitted arm P, and replaced its numbers. The audit's request for a ceiling fixed in points is the fixed-ceiling bullet above.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• One substation and one year. The headline interval is 98.75% from 12 monthly blocks, and it spans -0.214 to -0.033 MW. The clip ceiling was chosen on 6 tuning months at the same substation.
  • The clip ceiling is a share of the capacity held after each cut. It follows the pinned capacity, so a step in D5's capacity moves the ceiling with it.
  • The learned response was not tested. Whether it beats the clip at D5 is unknown.
  • The gain is concentrated late in the scored year. The audit found 80% of it in April to June 2026, though dropping any one month leaves it between -0.100 and -0.147 MW, and every lead band improves (-0.087 MW at 0 to 24 hours to -0.147 MW).
  • The clip is a partial fix. On clear summer days D5's net power stays flat from about 08:00 to 15:00 UTC, as an export limit would make it, and D10 and D16 show no plateau. The shoulder half-hours keep an error, and the sunny rows keep a negative bias (the forecast is too low by 0.36 MW for the control and 0.39 MW for arm K).
  • Shared limits of the chain. The monthly fits train on the CAMS-derived shape of experiment 106's cache and the forecasts use a shape recomputed from the same irradiance, which is identical to 1e-9 for the fleet. Arm P's selection scored all half-hours with a reading, including those in the switching events.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Re-score the 60% ceiling at D5 on a later year, once the hold-out from 2026-07-01 is lifted.
