• Median minus mean forecast, per substation (located-onset arm, part 2 rows). D10 -0.110, D11 -0.055, D14 +0.022, D16 +0.035, D5 -0.367, D9 -0.074 points. The part 1 values are those of experiment 171.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile contrast. Part 2, alarm time minus located onset: +0.556 (+0.253 to +0.873) in the mean absolute error, the same direction as the quantile score. Part 1 reuses experiment 171's score tables, and its mean-forecast check (+0.064) was not recomputed after the removal.
  • Audit triggers. None fired on the injected rows. On the 15 real transfers the true-onset mask (7.695) scores worse than no mask (6.899) and worse than the alarm-time mask (7.065), so the true-onset mask is not a floor on real data; those rows decide nothing. No control failed, the result does not contradict an earlier finding or the prediction, the quantile and mean-forecast contrasts agree, leaving one substation out changes no verdict, and no nested arm beats the arm that contains it. The interval of part 1 (half-width 0.036) is 0.86 of experiment 171's 0.042. No audit was run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The alarm-time mask is a comparison arm, not an earlier design. Experiment 171 already masks from the detector's step stamp, so C2 mainly shows what masking back to the step is worth.
  • Part 1's removal lowers the contrast by construction. Rows with a gated alarm active carry the whole difference, so removing confirmed events removes some of it. The informative results are the small confirmed share, the 5.6% placebo share, and the harm that stays on unconfirmed alarms.
  • The confirmation rule has no positive control. Its recall was not measured on logged transfers or injected events, so a low confirmed share could also mean a low-power rule. The 5.6% placebo share bounds only the chance rate.
  • The confirmation rule is one choice. A looser step test, or one that used the metered neighbours' own power, could confirm more alarms.
  • Counts of transfers. The 247 injected transfers are (world, substation, transfer, alarm) rows, 210 distinct (world, substation, transfer) combinations, because a transfer found by both alarms counts once for each; the pooled interval treats them as independent, and the whole-world resampling partly covers this. The location errors are over all 153 pair-alarm and 430 RO-NC matches, of which 87 and 160 have scored forecast rows.
  • The step stamp's location error is truncated. An alarm counts as finding a transfer only when its step stamp lies within 24 hours of the true onset, so the step stamp's error cannot exceed 48 half-hours, while the located onset (searched 24 hours either side of the step stamp) can. That truncation favours the step stamp in the location comparison.
  • The alarm-time mask starts at the known stamp. The plan said the first usable origin's newest stamp; the code masks from the known stamp, up to 11 half-hours earlier (mean 5.0 to 5.7). That makes the alarm-time arm slightly better than registered and biases C2 downward.
  • Overlapping alarms. Every alarm at a substation is applied to every scored row there, so a row scored for one transfer can see another alarm's located onset, computed from readings up to 11 half-hours after that row's cutoff. The share of rows affected was not counted.
  • The overall verdict is a judgement. The plan registered a verdict for each part only.
  • The real logged transfers are few. 15 transfers found by an alarm, and the logged onset is coarser than a half-hour.
  • Lab shortcuts. The residual comes from the analysis proxy (a weather estimate for the recent past), the transfers are injected as constant-weight shares, and the end rule is that of experiments 147 and 148.
  • The forecasts are daily. A 6-hourly cadence is simulated by taking, per found transfer, the one daily run whose newest stamp lies in the first 24 hours after the first origin that sees the alarm. The located onset is computed once, at that first origin.
  • The retraining schedule does not affect the contrasts. The cached forecasts are the frozen stack of experiment 171, with no refitting, so the contrasts do not depend on a retraining schedule.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next question is why D10's gated alarms raise the error when most of them match no opposite step: whether they are false alarms that a stricter gate would drop, which would show in a gate tuned on the rows with an active alarm. Showing no harm needs about 54 months of forecasts, as in experiment 171.

docs.title: Experiment 189: can a small neural network, trained on realistic injected transfers, find real load shifts?
docs.text:
A small neural network (33,604 learned weights), trained only on synthetic transfers, found 7 of the 35 real transfers that lasted longer than 1 day. The rule-based detector RO-NC found 18. A transfer is a period, labelled by hand in experiment 41, in which switching moved load from one Primary substation (a substation that steps transmission voltage down to distribution voltage) to neighbouring Primary substations. A transfer counts as found when an alarm falls within 2 hours of its start and the alarm's end falls within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration of the true end. RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector of experiment 82, scored at 80 unexplained alarms in experiment 181: an unexplained alarm is one not near a logged closure or labelled transfer, and the count is over odd-numbered months.

We built an injector that adds synthetic transfers to the real residuals (observed minus forecast power from the convex demand model of experiment 130). Its depth, duration, start time, shape, and receivers are fitted to the real events. We trained the network on 7-day windows of one Primary substation's residual and its neighbours', and scored it on real transfers of Primary pairs it had never seen. The verdict is refuted, because the pre-registered prediction was at least 15 found. The start of a transfer is learnable, and the end is the weak part. The network placed the start within 2 hours for 12 of the 35 transfers (17 after a second, longer training run), against 20 for RO-NC, and the median start error among transfers found was 0.5 hours.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Architecture. Dilated one-dimensional convolutions, 33,604 weights. Inputs: 336 half-hours of the Primary's residual and the four most-read neighbours' (each divided by its noise unit, with a present-or-not channel), the hour of day, and a bank-holiday flag. Outputs: a start alarm, an end alarm, and a per-half-hour map for each. The network assigns each onset alarm the earliest end alarm after it as its end.
  • Training data. D8 and D9 are two of the 16 Primary substations. Windows come from even-numbered months only: 80,000 windows per fold (40% with an injected transfer, the rest real stretches with no logged or labelled event, a fifth near bank holidays, a fifth on D8, a fifth on D9). The network never sees a real event.
  • Folds. The 66 labelled transfers fall in 23 Primary pairs, grouped into 3 folds. Each fold's network and injector are fitted without that fold's pairs (including D8 drops that overlap them).
  • Real transfers over 1 day (35), 80 unexplained odd-month alarms, experiment 130's rule (start within 2 hours, end within the larger of 6 hours and 10%):
Detector Start and end found Start only found Pair alarm (experiment 156, quoted) 5 not run RO-NC on the convex residual 18 20 Network, 14 epochs (pre-registered, seed 0) 7 12 Network, 40 epochs (post hoc, seed 1) 8 17
  • All 66 labelled transfers: the 14-epoch network finds 12 (start only 23) and the 40-epoch network 19 (start only 31), against 18 for RO-NC. The 31 transfers of 24 hours or less are mostly found by start alone.
  • Found against alarms (35 transfers). Pre-registered network at 20, 40, 80, 160, and 320 alarms: 1, 5, 7, 9, 15. Post hoc network: 2, 4, 8, 12, 14.
  • Median start error of found transfers: 0.5 hours (both networks).
  • Injected transfers (odd months, same thresholds), start and end found: 21% to 34% for the 14-epoch network (21% on Primary pairs it never saw, 34% on the pairs the injector was fitted on), 21% to 23% for the 40-epoch network. The network is as weak on injected as on real transfers, so the failure is not that the injector is easier than the real events.
  • Realism check 1. A logistic regression on nine features measured from the residual (log depth in noise units and in MW, log duration, start hour as sine and cosine, weekend flag, day-night difference, count of opposite neighbours, balance, series count) separates real from injected events with area under the curve 0.59 (95% 0.52 to 0.66; 63 real events against 336 injected). The point estimate meets the pre-registered limit of 0.65, the upper end of the interval does not.
  • Realism check 2. A stand-in for RO-NC (a 24-hour step above its threshold) has onset recall 67% on real transfers over 1 day and 54% on injected ones, a gap of 12 points against the pre-registered tolerance of 10; for all durations the gap is 9 points (38% against 29%). The injected events are slightly harder than the real ones. The check therefore marginally fails for transfers over 1 day.
  • 17 unlabelled block days of experiment 175. Each fold's network is scored on all 17 days at 80 alarms. The 14-epoch networks find 1, 0, and 0 days, the 40-epoch networks find 1, 1, and 1, and the block detector of experiment 181 found 0.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, mean-forecast error, tail calibration, curtailment cost: not applicable, because no forecast is scored.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 fired (the result contradicts its prediction of at least 15). The explanation tested here is that the injector might be too easy: it is not, because the network also fails on injected transfers. No Opus audit was run (the Sonnet leakage review is below). The other six audit triggers of the ml-experiment skill did not fire; the check that leaves one site out was not run.

docs.title: Review and deviations
docs.text:
• A Sonnet code review found a leak, fixed before scoring: D8 drops overlapping two labelled transfers entered every fold's injector fit. Drops that overlap a held-out transfer are now excluded. A second fix: an all-missing donor window produced NaN inputs.
  • Reviewer findings not acted on. The threshold ignores alarms inside labelled spans and gives the end alarm its own 80-alarm budget, so the combined budget is looser than RO-NC's; this favours the network, which still fails. Early stopping used even-month windows after the review. The classifier features cannot see edge sharpness or noise; a convolutional discriminator on raw windows would be a stronger test. The stand-in's threshold was tuned on the same real events. Logged closures at a held-out Primary with a different side tuple are not excluded from the duration fit.
  • Post hoc. The 40-epoch run (seed 1) was added after the 14-epoch run failed; its validation loss was not lower, so it is a second draw and not an improvement. Only seed 0 is pre-registered.
  • Lab shortcuts. The residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late. The end alarm uses the days after the end (hindsight). Transfers are injected into the residual, not the power.
  • Not done. The brief's optional learned alarm reliability classifier (item 2).
  • Interim report. The experiment manager's session was inactive, so no interim message was sent.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
One option is to pair the learned start alarm with RO-NC's end rule, because the start alone finds 12 to 17 transfers and the end is where the network fails. Another is a window long enough to hold the end of a multi-day transfer, with the injector's durations fitted to the labelled transfers only.

Code: ml-experiments/00189-switching-neural-onset-end-block-detector/; numbers are printed to printed_realism.txt, printed_score_seed0.json, and printed_score_seed1.json in that folder.

docs.title: Faster Kalman level state when the residual keeps one sign
docs.text:
Take-home: this test could not tell whether a faster level state helps. The gated version scored the same as the current filter and the always-fast version scored worse. The gate could not have been passed by any filter with one state per hour band, so the null says little about filter speed. A redesigned gate and a wider grid of multipliers are the fair test.

We asked whether a Kalman filter that speeds up its level state when the recent forecast errors keep one sign cuts the loss on days when the forecast error keeps one sign for hours, without harming ordinary days. The level state is the slowly moving offset that the filter adds to the forecast. The filter is that of the convex demand model (experiment 111), and the forecast it corrects is the best-guess forecast of experiment 155 (arm D). We first added a known one-signed offset to the observed power of ordinary days and measured how much of its extra loss each filter removed. We then scored the filters on the real scored year at the five decision Primaries. Arm D is rebuilt here to the stored quantile score (2.7562 points against 2.756 points, inside the plan's tolerance of 0.005 points).

Verdict: inconclusive, by the pre-registered rule that a failed gate caps the verdict. The gate asked for at least 50% recovery of the extra loss, for an offset of 0.10 of the day's median load lasting 16 hours and lasting 36 hours. The gated boost recovered -0.6% (95% interval -3.6% to +0.9%) and +0.4% (-1.3% to +2.2%). The audit found that the gate's ceiling lies far below the pass mark (see "Audit").

docs.title: Arms and method
docs.text:
• A0: arm D of experiment 155: the T-all fits on the ensemble-mean weather (experiment 136's A2), the winter night offset, and recipe R, with the spread refitted on the tuning months.
  • A1, A2, A3: only the level's process noise changes, as in the plan. A1 multiplies it by m while the counter is on. A2 multiplies it at every reading. A3 is A1 with the level increment shared across the four hour bands. The counter reads the one-step innovations in time order across bands.
  • Tuning: the grid of 18 settings was scored on the odd tuning months of 2024-07 to 2025-06 at stage 1, with A0's spread held fixed. The pre-registered point (m 5, k 6, z 1.0) scored 2.7506 against A0's 2.7486. The best cell (m 5, k 8, z 0.5) scored 2.7450, 0.0056 below the pre-registered point, which passes the 0.005 rule, so the frozen setting is m 5, k 8, z 0.5.
  • Row set: fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the five decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, 464,363 rows outside switching events. Telemetry delay 3.5 hours. Retraining schedule: monthly T-all fits stored by experiment 136; the contrast could depend on the schedule only through the filter's residuals, which every arm shares.
  • Gate (lab shortcuts): offsets of 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20 of the day's median load lasting 8, 16, and 36 hours, 8 days per substation per cell (40 per cell), on days of the even months. The forecast of a half-hour is the proxy-weather prediction plus the filter's correction, with origins every 6 hours. The loss uses a quantile table from the clean tuning-month errors. A matched 40 days without injection show the harm.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Scores, scored year, quantile score in points (lower is better):

  • A0 2.7562, A1 2.7564, A2 2.7791, A3 2.8336 (spread refitted). Stage-1 versions: 2.7910, 2.7904, 2.8232, 2.8969.
  • With experiment 169's calibrated spread held fixed: A0 2.7521, A1 2.7568, A2 2.7897, A3 2.8499.
  • C1 A1 minus A0: +0.0002 (95% interval -0.0046 to +0.0062; 1 of 5 substations better). With the fixed spread: +0.0048 (+0.0004 to +0.0103), a small loss.
  • C2 A2 minus A0: +0.0229 (-0.0023 to +0.0482). C3 A1 minus A2: -0.0227 (-0.0489 to +0.0045). C4 A3 minus A1: +0.0773 (+0.0450 to +0.1136; 0 of 5 substations better).
  • The gate's counter was on for 0.6% to 1.2% of readings at the five substations (326 to 585 triggers).

Pre-registered predictions:

  • P1 fails. On the 15 smooth-offset days of experiment 175, A1 changed the excess loss by -1.4% (interval -2.5% to +0.3%); a cut of 20% was predicted.
  • P2 holds with the refitted spread. A1 minus A0 is +0.0002 and the upper bound is +0.0062. With the fixed spread the upper bound is +0.0103, just above the +0.01 limit.
  • P3 holds on the point estimate only. A1 beats A2 by 0.023 points, with an interval that includes zero (excluding it with the fixed spread: -0.033, -0.057 to -0.007).
  • P4 fails. A3 changed the excess loss on the smooth-offset days by -9.5% (-20.4% to +6.4%), worse than A1.
  • P5 holds. On the 17 block days A1 cut the excess loss by 1.5% (+0.1% to +3.7%).

Known-answer gate:

  • A1 recovered -0.4%, -0.6%, and +0.4% of the offset's excess loss at the 0.10 size for 8, 16, and 36 hours. At the 0.20 size the values for A1 were within about 3% of zero.
  • The excess loss of A0 at the 0.10 size was 1.5, 1.0, and 0.9 points of quantile score, so there was loss to recover.
  • A1 minus A0 on the 40 left-alone days: -0.001 points (-0.014 to +0.014); A2 +0.079 (+0.001 to +0.159); A3 +0.015 (-0.074 to +0.111).
  • Post hoc, a multiplier of 100 on A1, A2, and A3 recovered less: -110% to +10% at the 0.10 and 0.20 sizes (A1: -25% at 16 hours, A2: -45%, A3: -114%), 40 cases per cell.
  • The harm half of the gate also failed: A1 minus A0 on the left-alone days has an interval of -0.014 to +0.014, wider than the pass mark of +0.005, and the post hoc multiplier of 100 on A1 raised the quantile score by 0.28 points (+0.15 to +0.42).
  • Wiring check (e00190_wiring_check.py): on a stream with no noise, A0 follows a 7.8-point offset to between 4.9 and 7.1 points, A1 to between 5.2 and 7.1, and A3 also moves the bands that have not yet been read, as designed (8.6 points in one band). The code does what the plan specifies.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
The audit (a fresh Opus agent, private brief e190_audit.md) re-derived the gate losses to within 4e-15 points, and found no bug in the injection, the filter, the reproduction, or the tuning. It made three findings about the design:

  • The gate's ceiling lies below its pass mark (F1). The filter keeps one state per hour band, the telemetry delay is 3.5 hours, and the first origins come 6 hours before the offset starts. On most pairs the target's band has not been read since the offset began, so every per-band filter gives the clean correction there. An oracle that knew the offset exactly, but only where the target's own band had been read, would recover 0.5% (16 hours) and 9% (36 hours) at the 0.10 size. An oracle that used any band would recover 25% and 39%. No filter could have reached 50%.
  • Faster filters do recover where the offset is visible (F2). On pairs whose band had been read since the offset began, the always-on boost recovered 52% (0.10 size, 36 hours) and a multiplier of 100 recovered 69% (0.20 size, 36 hours). Those pairs are a small share of all pairs (2% to 38%).
  • A multiplier of 5 barely changes the filter (F3). At steady state the level gain rises from 0.066 to 0.082, because the autoregressive transient already supplies a total gain of about 0.38. The gated boost is therefore close to arm D by construction.

The scored-year contrasts and the verdict stand.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast per site: 0.00 at every site and arm.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score: C1 on the mean absolute error is +0.0060 (-0.0011 to +0.0139), the same direction as the quantile score; C3 is -0.0567 (-0.0971 to -0.0157).
  • Tails (all rows, q95 coverage 0.947 to 0.949 for every arm; q99 0.983 to 0.984). On the 5,395 cold-night rows: q95 coverage 0.837 (A0), 0.841 (A1), 0.858 (A2), 0.763 (A3); quantile score 3.342, 3.317, 3.309, 3.765.
  • Rows within 24 hours after a trigger (194,765 rows): C1 +0.0009 (-0.0060 to +0.0083).
  • Audit triggers: trigger 1 fired (the known-answer gate failed) and the audit above ran.
  • Curtailment cost was not scored: this experiment has no generator forecasts to feed the node-plus-generators metric.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The gate runs on the proxy-weather forecast, not on ensemble weather, so it removes weather error from the comparison.
  • The gate as run cannot be passed (see "Audit"), so its recovery numbers are not a measure of filter speed.
  • Tuning used the stage-1 score, not arm D's, and every setting was scored with A0's spread table, which understates the gain of a setting whose errors are smaller.
  • The counter counts readings, so after a gap in the data it can span more than the stated hours.
  • The subsets "within 24 hours after a trigger" and cold nights are defined after the fact, from triggers and temperatures that a run at the origin could not yet see.
  • The post hoc settings (a1_fast, and the multiplier of 100) are diagnostic only.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Redesign the gate: score recovery only on pairs whose target band has been read since the offset began, or as a share of the oracle ceiling, and start origins after the offset starts.
  • Widen the grid of multipliers beyond 10 (the audit's multiplier of 100 recovered 69% where the offset was visible), and test whether a shared level across bands removes the per-band limit.
  • Look at the mean model as well: on the plotted day every arm forecasts about 10 points too high all day.
  • A small learned correction that reads whether several neighbouring Primaries show the same-sign residual (a neural head on the filter's innovations). The prediction that could fail: it recovers at least 20% of the excess loss on the 15 smooth-offset days, which none of the four filters here did.

docs.title: Experiment 191: can price-following assets be modelled in the history so the forecast improves?
docs.text: Take-home message: modelling a price-following asset in the history does not improve the forecast at D8 or D14. D8 and D14 are two primary substations of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) in the Boston area. A price-following asset is a generator or battery whose output follows the electricity price. Experiment 186 found that D8's multi-day drops in demand look partly like a gas engine that runs when the spark spread is positive. The spark spread is the system price minus the gas cost of generating one MWh of electricity. In the data we have, a price is not forecastable days ahead, so we asked a narrower question: if the demand model sees the price in its training history, does it learn a cleaner picture of the rest of the demand, and does the forecast improve even when the price is unknown at forecast time? We added four price indicators to a convex demand model (GAM-K, a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on recent errors), each lowering net load by a fitted, non-negative amount, switched on from the connection date of a registered 6 MW gas engine. We tested four arms (H, M, P and T, defined under Arms) that differ in what stands in for the price at forecast time, and scored the forecasts on the year 2025-07 to 2026-06, which no fit had seen. The best arm, H, which uses the true price at forecast time and so cannot run live, lowers D8's mean absolute error by 0.6%, with a 95% interval that includes zero. The pre-registered bar was a 5% fall, so the verdict is not supported. The reference demand model reproduces experiment 152 to numerical precision (see Checks), and the gas engine's response is visible in the fitted coefficients, but the response does not carry forward to the scored year.

docs.title: Inputs and arms
docs.text:
• The register. NGED's Embedded Capacity Register (August 2026) lists one connected gas engine that is not combined heat and power under the Primaries with metered series: 6 MW, connected on 2023-06-13, 0.4 km from D14's coordinates and about 0.8 km from D8's. D8 itself lists only solar and a 1.35 MW row of unknown type. D5 has a 1 MW gas engine connected in 2021. Batteries of 0.2 to 0.25 MW are connected at D2, D9, and D11 (2024 to 2026), and two more are accepted but not connected, at D3 and D16. The demand-side-response sheet holds no rows. The eight other Primaries that the register covers list no price-following asset (printed_ecr.txt).
  • Reference (A0). The ensemble-driven convex demand model of experiment 152 (fitted solar capacity, monthly refits on a 24-month window, shared Kalman filter, spread fitted on tuning months), with no price input. At D8 it has 12 monthly fits from 3 to 14 months of history, because the series is valid only from 2025-04-01. At D14 it has 27 fits. It is not the best-guess stack of experiment 155: the winter night offset and the 14-day error profile are absent, because D8 has no tuning months to fit the offset on. At D14 the reference's mean absolute error is 3.84 points against 3.69 for the best-guess stack.
  • Arms. H uses the true price at forecast time (a ceiling). M uses the expected indicator given the half-hour of the day, day type and quarter. P uses the last settled day's indicator at the same half-hour, the only price known at the 09:00 UTC origin. T removes the half-hours that the fitted price term explains from training and forecasts without a price term. A diagnostic arm (JB) is the price-aware fit's base model with its price term switched off at forecast time. The learned monotone price curve (the plan's optional neural arm) was not run.
  • Price indicators. System price above its 50th, 75th, and 90th percentile, and a positive spark spread at 40% efficiency (system price minus the gas cost of one MWh of electricity minus 5 pounds per MWh), from public data, 2023-06 to 2026-06 (2023-05-31 to 2026-07-01 in UTC). The percentile thresholds are fixed over the whole of that price history, including the scored year, so the cut-off values (not any individual price) look ahead slightly; the "high price" scoring cut shares that definition. The gate is 1 from the engine's connection date and 0 before, so a site with no asset has no price term.
  • Masking rule (fixed after one coefficient check, before any score was read). T drops a training half-hour when the fitted price output there is at least 25% of the largest fitted output and that largest output is at least 1 point (1% of the substation's effective capacity). Without the 1-point floor the rule dropped half of D14's training rows for a response of 0.04 MW.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Absolute scores (D8, scored year, all rows, leads 0.5 to 168 hours). Reference: mean absolute error 15.18 points (1.6 MW), quantile score 10.95, q05-to-q95 coverage 0.42 (42%). D14: mean absolute error 3.84, quantile score 2.16, coverage 0.89.
  • Mean absolute error against the reference, D8. H -0.64% (-2.53% to +1.11%), M +0.88% (-0.37% to +2.28%), P +4.41% (+3.00% to +5.83%), T +3.44% (+0.84% to +6.41%), JB +5.73% (+2.56% to +8.66%). The quantile score gives the same signs: H -1.04%, M +1.00%, P +5.36%, T +4.56%.
  • Mean absolute error against the reference, D14. H +0.49% (+0.23% to +0.78%), M +0.02%, P +0.16%, T +0.14%, JB -0.13% (-0.54% to +0.24%).
  • High-spread half-hours (spark spread above zero), D8. The reference's error is 16.37 points against 13.96 on other half-hours. H -0.74%, M +1.08%, P +3.73%, T +5.27%. No arm is significantly better where the price signal should be strongest.
  • By lead, D8, H. The quantile score falls 2.2% (interval -4.3% to -0.05%, not corrected for the number of cuts) at 0 to 24 hours, 1.8% at 24 to 72 hours and 0.4% at 72 to 168 hours.
  • In-sample gain (the ceiling). On each fit's own training rows the price columns lower D8's mean absolute error by 4.1% on average over the 12 fits (2.7% to 4.8%). The fitted response, with all four indicators on, is 1.9 MW at the first fit and 1.2 MW at the last. At D14 the in-sample gain is 0.0% and the response is 0 to 0.13 MW. At D5 it is 0.0%.
  • No-harm check. The largest rise in quantile score at any of the five decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16) is 0.011 points, at D14 for H, against the 0.02 limit. With the gate switched on for the whole history at sites with no asset (placebo), D10 rises by 0.009 points for H.
  • Tails. At D8 the reference's q05 quantile lies above 30.8% of readings (nominal 5%), q95 above 73.1% (nominal 95%), q01 above 20.6% (1%) and q99 above 83.9% (99%). H changes none of them by more than 0.5 points. D14 is close to nominal (q05 6.4%, q95 95.1%). The D8 spread comes from six other Primaries and is far too narrow for D8, so D8's quantile scores are weaker evidence than its mean absolute errors.
  • Post hoc: settlement-day indicators. Replacing the half-hourly indicators by the settlement day's mean price and spread lowers nothing: D8 H +2.23% (+0.42% to +4.28%), M +2.40%, P +3.83%, T +5.75%.
  • Not computed. The curtailment-cost metric (it needs a node and its generators) and the climatology and manual-heuristic baselines named in the plan's benchmark, so absolute skill is reported against the reference only.
  • Intervals. The intervals printed here are 95% month-block bootstrap intervals. The plan registered a 99.4% Bonferroni level, which would widen every interval and cannot change the verdict, because H's 95% interval already includes zero.
  • Post hoc daily variant, arm P. In the settlement-day variant below, arm P uses a day mean that can include half-hours after the 09:00 UTC origin, so that one P row is not a live arm.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits on a 24-month window, as in experiment 152, not weekly refits, so the absolute scores are not production-setting scores. The contrasts could depend on the schedule at D8, where a longer history would help the price columns.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Control. The reference reproduces the stored arm N of experiment 152 at D8 (mean absolute gap 1e-12 on 97,012 rows) and studies.dp_gam.fit_gam at one cut (largest coefficient gap 2e-10). Where the gate is off (D10, D11, D16) every arm equals the reference.
  • Median minus mean forecast. 0.000 points at every site and arm, because the spread is symmetric about the corrected mean.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score. Both are reported in Results and have the same sign in every contrast of the main tables.
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 2 fired: H gained 0.6% against a pre-registered 5%. The explanation was tested and is the in-sample figure: even on the rows the price columns are fitted to they explain at most 4.8%. Trigger 5 fired: at D14 H, which contains the reference, is 0.49% worse than the reference. JB, which keeps the base fit and drops the price term, is within 0.13% of the reference, so the loss comes from the price term, whose coefficients move between 0 and 0.9 points from fit to fit. No Opus audit was run, because neither result changes the next step. Triggers 1, 3, 4, 6, and 7 did not fire.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does a spread fitted on D8's own residuals change the picture? The reference covers 42% of readings where it should cover 90%, so D8's interval scores are weak evidence.
  • Does a wider band on spark-spread-positive days help? D8's error is 17% larger on those half-hours. This was not tested.
  • What does the engine's own output show? The price indicators reach at most 4.8% of the error on their own training rows, and the engine's half-hourly output would test the cause directly.

docs.title: Experiment 192: ensemble members through the temperature terms, scored on cold nights
docs.text:
Running each ensemble member's temperature through the demand model's heating terms does not improve the forecast bands on cold winter nights. The 51 members' temperatures differ by too little for their disagreement to carry a detectable signal about the day's error. Experiment 187 found that passing the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble through the solar term of the demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. The maintainer expected the same on cold nights, where heating responds to temperature nonlinearly and the ensemble mean smooths away the cold tail. We reused experiment 187's method: the demand model is linear in its fitted weights, so each member's forecast is the best-guess mean forecast (arm A) plus the member's response, and the 11 quantiles are those of the 51 forecasts, each forecast getting arm A's 11 quantile offsets added around that forecast. Arm T passes only the members' temperature (current and trailing means, through the heating hinge and the photovoltaic (PV) cell-temperature derating), arm ST passes every weather input, and the quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand; lower is better). D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised substations. A cold night is a half-hour with an ensemble-mean forecast temperature under 2 degrees C between 17:00 and 08:00 local time. The scored year is 2025-07 to 2026-06, and the replicate months are the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06.

The pre-registered prediction failed. Arm T lowers the cold-night score by 0.08% (97.5% interval -1.96% to +0.38%) against the required 1.5%, and cold-night coverage of the q05-to-q95 band moves away from 0.90, to 0.857 from 0.880. Arm ST gives the same numbers, because the solar term does nothing at night. The cold-night gain is far below the daylight gain of experiment 187.

  • Arms and row set. A: reference (experiment 187's arm A, the full best-guess stack; 2.494 points on cold nights, 2.752 on all rows in the scored year). T: members through temperature. ST: members through every input (experiment 184's all-input responses, reproduced exactly by this experiment's code). M: experiment 187's solar-only members, applied on every row. The row set is fold_a_daily_gap_v1: substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, forecast leads of 0.5 to 168 hours, excluding hand-filtered switching events. Each arm's factors on arm A's offsets (one per lead band and per daylight, twilight, or night) were fitted on the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06. Mean forecasts are experiment 155's monthly refits.
  • Weather used. Calibrated ECMWF ensemble temperature of experiment 111, available at forecast time; trailing temperature means stitch the analysis proxy before the forecast origin. Lighting depends only on solar elevation, so it receives no member input, and the demand model has no wind or cloud input, so the planned arm W was not run.
  • Pre-registered contrasts (cold nights, change from A, 97.5% interval). Scored year: T -0.08% (-1.96% to +0.38%), ST -0.08% (-1.96% to +0.38%). Replicate months: T -0.12% (-1.24% to +1.50%), ST -0.11% (-1.23% to +1.50%). Verdict rule: not met.
  • Absolute scores, cold nights (quantile score; scored year, replicate months). A 2.494, 2.021; T 2.492, 2.018; rescale only (no members) 2.496, 2.016. Mean absolute error (MAE) of the median forecast, in points: A 4.232, 3.548; T 4.234, 3.554.
  • Calibration on cold nights (scored year, replicate months). The q05-to-q95 coverage (nominal 0.90) is 0.880, 0.900 for A; 0.857, 0.879 for T; 0.862, 0.881 for rescale only. The share of readings at or under q95 (nominal 0.95) is 0.939, 0.940 for A; 0.924, 0.930 for T. Mean band width q95 minus q05: A 18.6 points, T 17.0, rescale only 17.4. The prediction quoted a cold-night q95 coverage of 0.896 for arm A; this experiment's two coverage statistics are 0.880 and 0.939, and the source of 0.896 was not traced.
  • Tails on cold nights (scored year; pinball loss A to T). q01 0.230 to 0.237, q05 0.691 to 0.686, q95 0.668 to 0.679, q99 0.220 to 0.233. Only q05 improves slightly (0.691 to 0.686); q01, q95, and q99 worsen.
  • Other cuts (scored year, change from A: T, ST). Coldest 5% of evening-to-morning rows (at or under 2.6 degrees C): -0.12%, -0.13%. Winter evenings (November to February, 17:00 to 23:00): -0.29%, -0.30%. Evening-to-morning rows at 2 to 6 degrees C: -0.34%, -0.40%. All other rows: -0.55%, -1.74%. Daylight: -0.28%, -2.22% (experiment 187's M is -2.23%). Night with the sun below the horizon: -0.90%, -0.90%.
  • By lead band, cold nights, arm T (scored year). Under 24 hours +0.12%; 24 to 72 hours -0.10%; 72 to 168 hours -0.11%. The replicate months' under-24-hour band is -1.61%, and the rescale-only arm gives -1.75% there.
  • By substation, cold nights, arm T (scored year, 97.5% interval). D5 -1.53% (-2.37% to +0.23%); D10 -0.22% (-3.70% to +1.12%); D11 +1.10% (-2.05% to +2.04%); D14 -1.20% (-2.22% to +0.42%); D16 -0.62% (-3.18% to +2.72%). D5's heating share does not make its result differ in kind: all five intervals include zero.
  • Controls. Known-answer gate G4 (fake ensemble: ERA5 temperature of 6 winter runs at D10 plus 51 offsets from -4 to +4 K, true irradiance in every member): passes on all 633 night rows under 8 degrees C (response non-increasing in the member's temperature; the extreme members ordered); the zero-offset member's response is 0.0. The planned check that responses vanish above 21 degrees C had no rows in winter runs and was not tested. Shuffled-members placebo (members from another day of the same substation, month, hour band, lead day, and temperature band): -0.01% on cold nights, so the day's own members add nothing. Two-number version (a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the responses): -0.06%, the same as T. Rescale-only placebo (zero responses): +0.09%; T minus rescale only is -0.17% (95% interval -0.36% to -0.06%) in the scored year and +0.11% (-0.08% to +0.37%) in the replicate months. Equal coverage: T and rescale-only have nearly equal coverage (0.857, 0.862), and their scores differ by 0.2%. The night placebo for the solar arms: M changes all night rows by -0.56%, the same as rescale only, because the solar response is zero at night.
  • Why the null. The standard deviation of the 51 members' temperature responses is 0.72 points on cold nights (0.73 in the replicate months), against 3.8 points for the solar responses in daylight and a half-width of 9.0 points for arm A's q05-to-q95 band. The mean temperature response is 0.000 points, so the pass does not shift the forecast either.
  • Checks. Median forecast minus mean forecast on cold nights: arm A's median equals its mean by construction, and the members' temperature responses have a mean of 0.000 points, so T's median minus A's median is +0.02 (D5), +0.03 (D10), -0.00 (D11), +0.01 (D14), and 0.00 (D16) points. The error of the median forecast (MAE) moves +0.05% for T on cold nights, in the same direction as no gain. Triggers from the audit rules: (3) the quantile-score and error contrasts are both zero within noise, not opposite; (4) no leave-one-out flips the verdict, because only D5 alone reaches -1.5% and its interval includes zero; (5) the rescale-only control moves non-cold rows by -0.39% against a half-width of 0.28%, because its night and twilight factors (0.85 to 0.90) narrow the bands; arm T scores -0.17% (95% interval -0.36% to -0.06%) beyond it. No separate audit was run. The verdict rests on a spread of 0.72 points, which the gate and the exact reproduction of experiment 184's all-input responses check.
  • Caveats. The scored-year cold nights fall in 6 valid-time months (2025-11 to 2026-04, one with 2 rows), so the month-block intervals may be too narrow or too wide. Cold nights lie far below the heating hinge at 15.5 degrees C, so the response is linear there and its mean of 0.000 points is guaranteed, not a finding; only the spread could help. The ensemble calibration of experiment 111 maps temperature to the training weather before the pass and may shrink the members' spread; the spread of the raw members was not measured. The cold-night sample has 11,064 rows in the scored year, spread over a few winter weeks, so the intervals are wide (the scored-year interval of -1.96% to +0.38% does not exclude a gain of 1.5%, so the result is "no detectable gain", not proof of none).
  • Prediction check. The prediction failed on the gain (-0.08% against at least -1.5%), on coverage (0.857 against 0.90), and on the comparison with the daylight gain. It held on non-cold rows (T -0.55%, never worse than +0.3%).
  • Neural suggestion (ranked, as the common brief asks). (1) A small learned heating curve would only reshape a response whose spread is already 0.72 points, so its headroom on cold-night bands is small; the prediction that could fail is a gain of 0.3% or more. (2) A small neural network that corrects the cold-night error could reach the 9-point band half-width, which is where the error is.
  • What to try next. (1) Fit the band factors on cold-night rows separately, then test the coverage at equal width (prediction that could fail: q05-to-q95 coverage returns to 0.90 with a score gain of 0.5% or more). (2) Add the ensemble's wind speed and night cloud cover as inputs to the demand model's heating term, then pass the members through (prediction that could fail: the members' response spread on cold nights rises above 2 points). (3) Look at the 20 worst cold nights by substation to see whether switching or other causes dominate.

docs.title: Experiment 193: two numbers per half-hour in place of 51 ensemble members in the solar term
docs.text:
Two numbers per half-hour, the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 ensemble weather members' estimates of solar output, keep 98% of the improvement that running all 51 members gives to the daylight forecast bands. The weather layer can therefore store two columns per half-hour instead of 51.

Experiment 187 passed each of the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble through the solar-power part of the demand model, so each member gave its own change to the forecast (a "solar response"). That lowered the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. A Gaussian shape with each half-hour's own mean and standard deviation of the 51 responses recovered 95% of that gain.

Here we rebuilt the forecast bands from those two numbers alone. We also rebuilt them from four numbers, adding the 10th and 90th percentiles of the responses. The bands are the forecast's 11 quantiles. For each lead band, a fitted offset factor rescales the quantiles' distance from the mean forecast, and a fitted spread factor rescales the spread of the responses. The rows are the same as in experiment 187.

The score is the quantile score, twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand); lower is better. Arm A is the full best-guess forecast of experiment 187 (a Kalman-filtered convex demand model with a winter night offset and a 14-day error profile). Arm M is its 51-member arm. Arm Q2 uses the two numbers and arm Q3 the four. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised substations. BG2 is the production-style blend of five XGBoost models. The scored year is 2025-07 to 2026-06; the replicate months are 2024-08, 2024-10, 2024-12, 2025-02, 2025-04, and 2025-06. Each interval is a 95% interval from resampling whole months.

The rule registered before the run was met in both periods: Q2's daylight gain is at least 80% of M's, with an interval wholly below zero. The verdict is supported.

  • Arms and row set. A and M are experiment 187's, read from experiment 184's stored arrays. Q2: 51 Gaussian points with each half-hour's mean and standard deviation of the member responses (the spread multiplied by a fitted factor), each with arm A's 11 quantile offsets times a fitted factor, pooled. Q3: the same, with a two-piece normal shape set by the 10th and 90th percentiles in place of the Gaussian. Q2s1: Q2 with the spread factor fixed at 1. Both factors are fitted per lead band on the tuning months (odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06). Fitted Q2 offset and spread factors by lead band: 0.90 and 1.3 (under 24 hours), 0.90 and 1.2, 0.90 and 1.0, 0.85 and 1.0; M used offset factors 0.95, 0.90, 0.90, 0.85. Row set fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the same five substations, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered switching events. Mean forecasts are experiment 155's monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. Ensemble weather is available at forecast time.
  • Headline C1 (daylight, change from arm A, 95% interval). Scored year: Q2 -2.20% (-2.88% to -1.48%), M -2.23% (-2.97% to -1.48%), Q3 -2.26% (-2.97% to -1.52%), Q2s1 -2.13% (-2.79% to -1.45%). Replicate months: Q2 -1.64% (-2.42% to -0.93%), M -1.76% (-2.57% to -1.02%), Q3 -1.71% (-2.51% to -0.99%), Q2s1 -1.60% (-2.32% to -0.92%). C1 is this change. The registered thresholds were 80% of M's change: -1.78% and -1.41%. Night and twilight (sun under 5 degrees above the horizon) are unchanged because only daylight rows change.
  • Retained share of M's gain. Scored year 98% (95% interval 93% to 105%); replicate months 93% (84% to 101%). Q2 minus M, as a percentage of M's score: +0.04% (-0.10% to +0.19%) and +0.12% (-0.01% to +0.27%).
  • Absolute scores (quantile score). Scored year, daylight: A 3.632, M 3.551, Q2 3.553, Q3 3.550; all rows A 2.752, Q2 2.716. Replicate months, daylight: A 3.453, M 3.392, Q2 3.396, Q3 3.394. Night is 1.981 (scored year) and 2.027 (replicate months) for every arm except the night placebo (2.112 and 2.128).
  • Coverage (daylight q05-to-q95, scored year; replicate months). A 0.854, 0.871; M 0.894, 0.901; Q2 0.896, 0.903; Q3 0.897, 0.903.
  • By lead band (daylight, A to Q2, scored year). Under 24 hours 3.095 to 3.038 (-1.84%, M -1.55%); 24 to 72 hours 3.343 to 3.278 (-1.94%, M -1.96%); 72 to 168 hours 3.906 to 3.813 (-2.38%, M -2.48%); 12 to 36 hours 3.227 to 3.164 (-1.97%, M -1.82%).
  • By clear-sky band (scored year, Q2 and M). Overcast 3.127 to 3.103 (-0.77%, M -1.04%); partly cloudy 3.861 to 3.756 (-2.71%, M -2.71%); clear 3.483 to 3.419 (-1.82%, M -1.87%). The overcast band keeps the least (74% of M's gain), and its Q2 interval (-1.54% to -0.12%) is wide.
  • By substation (daylight, Q2 against A, scored year; M in brackets). D5 -3.27% (-3.15%); D10 -1.18% (-1.30%); D11 -0.99% (-1.09%); D14 -1.65% (-1.73%); D16 -3.35% (-3.42%). Without D5 -1.79% (-1.89%). In the replicate months D11 is -0.72% with an interval that includes zero (-1.81% to +0.48%), as for M.
  • Placebos (daylight change from arm A, and the share of Q2's gain each recovers; scored year, then replicate months). Rescale only, with every response zero: -0.23%, 10%; +0.04%. Two numbers taken from another day of the same substation, month, and hour band: -0.44%, 20%; -0.01%. Taken from another day of the same lead day and cloud band as well: -0.87%, 40%; -0.43%, 26%. So about 60% (74%) of the gain needs the day's own two numbers. Night placebo (night rows given a daylight row's two numbers, same substation, month, and lead day): the night score is 6.6% worse (95% interval 2.7% to 11.5%) in the scored year and 5.0% worse (1.0% to 9.3%) in the replicate months, so the summary does not help where it should not.
  • Gap to BG2 (arm minus BG2, so positive means worse than BG2) on the sunniest third of daylight half-hours (mean absolute error of the median, five substations, 74,728 half-hours, scored year). A +0.044 MW (95% interval +0.007 to +0.072); M +0.026 (-0.020 to +0.059); Q2 +0.028 (-0.017 to +0.060); Q3 +0.027 (-0.019 to +0.059). Without D5: A +0.007, M -0.007, Q2 -0.005 MW. At D5: A +0.202, M +0.170, Q2 +0.171 MW.
  • Tails (daylight, scored year; coverage / pinball loss). Q2: q01 0.013 / 0.233, q05 0.051 / 0.839, q95 0.947 / 0.879, q99 0.986 / 0.242. M: 0.013 / 0.230, 0.053 / 0.837, 0.947 / 0.880, 0.986 / 0.242. A: 0.027 / 0.265, 0.078 / 0.907, 0.933 / 0.924, 0.979 / 0.262.
  • Checks. The median forecast minus the mean forecast at 12 to 36 hours for Q2 is -0.14 (D5), -0.03 (D10), -0.05 (D11), -0.04 (D14), and -0.05 (D16) points (M: -0.14, -0.05, -0.05, -0.05, -0.05), the shift probably comes from asymmetry in arm A's quantile offsets, which Q2's symmetric Gaussian centres do not remove; arm A is 0.000. The mean forecast shared by M, Q2, and Q3 (arm A's mean plus the mean response) has a daylight mean absolute error of 6.366 against A's 6.375, a change of -0.13% (-0.45% to +0.27%), in the same direction as the score. No trigger from the audit rules fired. No control failed: the rescale-only placebo moves the score by -0.23% against a half-width of 0.26, and the night placebo worsens night. The result matched its prediction on every point (Q2 -2.20% against a predicted near -2.1%; Q3 changes the score by 0.06 points against under 0.2; the strict shuffle recovers 40% against under 45%). Q2 beats Q2s1, the arm nested in it, by 0.07 percentage points, so no nested arm beat its container. The interval widths match experiment 187's.
  • Serving-path saving. The two numbers replace 51 member responses per half-hour with 2, a drop from 204 to 8 bytes in float32. The solar response is linear in the member's unit photovoltaic (PV) shape (experiment 187), so the same two numbers are the fitted solar coefficient times the mean and standard deviation of the 51 members' unit PV shapes. The 51 members' irradiance is still needed once, when the weather layer computes the two numbers; the saving is in the stored columns and in the 51 passes through the demand model per run. No runtime was measured.
  • Caveats. The scored contrasts reuse experiment 187's rows and arm M, so the experiment tests one new summary on rows and arms already scored. Q2 carries two fitted factors per lead band where M carries one, all fitted on the tuning months. The replicate months hold 6 months, so their intervals are wide, and Q2's retained share in the replicate months (93%) has an interval reaching 84%.
  • Optional neural arm (Q5). Not run. Q2 and M differ by 0.04% of the score, so a learned scale function has at most the upper end of that interval (0.19%) to gain, and the point estimate gives it none.
  • What to try next. (1) A follow-up experiment could put the two numbers into the weather layer and the serving path and measure the runtime saving. (2) Test whether the standard deviation can be computed from the ensemble's irradiance mean and spread without running each member through the unit PV shape (prediction that could fail: the computed standard deviation keeps at least 80% of the gain). (3) Score Q2 on the curtailment-cost metric of studies.node_curtailment, because the pinball-loss reduction from A to Q2 is largest at q01 (12%, against 5% to 8% at the other three tail quantiles).

docs.title: Experiment 194: D8's drops follow one engine whose output stopped being added back
docs.text:
We asked whether the long stretches in which D8 (one of the 16 Primary substations in the trial) draws less power than a fitted model expects come from one 6 MW gas engine, labelled G2 on this page. NGED's notes say that G2's output is added to D8's reading, so that D8 shows demand plus the engine's output, and that G2's own telemetry channel (its analogue) does not work. We reran the design note's calculations from committed code. We call the share of half-hours in which D8's metered power sat more than 2.5 MW below the fitted model's expected power the "shortfall share". We found the date on which that share jumped. We also checked the same share on three comparison Primaries (D3, D5, and D14) with no known engine.

The design note's numbers reproduce, and its account of D8's drops holds in outline. While G2's output arrived, D8's reading rose with G2's output (D8's reading rose by 0.02 MW for each 1 MW of G2 output; had the output not been added back, D8's reading would fall by 1 MW for each 1 MW). The shortfall share stepped from 0.010 to 0.257 in the week of 2023-08-14, the week G2's last output reading arrived. It stayed between 0.10 and 0.46 in every month to January 2026. The shortfall share of the three comparison Primaries stayed near zero.

Two findings differ from the design note's wording. G2's readings did not stop arriving: 98 later days carry all-zero readings, and D8's shortfall share is the same with a zero reading present as with none. D8's shortfall also fades from March 2026 with no matching change in G2's readings (they already stopped on 2026-01-26). Experiment 191's scored year (2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30) therefore holds both high-shortfall and low-shortfall months.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Figure 1. D8's weekly shortfall share against D3, D5, and D14 (near zero throughout).

Figure 2. The break by day: D8's shortfall starts on the day G2's last output reading arrives.

Figure 3. G2 ran in 9% of the cheapest fifth of half-hours and 26% of the dearest.

Figure 4. D8's residual in four periods. The negative tail after August 2023 is broad, not clearly quantised in units of 2 MW.

Figure 5. Monthly shortfall share. The blue band is the scored year of experiment 191.

docs.title: Reproduction of the design's numbers (PS1)
docs.text:
• Stop rule: passed. 2,054 half-hours join to the system price, exactly the design's count.
  • G2's output (2023-07-03 to 2023-08-15, 44 days): units running 0, 1, 2, 3 in 1,704, 137, 133, 80 half-hours (exact). Running share 0.170 (Wilson 0.155 to 0.187). Only 440 of G2's 441 positive readings fall in these weeks; the other is 0.2 MW on 2026-01-23.
  • Running by price fifth, cheapest to dearest: 0.089, 0.152, 0.151, 0.198, 0.259, against the design's 0.090, 0.151, 0.152, 0.191, 0.271 (the top fifth differs by 0.012). The cheapest and dearest fifths' intervals are 0.065 to 0.120 and 0.220 to 0.303. Spearman correlation of price with running 0.160.
  • By hour (UTC): 0.02 to 0.20 from 00:00 to 05:59 (design 0.02 to 0.10) and 0.25 to 0.28 from 19:00 to 21:59 (exact). The design's low range misses 05:00 UTC (0.20), where running starts.
  • Running spells (consecutive half-hours with G2 running): 56 (design 55), lengths 1 to 29 (exact) and median 4 half-hours (design 6; not reproduced, probably because a missing reading ends a spell here).
  • D8's residual while G2 ran, median at 1, 2, and 3 units running: over 2023-07-03 to 2023-08-15 we find +0.49, +0.43, and +0.23 MW. The design quotes +0.49, +0.53, and +0.23 MW for July, so the 2-unit value is not reproduced and the design's label ("July") does not match its first and last values. For July alone the medians are +0.19, +0.37, and +0.60 MW, which rise with output. All six medians are positive.
  • Shortfall share by month: May 2023 0.001 (design 0.000), July 0.000, September 0.353, October 0.357 (design 0.353), November 2025 0.147, January 2026 0.292, April 2026 0.008, May 0.022, June 0.039. The June and August 2023 values (0.035 and 0.112) are exact.
  • By calendar quarter, 2023Q4 to 2025Q4: 0.198 to 0.338 (design 0.197 to 0.343, which used quarters starting in September). 2023Q3 is 0.153 because July and August were mostly clean.
  • Springs: March to May 0.267 in 2024, 0.228 in 2025, 0.034 in 2026.

docs.title: Prediction and decision rule
docs.text:
• July 2023 at most 0.02: held (0.000, Wilson 0.000 to 0.003).
  • At least 0.10 in every month from September 2023 to January 2026: held, narrowly. The lowest month is February 2025 at 0.102.
  • Change point between 2023-08-10 and 2023-09-10: held. The weekly step is at 2023-08-14 (likelihood-ratio set and bootstrap 95% both 2023-08-14 to 2023-08-21).
  • No control within 30 days: held, with a caveat. D3 and D5 have no step (0.000). Their best split falls on the earliest allowed week, 2023-06-26, 49 days before D8's, because the likelihood is flat and the search returns the first tie. D14's step is +0.005 at 2025-09-29.
  • Two-step fit of D8 over the whole window: up at 2023-08-14 (0.010 to 0.254), down at 2026-03-09 (to 0.029).
  • Sensitivity: a threshold of 0.241 times each site's capacity equals -2.5 MW at D8, so D8's fit is unchanged. The controls stay below a step of 0.007, though D5's best split moves to 2025-11-10.

docs.title: Does the account hold?
docs.text:
• Gross while G2's output arrived: yes. Had D8 been net of G2, 10.2% of those half-hours would fall below -2.5 MW. The observed share is 0.0%.
  • Net afterwards: yes, from the shortfall's timing. The shortfall starts on 2023-08-15, when G2's readings stop mid-day (22 of 48 readings that day).
  • "Reading stopped arriving": only partly. G2 has 98 days with readings after 2023-08-24, all zero except the 0.2 MW. D8's shortfall share is 0.329 with a reading present and 0.270 with none (2023-08-25 to 2023-12-31; the intervals do not overlap), and 0.232 and 0.255 in 2024 to January
  • The difference has no consistent sign, and G2's later readings give no record of the engine running.
  • Quantised steps (output rising in units of 2 MW, one per running engine unit): not shown. The histogram's local peaks are at -4.1 MW and -3.1 MW, where steps of 2 MW would put them at -2, -4, and -6 MW. Noise in the expected power is wide enough to blur 2 MW steps.
  • 2026: the shortfall share falls from 0.292 in January to 0.070 in March and 0.008 in April while G2 has no readings after 2026-01-26. Either the engine stopped running, or NGED resumed adding the engine's output to D8's reading. The data cannot tell which.
  • Experiment 191's window (its constants: D8 data from 2025-04-01, scored runs 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30): in those 12 months, 59% of half-hours fall before February 2026 (shortfall share 0.292) and 41% from February 2026 onwards (0.061). The window includes the 2026 change.
  • Register entries near G2 (MW and distance only): a 6 MW gas engine connected 2023-06-13 at 0.00 km in the ECR (under D14 in the register's Primary column); two Capacity Market gas-fuelled components at 0.05 km (six-figure grid reference, so about 0.07 km precision); a connected 10.98 MW battery at 0.27 km, registered under none of the 16 Primaries.

docs.title: PS5: census
docs.text:
• Series notes: 5 of 33 series carry an information note. Among the 16 Primaries, only D8 has an added-back note, and its note says that generators' analogues are not working. Of 13 metered generators and batteries, 4 carry a note: 1 solar analogue "not working", 1 solar analogue "suspect", G2 "not working", 1 biofuel customer "has not exported since June 2026".
  • Reading availability, 2024-01-01 to 2026-06-30: 11 of the 13 generators and batteries have readings in at least 74% of half-hours. G2 has 4% (last 2026-01-26), and 1 solar farm has none since 2024-09-26.
  • Shortfall share across all 16 Primaries: D8 is the only Primary with a sustained upward step of at least 0.10 (+0.246). D9's usable weeks start in January 2024 and open with a four-week burst (weekly shares 0.08, 0.52, 0.65, 0.34 from 2024-01-08), after which the share is near zero, so the fit reads a step of -0.198 at 2024-02-26. D18 has 27 usable weeks and one week at 0.301 in October 2025, fitted as a step of -0.038. D15 has no usable weeks. D14's highest week is 0.074.
  • ECR price-following assets under the 16 Primaries (connected): 2 gas or oil engines of 7.00 MW (6.00 MW at D14 from 2023-06-13, 1.00 MW at D5 from 2021-03-11) and 3 batteries of 0.65 MW (D11, D2, D9). 2 batteries (0.2 MW each, D16 and D3) are accepted to connect. 9 Primaries have none. The demand-side response register holds no rows. CHP: 2 slots, 1.40 MW, both at D10, none gas or oil engines.
  • Whole register: 168 connected gas or oil engines of at least 1 MW each, totalling 1,265.8 MW. Engines of this size are therefore not confined to the trial's Primaries.
  • PS5 prediction: held for sustained upward steps. D9's transient burst fits a step down of more than 0.10, and D15 and D18 lack the data for a fit, so "no other series" covers 13 of 16 Primaries fully.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site and mean-forecast error beside each contrast: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Audit triggers: none fired. No control failed, the result matches its prediction, and no planned contrast exists to flip. Later experiments (PS2 to PS4) depend on this result, and this experiment is the replication the design asked for.
  • Caveats: the stored residual panel comes from experiment 130's frozen convex model driven by ERA5, so a changing model error shifts the shortfall share. The threshold of -2.5 MW is the design's; D8 is measured in apparent power (MVA, not MW), so a dip in apparent power at low demand can look like generation. The bootstrap interval resamples weeks within each side of the fitted split, so it is narrow by construction; the likelihood-ratio set is the more cautious interval.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Ask NGED whether G2's output is still added back to D8, from when, and whether its analogue was repaired (design questions 1 to 3).
  • PS2 may use G2's 44 summer days as a known answer, and must treat D8 as gross before 2023-08-15 and net after.
  • PS3 and PS4 need an "engine visible in the target" flag, set to off from March 2026 until NGED answers.

docs.title: Experiment 195: a learned score on detector features finds 24 of 35 real transfers, not 19
docs.text:
On 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, a small learned score found 22 to 24, against 19 for RO-NC, the rule-based switching detector with the best score of those we tested, at the same 80 unexplained alarms. A transfer is a period, labelled by hand in experiment 41, in which switching moved load from one Primary substation (a substation that steps transmission voltage down to distribution voltage) to its neighbours. An alarm is unexplained when no logged closure or labelled transfer lies within 24 hours of it, and the 80 are counted over odd-numbered months. RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector of experiment 82: it raises a candidate alarm wherever the 24-hour step in a Primary substation's forecast error reaches 2.5 noise units, and it keeps the candidates that a logistic score ranks highest. Our re-run finds 19 transfers where its original run found 18, probably because our end rule differs in one detail from experiment 130's.

A learned score re-ranks RO-NC's candidates, and a logistic regression does nearly as well. Each score reads 25 numbers per candidate, among them the 24-hour step, the opposite step at a neighbouring Primary substation, and the hour and season. We trained each score only on synthetic transfers, added to the forecast error with the injector of experiment 189 (pull request 1494), plus real stretches with no logged or labelled event. We scored each on real transfers of Primary pairs it had never seen. The best score, a neural network that also reads 4 days of the raw forecast error, found 24 and lost none of RO-NC's (+0.074 in the share of moved MW found, 95% interval +0.013 to +0.175, resampling whole Primary pairs).

The verdict is partly supported, because the re-ranker clears the recall bar only with a feature that reads 2 days after the step. RO-NC's score reads no such feature. Without it, the re-ranker finds 22 and its interval reaches below zero (-0.002), so only the count bar holds. The logistic regression finds 22 with or without that feature. The extra transfers are small. The learned scores find no more injected transfers than RO-NC does. The gated-mask bar was not run.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. F: features only, as a logistic regression, a gradient-boosted tree, and a neural network of 2,449 weights ("F network"). R: re-ranker of RO-NC's candidates, a neural network of 10,249 weights that reads the features and a raw window of 4 days. C: logistic stack of the F network, RO-NC's score, and the pair statistic (the smaller of the 6-hour step and the opposite step at the best neighbour), fitted on validation worlds only. U and I: union and intersection of a learned arm with RO-NC or the pair alarm, with the split of the alarm count chosen on validation worlds. Comparators: RO-NC, the pair alarm of experiment 156, and their rule-based union.
  • Rows. The 35 real transfers over 1 day, out of 66 labelled transfers, in 18 Primary pairs divided into 3 folds that hold out whole pairs. Alarms are chosen at 80 unexplained odd-month alarms per fold (0.185 per Primary-month, equal for every arm by construction). A transfer is found when an alarm starts within 2 hours of its start and ends within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration of its end (experiment 130's rule). Every arm uses RO-NC's end rule.
  • Real transfers over 1 day found, out of 35 (MW-weighted recall and difference from RO-NC, 95% intervals; "gained" and "lost" count transfers found by the arm and not by RO-NC, and the reverse):
Arm Found Start only MW-weighted recall Minus RO-NC Gained / lost RO-NC (this re-run) 19 22 0.678 [0.479, 0.799] 0 0 / 0 Pair alarm 5 5 0.166 [0.042, 0.364] -0.512 [-0.697, -0.224] 1 / 15 Union of RO-NC and pair alarm (rule) 18 20 0.657 [0.447, 0.782] -0.021 [-0.087, 0.000] 0 / 1 F logistic regression 22 24 0.721 [0.538, 0.844] +0.043 [-0.003, +0.124] 4 / 1 F gradient-boosted tree 22 24 0.721 [0.538, 0.844] +0.043 [-0.003, +0.124] 4 / 1 F network 22 25 0.728 [0.555, 0.839] +0.050 [-0.002, +0.132] 4 / 1 R re-ranker 24 26 0.752 [0.582, 0.867] +0.074 [+0.013, +0.175] 5 / 0 C stack 22 25 0.728 [0.555, 0.839] +0.050 [-0.002, +0.132] 4 / 1 Union F network + RO-NC 22 24 0.721 [0.538, 0.844] +0.043 [-0.003, +0.124] 4 / 1 Union R re-ranker + pair alarm 24 26 0.752 [0.582, 0.867] +0.074 [+0.013, +0.175] 5 / 0 Intersection F network and RO-NC 21 24 0.717 [0.533, 0.831] +0.039 [-0.023, +0.123] 3 / 1
  • Pre-registered bars, with every feature. Primary bar: the re-ranker, and the union of the re-ranker with the pair alarm, have a lower interval end above zero and find more than the rule-based union (24 against 18). Count bar: 24 is at least 22, and 5 transfers are gained with none lost. The logistic regression and the F network agree within 2 transfers (22 and 22), as predicted. The other learned arms' lower interval ends run from -0.023 to -0.002, so they do not meet the primary bar. The prediction that recall falls by under 15 percentage points when the receiver is unmetered is met: 0.215 against 0.290 for the re-ranker on injected transfers. The gated-mask bar was not run.
  • The extra transfers are small. The re-ranker's five gains are 0.4 to 0.9 MW each (3.2 of the 42.7 MW in the 35 transfers) and sit in 4 of the 18 Primary pairs, 48 to 93 hours long. The three pairs that carry most of the moved MW keep their RO-NC counts. Dropping any one pair leaves the re-ranker 3 to 5 transfers ahead of RO-NC, and the F network 2 to 3.
  • Transfers that both forecast-error models can see (29 of the 35). Re-ranker 20, RO-NC 15, F network 18. The two models are the convex model and the XGBoost model of experiment 181.
  • The candidate ceiling is 26. RO-NC's candidate list contains an alarm within 2 hours of the start of 29 transfers, and a candidate with the right start and end for 26. The pair-alarm candidates add none. The re-ranker's 24 is 2 below that ceiling.
  • Start error. The median start error of found transfers is 0.5 hours for every arm.
  • Alarm accounting (per fold, at 80 unexplained odd-month alarms). Alarms that look like a balanced transfer (an opposite step at a neighbour of 0.4 to 2.5 times the own step) number 10 for RO-NC, 13.3 for the F network, and 14.7 for the re-ranker. Those extra balanced alarms may be unlogged real transfers, so we do not count them as failures. Unexplained alarms over all months fall from 149 (RO-NC) to 94 (re-ranker), but the scores were trained on the even-month candidates, so that fall is in-sample and is not a result.
  • Injected transfers (odd months, 998 injected transfers on pairs the injector never saw). Start-and-end recall is 0.259 for RO-NC, 0.265 for the re-ranker, 0.261 for the F network, and 0.264 for the logistic regression. Recall with no metered receiver is 0.198 for RO-NC and 0.215 for the re-ranker, against 0.290 and 0.290 with a metered receiver, so the learned scores do not collapse without a metered partner. The pair alarm falls from 0.146 to 0.018, and its intersection with the F network inherits that fall.
  • Hindsight control (post hoc, after the code review). Dropping the "level after the step" feature, which reads 1 to 2 days after the candidate, leaves the logistic regression at 22 (+0.043 [-0.003, +0.124]), and the re-ranker falls to 22 (+0.050 [-0.002, +0.132]). The re-ranker's raw window still reads 4 days ahead. Tables are in printed_report_ablation_no_persist.txt.
  • Post hoc ablation. Without the noise scale (a proxy for the series), the hour, and the season, the re-ranker finds 23 of 35 (+0.064 [+0.012, +0.154]) and the logistic regression 23 (+0.064 [+0.012, +0.154]). The F network falls to 21 (-0.041 [-0.261, +0.115]) because it loses one large transfer. The ablated networks have 2,209 and 10,089 weights. Tables are in printed_report_ablation.txt.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, mean-forecast error, tail calibration, curtailment cost: not applicable, because no forecast is scored.
  • Audit triggers. None fired. No control failed: the re-implemented pair alarm finds 5, as in experiment 156. The result meets its prediction. Dropping any one pair never changes the sign of the re-ranker's lead. No nested arm beats the arm that contains it. No later design depends on this result yet. No Opus audit was run.
  • Even-month transfers gain more. The re-ranker's net gain over RO-NC is 4 transfers in even-month transfers, the months its injected training transfers sit in, and 1 in odd-month transfers (RO-NC 8, F network 8, and re-ranker 9 of 15). The ablation without season, hour, and noise scale keeps the gain, which argues against a seasonal shortcut, but 15 transfers cannot settle it.

docs.title: Caveats and lab shortcuts
docs.text:
• RO-NC is re-implemented. It finds 19 here against 18 in its original run. Every arm uses the same end rule, so the contrasts are paired.
  • Hindsight inputs. The feature "level after the step" reads 2 days after the start, and the raw window reads 4 days after it, so the learned scores alarm days late. Reading future data is a lab shortcut.
  • Residual leakage. The convex model behind the real forecast errors was trained with the labelled transfers masked, which makes the features of the real transfers look cleaner than they would at serving time. We did not recompute the features from an unmasked model.
  • Negatives. Training negatives are real unexplained candidates in even months. They include probable unlogged transfers, which lowers every learned score slightly. The multi-day drops of one Primary substation that a gas peaker explains (D8), the 17 unlabelled block days of experiment 175, and all labelled or logged spans are excluded from the training negatives. An injected transfer that lands next to one of them still counts as a positive, and none of them is removed from the pool that sets the 80-alarm threshold (the same for every arm). The validation worlds hold the same real negatives as the training worlds, so early stopping, the tree's settings, and the stack were chosen on in-sample negatives and fresh positives.
  • Held-out pairs are held out by pair, not by Primary substation. A Primary substation of a held-out pair can sit in another fold's pair, so training sees synthetic transfers and real quiet stretches on the same Primary substations as the held-out transfers, as in experiment 189.
  • Best of several arms. The re-ranker's interval is not corrected for being the best of 11 learned and combined arms, and its lower end sits just above zero.
  • Intersection arms on injected transfers. Alarms of one world can match alarms of another world on the same series, which inflates the intersection arms' injected recall slightly. The real-record scores are unaffected.
  • Scoring months. Thresholds come from odd months, and transfers are scored in every month, as in experiment 189. We did not rescore on even months with thresholds from odd months only.
  • Not done. The gated-mask test of experiments 163 and 171, features from an unmasked model, and training that leaves one pair out (the leave-one-pair-out table drops a pair from the scores and does not retrain).

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test the extra alarms in the gated mask, because that bar decides porting.
  • Swap the odd and even months for training and thresholds, to settle whether the even-month gain is real.
  • Make the injector more realistic. The learned scores find injected transfers no more often than RO-NC does, so injected recall cannot rank detectors yet. A neural component is not the next step, because the logistic regression already matches the features-only neural network.

Code: ml-experiments/00195-switching-neural-plus-detector-features/; the printed numbers are in printed_report.txt, printed_report_ablation.txt, and printed_report_ablation_no_persist.txt in that folder.

docs.title: Can a hidden Markov model of 0 to 3 engine units find D8's price-following engine in its residual, and does it pass a known-answer test built from the engine's own recorded output?
docs.text:
An engine of up to three units, with a unit of about 1.75 MW, is detected in the recorded engine output that we injected into D8, but the detector cannot yet be trusted after March 2025. We asked whether a hidden Markov model whose state is the number of engine units running (0 to 3), read through the magnitude meter with no price input, can find a gas engine in the residual of D8 (the reading minus the expected power). To test it, we subtracted the recorded output of a metered generator (a gas-engine generator, G2) from D8's reading, once at the true times (K1) and once at nine other places in D8's history that had no engine (K2), and counted how many running half-hours the model found again. The model found all of the half-hours with 2 or 3 units running and 83% to 85% of those with 1 unit, and step detectors found at most 24%. The pre-registered verdict is not supported, because the false-alarm bar fails at three Primaries, and the over-flagging after 2025-03 is a larger problem than the false alarms at the three Primaries.

Ideas from Hart (1992) and Kolter and Jaakkola (2012) (load disaggregation with a discrete state per appliance) are applied here; the autoregressive error, the magnitude meter and the known-answer test are this project's.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Row set and detector. The detector fitted on D8 from 2023-09 to 2025-12 (40,900 half-hours). It flags a half-hour when the smoothed probability of at least 1 unit exceeds 0.5. Noise was fitted on odd months of D8's engine-free history (2022-01 to 2023-06-12 and July 2023). No convex demand model was refitted: the expected power is the stored panel's, and each retrain step re-centres it by a monthly offset and an hour-by-day-type profile.
  • K1 (G2's output replayed, 2,054 scored half-hours: 1,704 at 0 units, 137 at 1, 133 at 2, 80 at 3). Recall at 2 or 3 units 1.00 (95% 1.00 to 1.00); at 1 unit 0.83 (0.63 to 0.97); precision 0.84 (0.67 to 0.97); energy error -1.3% (-10% to +13%). All four thresholds pass.
  • K2 (nine shifted copies, 18,486 scored half-hours). Recall at 2 or 3 units 1.00; at 1 unit 0.85 (0.79 to 0.91); precision 0.93 (0.89 to 0.96); energy error -8.4% (-10.8% to -5.8%). All four thresholds pass. Intervals resample whole days.
  • Synthetic spells at 0.5 and 2 times G2's running rate (secondary). Recall at 1 unit 0.94 and 0.94; precision 0.82 and 0.96; energy error -0.1% and -6.2%. All pass. Reactive-power floor of 0, 0.5, and 1.0 MVA: recall at 1 unit 0.85 to 0.86, precision 0.89 to 0.92, all pass.
  • False alarms on D8's clean history. 0.7% of half-hours flagged (5 false active days in 559 days, 0.27 a month); on even months, which the noise fit did not use, 0.008%.
  • False alarms at the other Primaries (share flagged; false active days a month). D3 0.5%, 0.34; D5 1.7%, 2.02; D10 0.7%, 1.05; D11 3.2%, 1.12; D14 0.3%, 0.30; D16 0.02%, 0.04. D5 has a 1 MW gas engine in the Embedded Capacity Register and D11 a small battery, so some flags may be real. The pre-registered bars (3% of half-hours; 1 false active day a month) fail at D5 (2.02 days), D10 (1.05 days), and D11 (3.2% flagged). The audit judged that arguing these Primaries hold real assets would be post hoc, so the verdict stands.
  • Unit size. The fit puts it at 1.75 MW, on a grid of 0.25 MW, in the final round (1.5 MW in the first), with the design prior (centre 1.97 MW) and the wide prior (centre 2.5 MW) alike, and with the fit window cut at 2025-02. The log-likelihood is 2,300 nats lower at 2.0 MW than at 1.75 MW, so the log-likelihood favours a smaller unit than G2's 1.97 MW. The prediction (1.7 to 2.3 MW) holds only at its lower edge.
  • Step detectors on the same injections (half-hours inside a found spell, K1 and K2). RO-NC at 24 hours: 0.08 and 0.02 alone, 0.00 and 0.00 with the neighbour check; RO-NC at 4 hours: 0.24 and 0.20 alone, 0.00 and 0.01 with the neighbour check; block detector 0.09 and 0.09. One of five operating points (RO-NC at 4 hours) reaches 20% or more on both injections, so the prediction of under 20% holds for four of five.
  • Regimes. Share flagged against share below -2.5 MW: 2023-09 to 2025-12, 40% against 26%; 2026-02 to 2026-03, 41% against 12%; 2026-04 to 2026-06, 43% against 2%. D8's residual noise (median absolute step-to-step error) is 0.17 to 0.27 MW in clean months and 0.35 to 0.75 MW from 2024-05, rising most after 2025-03, when 8.91 MW of solar was connected. A local noise multiplier (post hoc) leaves the flagged share at 39% in 2026-04 to 2026-06. The audit found the cause is the observation model, not re-centring and not an engine: from 2025-03 steps of 1.5 to 2.5 MW occur about 69 times per 1,000 half-hours against 0.5 in clean history, in both directions, and upward excursions of more than 1 MW (26% of half-hours) outnumber downward ones (18%), which an engine cannot produce. With error correlation 0.906 the level carries little weight in the emission, so the detector reads steps.
  • Positive spells at D8 (4 or more half-hours more than 1.5 MW above a 30-day rolling median): 2.5 per 100 days in clean history, 35 in 2023-09 to 2025-02, 67 in 2025-03 to 2025-12, and 89 in 2026-04 to 2026-06. The rolling median is pulled down by the engine, so this measure cannot tell battery charging from a biased offset.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable; the experiment makes no forecast.
  • Mean-forecast error beside a quantile-score contrast: not applicable.
  • Triggers that fired: trigger 1 (a control failed: the false-alarm control at D5 and D11) and trigger 2 (the step detector at 4 hours reached 24%, against a prediction of under 20%, and the unit size sits at the edge of its predicted range). An Opus audit ran, and its findings are below.
  • The gate is easy where it was run. Every injection sits in 2022-23 or July to August 2023, when D8's noise is low, so passing says nothing about 2025-26. In the audit, adding noise of 0.40 MW lowered K1 precision to 0.51 and K2 precision to 0.61, and shifting G2's record into 2026-04 gave precision 0.29. D8's innovation scale is 0.21 MW in the injected history against 0.37 to 0.53 MW in the periods the labels are needed for.
  • Lab shortcuts. ERA5-driven expected power (from the stored panel), smoothed rather than filtered posteriors for the scores (the filtered recall of any running is 0.91 to 0.94), and the unit size quantised to 0.25 MW.
