BSP Child Unit First usable reading Years of readings Enters D13 D9 Trusthorpe MW 2023-08-23 3.05 (b), (c), (d) D13 D10 Spilsby MW 2019-09-17 6.95 (b), (c), (d) D13 D11 Horncastle MW 2019-09-17 6.99 (b), (c), (d) D13 D2 Warth Lane Skegness MVA 2019-09-17 6.99 (c), (d) D13 D4 Ingoldmells MVA 2019-09-17 6.98 (c), (d) D13 D19 Chapel St Leonards MVA 2019-09-17 6.99 (c), (d) D13 D21 Alford MVA 2019-09-17 6.94 (c), (d) D17 D5 Kirton MW 2019-09-17 6.97 (b), (c), (d) D17 D14 Mount Bridge Boston MW 2019-10-21 6.89 (b), (c), (d) D17 D16 Donington MW 2020-12-22 5.68 (b), (c), (d) D17 D3 Sleaford Road Boston MVA 2019-09-17 6.97 (c), (d) D17 D8 Marsh Lane MVA 2019-09-17 6.98 (c), (d) from 2025-04-01 D17 D12 Stickney MVA 2019-09-17 6.97 (c), (d) D17 D22 Langrick MVA 2019-09-17 6.97 (c), (d) D17 D15 Wrangle T1 MW 2025-02-06 1.56 (e) only D17 D18 Wrangle T2 MW 2024-12-11 1.64 (e) only

The two Wrangle transformers have under 8 months of readings at the first scored run, so no arm D forecast exists for them. NGED's hierarchy also lists metered generators under each BSP (wind, solar, biofuel, and battery sites). They are not Primaries and stay in the remainder, as in experiment 161. Experiment 152's Step 0 found reverse flow at D12 only (every sunny midday); D22 has 3.7% and the other six apparent-power children have none, so arms (c) and (d) differ materially at D17 only.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
All arms are scored on the same runs as experiment 161 (the 291 daily runs of 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads 0.5 to 168 hours. Every arm turns a mean forecast into quantiles with experiment 155's top-down spread table, row by row, so the comparison isolates the mean. Experiment 161's bottom-up arm refitted its table on the sum's corrected errors, and that narrowed its tails and gave C1 its positive sign (experiment 161's C5). Experiment 152 stored forecasts for the apparent-power children only in the scored and replicate years, with no tuning months, so a table fitted on the sum's own residuals could not be built for the full arms in any case.

Arm Forecast of the BSP (a) top-down Arm D's chain on the BSP's reading alone (reference; stored by experiment 161) (b) partial bottom-up Experiment 161's sum over the three MW children plus arm D's forecast of the remainder; scored with its own table (reproduction) and with the top-down table (c) full, naive Sum over all children with a long history, each apparent-power child's reading and forecast taken as signed (experiment 152's arm N mean), plus arm D's forecast of the remainder BSP - sum(w_i * y_i) (d) full, fold-aware The same sum with each apparent-power child's signed flow forecast by experiment 152's fold-aware model (the latent flow column of arm F, not the folded quantiles), and the remainder built from the child's estimated signed history (e) full plus short-history children (d) plus D15 and D18, forecast with the pooled shapes of experiment 158 at 5 to 7 months of history; D17 only, reported separately oracle (d) with the children's observed readings in place of their forecasts (control, no verdict)

Signed history of an apparent-power child. The remainder chain trains on BSP - sum(w_i * y_i), which needs each child's observed signed flow. The observed signed flow does not exist for a child that reports only magnitude. Arm (c) uses the magnitude as it stands. Arm (d) uses the magnitude times 0.97 (the power factor of experiment 124, which turns apparent power into active power, the quantity the latent flow forecast measures), with the sign set negative on every half-hour where the reverse-flow probability exceeds 0.9 (experiment 152's "sure" rule). The probability comes from the monthly meter fit of experiment 152 that was trained before that half-hour's cut (work/fits/real/*_meter.pkl), not from experiment 110's single fit, so no sign uses a later reading. A sensitivity arm (d-p50) sets the sign at probability 0.5 instead. The history changes at D12 on sunny middays and at essentially no other child. The sign of the converted flow is the main risk, so Step 1 prints it for D12 before anything is fitted. The sign error enters the remainder and the child forecast through the same meter fit, so the two are coupled, not independent.

Weights. Non-negative least squares of the BSP's reading on all children's signed readings with no intercept, on the winter window 2023-10-01 to 2024-03-31 of experiment 161, bounded to 0.8 to 1.2. The unbounded fit is printed as a diagnostic only. Winter has no reverse flow, so the weights do not depend on the sign convention. D8's series changes meaning in April 2025 (experiment 152), so its weight is fixed at 1 and it enters only from 2025-04-01; D17's full arms are therefore scored in the scored year only, and D13 also has a replicate year.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Feasibility, before any chain runs. Print the child table above from the stored files, the covered share of each BSP's effective capacity for every arm, and the per-half-hour sign estimate at D12 (share of sunny-midday half-hours with reverse flow, by month). Stop and report if the signed history of D12 cannot be rebuilt from stored experiment 110 outputs or a re-run of studies.dp_meter on D12 alone.
  2. Controls. Reproduce experiment 161's top-down and partial bottom-up scores to three decimals. Known-answer check. For the five MW Primaries of experiment 152's injection test (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16), take its folded series at injection levels 0, 1.0, and 2.0 times the midday median, sum the five children, and compare the sum's mean forecast built as in (c) (arm N's mean) and as in (d) (arm F's flow) with the signed sum from the signed files. The pass criterion uses the power-factor-0.97 folding (pf97, which matches real meters); the idealised q0 folding is reported beside it. This check tests experiment 152's latent-flow forecast only. It does not test the signed-history rule or the remainder chain. Pass: at level 2.0 the mean absolute error of (d)'s summed signed flow is at least 20% below (c)'s, and at level 0 (d) is no more than 5% worse than (c). Experiment 152 stored these forecasts, so the check costs minutes.
  3. Chains. Remainder chains for (c) and (d) at both BSPs, and for (e) at D17: experiment 161's copy of experiment 136's A2 and experiment 155's arm D. The oracle reuses the (d) remainder.
  4. Score. The contrasts below, the tail table, absolute skill for climatology and manual_heuristic, and the covered share beside every arm.

docs.title: Planned contrasts
docs.text: C1 (d) minus (a), headline, at D13 and D17. C2 (d) minus (c). C3 (c) minus (b), the effect of adding the apparent-power children without a sign model. C4 C1 by lead band (under 24 hours, 24 to 72, 72 to 168). C5 (e) minus (d) at D17. C6 (d) minus (a) at the tail quantiles. C7 oracle minus (a). C8 (d) minus (a) leaving D12 out of the sum, which tests whether one child with reverse flow decides D17. Each is read through studies.bootstrap. The reported checks include the mean forecast's error beside every quantile-score contrast and the median minus mean forecast, per BSP.

docs.title: Triggers and size
docs.text:
• Stored: private files only.
  • Serving path: not touched.
  • Degradation rule: not touched.
  • More than one defensible design: yes, three, each pre-registered above.
  • Callers not nameable without searching: no, the scripts copy experiment 161's.

Audit triggers watched: a failed control (the known-answer check, the oracle), a result that contradicts experiment 161 (it should not, since (b) reproduces it), and the mean's error pointing the other way from the quantile score. One Opus audit is allowed and, if a trigger fires, it checks the sign convention of the converted flow.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: CPU only, at most 4 cores with every thread cap at 1, each job under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=16G -p OOMPolicy=continue. No GPU. The children's forecasts of experiments 152 and 155 and the spread tables of experiment 161 (d_tuning_D13, d_tuning_D17, and its bu_r_tdspread files) are reused. Arm (e) needs new pooled-shape fits and chains for D15 and D18, so it runs last and is dropped if the earlier arms use up the budget.

docs.title: Advice followed and departures
docs.text:
• Followed: experiment 161's advice to fix the weights' bounds and forecast the apparent-power children before expecting a gain; experiment 152's advice to keep the meter fit and fold only where reverse flow exists (here, D12). The latent flow of experiment 152 is a signed corrected apparent power, so it is multiplied by the power factor 0.97, as the signed history is.
  • Departure from the brief's wording: the brief asks for a gain of 5% with an interval wholly below zero. This plan requires the interval to lie wholly below minus 5%, which is stricter. For (d) beats (c), the plan requires only that (d) is no worse (upper end at most +0.03), because no apparent-power child at D13 has reverse flow. At D17 the predicted gain is 0% to 5%, so supported is expected to be reachable at D13 only.
  • Departure: the spread table. All bottom-up arms use the top-down table, which experiment 161 showed isolates the mean, instead of a table refitted on the sum.
  • Departure from the brief's wording: the brief says the 5% threshold is experiment 161's. Experiment 161 used 2%. This plan uses the brief's 5%, and also reports the 2% reading.
  • Chain mismatch: the apparent-power children's forecasts come from experiment 152's GAM-K chain (meter fit, additive filter), which has no winter night offset or error-correction recipe, so the MW children (arm D) and the apparent-power children are corrected differently. The page says so.

docs.title: Gap robustness of the convex model with a Kalman filter: coast or fall back
docs.text:
Take-home: when power readings stop, keep the Kalman filter running without new readings ("coasting") and widen the bands. At each of the four gap lengths tested (3, 6, 24, and 72 hours) that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction. A quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better. Whether dropping only the filter would beat coasting at about 72 hours could not be told. The formal verdict is inconclusive: each comparison planned in advance against the same forecast with the filter dropped has an interval that includes zero.

We asked what a live forecast should do when power readings go missing: let the filter coast, coast and also widen the bands, or drop the filter. The demand model is the convex generalised additive model of experiment 111 with a Kalman filter on its recent errors (GAM-K, a method re-implemented from de Vilmarest and Wintenberger (2022)), plus the winter night offset and recipe R of arm D of experiment 155. We hid every reading in the 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours ending at the forecast's data cutoff (the time of the last usable reading), for up to 56 forecast runs (events) at each of five substations (275 events in all), and scored the forecast over the next 168 hours. With coasting, the quantile score (2.747 points with no gap) worsened by 0.011 points after a 3-hour gap and by 0.206 points after a 72-hour gap. With the filter dropped, it worsened by 0.158 to 0.193 points at every gap length.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
All differences are in points of quantile score, over leads of 0.5 to 168 hours. An interval is the 99.4% bootstrap interval, resampled by calendar month, and "spans zero" means it includes zero. Rule letters: (a) coast, (b) coast with wider bands, (c2) drop the filter, (c) the frozen model alone.

  • Rules. (a) The filter on the gapped readings, then the winter night offset (a monthly refitted correction to winter night forecasts) and recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean forecast-error profile of the previous 14 days). (b) Rule (a) with the quantile offsets widened by the filter's variance growth since the last reading. (c2) Rule (a) with the filter dropped. (c) The convex demand model with no filter, offset, or recipe R, called the frozen model. The plan below fixes these rules before any score was read.
  • Events. Five decision substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16) with 53 to 56 events each (275 in all), one randomly drawn forecast run per 8-day block. The gap ends at the data cutoff (k = 0, where k is the number of hours between the gap's end and the cutoff). The spread tables, which hold the quantile offsets from the mean, come from the no-gap forecast of experiment 136's arm A2.
  • Absolute scores. No gap 2.747. Rule (a) 2.758, 2.790, 2.857, and 2.953 at 3, 6, 24, and 72 hours. Rule (b) 2.759, 2.788, 2.857, and 2.948. Rule (c2) 2.905, 2.905, 2.914, and 2.940. Rule (c) 3.198, whatever the gap.
  • Coasting minus dropping the filter (rule (a) minus rule (c2)). 3 hours -0.147 (-0.321 to +0.030). 6 hours -0.116 (-0.287 to +0.060). 24 hours -0.057 (-0.232 to +0.123). 72 hours +0.013 (-0.152 to +0.203). All four span zero, so no crossover length is established and the pre-registered test fails. Over leads under 24 hours the contrast is below zero at 3, 6, and 24 hours (-0.480, -0.401, and -0.295) and spans zero at 72 hours (-0.167, -0.353 to +0.022).
  • Coasting minus the frozen model alone (rule (a) minus rule (c)). -0.439 (-0.666 to -0.241), -0.408, -0.341, and -0.245 (-0.478 to -0.040) at 3, 6, 24, and 72 hours. The plan treats this contrast as descriptive.
  • Wider bands (rule (b) minus rule (a)). The score changes by -0.004 to +0.000 at every length, and every interval spans zero (72 hours: -0.004, -0.033 to +0.014). The share of actual readings below the predicted 5% quantile (q05) changes by -0.006, -0.011, -0.023, and -0.028 (24 hours: -0.032 to -0.015), and the share below q95 by +0.003, +0.007, +0.014, and +0.018.
  • Coverage. Under rule (a), 7.3%, 7.6%, 7.7%, and 8.4% of actual readings fall below q05 at the four gap lengths, and 95.1%, 94.9%, 94.5%, and 94.2% fall below q95. Under rule (b) the shares are 6.6%, 6.4%, 5.5%, and 5.6% below q05 and 95.5%, 95.6%, 95.9%, and 95.9% below q95. With no gap the shares are 7.1% and 95.1%.
  • Rule (b) meets the plan's criterion for replacing rule (a). The mean absolute distance of the q05 and q95 shares from nominal is 0.016 for rule (a) and 0.007 for rule (b) at 24 hours, and 0.021 and 0.008 at 72 hours. The intervals of the coverage differences exclude zero (24 hours: q05 -0.032 to -0.015, q95 +0.010 to +0.018), and the score difference is at most +0.000 against the +0.01 limit. The coverage differences use the month-resampled interval rather than the plan's binomial standard error, because forecast errors in the same month are correlated.
  • Tails under rule (a), 3 to 72 hours. The pinball loss at the 1% quantile is 0.222 to 0.257 and at the 99% quantile 0.231 to 0.242. The share of readings below the 1% quantile is 2.5% to 3.2% and below the 99% quantile 98.1% to 98.4%. Under rule (b) those shares are 1.6% to 2.2% and 98.6% to 98.8%.
  • Recovery. Recovery is the smallest k from which the score stays within 0.02 points of the no-gap score. After a 24-hour gap, rule (a) minus the no-gap score is +0.110, +0.074, +0.061, +0.060, +0.012, and +0.025 points when k is 0, 3, 6, 12, 24, and 48 hours, so the pre-registered recovery (6 hours or less) fails. The filter alone (rule (a0)) is within 0.02 points from 24 hours on. After a 3-hour gap, recovery takes 0 hours; after a 6-hour gap, 24 hours; after a 72-hour gap, the score has not recovered at 48 hours.
  • Differences between substations (rule (a) minus rule (c2)). At 3 hours: D10 -0.171, D11 -0.228, D14 -0.342, D16 +0.056, and D5 -0.040. At 72 hours: D10 +0.033, D11 -0.012, D14 -0.235, D16 +0.222, and D5 +0.061.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. Exactly 0.000 at every substation and rule, because the centred spread table places the median at the mean. The check cannot expose a shifted forecast here.
  • Mean-error contrast beside the quantile score. Rule (a) minus rule (c2) on the absolute error of the mean forecast is -0.270 (below zero), -0.219, -0.124, and -0.006 points at 3, 6, 24, and 72 hours. The sign matches the quantile-score contrast at 3, 6, and 24 hours and differs at 72 hours, where both contrasts span zero (mean error -0.233 to +0.234).
  • Controls. The rebuilt no-gap forecast reproduces experiment 155's stored arm D exactly (the largest mean difference is 0.0 at all five substations). Widening by zero variance leaves the quantiles unchanged. Replacing every actual at or after a run's origin with random numbers leaves the mean forecasts of three tested runs unchanged.
  • Audit. The skill's audit check fired because leaving out D14 moves the 24-hour contrast from -0.057 to +0.001, and leaving out D16 moves the 72-hour contrast from +0.013 to -0.040. An independent reviewer re-derived the contrasts from the stored forecasts, and they match to 4 decimal places. The reviewer found no path by which future readings reach the forecast. The reviewer traced both sign changes and the 72-hour sign to one date, 2026-01-13, at D5 and D16 (the first finding below). Both contrasts span zero, so the verdict does not change.

docs.title: Audit findings
docs.text:
• One switching date carries the 72-hour sign and both leave-one-out flips. On 2026-01-13 the no-gap forecast scored 15.3 points at D16 and 16.9 at D5, against 1.7 and 7.6 for rule (c2). The 14 days before that cutoff all fall inside a hand-filtered switching event, but the filter still read those readings. It had learned the changed load, moving its level estimate by +22 points at D16 and by -9 points at D5. The hidden gap did not cause the large errors. Dropping that date after the fact (a post-hoc cut, not the verdict) gives rule (a) minus rule (c2) of -0.204 (-0.363 to -0.059) at 3 hours and -0.171 (-0.327 to -0.023) at 6 hours, both below zero. The same cut gives -0.112 and -0.037 at 24 and 72 hours, both spanning zero. On that cut the pre-registered rule would read partly supported. The 72-hour sign, coasting worse, is not a basis for a rule that drops the filter.
  • At 3 and 6 hours the contrasts mostly measure the filter's no-gap value. Every forecast starts at 09:00 UTC and its data cutoff is 05:30 UTC, so a 3-hour gap covers only the night hour band (and the morning band in summer time). A band here is a block of hours of the day that gets its own correction. The contrast splits into +0.011 from the gap and -0.158 from the filter's no-gap advantage. A gap ending in the evening would test more.
  • The widening is crude. Most of the extra variance comes from the filter's short-lived transient component. The method applies it unchanged at every lead up to 168 hours, although it should shrink as the lead grows. Part of the coverage gain also corrects under-coverage that the no-gap forecast already has (7.1% of readings fall below q05, against a target of 5%).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Gaps are injected, not real. Hiding readings in clean data does not reproduce a stuck meter, a communications fault that backfills later, or a gap at a switching event.
  • The demand model's monthly refits continue during a gap. A gap that spans a refit cut would also thin the training data, and that effect is not modelled.
  • The quantile offsets differ slightly from those of the no-gap forecast. The offsets differ by up to 1.4 points, because the winter night offset and recipe R move on rows near a gap. Rule (c) has its own table.
  • Hidden readings stay hidden for later runs. A telemetry backfill would restore them, so the recovery shown is a worst case.
  • The 275 events lie in 18 calendar months, and the intervals resample those months.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Real outages would be a more realistic test. They could be scored once the cleaned power table's outage periods are listed. Resolving the 72-hour question would take more events or real gaps.
  • Masking switching readings from the filter could be tested. One date shows that unmasked readings can raise the quantile score by 14 points. A test that masks them would also settle the 72-hour comparison.
  • A small neural network could shorten the recovery. It would take the filter state and the hours since the last reading and rescale how fast the transient decays. If it works, the score after a 24-hour gap would be within 0.02 points of the no-gap score 12 hours after the gap ends.

docs.title: Planned design
docs.text:
The design below was fixed before any score was read. Two details changed after the plan review and before any run: the comparator for the headline contrasts is rule (c2), and the gap hides the actuals from the offset and recipe R as well as the filter.

Question. In production the convex demand model with a Kalman filter (GAM-K, the Kalman filter on recent errors of experiment 111; the method re-implements de Vilmarest and Wintenberger (2022)) will sometimes receive no power readings for hours or days. We ask which rule to serve then, and whether a gap length exists beyond which the filter should be dropped.

Design.

  • Inputs. The unfiltered forecast of every run (experiment 136's A2: the T-all fits driven by the calibrated ensemble mean), rebuilt from the stored fits and ensemble arrays as in experiment 197, and the filter's residual stream. The full pipeline is the arm D of experiment 155: the filter, the winter night offset, and recipe R (minus 0.75 times the 14-day mean error profile).
  • Events. For each substation the origins of the replicate and scored runs (excluding the every-fifth-day stride runs and any origin before 2024-07-16) are cut into blocks of 8 days, and one run is drawn at random (seed 205) from the first 3 days of each block, so two events are at least 6 days apart and no gap window reaches the previous event's cutoff. The same event runs are used for every gap length and rule.
  • Gap. The readings of all four hour bands are removed for the L hours up to k hours before the event run's data cutoff, with L in {3, 6, 24, 72} and k in {0, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48}; all 24 combinations are scored, and the headline contrasts use k = 0. One filter pass per (substation, L, k) applies the gaps of all that substation's events together, which is equivalent to one pass per event because the windows do not overlap.
  • What each stage sees. The filter reads the gapped stream. The winter night offset is refitted monthly on the errors of the earlier rows of the gapped timeline, as in experiment 155, with the actuals inside gaps hidden. Rows of the tuning months keep the no-gap filter's forecast, so every rule's spread table is the no-gap one even where a gap reaches back into a tuning month. Recipe R is recomputed from the gapped timeline: it uses the errors of the earlier runs from the gapped filter, and the actuals whose valid time falls inside any gap are hidden from its error blocks (a block with fewer than 40 readings is unusable, as in experiment 155). Scoring reads the true actuals of the event run's own rows, which all fall after its origin.
  • Rules. Each rule's offset, R profile, and spread come from that rule's own forecast errors. (a) Coast: the gapped filter, then the offset and R. (b) Coast with widened bands: rule (a)'s 11 quantiles with their offsets from the mean multiplied by sqrt(1 + v / s^2), where s = (q95 - q05) / 3.29 of the row, in points, and v is the extra predictive variance of the level and transient, in points squared, over the no-gap filter at the same cutoff. With n and n0 the half-hours from the target band's last reading to the cutoff in the gapped and the no-gap stream, v = max(0, w(n) - w(n0)), where w(n) = q n / 48 + sigma_z^2 (1 - phi^(2n)) / (1 - phi^2), using the single pooled setting (q, phi, sigma_z) of experiment 133 that arm A uses. (c2) The no-gap pipeline with the filter dropped for all runs: the frozen GAM plus its own offset and R. (c) The frozen GAM alone, with a spread refitted on its tuning months, no offset and no R. Secondary: (a0) and (b0) are (a) and (b) with the filter alone, no offset and no R, spread refitted on the filtered tuning errors.
  • Scored. Five decision substations, D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, then under 24 hours and 12 to 36 hours; per-substation contrasts and the number of events per substation and length are reported beside the pooled ones.
  • Compute. CPU only, 4 cores, no new fit; the filter re-runs on a masked stream per (substation, L, k).

Prior advice followed: the Kalman state is the one of experiment 111 with the POOL setting (experiment 136, A2); no faster level is used (experiment 197); recipe R at every lead and no offset on top of R is experiment 155's finding, but this plan keeps arm D, the pipeline that experiment 155 tested, so the offset stays in the gapped pipeline and the comparison stays with the stored arm D.

docs.title: E1: do a solar farm's meter outages show up in its Primary's power?
docs.text:
Metered-farm outages do not show up as extra solar generation at D10: the Primary's power does not change by the output of a metered solar farm when that farm's readings drop to zero. NGED removes the output of a metered solar farm from the power supplied by the Primary substation the farm sits under. If a farm's meter fails, the farm's output should then reappear in that Primary's power, which would look like a step up in the Primary's unmetered solar capacity. We found the outages of the six metered solar farms (labelled A to F) that last 3 days or more through the clear-sky hours of the day, and compared the Primary's power on those days with the 14 days either side. The Primary is the nearest one that shares the farm's bulk supply point, which is a guess, because NGED has not given the connections. Farm outputs are scaled by the farm's 99th-percentile output. At D10, the three zero-output outages that could be tested (farms A and C) changed the Primary's solar generation by -1% to -6% of the farm's output, the opposite sign to the prediction of +50% to +150%. The result narrows the search: meter failures at farms A and C do not explain capacity steps at D10, and the other decision Primaries could not be tested.

Verdict not supported. The pre-registered rule needed at least two thirds of the tested outages to show the shift, and 0 of 3 did. The brief's stop rule therefore holds: experiments E3 and E4 are not run. Experiment 207 (E2) ran at the same time, as instructed, and is a separate result.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Tested outages at the assigned Primary, as a share of the farm's 99th-percentile output (more solar is positive): farm A in March 2020 at D10 is -0.01 (95% interval -0.04 to 0.03), farm A in April 2021 at D10 is -0.05 (-0.15 to -0.01), and farm C in April 2021 at D10 is -0.06 (-0.11 to -0.02). In megawatts the Primary's power rose by 0.05, 0.29, and 0.49 MW, against farm outputs of 6.2, 6.2, and 8.1 MW. The two April 2021 outages overlap in time, so they are not independent.
  • Untestable: farm F's zero outage (August 2025) has 1 sunny half-hour at D5, and farm B's zero outages are at D15 and D18, which are not decision Primaries. No farm is assigned to D11 or D16.
  • Noise of the test: in 840 placebo windows with no outage (39 to 200 per farm), 7 shifted by 0.5 to 1.5 farm outputs in either direction (3 in the predicted direction), all at farm D. The 5th to 95th percentile of the placebo shift is within -0.15 to 0.10 of the farm's output for farms A, B, C, E, and F and -0.39 to 0.52 for farm D, whose output is only 1.2 MW.
  • Other nearby substations: none of the 9 zero outages tested at the MVA Primaries (which carry no sign) and none of the 1 tested at another MW Primary shows a shift. Of the 13 outages with no readings, 1 of 20 MVA tests (farm D, August 2022, at D8: 1.19, interval 0.63 to 1.76) is in the band.
  • Farm D's 101-day stretch without readings (March to July 2020) shifts its assigned Primary D14 by 1.95 farm outputs (1.49 to 2.59). The stretch is 7 times longer than the 14-day reference windows and spans the start of the 2020 lockdown, so the shift mixes demand and season changes with any generation effect.
  • Bulk supply point D13, post hoc and with no placebo: two of farm E's three stretches without readings coincide with a rise of 9 to 10 MW in D13's power, -0.57 and -0.56 of farm E's output (more solar is positive); the third, from July to September 2025, is -0.49 (-0.69 to -0.26). Farms A and C's overlapping April 2021 outages coincide with a rise of about 10 MW, -1.54 and -1.25 of their outputs, and one event could cause both. Farm A's March 2020 outage shifts D13 by +0.51 (0.00 to 1.10), in the predicted direction.
  • Audit triggers: the result contradicts its own prediction, so the ml-experiment skill's second trigger fired. We tested two explanations, a wrong parent Primary (the MVA Primaries, above) and a connection above the Primaries (D13, above); neither shows the predicted shift at a Primary. The placebo control passed. No forecast is scored, and no later experiment is built on this result.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Row definition: a Primary's half-hourly supplied power in MW (the feature cache of experiment 106, with switching-event half-hours dropped), on sunny daylight half-hours only (clear-sky irradiance above 300 W/m² and CAMS irradiance at least 80% of clear-sky). No forecast is scored.
  • Outages: 19 found (farm A 2, B 3, C 2, D 5, E 3, F 4), of which 6 are zero outages and 13 missing. Farm E counts from its commissioning on 2024-10-06.
  • Farm-to-Primary map: NGED's hierarchy file gives bulk supply points for five of the six farms and no Primary, so the assigned Primary is the nearest MW Primary with the same bulk supply point (D10 for farms A, C, and E; D15 for B; D14 for D; D5 for F). The nearest Primaries of several farms report in MVA, which carries no sign, so the true parent may be one of those. The distances are 3.1 to 9.2 km.
  • Amendment before any shift was seen: the minimum sunny half-hours were lowered from 100 and 300 to 20 and 60 (recorded on the plan before the first shift was computed).
  • Differences from the plan, found in code review: the minimum is 2 sunny samples per half-hour of the day in each window (the plan said 3 before the amendment, which lowered it to 2); an outage bridges up to 4 calendar days that have fewer than 4 clear-sky half-hours; a placebo window must hold no bad day (at least 80% of clear-sky half-hours flagged or missing) and at least 3 eligible days, and starts in March to September; and the farm's 99th-percentile output is taken over unflagged half-hours with clear-sky irradiance above 20 W/m², which differs slightly from the capacity unit of experiment 129.
  • Post hoc, labelled: MVA Primaries and the bulk supply point D13 were tested after the decision rule was applied, to explain the result. The bulk supply point uses the CAMS irradiance of D10 for its sunny mask.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: A connection list from NGED would show where the farms connect. The farms' outages are not visible at the substations we could test. The list would show whether the farms feed the MVA Primaries, and the bulk supply point's response to farm E suggests the farm feeds a substation above the Primaries.

docs.title: E2: can a step in solar capacity be seen? A known-answer test
docs.text:
A solar capacity that can change each month finds a known step in solar output, in size and to within a month, but at the pre-registered penalty it also invents steps at 2 of 5 Primaries (D10 and D11), so the gate fails. We asked whether the demand model of studies.dp_gam (a regression that stays convex, so it has one best fit) can find a sudden step in the solar capacity it infers for a Primary substation, which is a substation that feeds homes and businesses. The pinned capacity is the real-time estimate of the Primary's solar capacity that experiment 45 produced. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm to a Primary's power, from a known month onward or before it, at 30% or 60% of the Primary's pinned solar capacity, and checked how much of the step the fit found. The fit used April to August rows before 2025-07-01 only. We repeated the test for 20 injections at each of the 5 decision Primaries (5 farms, 2 sizes, on and off), and compared three capacity paths on the same rows. A path is the capacity in each month. The step path penalises the sum of the month-to-month changes, so it stays flat except where the data need a jump; the weight 0.3 is the pre-registered strength of that penalty. At that weight the step path found a median 0.98 to 1.00 of the injected step (the capacity change found, over the capacity change added), the smooth monthly path of experiment 157 found 0.87 to 0.91, and experiment 129's capacity that changes once a season-year found 0.24 to 0.49. The result narrows the search: a step as large as one farm's output is visible in summer data, so the open question is whether the real series contain such steps (experiment 206 found no meter-failure signal).

Verdict partly supported. At the pre-registered weight 0.3 the step path passes the size test (median in 0.75 to 1.25) at 5 of 5 Primaries. The step path passes the date test (at least 75% of dates within one month boundary of the true date) at 5 of 5 Primaries. The false-step test (fewer than 1 step above 0.5 MW per placebo year) passes at 3 of 5, so all three tests pass at 3 of 5 Primaries and the pre-registered gate, which needs 4 of 5, fails. D10 and D11 fail with 1.73 and 1.00 false steps per year. At weight 3, one of the pre-registered sensitivity weights, all three tests pass at 5 of 5, but the weight was picked after seeing the results. The smooth path also passes the size and date bands, so the claim that it blurs the step is not supported: it shrinks the size to 87% to 91%.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Gate table (tests passed, out of 5 Primaries), size / date / false steps / all three: weight 0.03 is 5 / 5 / 2 / 2, weight 0.3 is 5 / 5 / 3 / 3, weight 3 is 5 / 5 / 5 / 5, weight 30 is 1 / 5 / 5 / 1, and weight 300 is 0 / 2 / 5 / 0 (no step is allowed).
  • False steps per placebo year at weight 0.3 (no injection, mean of 5 row sets over 2022 to 2024): D5 0.00, D10 1.73, D11 1.00, D14 0.93, D16 0.60. At weight 3 they are 0.00, 0.60, 0.67, 0.53, and 0.13. A false step is a month-to-month change above 0.5 MW between two summer months, or the net change from the August level to the next April level. The largest false step at weight 0.3 is 1.79 MW. A step in the no-injection fit may be a real change in capacity, so the count is an upper bound.
  • Absolute recovery, median (95% interval over the 20 injections), weight 0.3: D5 0.98 (0.97 to 0.99), D10 0.99 (0.96 to 1.00), D11 1.00 (0.99 to 1.01), D14 1.00 (0.98 to 1.02), D16 1.00 (0.97 to 1.01). Smooth path: 0.87, 0.88, 0.90, 0.91, 0.89. Season-year steps: 0.24, 0.34, 0.49, 0.43, 0.37.
  • Date within one month boundary (31 days): 100% of injections for the step path (weights 0.3 and 3) and the smooth path at every Primary and 40% to 90% for season-year steps. The exact month is found in 100% of injections for the step path at weight 0.3 and the smooth path, 95% at D11 for weight 3, and 15% to 45% for season-year steps. The date is read on month boundaries, so the test cannot tell a step placed a few days into a month from one at its start.
  • Spread over the injections: the median ratio is 0.99 to 1.00 for each combination of size and direction, and 0.89 (farm B) to 1.02 (farm D) by farm.
  • Non-negativity of the level was not enforced: the lowest level is -0.68 points (a point is 1% of the Primary's effective capacity) at weight 0.3, in 3 path values.
  • Audit triggers: the first trigger of the ml-experiment skill fired, because the placebo control fails at D10 and D11 at the pre-registered weight (1.73 and 1.00 against a limit of 1), although the false steps are marginal and may be real steps. No forecast is scored, and no later experiment is built on this result.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Arms: the step path (weights 0.3, 0.03, 3, 30, and 300 per unit of step, as a share of the mean diagonal of the month Gram matrix; 30 and 300 were added after the first results), experiment 157's smooth monthly path (growth share 0.1), and experiment 129's season-year steps (ridge 0.1). All use one Gram matrix, so the row set is the same.
  • Row definition: half-hourly rows of April to August, before 2025-07-01, with a reading for the injected farm, about 26,000 rows per fit. No forecast is scored, so there is no lead range. Injected steps were 0.83 to 2.36 MW.
  • Step dates: the first of May, June, or July of 2022 to 2024 (seeded). A step in winter is not tested, because winter rows are not in the fit.
  • D9 is left out: its readings start in 2025, so no 2022 to 2024 step can be injected.
  • Disclosed differences from the plan: the bounded solver keeps the smooth path's levels at or above zero but not the step path's (the lowest step level is -0.68 points at weight 0.3, in 3 path values). The date tolerance is 31 days, so a step one month boundary away passes. The first draft counted only single month-to-month changes as false steps; a reviewer pointed out that the fit has no winter rows, so the count now also includes the net change from one summer to the next.
  • Injection: the farm's output is scaled by its 99th percentile and subtracted from the target from the step month on (on-step) or before it (off-step). Recovery is the change in the fitted level across the step, injected fit minus the fit without injection, over the injected capacity.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Experiment 206 found no meter-failure signal at the Primaries, so experiments E3 and E4 of the brief are not run. A later experiment that needs steps would fit the step path with weight near 3 and read candidate steps as "inferred, unconfirmed". The recovery here is a ceiling: a real meter-regime step has its own shape and may sit in winter, where this fit cannot see it.

docs.title: When does the forecast benefit from knowing about switching transfers, and what is a better or worse detector worth?
docs.text:
Telling the forecast about a switching transfer lowers its error by about 1.5 points of capacity during the transfer and in the 48 hours after it ends, but by only about 0.005 points averaged over a year, and none of the five real alarm sources tested stays inside the ordinary-day error limit. A switching transfer moves load from one Primary substation (one fed at a higher voltage than its customers) to its neighbours for hours or days. We tested one way of using that knowledge. The forecast is a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its recent errors. A "mask" sets the filter's recent power readings aside while a transfer is known, so the forecast leans on weather and calendar alone. An "alarm source" is a detector that flags a transfer from the power record. A score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, as a percentage of the substation's effective capacity ("points"); lower is better, and a gain is the no-mask score minus the arm's.

We answered three questions. The answers rest on 371 transfers that we simulated on the 27-month power record of six substations (44 simulated copies of the record), and on NGED's log of real transfers.

  • Is a detector worth having? Perfect knowledge gains 0.005 points averaged over every forecast row in the year. The pre-registered verdict is not supported because the hypothesis predicted a gain of at least 3 points after a transfer and the measured gain is 1.50 (1.08 to 1.96).
  • Where is the benefit? It sits during a transfer (+1.46, 0.69 to 2.29) and in the 48 hours after it ends (+1.50). It is smaller before an alarm would normally arrive (+0.61), rises with forecast lead (+0.81 at 0 to 12 hours, +1.79 at 36 hours to 7 days), and ranges across substations from +0.12 to +4.88.
  • What is a better or worse detector worth? RO-NC finds 37% of the simulated transfers and recovers 53% of the 48-hour gain. The share recovered rises steeply with the share of transfers found, and falls with delay only beyond 2 days.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Sources compared. K0 is no mask. PERFECT knows each transfer from its true onset and its end at once. PERFECT_LAG knows it with the live delays (onset 96 half-hours after the step, end 60 after the end). RO-NC is the stored detector of experiment 147. LOGGED is NGED's switching table. On the real record, the re-ranker (LEARNED_R) is experiment 195's learned score, and the pair alarm (PAIR_NEW, and PAIR_GATED when its balance score is 0.7 or more) is that of experiment 156. CLEAN is recent power without the simulated transfer, and GAM_ONLY ignores recent power. The simulated transfers are those of experiment 141, scored against the true normal-arrangement series as in experiment 151; the forecast and masks are those of experiment 163 and experiment 203. Nothing is retrained, and the weather is the analysis proxy of those experiments.
  • The gain after a transfer is 1.50 points (1.08 to 1.96) for perfect knowledge. The rows are the 213,533 forecasts for transfers of 25% of load or more lasting over 1 day (133 transfers during, 301 after, 353 before the alarm). Gains over K0 by phase, before the alarm, during, and after: PERFECT +0.61 (0.43 to 0.81), +1.46 (0.69 to 2.29), +1.50 (1.08 to 1.96); PERFECT_LAG +0.29, +1.46, +1.47; RO-NC -0.09 (-0.34 to +0.16), +0.44 (-0.02 to +1.03), +0.79 (0.44 to 1.19). K0 scores 4.17 after a transfer and CLEAN 2.46. Averaged over every forecast row of the year, PERFECT gains +0.0053, PERFECT_LAG +0.0045, and RO-NC +0.0013.
  • RO-NC recovers 53% (35% to 69%) of the 48-hour gain, which is fragile. The share is 61% (45% to 77%) without RO-NC's false alarms, 98% for PERFECT_LAG, and 71% (59% to 80%) for GAM_ONLY, which uses no detector. Subtracting RO-NC's moved megawatts instead of masking recovers 30% (2% to 52%) of the gain of subtracting the true megawatts. Leaving out one substation gives 44% (without D9) to 86% (without D11). CLEAN gains 115% of PERFECT's gain.
  • The pre-registered bar, "worth having", is not met. The bar needs the detector to recover at least 50% (point estimate) of the perfect gain in the 48 hours after a transfer and the ordinary-day error to have a 95% interval inside +/-0.05 points. RO-NC meets the first clause on the point estimate. No real alarm source meets the second.
  • Ordinary days (1,579,711 rows, 27 months; mask minus no mask, points; interval from resampling whole calendar months). PAIR_GATED +0.030 (-0.012 to +0.074), PAIR_NEW +0.055 (+0.009 to +0.105), re-ranker +0.031 (-0.020 to +0.086), logistic regression of experiment 195 +0.109 (+0.022 to +0.226), RO-NC re-run of experiment 195 +0.144 (+0.054 to +0.258). The last three intervals show a rise for PAIR_NEW, the logistic regression, and RO-NC.
  • The extra error scales with the number of alarms. Per alarm it is about +0.0003 points for random false alarms (+0.013 over 46 alarms, at precision 0.5), the pair alarm (+0.055 over 242 alarms), and the re-ranker (+0.031 over 104 to 150 alarms), and about +0.0014 for RO-NC (+0.144 over 104 alarms). Random false alarms at precision 0.75 (16 alarms) raise it by -0.000 (-0.000 to +0.000). Random alarms copy the durations of logged transfers, which real alarms need not match. The real sources raise 104 to 242 alarms of which 15 to 20 match a logged transfer, a precision of under 0.2 against the log (an unmatched alarm may be a real, unlogged transfer).
  • On the real record the gain is small once averaged over rows. In the 48 hours after a logged transfer ends, LOGGED gains +7.40 points (2.32 to 10.22), PAIR_GATED +6.35, the re-ranker +6.31 (interval 0.11 to 11.99), and RO-NC +6.18, over six windows of transfer and substation. Averaged over ordinary rows plus these rows the gain is about +0.017 for every real source and +0.020 for LOGGED, below the ordinary-day rise of +0.03 to +0.14 for four of the five sources. During a transfer the mask loses 4.75 points (LOGGED, 1.5 to 7.2), because the metered power really does include the transfer.
  • The value curve is steep in recall and flat in delay up to 2 days (share of the PERFECT gain, after the end; during; before the alarm). Recall 0.25: 37% (25% to 51%); 37%; 36%. Recall 0.5: 63% (47% to 80%); 72%; 48%. Recall 0.75: 77%; 96%; 66%. Onset delay up to 24 hours: 100% after the end (by construction, because those rows start 48 hours after the onset). Delay of 2 days: 100%; 100%; 46%. Delay of 3 days: 83%; 90%; 36%. Delay of 4 days: 64% (48% to 75%); 81%; 24%. Error of 25% or 50% in the megawatts, for subtraction: 86% or 72%. Repairing 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of RO-NC's missed transfers: 59%, 72%, 73%, or 85% (69% to 99%). The delays of 2 to 4 days were added post hoc. RO-NC finds 393 of 1,063 simulated transfer-substation pairs (37%), and 19 of 45 logged real transfers by this experiment's matching rule.
  • Quality needed for 50% after the end, other axes perfect. Recall of 0.25 is below the threshold and 0.5 above, but each interval spans 50%, so "about 0.4" is an interpolation. No tested delay or megawatt error falls below it.
  • Strata after a transfer (perfect knowledge). Winter (November to March) +1.60 (0.94 to 2.26) and summer +1.48 (1.00 to 2.00); RO-NC recovers 74% in winter (57 transfers) and 50% in summer. Substations: D10 +4.88, D11 +2.08, D9 +1.54, D14 +1.36, D16 +0.59 (-0.27 to +1.28), D5 +0.12 (-0.25 to +0.53). Every simulated transfer moves 25% of the load or more, and almost all last over 1 day, so the size and duration strata below those cannot be scored. The receiver metered or unmetered stratum is not scored, because the simulated transfers do not record it.
  • Tails after a transfer (coverage at q95 and q99, nominal 0.95 and 0.99; pinball at q05 and q95). K0: 0.758 and 0.864; 1.00 and 1.41. PERFECT: 0.948 and 0.983; 0.63 and 0.77. RO-NC: 0.845 and 0.916; 0.78 and 1.06. K0's upper quantiles sit too low after a transfer; PERFECT's are close to nominal.
  • Checks. The median minus the mean forecast per substation is the same for K0 and PERFECT (D5 -0.31 to D14 +0.10). The error of the mean forecast agrees with the score contrasts: K0 6.90, RO-NC 5.74, PERFECT 4.63, CLEAN 4.27. The controls reproduce experiment 203's K0 10.129 and PAIR_NEW 6.083 on 11 real transfers, PAIR_GATED +0.030 (-0.012 to +0.074), and K0 2.718 on ordinary rows. Audit trigger 2 fired: the perfect gain (1.50) and RO-NC's share (53%) missed their predictions (3 or more, and 15% to 40%). One possible explanation is size. The simulated transfers move a median of 9.5 points of capacity and the logged ones 15.4, and K0 scores 4.17 after a transfer on the simulated record against 13.6 on the real one. Size does not account for the whole gap (+1.50 against +7.40), and the two scores use different references. The other triggers did not fire. No Opus audit was run.
  • Deviations from the plan. The learned score of experiment 195 does not exist on simulated transfers, so RO-NC stands in there. The controls are experiment 203's printed numbers on 11 transfers. Tail coverage and pinball resample transfers, not months. The real-record phases before the alarm and during a transfer are scored against metered power. A debug run on 8 of the 44 simulated copies was read before the final run.
  • Next steps (options). An alarm source with far fewer alarms per matched transfer (for example a pair alarm that also needs balanced steps); a soft use of the alarm that keeps recent power; and a small neural gate that scores each alarm before masking, with the convex forecast as the comparison arm. Simulating transfers below 25% of load and under 6 hours would fill the empty strata. For a 2,500-series deployment, the logged-table results need NGED's labels; the detector results and the sweep do not.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: is a neural network needed to recalibrate arm D, or does a table do the same?
docs.text:
Take-home: lookup tables of corrections to arm D lower its score by only 0.03 to 0.04 points, while a neural network given similar inputs and no recent errors lowers it by 0.10, so this table design does not match the network and the cause is not yet isolated. Arm D is our best day-ahead demand forecast, from experiment 155. In experiment 200 a neural network learned corrections to arm D's median and uncertainty bands, and a copy of it that was given no recent forecast errors (the "network without error inputs") still gained 0.10 points. A lookup table had come within 0.01 to 0.02 points of that copy when both trained on one year of data. We asked whether a table still matches the network when both train on every year from 2020 on, and whether a term for temperature extremes (found in experiment 201) helps the table.

Answer: no table matches the network, and the temperature term helps by under 0.001 points. All scores are quantile scores in points of effective capacity, where a lower score is better. On the five decision substations in 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, the plain table (T0) scores 0.065 points worse than the network without error inputs (T0 minus network; 99% interval over resampled months 0.042 to 0.086). Four table variants (T1 to T4) stay within 0.006 points of T0. The verdict is not supported, because the rule fixed before the run needed the table to come within 0.02 points of the network.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Setup. Arm D is the best forecast of experiment 155. Each table is a sum of lookup terms, with no hidden layer, fitted by gradient descent on the pinball loss (Koenker and Bassett (1978)) over 11 quantiles. The terms shift arm D's median and scale its quantile offsets. Rows, training window (2020 to 2025-06-27), validation block, and scored rows (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, 15.5 to 39 hours ahead, outside switching events) are those of experiment 200. The network scores are experiment 200's stored rows. The table fits ran on CPU, with the median shifts and log-scales averaged over three seeds. The network rows are experiment 200's stored rows.
  • Arms. T0: median shift by site and half-hour, site and weekday, site and lead band, half-hour and weekday, site by arm D's forecast level (12 bins) by weather era, and the ensemble-era flag. T1: T0 plus a temperature-extremes term. T2: T0 without the forecast level by era term. T3 and T4 are post hoc: T3 fits the calendar terms separately for each weather era, and T4 adds forecast level by six-hour block by era and forecast level by weekday by lead band.
  • Scores (five decision substations, quantile score in points; lower is better). Arm D 2.432, T0 2.397, T1 2.396, T2 2.391, T3 2.395, T4 2.395, network without error inputs 2.332, network with error inputs 2.307.
  • Contrasts against arm D (99% month-resampled intervals). T0 -0.035 (-0.058 to -0.014), T1 -0.036 (-0.060 to -0.015), T2 -0.041 (-0.061 to -0.022), T3 -0.036 (-0.057 to -0.014), T4 -0.037 (-0.062 to -0.015), network without error inputs -0.100 (-0.140 to -0.064), network with error inputs -0.125 (-0.207 to -0.060).
  • Decision contrasts. T0 minus network without error inputs +0.065 (+0.042 to +0.086). T0 minus network with error inputs +0.090 (+0.038 to +0.171). T1 minus T0 -0.0009 (-0.0022 to -0.0001). T2 minus T0 -0.006 (-0.014 to +0.001), so the forecast level by era term does not help the table. T3 minus T0 -0.002 (-0.013 to +0.009). T4 minus T0 -0.002 (-0.009 to +0.004).
  • Tails (T0, decision substations). Coverage at q95 94.8%, at q99 98.3%, at q05 6.3%, at q01 2.0%. Pinball at q99 0.385 and at q01 0.352, against arm D's 0.411 and 0.386.
  • Per substation, T0 minus arm D. D5 -0.056, D10 +0.026, D11 +0.014, D14 -0.099, D16 -0.063, D9 +0.018. Leaving one decision substation out keeps T0 minus the network without error inputs between +0.039 and +0.077.
  • Pre-registered predictions. The table within 0.02 points of the network failed (+0.065). The temperature term lowering the score by 0.01 to 0.04 points failed (0.0009). The decision rule's gain condition for the temperature term (an interval wholly below zero) is met, but at 0.0009 points the term is not worth porting. The prediction that an additive table without the era term scores worse than arm D was not tested as written: T2 drops only the forecast level by era term and keeps the era flag, and it beats arm D by 0.041.
  • Caveats. The network has continuous inputs (lead, the sine and cosine of the half-hour, arm D's forecast) where the table has bins, and a spread head. The experiment does not say which of these the network needs. The table's spread scale is a lookup by site, lead band, and six-hour block. The temperature term is a linear hinge per substation. The driver temperature is the ensemble mean in the ensemble era and past weather before it.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site and the error of the median forecast were not computed: the stored rows hold quantile scores only, and every table shifts the median directly. The contrasts rest on the quantile score alone.
  • Triggers fired: trigger 2, because the result contradicts the pre-registered prediction and the reading of experiment 200's audit. The post hoc arms T3 and T4 tested two explanations and did not close the gap. The ML manager instructed that no audit run for this experiment.
  • Row alignment: the rows match experiment 200's stored rows (arm D losses agree within 0.001).

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Ablate the network without error inputs one input at a time (lead, half-hour, forecast level, era) to find the input whose smooth use the table misses.
  • Fit a gradient-boosted model with the pinball loss on the same inputs, as a second route to the same gain with an interpretable form.

docs.title: Does the noise in NGED's metered wind series occur only at low wind speed, so that ERA5 wind speed alone can find the rows to drop?
docs.text:
The noisy near-zero rows in NGED's three metered wind series are not confined to low wind, so ERA5 wind speed alone cannot find them. A rule that excludes every half-hourly reading below a wind-speed threshold removes 8.9% (W1), 9.9% (W2), and 15.2% (W3) of the readings. The rule still leaves about 60% of the idle-band readings in the data. A probable cause, which we did not test, is that ERA5 gives the wind in a 25 km cell, which can differ from the wind at the turbines by more than the width of the cut-in region (the wind speed at which turbines start generating). The rows we flag are stored in mask.parquet for the main wind-farm experiment to use.

We asked whether the idle noise (readings near zero, with repeated values, and in MVA a small non-zero floor) happens only when the wind is too light to turn the turbines. This is hypothesis H0, written down before any plot. We took half-hourly power from three of NGED's (National Grid Electricity Distribution's) metered wind farms, labelled W1 to W3 to keep them anonymous. W1 and W3 report apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA), which includes reactive power, and W2 reports real power in megawatts (MW). We took the wind speed at 100 m from ERA5, a weather reanalysis, at each farm's cell (Hersbach et al. (2020)). We then measured how often power sits in the idle band, which is the 5% to 95% range of power at ERA5 wind below 2 m/s, at each wind speed. The answer narrows the next step: a threshold on ERA5 wind speed is worth using only as one flag among several.

Verdict: not supported for all three farms. The prediction failed on both counts at every farm.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Data and alignment: 121,878 (W1), 121,940 (W2), and 121,535 (W3) half-hours from 2019-09 to 2026-09, with no nulls or duplicate times. The cleaning rules flag none of the three series. W1 has 185 gaps over 30 minutes (longest 5.0 days), W2 has 62 (longest about 10 days), and W3 has 227 (longest 38 hours). The longest identical-value runs are zeros of 108 to 155 half-hours. Power correlates best with ERA5 wind at lag 0 (0.858, 0.853, and 0.806), so no shift was applied.
  • Weather used: ERA5 100 m wind speed, linearly interpolated between the two hourly instants either side of each half-hour's midpoint (the stored timestamp minus 15 minutes). ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, so ERA5 is a research-only input and the detector below could not run live on it. The two farms W2 and W3 share one ERA5 cell, so their weather is one series.
  • Idle floor (ERA5 wind below 2 m/s): W1 median 0.299 MVA, 5% to 95% band 0 to 0.608, 41% exactly zero, 30% repeating the previous value. W2 median 0.000 MW, band -0.033 to 0.482, 40% negative (minimum -0.071), 19% exactly zero, 15% repeating. W3 median 0.025 MVA, band 0 to 0.243, 41% exactly zero, 27% repeating.
  • A dip only at W1, and a tiny one: the lowest bin median between 2 and 5 m/s minus the idle median is -0.017 MVA at W1 (0.08% of capacity), 0.000 MW at W2, and +0.001 MVA at W3. No bin median falls below the idle floor's 5% value, so the expected dip is barely visible at half-hourly, farm-level resolution.
  • H0 fails (pre-registered test): cut-in came out at 4.5 m/s for W1 and was set to the 3.0 m/s default for W2 and W3, whose empirical estimates (5.5 and 7.0 m/s) fell outside 2.5 to 4.5 m/s. So "above 1.5 times cut-in" means wind above 6.75 m/s (W1) and 4.5 m/s (W2 and W3). The 5% to 95% width per bin above that wind exceeds the reference residual width in 78% (W1), 100% (W2), and 100% (W3) of bins (median bin width 8.21 against 3.89 MVA, 4.38 against 0.99 MW, 1.68 against 0.34 MVA). The share of those rows in the idle band is 1.6% (W1), 13.0% (W2), and 29.9% (W3), against the 1% limit.
  • The idle share falls to 1% only at high wind: the idle share crosses 1% at about 9 to 10 m/s for W1 and W2 and about 16 m/s for W3, which stays noisy around 1% beyond that (Figure 3). Above 10 m/s it is 0.8% (W1), 0.8% (W2), and 6.2% (W3). It is 11% to 27% at 5 to 6 m/s for W1, and 50% to 26% at the same speeds for W2.
  • Idle share by year: at W1 and W2 the idle share above 1.5 times cut-in is steady across years (W1 1.0% to 3.1%, W2 11% to 14%). At W3 it is 70% in 2019, 45% in 2020, and 23% to 32% from 2021 to 2026, and above 10 m/s it is 1.5% from 2021. The first 2 years of W3 therefore carry a regime change, not a wind effect (post hoc).
  • W3 has a half-capacity level: at wind above 15 m/s, 13% of W3's half-hours sit between 40% and 60% of capacity and 1.6% below 10%, which suggests part of its capacity is often out of service. W1 (0.9%) and W2 (3.4%) show the same pattern far less (post hoc).
  • Outage rows (at least 12 hours in the idle band at wind above 1.5 times cut-in): W1 has 9 runs, 160.5 hours in total, longest 24 hours, began in 2020 (3), 2022 (1), 2023 (1), and 2024 (4). W2 has 23 runs, 427.5 hours, longest 55 hours, began in every year from 2019 to 2026 (7 in 2023). W3 has 151 runs, 2,741.5 hours (4.5% of its half-hours), longest 49 hours, with 80 of them began in 2019 and 2020.

Detector (threshold on ERA5 wind speed, largest threshold with at most 5% false drops on the training years):

Farm Threshold, all years (m/s) Dropped False drops Idle-band rows missed W1 3.2 8.9% 4.8% 61.5% W2 3.7 9.9% 4.9% 61.7% W3 4.5 15.2% 4.9% 59.8%

Out of sample, odd years to even years: W1 3.4 m/s, 10.0% dropped, 5.3% false, 57.8% missed; W2 3.5 m/s, 8.8%, 7.0%, 61.0%; W3 4.0 m/s, 11.5%, 4.5%, 69.2%. Even years to odd years: W1 3.1 m/s, 8.4%, 5.0%, 62.1%; W2 3.9 m/s, 11.2%, 3.6%, 61.2%; W3 5.0 m/s, 19.6%, 5.9%, 51.0%. The 5% false-drop limit applies to the training years, so a test-year rate can exceed it (W2 odd to even, 7.0%). A false drop is a dropped row with power above the idle band's 95% value plus 2% of capacity. A miss is an idle-band row, outside the suspected-outage runs, that the rule keeps.

  • The mask: the stored table mask.parquet holds 11,142 (W1), 12,903 (W2), and 24,009 (W3) rows, with drop_reason low_wind_idle (10,821, 12,048, and 18,526) or outage_suspected (321, 855, and 5,483). Those rows are 9.1%, 10.6%, and 19.8% of all rows.
  • Effect on the retained rows (median, 5%, 95%): W1 from 2.890, 0.000, 17.648 to 3.396, 0.251, 18.026 MVA. W2 from 1.538, 0.000, 7.875 to 1.856, 0.089, 8.013 MW. W3 from 0.374, 0.000, 2.095 to 0.617, 0.000, 2.211 MVA.
  • Dropped share by month: highest from May to July (W1 about 13%, W2 about 14% to 17%, W3 about 25% to 28%) and lowest in February and December (W1 4% to 6%, W2 4% to 7%, W3 8% to 14%).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, and quantile-score contrasts: not applicable, because the experiment fits no forecast and scores no quantile.
  • Audit triggers: trigger 2 fired in the plain sense that the result contradicts its prediction. No explanation was tested. The idle share falls smoothly over 3 to 10 m/s (Figure 3), which fits ERA5's wind error but also fits curtailment or turbine availability, and the W3 excess by year fits a regime change but does not show one. Trigger 7 may apply, because the main wind-farm experiment depends on the mask; the manager decides whether an audit runs. Triggers 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 do not apply (no control, no forecast contrasts, no nested arms).
  • Sensitivity not run: the nearest-hour wind in place of the interpolated wind, and a cut-in speed other than the pre-registered estimate. The idle share at 10 m/s and above does not depend on the cut-in speed. It meets the 1% limit at W1 and W2 (0.8% each) and fails only at W3 (6.2%), so H0 fails over the 5 to 9 m/s range at all three farms, and above 10 m/s at W3.

docs.title: What this narrows
docs.text:
• The idle floor exists, and above about 10 m/s it nearly disappears at W1 and W2, but ERA5 wind speed in a 25 km cell does not locate it. A rule on wind speed drops 9% to 15% of rows and finds only 30% to 50% of the idle-band rows out of sample.
  • The main experiment can keep the mask as a default, with the caveat that it is a coarse, hard drop. An alternative to test is to leave the rows in and let the forecast's lower quantiles absorb the idle band.
  • W3's first 2 years look like a different regime from the later years and hold most of W3's idle rows at high wind (idle share above 1.5 times cut-in 70% in 2019 and 45% in 2020, against 23% to 32% from 2021).
  • Next: a detector that uses the farm's own recent power (available live after a 3.5-hour delay) rather than ERA5 alone, and a test of whether NGED's meters or turbine availability explain the 12-hour runs.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Cut-in speed, hub height, and turbine model are unknown, and the 1.5 times cut-in rule uses an estimate taken from ERA5, so the exact wind at which H0 is tested is soft. The idle share above 10 m/s does not use the cut-in estimate, so it is the check free of that softness.
  • W2 and W3 share one ERA5 cell, so they are one independent weather series.
  • The mask rule uses ERA5, which is not available at forecast time. It is for training and evaluation rows only.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: can a boosted-tree calibrator capture the gain of the network without error inputs?
docs.text:
Take-home: a boosted-tree model captured 0.064 of the 0.065 points that lookup tables missed, so a boosted-tree calibrator is a candidate to replace the neural network, though the interval allows a loss of up to 0.026 points. Arm D is our best day-ahead demand forecast, from experiment 155. In experiment 200 a neural network that was given no recent forecast errors (the "network without error inputs") lowered arm D's score by 0.10 points. Experiment 209 showed that no lookup table gets beyond 0.041. We asked whether a gradient-boosted tree model gets the full 0.10 points without a neural network on the serving path, and which input of the neural network carries the gain.

Answer: yes by the rule fixed before the run, and forecast level and weather era carry the gain. All scores are quantile scores in points of effective capacity, where lower is better. On the five decision substations in 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, the boosted-tree model scores 0.098 points below arm D, and 0.0015 points above the network without error inputs (99% interval over resampled months -0.028 to +0.026). The point estimate is within the 0.02 limit and the interval includes zero, so the verdict is supported. The interval is also wide enough to include a loss of 0.026 points, above the limit, so the data do not show that the tree model is as good as the network, only that they could not separate the two.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Setup. Rows, training window (2020 to 2025-06-27), validation block, and scored rows are those of experiment 200. The boosted-tree model is XGBoost with the pinball loss (Koenker and Bassett (1978)) at the 11 quantiles, fitted to arm D's quantile residuals on the network's inputs: substation, lead, half-hour, weekday, arm D's forecast level, the ensemble-era flag, and four of arm D's quantile offsets. Column subsampling is off, so that every arm sees every input. Depth 6, learning rate 0.1, minimum child weight 50, early stopping at round 288 on the validation block. The retrained network and its four ablations ran on CPU, with one seed each.
  • Scores (five decision substations, points; lower is better). Arm D 2.432, lookup table (T0) 2.397, network without error inputs (stored, experiment 200) 2.332, the same network retrained here 2.341, boosted-tree model 2.334.
  • Decision contrast. Boosted-tree model minus stored network +0.0015 (-0.028 to +0.026). Minus the retrained network -0.0072 (-0.036 to +0.018). Minus table T0 -0.064 (-0.085 to -0.044). Minus arm D -0.098 (-0.131 to -0.065).
  • Ablations (each minus the retrained network, 99% intervals). No lead -0.0009 (-0.0049 to +0.0030). No half-hour +0.0097 (-0.0031 to +0.0253). No forecast level +0.041 (+0.021 to +0.065). No era flag +0.042 (+0.021 to +0.065). The retrained network gains 0.091 over arm D, so removing the forecast level or the era flag gives back 45% and 46% of the gain.
  • Retrained against stored network. The retrained network scores 0.0087 above the stored one (+0.005 to +0.012), from a different seed and a CPU run. The ablation contrasts use the retrained network as the reference for this reason.
  • Tails (boosted-tree model). Coverage at q95 95.0% and at q99 99.3%. Pinball at q99 0.373 and at q01 0.338 against T0's 0.385 and 0.352. Coverage at q05 and q01 was not computed.
  • Leave one substation out. Boosted-tree minus retrained network stays between -0.015 and -0.002 when any one decision substation is dropped.
  • All six substations. The decision contrast is +0.0038 (-0.023 to +0.029); no ablation contrast changes by more than 0.005.
  • Pre-registered predictions. Boosted tree within 0.02 of the network: held. Removing forecast level or era removes at least half the gain: the point estimates (45% and 46%) fall just under half, and the intervals include half. Removing lead or half-hour changes the score by under 0.02: held.
  • Caveats. One seed for each network arm. The tree model has no ablations of its own, so the experiment does not show that the tree model relies on the same two inputs. The 99% interval rests on about 12 resampled months and five substations.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site and the error of the median forecast were not computed: the stored rows hold quantile scores only.
  • Triggers fired: none. The result agrees with the pre-registered prediction, except that the two largest ablations removed 45% and 46% of the gain, just under the predicted half. No input was changed to make it hold, and the rows are those audited in experiment 200.
  • Row alignment: arm D's losses agree with experiment 200's stored rows within 0.001, and the table T0 rows are those of experiment 209.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Fit the boosted-tree model on all 16 Primary substations and a second scored year, to narrow the interval that currently allows a 0.026 loss.
  • Ablate the tree model's inputs, to check that it relies on forecast level and era as the network does.

docs.title: Can alarms raised by a live switching detector replace hand labels when the forecast model is trained?
docs.text:
Masking switching transfers when the forecast model is trained barely matters, so a detector has almost nothing to replace. A switching transfer moves load between Primary substations for hours or days. Every earlier forecast in this project trained with the logged and hand-labelled transfers set missing, and nobody had measured what that masking changed. We refitted experiment 111's forecast model at five Primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16). That model is a convex additive model (GAM) with a Kalman filter that corrects its recent errors (GAM-K), refitted each month on the previous 24 months of readings. We refitted it three ways: with no training mask (arm A), with the hand labels masked (arm B, experiment 111's own fits), and with the alarms of experiment 195's detector masked (arm C). The detector is a learned score that flags a likely transfer in the readings. Arm C used only the alarms raised by each refit date, as a live service would have them. We scored each arm on clean rows (the scored year, outside every logged transfer and the 72 hours after it) and on rows after a logged transfer. The score is the quantile score in points of effective capacity, the error as a percentage of each substation's effective capacity, where lower is better. We repeated the comparison on 476 simulated transfers (generated with experiment 195's injector) added to the training readings, in "worlds" of simulated records, and scored against the true readings. Arm A is 0.002 points worse than arm B on clean rows and 0.003 worse on rows after a logged transfer. Simulated transfers widen the gap to 0.009. All three gaps are far below the 0.05-point improvement that the pre-registered plan required, so the verdict is inconclusive: there is little for a mask to repair, and the detector did not fail.

The refits build on three earlier experiments. The alarm intervals, the 4-day delay before an alarm is known, and the end rule come from experiment 203. The step stamp as the mask's start comes from experiment 188. Experiments 163 and 171 masked the recent-power correction instead of the training rows.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• The positive control passes, and the verdict is inconclusive. Arm B's coefficients equal experiment 111's stored fits exactly (maximum relative difference 0) at all 27 monthly refit dates of the five substations (printed_control.txt). Its scores equal experiment 203's no-mask scores row by row (maximum difference 0). Arm A minus arm B is under 0.05 on rows after a logged transfer (+0.0025) and in the worlds (+0.0091 net of the real record). That triggers the first row of the pre-registered verdict table, inconclusive.
  • The gates, reported although the table stops earlier. G1 holds: arm C minus arm B on clean rows is +0.0065 (-0.0069 to +0.0246). G2 fails: arm A minus arm C on rows after a logged transfer is +0.0005 (-0.0077 to +0.0072), against the 0.05 bar. G3 holds on its two conditions (arm C minus B +0.0051, arm A minus C +0.0040 with an interval of +0.00003 to +0.0093), but the gap that arm C could close in the worlds is only 0.009.
  • Absolute scores. Clean rows (scored year, 462,137 rows): A 2.7913, B 2.7890, C 2.7955. Rows after a logged transfer that the detector can know about (1,130,781 rows, 17 logged transfers): A 2.8215, B 2.8191, C 2.8210. Rows within 4 days after a transfer (14,895 rows, 4 months): A 3.5462, B 3.6304, C 3.5452. The 4-day rows are too few to resolve anything: arm A minus B is -0.0842 (-0.2209 to -0.0064) there, with arm A scoring better.
  • Rows after a logged transfer are 86% of the ordinary rows, so that contrast is diffuse. They are every cached run from 2024-04 whose latest monthly fit has, inside its 24-month window, a logged transfer that ended at least 4 days before the refit date.
  • The hand mask is too small to matter much. It holds 0 to 2,406 half-hours in the 24-month window at the last refit (D5 2,406, D10 1,044, D11 0, D14 592, D16 2,085) out of about 35,000 training half-hours. Arm A therefore trains on exactly that many more half-hours than arm B. The ridge penalty and the long window dilute a transfer's pull on the coefficients.
  • The detector's alarms cover the hand mask poorly. The share of the hand mask covered, per fold of experiment 195, is D5 41%, D10 48% to 52%, D14 32% to 43%, and D16 67%. D11 has no hand mask. Between 50% and 100% of an alarm's half-hours lie outside the hand mask.
  • Replacing hand labels with the detector worsens the score slightly. Arm C minus arm B on clean rows is +0.0065 (-0.0069 to +0.0246), and each of the three folds gives +0.0057, +0.0070, or +0.0068. In winter (November to March, 182,832 rows) the contrast is +0.0267 (-0.0015 to +0.0632), outside the plan's +/-0.02 band on its point estimate. On the odd months, which the learned score was not trained on, it is +0.0167 (-0.0047 to +0.0483). On the even months, which it was trained on, it is -0.0036 (-0.0153 to +0.0102).
  • Simulated transfers raise the gap only to 0.009. 12 of experiment 195's held-out worlds (3 folds, 4 worlds each) put 476 simulated transfers on 47 substation-and-world cells, and the detector found 125. Net of the real record (each arm against the real-record arm of the same fold), arm A minus arm B is +0.0091 (+0.0039 to +0.0150), arm A minus arm C +0.0040 (+0.00003 to +0.0093), and arm C minus arm B +0.0051 (+0.0013 to +0.0101). Worlds with 17 to 19 transfers on D5 worsen arm A by 0.10 and 0.13 points, and the other cells sit below 0.05, so the average rests on a few D5 worlds.
  • Checks: mean-forecast error. The error of the mean forecast points the same way as every quantile-score contrast on clean rows: C minus B +0.0061 (-0.0198 to +0.0382), A minus B +0.0053 (-0.0034 to +0.0135), A minus C -0.0008 (-0.0404 to +0.0312).
  • Checks: median minus mean forecast per site (clean rows, points). B: D5 -0.1345, D10 -0.0639, D11 -0.0266, D14 +0.0331, D16 +0.0144. A differs from B by at most 0.0006.
  • Checks: leaving one substation out. Arm C minus B on clean rows stays between +0.0006 and +0.0105 and positive without each substation. Arm A minus B changes sign without D16 (-0.0005) and stays between +0.0028 and +0.0035 otherwise. Arm A minus C on rows after a logged transfer runs from -0.0024 (without D16) to +0.0037 (without D11), changes sign without D5 or D16, and has an interval that includes zero in every case.
  • Checks: audit triggers. Two audit triggers fired and no audit was run. The result contradicts the prediction that arm A minus arm C would reach 0.05. The explanation, that the hand mask is at most 7% of training half-hours, is tested by the worlds, where 476 simulated transfers still worsen the score by only 0.009 points. Two leave-one-out contrasts changed sign, arm A minus B without D16 and arm A minus C without D5 or D16. Both contrasts are under 0.003, and either sign sits far from the 0.05 bar, so the verdict is unchanged.
  • Tail calibration on clean rows (share of readings below the quantile; nominal 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99). A: 0.0150, 0.0484, 0.9564, 0.9873. B: 0.0148, 0.0478, 0.9564, 0.9872. C (fold 0): 0.0150, 0.0480, 0.9555, 0.9865. Pinball loss at those quantiles and the curtailment-cost saving were not computed, because the contrasts are under 0.01 points.
  • The refits used monthly refit dates and a 24-month window. This is experiment 111's schedule. A weekly schedule would refit on mostly the same rows, so the contrasts are unlikely to depend on it.
  • The alarms are not label-free. Experiment 195's features come from the residual of a GAM trained with the labelled transfers masked. Its learned score was trained on the even months of the whole record, and its threshold of 80 alarms counts alarms that the logged transfers do not explain.
  • Five departures from the plan. D9 is not scored. The detector's intervals are not padded like the hand mask, because the cache does not record the hand mask's padding. An alarm known exactly at the refit date counts as known, which moves one half-hour and is copied from experiment 203. In the worlds, a receiver takes an equal share of the moved MW, the random drift of experiment 195's profile is omitted, and 4 of the 6 worlds per fold are used.
  • Intervals resample whole clusters. The interval for rows after a logged transfer resamples the 17 logged transfers, and the clean-row interval resamples 12 calendar months. Arm C is the mean of the scores of the three folds' alarm tables, as experiment 203 scores ordinary rows, because a substation sits in Primary pairs of several folds. The three folds' own contrasts are listed above.
  • What this narrows. A training-time mask is not where a detector helps most. The forecast's recent-power correction is where experiments 163 and 171 found changes of several points. An open question is how the unmasked GAM copes at D5, where large simulated transfers worsened the score by up to 0.13 points.

docs.title: Experiment 213: online band adaptation from recent coverage misses
docs.text:
Learning the band widths from the misses of the last few days did not lift cold-night coverage reliably, and a fixed widening of the upper quantiles did as well, with almost no change in the all-row score. A quantile is a level of the forecast's error distribution: the q95 is the value that the demand reading should fall at or under on 95% of rows. Coverage is the share of rows on which it does. A cold night is a winter night (November to March, evening or night hours) whose ERA5 day-mean temperature (the ECMWF reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) is below 2 °C.

We asked whether the quantile offsets of the best demand forecast so far can learn from recent misses. That forecast is arm A of experiment 169. An offset is the distance from the mean forecast to a quantile. After every reading that is at least 3.5 hours old, the offset grows if the reading fell outside the quantile and shrinks if it fell inside. The aim was cold-night q95 coverage of 0.90 or more without a second fitted model of the forecast's spread. The update is that of adaptive conformal inference (ACI, Gibbs and Candes (2021)).

The result is a small gain in one period, a loss in the other, and a worse score. In the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29) the best of three learning rates (gamma, the size of each update) lifts coverage from 0.896 to 0.906. It also worsens the all-row quantile score by 0.013 points of effective capacity (percentage points of each substation's rated demand; lower is better), which is over the pre-registered limit of 0.010. In the replicate months (other months of the earlier year), ACI at gamma 0.01 lowers coverage from 0.913 to 0.892. The pre-registered rule gives the verdict inconclusive, because the coverage gain (+0.0102) is just over the 0.01 below which the rule says refuted. In substance, online adaptation did not do what it was meant to do.

  • Arms. Arm A: experiment 169's arm A. Arm ACI: arm A with each of the quantile offsets at q01, q05, q10, q25, q75, q90, q95, and q99 times exp(u), where u is learned per series, hour band, and level by u += gamma * (miss - alpha) after each reading and clamped to [ln 0.7, ln 2.0].
