The gamma grid is 0.01, 0.03, and 0.1. Arm CW (reference, post hoc): arm A with the q90, q95, and q99 offsets times 1.06, 1.06, and 1.11, the intercept-only values of experiment 169's audit.
  • Contrasts. C1: ACI minus A in all-row quantile score. C2: ACI minus A in cold-night q95 coverage. C3 (descriptive, post hoc): ACI minus CW in cold-night q95 coverage. Each is a paired difference with a month-resampled 95% interval.
  • Row set and schedule. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, the five decision substations D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (D9 written beside, in no contrast), leads 0.5 to 168 hours, rows outside the hand-filtered switching events: 464,363 rows in the scored year and 299,306 in the replicate months. The mean forecasts are experiment 155's stored monthly refits, so no contrast depends on the retraining schedule. The tuning and replicate months are alternate months, so the state restarts at 0 whenever readings are more than 36 hours apart; the restart may handicap ACI in those months.
  • Gamma selection (deviation from the plan). No gamma had a tuning-month C1 upper bound at or under +0.01 (+0.012 at gamma 0.01, +0.051 at 0.03, +0.108 at 0.1), so the pre-registered selection rule selected no gamma. The script fell back to the smallest gamma, 0.01, which the plan did not state. Cold-night q95 coverage in the tuning months: A 0.918, ACI 0.925, 0.921, and 0.901 at the three gammas.
  • Headline, scored year (gamma 0.01). Cold-night q95 coverage 0.906 against A's 0.896 (+0.010, 95% interval -0.007 to +0.025; 5,395 rows). All-row q95 coverage 0.947, all-row q05 coverage 0.055 (A: 0.948 and 0.065). C1, all rows: +0.0132 (-0.0010 to +0.0295). Of the pre-registered pass conditions (cold-night coverage, all-row coverage, score bound), only the score bound fails.
  • Headline, replicate months. Cold-night q95 coverage 0.892 against A's 0.913 (-0.021, -0.041 to 0.000). C1 -0.0017 (-0.0208 to +0.0189). ACI fails the coverage condition and the score bound.
  • Gamma sweep, scored year (cold-night q95 coverage, C1). 0.01: 0.906, +0.013; 0.03: 0.941, +0.030; 0.1: 0.909, +0.034. Replicate months: 0.892, 0.874, and 0.889, so no step size passes both periods (post hoc reading of the sweep, not a selection).
  • Absolute scores, scored year, decision substations. A 2.7519, CW 2.7532, ACI 2.7651, BG2 (the best-guess forecast of experiment 87) 2.7804, manual heuristic 3.4968, climatology 3.8038.

  • Cold spells, scored year (cold-night q95 coverage; A, ACI, CW). First night of a spell: 0.870, 0.857, 0.876 (516 rows). The 3 days after it: 0.917, 0.916, 0.925 (2,242 rows). Later nights: 0.884, 0.908, 0.904 (2,637 rows). A night is keyed to the evening on which it starts. The stages hold 2, 5, and 8 distinct night dates, so these are point values without intervals. Replicate months: first night 1.000 for all three arms (804 rows); 3 days after 0.884, 0.856, 0.893; later nights 1.000 (112 rows).

  • Special days, scored year (A, ACI). Bank holidays (9,812 rows): q95 coverage 0.934, 0.928; C1 +0.086 (+0.019 to +0.131), so the score worsens. Christmas, 24 December to 1 January (8,641 rows): q95 coverage 0.934, 0.951; q05 coverage 0.075, 0.094; C1 +0.093, and no interval is quoted because the period lies in one month, which leaves the month-resampled bootstrap nothing to resample.

  • Tail calibration, scored year (coverage / pinball loss; A, ACI). All rows: q01 0.022 / 0.216 and 0.017 / 0.210; q05 0.065 / 0.714 and 0.055 / 0.718; q95 0.948 / 0.745 and 0.947 / 0.756; q99 0.982 / 0.232 and 0.984 / 0.233. Cold nights: q01 0.045 / 0.392 and 0.031 / 0.354; q05 0.090 / 0.950 and 0.099 / 0.943; q95 0.896 / 0.819 and 0.906 / 0.858; q99 0.959 / 0.282 and 0.959 / 0.291.
  • Against the constant widening. ACI minus CW in cold-night q95 coverage: -0.004 (-0.019 to +0.006) in the scored year and -0.028 (-0.055 to 0.000) in the replicate months.
  • Caveats. The scored year holds 10 cold days, so cold-night figures rest on a handful of spells, and the interval on the cold-night coverage gain is wide (-0.007 to +0.025). Leaving one substation out moves ACI's scored-year cold-night coverage to 0.901 (D5), 0.921 (D10), 0.925 (D11), 0.879 (D14), and 0.907 (D16), so the 0.90 pass depends on D14. The chosen gamma is the fallback described above. Arm A's q05 coverage (0.065) already misses the plan's rule that coverage stay within 0.01 of nominal, so the plan used "no further from 0.05 than A, plus 0.01". The replicate-month result may reflect the monthly state restarts. That explanation was not tested. The curtailment-cost metric was not run: experiment 169's figures show that it cannot rank forecasts this close.
  • What to try next. (1) A bias correction of the mean forecast at ensemble-mean temperatures of 0 °C or below, since bands that learn from misses cannot react before a cold spell starts. (2) If an online band is still wanted, one that learns separately for ensemble-cold days, scored over at least two winters, with a continuous history instead of alternate months.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site. 0.000 for every arm at every substation: no arm scales the q50 offset.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast is identical across all arms (4.7096 points in the scored year), because the mean is unchanged, so the quantile-score contrasts cannot come from the mean.
  • Reproduction. Arm A rescored from experiment 169's stored forecasts gives 2.7521 on all five decision substations' rows in this experiment's scorer (2.7519 on the rows shared with BG2), a gap of 0.0002 from the printed 2.7519, inside the 0.001 cap. A gamma of 0 reproduces arm A's quantiles exactly at every substation and period (the script raises otherwise).
  • Prediction check. Cold-night coverage rose by 0.010 in the scored year (predicted 0.00 to 0.03), but fell by 0.021 in the replicate months. The all-row score changed by +0.013 (predicted -0.01 to +0.01), just outside the range.
  • Audit triggers that fired. Two of the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill fired. (Trigger 2) The prediction failed in the replicate months, where coverage fell, and the monthly state restart is an untested explanation. (Trigger 6) The C1 interval in the scored year (-0.001 to +0.030, width 0.031) is 2.3 times as wide as experiment 169's C2 interval on the same rows (width 0.013). An online scale that changes from month to month is expected to vary more than a fixed multiplier, but that expectation was not tested. No Opus audit was run, because this experiment's brief excluded Opus. The verdict is inconclusive, so an audit finding could only confirm or weaken it, and the decision to merge without an audit is left to the maintainer.

docs.title: Does capping D5's solar output at 60% still help when the cap is chosen using only earlier data?
docs.text:
Choosing the 60% cap at D5 from earlier data alone keeps almost all of its gain, and none of the other five Primaries shows the same pattern clearly. A Primary substation is a substation that feeds homes and businesses; D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised labels for six of them. Experiment 180 found that the D5 forecast has lower error on sunny half-hours when the solar output the forecast subtracts from the substation's power is capped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5. That cap mimics an export limit on the solar generators behind D5. Experiment 180 chose 60% on some months and scored it on a later year, so the choice never used only earlier data.

We asked two questions. First, does the gain remain if the cap is chosen at each monthly retraining from the previous 12 months of forecasts, rather than using the scored year? Second, do the other five Primaries show the same levelling-off of net power as the sun rises? Here "as-of" means chosen using only data from before the retraining. The gain is the change in mean absolute error of the median forecast, in megawatts (MW), against a control that has no cap; "sunny" means the sunniest third of a substation's daylight half-hours. The as-of cap kept 97% of the gain (-0.129 MW against -0.133 MW). Only D5 showed the levelling-off. D9 improved by 0.032 MW and D11 worsened by 0.017 MW, and the intervals of both include zero.

Figure 1 shows each Primary's change in error, with D5 and D9 also shown with the cap chosen as-of.

Figure 2 shows the change in error at each fixed ceiling, at D5 and D9.

Figure 3 shows, per Primary and summer, the solar output implied by net power against the fleet solar shape, a south-facing panel's expected output scaled by the sun's height and the irradiance. Only D5 falls towards the sunniest half-hours.

Verdict partly supported. The D5 prediction we wrote down before fitting holds. The as-of cap lay in 50% to 70% at 12 of 12 refits (60% at 11, 50% at one), and the as-of arm keeps 0.129 MW of the 0.133 MW gain against a required 0.08 MW. The D5 interval is wholly below zero, and D10 and D16, which we expected to be unaffected, moved by under 0.02 MW. D9's estimated gain is 0.032 MW, which meets the 0.03 MW threshold. Its interval includes zero, and supported required the interval to lie wholly below zero. The decision rule did not cover that case, so we labelled it partly supported. D11's estimate (+0.017 MW) exceeds the 0.01 MW we predicted for the other Primaries, but its interval spans zero.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Rows: the 292 forecast runs of the scored year (2025-07 to 2026-06) used in experiment 178, leaving out half-hours affected by switching events, leads 0.5 to 168 hours. The forecasts are the monthly retrainings of the generalised additive model (GAM) of experiment 180, so only the cap differs between arms and the contrast does not depend on the retraining schedule. D5 has 14,045 sunny half-hours and D9 has 15,415. BG2 is the best-guess forecast that experiment 180 compared against.

Sunny daylight, mean absolute error (MW) Control As-of cap Fixed 60% BG2 D5 0.655 0.527 0.523 0.453 D9 0.497 0.465 0.460 0.418
  • D5 against the control (as-of, 98.33% interval from resampling whole months): -0.129 MW (-0.212 to -0.029). Pinball loss averaged over 11 quantiles is 0.185 for the control, 0.155 as-of, and 0.154 at fixed 60%. The gap to BG2 falls from +0.202 MW to +0.073 MW (+0.028 to +0.099).
  • D9 against the control (as-of): -0.032 MW (-0.076 to +0.007). The cap is 60% at 10 of 12 refits and 50% at two. The gap to BG2 falls from +0.079 MW to +0.047 MW (-0.008 to +0.080).
  • The other four Primaries at a fixed 60% cap, against the control: D10 +0.004 MW (-0.024 to +0.037), D11 +0.017 (-0.005 to +0.041), D14 -0.001 (-0.049 to +0.049), D16 -0.004 (-0.050 to +0.048). Pooled: +0.004 (-0.029 to +0.043).
  • As-of choice at D5: 60% at 11 refits and 50% at the refit of 2026-03-01 (mean error over the previous 12 months 0.468 MW at both). At the first refit the errors were 0.494 MW at 60%, 0.502 at 50%, 0.519 at 70%, and 0.591 with no cap.
  • Screen (figure 3): we ranked each Primary's clear May to August half-hours by the fleet solar shape and compared the implied solar output in the top two tenths with that in the fourth to sixth tenths. A ratio well below 1 means solar output levels off as the sun rises. The ratio is 0.77, 0.68, and 0.73 at D5 in the summers of 2022, 2023, and 2024, and 0.98 to 3.74 at D10, D11, D14, and D16. D9 has 0 and 28 clear half-hours in 2022 and 2023, and its 2024 ratio is undefined because the middle tenths are negative, so D9 fails the screen.
  • Replicate months: letting the as-of window grow from 3 to 11 months picks 60% at every refit again (gains of -0.124 MW at D5 and -0.031 MW at D9). Experiment 180 used these months to choose 60%, so this repeats the choice and is not independent evidence.
  • Ceiling sweep (figure 2): at D5 the gain peaks at 50% to 60% (-0.126 and -0.133 MW) and is -0.007 MW at 90%. At D9 the shape is the same at about one third of the size.
  • Caveats: D9 has about six months of data before 2024-07, so its as-of sunny threshold (top third of the daylight shape before 2024-07) differs from the scored year's threshold. The as-of rule selects on the quantity scored.
Sunny rows at D5, as-of against control q01 q05 q95 q99 Share of actuals below the forecast, as-of 0.056 0.178 0.996 0.999 Share of actuals below the forecast, control 0.051 0.168 0.967 0.993 Pinball loss (MW), as-of 0.0230 0.0841 0.0765 0.0209 Pinball loss (MW), control 0.0252 0.0972 0.0806 0.0218

The 95% and 99% quantile forecasts lie above the actual value more often than 95% and 99% of the time, and the cap makes this worse.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: the new fixed-60% forecasts at D5 are identical to experiment 180's (largest difference 0 in the median forecast and in the 99% quantile forecast; e00214_checks.py).
  • Median against mean forecast: stage 2 of the forecast chain sets the mean forecast equal to the median, so the difference is 0 by construction and the check cannot show whether the spread of the forecast shifts it. The error contrast of the mean forecast is therefore the same as the median's, and this experiment cannot test whether the two point in different directions.
  • Audit conditions: none was met. The reproduction passed, D10 and D16 stayed inside 0.02 MW, the as-of arm does not beat the fixed-60% arm that it contains, and the D5 interval has about the same width as experiment 180's. Leaving out D11 moves the pooled estimate for the other four Primaries from +0.004 MW to -0.000 MW, and leaving out any other Primary leaves it between +0.004 and +0.007 MW (e00214_checks.py). The pooled interval includes zero in all five cases.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• The as-of rule adds one ceiling-selection step to each monthly retraining, and it is ready to consider for the next model release.
  • Repeat the screen and the contrast at D9 once it has at least two summers of data before the scored year.
  • The planned combination check can use the as-of ceiling rule in place of the fixed 60% ceiling.

docs.title: Do the real Primary series show jumps in solar capacity that match feed-in tariff installation dates?
docs.text:
The fit finds no more jumps in solar capacity in the real Primary series than it invents on test series where none exists, and the list of feed-in tariff solar installations stops before the months the fit uses, so no jump can be confirmed. We asked whether the power drawn at six Primary substations (labelled D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), which feed homes and businesses, shows sudden changes in the capacity of the solar panels connected to them. Experiment 207 built an estimate of solar capacity that is allowed to jump from one month to the next, and showed that the estimate finds a solar farm that we had added to a substation's power. Here we ran that estimate on the real April-to-August power of each Primary from July 2021 to June 2026, with nothing added, and listed every change of more than 0.5 MW. We found 7 such changes across 4 of the 6 Primaries. The only dated record of installations we hold, the feed-in tariff register (a list of small solar installations paid under a UK subsidy scheme), ends on 2021-03-24. The project excludes every row before 2021-07-20 from training, because of the COVID-19 lockdown. No change can therefore be matched to an installation date.

Figure 1: the fitted capacity rises at D10 to D16 and stays within 2.2 to 2.8 MW at D5, and the marked month-to-month changes above 0.5 MW are few.

Figure 2: the real series show no more changes per year than experiment 207's series with no change, except at D16.

Figure 3: no month the fit trains on comes before the register's last commissioning date.

The prediction is partly supported: changes of 0.5 MW or more exist at 4 Primaries, none can be matched to an installation, and the placebo Primaries stay under 1 change per year. Whether a change at D10 or D16 lies within 60 days of a register cluster could not be tested, so that part of the prediction is neither confirmed nor refuted. D5 shows 0 changes and D14 shows 0.20 per year. The check that the scan code reproduces experiment 207's stored result at D10 passed (largest difference 1.7e-13, in the units of the fitted capacity).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
We used April to August half-hours from 2021-07 to 2026-06 at each Primary (D9 from 2024-04), after dropping the lockdown months and the periods of switching, which leaves 34,690 to 35,804 half-hours per Primary and 19,041 at D9. The fit uses every row, including rows after the date it describes, so it is a retrospective scan and not a forecast. The penalty on the total change in capacity has weight 3, as in experiment 207.

Primary Month-to-month changes August-to-April changes Per year Experiment 207, per year, no change added D5 0 0 0.00 0.00 D9 (2.25 years) 0 0 0.00 none D10 2 1 0.60 0.60 D11 1 1 0.40 0.67 D14 0 1 0.20 0.53 D16 0 1 0.20 0.13
  • All 7 changes are increases. D10: +0.60 MW (August 2022), +0.51 MW (May 2023), and +0.54 MW from August 2022 to April 2023. D11: +1.08 MW (August 2022) and +1.46 MW from August 2021 to April
  • D14: +1.45 MW from August 2021 to April 2022. D16: +0.58 MW from August 2022 to April 2023. An August-to-April change is a net change across the winter. Its date is unknown within the winter, because the fit uses only April to August rows.
  • The two changes of about +1.45 MW in the first winter, at D11 and D14, are probably fit artefacts. The two values are equal to within 0.02 MW, and the fit has no earlier summer to anchor either.
  • No change falls in the register's period, so none can be matched. Between 2019-09 and 2021-03, no 60-day window at any Primary holds 0.5 MW or more of share-weighted registered capacity (the base rate is 0%). The register holds almost nothing from those months: 393 installations were commissioned across the whole register from April 2019 to March 2021, against 860,064 before April 2019, so even a fit that covered 2019 to 2021 could not find a cluster. Every change is therefore described as inferred, unconfirmed.
  • Sensitivity (post hoc, not part of the verdict): at penalty weight 0.3 the fit finds 9, 3, 4, and 6 changes at D10, D11, D14, and D16 (none at D5, 2 at D9). At penalty weight 30 it finds one change each at D10, D11, and D14. The count falls as the penalty grows, as experiment 207 found.
  • The fitted capacity at D10 rises from 0.4 MW in 2021 to 2.7 MW in 2026, and 1.7 MW of that 2.3 MW rise is in changes above 0.5 MW. D5 stays between 2.2 and 2.8 MW.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: refitted using only the data up to 2025-07-01, experiment 207's cut-off, the scan's base path at D10 for weight 3 matches experiment 207's stored path in all 48 months (largest difference 1.7e-13, in the units of the fitted capacity). e00215_scan.py prints it.
  • Forecast checks: this experiment scores no forecast, so the forecast checks do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: none fired. The untested match is explained in the verdict paragraph and is not an unexplained contradiction.
  • Plan correction: the plan expected that changes in the summer of 2020 could be matched. The lockdown window removes that summer from training.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Match the changes to a register that covers 2021 to 2026, or to the metered record of a known installation, before reading any change as a commissioning.
  • Show the changes on the substation cards as inferred, and only once one is confirmed as real.
  • Find a way to use the lockdown months without biasing the fit, so that the fit has a summer before 2021 to anchor the first winter.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: can a more flexible temperature curve in the convex model carry the network's correction?
docs.text:
Adding extra terms for very hot and very cold weather to arm D, our convex demand forecast, recovered 20% to 27% of the quantile-score gain that a neural network gives over arm D in the scored year, and the recovery was not confirmed in a second year. The neural network's correction is spread over all temperatures instead of sitting at the extremes, and a smooth function of temperature explains under 1% of it. The neural network therefore uses an input other than temperature. Calendar and seasonal inputs are where the remaining gain may lie. Under the pre-registered rule, prediction 1 is partly supported at both the 0.05 and the 0.02 threshold: both arms gain 0.027 to 0.036 points in the scored year, and neither gains in the replicate year. The verdict is inconclusive because the placebo check of the pre-registered known-answer test failed (10.2% in sample and 12.5% on held-out months, against a limit of under 10%); the shortfall against the neural network does not depend on that check.

This experiment asked whether the correction that a small neural network gives the best-guess convex demand forecast (arm D of experiment 155) is a shape the convex model could carry. Experiments 200 and 201 found that the network lowers the quantile score by 0.09 to 0.125 points, and experiment 209 found that a binned table recovers only 0.035 to 0.041. We refitted the convex model with extra hinge terms in the hot and cold tails of each substation's temperature range, rebuilt arm D from the refits, and compared the result with the stored network on the same rows. We then fitted a convex surface to the neural network's correction. The fit shows how much of the correction a function of temperature, hour band, and day type can express. A hinge term is zero below a given temperature and rises linearly above it. "Points" below are points of the quantile score, in percentage points of effective capacity. The scored year is 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29, and the replicate year is the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. R0 is arm D as stored; the rebuilt control reproduces it exactly (2.7562 points in the scored year, all 464,363 rows). F1 adds 32 tail hinge columns per substation (cold knots at the 5th and 1st percentiles and hot knots at the 95th and 99th percentiles of the training rows' 6-hour and 24-hour averaged temperature). F2 adds the same on the 72-hour average plus an unconstrained linear term in it (20 more columns). The stored network is arm 2 of experiment 201, three seeds.
  • Schedule and rows. Monthly refit on 24 months, as in experiment 155; six substations, with the five decision substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16) in the contrasts. A weekly refit might change the contrast, because the tail knots move at each cut.
  • Prediction 1 (convex route recovers half of the neural network's gain): failed. Under the pre-registered rule it is partly supported, because the scored-year intervals are wholly below zero but the gain is under 0.05 and the replicate year disagrees; the same holds at 0.02. In the scored year F1 scored 2.7293 (-0.027 against R0; 97.5% interval -0.052 to -0.007) and F2 2.7205 (-0.036; -0.074 to -0.007). The network scored 2.6197, 2.6153, and 2.6396 across seeds (-0.137, -0.141, -0.117 against R0), so F1 recovers 20% and F2 27% of the mean gain. In the replicate year (the even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06; the network is not stored there, so the comparison is with R0 only) F1 was +0.007 (-0.006 to +0.023) and F2 +0.026 (-0.010 to +0.086), with intervals that include zero. D10 alone drives this: without D10 F1 is -0.017 and F2 -0.016, and four of five decision substations improve with F1. Under 6 hours F1 gains in the replicate year (-0.027) and over 6 hours it does not, the reverse of the scored year. The decision rule's median monthly difference was not computed.
  • Prediction 2 (convex surface explains 70% of the correction): failed. Temperature by hour band by day type explains 9.9% of the variance of the neural network's median correction in sample and 0.8% on held-out months (leave-one-month-out; 0.06% to 0.8% across three smoothing weights). Adding arm D's filter state gives 0.9%, day of year 10.6%, and both 9.5%. Held-out rows inside the other months' temperature range are 99.97% of the rows, so the low score is not an extrapolation artefact.
  • Prediction 3 (gain sits in the outer deciles): failed. Deciles 1 and 10 hold 24.8% of the network's gain (95% interval 11.0% to 49.3%), 28.2% of F1's (-33.7% to 64.7%) and 23.0% of F2's, against 23.5% of the rows and 22.3% of arm D's score. The network's gain peaks in deciles 3, 8, and 9.
  • Tuning. The tail ridge ratio was chosen on the tuning months from {1, 0.1, 0.01}. The mean absolute error of the filtered mean forecast on outer-decile rows was 4.591, 4.680, and 4.721 against 4.602 for arm D, so the base ridge (ratio 1) was chosen and the weaker penalties the brief asked for lost.
  • Where F1 gains. The scored-year gain is at leads of 6 hours or more (-0.028; -0.054 to -0.007); under 6 hours the gain is -0.001 (-0.021 to +0.021). The gain is -0.015 to -0.035 at every substation, and no leave-one-out flips it (-0.025 to -0.030).
  • Tail calibration (five decision substations, scored year; coverage and pinball loss):
Arm q01 q05 q95 q99 R0 2.4%, 0.215 7.0%, 0.712 94.7%, 0.749 98.3%, 0.232 F1 2.3%, 0.213 6.9%, 0.706 94.9%, 0.745 98.4%, 0.232 F2 2.3%, 0.213 6.8%, 0.704 95.1%, 0.741 98.4%, 0.231

docs.title: Known-answer test and placebo check
docs.text:
• Known-answer test (hot-tail step). With 3% of the training window's mean absolute demand added to the target above the 95th percentile of temperature, F1 recovered 62% (F2 66%, arm D 20%) on the injected rows and 55% (58%, 21%) on held-out months, at every one of the 6 substations (59% to 66%). A ramp injection was recovered 68% and 66% against 11%; a cold-tail step 65% and 66% against 45%.
  • Placebo. An injection in the middle half of the temperature range changed F1's fitted values on hot-tail rows by 10.2% of the amount in sample and 12.5% on held-out months (15% at D5, D10, and D11); F2 changed them by -0.8% and arm D by 23.7% in sample. F1 therefore fails the pre-registered limit of under 10%. Arm D leaks more than F1, so the leak is the smoothness of the convex demand model and not the tail columns. The verdict follows the pre-registered cap.

docs.title: Consistency checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per substation: 0.000 at all six, because the stored quantiles centre on the corrected mean.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each contrast: F1 -0.053 (97.5% interval -0.108 to -0.012) and F2 -0.069 (-0.149 to -0.011) in the scored year, the same direction as the quantile score; in the replicate year +0.011 and +0.038, both with intervals that include zero.
  • Triggers fired: trigger 4. In the replicate year F1's contrast is -0.017 without D10 and +0.009 to +0.019 without any other substation, because D10 alone is +0.107. Trigger 1 (a control fails: the placebo) and trigger 7 (the series of neural-network experiments depends on the headline) are also arguable. Audit trigger 4 fired and no audit was run, because of the quota. The verdict is inconclusive and nothing is ported on it. Read the replicate-year F1 contrast as unreliable: it flips sign when D10 is left out.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The replicate year has 6 resampling units (the even months), and the network is not stored there, so prediction 1's replicate clause compares the tail columns with arm D only.
  • Deciles use the analysis-frame 24-hour temperature at the valid time, not the ensemble-mean temperature. The share of scored rows on which each tail hinge is active under the ensemble-mean weather was not computed.
  • Arm S's leave-one-month-out folds are by the month of the run's origin, and a run's valid times reach up to 7 days into the next month, so the held-out score may be slightly inflated. The in-range share (99.97%) is measured against the global temperature range, not per hour band and day type, so it does not prove that no cell was extrapolated. Both faults would strengthen the conclusion only if the true score were higher, and the reported score is already under 1%.
  • The pre-registered hypothesis range of 0.09 to 0.125 points came from experiment 201's six-substation figures; on the five decision substations the neural network's gain is 0.117 to 0.141.
  • Only day of year was tested among the calendar inputs; lagged errors and holiday flags were not, so which inputs the neural network adds is not settled.
  • The hot-hinge gain by hour band is mixed: F1 gains 0.10 in the night band and 0.05 at midday but loses 0.04 in the evening band on hot rows, so some of the hot-tail gain may be solar error.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test calendar and seasonal inputs. Day of year takes a convex surface from 0.8% to 10.6% of the neural network's correction on held-out months, about a tenth of it, which may point at a seasonal or calendar effect that arm D's heating terms do not carry. A learned small network on day of year and hour, with the convex model as the comparison arm, is the ranked suggestion; it could fail if the gain vanishes in the replicate year.
  • If hot-tail terms are tried again, cap the hot slope or test a stronger ridge.

docs.title: Does one threshold in noise units give predictable alarm rates across Primary substations, with no load-shift labels?
docs.text:
Take-home: a threshold in noise units gives similar alarm rates across Primary substations only when it is low. Flexpectation version 2 therefore needs an automatic per-Primary rule for any threshold above about 3 noise units. A switching detector raises an alarm when it sees a sudden step in a substation's demand that the weather-driven demand model did not predict. At 4.35 noise units, the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) raises between 0.9 and 19 alarms per Primary-year across 15 Primaries. Of the 13 Primaries other than D8 and D9 (two substations whose alarms stood out in an earlier analysis), 9 fall within a factor of 2 of the median of 4.7 alarms per Primary-year. The pre-registered bar was 11 of 13, so the first part of the prediction fails. Post hoc, the same detector at 2.5 noise units puts 13 of 13 within a factor of 2 (median 27 alarms per Primary-year). The agreement between Primaries worsens steadily as the threshold rises. At 4.35 noise units D8 and D9 are within a factor of 3 of the median, no more extreme than D18 or D10. Of the statistics we measured on the residual, the share of days on which the demand model's daily mean error exceeds 3 noise units predicts the RO-NC alarm rate best of the 30 or so statistics we tried, on 15 Primaries.

We asked whether a detector's alarm rate on a new Primary can be predicted from that Primary's residual alone, so that Flexpectation version 2, which will have no switching labels, needs no per-Primary tuning. We ran RO-NC and the pair alarm (an alarm that needs a connected substation to step the opposite way) at the thresholds in noise units that experiment 130 and experiment 156 stored. The residual is the gap between observed demand and the frozen convex demand model of experiment 130. We used the whole history of every Primary with 12 or more months of residual. We counted all alarms and read no switching label, logged closure, or labelled transfer. We also read the stored alarms of the learned score of experiment 195, which is trained on switching labels. One noise unit is the scale of the 24-hour step statistic, estimated from odd months. The result narrows the search for version 2 to a per-Primary rule that sets a threshold from the residual's tail, not only from its noise scale.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
• Prediction, part 1 fails. RO-NC at 4.35 noise units: 9 of 13 other Primaries are within a factor of 2 of the median (69%; 11 were needed). The pair alarm at 3.75 noise units: 5 of 13. Dropping any one Primary in turn leaves between 8 of 12 and 9 of 13, so no single Primary changes this result.
  • Prediction, part 2 holds, but was never at risk. D8 is 2.14 times and D9 is 0.51 times the median under the current noise estimate, so both were inside a factor of 3 before any change. The two robust estimates keep them inside (figure 4). The verdict therefore rests on part 1. The pair alarm, which carries no verdict, fails both parts: 5 of 13, and D9 has no alarms in 2.5 years.
  • The two robust estimates do not narrow the spread. R1, the median absolute deviation (MAD) of all months, equals the current odd-month MAD within 8%, so R1 changes most rates by less than 10%, and doubles D12's from 0.9 to 1.8 (9 of 13; standard deviation of the base-2 logarithm of the rate 1.00 against 1.17). R2, the 95th percentile divided by 1.96, more than halves the median rate to 2.0 and leaves 9 of 13 (1.30).
  • The label-tuned detectors are not clearly more uniform. RO-NC XL (stored alarms, threshold tuned so that at most 80 alarms in odd months match no logged closure) has 9 of 13 within a factor of 2, and D9, at 3.2 times the median, is outside a factor of 3. The learned re-ranker has 10 of 13 within a factor of 2, and the learned logistic score has 7 of 13.
  • Rate against threshold (post hoc). Other Primaries within a factor of 2 of the median: 13 of 13 at 2.5 noise units, 12 at 3.0, 11 at 3.5, 9 at 4.35, 8 at 5.0, 6 at 6.0, and 4 at 8.0 (figure 3).
  • Best predictor, for RO-NC only. The share of days on which the day's mean residual exceeds 3 noise units predicts the base-2 logarithm of the RO-NC alarm rate best. Each prediction is made without the Primary it predicts. The mean absolute error is 0.58 (about a factor of 1.5 in the rate), against 1.14 for the baseline of predicting the median of the other Primaries' log rates. 13 of 15 predictions fall within a factor of 2 (correlation 0.81, figure 2).
    • Without D18, which has 1 year of residual and the largest share (0.42), the correlation is 0.72 and the error 0.62 against a baseline of 1.19.
    • The tail ratio (95th percentile over MAD) comes next (error 0.93). The noise scale at any window gives 1.03 to 1.04, barely better than the baseline.
    • For the pair alarm the best statistic, the tail ratio, gives 1.46 against a baseline of 1.80. No statistic beats the baseline of 1.34 for RO-NC XL. No single statistic worked for the pair alarm or RO-NC XL.
    • The 0.58 is the best of about 30 candidate statistics ranked on 15 Primaries, not a nested leave-one-Primary-out, so it is optimistic.
  • Winter against the rest. Pooled over Primaries, RO-NC raises 5.4 alarms per Primary-year in December to February and 4.7 in the other months. The pair alarm raises 4.0 in winter and 4.7 in the other months. The per-Primary split is in the table. These pooled rates have no interval, so the difference is not evidence of a seasonal effect.
  • D8 and D9 are within a factor of 3 of the median at 4.35 noise units. D8 is the highest of the 13 other Primaries between 3.0 and 3.5 noise units (2.5 to 2.7 times the median). D8 has the largest noise (a 24-hour step scale of 0.62 MW against a median of 0.16) and the heaviest upper tail (95th percentile 0.94 MW), but at a fixed threshold in noise units its rate is 2.1 times the median, not an outlier. D9 is ordinary on the noise, tail, and misfit statistics (misfit share 0.14, equal to the median; kurtosis 2.7), but its holiday misfit share, 0.26, is the fourth highest of 15,, and raises 6 RO-NC alarms in 2.5 years at 4.35 noise units. Its 34 alarms under RO-NC XL come from the label-trained score, which admits alarms at a lower threshold in noise units; these data do not say which of that score's inputs raises them.
  • Tail calibration and curtailment. Not applicable: no forecast is scored.

docs.title: Residual statistics and alarm rates per Primary
Checks
docs.text:
• Forecast checks (median minus mean forecast, mean-forecast error beside each contrast): not applicable, because the experiment scores alarm counts, not forecasts.
  • Audit triggers: none fired. There is no control. An earlier analysis (not published) found that D8 and D9 raise 61 of 148 alarms that match no logged closure. This result differs, because at a fixed threshold in noise units D8 and D9 are not outliers. Only the label-tuned RO-NC XL puts D9 outside a factor of 3 (figure 4), so the detector, not the series, produces that finding. Dropping any one Primary never reaches 80% (between 8 of 12 and 9 of 13). No nested arms, sister experiment, or later design depends on this result yet.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Residual and alarms share the same data. The misfit share and the tail ratio are measured on the residual from which the alarms are computed, so the link between each statistic and the alarm rate is partly built in. The leave-one-Primary-out test shows the link holds across Primaries, not that the statistic is independent of the alarms.
  • Thresholds were tuned on labels elsewhere. This experiment reads no label, but the thresholds of 4.35 and 3.75 noise units were chosen in experiments 130 and 156 against logged closures. "Label-free" describes what this experiment reads, not those thresholds. The misfit day compares the day's mean residual with the scale of the 24-hour step statistic, the same scale the alarm threshold divides by.
  • Only 15 Primaries. D18 has 1 year and D9 2.5 years of residual. The intervals in figure 1 are wide, and alarms in the same week are not independent.
  • Lab shortcuts. The residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late, and a convex model refitted on the 1st and the 16th of each month, as in experiment 130. A live service would have ensemble forecast weather instead. The learned-score alarms are the stored cross-fitted alarms of experiment 195, averaged over its three folds, and the learned-score thresholds use switching labels.
  • Post hoc. The threshold sweep (figure 3) and the robustness checks were not in the plan. The noise estimates R1 and R2 were named in the plan before any rate was seen.
  • The 35 logged transfers, the real load transfers in the switching log, were not read.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a per-Primary alarm budget give uniform rates with no labels? Set each Primary's threshold so that its alarms equal a target number per Primary-year, estimated from its own history, and check that the rate holds on a later year. The prediction that could fail: the rate in the held-out year stays within a factor of 2 of the target for at least 80% of Primaries.
  • Does the misfit-day share carry over to a held-out period? Compute it on one year and predict the next year's alarm rate.

docs.title: Does a per-farm plant model fit the six metered solar farms better than the fleet shape?
docs.text:
Giving each of the six metered solar farms its own plant parameters barely improves the fit, so the plant is probably not what limits it; the sunshine data is the likelier source. NGED meters the output of six solar farms in its trial area, which this page labels A to F. We asked whether a plant model with a fitted panel tilt, panel azimuth, ratio of direct-current (DC) to alternating-current (AC) capacity, heat loss, and soft inverter clip (a smooth cap on AC output) fits each farm's metered output better than one fleet shape, a single generic south-facing plant (tilt 35 degrees, 0.4% loss per kelvin) whose only fitted number is a scale. We fitted each plant on the months before 2025-09 and scored it on the next 12 months (a "fold"), using satellite-derived irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) and ERA5 air temperature. The fraction of metered output fitted, defined as one minus the squared error over the squared metered output on daylight half-hours, rose from 0.950 to 0.953. We had predicted 0.97 or more, a rise from the 0.93 that experiment 157 found for one scale of the fleet shape on other rows.

The prediction we wrote before fitting fails, and the stop rule we wrote with it fires. The median over farms of the fraction of output fitted is 0.953 for arm 2 (the per-farm plant), with a 98.75% interval of 0.933 to 0.966 from resampling the 12 scored months. Arm 1 (the fleet shape with one fitted scale per farm) scores 0.950. The gain is 0.003 (0.0004 to 0.014), under the 0.02 threshold. The best tilt is 20 degrees and the best azimuth is 180 degrees (south) at all six farms, but 20 is one of seven values on a coarse grid (10, 20, 30, 35, 40, 50, and 60). The DC:AC ratio (the fitted scale over the fitted AC limit) is 1.04 to 1.17 at five farms; at farm A the limit sits above the scale (ratio 0.80), so its clip never bites. The heat loss is 0 at five of six farms, the lowest value of the grid. Pooling the geometry and heat loss from the other five farms picks the same tilt, azimuth, and heat loss at every farm, so contrast C4 equals contrast C3 and tests nothing about pooling. Arm 1 has no clip, so C1 bundles geometry, heat loss, and clip; the no-clip ablation scores 0.9526, so the clip accounts for 0.0004 of the 0.003.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Fold 1 (tuned before 2025-09, scored 2025-09 to 2026-08, CAMS irradiance), median over farms: arm 1 0.950 (0.922 to 0.963), arm 2 0.953 (0.933 to 0.966), arm 3 0.944 (0.917 to 0.959), arm 4 0.953 (0.933 to 0.966), no-clip ablation 0.953, fleet-geometry ablation 0.952.
  • Contrasts, fold 1, 98.75% intervals: C1 (arm 2 minus arm 1) 0.003 (0.0004 to 0.014); C2 (arm 3 minus arm 2) -0.009 (-0.019 to -0.004); C3 (arm 2 minus arm 4) -0.0002 (-0.0008 to 0.0007); C4 (arm 2 minus pooled geometry) -0.0002 (-0.0008 to 0.0007). Arm 2 beats arm 1 in 55 of 72 farm-months (6 farms times 12 scored months), and in all six farms (+0.0005 to +0.012).
  • Fold 2 (tuned before 2024-09, scored 2024-09 to 2025-08, farm E absent): arm 1 0.947, arm 2 0.954; C1 0.007 (0.002 to 0.024), C2 -0.008 (-0.012 to 0.004). Fold 2 reuses fold 1's tuning months, so fold 2 is a replication and not an independent test.
  • Error in capacity points (fold 1, median over farms): arm 1 7.5, arm 2 7.4. In MW per farm, arm 2 gives 0.45, 0.56, 0.52, 0.10, 1.59, and 0.40 for farms A to F.
  • Tail slices, median fraction fitted (arm 1, arm 2): sunny half-hours (clear-sky irradiance above 650 W/m²) 0.968, 0.973; hot half-hours (air temperature above the farm's 90th percentile) 0.977, 0.977; shoulder months (March, April, September, October) 0.946, 0.946.
  • Forecast-time weather: the same fold-1 plants driven by the ECMWF ensemble mean at 12 to 36 h leads fit 0.910 (arm 1) and 0.912 (arm 4), against 0.950 and 0.953 with CAMS on the same half-hours. Error is 10.3 and 10.5 points of capacity.
  • Is the flat top explained? No arm explains it out of sample. Experiment 183's seasonal range of the 90th-percentile flat level (April to August, farms C to F) is 7.3%, 8.9%, 5.9%, and 8.5% metered when every fold-1 half-hour is used, pooling years as experiment 183 did. On those rows, which are mostly the tuning months, the mean gap between a model's range and the metered range is 5.1 points for arm 2, 5.1 for arm 4, 2.0 for the no-clip ablation, and 5.1 for arm 1. By the rule we wrote before fitting, neither the heat term (arm 2 against arm 4: no difference) nor the clip (arm 2's gap is 3.1 points larger than the no-clip ablation's) explains the fall. On the scored year alone (post hoc, metered ranges 5.5%, 10.0%, 6.4%, and 9.5%) the gaps are 4.3 points for arm 2, 4.7 for the no-clip ablation, 3.3 for the fleet-geometry ablation, and 6.6 for arm 1. The fitted clip flattens the level (arm 2's ranges are 2.5% to 4.5%), and the no-clip plant overshoots (8% to 13.5%). The 99th-percentile gap is 1.8 points for arm 2 and 5.6 for no clip.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable, because every arm is a point forecast. The mean-forecast error is the error reported above, so trigger 3 does not apply.
  • Triggers fired. Trigger 2 (the result contradicts the prediction of 0.97): the explanation, that the ceiling is in the irradiance, was tested. On sunny half-hours the plant already fits 0.973, and with ensemble irradiance it fits 0.91. Trigger 5 (a nested arm beats the arm that contains it): arm 4 beats arm 2 by 0.0002 (interval -0.0008 to 0.0007), because arm 2 picked a heat loss of 0.2%/K at farm A on tuning error; and arm 3 scores 0.009 below arm 2. A post hoc refit of arm 3 with penalty 100 scores 0.941, so the table loses 0.012 by projecting arm 2 onto irradiance and elevation (the table has no azimuth, beam-diffuse split, or temperature). Trigger 4 (leave-one-farm-out): C1 is positive at all six farms, so no farm flips it. No audit was run; the verdict follows the stop rule and would not change if arm 4 replaced arm 2.
  • Caveats. Arm 3's penalty is chosen with arm 2's prediction fitted on all tuning rows as the prior, which favours large penalties, and the contiguous month blocks of its cross-validation each remove a season from training. The soft clip's AC limit is an asymptote: the curve reaches about 0.89 of the limit when the unclipped power equals it, so the DC:AC ratio is only approximate. ERA5 temperature is applied to both half-hours of its hour. Farm E has 10 tuning months and fits worst (0.87). The 12-block interval is close to the range of the draws. Cloud acts on the observed and modelled flat levels alike in figure 4. The heat loss sits at the lowest value of its grid at five farms, so a heat gain was not tested.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a different irradiance product (for example, a blend of CAMS and a numerical weather forecast) lift the fraction fitted on the same plants, since the plant is not the limit?
  • The fitted clip flattens the falling flat top and no clip overshoots it. Does a clip limit that varies with the season, or with cell temperature, fit the scored year's 5.5% to 10.0% fall?

docs.title: Plan amendments (made before any fit)
docs.text:
• The 0.97 is a point estimate of the median over farms on fold 1; the interval is reported beside it. Arm 1 on the same rows is the reference, and the 0.93 of experiment 157 is quoted only as background. The fraction uses squared error against a zero baseline, so MAE in MW and in points of capacity is reported beside it, with slices for sunny half-hours (clear-sky irradiance above 650 W/m²), hot half-hours (air temperature above the farm's 90th percentile), and the shoulder months (March, April, September, October).
  • Folds. Fold 1 tunes on every month before 2025-09 and scores 2025-09 to 2026-08. Fold 2 tunes on months before 2024-09 and scores 2024-09 to 2025-08; fold 2 is a replication with less tuning data, not an independent test. A farm needs at least 12 tuning months to enter a fold, so farm E is out of fold 2.
  • The bootstrap resamples the 12 scored calendar months with replacement, the same months for all farms at once, 10,000 draws, seed 218. The number of months where arm 2 beats arm 1 is reported too, because 12 blocks give an interval close to the range of the draws.
  • Arm 3's penalty is chosen by 5-fold cross-validation over contiguous blocks of whole tuning months. "Cell means" are the weighted means of arm 2's prediction inside each (irradiance, elevation) cell of the hat basis, and the fit is a non-negative least-squares problem on the increments, which is a convex bounded quadratic.
  • Arm 4 re-searches tilt and azimuth with the heat coefficient fixed at 0, so C3 measures the heat term after refitting. DC:AC ratio is the fitted DC scale over the fitted AC limit.
  • C4 pools tilt, azimuth, and heat from the other five farms (summed tuning error divided by each farm's squared output), and each farm still fits its own scale and clip. C4 has no gate; a positive value favours a farm's own geometry.
  • The flat-top test. For farms C to F, take the range over its mean of the monthly 90th percentile of power over capacity from April to August, on half-hours with clear-sky irradiance above 650 W/m², for the metered series (experiment 183's figure) and for each arm's predictions on the same half-hours, with the actual CAMS irradiance so that cloud acts on both. The gap is the absolute difference of the two ranges. The heat term explains the fall when arm 2's mean gap over C to F is at least 2 points smaller than arm 4's, the soft clip when it is at least 2 points smaller than the no-clip ablation's, both when both hold, and neither otherwise.
  • Deliverables also include the fitted parameters per farm and fold (tilt, azimuth, DC:AC ratio, heat coefficient, clip sharpness fixed at 6) for the farm page.
  • Weather names. Fit: CAMS irradiance (about 2 days late) and ERA5 temperature (about 5 days late), neither available at forecast time. Forecast-time repeat: ECMWF ensemble mean irradiance and temperature at 12 to 36 hour leads, available at forecast time, for the arm with the highest fold-1 median.

  • Schedule. One CPU job on 4 cores, no GPU; the grid search is exhaustive, with no seeds.

  • A departure from the plan. A farm needs at least 10 tuning months and not 12, because farm E has 10 months before 2025-09. Farm E fits worst, so it is flagged.

docs.title: How many large load transfers exist, estimated without labels by capture-recapture between detectors?
docs.text:
Take-home: comparing the three detectors with each other cannot tell us how many large load transfers exist, or how many each detector misses. We asked whether the number of large load transfers (demand moved from one Primary substation to another for at least 3 hours, with a step of at least 10% of the Primary's 99th percentile of demand, p99) can be estimated without a switching log. The method is capture-recapture: if two detectors search independently, the share of one detector's events that the other also finds says how many events both missed. We ran it on three detectors that read the same demand-model residual (observed demand minus the weather-driven forecast of a demand model): the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), the pair alarm (an alarm that needs a neighbouring Primary to step the opposite way), and a learned score that re-ranks the candidate alarms of the other two detectors. The detectors ran over 15 Primary substations with 61.8 Primary-years of data in all (the years of data of each Primary, summed). Together the detectors found 233 to 244 distinct events (the range is over three folds of the learned score), 3.8 per Primary-year. RO-NC and the pair alarm share only 23 events, so most events were found by one detector only. The estimate that uses all three lists of events (the three-list estimate) is 1,010 to 1,530 events (16 to 25 per Primary-year), and it puts RO-NC's recall at 0.09 to 0.14. Experiment 146 (a recall measurement on logged transfers) measured a recall of 0.51 for RO-NC on the 35 logged transfers (transfers recorded in the switching log).

The method also fails a known-answer test. In experiment 195, 419 synthetic transfers were injected into the demand history, so the true count is known, and we ran the same estimators on what each detector found. The estimate falls 23% to 59% short of the known count, mainly because 158 of 419 injected events are missed by all three detectors. A recall estimate for Flexpectation version 2 would need a list that does not come from the residual, such as a meter-based list of switching actions or a hand-checked random sample of alarms.

The three detectors come from experiments 148, 156, and 195. The estimators are the Lincoln-Petersen estimate for two lists, the no-three-way-interaction estimate for three lists, and Chao's lower bound (Chao, 1987). Each detector's set of events is one list. RO-NC is the detector of experiment 148, with its 6-hour-lookahead end rule and 24-hour merge. The pair alarm is that of experiment 156. The learned score is the re-ranker of experiment 195, with one alarm set per held-out fold of Primary pairs (three folds). Experiment 217 supplied the Primaries and their years of data. Two intervals are the same event when they share a Primary and overlap by at least half of the shorter interval. A partner-side interval of the pair alarm counts with its own alarm-side interval. Strata are the event's step size (as a share of p99), its duration, and whether the pair alarm saw a metered partner. No switching log is read; the 35 logged transfers are compared at the end only.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
All counts are medians over the three learned-score folds unless a range is given.

  • The prediction fails on both parts. RO-NC's label-free recall is 0.12 (folds 0.09, 0.14, 0.12; interval 0.03 to 0.25), outside 25% of 0.51 (0.38 to 0.64). Chao's lower bound on the event count gives an upper bound on recall of 0.36 to 0.39, which straddles the lower edge of the band; the pre-registered three-list estimate does not. The injected arm is within 25% in 1 of 3 size strata (large third 0.77 of the known count, middle third 0.71, small third 0.41).
  • Events seen. RO-NC 137, the pair alarm 72, and the learned score 119 to 140, with 233 to 244 distinct events in all. RO-NC and the pair alarm share 23 events, RO-NC and the learned score 61 to 70, and the pair alarm and the learned score 27 to 30 (figure 1).
  • Estimates over all large events. Lincoln-Petersen gives 429 events (RO-NC and the pair alarm), 248 to 274 (RO-NC and the learned score), and 317 to 336 (the pair alarm and the learned score). The three-list estimate is 1,010 to 1,530 events (16.4 to 24.7 per Primary-year; 95% interval of the median fold 548 to 4,190, from resampling whole calendar months). Chao's lower bound is 348 to 385 events (5.6 to 6.2 per Primary-year).
  • By size (share of p99). At 10 to 20%, 151 events seen, three-list estimate 644 (folds 545 to 783), Chao 230. At 20 to 40%, 77 seen, estimate 357 (folds 166 to 420), Chao 118. At 40% or more, 7 seen and Chao 8.0 to 9.7 (0.13 to 0.16 per Primary-year), where the three-list estimate is undefined. RO-NC finds all 7 events at 40% or more, so its recall there is 0.72 to 0.88, an upper bound.
  • By duration and partner. Events under 3 days: 134 seen, estimate 503. Events of 3 to 14 days: 92 seen, estimate 689. Events of 14 days or more: 9 seen, Chao 13. Events whose partner the pair alarm saw: 57 seen, Chao 86. Events without such a partner: 178 seen, estimate 542. The estimates are unstable in every stratum except the 40%-or-more size band, the 14-day-or-more duration band, and the metered-partner stratum; the three-list estimate is undefined in those three, so each is Chao's lower bound.
  • Sensitivity. With a size cut-off of 5% or 20% of p99, or the unmerged end rule, the three-list estimate is 5 to 43 events per Primary-year (up to 53 when the unmerged end rule is combined with the 5% cut-off) and RO-NC's recall never exceeds 0.24.
  • Injected arm (experiment 195's held-out injected transfers of 24 hours or longer, 419 events). The detectors saw 261 (62%). The three-list estimate is undefined in every stratum (an empty cell), so the estimate is Chao's lower bound, 263 (interval 236 to 291). The two-list estimates are 256 to 263. The true recall is 0.575 for RO-NC, 0.592 for the learned score, and 0.215 for the pair alarm. The estimated recall is 0.92, 0.94, and 0.34. By size third (140, 139, and 140 known events) the estimates are 57, 99, and 108, which is 41%, 71%, and 77% of the known count.
  • Label-free recall by size. At 40% of p99 or more, RO-NC 0.72, the pair alarm 0.10, the learned score 0.31 to 0.50, against 0.51, 0.14, and 0.66 (23 of 35) on the 35 logged transfers.

docs.title: Why the estimate fails
docs.text:
• Many events are missed by all three detectors. In the injected arm, 158 of 419 events are found by none, and no overlap-based estimate sees them. RO-NC and the pair alarm are not nested there either, and their two-list estimate is still 258.
  • The learned score is nearly nested in RO-NC. The learned score re-ranks RO-NC's candidates and the pair alarm's, so most of its events are also RO-NC's: 233 of RO-NC's 241 injected finds and 248 of the learned score's are shared.
  • On real data the detectors mostly find different events. Only 18 of 235 events are found by all three (figure 1), so the three-list estimate divides by small shared counts and is unstable. Alarms that are false positives add single-list events, and the method counts every alarm as an event.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, and mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast: not applicable, because the experiment forecasts nothing.
  • Audit triggers fired: the known-answer test failed (injected arm), and RO-NC's label-free recall contradicts experiment 146. A fresh Opus audit re-derived every headline number from the stored inputs, and its report is in the private briefs folder. Findings and triage:
    • The pair alarm's partner-side intervals were counted as separate events, which inflated its list. Accepted: partner-side intervals now join their alarm-side interval, and the census was re-run. The three-list estimate fell from 1,650 to 2,590 events to 1,010 to 1,530, and RO-NC's recall rose from 0.05 to 0.09 to 0.09 to 0.14. The verdict is unchanged.
    • The injected arm and the 40%-or-more band report Chao's lower bound, because the three-list estimate is undefined there. Accepted: the page says so, and an advice item that quoted the 40% band was changed.
    • The injected arm uses experiment 195's 6-hour pair alarm, not the 4-hour pair alarm of experiment 156 that the real census uses. Accepted as a caveat: the injected arm therefore does not test the real census exactly.
    • The learned score is nearly nested in RO-NC, not in the pair alarm; wording corrected.
    • The size strata now use the same threshold as the large-event filter (the smaller of the two Primaries' p99). The sentence on the pair alarm's median step was removed, because the figure measured a different quantity.
  • The bootstrap intervals mix the three-list estimate and Chao's bound in resamples where the three-list estimate is undefined, which matters only in the sparse strata.
  • No data-processing finding to add to the data-processing page.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The detectors' alarm sets were fitted on switching labels: the operating point of 80 unexplained odd-month alarms of experiment 195, and a learned score trained on injected events drawn from the logged transfers of the other Primary pairs. The census reads only detector outputs. Label leakage of this kind would raise recall, so it cannot explain a recall that is too low.
  • The injected arm's found flags come from matching to the known event, so the arm tests the estimators and not the blind matching rule that the real census uses.
  • The 35 logged transfers last longer than 1 day, of any size, while the large events are defined by step size, so the recall comparison is approximate.
  • The 10% of p99 cut-off, the 50% overlap, and the size, duration, and partner strata were fixed before the run. The 5% and 20% cut-offs are sensitivities.

docs.title: Questions this result leaves open
docs.text:
• Can a hand-checked random sample of alarms give the precision of each detector, and a meter-based list give its recall?
  • How many events of 40% of p99 or more does the switching log for the trial area contain, compared with the 7 to 10 events this experiment found?

docs.title: Do the solar summary, the pooled correction network, and the gap rule stack on the best-guess demand forecast, or do they remove the same error?
docs.text:
Take-home. A small neural network that corrects the demand forecast's median and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response lower the best-guess forecast's quantile score by 0.136 points of substation effective capacity (5%). That is the sum of what each part gains alone. The network and the solar summary remove different errors, so both belong in the next stack. The network's own uncertainty bands scored 0.048 points better than the hand-fitted bands plus the network's correction (A+H), and about 0.01 better than A+H+S, a difference inside the noise of C1 (on cold nights A+H+S scores 2.838 and H-own 2.866), so the band fixes of experiments 160 and 164 may not be needed once the network is in the stack. The coast-and-widen rule for missing readings was not combined with the stack (see "What was not done").

We asked whether three parts added to the best-guess forecast since experiment 170 stack, meaning that their gains add. We asked because experiment 167's drift gain of 0.50 points fell to -0.03 inside the full stack. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of a substation's effective capacity (lower is better). Coverage of a quantile is the share of readings at or under it. "Drop-one" means removing one part from the stack and scoring the rest. The labels are:

  • A is the best-guess forecast: the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, a winter night offset, and recipe R (a 14-day error profile subtracted from the forecast), from experiment 155 (its arm D), with the bands of experiment 169.
  • S is the solar summary: the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar response, from experiment 193 and its rolling replay, experiment 202 (built on experiment 187). A+S is A with S.
  • H is the correction network: the two-hidden-layer neural network of experiment 201 that shifts A's median, with experiment 200 and experiment 209 as its evidence. A+H is A with its median shifted by H; A+H+S has both. H-own is the network's own 11 quantiles, with none of the band fixes of experiments 160 and 164.
  • C is the coast-and-widen rule for missing readings of experiment 205. It was not scored here.

We re-scored the stored forecasts of all three parts, refitted nothing, and scored the combinations on one shared set of rows: the five decision substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16), over the scored year 2025-07 to 2026-06, outside the hand-filtered events (stretches of telemetry that a hand-made list marks as unusable). D9 is a sixth substation that appears in the six-substation tables only. A cold night is a winter (November to March) evening or night whose ERA5 (the ECMWF reanalysis, an estimate of past weather) daily mean temperature is below 2 °C. Contrasts are written C1 (A+H+S minus A), C2 (the stacking ratio), C3 (H-own minus A+H), and C5 (each drop-one row minus A+H+S). A negative score difference is a gain.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and row set. A 2.752; A+S 2.714; A+H 2.653; A+H+S 2.616; H-own (the network's own 11 quantiles) 2.605. Five decision substations, 464,363 rows, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered events. Leads 15.5 to 39 hours (66,844 rows): A 2.430; A+S 2.402; A+H 2.347; A+H+S 2.321; H-own 2.314. Six substations with D9 (561,363 rows): A 2.688; A+H+S 2.578; H-own 2.568.
  • Schedule. The weekly-refit mean forecast and bands are experiment 155's and 169's stored forecasts; the network was trained once on rows before 2025-07; the solar factors are refitted monthly (experiment 202). Nothing was refitted here. The network's correction and quantiles are the mean over experiment 201's three seeds. We scored one year only, because the network and the solar summary were built for that year alone.
  • The network and the solar summary add (prediction 1 passed). C1 (A+H+S minus A) is -0.136 (95% -0.223 to -0.065; 99% -0.253 to -0.047). A+H alone is -0.099 (-0.191 to -0.027), A+S alone -0.038 (-0.052 to -0.025). The stacking ratio C1 / (A+H + A+S) is 0.99 (95% 0.95 to 1.05), the interaction +0.002 (-0.004 to +0.008). At leads 15.5 to 39 hours, C1 is -0.109 (-0.160 to -0.060) and the stacking ratio is 0.98.
  • The network's own bands match the band fixes on cold nights but score better overall (prediction 2 failed on its score clause). H-own's cold-night q95 coverage is 0.904 (A 0.896), so the coverage clause passed. H-own scores 0.048 below A+H (-0.081 to -0.021), a gap outside the pre-registered 0.02. The clause was two-sided, so it failed because H-own was better than predicted, which is a favourable failure. A post hoc check (run after seeing the scores; e00220_posthoc.py) shows that single-seed networks give gaps of -0.040, -0.042, and -0.043, so averaging the three seeds does not explain the gap. At D10 alone it is -0.138, -0.121, and -0.129 across the seeds, and without D10 it is -0.014 to -0.021; the network's bands fit D10 much better than arm A's bands.
  • The network matters most in the drop-one table (prediction 3 passed). The score rises when a part is removed, by +0.098 for the network (+0.028 to +0.187), +0.036 for the solar summary (+0.023 to +0.049), +0.034 for recipe R with the network kept (+0.021 to +0.051) and +0.019 without it (+0.007 to +0.033), +0.004 for the winter night offset with the network kept (+0.001 to +0.008) and -0.001 without it (-0.005 to +0.004), and -0.0003 for experiment 164's cold-day widening (-0.002 to +0.0015). We did not retrain the network without recipe R or the offset. The network was trained on arm D, which contains both, so removing R from the stack understates how much R helps.
  • Tail calibration, coverage / pinball loss (five substations). All rows: A q01 0.022 / 0.216, q05 0.065 / 0.714, q95 0.948 / 0.745, q99 0.982 / 0.232; A+H+S 0.012 / 0.177, 0.046 / 0.638, 0.954 / 0.703, 0.985 / 0.216; H-own 0.020 / 0.173, 0.069 / 0.621, 0.940 / 0.704, 0.980 / 0.224. Cold nights (5,395 rows): A 0.045 / 0.391, 0.090 / 0.950, 0.896 / 0.819, 0.959 / 0.282; A+H 0.054 / 0.407, 0.097 / 0.939, 0.964 / 0.622, 0.986 / 0.174; H-own 0.051 / 0.384, 0.108 / 0.908, 0.904 / 0.716, 0.955 / 0.271. Daylight (211,576 rows): A 0.027 / 0.265, 0.078 / 0.907, 0.933 / 0.924, 0.979 / 0.262; A+S 0.016 / 0.236, 0.058 / 0.838, 0.941 / 0.877, 0.983 / 0.245; A+H+S 0.013 / 0.218, 0.052 / 0.805, 0.944 / 0.850, 0.985 / 0.234.
  • Substations. A+H+S minus A: D16 -0.350, D5 -0.161, D14 -0.113, D10 -0.049, D11 -0.019, D9 +0.018. Leaving out one decision substation keeps C1 between -0.083 (D16 out) and -0.167.
  • Gates (all passed). Arm A 2.7521 (target 2.7519, within 0.005); arm A equals experiment 202's stored A on every shared row and experiment 201's actual matches (difference 0); R2's daylight change -2.30% (target -2.30%); arm D scores 2.756 at five substations (printed 2.756), and the three seeds of experiment 201's second arm score -0.109, -0.110, and -0.093 below arm D at six substations (the mean of the three is -0.104, matching the printed -0.104; the seed-averaged quantiles used elsewhere here give -0.123); building A+H+S directly and as A plus the R2 change plus delta agrees to 7.6e-6, the float32 storage precision (this checks arithmetic and storage only, since both sides use the same stored arrays).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, 12 to 36 hours, per site. A and A+S: 0.000 and -0.03 to -0.14 (the solar summary). A+H: D10 +0.67, D11 -0.32, D14 -0.17, D16 -0.59, D5 +0.18, D9 -0.47, which is the network's correction by construction.
  • Error of the median beside each quantile-score contrast. The mean absolute error of the median moves the same way as the score: C1 -0.146, A+H -0.145, A+S 0.000, removing R with the network +0.079, removing the network +0.146. H-own minus A+H is 0.000 on this error but -0.048 on the score, so the gap is in the bands.
  • Audit conditions (the seven in the ml-experiment skill). None was met. Condition 2 (H-own beat A+H by more than predicted) was tested with the single-seed and leave-D10-out runs above (e00220_posthoc.py), which locate the gap at D10. The nested-arm condition was not met: removing the widening changes the score by -0.0003, inside its interval.

docs.title: What was not done
docs.text:
• The coast-and-widen rule (arm A+H+S+C) was not scored. Experiment 205's code imports a GPU-only library through a chain of six modules, and the environment here has no GPU group installed. Composing a gap's effect onto the network and the solar summary would also be a post hoc approximation. Experiment 205's own gain, 0.25 to 0.44 points on gap rows, stands as measured against a forecast without the correction.
  • No replicate year. The network and the solar summary were built for the scored year only.
  • No curtailment-cost figure. The node-level curtailment metric was not run on the new arms.
  • Network not retrained in the drop-one rows. The two score losses from removing recipe R or the offset are lower bounds.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• One year and five substations. D16 carries 0.35 of the gain at its own site, and D9 gets worse. Cold-night intervals rest on 3 months and are not quoted.
  • Cold nights use realised weather. The mask is the ERA5 mean temperature of the UTC calendar day, which is not known at forecast time, so the cold-night coverage is not what a forecaster would see when it must predict that a night is cold. No arm is fitted on the mask.
  • A+H overshoots on cold nights. Coverage at q95 is 0.964 against 0.95, and at q05 0.097 against 0.05, because the correction lifts A's bands that experiment 164 had already widened.
  • Next. Test the network's own bands inside the stack with the solar summary applied to them, then add the gap rule once experiment 205's code runs without the GPU group. Prediction that could fail: H-own plus the solar summary scores at least 0.02 points below A+H+S over all rows.

docs.title: Does a small neural-network head on the stored wind best guess lower the three wind farms' error at lead days 1 and 2, and how much of any gain does a blind head reproduce?
docs.text:
A small neural-network head on the stored wind forecast did not lower the error of three wind farms' power forecasts at 1 to 2 days ahead, so on this evidence the stored forecast needs no head. The stored forecast ("the best guess") is the wind-power forecast of experiment 33: nine quantiles per half-hour, from the 51 members of the ECMWF ensemble forecast (ENS) and a wind-power model. A head is a small neural network that shifts and rescales those nine quantiles. We trained one head on all three farms together, using only earlier months, and scored it on the following month, for the 9 months from October 2025 to June 2026 (July to September only trained the first head). The error measure is the quantile score, in points of capacity (a point is 1% of the farm's capacity), where a lower score is better. The head fed the ensemble's mean wind speed, spread, and direction scored 0.180 points worse than the best guess. The 95% interval, from resampling whole months and the three fitting seeds, is -0.141 to +0.576. A blind head, which saw only the hours ahead and the calendar, scored 1.109 points worse. The result is consistent with a head that fits 9 months of history from three farms learning those months, and not a correction that carries over. A head may therefore need far more farms or years, or far fewer parameters.

The method follows experiments 200, 201, and 209, which found gains from a pooled head on demand forecasts. The head's form is experiment 200's (a median shift and a log-scale applied to the base quantiles). The three farms are labelled W1 to W3.

Verdict: inconclusive. Lead days 1 and 2 are the two calendar days after the date of the ENS run. The decisive contrast C1 is the head with weather (A2) minus the best guess at those leads. It is +0.180 (-0.141 to +0.576), so it does not lie below -0.1, and it does not lie wholly above zero. The prediction (a gain of 0.05 to 0.2) failed. The blind share is undefined, because C1's point estimate is above zero. The stop rule on the blind head did not fire: the blind head is worse than the head with weather (A2 minus A3, C3: -0.929, -2.381 to +0.092). The intervals resample whole months (9) and the three seeds, and describe these three farms only.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and absolute scores (quantile score at lead days 1 and 2, points of capacity; scored rows): A0 best guess 7.223; A1 head on quantiles and lead 7.174; A2 head with ensemble wind 7.403; A3 blind head 8.332; A4 head on the ensemble-mean forecast 7.627 (A4's base forecast alone, without a head, 7.384); A5 table of shifts and scales 7.196. All arms cover the same 30,240 cases at lead days 1 and 2 (213,882 over all leads).
  • Contrasts at lead days 1 and 2 (arm minus A0, 95%): A2 +0.180 (-0.141 to +0.576); A3 +1.109 (+0.225 to +2.491); A1 -0.049 (-0.204 to +0.123); A4 +0.404 (-0.113 to +1.041); A5 -0.026 (-0.094 to +0.041). Other contrasts: A2 minus A3 -0.929 (-2.381 to +0.092); A4 minus A2 +0.224 (-0.125 to +0.614).
  • At days 3 to 6: A1 -0.097 (-0.433 to +0.250); A2 +0.171 (-0.310 to +0.722); A3 +1.478 (-0.172 to +3.439); A5 -0.278 (-0.527 to -0.044). Over all leads: A1 -0.210 (-0.528 to +0.142); A5 -0.415 (-0.597 to -0.192).
  • Tail calibration (lead days 1 and 2; the stored best guess holds the nine levels 0.05 to 0.95 only, so 0.01 and 0.99 are not scored):
Arm Coverage of 5% to 95% band Share below 0.05 Share above 0.95 Pinball 0.05 Pinball 0.95 A0 best guess 0.908 0.038 0.054 1.129 1.479 A1 0.822 0.125 0.053 1.248 1.515 A2 0.798 0.135 0.068 1.353 1.646 A3 0.767 0.169 0.063 1.776 1.727 A5 0.821 0.124 0.055 1.197 1.479
  • Every head narrows the band, and most of the lost coverage is below the 0.05 quantile. The share of actuals below the 0.05 quantile rises from 0.038 to between 0.12 and 0.17. A2's 0.05 pinball is worse than A0's by +0.223 (+0.071 to +0.546) and its 0.95 pinball by +0.167 (+0.017 to +0.440).
  • Leave one farm out (lead days 1 and 2, minus A0): A1 +0.594 (+0.412 to +0.782), A2 +1.222 (+0.853 to +1.610), A3 +1.276 (+0.504 to +2.406). A head does not transfer to a farm it never saw. A2 held out minus A2 pooled is +1.042 (+0.445 to +1.635).
  • By farm (lead days 1 and 2, minus A0): A2 +0.177 (W1), -0.378 (W2), +0.760 (W3); A1 -0.141, -0.508, +0.523. The only farm where a head's interval lies below zero is W2 under A1 (-0.508, -0.840 to -0.084).
  • Post hoc: the heads fit the rows they train on. Scored on its own training rows, A2 is 0.64 points better than A0 at days 1 and 2 (6.362 against 7.003) and A1 0.30 better (6.704), with coverage 0.86 to 0.87. The in-sample rows are counted once per refit, so the earliest months count most.
  • Post hoc: a 2-epoch head and a linear head (no hidden layers) do no better at days 1 and 2. Minus A0: A1 2-epoch +0.070 (-0.073 to +0.254), A2 2-epoch +0.079 (-0.057 to +0.270), A1 linear +0.032 (-0.090 to +0.162), A2 linear +0.123 (-0.042 to +0.302). At days 3 to 6 they score better: A1 linear -0.352 (-0.698 to -0.041), A2 linear -0.359 (-0.755 to -0.024).
  • Post hoc: the best guess's spread is already close to the best width. Rescaling its quantiles about the median by the single factor that minimises the score on the scored rows gives 7.209 against 7.223 at days 1 and 2 (factor 0.90, coverage 0.863), and 10.571 against 10.578 at days 3 to 6 (factor 0.95). The quantile score rewards a band covering about 0.86, not the 0.90 target, so a head narrows the band even when the narrowing does not help.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site (points of capacity, whole scored period): A0 -5.81 (W1), -5.80 (W2), -4.80 (W3); A2 -5.58, -5.34, -4.25; A3 -4.70, -4.67, -3.78. The "mean" is the mass-weighted mean of the nine stored quantiles, which cannot reach the tails, so the gap shows the skew of the wind-power distribution and not a shift.
  • Mean and median forecast errors beside the quantile-score contrasts (lead days 1 and 2, minus A0): A2 median error +0.055 (-0.354 to +0.518), mean error +0.423 (-0.036 to +0.946); A1 median error -0.165 (-0.370 to +0.078), mean error +0.151 (-0.081 to +0.379); A3 median error +1.313 (+0.105 to +3.272). A1's mean error and its quantile score point in opposite directions, but the mean of nine quantiles is not a proper score for an absolute-error target, and A1's median error has the same sign as its quantile score.
  • Triggers fired: 2 (the result contradicts the prediction and earlier demand experiments), 3 (A1's mean error against its quantile score), and 5 (A1 beats A2, which contains A1's inputs). A fresh Opus audit re-derived C1 by its own code and found the headline numbers stand (the audit's interval for C1 is -0.137 to +0.569). No finding changes a verdict. The audit's findings and their triage:
    • Bug in A4's base forecast, fixed and rerun. The base forecast fed the wind-power model the magnitude of the vector-mean wind, and that magnitude shrinks as members disagree on direction. e00221_inputs.py now feeds the mean of the members' speeds. A1 to A3, A5, and C1 are unchanged, and A4's days 3 to 6 score moved from 11.436 in the first run to 10.925.
    • Under-coverage is mostly what the quantile score rewards. Written into the results above (the oracle rescaling).
    • A2's loss to A1 concentrates in months whose wind lies outside the head's training range, most of all October 2025. This is an audit reading that the committed scripts do not print. A2's 10 weather inputs let a 64-unit neural network extrapolate.
    • The best guess's spread factor differs by month, which is immaterial. An audit refit with the factor matched changed C1's point estimate by about 0.03 (audit only).
    • The head's loss pools all leads. Leads of 7 days and later hold about 55% of the training loss (audit figure). Accepted, because the weighting was pre-registered.
    • error_mean is not a proper score. It is the error of the mean of nine quantiles, and is labelled as such above.
  • Code review (Sonnet): no defects found in leakage, masking, head form, leave-one-farm-out, direction convention, or scoring.

docs.title: How the experiment was run, and where it departs from the plan
docs.text:
• Rows: experiment 33's wind cases with experiment 210's mask applied to training and scoring; masked share 9.9% of rows (6.7% at W1, 9.0% at W2, 14.1% at W3, from input_checks.json). A0 recomputed on all rows reproduces experiment 52's printed scores (6.701 and 11.037, gaps under 0.001).
  • Scored months: October 2025 to June 2026, each from a head trained on all earlier months (valid times at least 4 hours before the month). July to September only train.
  • Schedule: the head is refitted monthly on an expanding window; the base forecast is the stored table, so the contrast does not depend on a retraining cadence. Fixed 12 epochs, no tuning on scored months.
  • Weather at forecast time: the ensemble mean, spread, and direction come from the ENS run the best guess already used, so they exist at forecast time.
  • Departures: the stored best guess holds nine levels, so 0.01 and 0.99 are not scored and the predicted concentration at those levels is untested. The node curtailment metric and the manual-heuristic cost saving do not apply to three separate farms and are not computed. The post hoc rows (in-sample check, 2-epoch and linear heads, oracle rescaling) are labelled post hoc and change no verdict.
  • Data processing: no new finding for data-processing.md.
  • Code: ml-experiments/00221-wind-correction-head-on-stored-predictions/.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test a head trained on many more farms or years (the stored best guess on more wind farms, or a long backtest of the best guess), because the in-sample gain shows the head can find structure that 9 months do not confirm.
  • Fit the head's loss to the metric and the coverage target together, for example by adding a coverage penalty, because the pinball loss alone pulls coverage towards 0.86.
  • Leave the ensemble-mean base forecast alone: A4's head-free forecast is worse than the stored mixture at days 1 and 2 (+0.161, +0.053 to +0.275).
