docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per arm: 0.00 points for every arm built here (printed in the report); the -0.96 points for arm 4 arm_emp comes from experiment 264's stored forecasts.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile score. Arm 3's mean absolute error is 17.38 against arm 1's 16.29 (worse, as is its quantile score); the matched arm's is 15.78 (better, as is its score). The two metrics agree.
  • Audit triggers. One trigger fired: arm 3 contains the single-model arm and the indicator-only arm, and both score better than arm 3. We tested an explanation, that the coefficient was trained on the state at the half-hour and applied to a day-old state, and the matched arm trained on the lagged state removes the loss. No independent audit of the method was run. The other six triggers (a failed control, a result against its prediction without a tested explanation, a disagreement between the quantile score and the error of the mean forecast, a leave-one-site-out flip, an interval width against a sister experiment, and an unreplicated result that a later design depends on) did not fire.
  • Row set. All arms share the same 97,012 D8 rows (keys joined across arms).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should answer whether the engine's state can be known before the half-hour it affects. The state of the last settled day is worth 0.15 MW out of sample, which cannot be told from zero. Options that this experiment did not test are a forecast of the state from the gas price, a longer or lead-dependent lag, and NGED's own record of the engine's running hours. Any of them should be scored with a state that no reading of the target half-hour enters.

docs.title: Can persistent regimes be segmented in a Primary's history without labels?
docs.text:
We asked whether a Primary substation's history can be split into regimes using only the errors of a forecast. The answer is partly. A Primary substation steps 33 kV down to 11 kV for homes and businesses. A regime is the whole period, without gaps, in which one configuration holds. For D8, a Primary whose meter began including a gas engine in August 2023, the regime is the whole period that includes the engine, even in the spells when the engine is off. Whether the engine runs, or a load shift (an operator moving part of one Primary's demand to another for days) is in force, is a state inside a regime.

The segmentation found a sudden, lasting change of 25% of a Primary's load and dated it with a median error of 0 days, but found only about half of the 10% changes. It also could not reliably tell a load shift from a lasting change. We fitted a generalised additive model (GAM), a forecast that uses no recent power readings and is fitted by convex least squares, to each Primary's whole history. We took the residual (the reading minus the forecast) and summarised each day by four numbers: the share of that day's half-hours with a dip (a residual more than 2.5 noise units below zero), the 5% and 95% quantiles of the day's half-hourly residuals, and the night-minus-day mean residual. A penalised search for the best split points (Killick et al. (2012)) then placed boundaries. The penalty sets how large a change in the four numbers must be before the search places a boundary, so a higher penalty gives fewer boundaries. A boundary is a state change when the four numbers return to their earlier values within 120 days, or a neighbouring Primary shows the opposite change within 3 days, and a regime change otherwise. We tested the segmentation on D8's break on 2023-08-15, on changes that we added to the recorded power of the other Primaries (lasting steps, and load shifts of 14 to 60 days), and on the unmodified series.

Verdict not supported: two of the four parts of the prediction held. The two recall bullets below form one part. The penalty (64) and the minimum segment length (7 days) were chosen on injections in odd months at 7 tuning Primaries. Every number below is from the 7 held-out Primaries and even-month injections, except D8.

  • D8's break (failed, narrowly). The nearest boundary is 2023-08-30, 15 days late. Penalties of 16 or less place the break on 2023-08-15 exactly, at 2.5 or more regime changes per Primary-year at the held-out Primaries (Figure 2).
  • False regime changes (held). The segmentation found 0.87 per Primary-year (98.75% interval 0.46 to 1.39). Of 33 regime changes, 8 look like solar capacity steps (a daytime shift at least twice the night shift; PV is photovoltaic) and 15 fall in April to August.
  • Persistent steps (failed). The segmentation labelled 70% persistent (0.58 to 0.85): 25% steps 89% to 95%, 10% steps 45% to 50% (Figure 1). Found steps are dated to a median of 0 days.
  • Temporary shifts (failed). The segmentation labelled 42% as states (0.21 to 0.64): 27% at 14 days, 45% at 30, 55% at 60. A permanent transfer between two Primaries is labelled a state 73% of the time, as the prediction expected.
  • Engine spell edges (held, trivially). After 2023-08-15 the engine detector (experiment 199) shows 121 times the engine switched on or off for at least 3 days. At penalty 64, 2% of these edges have a boundary within 3 days, and 2% at random dates, because only 3 boundaries remain. At penalty 16, 15% against 12% at random dates, with 19 regime-change boundaries inside the regime; at penalty 4, 39% against 29%.
  • The 2026 fade. Penalties of 32 and above put a boundary on 2026-03-10, labelled unconfirmed (less than 150 days before the end of the data), where the dip rate falls by 0.15 to 0.23. The engine detector's flagged share falls from 0.53 (October 2025 to February 2026) to 0.43 (from 15 March 2026), so the residual cannot say whether a regime ended or the engine ran less.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
Figure 1. Recall of injected steps and shifts against the penalty, and the rate of regime changes at the unmodified held-out Primaries. A larger penalty finds fewer false changes and fewer real ones.

Figure 2. D8's dip rate, 5% quantile, and engine detector flagged share, with boundaries at penalties 16 and 64 and the known break.

Figure 3. Forecast error after an injected step with no offset, with a trailing 60-day offset, with the latest-boundary offset, and with the latest-regime offset.

docs.title: Forecast gain from an offset for the latest regime
docs.text:
• Setup. At each monthly cut (24-month window), the GAM's in-sample residual is segmented using days before the cut only. The latest-boundary offset is the mean residual since the latest boundary of any kind. The latest-regime offset skips boundaries labelled as states (by the return rule alone, with no neighbours) and the boundary that ends each state, and uses the mean residual since the latest remaining boundary. Scored over the month after the cut, for 6 months after each injected persistent step (14 Primaries pooled, 8 onset dates in even months, 4 step types: 10% and 25% of load, each flat or following the Primary's own demand). Intervals resample whole Primaries.
  • Injected steps. Mean absolute error 9.81 points with no offset, 7.59 with the latest-boundary offset, 7.64 with the latest-regime offset, and 7.44 with the trailing 60-day offset. The latest-regime offset beats no offset by 2.17 points (98.75% interval -2.87 to -1.46) and is 0.20 points worse than the trailing offset (-0.07 to 0.47). The latest-boundary offset is 0.15 worse than the trailing offset (-0.12 to 0.40). Neither difference from the trailing offset is clear of zero.
  • D8's real break. No offset 16.94, latest-boundary and latest-regime 16.93, trailing 16.09. The differences have intervals that include zero (6 cuts).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Mean minus median forecast. Zero by construction: the GAM gives one point forecast.
  • Quantile score beside the error of the mean. No quantile score is contrasted here.
  • Audit triggers. One trigger fired: the known-answer test (D8's break) missed its 14-day bound by one day at the chosen penalty. The explanation, that the penalty was set on injections and not on D8, is tested by the penalty grid in Figure 2 and the sweep in printed_report.txt. A fresh Sonnet agent (not Opus, on the manager's instruction to save credits) audited the derivations from the stored parquet files, and reproduced the chosen penalty (64, 7 days), the held-out recalls (0.699 persistent, 0.424 temporary), the 0.87 regime changes per Primary-year, and D8's dating (exact at penalties 4 to 16, 15 days late at 32 and above). It found no leakage. It found two small traps, now in the caveats. No other trigger fired; whether a later experiment depends on this result is not known to us.
  • Comparison with the first design. The first design segmented the daily mean level. On the 5 Primaries both designs ran (D10, D11, D12, D14, and D16, with a 14-day minimum segment), at the same penalty the level design finds more 10% steps and temporary shifts but also more regime changes per Primary-year. At a matched rate the two agree: the level design at penalty 64 (1.18 per Primary-year) has recall 0.73 for 25% steps, 0.34 for 10% steps, and 0.57 for temporary shifts, and the distribution features at penalty 32 (1.38) have 0.69, 0.34, and 0.57 (printed_level_only.txt).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The tuning choice is a tie. Penalty 64 with minimum segment 7 and with 14 have the same tuning objective, and D8 is dated 15 days late at both.
  • A boundary already in the unmodified series can count as finding an injection. At the chosen setting, 14 of 308 held-out persistent and temporary injections have such a boundary within 14 days of the onset, and 10 of them were scored found, so persistent recall is biased upward by at most 8 of 176 injections (4.5 points).
  • Injection dating. The injected step begins at the first half-hour after midnight on the onset date, and the match window runs from 13 days before to 15 days after that date. The stored dating error is relative to the following day, so the printed median adds 1 day.
  • The injected steps are easier and harder than real ones. They are added to the recorded power at a fixed date with no change to the weather, and the GAM is fitted on the injected series, so month and weather terms absorb part of the step (a median of 2% for persistent steps and 6% for temporary shifts).
  • The engine spells come from a detector that did not pass its gate (experiment 199, night-only v1), and the spell-edge share is not a measure of the engine's true spells.
  • D15 has no training rows, so 14 Primaries other than D8 were used, not the 15 planned. D9 and D18 have under two years of readings, so their onsets are fewer.
  • The PV check approximates. Experiment 207's step path was not refitted. A PV-like change is one whose daytime shift is at least twice its night shift.
  • Real regimes in the controls count as false changes, so 0.87 per Primary-year is an upper bound.
  • Embedded Capacity Register context. The register lists one connected entry of 8.9 MW at D8, dated 2019 or later, which is probably the engine. We did not use the register.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Whether a second signal, such as the engine detector's flagged share together with the dip rate, separates a regime change from an engine that is off, because the residual alone cannot.
  • Whether a lower penalty with a rule that merges boundaries within 14 days, which keeps the D8 break exact, brings the false regime changes under 1 per Primary-year.

docs.title: How much of the value of knowing about load shifts comes from long and deep shifts, and how much from smaller ones?
docs.text:
A load shift moves demand from one Primary substation to its neighbours for hours or days. We asked how much of the forecast improvement that comes from knowing every shift exactly (its true start, end, and megawatts) comes from long and deep shifts, so a detector that finds only those would still deliver most of the improvement. We call that improvement the benefit: the reduction in a forecast score compared with a forecast told nothing about the shifts. The two scores are the upper-tail score (twCRPS, which weights errors at high power) against the power the substation would have carried in its normal running arrangement (NRA), and the curtailment cost, which scores how badly a forecast misjudges when demand breaches a limit. We simulated 1,152 shifts at six Primary substations, in a grid of six durations (2 hours to 60 days) by four depths (5%, 10%, 25%, and 50% of the substation's load), and scored forecasts that know all of them, only the long and deep ones, or only the others. Knowing only shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of load captures 95.9% (94.3 to 97.2) of the upper-tail benefit and 90.3% (86.8 to 93.3) of the curtailment-cost benefit, in the central one of three assumed mixes of how often shifts of each duration and depth occur (95% intervals). The result rests on simulated shifts and on assumed frequencies of each depth.

Curtailment figures compare forecasts with each other and do not state money saved. A Primary substation has no published export limit and no known generator beneath it, so the metric treats its demand as the flow that can breach, as experiment 283 did.

Realistic detectors are not scored here. The shares above assume a detector that finds every shift of its class at once. Weighting each class by the recall of the long-and-deep detector, and subtracting its false-alarm harm, is a follow-up that waits for Part 1 of the long-deep detector experiment (see the plan page of the LSC detectors theme).

docs.title: Share of the benefit by class of shift
docs.text:
Each cell is the share of the benefit of an oracle that knows every shift (PERFECT) that an oracle knowing only one class of shift (PERFECT_LD, the long and deep shifts, or PERFECT_SMALL, all other shifts) captures, in rows within 7 days of a shift, with a 95% interval from resampling whole shifts within each cell. The benefit of an oracle is the sum over those rows of the no-knowledge score minus the oracle's score. The upper-tail score is the threshold-weighted continuous ranked probability score (twCRPS) at the 95th percentile of earlier power, against the power the substation would have carried in its normal running arrangement (NRA), with readings inside a known shift set aside (the design of experiment 283). The cost column is the node-only curtailment cost against observed power at the 0.5 scaled limit, with the known shift's megawatts added back to the forecast (experiment 283's post hoc design, needed because setting readings aside predicts the wrong series against observed power).

Scenario Class Upper-tail score vs NRA Curtailment cost vs observed power Few small shifts Long and deep (2 days or more, 10% or more) 96.9% (95.4 to 98.0) 91.4% (87.6 to 94.6) Few small shifts Under 12 hours or under 10% of load 0.6% (0.3 to 1.1) 0.9% (0.3 to 1.6) Central Long and deep 95.9% (94.3 to 97.2) 90.3% (86.8 to 93.3) Central Under 12 hours or under 10% of load 1.6% (0.8 to 2.6) 2.4% (1.3 to 3.6) Many small shifts Long and deep 87.9% (83.0 to 92.2) 80.8% (74.7 to 86.5) Many small shifts Under 12 hours or under 10% of load 7.3% (3.4 to 11.7) 9.0% (5.0 to 13.2)

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Pre-registered prediction held: the long-and-deep share is 95.9% (94.3 to 97.2) on the upper-tail score and 90.3% (86.8 to 93.3) on cost, against 70% or more, and the share of the benefit from shifts under 12 hours or under 10% of load is 1.6% (0.8 to 2.6) and 2.4% (1.3 to 3.6), against under 15%. All three scenarios give the same verdict; in the many-small-shifts scenario the long-and-deep share falls to 87.9% and 80.8%.
  • Duration matters more than depth. An oracle with a minimum duration of 6 hours instead of 2 days (and a minimum depth of 10%) adds 2.7% (1.7 to 4.0) of the benefit on the upper-tail score and 7.7% (4.9 to 11.0) on cost. A minimum depth of 5% instead of 10% adds 0.8% (0.3 to 1.5) and 1.7% (0.9 to 2.8). A minimum duration of 7 days is too long: the oracle then keeps 80.3% (74.9 to 84.6) of the upper-tail benefit and 44.2% (38.5 to 49.8) of the cost benefit (figure 2).
  • All other shifts: the shifts outside the long-and-deep class, which include those from 12 hours to 2 days at 10% of load or more, carry 4.1% (2.8 to 5.7) of the upper-tail benefit and 9.7% (6.7 to 13.2) of the cost benefit. The "under 12 hours or under 10% of load" class is a subset of them.
  • Frequency at which the conclusion changes: the shifts outside the long-and-deep class would have to be 10 times as frequent (upper-tail score) or 4 times as frequent (cost) as in the central scenario before the long-and-deep share fell to 70%.
  • Cells that carry at least 5% of the benefit on their own (central scenario): for the upper-tail score, shifts of 7 to 30 days at 50% of load (43.5%), 7 to 30 days at 25% (14.9%), over 30 days at 50% (14.0%), and 3 to 7 days at 50% (10.2%). For cost, 3 to 7 days at 50% (25.5%), 7 to 30 days at 50% (24.1%), 7 to 30 days at 25% (13.9%), 1 to 3 days at 50% (11.1%), and 3 to 7 days at 25% (7.8%) (figure 3).
  • By phase (central scenario, long-and-deep share): before a live detector would have flagged the shift, 73.8% (64.5 to 82.3) of the upper-tail benefit and 84.6% (78.8 to 89.7) of the cost benefit; during the shift 99.8% (upper-tail) and 98.6% (cost); in the 48 hours after the shift ends 98.5% and 96.7% (94.2 to 98.7) (figure 5). Smaller shifts matter most before the alarm arrives.
  • Shape and site: the long-and-deep share is 97.2% (95.7 to 98.4) for constant shifts and 94.4% (91.0 to 96.8) for demand-shaped shifts on the upper-tail score, and 92.5% and 88.2% on cost. Leaving out any one of the six Primaries gives 94.6% to 96.8% (upper-tail) and 88.1% to 91.9% (cost), so no site decides the result.
  • Cost against observed power needs the megawatts added back: with readings set aside the cost within 7 days of a shift is 87.5% worse than with no knowledge, as in experiment 283, so the cost shares use the megawatts-added-back arms. The cost benefit is 16.9% of the no-knowledge cost for shifts that add load and 18.1% for shifts that remove it.
  • Absolute scores, rows within 7 days of a shift, points of effective capacity (against the NRA): CRPS 6.098 for no knowledge, 3.050 for PERFECT, 3.070 for PERFECT_LD, and 6.091 for PERFECT_SMALL; mean absolute error of the median 9.194, 5.312, 5.340, and 9.186; twCRPS 1.672, 0.677, 0.683, and 1.669. PERFECT_ADD scores against observed power: CRPS 3.648, twCRPS 1.062.
  • Tail calibration (the score tables hold the 0.05, 0.5, and 0.95 quantiles only, so 0.01 and 0.99 are missing): no knowledge puts 15.8% of readings below the 0.05 quantile and 14.8% above the 0.95 quantile within 7 days of a shift; PERFECT 6.3% and 5.9%; PERFECT_LD 6.6% and 6.1%; PERFECT_SMALL 15.7% and 14.7%. Pinball loss at 0.05 and 0.95: 2.131 and 2.017, 0.782 and 0.804, 0.790 and 0.810, and 2.129 and 2.014.
  • Ordinary rows: knowing every shift changes CRPS by +0.41% (0.23 to 0.65) and twCRPS by +0.47% (0.22 to 0.85) over 3.57 million rows (months resampled). A forecast that knows the shifts is not worse on ordinary rows; the small gain comes from rows where no-knowledge forecasts still carry the effect of a shift that ended earlier.

docs.title: Frequency
docs.text:
• Duration frequencies come from the log. The 537 logged operations of 2 hours to 48 days, between January 2022 and March 2026, give 926 shift sides on the 16 series, which is 6.27, 3.65, 1.54, 1.29, 0.84, and 0.13 shifts per series-year for the six duration bins (2 to 6 hours up to over 30 days).
  • Depth frequencies are assumptions. Only 16 of the 537 operations have a measured depth. The depth mix (5%, 10%, 25%, and 50% of load) is 10%, 15%, 35%, and 40% in the few-small-shifts scenario, 25%, 25%, 30%, and 20% in the central scenario, and 45%, 30%, 18%, and 7% in the many-small-shifts scenario, which also multiplies the two shortest duration bins by 3 because the log lists short shifts least (figure 4). The break-even multipliers above are the sensitivity test.
  • Undercounted classes: short and small shifts are the hardest to see, and the log lists only some of them. The 17 block days and 37 unlabelled worst days of experiment 175, the detectors' census, and D8's drops are not added, because none of them records depth in a form this page can use, so the long-and-deep class may be undercounted too.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site: the mean absolute error (MAE) of the median forecast minus that of the mean forecast lies between -0.048 and +0.011 points for no knowledge and for PERFECT, and changes by at most 0.014 points between them (D5), so the width of an arm's forecast distribution does not move its median forecast.
  • Mean forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast: within 7 days of a shift PERFECT lowers the MAE of the mean forecast by 42.2% and the CRPS by 50.0%, the same direction.
  • Explicit arms against selection: the explicitly run PERFECT_LD arm captures 96.6% of the upper-tail benefit and 91.1% of the cost benefit, against 95.9% and 90.3% from selecting the long-and-deep shifts out of the PERFECT arm. The explicit PERFECT_SMALL arm captures 3.0% and 8.8%.
  • Trigger that fired: the long-and-deep detector experiments are designed on this result, which has not been replicated. A fresh Sonnet agent audited the method (Opus was not used, as the brief required); see "Audit". No Opus audit run.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
• Headline reproduced from the raw score tables with independent code: 95.90% on the upper-tail score and 90.28% on cost, 1,079 scored shifts, explicit PERFECT_LD 96.65% and 91.12%, explicit PERFECT_SMALL 3.02% and 8.82%. Accepted.
  • No leakage found: for 283,439 rows whose forecast cutoff precedes every shift onset in the world, every arm equals no knowledge exactly. Accepted.
  • The ambiguous-row rule matters: without it the selected long-and-deep share is 87.0% (upper-tail) and 79.8% (cost) against 96.4% and 92.6% for the explicit arm, and with it the gap is under 1 point. Accepted; the explicit arms are quoted beside the headline.
  • Per-shift additivity is not exact: on shifts outside the long-and-deep class, PERFECT_LD alone earns 33% (upper-tail) and 11% (cost) of PERFECT's benefit, because the filter of no knowledge still carries a neighbouring long shift. Those shifts hold under 5% of the total, so the totals agree. Accepted as a caveat.
  • Row weighting: normalising each shift's benefit by its number of scored rows gives a long-and-deep share of 88.5% (upper-tail) and 80.4% (cost), still above 70%. The page headlines the row-summed share, because a long shift changes more rows. Accepted as a caveat.
  • Depth mix can decide the cost verdict: with only 5% and 10% depths, the long-and-deep share falls to 72.0% (upper-tail) and 63.5% (cost), below the 70% bar on cost. The depth mix is an assumption, so a measured depth for the logged operations is the first step before porting anything. Accepted as a caveat.
  • Not checked: the realism of the simulated worlds, and the months used to tune the filter, which interleave with the scored months for every arm alike.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Shifts are simulated and idealised. The true start, end, and megawatts are known, shifts at one site are at least 7 days apart, and half remove load and half add it. Solar-shaped shifts are not run.
  • Rows within 7 days of two shifts are left out. The score table gives such a row to the later shift, so its score would credit that shift with the effect of the earlier one. The rule drops 697,129 of 6,563,096 near-shift rows (10.6%).
  • Cells are uneven. 1,079 of the 1,152 shifts have scored rows after the rule, 37 to 48 per (duration, depth) cell with both shapes pooled. The two shapes are not scored separately beyond the check above.
  • Benefit weights rows equally, and the depth mix is assumed. A long shift has more rows, so its benefit grows with its length. The share is a share of forecast skill summed over rows, not over shifts. With only 5% and 10% depths the cost share falls to 63.5% (see "Audit").
  • The forecasts are experiment 208's cached member forecasts with a Kalman filter on recent errors, with no retraining, so the contrast cannot depend on a retraining schedule.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Weight the shares by realistic recall. Multiply each cell's benefit by the recall of the long-and-deep detector in that cell, and subtract its false-alarm harm, once Part 1 of the long-deep detector experiment reports.
  • Measure depth for the log of operations. A measured depth for every logged operation would replace the assumed depth mixes.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• Arms: no knowledge (K0); PERFECT, PERFECT_LAG, PERFECT_LD, and PERFECT_SMALL with readings set aside; the same four with the known megawatts subtracted from the readings and added back to the forecast (post hoc). Ladder arms (minimum duration and depth) are computed by selection.
  • Rows: 143 simulated worlds, 1,079 scored shifts, six Primaries (D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16), rows within 7 days of a shift (target times from August 2024 to June 2026), plus every fourth daily run's ordinary rows.
  • Cost: node-only, 12 to 36 hour leads, scaled limit 0.5 (0.75 and 0.9 give 91.2% and 93.1%), GBP 2,000 per MWh.

docs.title: Do forecasts with no load shift detector match the best LSC detector?
docs.text:
This experiment asks whether a forecast needs a load shift detector at all. A load shift moves demand from one Primary substation to its neighbours for hours or days. A detector finds those shifts in the power readings, and the forecast then sets aside the readings inside each detected shift (a "mask"). We simulated 411 load shifts (44 copies of the real power record, six Primary substations labelled D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, from experiment 141). We compared forecasts that use a detector with seven forecasts that use none, scored as in experiment 283. The detector is RO-NC (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector), because LR_b20 (a learned detector built on RO-NC's alarms) was never run on the simulated shifts. Against RO-NC, a detector is not shown to be needed. The page does not conclude that no detector is needed, because RO-NC is the weaker of the two detectors.

K0 is the Kalman filter on recent power with no knowledge of shifts; every gain is a percentage of K0's score, and positive is better. The "upper-tail score" is the continuous ranked probability score weighted towards values above the 95th percentile of earlier power (twCRPS). G1 is ordinary rows, G4 is the 48 hours after a shift ends, G5 is the 7 days either side of a shift and the shift itself, and "shift rows" are the before-alarm, during, and after rows of G5. Primary substations have no published export limit, so curtailment figures compare forecasts and state no money saved. Intervals resample whole shifts, or whole calendar months for ordinary rows.

docs.title: Gains over K0 near a shift
docs.text:
Arm Upper-tail score, 48 h after (G4) Upper-tail score, within 7 days (G5) Curtailment cost, within 7 days (G5) GAM_ONLY (no correction) +18.4 (9.8 to 30.0) +2.3 (-2.5 to 7.5) -7.5 (-10.8 to -4.6) Band table by disagreement +1.6 (-5.4 to 7.2) +6.7 (5.0 to 8.7) -0.9 (-2.0 to +0.0) Band quantile head +14.7 (6.7 to 20.9) +11.5 (9.7 to 13.4) +2.0 (1.0 to 3.1) As-of widening +14.2 (6.3 to 24.6) -0.3 (-4.6 to 4.5) -4.0 (-5.7 to -2.3) Lead-decay filter +1.3 (-2.6 to 6.6) +9.6 (6.7 to 12.9) -3.5 (-6.0 to -1.6) RO-NC mask +13.9 (0.9 to 26.5) -35.0 (-48.8 to -23.0) -6.1 (-9.9 to -2.7) Perfect mask +23.1 (8.7 to 39.1) +6.3 (2.8 to 10.0) -1.4 (-4.9 to +1.6) Perfect, megawatts added back (post hoc, scored against observed power) +18.1 (6.0 to 31.5) +6.6 (3.3 to 9.7) +8.1 (6.4 to 10.0)

Every cell is a percentage gain over K0 with a 95% interval.

docs.title: Decision contrasts
docs.text:
• Decision rule against RO-NC (half B of the worlds; the best no-detector arm, the band quantile head, was chosen on half A). The RO-NC mask loses 57.9% (34.1 to 88.8) of the upper-tail score against the head within 7 days of a shift, and scores 0.178 points (0.070 to 0.298) worse on ordinary rows. RO-NC with megawatts added back loses 3.9% (0.1 to 9.1) of curtailment cost. The decision rule is not met.
  • Perfect knowledge against the same head. On the upper-tail score within 7 days it loses 5.7% (1.1 to 10.9). On the 10.4% of those rows where a shift acts it gains 10.2% (-7.0 to +25.0), so the interval spans zero. On curtailment cost, with the true megawatts added back, it gains 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2) in G5 and 14.9% (6.3 to 23.4) on shift rows. The ordinary-row clause fails: the perfect mask scores 0.048 points worse than the head on ordinary rows (interval for perfect minus head: -0.149 to +0.019). The head also costs 2.9% (0.7 to 5.7) more curtailment than K0 on ordinary rows.
  • Leaving out one Primary substation changes the contrasts. Without D16, the perfect mask against the head moves from -5.7% to +0.4% (-5.1 to +5.6) on the upper-tail score in G5. Without D11, RO-NC with megawatts added back moves from -3.9% to +1.4% (-2.4 to +5.2) on cost.
  • Held-out check of the head (post hoc). The head's fit used the same worlds as its scoring, on the other month parity. Refitting it on even-seed worlds only and scoring odd-seed worlds only keeps the gain: +10.1% (8.2 to 12.3) within 7 days against +11.8% (9.2 to 14.9) for the cross-fitted head on the same worlds, and 4.07% (2.44 to 5.94) of readings above q99 after a shift against 3.85% (2.30 to 5.68). The injector and the real record are shared, so a leak through either is not removed.

docs.title: Predictions
docs.text:
• P1 failed. GAM_ONLY loses 0.222 points (0.029 to 0.374) of CRPS on ordinary rows at leads of 24 to 168 hours, against the bar of 0.10. In the 48 hours after a shift 0.16% (0.07 to 0.28) of true readings fall below its q01 and 3.97% (2.46 to 6.25) rise above its q99, outside the 2-percentage-point bar.
  • P2 failed as written. K0's share below q01 after a shift is 2.24% (1.14 to 3.55), not the brief's 9.1%, so K0 meets the 3% bar. The share above q99 is the real fault: 14.23% (10.92 to 17.74) for K0 and 3.54% (2.22 to 5.05) for the head. The head lowers ordinary-row CRPS by 0.046 points (-0.023 to +0.150), more than the 0.01 bar allows.
  • P3 failed. The lead-decay filter recovers 5.8% (-11.9 to 30.0) of the perfect mask's gain in the 48 hours after a shift, against 60%. Arms outside the prediction recover more: GAM_ONLY 79.5% (57.2 to 134.1), as-of widening 61.7% (41.5 to 93.4), and the head 63.6% (22.4 to 210.6).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site: the mean absolute error of the median forecast minus that of the mean forecast lies between -0.274 (band head) and +0.088 (band table, plain) points. The band arms keep K0's mean forecast, so their mean-forecast error equals K0's by construction, and the head moves the median by design.
  • Absolute CRPS against the true series (points of effective capacity, K0 / head / perfect mask): 2.71 / 2.66 / 2.71 on ordinary rows, 4.14 / 3.43 / 2.69 in G4, and 2.96 / 2.74 / 2.64 in G5. The printed report holds every arm.
  • Triggers that fired: the prediction-contradiction trigger (all three predictions failed; the tested explanation is K0's measured 2.24% below q01 against the brief's 9.1%), the leave-one-site-out trigger (D16 and D11 flip contrasts), and the replication trigger (the next program step builds its bar on the best no-detector arm). An audit by a fresh Sonnet reviewer reproduced the headline contrasts from the stored scores. Its main finding, that the head's advantage over the perfect mask in G5 sits in margin rows (89.6% of G5), is in the contrasts above. Its estimate that the head's gain falls from +11.5% to +4.9% when ordinary rows are reweighted like near-shift rows is not in the printed report, and BAND_TABLE_PLAIN (+1.8%, 1.1 to 2.6, the same arm without the filter level) is the printed control.

docs.title: How BAND_HEAD was trained, and its real-record results (added by experiment 312)
docs.text:
• Training: every head is fitted on the rows of all 44 worlds whose month has one parity and scored on the other parity, then the roles swap. Rows near a shift take the parity of the shift's onset month, and ordinary rows weigh 4. A world shares the injector, the real record, and the months with the other worlds, so the held-out check above removes the scored worlds and seeds from fitting but not the injector.
  • Real record (experiment 312): against K0 the head changes the quantile score on ordinary rows by +1.1% (-1.1 to +3.7), so it does no harm. Readings fall below q01 in 0.9% of ordinary rows and above q99 in 0.9%, against 1.8% and 1.1% for K0. In the 48 hours after a logged transfer the shares are 1.3% and 1.1%, against 2.4% and 1.0%.
  • Not compared: experiment 264's rows are at D8 and experiment 209's heads belong to arm D, so neither shares rows with BAND_HEAD.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• RO-NC is a weak stand-in. Its false alarms are the likely cause of the 35% loss, although the report does not separate them from late ends. LR_b20 may behave differently, and experiment 208 noted that its learned score was trained on the real record.
  • The comparison is not like for like on bands. The detector arms keep K0's bands, and the head has refitted bands, so part of the head's lead is a calibration gain that a detector forecast could also have.
  • Lab conditions. The megawatts-added-back arms use the true megawatts and the true end of each shift, and the detector arms use hindsight ends.
  • The simulated shifts are all 25% of load or more and last over a day.
  • Not done. The head was not scored on the real record (7 logged transfers), which resolves no curtailment difference (experiment 277). The as-of widening arm is a simplified port of experiment 264's idea, and no comparison with experiment 209's heads was made.
  • Spreads and folds. GAM_ONLY and as-of widening fit their spreads on the clean series, which flatters both arms slightly. Rows near a shift are folded by onset month, so a few target timestamps fall in the other parity's months.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• Arms: K0; GAM_ONLY (no correction, spread fitted on the other month parity); the same with K0's bands; a band table (lead band by hour band); a band table by disagreement (also binned by the filter's correction in units of its own history); the band quantile head (XGBoost, 11 quantiles, depth 3, 100 rounds, trained on residuals against observed power); as-of widening; the lead-decay filter; RO-NC with and without megawatts added back; perfect knowledge with and without megawatts added back.
  • Training: every fitted arm is trained on all worlds' rows of one month parity and scored on the other parity, then the roles swap. Rows near a shift take the parity of the shift's onset month.
  • Rows and schedule: experiment 283's rows (22.9 million weighted rows, 411 shifts); no retraining, the forecasts are cached member forecasts of experiments 111 and 115.
  • Weather: the cached ensemble member forecasts; the readings are the real residual stream plus injected megawatts.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Run LR_b20 on the injected worlds, after checking whether the learned score needs retraining there, and judge it against the head and against perfect knowledge on shift rows.
  • Give the detector arms the recalibrated bands, so that detector and no-detector forecasts differ only in the detector.

docs.title: Does leaving detected load shifts out of the refit of a no-lag forecast stop it learning them as normal?
docs.text: Six detectors that read the daily mean forecast error find about as many long, deep real load shifts as LR_b20, a learned score from experiment 302, and leaving their flagged days out of the monthly refit cuts what a 30-day transfer teaches the forecast by a third to a half, but not to the 5% that was pre-registered. A load shift (also called a transfer) is a spell in which an operator moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto a neighbouring Primary. Primary substations step 33 kV down to 11 kV. We used the generalised additive forecast with no lagged power (GAM_ONLY), refitted every month. Detectors A to C test the daily mean of its error. Detectors D to F add a check against the neighbouring Primaries. We scored them on the real record and on transfers that we added to the demand series. We then refitted GAM_ONLY with the days a detector had flagged left out of training. The "share learned as normal" is the part of an added transfer that the refitted forecast absorbs into its idea of normal load. The "oracle" is cleaning that leaves out exactly the true transfer days. The verdict is not supported, because pre-registered predictions 1 and 2 failed, and prediction 3 failed on its 5% target. The oracle shows the ceiling: leaving out the true days cuts the share learned to 2.8%.

docs.title: Detectors on the 19 real load shifts that are long and large
docs.text:
The headline comparison is on the 19 real load shifts that last at least 2 days and move at least 10% of load, the group that experiment 302 fixed before this experiment's results were read. The other 16 of the 35 labelled real transfers over 1 day are "other". "Matches" counts shifts with an alarm during them or within a day. "Alarms per match" is every alarm over the whole record divided by the matches. "MW-weighted" weights each match by the shift's recorded megawatts. printed_stratum.txt holds the full table. RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector.

Detector Matches, 19 long and large Alarms per match MW-weighted Matches, other 16 MW-weighted LR_b20 (experiment 302) 12 8.8 0.72 9 0.69 RO-NC, 2nd operating point 12 10.8 0.71 10 0.80 RO-NC, carried operating point 16 18.1 0.86 13 0.92 Learned re-ranker 18 21.3 0.95 14 0.94 A3 (mean of 3 days) 10 13.3 0.65 4 0.43 B (cumulative sum) 10 15.0 0.66 3 0.18 C (3 days against 28) 11 11.4 0.67 5 0.38 E3 (pair test) 12 11.4 0.68 2 0.09 D-A3 (neighbour check) 8 16.4 0.54 4 0.34 F-C (neighbour cover) 9 13.8 0.58 4 0.22

On the 19 long and large shifts the daily-mean detectors match 8 to 12, against 12 for LR_b20, with more alarms per match; on the other 16 shifts they are clearly worse. RO-NC and the learned re-ranker match more at their carried operating points, but at 18 to 21 alarms per match.

The same split on the injected shifts (25% of load, no metered partner, even-month onsets, 2 or more days against 1 day): variant C finds 62% of 1,440 long shifts (3.2 alarms per match, MW-weighted 0.85) and 13% of 240 one-day shifts. E3 finds 61% and 6%. F-C finds 55% and 8%.

docs.title: Part 1: the detectors
docs.text:
• Real record, tuned to 2 false alarms per Primary-year in odd months. A "world" below is one injected-transfer scenario at one Primary. Variant C, which odd-month injected transfers picked as the best any-alarm variant, found 0 of 17 block days, 11 of 29 D8 drops, and 16 of the 35 real transfers, with 1.48 false alarms per Primary-year in even months. Variant B found 27 of 29 D8 drops and 1 of 17 block days at 1.59 false alarms. The block days are 12 hours or less, so a daily mean cannot see them. Prediction 1 fails on the block days and on the drops for C (11 against 15 needed), and holds on the false-alarm rate. The drops are probably a gas engine (experiment 291), so they are not counted as load shifts.
  • Neighbour checks at the same threshold cut false alarms by 68% to 73% (D-A3 against A3: 76 to 24 over the record), but lose 27% to 56% of the 22 real transfers that have two metered sides. Prediction 2's limit of a 20% recall loss fails.
  • The pair test E3 does not check neighbours. On injected transfers its recall is 73% with no metered partner, 81% with one, and 74% with a shifted-week placebo. D and F separate better (F-C at the same threshold: 65% with the partner, 42% with none, 39% with the placebo).
  • Permanent steps are not rejected. Variants D to F alarm on 50% to 99% of injected steps whose receiver is unmetered, against the 20% or less that prediction 2 allowed.
  • Timing. For found injected shifts of 6 days or more, the median alarm comes 24 to 48 hours after the start for A2, A3, C, E3, and F-C, and 72 to 96 hours for A7 and B. The median start error is 0 hours at day resolution, and the median end error is 0 hours except for F-C (-48 hours) and D-C (-24 hours).
  • Depth. Recall for 7 to 90 days at 10% of load is 16% to 44%, at 25% it is 66% to 83%, and at 50% it is 66% to 92%.

docs.title: Part 2: cleaning the refit
docs.text:
30 days, 25% of load Share learned, 48 h after the end 2 to 33 days after No cleaning 19.4% (18.2 to 20.5) 12.0% Oracle 2.8% (0.4 to 5.1) 2.0% Detector C 13.0% (10.4 to 15.7) 6.0% Detector E3 10.1% (6.9 to 13.2) 4.5% Detector F-C 13.2% (10.3 to 16.0) 5.9%
  • Paired difference from no cleaning: oracle -16.6 points (-18.9 to -14.4), C -6.3 (-9.3 to -3.6), E3 -9.3 (-12.6 to -6.1), F-C -6.1 (-9.2 to -3.5). Prediction 3's target of under 5% fails for every detector.
  • Short shifts. Cleaning removes most of the learning for 3 to 14 days (14 days: 18.1% uncleaned, 3.9% oracle, 6.1% to 7.4% detectors). A 7-day, 25% shift is learned at 9.3% with no cleaning and at 3.0% to 3.4% with a detector.
  • Long shifts and steps. A 90-day shift is learned at 32% with no cleaning and at 22% to 28% with the oracle or any detector, because the run of excluded days is capped at 60. A permanent step of 25% is 45% learned after 12 months with no cleaning, 24% with the oracle, and 24% (E3) to 34% (F-C) with detectors.
  • Clean rows. On the 14 Primaries with no shift, cleaning changes the mean absolute error by +0.013 (-0.028 to +0.068) points for C, +0.007 (-0.030 to +0.053) for E3, and -0.008 (-0.033 to +0.024) for F-C. Prediction 3's limit is a rise of under 0.01 points, which E3 and F-C meet and C does not. D8 (+0.31 for C) and D12 (+0.16 to +0.26 for E3 and F-C) carry the positive values.
  • Self-reinforcement. Refitting without the flagged days and re-running the detector on the new residuals flags 74% to 97% of the same days again, so the exclusion is stable. The recheck uses in-sample residuals for the days that stayed in training.
  • Wrong exclusions. Over the whole run each detector flags 7.5 to 8.2 days per 30-day world, and 5 to 7 days per world of 1 to 7 days, outside the true shift.
  • Near-a-shift scores against the true normal-arrangement series (30 days, 25%): mean continuous ranked probability score 4.66 points with no cleaning, 4.54 for the oracle, and 4.59 to 4.61 for the detectors. The threshold-weighted score is 0.63 for every arm. The spread is a fixed Gaussian width fitted to the clean forecast's own error, so these scores rank the centres only.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast against mean forecast. GAM_ONLY forecasts the mean only, so there is no median to compare with it.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the scores. The mean absolute error against the true series falls in step with the continuous ranked probability score (6.26 uncleaned, 6.11 oracle, 6.17 to 6.20 detectors).
  • Audit triggers fired. A control failed: E3 does no neighbour check (73% with no partner, 81% with one, 74% with the placebo). The result contradicts the pre-registered predictions, and the explanation we tested, the detector's delay of 1 to 3 days, fits but was not isolated. A nested arm lost to the arm it contains: the oracle, which should contain every detector arm, leaves 27.4% learned for a 90-day, 25% shift against 22.3% for E3 (intervals 24.6 to 30.6 and 17.9 to 26.3), because the oracle's run of excluded days is capped at 60 while the detectors' separate runs are not.
  • No Opus audit was run, because this session was limited to Sonnet models.
  • Reviews. One Sonnet code review found 12 issues. We fixed four (a pair-noise cache shared between worlds, a placebo shifted by less than the transfer, hits that ignored the sign of the alarm, and stored-alarm counts on a different basis) and documented the rest below. One Sonnet review checked the numbers and one checked the prose.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• Thresholds for D-A7, D-C, and F-A7 reach the bottom of the grid, so they are not at equal false-alarm rate with A to C. Recall on the real record is counted in all months, so it is partly in the tuning months. Variant B's long spans count as hits on any overlap.
  • The hindsight start moves back by up to the window length minus one (6 days for A7 and E7), not the planned 2. The partner in a metered world is refitted but never cleaned, and the load level used by the depth rule is the clean level.
  • Permanent steps start at the four fixed onsets and run 15 months, not 3, 6, and 12 months before the end of the data. The weather is ERA5 and CAMS, which arrive days late, so these detectors had better weather data than a live service would have, and live results will be worse.
  • D15 has no panel because its history starts in 2025, so 15 of the 16 Primaries are scored.
  • Next. The gap between the detectors (10% to 13% learned) and the oracle (2.8%) is mostly the 1 to 3 days before a detector fires and the long transfers it misses. The result points to the next experiment: a detector that fires on the first day, or a refit that downweights the most recent days when the residual is high.

docs.title: When does the best-guess demand model fall behind BG2 in spring, what causes D10's night offset, and does the error-correction layer make the spring excess worse?
docs.text:
The spring excess of arm D over BG2 grows with sunshine and is not a one-date step at the clock change. Arm D is our best-guess demand forecast without its neural-network head: a convex model with a Kalman filter on recent errors. BG2 is the production-style XGBoost forecast of experiment 87. We asked three questions of experiment 266's stored forecasts. When does arm D fall behind BG2? What is the night-time level error at D10? Do the Kalman filter and the neural-network correction heads make the spring excess larger? Nothing is refitted.

D5, D9, and D10 are anonymised Primary substations. The excess sits on clear midday half-hours at D5 (+1.67 points) and across the whole day at D9, at every lead. The Kalman filter changes the excess by +0.02 and +0.06 points, and at D5 the three correction heads lower it. D10's night residual (actual minus forecast) has no single step. A clock-change effect is not ruled out, because it cannot be separated from the rising sun.

The scores are quantile scores on 561,207 rows. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of a substation's rated demand); lower is better, and "excess" means arm D's score minus BG2's. The rows cover six substations, 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, forecasts issued at 09:00 UTC, leads (hours ahead) 0.5 to 168, outside hand-filtered load shifts. Intervals resample whole ISO weeks of forecast initialisation time (14 weeks in April to June).

None of the three pre-registered predictions held. The excess is not concentrated within 4 weeks of the clock change or at short leads (Part 1), D10's offset is not one step (Part 3), and removing the filter or a head does not lower the excess by 30% (Part 2; refuted at D5, undecided at D9 for the filter).

Figure 1. Weekly daylight excess at D5, D9, and D10: it builds from April, with no clean step at either clock change.

Figure 2. The April-to-June excess by lead band: it is not concentrated at short leads.

Figure 3. D10's nightly residual and its monthly mean: the monthly mean wanders and shows no single step.

Figure 4. The share of the April-to-June daylight excess that removing each layer removes: no layer reaches the 30% bar.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Check that reproduces experiment 266: arm D minus BG2 in April to June is +0.319 (+0.198 to +0.430) points, the figure of experiment 266.
  • Part 1, timing (predicted, and failed): the stored rows start with the forecasts issued on 1 April, so the window is forecasts issued 1 to 25 April 2026. It holds 29% of D5's April-to-June daylight excess (27% of its rows) and 10% of D9's (26% of rows); the required share was 50%. The shares are point estimates without intervals. Leads under 24 hours hold 14% of D5's excess (14% of rows) and 6% of D9's (14% of rows); the required share was 50%. Neither the 4-week test nor the 24-hour test is met at either substation, so the excess does not concentrate in either window. The 0-to-6-hour band holds more of the excess than of the rows at D5 (+2.45 points against +0.30 at 6 to 24 hours), so BG2's use of recent power is not excluded as a contributor at the shortest leads.
  • Lead and sunshine, April to June daylight (points): D5 +2.45 at 0 to 6 hours, +0.30 at 6 to 24, +1.22 at 24 to 48, +1.10 at 48 to 168; D9 +0.25, +0.35, +0.59, +0.84. By realised clear-sky index at D5: clear +1.67 (+1.23 to +2.11), mixed +0.72, overcast -0.31 (-0.90 to +0.35). At D9: clear +1.02, mixed +0.47, overcast +0.25.
  • Hour of day, April to June, local time (hour of the half-hour's start): D5's excess is +2.0 to +3.5 points from 11:00 to 15:00 and near zero at night. D9's is +0.4 to +1.0 from 06:00 to 23:00 and +0.1 to +0.2 from 00:00 to 05:00, so D9's excess is not shaped like solar output alone.
  • Clock-change comparison (descriptive): D5's daylight gap is -0.03 in the 4 weeks before 29 March 2026 and +1.12 in the 4 weeks after, but in the autumn it falls from +0.52 to +0.13 across 26 October 2025. The jump at D5 and the fall in autumn both match sun elevation and sunshine, and this design cannot separate a clock-change effect from them. D10 shows a larger jump near the same date: its night excess goes from -0.13 (-0.25 to +0.01) in the 4 weeks before 29 March to +0.89 (+0.70 to +1.08) in the 4 weeks after, and in autumn from +0.92 to -0.85 (-2.40 to +0.87); its daylight excess goes from -1.03 to +0.16.
  • Season at D5 and D9: July to September daylight excess is +0.31 (D5) and +0.17 (D9), against +1.12 and +0.73 in April to June. D10's April-to-June excess is +0.20 points by day and +0.60 at night.
  • Part 3, D10 night level (predicted, and failed): over 635 nights (2024-07 to 2026-06, leads 12 to 36 hours, rows outside hand-filtered load shifts, which is a subset of the rows the earlier experiments scored), the best single-step fit explains 0.9% of the variance of the nightly mean residual; a fit on the 24 year-months explains 12.7% (9.4% adjusted for its 24 parameters, against 0.6% for the step) and on temperature band and year-month 13.3%. Within the scored year the step explains 2.6% (1.9% adjusted) and the 12 year-months 8.7% (5.0% adjusted). The monthly means do not repeat across years, so a month-of-year term would not capture them. The change-point date has a 95% interval of 623 days (whole period) and 310 days (scored year), far above the 2-week bar. The April-to-June mean residual is -0.55 points in 2025 and -0.95 in 2026. Day of week (of the evening the night starts) explains 1.2% (Monday and Sunday evening nights -1.0 and -1.2 points). No candidate date is inferred.
  • Part 2, error correction (predicted, and not supported), April-to-June daylight: removing the Kalman filter from GAM-K (experiment 111's GAM-K, a generalised additive model with the filter, against its filterless version GAM0) lowers the excess by 1.7% at D5 (-18.7% to +21.5%) and 8.1% at D9 (-54.9% to +38.3%). By the decision rule D5 is refuted (upper bound under 30%) and D9 is undecided (upper bound 38.3%). The July-to-September condition fails at D9, where removing the filter raises the score by 0.60 points. Removing a correction head (experiment 201's arms 1, 5, and 6 against arm D) raises the D5 excess: the heads lower the score by 0.49 (-0.81 to -0.16), 0.63, and 0.58 points. At D9 the heads change the score by -0.20 (-0.49 to +0.10), -0.14, and +0.10 (+0.04 to +0.15) points, so the D9 effect is mixed and arm 6 raises the excess there.
  • Filter by season, all six substations, GAM-K minus GAM0: -0.14 (-0.39 to +0.06) points in April to June daylight and -0.30 (-0.42 to -0.19) in July to September daylight.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, arm D, per substation: exactly 0.000 points at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, because arm D's median is its mean, so the mean-forecast and median-forecast errors are identical (mean absolute error of arm D: D5 6.01, D9 4.21, D10 5.31, D11 4.21, D14 3.69, D16 4.48 MW; printed by e00299_timing.py). The head-arm and filter joins assert that no row is lost, and every arm scores all 561,207 rows.
  • Triggers: 1 (a control fails), 3 (quantile score against mean-error direction), 4 (leave-one- out), 5 (nested arm), and 6 (interval width) do not apply, because the experiment has no controls, no leave-one-out contrast, and no sister experiment on these contrasts. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction) fired for every prediction; we record an explanation for each (sun elevation and sunshine, a month-scale drift, and the heads helping), and the head result agrees with experiments 200, 201, and 266. Trigger 7 holds for the planned solar-times-temperature experiment, whose design depends on the D5 and D9 excess being a clear-sky effect that the generalised additive demand model cannot give different weights; the experiment manager decides whether that needs an audit.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Part 2 is stored pairs only. Arm D without its filter is not stored, so the filter test uses the older GAM-K and GAM0 of experiment 111, which differ from arm D (no night offset, no recipe R). A refit of arm D without the filter was not run.
  • D10's night residual here is smaller than the -2 points of experiment 281. This page uses arm D at leads 12 to 36 hours over 21:00 to 07:30 UTC outside load shifts; experiment 281 used a different arm and lead set.
  • Intervals are wide. April to June holds 14 weeks of forecast initialisation, and the nightly series are noisy; the single-step test has little power, which the page reports through the interval width.
  • Retraining schedule: not applicable, because nothing is refitted.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Test the solar term's response on clear, high-sun half-hours at D5 and D9 directly, for example with the experiment 4 interaction terms of dp_summer_gap_next_experiments.md, using realised clear-sky index strata as the first read.
  • Test a night term that varies by month at D10 instead of looking for a date.
