docs.title: How good is the assembled best-guess day-ahead forecast for the six metered solar farms, and what does a new farm with no history get?
docs.text:
The assembled forecast scores 3.3% better than XGBoost on the quantile score (lower is better) and 43% better at the 0.99 pinball loss when a farm trains on its own history. With no history for the farm, it scores 2.0% better than XGBoost on the quantile score. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F here. We scored the forecast that experiments 270, 287, and 260 selected against four references: XGBoost (a gradient-boosted tree model, Chen and Guestrin, 2016), manual_heuristic, climatology, and the physical power model alone. The forecast starts from a physical power model of each farm, called "P2". A generalised additive model (GAM) and a mixture-density neural network (MDN) each correct P2's 11 quantiles. The forecast blends the GAM's, the MDN's, and XGBoost's quantiles, level by level. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over the 11 quantile levels, in points of capacity, and a negative change in it is an improvement. We refitted every forecasting method each month for the 12 scored months, September 2025 to August 2026. "Own history" means a model trains on the farm's earlier months, and "zero history" means a model trains on the other five farms only.

The verdict is partly supported. The own-history score gain (-3.3%, 98.75% interval -4.3% to -2.0%) and the 0.99 pinball-loss gain (-42.8%, -49.2% to -36.0%) cleared the bars in the decision rule. The zero-history gain (-2.0%, -2.8% to -1.0%) did not reach the 3% we predicted, although its interval excludes zero. The own-history score gain is larger than the 1% to 2% we predicted. The Audit triggers bullet under Checks compares it with experiment 287's XGBoost score and explains the difference.

The scores cover leads of 12 to 36 hours only, and NGED cares about 1 day to 10 days ahead. The stored ensemble tables hold only the 00 UTC run's first 36 hours, so nothing here says how the candidate compares with XGBoost at 2 to 10 days.

docs.title: Each model family alone beside the blend
docs.text:
The fits for every row of this table are stored, so the table needs no new run. A negative change is an improvement. The best single family is chosen on the scored year, which favours it slightly.

Model Score, own history 0.99 pinball loss, own Score, zero history 0.99 pinball loss, zero GAM alone 5.43 0.331 5.59 0.348 MDN alone (5 seeds averaged) 5.34 0.300 5.55 0.321 Plant-fed XGBoost 5.45 0.541 5.56 0.549 Blend of the three 5.27 0.310 5.45 0.327
  • The MDN is the best single family on the quantile score in both settings.
  • The blend adds 1.3% over the MDN in own history (98.75% interval -2.6% to -0.2%) and 1.7% in zero history (-2.5% to -0.6%).
  • The blend adds nothing at the 0.99 quantile. The blend's 0.99 pinball loss is 3.1% higher than the MDN's in own history (-0.5% to +8.5%) and 1.9% higher in zero history (-3.9% to +8.0%).
  • Plant-fed XGBoost is the weakest family at the 0.99 quantile (0.54, against 0.30 to 0.35 for the other two) and scores within 0.4% of the GAM on the quantile score in own history.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Quantile score (points of capacity; own history, then zero history). Candidate blend 5.27 and 5.45, blend of GAM and XGBoost 5.32 and 5.47, MDN (five seeds averaged) 5.34 and 5.55, XGBoost 5.45 and 5.56, GAM 5.43 and 5.59, P2 5.54 and 5.71, climatology 8.64, manual_heuristic 8.69. The candidate is 39% below manual_heuristic in own history (-42.3% to -36.3%) and 37% below in zero history.
  • Planned contrasts, candidate minus XGBoost (98.75% interval). Own history: score -3.27% (-4.30 to -2.04); 0.99 pinball loss -42.8% (-49.2 to -36.0); error of the median -1.74% (-2.92 to -0.15). Zero history: score -1.99% (-2.84 to -0.96).
  • What each stage adds (own history). Candidate minus P2 -4.75% (-7.84 to -2.96). GAM minus P2 -1.9% (the ablations' reference). MDN minus GAM -1.57% (-2.91 to -0.44). Candidate minus the blend without the MDN -0.87% (-1.32 to -0.31). In zero history MDN minus GAM is -0.80% (-2.61 to +0.70) and the candidate minus the blend without the MDN is -0.46% (-1.12 to +0.21).
  • Inputs. The ensemble spread is the standard deviation of the plant's response across the 51 ensemble members. The availability ratio is the farm's output one or two days earlier divided by the plant's forecast for that time. The plant scale and output ceiling scale P2's forecast and cap it.
  • Ablations on the GAM (score change against the full GAM; own history, zero history). No spread +0.31% (-0.83 to +1.09) and +0.58% (-0.38 to +1.24). No lagged power +0.01% (-0.06 to +0.07) and -0.01%. No availability ratio +0.17% (-0.01 to +0.35) and +0.27% (+0.13 to +0.42). Lagged power and the availability ratio add almost nothing.
  • Tail calibration (own history; nominal 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, 0.99). Candidate coverage 0.036, 0.070, 0.957, 0.990; XGBoost 0.035, 0.083, 0.946, 0.991. Pinball loss at 0.99: candidate 0.31, XGBoost 0.54, manual_heuristic 0.58, climatology 0.43. Actual output falls below the 0.01 quantile 3.4 to 3.6 times as often as the nominal 1% for every forecast arm (the manual_heuristic floor: 9.6 times). It falls below the 0.05 quantile 1.3 to 1.5 times as often as the nominal 5% for most arms, and 1.7 times as often for XGBoost.
  • Where the gain sits (own history). By season the candidate beats XGBoost by 4.1% in June to August (-5.5 to -2.9), 3.2% in March to May, and 2.3% in September to November and in December to February, where the December to February interval includes zero. By clear-sky band the candidate is 8% below XGBoost under cloud (index below 0.3), 5% below under clear sky (0.9 and above), and 2% below in between. In each setting the candidate is worse than XGBoost in one month: December 2025 in own history and April 2026 in zero history.
  • Lead axis. The stored ensemble tables cover leads of 12 to 36 hours from the 00 UTC run, and daylight leaves 3-hour bins starting at 12, 15, 18, 27, 30, and 33 hours. The candidate scores 6.7 at the lowest bin and 6.5 at the highest, and about 1.1 to 1.2 at the 18 and 27 hour bins. The lead range of 0.5 to 54 hours that the brief asked for needs other ensemble runs and was not scored.
  • Farm cards (own history, August 2026 refit; fractions of capacity). The plant scale is 1.00 to 1.16 and the output ceiling 1.05 to 1.11. The mean width of the 5% to 95% band is 16 to 23 points of capacity under cloud (clear-sky index below 0.3), 48 to 55 under partly clear sky (0.6 to 0.9), and 29 to 39 under clear sky (0.9 and above). Across farms and bands, the band holds 85% to 95% of actual output against a nominal 90%. The per-farm tables are in the private data folder.
  • What the candidate cannot do. It cannot forecast outages or curtailment by the network operator, and a 25% loss of capacity is detected too slowly to act on. A drift under about 0.5% per year is invisible to it (experiment 286).
  • Curtailment value. Not scored. The node-plus-generators metric needs a substation node with its generators, and these six farms are single series, so the comparison against capacity_forecast could not be run. Experiments 255, 268, and 277 give the metric's limited power.
  • Reference rows, quoted and not refitted. The plant given observed weather explains a sunny fraction of 0.973, and the plant given the ensemble mean 0.91 (experiment 218).
  • Schedule and weather. The models are refitted monthly on all earlier months, and each month's training rows end one day before the month starts. The forecast weather comes only from the ECMWF ensemble 00 UTC run, and the farm's own power comes from one or two days earlier; both exist at forecast time. Weekly refits were not run, so the absolute scores could shift a little. The MDN has five seeds, and the ablations use the GAM only.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, own history (points of capacity, farms pooled). Candidate +0.01, XGBoost -0.92, GAM +0.29, MDN +0.37, P2 +0.40. XGBoost's median sits below its mean forecast; no other arm's does by more than 0.4.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside each score contrast. Candidate minus XGBoost in own history: mean-forecast error -3.78% (-5.82 to -2.43), against a score change of -3.27%. The score and the mean-forecast error point the same way, so trigger 3 did not fire.
  • Audit triggers. Trigger 2 (a result contradicting its prediction) fired in size only: the own-history gain is 3.3% against the predicted 1% to 2%. The XGBoost arm here has no past-weather rows, because those arrive about 5 days late. Experiment 287's XGBoost scored 5.40 with past weather in a single fit, and the candidate is 2.4% below that figure, which brings the result into the predicted range. The two schedules differ, so the comparison is approximate. Trigger 4 did not fire: dropping each farm in turn leaves the own-history score change between -2.9% and -3.5%, and the zero-history change between -1.8% and -2.2%. Trigger 5 did not fire: the ablated GAMs score within 0.6% of the full GAM, and none scores better by more than the interval's half-width. Triggers 1, 3, 6, and 7 did not fire. No audit ran.
  • Row set. Every arm holds the same 41,676 rows in each setting (the code checks equal counts).

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Zero history is not fully blind. In zero history the blend's weights for a farm are fitted on the other five farms' earlier rows only. The lagged-power inputs still use the scored farm's own power from one or two days before the run, which exists at forecast time.
  • Post hoc. The blend without the MDN is an added arm and not a planned contrast. The 98.75% level covers the four planned contrasts only.
  • Not covered. This experiment did not cover leads under 12 hours, leads over 36 hours, weekly refits, or the curtailment value.
  • Next. The next experiment should score the candidate and XGBoost at leads of up to 10 days, which is the horizon NGED cares about. After that, score the candidate with the node metric once a farm is paired with its substation.

docs.title: Does an availability state improve the solar-farm forecast band during and after outages?
docs.text: Outages of the six metered solar farms are too rare in the scored year to test an availability state, so the experiment stopped at its stop rule without fitting any model. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F here. We asked whether a farm's state (running, partly down, or switched off), inferred from its last 6 to 48 hours of power, improves the lower quantiles (0.01 and 0.05) of the day-ahead forecast band during and after an outage. The stop rule says to stop if fewer than 200 outage half-hours fall in the scored year (2025-09 to 2026-08) at 4 or more farms. An outage half-hour is a daylight half-hour (sun more than 5 degrees above the horizon) in which the farm produced under 5% of the physical power model's forecast, when that forecast exceeded 15% of the farm's capacity, on a day with at least 6 such half-hours. No farm has 200: five have at most 34, and farm E has 165.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Outage half-hours in the scored year (daylight, 12 to 36 h leads). A 15 (2 days), B 14 (2 days), C 0, D 34 (5 days), E 165 (15 days), F 10 (1 day). All six are under 200, so the stop rule fires.
  • A looser count gives the same answer. Counting every low daylight half-hour, without the 6-per-day requirement, gives 26 (A), 22 (B), 5 (C), 227 (D), 215 (E), and 21 (F). Farms A, B, C, and F stay under 200. Farms D and E pass 200 only because the loose count includes many short dips on 96 days (D) and 47 days (E), which the 6-per-day requirement removes.
  • Months before the scored year hold more low half-hours at some farms. The loose count before 2025-09 is 118 (A), 46 (B), 47 (C), 515 (D), 50 (E), and 78 (F).
  • Not run. The availability-state arms, their pinball loss, coverage, false alarms, and the control that shifts the power by one week.
  • The count preceded the plan commit. e00301_count.py ran before the plan was committed, so the stop rule acted as a pre-check and not as a pre-registered test.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Forecast checks do not apply. No forecast was made, so there is no median-minus-mean forecast and no mean-forecast error to read beside a quantile-score contrast.
  • No audit trigger fired.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Label. The outage label uses hindsight output against the plant forecast. A looser label finds more outage half-hours at farms D and E, and a stricter label finds fewer.
  • Next step. If outages matter for curtailment, test the availability-state model on the full history of farms A, B, and F, scoring outage half-hours only with blocked folds. That test needs its own plan.

docs.title: Does the learned LSC score keep its matches without NGED labels in training and thresholds?
docs.text:
A learned load-shift score trained without NGED labels in its negatives, with an alarm count taken from the labelled score, matched 14 of the 35 logged load shifts, against 20 to 21 with labels. The loss comes from the training negatives, not from the threshold. A load shift is demand that the electricity network operator moves between neighbouring Primary substations for hours or days. The 35 are the load shifts lasting over 1 day in NGED's switching log and hand labels. The score is the re-ranker of experiment 195, a small neural network that re-scores the candidate alarms of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC). A training negative is a candidate alarm that the network is taught is not a load shift.

Two arms use NGED labels and four do not. L0 is the carried setting of experiment 227 (LR_b20). It drops every logged or labelled span, every multi-day drop of the Primary substation named D8, and the 17 block days from its training negatives, and it sets its alarm threshold by counting candidates that no logged closure explains. L1 repeats L0 with the months swapped. L2 keeps every real candidate as a negative, and L3 adds an alarm rate per Primary. Terms defines the arms and a match. Flexpectation version 2 will have no NGED labels, so we asked whether L3 still matches about as many load shifts.

The prediction failed. We predicted that L3 would match at least 18 of the 35 at no more than 6.5 alarms per match. It matched 14 at 7.5. Its ordinary-day harm point estimate and 95% interval stayed inside the limit of 0.05 points (+0.017, -0.006 to +0.043). Points are percentages of a substation's effective capacity, and a lower score is better. Against the labelled score trained on the same months (L1), L3 lost 6 matches. The label-free negatives lowered matches by 7 (L2 against L1), and the label-free threshold raised them by 1 (L3 against L2). The verdict is not supported.

The whole loss sits in the load shifts that start in a month the score trained on (post hoc). In those 15 load shifts the labelled score L1 finds 7 and the label-free scores L2 and L3 find 0. Of the 15, 12 have a real onset candidate that L2 trains as a negative and L1 drops, which is a plausible mechanism that this page did not test. In the 20 load shifts that start in months the score never saw, L1, L2, and L3 find 13, 13, and 14. A service for future months resembles this split more than the whole 35, although the unseen months lie between trained months. Twenty load shifts cannot separate a difference of one or two matches.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Arms. L0 is the stored re-ranker of experiment 195, trained on even months, with a threshold that leaves 20 unexplained odd-month candidates. L1 is the same recipe trained on odd months, with a threshold that leaves 20 unexplained even-month candidates. L2 trains on the same odd months as L1, but keeps every real candidate that lies outside an injected span as a negative, and its threshold leaves as many merged alarms over the whole record as L0 raises in the same fold. L3 uses L2's score with one threshold per Primary: the fold's total alarm count is shared in proportion to each Primary's predicted RO-NC alarm rate times its years of residual. L3_5 and L3_2 pin the total at 5 and at 2 merged alarms per Primary-year, so they read no label in their alarm count.
  • The predicted rate. For Primary p, the base-2 logarithm of RO-NC's alarm rate at 4.35 noise units (experiment 217) is fitted on the base-2 logarithm of the share of days on which the demand model's daily mean error exceeds 3 noise units (plus 0.01), by a straight line fitted on the other 14 Primaries.
  • Match and alarm. A load shift is matched when an alarm's step is within 2 hours of its start and its estimated end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration (experiment 195's rule), scored with the fold that holds out the load shift's Primary pair. Alarms on one series within 24 hours merge, and the alarm count is the mean over the three folds.
  • Long and deep. A load shift of at least 2 days that moves at least 10% of load (19 of the 35; 8 load shifts of at least 2 days have no recorded share of load).
  • Confirmed. An alarm with at least one opposite step at a metered neighbour.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Verdict: not supported. L3 matches 14 of 35, below the bar of 18, and at 7.5 alarms per match, above 6.5. The harm bar holds.
  • Positive control reproduced. L0 recomputed from experiment 227's stored scores matches 21 of 35 at 5.0 alarms per match, and its harm on odd months is -0.015, as in experiment 227's odd-month figure (its all-month figure is -0.007).
  • Arms, all 35 load shifts (alarms are the mean over folds, over 15 Primaries and 61.8 Primary-years):
Arm Matched Alarms Alarms per match MW-weighted recall L0 labelled, even months 21 105.0 5.0 0.707 L1 labelled, odd months 20 101.0 5.0 0.662 L2 label-free negatives 13 105.0 8.1 0.413 L3 + per-Primary rate 14 104.7 7.5 0.444 L3 at 2 per Primary-year 14 123.0 8.8 0.444 L3 at 5 per Primary-year 18 311.0 17.3 0.537
  • Decisive contrast and its parts (pairs resampled, 95% interval). L3 minus L1: -6 matches (-10.0 to -2.6; lost 7, gained 1). L2 minus L1 (the negatives): -7 (-10.9 to -2.8). L3 minus L2 (the threshold): +1 (0.0 to +2.6). L1 minus L0 (months swapped): -1 (-5.5 to +3.3). The decision rule asked for L3 within 3 matches of L1, and L3 is 6 below.
  • Long-and-deep load shifts (primary stratum, 19). L0 12 (8.8 alarms per match), L1 10 (10.1), L2 8 (13.1), L3 8 (13.1), L3 at 5 per Primary-year 10 (31.1). L3 minus L1 is -2 (-5.6 to 0.0). MW-weighted recall in this stratum is 0.724 for L0, 0.634 for L1, and 0.469 for L3.
  • Neighbour-confirmed alarms. L0 9 of 35 (4.8 alarms per match), L1 11 (4.8), L2 7 (5.9), L3 7 (5.6). In the long-and-deep stratum L1 finds 7 of 19 and L3 6. Confirmed alarms lose fewer matches from label-free training (L1 minus L3 is 4 against 6) but match half as many load shifts.
  • Alarm rates (merged alarms per Primary-year). The overall rate is 1.7 for L0, 1.6 for L1, 1.7 for L2, and 1.7 for L3: the labelled budget of 20 is about 1.7 alarms per Primary-year, a third of the 5 per Primary-year chosen before the run. The number of Primaries within a factor of 2 of the median rate is 7 of 15 for L0 and L1, 8 for L2, and 11 for L3, L3_2, and L3_5. The per-Primary rule moves D10 from 2.4 (L2) to 4.5 (L3) alarms per Primary-year and D2 from 0.15 to 1.4. Leave-one-Primary-out predictions of RO-NC's rate run from 1.35 (D12) to 16.3 (D18).
  • Injected load shifts of held-out pairs (even months, 1,009 load shifts; start and end found). L1 0.248, L2 0.274, L3 0.270, L3 at 2 per Primary-year 0.272, L3 at 5 per Primary-year 0.289. Experiment 195's stored re-ranker (budget 80, odd-month injections, 998 load shifts) found 0.265. The label-free arms find at least as many injected load shifts as L1 and fewer real ones, so injected recall again cannot rank the arms (experiment 195 found the same).
  • Ordinary-day harm (arm minus no mask, 6 Primaries, whole-month 95% intervals, months the arm did not train on). L0 -0.015 (-0.078 to +0.021, 13 odd months), L1 +0.006 (-0.010 to +0.024, 14 even months), L2 +0.009 (-0.006 to +0.024), L3 +0.017 (-0.006 to +0.043), L3 at 2 per Primary-year +0.019 (-0.004 to +0.045), L3 at 5 per Primary-year +0.029 (-0.005 to +0.068). All point estimates are inside +/-0.05. The 95% intervals of L0 to L3 and L3 at 2 per Primary-year are inside it too; the interval of L3 at 5 per Primary-year (to +0.068) is not. Paired on the same months: L3 minus L1 +0.012 (-0.017 to +0.041), L2 minus L1 +0.003 (-0.019 to +0.024), L3 minus L2 +0.008 (-0.005 to +0.029).
  • Label contamination of L2's training negatives. Of 913 odd-month RO-NC candidates, 364 lie inside a logged or labelled span, 93 inside a D8 drop, and 2 on a block day (416, or 45.6%, in any of the three). Of the 15 logged load shifts that start in an odd month, 12 have a real candidate at the onset that L2 trains as a negative and L1 drops.
  • Forecast and training schedule. Harm uses experiment 227's harness unchanged: Kalman filter correction on cached daily 09:00 UTC forecasts, readings set missing inside known alarms, alarms known 192 half-hours after the step. The re-rankers train on 40 worlds of 200 injected load shifts, three seeds, early stopping on 8 validation worlds. No demand model is refitted.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Audit triggers. Trigger 1: no control failed (L0 reproduces 21 of 35, 5.0 alarms per match, and harm -0.015 on odd months). Trigger 2: the failure of the prediction is explained by a tested split of matches by whether the load shift starts in a training month (post hoc; 15 and 20 load shifts). Trigger 3: the mean-forecast absolute-error contrast against no mask agrees in sign with the quantile-score harm for L1 (+0.014 against +0.006), L3 (+0.003 against +0.017), and L3_5, and disagrees for L2 (-0.005 against +0.009), where both are inside 0.01 points and inside the intervals. Trigger 4: leaving out any one Primary keeps L3's harm between +0.011 and +0.022 and L1's between +0.001 and +0.007. Trigger 5: L2 finds more injected load shifts than L1 (0.274 against 0.248) while matching fewer real ones, a pattern that this page reads as injected recall failing to rank arms. Triggers 6 and 7 do not apply. No Opus audit was run: the verdict rests on a count of matches, which the L0 control reproduces exactly.
  • Median minus mean forecast for L3 (megawatts, per Primary). D5 -0.177, D9 -0.017, D10 -0.057, D11 -0.025, D14 +0.044, D16 +0.026.
  • Tail calibration and curtailment cost are not reported: the harm harness stores no quantile predictions beyond the mean quantile score, and this experiment tests an alarm source, not a forecast.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The odd and even month split is post hoc and small, and the threshold may add to it. L2 and L3 set their alarm count on scores over the whole record, and in the training months those scores are in-sample, so the shared alarm count falls mostly on the months the score never saw. It uses 15 and 20 load shifts. The pre-registered contrast is on all 35.
  • Matches are scored in every month, as in experiment 195, so every arm is partly in-sample in the months it trained on. L1's thresholds use even-month labels, L0's use odd-month labels.
  • Label uses that remain. The demand model behind the residuals was trained with the labelled load shifts masked. The injector is fitted on the 66 labelled load shifts, the logged closures, and D8's drops (leaving out the held-out fold's pairs), and places positives only in stretches with no logged or labelled event within 7 days. Version 2 could not copy either step without labels. Experiment 212's unmasked fits cover 5 of the 15 Primaries and a 15-series residual panel is not stored, so L4 (the unmasked demand model) was not run.
  • Pins use one labelled number. L2 and L3 take their alarm count from L0. L3 at 2 and 5 alarms per Primary-year do not. L3 at 2 per Primary-year was added to the plan before any match was counted, to bracket L0's 1.7.
  • The per-Primary rule predicts RO-NC's rate, not the learned score's, and RO-NC's threshold of 4.35 noise units was tuned on labels in experiment 130.
  • Folds share Primaries. A Primary of a held-out pair can sit in another fold's training pair, as in experiment 195.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Re-run the comparison on months the score never trained on, with L1 and L2 trained on a block of months and every load shift scored in later months. Twenty load shifts cannot separate a difference of one or two matches, so the test needs the other Primaries' logged load shifts or a longer record.
  • Test a negative-cleaning rule that needs no log. Logged or labelled spans hold 364 of L2's 913 negatives. Dropping negatives that sit within 4 days of a high-scoring candidate is one rule to try, scored on months the score never trained on.
  • Keep the per-Primary alarm rate unchanged for now: the per-Primary rate loses no matches and brings more Primaries within a factor of 2 of the median alarm rate (11 of 15), and its harm is inside the limit.

Code: ml-experiments/00302-lsc-learned-score-without-nged-labels/; the printed numbers are in printed_score.txt, printed_inj.txt, printed_report.txt, and printed_checks.txt in that folder.

docs.title: Does a small neural correction of the wind speed beat XGBoost plus a lookup table of offsets when the weather is the 51-member ensemble forecast?
docs.text:
Take-home: a small neural correction of the wind speed, fitted to ERA5 (the weather estimate used for training) and run on the 51 ensemble members, matches XGBoost plus a lookup table of offsets, and fitting the correction on the ensemble hindcast made it worse. The hindcast is 442 daily ensemble forecasts issued from April 2024 to June 2025; the scored year runs from July 2025 to June 2026. Scores are quantile scores (an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score) in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity); lower is better, and a negative difference means the first arm is better. With the offset table of experiment 259 on top, the adapter fitted to ERA5 (P3) scored 0.09 points better than XGBoost plus the table (P1; 95% interval -0.17 to -0.02). Fine-tuning the adapter on the hindcast (P5) scored 0.95 points worse than P1 (0.60 to 1.32). A repair chosen after seeing the results, which stops the ensemble spread being counted twice, cut that gap to 0.21 points (-0.05 to 0.49), so the adapter is still no better than XGBoost plus the table. Both the mean wind speed and the mean observed power were higher in the scored year than in the hindcast year, which may be why a correction fitted to the hindcast does not carry over; we did not test that.

We asked whether the small neural adapter of experiment 285, which scored better than XGBoost with ERA5 as the weather, also wins on the production weather input, the ensemble forecast, in the scored year. The adapter scales and shifts the wind speed that the physics model of a wind farm reads. We fitted it to ERA5, ran it on every member, mixed the 51 members with equal weights, and added experiment 259's offset table. We also fitted it directly to the ensemble hindcast. The 3 metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3) are scored on 53 Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026. Verdict partly supported: the decision rule (P5 beats P1 by at least 0.10) failed, and its fallback (P8 or P5 beats P1 by under 0.10, with an interval below zero) held for P8.

docs.title: Arms and rows
docs.text:
• Arms (all on the 51 members, then the spread factor of experiment 33). P0 is XGBoost trained on ERA5 before 2024-04-01, and P1 is P0 plus experiment 259's offset table (both read from experiment 285; this folder's code reproduces them exactly). P2 is the adapter (inputs: wind direction, the 10 m to 100 m speed ratio, 2 m temperature, hour of day) fitted to ERA5; P3 is P2 plus the table. P4 fits the whole physics model and an adapter on the hindcast alone, and P5 fine-tunes P2 on the hindcast; the P4 and P5 adapters also see the lead day and the members' standard deviation of the 100 m speed. P7 is P5 with an adapter that sees the 100 m speed only. P8 is XGBoost with the adapter's effective speed as an extra column, plus the table. P6 is P2 plus experiment 259's neural head (a small neural network that outputs 11 quantile offsets).
  • Cross-fit. P4, P5, and P7 take their hindcast predictions from models fitted without the held-out third of the hindcast runs (purged for overlapping valid times), so the spread factor and the residual quantiles never see an in-sample prediction. The scored predictions come from a model fitted to the whole hindcast, stopping on its last 90 days.
  • Post hoc arms (added after the results, so not pre-registered). P4m, P5m, and P7m use a loss on the members' mean power. The Sonnet audit found that the fine-tuned arms count the ensemble spread twice: the residual quantiles are fitted to the case-mean forecast (the forecast from the members' mean power) and applied to each member before mixing. That worsened P5's score by 0.39 points at W1 in the auditor's re-run of one seed. P4c, P5c, and P7c repair the double counting by applying the case-mean residual quantiles to the members' mean power and not mixing members.
  • Rows. A row is one farm, seed, run, and valid time. The rows are experiment 33's 53 Tuesday runs, 3 seeds, and 3 farms; "kept" rows (96,479 of 107,121) are those outside experiment 210's idle-band mask (the half-hours when a farm is idle). Intervals resample whole months of the run date and the three seeds (50,000 resamples); farms are not resampled. Eight contrasts were planned, so the Bonferroni level is 99.375%; the 95% intervals the brief asks for are quoted below, and the planned contrasts' Bonferroni intervals are in work/score.json.
  • Weather at lag times. The adapters and XGBoost read the ensemble's own wind, temperature, and hour of day at forecast time; ERA5 is used only to fit models before 2024-04-01, so no lagged past weather is read at forecast time.

docs.title: Planned contrasts (kept rows, points of capacity, first minus second; negative means the first arm is better)
docs.text:
• C1, P2 minus P0: -0.091 (-0.167 to -0.017). Predicted -0.05 to -0.2. Held.
  • C2, P3 minus P1: -0.090 (-0.166 to -0.015). Predicted a gain smaller than 0.1 points. Held: the table takes most of the gain.
  • C3, P5 minus P3: +1.044 (0.721 to 1.365). Predicted at most -0.05. Failed in the opposite direction.
  • C4, P4 minus P5: -0.266 (-0.361 to -0.188). Predicted positive (P4 worse). Failed: training from scratch scored better than fine-tuning.
  • C5, P6 minus P3: -0.159 (-0.283 to -0.041) on the quantile score, +0.005 (-0.037 to 0.043) at the 0.99 pinball loss. Predicted a 0.99 pinball loss at least 10% lower and a score no worse than +0.1. Held on the score (the head helped the middle of the distribution: median error 15.75 against 16.01) and failed at the tail.
  • C6, P8 minus P3: -0.010 (-0.034 to 0.014). Predicted at least as good. Held (a tie).
  • C7, share of the P3-to-P5 gap that P7 closes: 0.91 (0.77 to 1.06). Predicted under a third. Failed: the blind adapter did as badly as P5, so the extra inputs gave the fine-tuned arm nothing.
  • C8, P5 minus P1: +0.954 (0.599 to 1.324). The decision-rule contrast. Failed.

docs.title: Scores and tail calibration (kept rows unless stated)
docs.text:
• P6 had the lowest score of the pre-registered arms, 11.104, which is 0.248 points better than P1 (95% interval -0.380 to -0.112). It is not the headline, because P6 adds a second neural network (the head), its 5% to 95% coverage is the lowest of any arm (88.5%), and the 0.99 pinball loss did not improve (C5). Experiment 259 found that a table of offsets recovers most of what the head gains.

P5c minus P3 is +0.301 (0.071 to 0.539), P5c minus P1 is +0.212 (-0.049 to 0.493), and P5c minus P2 is -0.043 (-0.282 to 0.219): once the double counting is repaired, fine-tuning on the hindcast adds nothing over the ERA5 adapter, and the blind P7c scores 0.171 better than P5c (0.007 to 0.342), so the adapter's extra inputs add nothing.

Only the turbine count and rating from the Renewable Energy Planning Database would be known for such a farm; the adapter above was not given them.
  • Curtailment cost. Not scored: no arm's output was run through studies.node_curtailment because the metric scores a node with its generators and not three farms alone.

docs.title: Checks and the audit
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast (kept rows, pooled over the farms, points of capacity): P0 -4.97, P1 -4.81, P2 -4.82, P3 -4.71, P5c -4.61, P6 -3.91, P8 -4.72. The offset table moves the median by about 0.1 to 0.2 points, as experiment 259 found.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile contrast (C2, C3, C5, C6). The mean-forecast absolute error moves the same way as the score in C2 (-0.116), C3 (+0.888), and C6 (-0.006), and in the opposite direction in C5 (+0.133 against a score change of -0.159), because the head lowers the median's error (-0.258) and not the mean's.
  • Audit triggers fired: the blind control P7 scored no worse than P5, C3 and C4 contradicted the prediction, and P4 beat P5, which starts from more. A fresh Sonnet agent audited the code and the results; the maintainer asked for Sonnet only, so no Opus audit ran. Its findings and their triage:
    • The member mixture counts the ensemble spread twice for P4, P5, and P7. Accepted. The auditor's re-run of one P5 seed at W1 scored 11.72 with the mixture and 11.33 with the case-mean quantiles (not stored). The stored W1 scores are 11.707 for P5, 11.305 for P5m, and 10.833 for P5c. The repaired arms P4c, P5c, and P7c are post hoc, and the table above shows they do not change the conclusion.
    • The hindcast year differs from the scored year. Accepted. The shift table below (work/shift.json, from e00303_shift.py) shows that the mean observed fraction of capacity and the ensemble-mean speed both rose.
    • No mismatch between the hindcast and scored adapter inputs, and early stopping on one spring season is not the cause. No change.
    • P5 has two extra inputs that P2 lacks (lead day and spread), so C3 mixes the inputs with fine-tuning. Accepted as a caveat. P7, which has none of them, scored the same as P5 (C7).
    • P6's base was chosen from P2, P4, and P5 on their hindcast scores (P3 is P2 plus the table the head replaces). Accepted as designed. The hindcast scores of P4 and P5 are slightly in sample for the residual quantiles, and P2 won regardless.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Fit the correction to many years of ERA5 and to the ensemble hindcast together, with an indicator saying whether each row is ERA5 or ensemble data, so the correction does not depend on one year's relation between speed and power.
  • Find the reason the scored year had higher mean speed and mean power (turbine availability, a change of ensemble model cycle, or ERA5 drift) before trusting a one-year fit.
  • Give XGBoost the effective speed (P8) if the small gain of 0.099 points is wanted. It needs no second training stage, and the threshold for porting a change that adds a neural network is 0.10 points, so the gain falls just below it.

docs.title: How wide is the tail of the summed output of the solar farms under one bulk supply point?
docs.text:
Summing the 51 members of the weather forecast farm by farm gives a band for the three farms' total output that is almost as wide as adding the farms' quantiles, and both bands are too wide. A band from a Gaussian copula with a correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months comes closest to the stated probability. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F on this page. They sit beneath two bulk supply points (132 kV to 33 kV substations), which this page calls nodes: farms A, C, and E beneath node 1, and farms B, D, and F beneath node 2. Curtailment acts at a node, so the tail of the three farms' summed output matters more than each farm's own tail. The weather forecast is the 00 UTC run of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble, which has 51 members.

Each farm has a band of 11 quantiles of its output in MW, at levels 0.01 to 0.99, 12 to 36 hours ahead. Three sources of that band come from earlier experiments, and this page calls each source an arm. "P2" is the solar-farm power model whose band is binned by the forecast and the ensemble spread (experiment 270). "Blend" is the per-quantile blend of an additive model, a mixture-density neural network, and XGBoost (experiment 287). "XGBoost" is XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016) alone, also from experiment 287. For each arm we formed the node's band four ways, which this page calls sum methods. Method (a) adds the three farms' quantiles at the same level. Method (b) draws each farm's quantile level independently at random and sums the three values. Method (c) runs each of the 51 members through the three farms' forecasts, sums the three outputs for each member, and reads the quantiles off the 51 sums. Method (d) draws the three farms' quantile levels from a Gaussian copula, a distribution that keeps each farm's own band and sets how closely the farms' errors move together, with its correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months. We then measured coverage: the share of half-hours in which the observed total output of the three farms was at or below a quantile of the node's band. A 0.95 quantile is correct when its coverage is 95%.

Verdict: not supported. The prediction was that the coverage of (c) lands within 0.5 percentage points of the stated probability at both 0.95 and 0.99. At 0.95 it does not for any arm. At 0.99 it holds for P2 only. Method (b) is too narrow, as predicted, for every arm. Method (a) is above 99.5% at 0.99 for the blend and XGBoost but not for P2, so that part of the prediction held for two of the three arms. The table gives coverage pooled over both nodes, as a percentage of half-hours, with the 98.75% interval from resampling whole months in brackets for (c) and (d).

Arm Level (a) add quantiles (b) independent (c) members (d) fitted copula P2 0.95 96.66 90.10 96.79 [95.85, 97.60] 95.84 [94.94, 96.78] P2 0.99 99.34 95.97 99.27 [98.90, 99.59] 98.90 [98.50, 99.28] Blend 0.95 97.36 90.78 97.50 [96.76, 98.14] 96.48 [95.60, 97.24] Blend 0.99 99.70 96.62 99.64 [99.42, 99.84] 99.38 [99.04, 99.67] XGBoost 0.95 97.32 92.66 97.89 [97.14, 98.53] 97.36 [96.48, 98.12] XGBoost 0.99 99.82 97.90 99.75 [99.48, 99.94] 99.56 [99.14, 99.87]

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rows. 5,569 half-hours at node 1 and 6,536 at node 2 hold all three farms (daylight, sun more than 5 degrees above the horizon, 12 to 36 hours ahead, 2025-09 to 2026-08). The stop rule (under 2,000) did not fire. Node 2 holds a farm of 1.19 MW beside farms of 6.03 and 7.80 MW.
  • Why (c) is as wide as (a) (tested explanation). The ensemble's ranks imply a mean correlation of 0.95 to 0.97 between the node's farms in every clear-sky band, while the farms' forecast errors correlate 0.54 to 0.78 (Figure 2; blend arm). Summing members therefore treats the three farms as nearly one farm, which is the perfect dependence that (a) assumes. The control agrees: shuffling the members across days (breaking the dependence) gives 90.02% at 0.95 and 95.35% at 0.99 for P2, close to the independent form (b).
  • The fitted copula (d) is the closest form. Coverage of (d) at 0.95 is 95.84% for P2 (94.94% to 96.78%), 96.48% for the blend (95.60% to 97.24%), and 97.36% for XGBoost (96.48% to 98.12%). At 0.99 it is 98.90% (P2), 99.38% (blend), and 99.56% (XGBoost). (d) scores lower pinball loss at 0.99 than (c) for the blend by 6.5% (interval -0.0070 to -0.0020 MW per half-hour, excluding zero) and for XGBoost by 15.6% (-0.0214 to -0.0122), and by 1.6% for P2 (-0.0034 to +0.0011, includes zero).
  • Lower tail. At the 0.01 quantile the forms cover 0.3% (a), 5.5% to 5.9% (b), 0.4% to 0.5% (c), and 1.0% to 1.2% (d) of half-hours, against 1.0% intended. The sum of quantiles (a) and the member-wise sum (c) are far too wide below, as above.
  • Planned contrasts on pinball loss at 0.99 (MW per half-hour, 98.75% intervals). (c) minus (a): P2 -0.0002 (-0.3%, -0.0009 to +0.0010), blend -0.0004 (-0.6%, -0.0011 to +0.0007), so the two forms score alike; for XGBoost -0.0037 (-3.5%, -0.0045 to -0.0027). (c) minus (b): P2 -0.0268 (-27.2%, -0.0421 to -0.0107) and blend -0.0162 (-19.2%, -0.0306 to -0.0032), lower because the independent band is too narrow; for XGBoost +0.0116 (+12.5%, -0.0070 to +0.0304, includes zero).
  • Both nodes agree. Coverage of (c) at 0.95 is 97.0% and 96.6% (P2), 97.7% and 97.4% (blend), and 98.0% and 97.8% (XGBoost), at node 1 and node 2. The order of the forms is the same at both nodes, except that XGBoost's (a) and (d) swap places at 0.95 (97.45% against 97.65% at node 1, 97.22% against 97.12% at node 2).
  • Residual correlations (blend arm, pairs of farms beneath one node, all bands): 0.45 to 0.83 at node 1 and 0.64 to 0.68 at node 2. Correlation is higher under overcast skies (0.68 to 0.95) than under clear skies (0.33 to 0.78), and the all-band correlations differ by at most 0.08 between 12 to 24 and 24 to 36 hours ahead (within one clear-sky band the gap reaches 0.19 for one pair).
  • One-farm control (blend arm, a farm's own band): the 0.95 quantile covers 94.6% to 97.3% and the 0.99 quantile 98.8% to 99.6% of half-hours, so each farm's own band already over-covers, and every sum inherits that. The 0.01 quantile of the 1.19 MW farm D covers 12.1% and that of the 17.6 MW farm E covers 5.6%, both too narrow below. Farm D's small share keeps its excess from reaching node 2's sum. Farm E's large share may add to the lower tail at node 1.
  • Curtailment cost not scored. The event census of experiment 255 holds 5 half-hours beyond 0.75 times each node's maximum export and 2 beyond 0.9, under the 20 the plan required, so the coverage result stands alone.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per farm (blend arm, mean taken as the average of the stored quantiles weighted by level spacing, MW): A -0.018, C +0.012, E +0.103, B +0.030, D +0.004, F +0.030, against capacities of 5.96, 7.88, 17.6, 7.80, 1.19, and 6.03 MW. The largest is 0.6% of capacity, so the shape of the band barely moves the median forecast.
  • Error of the median forecast beside the pinball contrasts. The mean absolute error of the sum's median is 2.088 (a), 2.079 (b), 2.090 (c), and 2.078 (d) MW for P2, with overlapping intervals, so the contrasts on the tail do not come from a shifted median.
  • Audit triggers. Audit trigger 2 (a result that contradicts its prediction) applied once: (c) over-covers. The comparison of correlations in Results (Figure 2) tests the explanation, so no audit ran. Triggers 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 did not apply: the shuffled-members control behaves as a control should, the quantile and median errors do not disagree, neither node flips a verdict, no nested arm beats its container, there is no sister experiment on the same rows, and no later experiment depends on this result yet.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The copula (d) used future months. Its correlation for each month comes from the other 11 scored months, because the stored predictions cover only the scored year. A production copula would use earlier months only.
  • (d) does not use the ensemble. Method (d) is a Gaussian copula whose correlation is fitted by clear-sky band, and the ensemble's ranks play no part in it.
  • Two nodes and six farms. The intervals resample 12 months. The two nodes share the same weather forecasts, so the nodes are not independent evidence.
  • Each farm's own band. The bands come from experiments 270 and 287 at seed 0, trained on each farm's own earlier months. No refits ran, so the retraining schedule is the one those experiments used.
  • No lookahead in the weather forecast. The ensemble members are from the 00 UTC run, available before the forecast is used. No past-weather data enters.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a copula with correlation fitted on earlier months only keep its coverage within 1 percentage point of the stated probability at 0.95 and 0.99 on months it has not seen?
  • Does recalibrating each farm's own band, which over-covers slightly, bring the sum closer to the stated probability than the choice of copula does?

docs.title: Is the production-style XGBoost forecast better in April to June because of interactions between its inputs, or because of one input on its own?
docs.text:
Take-home: BG2 does not beat arm D at D5 and D9 in April to June through interactions of sunshine with temperature or with recent power. Forbidding them removes 2.7% of its advantage on the half-hours where arm D trails most, and 16% on all daylight half-hours. A refit allowed no interactions at all keeps 92% of the advantage on the worst half-hours but only 45% on all daylight half-hours. The result rules out the two planned interactions, and narrows the worst half-hours to arm D's single-input terms. Verdict: refuted.

BG2 is the production-style forecast, an XGBoost model per substation (experiment 87). Arm D is the convex best-guess demand model, which adds its terms up (an additive model); D5 and D9 are two anonymised Primary substations where arm D trails BG2 in April to June. We asked whether BG2 does better because XGBoost combines inputs, which an additive model cannot do. BG2's fitted models are not stored, so we refitted its recipe on CPU (one refit each for April, May, and June 2026, on the control ensemble member only). We then refitted it again with XGBoost forbidden from combining certain input families, and measured how much of the gap to arm D each ban removes. The gap is the quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in percentage points of effective capacity; smaller is better). The refit follows experiment 87's recipe, and the ban uses XGBoost's interaction_constraints.

The rows are the 6,755 half-hours where arm D trails stored BG2 most. They are the quarter of each substation's daylight half-hours (09:00 UTC runs of April to June 2026, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, experiment 266's row set) where arm D's quantile score exceeds stored BG2's by the most. The "share removed" S is (score with the ban - score of the unrestricted refit) / (score of arm D - score of the unrestricted refit). Intervals resample the 14 ISO weeks of forecast initialisation. The refits were monthly, so the contrast could shift slightly under weekly retraining. The five input families are solar (shortwave radiation, solar zenith, solar azimuth), temperature (air temperature, dew point), the three recent-power lags, the calendar (hour, day of week, lockdown flag, days to Christmas, lead time), and other weather (longwave radiation, pressure, precipitation, wind speed).

Figure 1 shows each ban's share removed, with placebos. Figure 2 shows each arm's score. Figure 3 shows how much the refit relies on each input family.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Gate (planned prediction P0) passed. The refit's median error on all April-to-June daylight half-hours is 6.91 at D5 and 5.59 at D9, against 6.69 and 5.47 for stored BG2 (3.4% and 2.3% higher), and arm D's is 8.90 and 6.69. The refit is a close but not identical copy of BG2, which blends five XGBoost models over 51 ensemble members.
  • Headline (P1) refuted. Banning both solar-by-temperature and solar-by-lags interactions removes S = 0.027 (95% interval 0.005 to 0.050) at D5 and D9 together. The plan required at least 0.5. Quantile scores: arm D 8.67, stored BG2 3.77, unrestricted refit 3.72, refit with both bans 3.86.
  • By substation. S is 0.024 at D5 (-0.002 to 0.051) and 0.030 at D9 (-0.010 to 0.087).
  • Single bans (P2) failed. Solar-by-lags alone removes 0.027 (0.005 to 0.048) and solar-by-temperature alone removes 0.002 (-0.004 to 0.010), against the 0.25 predicted for each.
  • Placebos (P3) held for the planned bans. D10 and D16 are substations where the gap to BG2 has another source. S is 0.018 at D10 (-0.022 to 0.051) and 0.044 at D16 (0.004 to 0.092), under 0.25.
  • Shapley and shuffling (P4) held. The solar family has the largest mean absolute Shapley value of the median forecast (0.142 points, against 0.066 for the lags, 0.018 calendar, 0.011 temperature, 0.008 other weather). The largest Shapley interaction is solar-by-lags (0.035, then solar-by-calendar 0.022). Banning that interaction removes under 3% of the advantage, so BG2 uses the interaction but arm D does not lose to BG2 for lack of it. Shuffling the solar family adds 1.62 quantile score points per half-hour, the calendar 0.46, the lags 0.45, other weather 0.23, and temperature 0.01.
  • Post hoc: an XGBoost refit that may use no interaction. Depth-1 trees (2,000 rounds) remove S = 0.084 (0.047 to 0.128) at D5 and D9 together, 0.052 at D5 and 0.128 at D9 (0.053 to 0.254). So 92% of the advantage on these rows needs no interaction. At D10 the same refit removes S = 0.226 (0.148 to 0.304) of a small gap, a hint that interactions matter more where arm D and BG2 are close. The hint is weak, because the absolute loss added at D10 (0.61) is close to D9's (0.52). This refit was run after the headline to explain a prediction that failed.
  • Sensitivity: all daylight rows at D5 and D9 (27,015 half-hours). The selection uses stored BG2's realised loss, so we also scored every daylight half-hour, where arm D scores 4.37 and the unrestricted refit 3.47. Both bans together remove S = 0.155 (0.091 to 0.252), solar-by-lags alone 0.167 (0.107 to 0.260), solar-by-temperature alone -0.001 (-0.019 to 0.016), and the refit that may use no interaction 0.547 (0.340 to 0.934). The planned bans stay under the 0.5 threshold on both row sets, so the refutation holds. The no-interaction refit does not: on typical rows about half of the advantage needs an interaction that the bans leave free (solar-by-calendar, solar-by-lead-time, or interactions inside the solar family). This sensitivity was added after the code review raised the selection effect.
  • No decomposition against arm D's own terms. The additive model's term contributions are not stored, so the comparison rests on the forecasts. The correlation between BG2's median minus arm D's median and each family's Shapley sum lies between -0.13 and 0.00, so no single family explains the difference row by row.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable, because the refit is one control member with quantile outputs and has no mean forecast.
  • Median-error contrasts and quantile-score contrasts: on the selected rows the median error is 15.55 for arm D, 6.80 for stored BG2, 6.70 for the unrestricted refit, 6.98 with both bans, and 7.29 with no interaction. The solar-by-temperature ban alone is the exception: its median error (6.69) is 0.01 below the unrestricted refit's while its quantile score is 0.01 above, a difference inside the noise of S = 0.002.
  • Triggers fired: trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction). The explanation tested is the post hoc refit above, which supports the refuted verdict, so no Opus audit was run. Leaving D5 out leaves S = 0.030 at D9 and leaving D9 out leaves S = 0.024 at D5 (both bans), so trigger 4 did not fire. The placebos stayed under their predicted bound, so trigger 1 did not fire.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• The bans leave solar-by-calendar, solar-by-lead-time, and interactions inside the solar family free, so what is refuted is an interaction between sunshine and temperature or recent power. The post hoc refit covers every interaction.
  • The rows are the quarter where arm D trails most, so the 92% describes those half-hours; on all April-to-June daylight half-hours the figure is 45%, with a wide interval (7% to 66%).
  • BG2's fitted models are not stored, so these are monthly refits of its recipe on the control member only.
  • Next, refit with the solar family, the lags, and the calendar dropped in turn, to say which main effect carries the advantage. Then re-run experiments 3 and 5 of the sunny-daylight fix design (private brief dp_sunny_daylight_fix_design.md) over April-to-June rows.
  • Compute: 69 CPU refits of about 6 minutes each on 2 threads, and no GPU.

docs.title: Does letting the solar term interact with temperature and day type close the April-to-June gap to BG2?
docs.text:
Letting rooftop solar interact with temperature and with the day of the week does not close the April-to-June gap to BG2. BG2 is the production-style XGBoost forecast of experiment 87. In April to June, on daylight half-hours up to 36 hours ahead, our convex demand model scores worse than BG2 at two anonymised Primary substations, D5 and D9. That score difference is the gap. The convex model is experiment 136's arm A2, a monthly refit of experiment 114's T-all model (a model that is linear in its coefficients) with a Kalman filter that corrects the forecast using recent errors. We added two columns that let the solar term vary: the solar shape times a heating hinge (how far the temperature falls below 15.5 degrees Celsius, divided by 10), and the solar shape times a weekend indicator. At D5 and D9 averaged, the two columns closed -0.4% of the gap (95% interval -6.3% to +4.7%), which is none of it. Two linear interaction columns therefore do not explain the gap. The next test is what BG2 uses that the convex demand model does not.

The scores are quantile scores on the 561,207 rows of experiments 228, 251, 266, and 289. A row is one substation, one forecast initialisation time, and one half-hour being forecast (valid time). The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of a substation's rated demand), and lower is better. "Excess" is the control's score minus BG2's, and "closure" is the share of the excess that an arm removes. Rows are daylight half-hours up to 36 hours ahead, as in experiment 289, and intervals resample whole ISO weeks of forecast initialisation time (14 weeks in April to June). The control is experiment 136's stored A2 fits run through this folder's forecast pipeline. The pipeline reproduces A2's stored quantiles to 0.0 points.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Verdict refuted. Prediction P1 (closure of at least 30% at each of D5 and D9) fails: closure is +4.7% at D5 (95% interval +1.6% to +7.7%) and -12.7% at D9 (-39.3% to +1.9%). The D5-and-D9 average of -0.4% is under the 10% threshold below which the decision rule refutes the hypothesis.
  • P2 fails. At D10 and D16 the both-column arm worsens the score by 0.068 points (95% interval 0.020 to 0.126 points worse), more than the 0.02 allowed.
  • P3 holds. July to September at D5 and D9 moves by +0.005 points (interval -0.023 to +0.033).
  • P4 holds. The placebo column (solar shape times day-of-year parity) closes +2.1% (interval -0.6% to +5.7%) at D5 and D9.
  • Excess of the control, April to June. D5 +1.354 (95% interval +1.032 to +1.652); D9 +0.555 (+0.336 to +0.780); D5 and D9 averaged +0.954 (+0.723 to +1.172). BG2 scores 3.419 at D5 and 2.762 at D9; the control scores 4.772 and 3.317.
  • Reduction against the control (points of quantile score; positive is better), D5 and D9 averaged. Both columns -0.003 (-0.058 to +0.046); heating only -0.037 (-0.070 to -0.008); weekend only +0.043 (-0.000 to +0.089); placebo +0.020 (-0.005 to +0.048). At D5 alone the weekend column lowers the score by 0.065 (+0.021 to +0.104), and the placebo column lowers the score by 0.019 (-0.025 to +0.064).
  • Clear midday half-hours at D5. These are the 643 half-hours in April to June, daylight, up to 36 hours ahead, with a realised clear-sky index above 0.8 and hour 10 to 14 in experiment 178's rows. The control's excess is +3.50 (interval +2.65 to +4.21), larger than the +1.67 that experiment 299 found over clear half-hours at all hours of the day. The both-column arm lowers the score by 0.267 (+0.042 to +0.510), 7.6% of the control's excess. Heating alone lowers the score by 0.024 (-0.066 to +0.112).
  • Tail calibration, April to June, daylight, up to 36 hours ahead, D5 and D9 pooled (control / both-column arm). Share of actuals at or below the 0.01 quantile 1.84% / 1.82%; the 0.05 quantile 7.95% / 8.87%; the 0.95 quantile 91.0% / 91.3%; the 0.99 quantile 96.4% / 96.3%. Pinball loss at 0.01 is 0.249 / 0.244, at 0.05 0.943 / 0.935, at 0.95 1.060 / 1.066, and at 0.99 0.326 / 0.343. Both arms are too narrow in both tails: 3.6% of actuals lie above the 0.99 quantile, and 8% to 9% lie at or below the 0.05 quantile. The interaction columns do not change those shares by more than 1 percentage point.
  • Analysis added after the results were seen: stored arm D. Stored arm D (experiment 220's forecast) is a close relative of the control, not the control: their per-row scores differ by 0.51 points on average in absolute value, and the control's mean score is 0.039 points higher. Shifting stored arm D's quantiles by each arm's change in the mean forecast, as experiments 251 and 289 do, gives the same answer: the both-column arm closes +0.6% at D5 and D9 averaged, with stored arm D's excess at 0.951.
  • Fitted coefficients (report.json). The weekend column's coefficient is positive in the last monthly fit at every substation: 5 to 10 points per unit of solar shape when the column is alone, and 3 to 11 in the both-column arm. On weekends the fit therefore reduces the weight of the pinned solar subtraction (the solar output at the capacity held fixed for each fit). The placebo column's coefficient is positive too (3.1 at D5), so a part of the weekend coefficient is a correction to the solar shape that holds on every day.
  • What the figures show. The excess at D5 and D9 steps up between March and April. The interaction arms follow the control closely (figure 2), and the gain of the weekend column at D5 is too small to move the monthly curve.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site. The quantiles are the mean forecast plus a residual table with median zero, so the difference is 0.0 at every site, for the control and the both-column arm.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the score. Mean absolute error of the mean forecast, April to June, daylight, up to 36 hours ahead, in points of effective capacity, control / both-column arm: D5 8.45 / 8.33, D9 5.97 / 6.12, D10 6.51 / 6.60, D16 6.09 / 6.27. The signs agree with the score contrasts (better at D5, worse elsewhere).
  • Leaving one site out flips the sign of the both-column contrast. The closure is +4.7% at D5 alone and -12.7% at D9 alone, and both are under the 10% threshold, so the verdict does not change.
  • A nested arm beats the arm that contains it. Weekend only (+0.043) beats both columns (-0.003), because the heating column worsens D9 (heating only: -0.092, interval -0.170 to -0.027).
  • Controls. The control reproduces experiment 136's stored A2 quantiles to 0.0 points at all six substations, and the placebo closes 2.1%, under 10%, so neither control fails.

docs.title: Method and caveats
docs.text:
• Arms. Control (a2): experiment 136's stored monthly T-all fits. s_both, s_heat, s_wknd, s_placebo: T-all refitted at the same 27 monthly refit dates with the extra column or columns, free in sign, with the ridge penalty of 0.1 that the heating columns use. The columns multiply the derated unit solar shape by the mean heating hinge over the four smoothed temperatures, by the weekend indicator (Saturday, Sunday, or bank holiday), or by the day-of-year parity. The filter noise, the calibration, the spread table, and the tuning months are as in arm A2. No neural-network head, export clip, or coasting is applied.
  • Collinearity. The new columns carry a ridge penalty of 0.1, which is small beside the Gram matrix of 24 months of rows, so they are effectively unpenalised. Their coefficients are large and move with the other columns (the heating column's coefficient is -1.8 at D5 and +8.4 at D9 in the both-column arm), which may contribute to the worse scores at D9, D10, and D16.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits on a rolling 24-month window, as arm D.
  • The columns live in this experiment's copy of experiment 114's design code, not as a studies.dp_gam option. The one-averaged-hinge form and free signs are one defensible design of several. A per-smoothing-window hinge or a sign-bounded column is untested.
  • The intervals resample only 14 weeks of April to June. Only two substations, D5 and D9, show the gap.
  • The headline closure is against the control, which differs from stored arm D (see the analysis added after the results were seen).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Item 5 of the summer-gap brief (what BG2 uses that arm D does not). Two linear interaction terms did not explain the gap. Two candidates not yet tested are BG2's interactions between irradiance and recent power, and its use of the realised past.
  • A small neural interaction term (ranked suggestion, per the common brief). A learned smooth response of demand to the solar shape, temperature, and hour, inside the convex fit, with the convex arm as the comparison. The prediction that could fail: the neural term closes under 10% of the D5 and D9 excess, as the two linear terms did. A run is worth the effort only if the maintainer wants to rule out a smooth interaction of any shape.

docs.title: Which property of the ensemble's wind speed is wrong, judged against the wind that the farms' own power implies?
docs.text:
Take-home: the ensemble's low wind-power forecast is mostly a wind-speed level error, not a spread or timing error. The forecast for three metered wind farms (W1 to W3) takes each of the 51 members of the ECMWF ensemble weather forecast (separate forecast scenarios), turns each member's wind into power with a fitted physics core (a wind-speed-to-power curve fitted to ERA5, our estimate of past weather, before 2024-04-01), and mixes the 51 power forecasts. Observed power was below the mixture's median on 34.1% of kept farm half-hours, where 50% is calibrated. A kept half-hour is one that the idle-row mask of experiment 210 does not remove, and the page counts every row as one farm half-hour of one forecast run.

We ran the core's curve backwards on the observed power to get the 100 m wind speed that each farm's own output implies (the implied wind). The members are on average 1.1 m/s slower than the implied wind, 0.4 m/s at day 0 (the first forecast day) and 1.6 m/s at day 9. Multiplying every member's wind speed by one factor of 1.13, fitted on the 442 daily forecast runs of 2024-04 to 2025-06, raised the share below the median on the scored year (53 Tuesday runs, 2025-07 to 2026-06) from 34.1% to 48.6%. The core fed ERA5 wind directly (the ERA5 oracle) has 52.8%, so the factor closes 77.6% of the 18.7-percentage-point difference. Widening the spread of the members closed none of it, and shifting the members in time by up to 3 hours closed at most 5.5%.

The hypothesis said that spread and timing would carry at least half of the difference, so the verdict is not supported. It also said that the high-resolution Met Office UKV (2 km, UK model) and DWD ICON-D2 (2 km, German model) forecasts would be closer than ERA5 to the implied wind. UKV is, and ICON-D2 is about as close. The question follows experiment 261, which put 89% of the low median in the ensemble's weather, and experiment 285, whose quantile mapping of member speeds to the ERA5 speed distribution closed about 18% of the difference. The physics core is from experiment 230, and the idle-row mask from experiment 210. The forecasts and offsets they build on are from experiment 259.

The wind speed that the farms imply is a slightly better target than ERA5 for calibrating the median. On the same rows (half-hours with an implied wind), a factor fitted to ERA5 closed 68.3% (58.1% to 81.6%) of the gap and the factor fitted to the implied wind closed 77.6%. The paired difference is 1.7 percentage points of share below the median (1.6 to 1.9). Fitted on all unmasked half-hours instead, the ERA5 factor closed 55.4%, so most of the difference between 55% and 78% is the choice of rows. The quantile score gives no preference: the ERA5-fitted factor scored 11.410 and the implied-wind factor 11.439 (lower is better).

The high-resolution check gives a mixed answer. The first forecast hour of UKV (from the AWS open-data bucket, the live feed) is closer to the implied wind than ERA5 is at 7 to 14 m/s (root-mean-square error 1.29, 1.41, and 1.52 m/s against ERA5's 1.43, 1.61, and 1.74 at 7 to 9, 9 to 11, and 11 to 14 m/s). The freshest ICON-D2 value is about as close as ERA5 at 5 to 14 m/s (1.40, 1.59, and 1.72 m/s at 7 to 9, 9 to 11, and 11 to 14 m/s) and further away below 5 m/s and above 14 m/s.

docs.title: Design and results
docs.text:
• Implied wind (step 1). The core (experiment 261's R1, fitted to ERA5 before 2024-04-01) is run backwards. The rows used are farm half-hours outside experiment 210's mask and outside stretches of 48 or more half-hours below 1% of capacity, where observed power lies between 5% and 90% of the curve's plateau. These filters leave hub-height speeds of about 3 to 11.4 m/s (W1), 12.4 m/s (W2), and 15.8 m/s (W3), and 79,000 to 82,000 half-hours per farm. The share of half-hours that can be inverted is 75% at ERA5 speeds of 5 to 7 m/s, 95% to 99% at 7 to 11 m/s, 91% at 11 to 14 m/s, 60% at 14 to 18 m/s, and 42% above 18 m/s. Near the plateau the curve is almost flat, so a small power error becomes a large speed error, which adds noise at the top of the range.
  • Stop rule. The rule asked whether the implied wind differs from ERA5 by more than 1 m/s on average at the invertible bins. We read it on the overall mean, which is +0.04 m/s (84,785 half-hours, 2024-04 to 2026-06, out of sample; root-mean-square error 1.61 m/s, correlation 0.80) and +0.16 m/s in sample. Read bin by bin, the difference exceeds 1 m/s at the edges (next bullet), which selection explains. The implied-minus-ERA5 difference by farm is +0.17, +0.11, and -0.14 m/s (W1, W2, W3). By season it is -0.36 (winter), +0.29, +0.27, and -0.10 m/s (autumn). Per direction sector it ranges from -0.14 to +0.37 m/s.
  • Selection effect. Binned by ERA5 speed, the implied wind is +1.5 m/s above ERA5 at 3 to 5 m/s and 1.9 m/s below it at 14 to 18 m/s (figure 2, blue). Selecting half-hours by observed power pulls every product's bin means towards the middle. Differences between products on the same half-hours are the comparison that survives this selection.
  • Ensemble against implied wind (step 2, scored year, 79,461 farm half-hours). The ensemble mean is 1.11 m/s slower than the implied wind; ERA5 is 0.04 m/s faster. The root-mean-square error is 2.60 m/s for the ensemble and 1.56 m/s for ERA5. By lead day the ensemble-mean gap is -0.42, -0.37, -0.26, -0.69, -1.07, -0.99, -1.08, -1.27, -1.67, and -1.55 m/s (days 0 to 9). The implied wind is below the members' 10th percentile on 4.3% of half-hours and above the 90th percentile on 21.7% (10% each if calibrated). The members' mean standard deviation (the 10th-to-90th percentile range divided by 2.56) is 2.38 m/s, and the standard deviation of the implied wind about the ensemble mean is 2.35 m/s. At day 0 the members' standard deviation is 0.94 m/s against 1.61 m/s.
  • Timing. The root-mean-square error of the ensemble mean against the implied wind is 2.599 m/s at 0 h and 2.600 m/s at +0.5 h, which the changing row set between shifts does not resolve. It rises to 2.67 m/s at -3 h and 2.64 m/s at +3 h.
  • Corrections (step 3). Each factor multiplies the 10 m and 100 m speeds alike and was fitted on the 442 daily forecast runs of 2024-04 to 2025-06. One factor is 1.13 (ERA5-fitted on the same rows 1.11, on all rows 1.09). The factor per lead day runs from 1.06 at day 0 to 1.17 at day 9. The factor per direction sector (ensemble-mean direction, eight sectors of 45 degrees) is 1.09 to 1.21, largest in sectors 0 to 3. The widening factor per lead day is 2.09 at day 0, falling to 0.83 at day 9, applied to each member's deviation from the case mean. It is the standard deviation of the implied wind about the ensemble mean over the members' standard deviation, so it includes the noise of the implied wind itself and over-states the widening needed.
  • Share of kept rows below the median, scored year (95% interval). Raw 34.1% (31.5 to 37.1); one factor 48.6% (45.8 to 51.6); factor per lead day 47.1% (44.4 to 50.1); factor per direction sector 48.9% (46.1 to 51.9); spread widened 33.9% (31.3 to 37.0); lead day, direction and spread together 47.6% (44.9 to 50.8); ERA5-fitted one factor 46.8% (44.1 to 49.9) on the same rows and 44.4% (41.7 to 47.5) on all rows; ERA5-fitted per lead day 45.4% (42.7 to 48.3) and 43.3% (40.7 to 46.3); ERA5 oracle 52.8% (50.3 to 55.1). Shifts: 35.1% at -3 h, 34.7% at -2 h, 34.3% at -1 h, 34.1% at +1 h, 34.2% at +2 h, 34.3% at +3 h.
  • Percentage points of the 18.7-point gap closed. One factor 77.6% (66.4 to 92.4); per lead day 69.8% (60.1 to 82.9); per direction sector 79.0% (66.8 to 94.6); spread -0.9% (-1.4 to -0.2); all three together 72.5% (61.1 to 87.6); shifts 5.5% (-3 h), 3.3%, 1.1%, 0.2%, 0.8%, and 1.3% (+3 h); ERA5-fitted one factor 68.3% (58.1 to 81.6) on the same rows and 55.4% on all rows; ERA5-fitted per lead day 60.3% and 49.4%. The direction-sector factor against one factor is +0.3 percentage points (-0.6 to +1.4), so splitting by direction adds nothing beyond the mean-speed correction.
  • The single factor over-corrects early leads. At days 0 to 2 it gives 60.8% of rows below the median, against 46.9% for the factor per lead day (days 3 to 6: 49.0% and 46.2%; days 7 and later: 44.2% and 47.7%).
  • Quantile score (twice the mass-weighted pinball loss at the nine levels of experiment 33, points of capacity, kept rows, no spread factor). Raw 11.823; one factor 11.439; per lead day 11.361; per direction sector 11.462; spread widened 11.993; all three together 11.456; ERA5-fitted 11.410 and 11.356 on the same rows (11.402 and 11.361 on all rows); shifts 11.84 to 12.18. Widening the members and shifting them both worsen the score (raise its value).
  • By farm (share of kept rows below the median: raw, one factor, ERA5 oracle). W1 32.9%, 47.8%, 50.3%; W2 28.0%, 42.0%, 50.9%; W3 41.8%, 56.5%, 57.5%. W2 stays furthest from its oracle.
  • High-resolution check (step 4, 51,797 farm half-hours of the scored year, 46,580 kept). ICON-D2 (Open-Meteo previous-runs archive, freshest value of each hour, converted from km/h) and UKV (AWS lead 0, 100 m level) cover 2024-01 to 2026-09 and 2024-10 to 2026-10, so both cover the scored year. Share of kept rows below the core's median with each product as the weather: ERA5 52.9%, ICON-D2 41.7%, UKV lead 0 34.1%, UKV lead 2 36.2%. Quantile score on these rows: ERA5 6.19, ICON-D2 5.74, UKV lead 0 6.21. The shares are not comparable in level, because the core's hub height and shear exponent were fitted to ERA5's 10 m and 100 m speeds, and another product's 10 m to 100 m ratio changes the exponent. The comparison with the implied wind does not depend on that fit.
  • Distance to the implied wind (root-mean-square error in m/s, 38,303 half-hours, binned by the mean 100 m speed of the three products so that no product's own speed defines the bins).
Speed bin (m/s) Half-hours ERA5 ICON-D2 UKV lead 0 below 5 920 1.44 1.78 1.71 5 to 7 7,662 1.23 1.14 1.17 7 to 9 11,183 1.43 1.40 1.29 9 to 11 9,636 1.61 1.59 1.41 11 to 14 7,529 1.74 1.72 1.52 14 and above 1,373 2.60 2.74 2.28
  • Schedule. One core fit before 2024-04-01 and one set of corrections fitted before 2025-06-17, with no refits, so the contrasts say nothing about retraining cadence.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. This experiment does not store a mean forecast, so the per-farm median-minus-mean check is not repeated. Experiment 261 gives -4.7, -4.5, and -3.8 points for the raw mixture at W1, W2, and W3, and the mean of the median forecast moves from 17.7 points (raw) to 24.2 (one factor), against 29.2 for the oracle and an observed mean of 28.9 (experiment 261).
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score. Not computed. The quantile score and the share below the median rank the corrections differently: the ERA5-fitted factor has the better quantile score and the worse median than the implied-wind factor, and the per-lead-day factor has the best quantile score and closes less of the gap than the single factor.
  • Tail calibration and curtailment cost. Not run: no arm is a production candidate, and the scores here are medians and one quantile score.
  • Control. The recomputed raw mixture median equals experiment 259's stored R1 median on every kept row (largest difference 0.0000), so the refit reproduces the earlier forecasts.
  • Triggers. Trigger 2 (a result contradicting an earlier experiment's finding) fired against experiment 285. A plain factor fitted to ERA5 closes 55% to 68% of the gap where experiment 285's quantile mapping closed about 18%, and this experiment has not tested why the mapping fell short. No audit has run. No other trigger fired: the one factor raises the share by 14.9, 14.0, and 14.7 percentage points at W1, W2, and W3, and no nested arm beat its container.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The implied wind exists only where observed power is between 5% and 90% of the plateau. Hub-height speeds above about 12 to 16 m/s are not invertible (the ERA5 speed bins above 14 m/s hold rows because ERA5's 100 m speed and the hub-height speed are different axes), so the finding says nothing about the highest speeds, which matter for curtailment.
  • The implied wind inherits the core fitted to ERA5. The core's hub height absorbs ERA5's own bias, and the implied 100 m speed uses ERA5's shear and air-density factor, so the implied wind is not independent of ERA5. The result says the ensemble is slower than that effective wind, not that ERA5 or the ensemble matches the wind at the turbines.
  • The corrections are fitted on observed power and so are a calibration, not a physics fix. The fit uses only the hindcast before 2025-06-17, so the scored year is out of sample, but a factor fitted to observed power would be expected to calibrate the median.
  • The spread test is weak. The widening factor includes the implied wind's own noise, and widening members symmetrically about their mean moves a median only through the curvature of the power curve. The result says that this widening does not help the median, not that the members' spread is right: at day 0 the members' spread is well below the implied wind's.
  • Direction sectors use the ensemble-mean direction, and the 10 m and 100 m speeds are scaled together so the shear exponent is unchanged.
  • Three farms and one weather year. Intervals resample the 12 months and not the farms.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does a per-lead-day speed factor survive in the production chain? Apply it before the core and XGBoost on the same rows, score with the offset table of experiment 259 on top, and include the tail levels (0.01 and 0.99).
  • Why did experiment 285's quantile mapping fall short? Re-run its mapping next to a plain factor on identical rows, and check whether mapping to the marginal ERA5 distribution flattens the members.

docs.title: Is the gap between a no-lag forecast and a forecast with lags a detector of LSC events?
docs.text: This experiment asks whether the gap between two forecasts can find load shifts. A load shift is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand (a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV) onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The network operator NGED has no access to the system that records these operations. The two forecasts it receives from us are K0 (a Kalman filter on recent power readings, added to the generalised additive model forecast) and GAM_ONLY (the same model with no recent power, which forecasts how the network is normally switched). We turned the gap between them, and averages of recent forecast error over 6, 24, and 72 hours (observed power minus GAM_ONLY), into alarms. We set each alarm threshold on odd calendar months, using no knowledge of where shifts happened, and scored the alarms on the other months and on all months. The scoring covered the 35 real load shifts lasting longer than 1 day, 411 artificial shifts added to 44 simulated copies of the power history (experiment 141), and false alarms in ordinary rows. A row is one Primary at one 6-hourly forecast origin, and it is ordinary when no logged switching touched the substation or a neighbour in the 72 hours before. An alarm "matches" a shift when it opens from 2 hours before the onset until the shift ends. The plain gap matched 11 of 35 real shifts, the learned score LR_b20 10, and RO-NC 20 (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector), when each gap threshold reproduces the benchmark's false alarm rate on odd months. The learned score (experiment 227) re-ranks RO-NC's candidate alarms. The 24-hour mean forecast error matched 20 of 35.

docs.title: Matched real shifts (35 shifts lasting over 1 day)
docs.text:
"While on" means an alarm episode opened from 2 hours before the onset to the end of the shift. "Within 4 days" (post hoc) counts an alarm that opens up to 4 days after the shift ends, because the learned score opens its alarms about 4 days after the step. "Share of moved MW" weights each shift by its size in megawatts. "Alarms per match" is all false alarms plus matched alarms divided by matched shifts. "Lag" is the forecast origin minus the onset. The threshold of each gap row reproduces the false alarm rate named in its row on odd months (1.29 per Primary-year for the learned score, 4.11 for RO-NC, and 0.86 for the pair alarm); the last column is read on even months.
