docs.title: Curtailment cost
docs.text:
We can now score a demand forecast by the curtailment cost of its errors at a bulk supply point, but the two supply points of the pilot hold too few events to rank forecasts at the headline limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export, so no forecast has yet been shown to curtail less there.

Curtailment is the capping of generators beneath a substation when its export would pass a limit. The scoring code plans the caps from a forecast of the substation's export, then charges the energy lost to the caps plus a penalty for export that stays over the limit. Both experiments of the theme are worked examples of that code, and neither had a registered prediction. Experiment 84 ran the scoring code on 2 bulk supply points, Boston and Skegness, and experiment 83 scored the tails of the forecasts of 20 demand series (16 Primary substations, 4 supply points).

Boston and Skegness together have 19 half-hours beyond 0.9 times their earlier maximum export in the scored year, and more than 100 per node only at half that maximum. The scored year runs from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30. The figure counts export and import in separate panels, and also plots Bicker Fen, which is not scored. Source: experiment 84.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The code runs and reproduces a hand-worked answer exactly. All eight quantities of a made-up half-hour (a 45.0 MW limit and two generators) agree with the hand calculation (experiment 84). The verdict of both experiments is inconclusive, because neither registered a contrast.

The pilot cannot rank forecasts at the headline limit. Each arm is a pair of forecasts, one of the substation's export and one of its generators' output. The scaled limit is a fraction of a node's maximum export before 2025-07-02. At 0.9 times, the cost rests on 19 half-hours (all 19 scored), and no difference between arms is significant at the 5% level. At 0.75 times, with 46 half-hours (41 scored), the stack costs GBP 2,440,720 more than the best guess (95% interval 96,371 to 6,686,043). At 0.5 times, with 323 half-hours (268 scored), the best guess costs GBP 10,802,520 less than climatology (-20,880,964 to -3,342,553), and its gap to the NGED baseline includes zero. We have no evidence that NGED operates at 0.5 times, so that limit is a rehearsal (experiment 84). The costs are retrospective, from an energy proxy (generator energy cut plus 20 times the energy left over the limit, at GBP 2,000 per MWh), and are a calibration to history, not a saving.

The two arms are experiment 84's, and match the glossary entries only in part. The stack is the substation forecast fitted once and corrected from its own recent errors, with a generator forecast fitted once. The best guess (weekly retrained) is the substation forecast retrained every week with each generator forecast retrained monthly. Experiment 84 does not state whether either arm applies a half-life or the glossary's spread factor of 1.15.

The best guess (weekly retrained) has the lowest avoidable cost of the arms at all three scaled limits, but only some of its gaps are significant. Avoidable cost is an arm's cost minus the perfect forecast's cost, where the perfect forecast has every quantile equal to the metered value. The figure has one panel per scaled limit at GBP 2,000 per MWh, and shorter bars are better. Source: experiment 84.

Most of the best guess's avoidable cost at 0.9 times is breach, not unneeded cuts. Breach is export that stayed over the limit because the forecast did not order enough cuts. Of the GBP 571,823 avoidable cost, 81% is breach: the forecast ordered 13.6 MWh of cuts on event half-hours against 35.1 MWh needed. Another 20% is output cut when metered export was within the limit (experiment 84).

A forecast that fits a whole distribution can plan far more curtailment. In experiment 97, on 17 half-hours at one node (it scores the stored BG2 forecasts of node-only mode, so its count differs from experiment 84's 19), Student-t and skew-normal fits planned 911 and 1,364 MWh of curtailment against 57.5 MWh for the stored forecast, which gave avoidable costs of GBP 2.36 million and 3.12 million against 618,171. The other recalibrations were not separable from the stored forecast (experiment 97).

In an exploratory run, the stored demand forecasts of experiment 48 were too narrow in both tails. The run pooled 20 demand series, every lead, runs from 2025-07-02, and the arms best guess stack, manual_heuristic, and climatology. Coverage of the 0.05 quantile was 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile 0.891 to 0.927, and weekly retraining had the lowest pinball loss at both levels. The experiment gives no interval, and the 0.01 and 0.99 levels were not stored (experiment 83, on forecasts stored by experiment 48). For the later BG2 forecast, q05 coverage reads 0.035 at the point estimate, which is too wide a lower tail (16 Primary substations, 12 to 36 hours, about 9 months, no interval given; experiment 97).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: The only metric design implemented plans caps from the 0.95 quantile of the substation's export forecast and scores at a limit scaled from the node's earlier maximum. The generators beneath the node cut the excess in proportion to their capacity, and the cost is the energy proxy with a breach ratio of 20 (experiment 84). Experiment 84 compared the price and the DCUSA form only, and tried no other quantile, sharing rule, or breach ratio. This is a metric design, not a forecast design: no forecast design curtailed less with significance at the headline limit.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: Nothing is ready. Both experiments are not-for-production. The cost-savings roadmap describes the metric and the larger delivery that would allow a ranking (cost-savings metrics).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Score curtailment at the substation, not at a single meter. Experiment 83 first built a single-series metric and withdrew it, because the limit binds at a substation (experiment 83). Otherwise the metric scores each meter against its own history, which does not measure curtailment. Re-check if a per-meter limit becomes known.
  • Count the events before ranking. At 0.9 times the maximum only 19 half-hours qualify, and no difference is significant (experiment 84). Otherwise a ranking rests on a few half-hours. Re-check when the delivery of about 2,500 series is scored.
  • Score at a scaled limit, and show the published thermal limit as a reference. Boston's export reached its published limit once, and the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding is that NGED curtails early to keep headroom (experiment 84). Re-check if NGED confirms its operating practice (issue #1318).
  • Label every cost "calibration to history, not a saving". The perfect forecast still costs GBP 87,460 at 0.9 times, because the cap also removes output above a generator's estimated capacity (experiment 84). Otherwise a cost reads as money NGED would have saved. Re-check if the metric is validated against a real curtailment event.
  • The NGED baseline is an assumption. It is the manual heuristic's substation forecast with every generator at full capacity, from the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of NGED's practice (experiment 84). Re-check once NGED describes its practice.
  • Rank under the energy proxy and under the DCUSA form separately. Changing the price does not reorder the arms, but the DCUSA form charges every instructed generator its whole headroom, and climatology's avoidable cost becomes negative under it (experiment 84). Otherwise the choice of cost form decides the ranking unnoticed. Re-check if a different price or cost form is added.
  • Report how many generator-half-hours had no forecast. Across the six arms, 13% had none, so those generators were not capped and added to breach (experiment 84). Otherwise a forecast set with more gaps looks worse for that reason alone. Re-check with other forecast sets.
  • Report the unscored half-hours. Scoring needs a stored forecast at 12 to 36 hours lead, which drops 5 of 46 events at 0.75 times, and the dropped half-hours hold 14% of the excess energy at 0.5 times (experiment 84). Re-check if the forecast lead window or the stored forecast sets change.
  • Check the sign of each node. Boston and Skegness are inferred as import-positive, Bicker Fen's sign is unconfirmed, and Walpole's is unknown, so the metric excludes them (experiment 84). A wrong sign swaps export and import. Re-check when NGED supplies the signs.
  • Store the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles, and score tails with studies.tail_calibration. The stored sets of experiment 48 stop at 0.95, so the tail table could not be read at 0.99 (experiment 83). Later sets store 11 levels (experiment 97). Re-check if a forecast set again stores fewer levels.
  • Publish generator figures only as sums over at least 4 generators. Experiment 84 reports no generator singly, and the table joining generators to substations stays in the private data folder (experiment 84). Re-check if a node has fewer than 4 generators.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether any forecast curtails less than another with significance, once about 2,500 series are scored (the January 2027 delivery).
  • How NGED chooses its operating limit, and how it allocates caps among generators.
  • Whether the tails of the forecasts are too narrow in general: experiments 83 and 97 disagree on the lower tail, on different forecasts and periods.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Curtailment cost: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00332 lsc-curtailment-cost-of-label-free-mask Treating as missing the readings that a label-free load shift detector flags (arm A of experiment 327) lowers curtailment cost during and after load shifts, against no mask (arm C), without raising it on ordinary half-hours. not supported not-for-production Masking the load shifts that a label-free detector finds lowers curtailment cost by about a third when the forecast is judged against the normal running arrangement. Judged against the power the electricity network actually carried, which is what a curtailment instruction responds to, the mask changes cost by -3.0% with an interval from -24% to +30%, and it costs 1.3% more on ordinary half-hours. Adding the true moved megawatts to the true spans lowered cost during a shift, but adding them to the label-free mask did not, so this result cannot say what a live service needs. also relevant 00327 lsc-label-free-detect-mask-train-pipeline A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) can be trained and corrected on power with the load shifts set to missing, where a label-free detector finds the load shifts. The detector reads only how unusual the observed power is inside the predictive bands of a demand model that uses no lagged power, and no NGED switching label enters any threshold, mask, or training row. partly supported candidate A forecast of the normal running arrangement recovers faster after a load shift when the readings that a label-free detector flags are treated as missing: during and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04 points of capacity. On ordinary days the masked forecast is no worse, and slightly better. Without one site (D11) the gain shrinks to 0.30 points, and retraining the demand model on masked power adds nothing beyond masking the filter. also relevant 00326 wind-research-default-1-change-arms Each of four changes, added alone to Wind farms research default 1, lowers the quantile score on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads: (a) 2 m temperature and an air-density column as XGBoost inputs, (b) hour of day and day of year as XGBoost inputs, (c) the ERA5-trained neural adapter's effective wind speed as an extra XGBoost column, and (d) one wind-speed scale factor, fitted on the hindcast to the implied wind, applied to every member's 100 m speed before the XGBoost model. At most one is adopted, in the order c, b, a, d. supported candidate Feeding XGBoost the neural adapter's corrected wind speed lowers the wind forecast's score by 0.10 points of capacity, about 0.9% of the default's score, at 1 to 10 day leads (99.75% interval -0.19 to -0.01). The change is negative at every farm and at short and long leads. The three other changes were not separable from zero. Only a port that puts the adapter in the production service can use the gain, so the maintainer decides. also relevant 00321 metered-farm-lower-tail-recalibration-and-tail-head Metered solar farms research default 1 (the blend assembled by experiment 300, scored to 10 days by experiment 310) lets the actual output fall below its 0.01 quantile 3.3% to 3.7% of the time, and no mixture-density head tried in experiment 318 changes that. Default plus a recalibration table, a zero-inflated lower tail, or a tail-targeted head brings the share of actual values strictly below the 0.01 quantile close to 1% at leads of 1 to 10 days, without raising the quantile score and without losing experiment 318's 0.99 gain. partly supported candidate The solar-farm forecast's lowest quantile was already close to correct: only 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below the 0.01 quantile, because the earlier 3.3% counted the 3.0% of half-hours that read exactly zero. A recalibration table, a zero-inflated head, and a tail head each lower the own-history score by 0.04 points or less (the unshrunk table raises it by 0.03 to 0.05 points), so none is adopted. A shrunk recalibration table does lower the score by about 0.05 points for a farm with no history, and two heads lower the 0.99 pinball loss by 3.7% to 8.5% while covering the 0.99 quantile only 98.3% to 98.9% of the time. also relevant 00312 lsc-how-good-must-a-detector-be-against-the-band-head A load shift detector that is far from perfect can still beat the best forecast that uses no detector, so a detector need not be near-perfect to be worth building. The one detector-based arm in experiment 297 that beat that forecast was the one that subtracts the true megawatts from the readings during a shift and adds them back to the forecast. This experiment degrades that arm one axis at a time to find where it stops beating the no-detector forecast. It also asks whether the surprise of recent readings against GAM_ONLY's residual bands (band position), or perfect knowledge of a shift, added as inputs to the no-detector quantile head, improves the head. This is question 3 of the LSC decision program, redefined by the Discuss ruling of 2026-10-23. not supported not-for-production A load shift detector does not need to be near-perfect to improve on the best forecast that uses no detector: with the true megawatts added back, finding half the shifts, learning of each up to 3 days late, or misjudging the megawatts by half still lowers curtailment cost against that forecast. The detector tested earlier (RO-NC) finds only a third of the shifts, below the break-even of one half (measured with every other property perfect). The surprise of recent readings against the forecast's bands (band position) found more, 37% of shifts on even months, but still under one half and with about 90% of its alarms false, so the next step is a detector that finds more shifts. also relevant 00309 lsc-two-forecast-gap-choosing-without-truth NGED sees two forecasts and not the true switching state. A forecast with no lagged power (GAM_ONLY) forecasts the normal running arrangement, and a forecast with lags (K0) forecasts what will flow while an abnormal arrangement lasts. A rule that reads only the gap between the two forecasts, how long it has lasted, and a neighbour check can choose between them nearly as well as knowing the truth. This experiment is part 2 of the brief briefs/sw_lsc_two_forecasts_divergence_and_selection_brief.md, and it builds on experiment 308. not supported not-for-production NGED cannot pick between the two forecasts from the gap alone. A rule on the gap, or on the 24-hour mean of measured power minus the no-lag forecast, did no better than always using the no- lag forecast in the injected worlds, and worse than always using the forecast with lags in the real record. An oracle that knows the true switching state gained little, except in the 72 hours after a real shift ended, so the most promising signal to test next is a flag for the end of a shift. The gap is a filtered copy of the measured-power residual, so it adds no information that the measured power lacks. also relevant 00304 metered-farm-node-sum-tail For the solar farms that share a bulk supply point, adding each farm's quantiles overstates the upper tail of the farms' summed output, adding independent bands understates it, and summing the 51 ensemble members' farm forecasts member by member gives calibrated 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles, because the ensemble carries the farms' shared dependence on cloud. not supported not-for-production The band for the combined output of the three farms beneath one substation comes out too wide if the weather forecast's 51 members are summed member by member, because the members' forecasts for the three farms move together almost perfectly while the farms' actual forecast errors are less closely linked. That band is almost the same as the band from adding each farm's quantiles. A band that assumes the farms' errors are unrelated is too narrow. A band from a Gaussian copula with a correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months comes closest to the stated probability. Only 5 half-hours in the scored year exceed 0.75 times a substation's maximum export, so this experiment cannot say what the band widths mean for curtailment cost. also relevant 00297 lsc-need-a-detector-no-detector-arms-against-the-mask A forecast that never learns which readings are load shifts can match a forecast that uses a detector, because its bands and its recent-power correction can be made to tell a load shift from ordinary variation by themselves. This is question 2 of the LSC decision program. not supported not-for-production A forecast with no detector that recalibrates its bands and reads how far the recent-power correction has moved scores better than the RO-NC detector near load shifts, so with RO-NC a detector is not shown to be needed. Perfect knowledge with the true megawatts added back still lowers curtailment cost by 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2) against that forecast, so the next step is to run the better LSC detector (LR_b20) on the same simulated shifts and judge it against a forecast that has the recalibrated bands. also relevant 00296 lsc-benefit-by-event-class-long-deep-versus-small-shifts Load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a Primary substation's load carry most of the benefit of knowing every load shift exactly, and shifts that are shorter than 12 hours or under 10% of load carry little. This is the question behind the "long-and-deep" detector of the LSC decision program. supported not-for-production A detector that finds only load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a substation's load would deliver about 96% of the upper-tail forecast benefit and about 90% of the curtailment-cost benefit of knowing every shift, if it were perfect. Detecting shifts from 6 hours to 2 days would add 3% to 8% more, and detecting shifts down to 5% of load would add 1% to 2%. The next step is to weight these shares by how often a real long-and-deep detector finds each class, which waits for Part 1 of the long-deep detector experiment. also relevant 00288 pooled-head-on-public-wind-farms A neural head that adds 11 quantile offsets to the XGBoost wind forecast (R0) and was trained on dozens of public onshore wind farms (metered output from Elexon's Balancing Mechanism Reporting Service) lowers the quantile score of the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3) against R0 alone, and a head trained on the pool beats the same head trained on W1 to W3 only, because experiment 259's head had too few farm-years to learn a correction that transfers. A second hypothesis: XGBoost keeps improving as the training history grows from 12 to 48 months while the physics core is flat after 24 months, and a pool of public farms replaces the missing history. not supported not-for-production Training the correction on 40 public wind farms did not help the forecasts for the three NGED wind farms. Applied directly, it made them worse, because the public farms' capacity, turbine rating, and hub height let the head memorise each farm. Without those inputs it did no harm, and after a short fine-tune on the three farms' own data it gained about as much as a simple offset table fitted on those farms, so the public farms added nothing measurable. also relevant 00284 metered-farm-tail-head-past-weather Experiment 275 found that adding years of past-weather rows lowered the 0.99 pinball loss of the neural head H5 by 4.6% while its overall score moved by 0.47%. A small neural network trained with a loss restricted to the tail quantiles (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99), on the same past-weather plus ensemble rows with an era flag, lowers the 0.01 and 0.99 pinball loss of a metered solar farm's forecast below that of XGBoost trained on the same rows. partly supported not-for-production A neural network trained only to forecast the extreme edges of a solar farm's output band does beat XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile (the upper edge that matters for curtailment) by 30%, but the existing H5 network does slightly better still, and most of the gain comes from building the band around the physical power model and not from tail-only training. The years of past-weather rows add under 1% at the 0.99 quantile, and at the 0.01 quantile the share of half-hours below it is outside 0.5% to 1.5% at three farms (marginally at A, because of exact zeros at D, and clearly only at E). also relevant 00283 lsc-perfect-knowledge-value-to-forecast-and-curtailment Knowing every load shift exactly (its true start and end) lowers the error of the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) in the 48 hours after a shift, and lowers the curtailment cost of the forecast of observed power in the days around a shift, while leaving ordinary rows unchanged. This is question 1 of the LSC decision program. partly supported not-for-production Perfect knowledge of load shifts lowers the forecast's error most in the 48 hours after a shift ends (23% lower upper-tail score, 95% interval 9% to 39%) and by under 1% over a whole year, because shifts are rare. Curtailment cost against observed power falls by 8% (6% to 10%) near a shift only when the known shift's megawatts are added back to the forecast, and does not fall when recent readings are merely set aside. The next step is to ask how good a detector must be to keep that gain, using the megawatts-added-back arm as the target. also relevant 00277 lsc-curtailment-metric-on-existing-forecasts The curtailment-cost metric of experiment 268 (studies.node_curtailment, sorted quantiles) ranks the four existing forecasts as the other metrics do, and can resolve the differences between them well enough to judge the load-shift questions of the decision program. supported not-for-production Over a year of ordinary days, the curtailment metric ranks the four existing forecasts the way the other scores do, and it can tell the GAM stack from BG2 (BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more on the six Primaries at the 0.5 limit, a figure that ranks forecasts and is not money saved). Inside the windows around the 7 logged load transfers, the GAM stack cannot be separated from BG2, because those windows hold only 926 to 2,923 scored half-hours. Questions about load shifts need injected worlds with many more shifts, not the real record. primary 00271 lsc-load-shifts-net-out-at-bulk-supply-points A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point (BSP) leaves the power flow at the BSP unchanged, so it barely changes the curtailment cost at the BSP, and only a load shift that crosses from one BSP to the other changes the cost noticeably. The step 7 program brief for the load-shift (LSC) decision program asks this in order to know whether the money question can be asked at BSP level. partly supported not-for-production A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point changes the curtailment cost at that bulk supply point by 0.2% at a random time and 0.7% just before days that would be curtailed (interval up to 1.08%), because the two Primaries' forecast errors partly cancel. A load shift across the boundary between the two bulk supply points changes it by 1.4% at a random time and 5.5% just before curtailed days. Only 4 of the 54 hand-filtered real events that involve two Primaries cross the boundary, so the curtailment metric at bulk supply points cannot say whether detecting load shifts is worth money, and that question has to be asked at Primary substations. also relevant 00268 lsc-curtailment-metric-v2-member-wise-ens A member-wise input path added to studies.node_curtailment (ensemble members of the node's demand and of each farm's output, paired by member, reduced to the quantiles the rule reads) gives the same avoidable cost as the quantile path when the members are drawn from the same quantile function, and scores nodes that experiment 255 could not (Primaries that connect a farm, and the bulk supply points D13 and D17 with member-wise inputs). partly supported not-for-production The curtailment metric can now take ensemble members for a substation's demand and for each solar farm, and on experiment 255's rows it reproduces the earlier answer. A third of the stored solar-farm forecasts list their quantiles out of order. Sorting them moves the cost of some forecasts by up to 3.7% and leaves every comparison between forecasts with the same sign, but it swaps which of two near-equal forecasts is cheapest. Forecasts that are already quantile sets can be scored now. Forecasts driven by ensemble members need member frames that we did not find in the experiment folders we searched. primary 00265 dp-gas-engine-bands-prior-and-visibility-switch Widening a Primary's forecast bands from its own past residuals (experiment 264, arm 2b) has coverage far from nominal in the first quarter, when there is no history, and after a change in the site's behaviour. A prior taken from the other Primaries' residuals, shrunk towards the site's own trailing residuals as they accrue, fixes the first quarter. A causal switch on the share of large drops in the trailing 30 days returns the widening to normal when D8's engine becomes visible in the readings (around April 2026). Together they hold D8's q05-to-q95 coverage within 5 points of 0.90 in every quarter, without raising the cost in quantile score, and without harming Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production In this year of forecasts, the other five Primaries' residuals did not predict D8's errors, so a starting estimate from them left D8's bands too narrow in the first quarter, and returning to normal widening after the engine's drops faded made them too narrow again. Widening from D8's own history (experiment 264) remained the best of the arms tried. We tested no other fix for the first quarter, and none of the other five Primaries had a heavy lower tail. also relevant 00264 dp-gas-engine-asymmetric-bands-at-d8 D8's forecast bands are too narrow in both directions, and part of the lower-tail miss is a 6 MW gas engine (probably three units of about 2 MW) that runs in spells and cannot be detected. A spread that widens as-of, using only residuals already resolved at the forecast origin, and that widens most in the direction the engine pushes (net demand falls), gives honest q05 to q95 bands at D8 without raising the quantile score at the Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production A forecast band that learns from the residuals it has already seen narrows most of the gap at D8: the quantile score falls by 9% to 19% and the share of readings inside the 90% band rises from 42% to between 80% and 87%. The extra gain of the engine mixture over simple widening is not evidence of an engine, because the mixture fits a running engine at two substations that have none. Plain two-sided widening with an earlier residual history is the option these results support, and NGED's own output for the engine would be the data to test an engine model. also relevant 00259 wind-plant-plus-quantile-offset-head For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a small neural network that reads the 51-member mixture of a wind model and the ensemble's wind summaries, and adds an offset to each of 11 quantiles, lowers the quantile score against the wind model alone (R1, the physics core), matches the XGBoost best guess (R0), and lowers the pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile, once it can learn from daily runs of the ensemble forecast over 15 months (about 440 runs) instead of the 13 to 40 Tuesday runs that experiment 221's head saw. partly supported candidate A correction learned from 15 months of daily ensemble forecasts lowered the wind forecast's quantile score by 4.5% to 5.5% on the three metered wind farms, but the neural network and the ensemble's wind summaries were not what earned it. The 51 ensemble members' median sits too low: the observed power was below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%. A lookup table with one offset per lead day, quantile, and farm recovers 92% of the gain. The open question is where that low bias comes from. also relevant 00255 metered-farm-node-curtailment-value When six metered solar farms beneath two bulk supply points are curtailed by the node-plus-generators rule of studies.node_curtailment, a forecast of each farm's output (the plant, XGBoost, or the plant with a neural head) avoids more curtailment cost than the NGED baseline, which assumes every generator runs at full capacity, and the neural head's lower 0.99 pinball loss does not show in the metric, because the rule uses only a farm's median. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting each solar farm's output instead of assuming every farm runs at full capacity cut the cost of curtailing at one of two substations (Boston, 40% lower) and raised it at the other (Skegness, 24% higher), so across both the saving is about a quarter, smaller than the uncertainty in the estimate. The neural network's better upper tail does not show in this cost, because the rule reads only each farm's median, and it lowers the cost by 3% against XGBoost, far under the 10% that would justify serving a neural network. Ranking farm forecasts by curtailment cost needs many more substations. also relevant 00251 dp-final-best-guess-assembly-clip-and-coast-against-bg2 The full best-guess stack of experiment 220 (arm D, the neural-network head, and the two-number solar summary) beats BG2, the manual heuristic, climatology, and a weak production-style XGBoost model over the scored year of 2025-07 to 2026-06. Adding the hand-set 60% clip at D5 lowers the D5 error on sunny half-hours when the neural-network head is absent, and adds nothing measurable when the head is present, because experiment 232 found the head cancels most of the clip's gain. supported candidate Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess demand forecast (arm D, a small neural network that corrects its median, and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5%; lower is better) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points, and it beats the manual heuristic on every headline metric we scored, including curtailment cost. The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. also relevant 00213 calibration-online-band-adaptation-from-coverage-misses Moving a scale on each quantile offset of experiment 169's arm A up after a reading falls outside that quantile, and down after a reading falls inside it, in the style of adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candes, 2021), lifts the cold-night q95 coverage to 0.90 or more without a second fitted spread model, because a run of misses on a cold spell widens the band before the spell ends. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the forecast widen or narrow its bands after each recent miss does not fix the under-coverage on cold nights: it lifts the 95% quantile's coverage from 0.896 to 0.906 in the scored year and lowers it in the other months, and it worsens the all-row, bank-holiday, and Christmas scores. A fixed widening of the upper quantiles does as well, so the cold-night gap is a shortfall that a signal arriving after the misses cannot learn in time, and the next step is to correct the mean forecast on the coldest days before any further work on the bands. also relevant 00169 calibration-combined-fixes-and-ensemble-spread The spread across the 51 ensemble members of the temperature and of the downward shortwave radiation at a substation predicts how wide the forecast's residuals are, beyond the hour band, calendar quarter, lead, and the cold-day widening of experiment 164. A convex quantile model that scales the quantile offsets by a non-decreasing function of those two spreads lifts the cold-night q95 coverage of the combined forecast to 0.90 or more. partly supported not-for-production Combining the smooth spread table with the cold-day widening reproduces its 0.896 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights, and adding the spread of the ensemble weather forecast (how much its 51 members disagree) lifts that to 0.907. The lift comes from widening the 95% and 99% quantiles by 4% and 10%, which the same model gives with its spread terms removed, so the ensemble spread is not what lifts cold-night coverage. A later experiment could test a bias correction of the mean forecast on the coldest days, and judge cold nights over more than one winter. also relevant 00164 calibration-cold-night-tail-under-coverage The q95 coverage of experiment 160's smooth-table forecast on cold nights (day mean temperature below 2 °C) stays near 85% because the spread table is too narrow when it is cold, not because the mean forecast is biased. Widening the quantiles on days the ensemble forecasts as cold, by a factor fitted on the tuning months, lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 90% or more without worsening the all-row score. refuted not-for-production On cold nights the 95% quantile of the best forecast is exceeded on about 15% of readings, and mostly because its prediction interval is too narrow, not because its mean forecast is biased. Widening only the upper quantiles on days the weather forecast calls cold reduces that share to about 10% without changing the all-hours score, but no fix reached the pre-registered 90% coverage in the scored year, and only 10 cold days back that year's figure. The coldest forecasts (0 °C or below) are also biased low, so correcting the mean forecast on those days is the next experiment to run. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00084 substation-limit-curtailment-cost-worked-example The substation-limit curtailment metric (studies.node_curtailment) can run end to end on the pilot's two bulk supply points, Boston and Skegness, and the pilot holds enough half-hours beyond a scaled limit to rank forecasts. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Two bulk supply points have 19 half-hours beyond a limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export in the scored year, so the pilot proves the arithmetic and cannot rank forecasts at the headline limit. primary 00083 curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-worked-example A tail-calibration table, built in packages/studies, can rank the stored quantile forecasts of experiment 48 by how well they cover the tails of the forecast distribution. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Every forecast is too narrow in both tails: coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927. primary

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Demand inputs
docs.text:
At Primary substations, a calendar-and-solar set of inputs lowered the demand forecast error by 0.1 points of capacity or more with an interval clear of zero: the hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, a Christmas column limited to the 14 days either side of 25 December, and an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output. A heating term gave 0.14 points in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead on one winter, which is under its 0.3 target. The electricity price, school terms, statistics of installed solar capacity, substation fingerprints, and the PV_Live estimate of solar generation gave no gain of 0.1 points that held up.

The experiments added one kind of information at a time to an XGBoost demand forecast and scored the change against the same XGBoost model without it. They scored 13 to 16 Primary substations (experiment 74: 5), over one or two validation years, and experiments 27 and 28 scored two grid supply points. Errors are in points of capacity, a negative change is an improvement, and each number names its metric: the error of the median (the mean absolute error of the middle forecast) or the quantile score. Several gains in the selection year (the year used to choose inputs) vanished in the confirmation year (the later year used to check them) or against a control.

For Primary substations on the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), adding the hour and weekday to the weather lowered the error of the median by 0.46 points (99.4% interval -0.61 to -0.30), the largest single input. The panels show the same contrasts for the 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points, which have too few series to settle. Source: experiment 6, an ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model on 14 Primaries.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, and a windowed Christmas column help; school terms do not. In experiment 6 the hour and weekday lowered the error of the median by 0.55 points on the selection year, a third of the 1.5 predicted, and the pre-registered COVID indicator by 0.26 (-0.40 to -0.10). The Christmas column is weaker evidence. The 15 December to 7 January window was chosen after the run, and the column lowered the Primary error there by 1.78 points (95% interval -2.30 to -1.26) and changed it by 0.00 elsewhere. The gain is concentrated: the median-error series barely moved (3.96 to 3.95 in the confirmation year) and a series picked after the fact fell from 22.23 to 4.13. Dropping the column from the chosen set changed the selection-year Primary error by +0.14 (-0.06 to +0.35), and the whole-year effect was -0.10. Experiment 11 found no gain from return-to-work or school-term columns on Lincolnshire Primaries: +0.20 at Easter (99.2% interval -0.19 to +0.59) and -0.29 in half-terms (-0.68 to +0.07). The experiment's own rule gives refuted, and its write-up reads Easter and half-terms as inconclusive.

The Christmas columns cut the Christmas error and leave other days unchanged. Source: experiment 6, post hoc windows (chosen after seeing the results), three folds.

An explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output lowers the daylight error; same-time analogues may too, and the data could not rank the two. In experiment 74, five Primaries refitted monthly and scored on daylight April-to-September rows, the explicit offset lowered the quantile score by 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007), against a monthly refit with neither. An offset built from another date's sunshine scored 0.246 worse than the real offset. Statistics of installed capacity did not help 16 Primaries (+0.006, -0.022 to +0.033; experiment 31).

Both ways of telling the XGBoost model about sunshine lowered the daylight error, and the intervals overlap. Source: experiment 74, 5 Primaries, one validation year.

Satellite sunshine as a training input gave no resolved gain, and a correction of the forecast sunshine a further small one. Training on CAMS irradiance changed the Primary quantile score by -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), refuted against 0.2 planned (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS lowered it by a further 0.067 (-0.094 to -0.039), which makes the pair 0.102 better than the ERA5-trained arm, but the monthly ratio to CAMS still ran from 0.81 to 1.13, so the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 14). PV_Live, Sheffield Solar's estimate of solar generation, gave no resolved gain at the two grid supply points Walpole and Bicker Fen (experiment 27, -0.03; experiment 28, -0.14 with interval -0.34 to +0.04).

The electricity price gave no gain that held against a control. The price at the target half-hour lowered the pooled error of the median by 0.52 in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) and 0.18 in the confirmation year (-0.50 to +0.08), and a price from another week matched about 0.45 of the 0.52 (experiment 15). Price changes (experiment 25) and lagged prices (experiment 10) did no better.

Substation fingerprints and a heating term gave little. Fingerprints changed the quantile score by +0.02 (-0.05 to +0.10; experiment 32). A heating term lowered it by 0.143 in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034) and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000), on 16 Primaries over one winter in which three ISO weeks hold 66% of the cold rows. The q95 forecast was still exceeded in 16.2% of those hours (experiment 94). Experiments 24 and 30 are in the candidates below.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: Among the experiments of this theme, no single one assembled the parts; the parts that beat their controls are below. Experiment 87 (the production-reference theme) assembled several of them in BG2. Give the weather-to-power XGBoost model the hour and weekday and the days to Christmas inside a 14-day window (experiment 6). Where a clean solar capacity estimate exists, add the forecast unmetered solar output as a base margin (experiment 74, using the offset of experiment 64; experiment 74 is not-for-production). In BG2 the offset lowered the score by 0.114 on its daylight April-to-September rows at the 5 Primaries that carry one, and by 0.010 over the whole year at all 16 Primaries (experiment 87). The stage 0 mapping (experiment 14) and the heating term (experiment 94) are candidates, not yet part of the design.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Five experiments here are marked candidate, and each rests on one validation year or an unconfirmed input.

  • Stage 1a inputs (experiment 6): the clock, the COVID indicator (-0.26), recency weights (-0.32, half-life 2 years), and the windowed Christmas column for the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model. A training start of 2023-09 stays unconfirmed (0.86 better on the confirmation year, 0.05 on the selection year).
  • Stage 0 (experiment 14): a quantile mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for a CAMS-trained stage 1a, 0.067 points better.
  • Pooling (experiment 24): one XGBoost model per substation type or size band (3 or 4 models instead of 20), 0.15 points worse (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), with the series identifier.
  • Weekly mean and median (experiment 30): two extra columns in N1 with the 14-day correction, 0.05 points better than N1 with it (-0.08 to -0.02). The arm is post hoc, and against the experiment 19 stack the 0.03 gain touches zero (-0.06 to +0.00).
  • Heating term (experiment 94): a per-series base margin. The experiment advises a second winter before porting.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Add a placebo twin of every added input, a copy with the same level but the wrong timing. A price from another week matched 0.45 of the 0.52-point price gain (experiment 15), the shuffled price matched most of the gain at the battery site (experiment 10), an offset from another date scored 0.246 worse (experiment 74), and a shuffled capacity control matched the register products (experiment 31). Without the twin, a column that only carries a level is credited. Re-check with a different data source.
  • Check a calendar column against a half-year flag and score it inside the special days. The unwindowed days-to-Christmas column flips sign every late June, so it acts as a half-year flag, and a time-of-year harmonic matched the Christmas gain but worsened summer (experiment 6). A column can also help a few days a year and barely move the yearly mean. Add a placebo calendar shifted by a fixed number of days (experiment 11). Re-check with more years than 3.
  • Fix colsample_bytree at 1.0 in every arm of a column ablation. Experiments 6, 30, 31, and 32 did so because column subsampling hands the wider arm a free win. None measured the size of that effect. Re-check if the arms are ever given equal column counts.
  • Give every arm the same starting level. A start at zero lowered the error by 0.071 (-0.099 to -0.047) against XGBoost's estimated base score in experiment 78, and experiment 74 quotes 0.07 to 0.10 points, so it started every arm at the median of the training labels (experiment 74). Experiment 76 did not test the effect. Re-check with a different pipeline.
  • Judge a lag set against N1 with the 14-day correction. The weekly lags gained 0.30 without the correction and lost 0.09 with it (experiment 30). Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Read a selection-year gain only after a confirmation year. The price gain at the battery site fell from -0.92 to -0.06 (experiment 10), and a 2023-09 training start gained 0.05 and then 0.86 (experiment 6). Re-check with a third year.
  • Test an input on the weather it will be served with. A CAMS-trained XGBoost model lowered the daylight error by 0.88 reading CAMS and by 0.04 reading ENS (experiment 9), and an ERA5-trained solar forecast ran 1.8 to 3.0 points too high on ENS members (experiment 28). Re-check with a different weather product.
  • Report a pooled share with and without the largest-residual substation. One substation set the pooled share in experiment 7. Re-check on new series.
  • Give every pooled XGBoost model the series identifier, and no fixed-window statistics for a held-out series. Dropping the identifier raised the score by 0.82 for by-type pools (experiment 24), and training-window statistics worsened a held-out substation by 1.39, probably because 7 series learn them as identifiers (experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Score cold-hour and special-day contrasts on more than one winter. Three ISO weeks held 66% of the cold rows at leads up to 48 hours (experiment 94), and the Christmas windows rest on three Christmases (experiment 6). Re-check when a second winter exists.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• A second validation year. The analogues on top of the offset (-0.066, -0.149 to +0.015) and the heating term need one.
  • Battery response to price. Only the largest battery site was testable, and national demand and wind scored at least as well as the price, so the price may be a proxy for them.
  • Stage 0 on more than 14 months of ENS and all members, and half-term effects with more than 9 half-terms.

The theme's research plan lists the proposals still waiting.

docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, adding a per-series heating term to the XGBoost model's base margin lowers the forecast error in cold hours (ENS 2 m temperature below 3 C), because the term extrapolates linearly beyond the coldest training hour and cannot be damped at long leads, whereas trees predict a flat response there. The term is the heating degree-hours (15.5 C minus the temperature, floored at zero) times a per-series, per-hour-of-day coefficient fitted by least squares on the training window only. small gain candidate The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). primary 00074 an1-same-time-analogues-vs-explicit-solar-forecast-demand At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, when the XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data (P-roll), an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output, given to the model as a starting offset (experiment 64's arm am), lowers the daylight April-to-September quantile score by more than same-time-of-day analogues do. An analogue is a recent day, at the same half-hour of the day and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday), whose satellite-based sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target. The model receives the observed power on the K nearest such days (K is 1, 3, or 5) as input columns. Once the explicit offset is in the model, the analogue columns add less than 0.05 points of capacity. inconclusive not-for-production Both ways of telling the monthly-refitted model about sunshine lowered the daylight error: the explicit forecast of the panels' output by 0.149 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and the 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007) against the reference. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). also relevant 00031 embedded-pv-features-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 trailing estimates of each substation's embedded (unmetered) solar capacity, built from the Embedded Capacity Register (ECR) as a prior for Primaries and a floor for BSP and GSP series, plus an amount learned from recent power and irradiance, lowers the quantile score on sunny days, and a linear PV offset or a sunshine-shaped correction does so more reliably than extra tree columns. inconclusive not-for-production C3, A3 (PV products with the register) minus B0, quantile score over all leads: +0.006 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.022 to +0.033). primary 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 the 13 power lags that manual_heuristic uses (the same weekday and time of day 1 to 6 weeks back, and 49 to 55 weeks back), as separate columns beside N1's three lags measured from the forecast origin, lowers the quantile score. inconclusive candidate C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). primary 00028 pvlive-forecast-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator a forecast of the GSP's solar generation at the target time, from a simple XGBoost model of Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate applied to ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather, lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without a solar forecast. inconclusive not-for-production C1, solar forecast minus no solar forecast, over all leads: -0.14 points of capacity (95% interval -0.34 to +0.04). primary 00027 pvlive-lags-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate of the GSP's solar generation at the lag times, next to the lagged delta (metered demand minus the stage 1a expectation), lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without PV_Live. refuted not-for-production C3, delta plus PV_Live minus no PV_Live, over all leads: -0.03 points of capacity (98.33% interval -0.13 to +0.09). primary 00025 price-change-features-stage1-demand Giving the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model the change in the intra-day price over the last half-hour, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 6 hours, in addition to the price at the target half-hour, lowers its error at observed power for Primary substations, and by more than the same columns built from a price taken from another week. Batteries and other dispatchable generation respond to how the price moves, not only to its level. small gain not-for-production On Primary substations, adding price changes to the price level lowered the error by 0.037 points of capacity in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.056 to -0.018) and 0.050 in the confirmation year (-0.083 to -0.018). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. also relevant 00015 same-time-price-stage1-demand Adding the intra-day price at the same half-hour as the target (Elexon Market Index Data, observed at time t, not forecast and not lagged) to the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model, which already sees the weather at time t, lowers its error at observed power across all fitted series pooled, and by more than a price taken from another week does. inconclusive not-for-production C1, price against no price, pooled: -0.52 points (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) in the selection year and -0.18 (-0.50 to +0.08) in the confirmation year. primary 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. also relevant 00011 school-term-and-return-to-work-columns-stage1a-demand For the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model at Primary substations in Lincolnshire, columns for the return to work after New Year and for Lincolnshire's school terms lower the mean absolute error of the median in the weeks after Christmas, at Easter, and in the half-term holidays, against the same XGBoost model with a Christmas column that is set only within 14 days of 25 December. refuted not-for-production Return and term columns against the base arm, Primary substations: +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 over the Easter window (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half-term holidays (-0.68 to +0.07). primary 00010 elexon-price-lags-stage1a-demand Adding the Elexon Market Index Data price from exactly 7 days earlier to the ERA5-trained stage 1a demand model lowers its error at the substations that host price-responsive batteries, and does so by more than adding the same-lag national demand and wind output, which price follows. inconclusive not-for-production C1 at B2, price against base: -0.92 points (98.3% interval -2.10 to +0.07) in the selection year and -0.06 (-0.38 to +0.23) in the confirmation year. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. also relevant 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. also relevant 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep For a weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 for substation demand, the local clock (hour of day and day of week) is the input that lowers the held-out error most, and the other non-lag inputs tested here (holiday encodings, time of year, trailing temperature means, sun position beyond zenith and azimuth, UTC offset, windchill, and a COVID indicator) each lower it by less. partly supported candidate P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. primary
