docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather)
docs.text:
This theme covers the demand model of a six-part series on forecasting with physical terms.

Background: Differentiable physics: background explains the models in plain terms.

The series builds models of Primary substation demand from a daily profile, holiday and heating terms, and a solar term, fitted by gradient-based optimisation. This theme holds the part that builds the model and asks whether more years of history help it. The series' finding so far is in experiment 104: the convex model trained on 12 months beat lagless XGBoost with its default start by 0.25 points (post hoc), and all years with drift are level with 12 months, so more years are not yet shown to help. Experiment 63 is an earlier, smaller linear test of the same decomposition into a weather baseline, a solar term, and transfer terms. The Experiments page lists every experiment, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00281 economy7-night-step-smooth-in-temperature A forecast of primary substation demand whose night level is a set of free levels for each UTC night half-hour (experiment 121's NS-U), and then a step whose size is a monotone function of the cold, scores better in the Economy 7 step hours and on cold winter nights than the same forecast with only the winter night offset (experiment 155), when the weather input is the ensemble-mean forecast and not past weather. Economy 7 is the tariff that switches storage heaters on shortly after 00:30 UTC. Experiment 121 found a gain of 0.233 points on winter nights on past weather and asked for a test on weather forecasts. inconclusive not-for-production Fitting the Economy 7 night levels inside the demand model, and not adding a winter night offset afterwards, lowered the day-ahead error by about 0.02 to 0.03 points of rated demand over all rows in both years and by about 0.04 points on winter nights, but the gain in the two hours after the step starts could not be shown: it changes sign between the two years and depends on two or three substations. Letting the step grow with the cold added almost nothing over free night levels. The Economy 7 term does not explain the night-time gap at D10 in April to June. primary 00279 dp-heating-curve-monotone-lagged-temperature-and-wind The heating response of the convex demand model T-all-K (a hinge at 15.5 C on four trailing-mean temperatures, split by day type) is too rigid. A smooth, monotone, non-negative curve on the same temperatures (A1), the same curve also on exponentially weighted and previous-day mean temperatures that carry the building's thermal lag (A2), or a small monotone neural network on three daily mean temperatures and the wind speed (A3), lowers the day-ahead quantile score on cold nights and winter days at the five decision Primaries, and the fitted curve is not a straight line. not supported not-for-production A smooth heating curve, a thermal lag, and wind each leave the day-ahead forecast within about 0.02 points of the straight-line heating response, so the evidence does not justify adding any of them. A small neural network learns a plausible curved heating response and lowers the error on cold nights by 0.13 points, but that gain comes from one cold spell in January 2026, did not appear in the previous year, and the network failed a test on synthetic data, so the substation card keeps the straight line for now. primary 00198 d8-summer-spikes-cooling-load-and-residual-test The summer spikes a colleague saw in D8's power (time series 26, Marsh Lane) are air-conditioning load: they rise smoothly with temperature, peak in the afternoon of the hottest days, and repeat every year. The best-guess forecast has a heating hinge but no cooling term, so its summer residual (metered minus forecast) rises with temperature, and a cooling hinge on the ensemble mean temperature fitted on past residuals lowers its summer score. inconclusive not-for-production D8's afternoon power does not rise with temperature, and its large summer departures from expected power are mostly downward shortfalls of 1.5 MW or more, which grow from 18% of summer half-hours in 2022 to 52% in 2025, so the spikes are not air-conditioning load. A cooling term added to the best-guess forecast changed the summer score at the five decision Primaries by 0.0002 points (interval -0.010 to +0.015), but the 4 fit months held too few hot days and the known-answer control failed, so the experiment cannot rule a cooling term out. On afternoons of 25 degrees Celsius or more, metered power exceeds the forecast by 0.6 to 5.1 points on average at each of six Primaries, so a term fitted on the full multi-year history of past weather, pooled across Primaries, is the next test. primary 00173 dp-christmas-more-years-and-sites The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, held to 0.75 of its size), which scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday over 24 December to 2 January at five substations in two Christmases (experiment 170), keeps a Christmas-to-weekday error ratio under 1.3 in every Christmas back to 2019-20 and at 14 or more of 16 Primary substations, and does not over- or under-forecast 25 and 26 December by more than 5% of that day's demand. inconclusive not-for-production Where the demand model had a winter of training data, the error over 24 December to 2 January was 0.97 to 1.22 times an ordinary weekday in all four Christmases from 2022-23 to 2025-26, so no special-day term is justified. The pre-registered run failed because the training rows of Christmas 2020-21 and 2021-22 (and of one substation in 2023-24) held little or no winter, since the lockdown window is left out of training. A forecast for a substation with under 180 days of usable history should be flagged, not trusted. also relevant 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k Averaging GAM-K's past day-ahead errors over the days most similar to the target day (same day type, with holiday identity for holidays, similar forecast daily mean temperature, and a season window of a few weeks either side of the date) gives a better correction than averaging the last 14 days alike (recipe R of experiment 115) or the same-day-type days of the last few weeks (experiment 134). The reasoning is that demand errors repeat on days that resemble each other. The errors that repeat most, on holidays and on cold days, are the ones that a 14-day average dilutes. small gain candidate Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. also relevant 00143 differentiable-physics-holiday-aware-updating-of-the-gam-k-filter The Kalman filter of GAM-K lets a holiday's reading error teach it a wrong level, which carries into the days after the holiday; leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update (and nothing else) lowers the day-ahead score on those following days, and does not hurt the holiday targets or the rest of the year. not supported not-for-production Leaving holiday readings out of the day-ahead filter's update does not reliably help the days after a holiday: the effect had the opposite sign after Christmas 2024 and Christmas 2025, and its 99% interval in the scored year (-0.309 to +0.036 points) includes zero. In 10 of 12 holidays, the holiday readings' error had the same sign as the error on the following days, so these readings are not usually contamination. Setting the correction to zero on holiday days, as experiment 118 did, is the action that hurts (+0.62 points on holiday days). Two Christmases give no basis for changing the filter this Christmas. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. primary 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. primary 00123 differentiable-physics-e7-storage-heating-night-step-estimation At Primary substations, demand steps up in the half-hours from 00:30 to 02:30 on winter nights, the step grows with cold, and the pooled step over the six decision series is positive at a daily mean of 3 C. At D5, D10, and D16, which were chosen because winter 2025-26 showed the step, it is 5 to 10 points (1% of each series' 99th percentile of demand); at the other decision series it is smaller. inconclusive not-for-production The night step at Primary substations is about 10 points on a 3 C day, where one point is 1% of a substation's near-peak demand, and it starts around 01:00 and looks fixed to UTC rather than the local clock (a check chosen after seeing the data). The rise on cold winter nights is the feature an operator would see: the day-ahead forecast runs 6 to 10 points below actual demand from about 01:00 at D5 and D16 on the two pre-registered winters, and at D10 in winter 2024-25 alone (7.6 points at 01:00); at D10 in winter 2023-24 the baseline is instead 9 to 17 points too high all night. The step appears at 13 of the 14 substations, and its full size rests on summer nights having no step, which the gate cannot test. The verdict is inconclusive because the gate is weaker than it looks: it holds one real test of the interval, and that test under-covers. primary 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. primary 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. primary 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. primary 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. also relevant 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): research plan
docs.text:
The cheap screens of inputs to the convex model are bundled into one experiment. Experiment 104 found that all years of history without drift scored worse than 12 months, and that a drift held constant recovered that. The recent-level drift and the day-type filter are covered by the KFE experiment, so this page lists the input screens only.

Experiment Question Priority Waits for State N3 and N4, interaction terms and heating threshold Do interaction terms in the convex model, and a heating threshold chosen per substation, lower its error? Done, partly supported None Interaction terms (N3) gained, mostly at one substation, and the per-site heating threshold (N4) tied (experiment 114) S1, cheap screens added to GAM-K (experiment 126) Do cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lower the score, winter first? Done, inconclusive None None of 13 screens showed a trusted gain; E-sol (-0.036 on dark winter evenings) is the lead for a retest on ENS weather; W-basis worse in every month, site and year; F-mix, W-stn undecided on 2 to 3 months E7F, Economy 7 night-step term in the forecast (experiment 137) Does an additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors, lower the day-ahead score on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC? Running None Planned; plan committed before any code Weather encoder retest Does a small learned encoder over a patch of weather cells lower the error on hard cases (convective and frontal days, wind and solar sites) once the base forecast is recalibrated? 3 A plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, which experiment 119 found accounts for most of the encoder's gain Queued, after the recalibration

Later parts are listed in their own themes.

docs.title: Bundled cheap screens
docs.text:
The six screens share one experiment and run on 6 CPU cores in about 2 hours. Each has one hypothesis:

  • Free temperature spline. A free spline of temperature fits better than the fixed 15.5 °C hinge.
  • Smoothed temperatures. Temperature smoothed at two decay rates, plus smoothed daily minimum and maximum, adds skill to the convex model's means of 6 hours to 1 week. The GAM papers on regional load use these terms: Obst et al. (2021) for French load, and Fasiolo et al. (2021) for the winning GEFCom2014 entry. No paper isolates the gain from the smoothing alone.
  • Humidity and wind chill. Feeding humidity and wind chill into the heating hinge lowers the winter error.
  • School-term calendar. A school-term term lowers the error in term-time weeks, once data availability is checked.
  • Lighting from solar elevation. Lighting modelled from solar elevation beats a fixed clock curve on dark winter evenings.
  • Filter-noise mixture. A filter noise that depends on the regime (cold snap, mild, holiday) beats one fixed noise.

docs.title: Weather encoder retest
docs.text: The retest repeats the weather-encoder comparison on the hard cases, with a recalibrated base forecast. The encoder replaces single-cell inputs with a learned view of a patch of cells, and the aim is a lower error on convective and frontal days, when a single cell misses the neighbouring weather. Experiment 119, the first encoder experiment, ended inconclusive, and about two-thirds of its gain survived when the network read the wrong date's weather. The retest therefore waits for a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, and runs on the GPU. The encoders technique page is the first thing to read.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: embedded generation
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted to the power a Primary substation draws. This theme covers the generation side of a Primary substation: whether the convex model can read an MVA meter, find a flat unmetered generator where one exists and not invent one where none does, represent an export-limited solar clip, and identify how much rooftop solar sits behind each substation. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: embedded generation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00306 summer-gap-solar-interactions-with-temperature-and-day-type The April-to-June daylight excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is an additive-structure problem. On cold clear spring days heating demand and rooftop solar output are both large, and an additive model must give the solar term one weight on every day. Experiment 299 found the D5 excess largest on clear midday half-hours (+1.67 points). Letting the solar shape interact with temperature (shape times the heating hinge) and with day type (shape times a weekend indicator) lets the model give those days a different solar weight. refuted not-for-production Letting the rooftop-solar term vary with temperature and with weekdays versus weekends does not close the April-to-June gap to BG2: at the two substations with the gap, the extra columns close about 0% of it. Two linear interaction columns therefore do not explain the gap. The next test is what BG2 uses that the convex demand model does not (item 5 of the summer-gap brief). also relevant 00299 summer-gap-timing-night-level-and-error-correction The April-to-June excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is a step that starts at the March clock change and sits at short leads, which would point at a local-time mismatch or at BG2's use of recent power. D10's night-time level offset of about -2 points (21:00 to 07:30 UTC) is a step on one date, not a smooth drift with temperature. The Kalman filter and the correction head are net harmful at D5 and D9 in April to June. not supported not-for-production The spring excess of the best-guess demand forecast over BG2 grows with sunshine, appearing on clear midday half-hours at D5 and across the whole day at D9. It is not concentrated in the 4 weeks after the clock change or at short leads, so the next test is the solar term's response on clear half-hours at D5. The Kalman filter and the correction heads are not the cause: removing the filter changes little, and at D5 the heads reduce the excess. D10's night-time offset varies partly with month and has no single date on which it changes. also relevant 00294 regime-aware-model-at-d8-engine-state-term D8's metered power excludes a gas engine's output (experiment 194) while the engine, which runs in spells (experiment 291), takes net load below what the weather and calendar predict. A single model trained across those spells has no way to know which half-hours the engine ran, so its forecast and its bands carry the engine as noise. A model that keeps the calendar, weather, and solar shapes shared across the whole history but adds one regime-specific term, an offset per half-hour the engine runs (non-negative, taking power off net load), forecasts D8 better than the single model. The offset is estimated from the data, and its size is not assumed. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast when D8's gas engine is running would make it much better when the state is read at the half-hour being forecast, but the detector builds that state from the very reading being forecast. With only the state of the last settled day, the engine term made the forecast 10% worse; trained on that stale state, it gained only 3%, no better than widening the bands from past residuals. A forecast of whether the engine runs, or NGED's own record of its running hours, would be the data to test next. primary 00291 d8-drops-engine-spells-load-shift D8's 29 multi-day drops (experiment 159) are spells in which a gas engine of up to three units runs, and D8's own metered power no longer includes the engine's output (experiment 194). If so, the engine detector of experiment 196 flags the drops' half-hours far more often than matched windows elsewhere on D8, the drops' depths cluster at multiples of one engine unit, and most of D8's load-shift alarms that fall inside drops are engine edges. partly supported not-for-production D8's multi-day drops coincide with the engine detector's running states, which is consistent with the gas engine running: the detector flags 27 of the 28 drops that began after the engine left D8's reading, against about 1 in 5 comparable stretches of D8, and it flags almost nothing at three other Primaries on the same dates. This cannot be called proved, because the drops and the detector both read D8's residual, and the depths of the drops do not fall at whole multiples of the engine's 1.97 MW unit. D8's drops should be flagged as a probable generator regime and reported apart from the load-shift scoring until NGED confirms the engine's running hours, and the next step is a forecast model for D8 that is told when the engine is running. also relevant 00289 summer-gap-weather-input-discriminator The best-guess stack's weaker April to June score than BG2 at the decision Primaries comes from the ensemble's sunshine forecast (or its ratio calibration), and not from demand absorbing the solar term or from the error-correction layers. partly supported not-for-production Giving the best-guess stack the sunshine that actually happened would close about 70% of its April to June gap to BG2, but the same change helps the stack nearly as much in July to September, when the stack already matches BG2. Most of the April to June gap beyond the July to September gap therefore stays. That points to the solar term in the demand model, or to the error-correction layers, and away from the ensemble sunshine forecast. A refit with realised sunshine as the solar driver, and a check of the solar term at D5 and D9 in April to June, are the next steps. also relevant 00282 pv-plant-curve-audit The curve that turns sunshine into power in our solar models departs from the metered farms' measured curve by more than 5% of capacity somewhere in the clear-sky range, and the departure is the flat-top level (the inverter limit), not the panel tilt or the temperature loss. not supported not-for-production The curve that turns sunshine into solar power stays within 5 percentage points of capacity at 3 of the 6 metered solar farms and departs from their measured output at the other 3 in different directions, so no single fix to the inverter limit repairs it. The best-guess demand stack assumes panels tilted 35 degrees and the farms fit best at about 20 degrees, which makes the stack over-predict output on clear half-hours in December (measured is 0.66 of the stack, median over farms) and under-predict it from April to July by 5 to 8%. Swapping in the pooled shape of the other farms does not help, so the next experiment should try the 20 degree tilt inside the stack. also relevant 00280 pv-empirical-shape-and-capacity-in-arm-d The April to June 2026 gap between arm D (the monthly-refit generalised additive model of experiments 155 and 220, scored on experiment 178's rows) and BG2 comes from its solar term: the pinned solar capacity is too high and the south-facing fleet shape is not the shape the metered farms show. Replacing the fleet shape by the pooled empirical shape of experiment 269, at the capacity that shape's real-series fit supports, lowers arm D's April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looks too high (D5, D9, and D16). not supported not-for-production Putting the empirical solar shape into the forecast, at the pinned capacity or at the lower capacity the real series supports, does not lower the April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looked too high. The change is under 0.01 MW against an error of about 0.5 MW, and the intervals are wide. A capacity cut that is correct for the whole of April to June is not the fix either: at D5 it raises the error. This experiment finds no sign that the shape or the capacity of the solar term closes the summer gap to BG2. primary 00269 pv-capacity-gain-decomposition Most of the 0.090 gain that experiment 238 found from using a nearby farm's recorded output as the solar shape comes from the farm's plant shape (tilt, orientation, flat top) and from the capacity unit in which recovery is read, and little comes from the farm's measured sunshine. partly supported not-for-production For the five substations and six farms tested, the measured sunshine at a nearby farm explains almost none of the extra solar output that its recorded output helped to find. The extra output found comes from the farms' plant shape (panel tilt, panel orientation, and the flat top of the output curve). A table learned from other farms' output and driven by the satellite irradiance reproduces that plant shape. Using the table finds 0.966 of an injected solar farm's output when recovery is read as the capacity ratio of experiment 231 (0.826 with the physical fleet shape), and 0.995 when it is read over clear-sky daylight energy. In these tests the satellite irradiance was not the limit, and a metered farm beside each substation was not needed. Switching to the table lowers the fitted solar capacities of the five decision substations by 0.2 to 0.4 MW. The effect on the sunny-half-hour forecast score has not been run. primary 00267 pv-capacity-early-years-and-register-floor The inferred capacity of unmetered solar at the five decision Primaries falls below the register floor in season-year 2021 (July 2021 to June 2022) because the capacity fit recovers only about 0.78 of an injected farm and the 2021 fit window is thin, not because the register is shared to the wrong district. Dividing by the median recovery of the metered farms, and using the output of a metered farm within 25 km as the sunshine shape, lifts the estimates to the floor. not supported not-for-production The 2021 shortfall at D10 and D11 is not a missing recovery correction and not a thin fit window: the card already divides by the metered farms' recovery, and the 2021 season-year has 12 months of data at every Primary. Using a nearby metered farm's output as the sunshine shape makes the shortfall no smaller (the estimates fall by 7% to 22%, partly because the two shapes are divided by different recoveries), so the shortfall at those two Primaries remains unexplained. Candidate causes are the register's postcode-district share, a gap of about 20 months in the early data, and a fit that is too low in its first full year. Show 2021 at D10 and D11 as a known shortfall. primary 00266 summer-gap-diagnostics-solar-term The best-guess demand stack (experiment 251's arm 1) trails BG2, the production-style XGBoost forecast, in April to June 2026 mainly because of its explicit solar term (the subtracted estimate of unmetered rooftop solar output), and not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response, the Kalman filter, or the heating and lighting terms. The same defect explains the loss at D5, an anonymised Primary substation, on sunny half-hours. partly supported not-for-production The best-guess stack trails BG2 in April to June because of the solar term at two of the six substations (D5 and D9 on daylight half-hours) and a night-time error at a third (D10), not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary, the Kalman filter, or the ensemble sunshine forecast; the head and summary actually reduce the gap. The pinned solar capacity looks too high in those months, not too low, and clear mornings are forecast worse than clear afternoons. Candidate next experiments are the export clip at D9, a morning-and-afternoon solar shape, and a look at D10's night residuals; the stack's added parts need no change for this gap. also relevant 00265 dp-gas-engine-bands-prior-and-visibility-switch Widening a Primary's forecast bands from its own past residuals (experiment 264, arm 2b) has coverage far from nominal in the first quarter, when there is no history, and after a change in the site's behaviour. A prior taken from the other Primaries' residuals, shrunk towards the site's own trailing residuals as they accrue, fixes the first quarter. A causal switch on the share of large drops in the trailing 30 days returns the widening to normal when D8's engine becomes visible in the readings (around April 2026). Together they hold D8's q05-to-q95 coverage within 5 points of 0.90 in every quarter, without raising the cost in quantile score, and without harming Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production In this year of forecasts, the other five Primaries' residuals did not predict D8's errors, so a starting estimate from them left D8's bands too narrow in the first quarter, and returning to normal widening after the engine's drops faded made them too narrow again. Widening from D8's own history (experiment 264) remained the best of the arms tried. We tested no other fix for the first quarter, and none of the other five Primaries had a heavy lower tail. primary 00264 dp-gas-engine-asymmetric-bands-at-d8 D8's forecast bands are too narrow in both directions, and part of the lower-tail miss is a 6 MW gas engine (probably three units of about 2 MW) that runs in spells and cannot be detected. A spread that widens as-of, using only residuals already resolved at the forecast origin, and that widens most in the direction the engine pushes (net demand falls), gives honest q05 to q95 bands at D8 without raising the quantile score at the Primaries that have no engine. not supported not-for-production A forecast band that learns from the residuals it has already seen narrows most of the gap at D8: the quantile score falls by 9% to 19% and the share of readings inside the 90% band rises from 42% to between 80% and 87%. The extra gain of the engine mixture over simple widening is not evidence of an engine, because the mixture fits a running engine at two substations that have none. For the five farms tested, one scale of the fixed fleet solar shape fits a median of 93% of a farm's output, so the target of 0.95 to 1.05 was out of reach for most farms before the fit ran. No forecast was run, and the monthly capacity is not worth taking to the forecast stage. primary 00152 dp-mva-fold-aware-gam-k-at-mva-only-primaries At the MVA-only Primaries, the GAM-K forecast driven by the ensemble mean (experiment 136's arm A2) forecasts the MVA reading better when it models the fold: it fits the demand model through the meter (experiment 110's L0), corrects the forecast with a Kalman filter whose state is the signed flow, and builds its quantiles by folding a signed predictive distribution. The gain is concentrated at Stickney (D12), the one trial Primary where reverse flow is the usual state on sunny middays, and the change is harmless at the Primaries without reverse flow. inconclusive not-for-production At Stickney (D12), the one Primary with clear reverse flow, drawing the quantiles around a signed flow and folding them at zero lowered the score by about 0.4 points on sunny middays against the same fit with symmetric quantiles, and it did no harm at the other seven Primaries. The whole-year gain against reading the apparent power as signed power is of similar size, but its interval in the scored year includes zero. The known-answer test on five Primaries with hidden farms passed on the sign at the larger injection and failed at the smaller injection and on the upper tail's coverage, so the experiment does not support a port yet. primary 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. also relevant 00139 differentiable-physics-pv-as-of-capacity-in-gam-k Feeding the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) the as-of solar capacity of experiment 129 in place of experiment 45's pinned capacity lowers the quantile score on the sunniest third of half-hours, and does not raise it on the darkest third. The mechanism is that the pinned capacity is a hindsight growth prior, and the as-of capacity is read from each Primary's own power before the forecast origin. refuted not-for-production Replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not improve the forecast, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm) only matched the pin, so the accuracy of the capacity number is not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error; it did not test the ensemble's cloud forecast, the solar shape, the Kalman filter, or the non-solar load. primary 00129 differentiable-physics-pv-capacity-known-answer-test The AC capacity of the unmetered solar behind each of the five decision Primaries can be inferred offline, one value per September-to-August season-year, from CAMS irradiance, ERA5 temperature, and the Primary's net power, with an 80% range that holds its coverage when the real panels differ from the assumed south-facing shape and when a day-long cloud-driven demand is present. partly supported not-for-production The capacity of the small solar panels behind five Primary substations can be read from the substations' power. For 2025/26 the arm 2 estimate is 3.3 to 4.5 MW of AC capacity per Primary, and it grew by 0.4 to 2.8 MW since 2021/22. The range around each estimate is 1.2 to 1.6 MW wide, but it is a spread over test scenarios and not a calibrated 80% interval. The method has not been shown to work on real panels that face other ways or on overcast-day demand, so a card should show the range with those caveats. primary 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. primary 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. primary

docs.title: N13: PV orientation mix
docs.text:
Experiment 114 dropped N13, so the design below is not queued. It stays as the design for any later experiment on solar orientation.

The proposal gives the convex model three non-negative solar capacities, one each for south, east, and west, in place of one south-facing unit shape. The model stays convex, and an east-west array should get a larger east and west share. The shares count as identified only if they pass the coverage rule of experiment 113, which asks that 80% intervals cover the injected truth 70 to 90% of the time. The experiment passes if the shares are identified and the score does not get worse. The run takes minutes on the CPU. It was first considered for the same bundle as the interaction-term and heating-threshold experiment, which ran without it as experiment 114.

The later parts of the differentiable-physics series are planned one at a time, from the result of the part before.
