docs.title: Differentiable physics: the forecast engine
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted by gradient descent. This theme covers whether such a model, driven by ECMWF ensemble weather forecasts, forecasts Primary substation demand up to 7 days ahead as well as the production recipe does, on its own or as the starting point of the production recipe's XGBoost model. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the forecast engine: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00306 summer-gap-solar-interactions-with-temperature-and-day-type The April-to-June daylight excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is an additive-structure problem. On cold clear spring days heating demand and rooftop solar output are both large, and an additive model must give the solar term one weight on every day. Experiment 299 found the D5 excess largest on clear midday half-hours (+1.67 points). Letting the solar shape interact with temperature (shape times the heating hinge) and with day type (shape times a weekend indicator) lets the model give those days a different solar weight. refuted not-for-production Letting the rooftop-solar term vary with temperature and with weekdays versus weekends does not close the April-to-June gap to BG2: at the two substations with the gap, the extra columns close about 0% of it. Two linear interaction columns therefore do not explain the gap. The next test is what BG2 uses that the convex demand model does not (item 5 of the summer-gap brief). also relevant 00305 summer-gap-what-bg2-knows-that-arm-d-does-not BG2 (experiment 87's production-style XGBoost forecast) beats the convex best-guess model (arm D) at the Primary substations D5 and D9 in April to June mainly through interactions of the sunshine inputs with temperature or with recent power, and not through the main effect of sunshine. refuted not-for-production The production-style forecast does not beat the convex best-guess model in April to June at two Primary substations through interactions of sunshine with temperature or with recent power: forbidding them removes under 3% of its advantage on the half-hours where the convex model trails most, and 16% on all daylight half-hours. A refit allowed no interactions at all keeps 92% of the advantage on the worst half-hours but only 45% on all daylight half-hours, so the worst half-hours come from the shape of single inputs and typical ones partly from other interactions. also relevant 00299 summer-gap-timing-night-level-and-error-correction The April-to-June excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is a step that starts at the March clock change and sits at short leads, which would point at a local-time mismatch or at BG2's use of recent power. D10's night-time level offset of about -2 points (21:00 to 07:30 UTC) is a step on one date, not a smooth drift with temperature. The Kalman filter and the correction head are net harmful at D5 and D9 in April to June. not supported not-for-production The spring excess of the best-guess demand forecast over BG2 grows with sunshine, appearing on clear midday half-hours at D5 and across the whole day at D9. It is not concentrated in the 4 weeks after the clock change or at short leads, so the next test is the solar term's response on clear half-hours at D5. The Kalman filter and the correction heads are not the cause: removing the filter changes little, and at D5 the heads reduce the excess. D10's night-time offset varies partly with month and has no single date on which it changes. also relevant 00266 summer-gap-diagnostics-solar-term The best-guess demand stack (experiment 251's arm 1) trails BG2, the production-style XGBoost forecast, in April to June 2026 mainly because of its explicit solar term (the subtracted estimate of unmetered rooftop solar output), and not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response, the Kalman filter, or the heating and lighting terms. The same defect explains the loss at D5, an anonymised Primary substation, on sunny half-hours. partly supported not-for-production The best-guess stack trails BG2 in April to June because of the solar term at two of the six substations (D5 and D9 on daylight half-hours) and a night-time error at a third (D10), not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary, the Kalman filter, or the ensemble sunshine forecast; the head and summary actually reduce the gap. The pinned solar capacity looks too high in those months, not too low, and clear mornings are forecast worse than clear afternoons. Candidate next experiments are the export clip at D9, a morning-and-afternoon solar shape, and a look at D10's night residuals; the stack's added parts need no change for this gap. also relevant 00251 dp-final-best-guess-assembly-clip-and-coast-against-bg2 The full best-guess stack of experiment 220 (arm D, the neural-network head, and the two-number solar summary) beats BG2, the manual heuristic, climatology, and a weak production-style XGBoost model over the scored year of 2025-07 to 2026-06. Adding the hand-set 60% clip at D5 lowers the D5 error on sunny half-hours when the neural-network head is absent, and adds nothing measurable when the head is present, because experiment 232 found the head cancels most of the clip's gain. supported candidate Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess demand forecast (arm D, a small neural network that corrects its median, and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5%; lower is better) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points, and it beats the manual heuristic on every headline metric we scored, including curtailment cost. The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. also relevant 00244 dp-deep-ensemble-heads-cold-night-bands On cold nights the demand forecast's error is partly something the correction network does not know (epistemic uncertainty, as opposed to the weather forecast's own uncertainty, which experiment 192 found the 51 ensemble members' temperatures do not signal). The disagreement between 20 independently trained copies of the pooled correction network therefore predicts the absolute cold-night error, and widening the bands by a non-decreasing function of that disagreement lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 0.90. inconclusive not-for-production The disagreement between 20 independently trained correction networks does not tell us how wrong the forecast will be on cold nights (correlation 0.00), so it cannot set the width of the cold-night bands: scaling the bands by it lifts the 95% quantile's coverage by 0.006, the same as a shuffled spread does. The check that the spread reacts to an unusual input failed for a realistic 4 C error, so the experiment cannot say more. The cold-night shortfall is therefore unlikely to be fixed by training more networks; the experiment cannot say what would fix it. primary 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 For Primary substation demand, a metered solar farm, and a metered wind farm, the best forecast that uses no XGBoost anywhere scores within 2% of the quantile score of the best forecast that uses XGBoost, at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. also relevant 00228 dp-bg-rolling-origin-stack-against-bg2 The best-guess stack (arm D with experiment 169's bands, plus the network head of experiment 201) beats BG2 in most monthly origins and at most substations, and its advantage is larger in winter than in summer. partly supported candidate Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the solar summary) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5% of BG2's 2.715; lower is better), and most of the gain comes from November to March. From April to June 2026 the stack is worse than BG2, and arm D without the neural network head is worse than BG2 in summer. The year-long gain is only just separable from zero, and we cannot test other years until BG2 is re-run for them. also relevant 00225 dp-network-heads-on-unlabelled-worst-days Experiments 172, 174, and 175 found that the worst 5% of substation-days carry 41.7% of the excess loss of arm D (the best-guess convex forecast of experiment 155), and that 37 of the 72 worst days at the five decision substations carry none of the labels (switching event, holiday, cold snap, flagged reading, Economy 7 step). Experiments 200 and 201 found that a neural network corrects arm D mainly on very hot and very cold days. The unlabelled worst days therefore sit at temperature extremes, and the neural network cuts their loss. partly supported not-for-production The neural network does cut the loss on the 37 worst days that no label explains, by about a fifth, and cuts it by more than on the 35 days that do carry a label. The unlabelled worst days are not at temperature extremes, so a neural network aimed at the hottest and coldest days would not target them. What helps on them is the forecast input: a neural network without one removes 4%. primary 00222 dp-network-before-filter-order Experiments 200 and 201 correct arm D after the Kalman filter. Their gain is mostly a systematic error of the convex model at some temperatures and loads, not a recent-error effect, and that systematic error currently sits in the filter's level state. A network that reads only the convex model's own output and inputs, and corrects the convex model before the filter, leaves the filter a cleaner residual stream and so beats the same kind of network applied after the filter. inconclusive not-for-production The gain of the network after the filter does not come from the convex model's own systematic error as seen in its past residuals. A network trained on those residuals learned patterns that do not carry to the next year, and when it was stopped on a later year it learned nothing and left the score unchanged. The test could not settle the order question, because the network failed to recover a known injected error. primary 00220 dp-bg-stage4-assembly-with-drop-one The three parts added to the best-guess demand forecast since experiment 170 remove mostly different errors, so their gains add. The parts are the two-number solar summary of the 51 ensemble members (experiments 193 and 202), the pooled correction network on arm D's mean (experiments 200, 201, and 209), and the coast-and-widen rule for missing readings (experiment 205). The solar summary changes only daylight bands, and the network corrects arm D's median from its own output, the calendar, and temperature, so the two act on different rows and different error. The network may remove what the winter night offset and recipe R removed (both correct arm D's mean by time of day), and it may make the bands' cold-night widening unnecessary. partly supported candidate Adding two parts to the best-guess demand forecast lowers its quantile score by 0.136 points (5%) of substation effective capacity. The parts are a small neural network that corrects the forecast's median, and a two-number summary of the 51 ensemble members' solar response. Each part's gain is almost exactly what it achieves alone, so the two parts remove different errors. The network's own 11 quantiles reached 0.904 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights without the hand-fitted band fixes, and scored 0.048 points better than the corrected forecast overall, mostly at one substation. The coast-and-widen rule for missing readings was not scored with the stack. primary 00216 dp-network-shape-on-arm-d-flexible-temperature-tails The neural network of experiments 200 and 201 lowers the quantile score of arm D (the best-guess convex forecast of experiment 155) by 0.09 to 0.125 points, mainly by raising the median on very hot and very cold days. That correction is a shape the convex model could carry. The convex model's only temperature terms are one-sided heating hinges at 15.5 degrees Celsius, so it has no term for cooling load and no extra slope in the cold tail. Extra hinge columns in the tails of the site's own temperature range, with a weaker ridge penalty on those columns, recover at least half of the network's gain without a network. inconclusive not-for-production Adding extra temperature terms for the hottest and coldest days to the convex demand model recovers only a fifth to a quarter of the neural network's improvement, and the recovery was not confirmed in a second year. The neural network's correction is spread over all temperatures instead of sitting at the extremes, and a smooth function of temperature explains under 1% of it, so the neural network uses an input other than temperature. The formal verdict is capped at inconclusive because a placebo check narrowly failed, but the shortfall does not depend on that check. primary 00211 dp-boosted-tree-calibrator-and-input-ablations The 0.065 points by which the network without error inputs (experiment 200) beats the best lookup table (experiment 209) comes from a smooth or higher-order dependence on a few inputs, so a gradient-boosted tree model fitted with the pinball loss on the same inputs captures it, and a boosted-tree calibrator can replace the neural network. One-at-a-time removal of the network's inputs shows which input carries the gain. supported candidate A gradient-boosted tree model given the same inputs as the neural network, and no recent errors, lowers the error score of our best day-ahead forecast by about as much as the network does (0.098 against 0.100 points). The interval is wide, so a loss of up to 0.03 points against the network is not ruled out. The gain comes mostly from two inputs, the forecast level and the weather-data era. primary 00209 dp-pinball-table-vs-network-head-on-arm-d The gain that experiment 200's network head and its blind copy get over arm D (0.100 to 0.125 points) is a recalibration that a table without hidden layers can reproduce. The table gives arm D's median a shift that depends on site, half-hour, day of week, lead band, and arm D's forecast level by an ensemble-era flag, and scales arm D's quantile offsets by site, lead band, and six-hour block. It is fitted by gradient descent on the pinball loss over the 11 quantiles, on the same rows as the network. A second arm adds a temperature-extremes term (a median lift below -3 degrees Celsius and above 24 degrees Celsius, from experiment 201's finding). not supported not-for-production A lookup table of corrections to our best day-ahead forecast lowers its error score by only 0.03 to 0.04 points, against 0.10 points for a neural network given similar inputs and no recent errors. This table design therefore does not match the network, and the cause is not yet isolated. A temperature-extremes term lowers the score by under 0.001 points. primary 00205 dp-gamk-gap-robustness-coast-or-frozen-gam When power readings go missing, a Kalman filter that coasts (keeps running with no update, so the transient decays and the level holds) beats the frozen convex model (GAM) alone for short gaps and loses to it for long gaps, so a crossover gap length exists between 6 and 72 hours. The mechanism is that the level is a random walk, so a short gap leaves it nearly right, while a long gap lets it drift away from the demand. Widening the quantile bands by the filter's own growth in predictive variance keeps the 5% and 95% quantiles calibrated at the gap lengths where coasting is still better than the frozen model. inconclusive candidate When readings stop for 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours, keep running the Kalman filter, which corrects the convex demand model using its recent forecast errors, without feeding it new readings, and widen the quantile bands. At each of those four gap lengths that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction (a quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better; the gain is 8% to 14% of the uncorrected model's score). At 72 hours the 99.4% bootstrap interval for the gain runs from 0.04 to 0.48 points, so the gain may be small. The data cannot show whether dropping only the filter beats coasting after a gap of about 72 hours: at every gap length the difference between the two forecasts is smaller than the variation between months. The forecast with the filter, winter night offset, and recipe R was still 0.025 points worse than its no-gap score 48 hours after a 24-hour gap ended. The filter alone was within 0.02 points of its no-gap score 24 hours after the gap ended. primary 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay Experiment 193 found that two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses) lower the daylight quantile score by 2.20% in the scored year. Its two fitted factors per lead band were fitted on interleaved months (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), some of them later than the replicate months they were applied to, and its numbers were held in float64. A replay of the live weather layer, which stores the two numbers as float32 columns computed from the one ensemble run published before each origin and refits the factors each month on history that has completed before that month, keeps most of the gain. supported candidate A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. primary 00201 dp-gam-residual-mlp A small neural network that reads the convex model's own design features, and later the calendar, the ensemble-mean weather, and lagged power, can learn an interaction the additive convex model lacks, and so lowers the quantile score of the best-guess convex forecast (arm D of experiment 155) when it adds a correction to the median and rescales the band widths. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network that reads the convex demand model's forecast lowers that forecast's quantile score by about 0.09 points (3%), and adding weather, calendar, or recent power does not help further. The neural network corrects an under-forecast on very hot and very cold days. That points to a missing temperature term in the convex demand model. The correction also scores worse on bank holidays and, in point estimate, on Christmas. primary 00200 dp-pooled-correction-head-on-kalman-state Experiment 142's small network failed its known-answer gate with about 1,100 samples from one year at five substations. The same kind of network, trained on rows pooled across many Primary substations and years, learns to correct arm D's forecast from the recent errors, the calendar, the lead, and the ensemble-mean weather, and so beats recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days) at day D+1. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network trained on arm D's own past errors lowers the day-ahead score by 0.07 to 0.12 points at five substations, but a copy that sees no recent error gets most of that gain. The gain comes from correcting how arm D's error depends on its forecast level and the calendar, and a pinball-loss table comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the network on one year of data. primary 00197 dp-kalman-level-adaptation-retest Experiment 190's known-answer gate could not be passed by a filter with one state per hour band, because the target's band is usually unread since an offset began. Scored only on pairs the filter can know about, (a) a faster per-band filter (A1) recovers at least 50% of a 0.10-size, 16-hour offset on target bands already read, and (b) a filter whose bands share one level while a same-sign run lasts (A3) recovers at least 50% on target bands not yet read, because it moves bands that no reading has reached. not supported not-for-production Making the Kalman filter's level state faster does not fix offsets that last for hours. Faster settings recover a long offset only late, and only by scoring worse on quiet days, and a level shared across the four hour bands recovered under a fifth of the offset, because its run counter cannot tell an offset from noise. No setting on the grid tried recovered an injected offset without scoring worse on quiet days, so level adaptation is dropped. primary 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary Experiment 187 found that passing each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term lowers the daylight quantile score of the full best-guess stack by 2.23%, and that a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the 51 responses recovers 95% of that gain. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. primary 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. primary 00123 differentiable-physics-e7-storage-heating-night-step-estimation At Primary substations, demand steps up in the half-hours from 00:30 to 02:30 on winter nights, the step grows with cold, and the pooled step over the six decision series is positive at a daily mean of 3 C. At D5, D10, and D16, which were chosen because winter 2025-26 showed the step, it is 5 to 10 points (1% of each series' 99th percentile of demand); at the other decision series it is smaller. inconclusive not-for-production The night step at Primary substations is about 10 points on a 3 C day, where one point is 1% of a substation's near-peak demand, and it starts around 01:00 and looks fixed to UTC rather than the local clock (a check chosen after seeing the data). The rise on cold winter nights is the feature an operator would see: the day-ahead forecast runs 6 to 10 points below actual demand from about 01:00 at D5 and D16 on the two pre-registered winters, and at D10 in winter 2024-25 alone (7.6 points at 01:00); at D10 in winter 2023-24 the baseline is instead 9 to 17 points too high all night. The step appears at 13 of the 14 substations, and its full size rests on summer nights having no step, which the gate cannot test. The verdict is inconclusive because the gate is weaker than it looks: it holds one real test of the interval, and that test under-covers. also relevant 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. also relevant 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. primary 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. primary 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. primary

docs.text:

docs.title: CAL: tail calibration and a coherence pass
docs.text:
The maintainer postponed CAL on 2026-10-20. The question is whether the tails of the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) on ECMWF ensemble weather are calibrated in every lead band, and which re-spreading of the same mean forecast fixes the bands that are not. Experiments 107 and 111 found the pooled tails close to the nominal 95% and 99%, so the work is in particular cells: some substations in winter, the night hours, and one or two lead bands. Curtailment depends on the upper tail, so those cells matter more than the pooled figure.

The mean forecast stays fixed, and only the spread changes. Four methods are candidates, each reusing the stored fits of experiment 111 so that no new model is fitted:

  • a rolling conformal offset per substation, lead band, and quantile;
  • the Kalman filter's own predictive variance, scaled by a table of standardised residuals;
  • the same variance widened by the spread across the ensemble members;
  • separate lower and upper widening factors per lead band.

A cell counts as calibrated when its coverage lies within a binomial band set by the number of distinct substation-days in the cell. A substation-day is the unit because the errors of one substation's half-hours within a day move together. Before any method is scored, a blocking known-answer test checks that the band does not flag a forecast that is calibrated by construction, and that the band and the methods detect and remove a miscalibration of the size that matters. The decision rule asks for a method that passes in the replicate months and in the scored year without raising the quantile score by more than 0.02 points of effective capacity.

The coherence pass tests whether the ensemble sums across substations are calibrated against the observed sum. Calibrated marginals for each substation do not make the sum of several substations calibrated, because the sum depends on how the errors of different substations move together. The test turns each substation's calibrated quantiles back into ensemble members with ensemble copula coupling (ECC), or with the Schaake shuffle, which orders the members by a template taken from history. It then sums the members across substations and scores the summed ensemble against the observed sum, and scores the joint distribution with the variogram score. The staged probabilistic forecast already specifies ECC and the coherence scores for the production forecast. The pass asks whether the convex model's spread, once calibrated, keeps the cross-substation dependence that those scores reward. It runs after the per-substation calibration, on the same rows.

docs.title: N7: paired residuals at switching events
docs.text: Where both sides of a hand-filtered switching event are metered, the donor's and the receiver's residuals should be anti-correlated and sum to roughly the moved power. The experiment reports the share of events where the two residuals sum to within 20% of the moved power. A high share would show that a later model can treat a transfer as a conserved flow between two nodes. Only a minority of the events have both sides metered, so the result describes those events and does not generalise to the rest. The run takes minutes on the CPU.

docs.title: Schaake shuffle against ECC
docs.text: The comparison tests which way of restoring dependence across substations gives the better summed ensemble. Ensemble copula coupling (ECC) orders each substation's calibrated quantiles by the ranks of the ensemble members. The Schaake shuffle orders them by a template taken from history. Both then give members whose sums across substations are scored against the observed sum, with the variogram score. It reuses the members of N8 (experiment 125) and takes about 1 CPU hour. It is the comparison that CAL's coherence pass needs, so CAL can reuse its result.

docs.title: Tail quantile regression on filtered residuals
docs.text: The proposal fits a quantile regression on the Kalman filter's residuals, with the model's prediction, its square, and the hour of day as covariates. de Vilmarest et al. (2024) did this for net load in the 14 GB grid supply point groups, and the regression gave a small gain over Gaussian quantiles on the same residuals. They also adapted the regression online by gradient descent on the pinball loss. In their results nearly all of the improvement came from filtering the mean, and the quantile step added 2 to 6%. Their data are regional and national load, so the gain at Primary substations is untested. The method replaces the residual-quantile spread of the convex model, and runs in CPU seconds.

docs.title: Conditional Pareto tails
docs.text: The proposal models the quantiles beyond 1% and 99% with a generalised Pareto distribution whose scale depends on covariates. Browell and Fasiolo (2021) found that plain quantile regression is not calibrated beyond those probabilities. A conditional Pareto tail cut the upward reserve requirement by up to 24.6% and the downward reserve by up to 10.8%, against a static Pareto tail. Their fit uses the R package mgcv, so a Python version needs a small custom maximum-likelihood fit, which takes CPU minutes per substation. The proposal serves the curtailment goal, which depends on the extreme upper quantiles.

docs.title: ERA5-only winter-by-winter backtest, earlier winters
docs.text: The backtest replaces the forecast weather with ERA5, so that the release candidate and XGBoost can be judged over the winters that the ensemble-weather experiments do not cover. Experiment 122 covers the winters of 2023-24 to 2025-26, so this backtest covers 2019-20 to 2022-23 and has low priority. The release candidate is the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K), plus whichever of the night steps and the multi-hinge heating terms win their experiments. XGBoost is the production recipe (BG2) and its lagless version. ERA5 removes forecast-weather error, so the result ranks model structure on past weather and does not give production skill. The report gives winter-by-winter paired contrasts next to the ensemble-weather result, and says whether the two rankings agree. The run is cheap and uses the CPU only.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: long history and drift
docs.text:
A Kalman filter on recent residuals lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points, using estimates of past weather, but whether old years of history help is still not settled.

The first experiment of this theme shows that the data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start most Primary substation series later than their first record, fix the lockdown window in advance, and count eligible long-history sites at each tuning year's first day. The second shows that a simple model of demand minus solar does not clearly gain from every usable year: without a drift term it scored worse than on the last 12 months, and with a drift term the model was level with 12 months. The third shows that the filter lowers the score, and that the benefit of old years changed sign between two scored years. This theme covers whether a differentiable-physics model of Primary substation demand can use old years of history and cope with drift in the demand level over the years. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: What the experiments found
docs.text:
• 00103 - Differentiable physics, part 1: The first months of 13 of the 16 Primary substations are cut (19.4 months at D4), the data does not isolate the 2020 lockdown from drift, and the power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of NGED's fix of 2026-03-26.
  • 00104 - Differentiable physics, part 2: A simple model of demand minus solar, fitted as one convex optimisation per substation, scored 0.25 points higher (worse) when trained on every usable year without a drift term than on the last 12 months. Adding a drift term lowered the score by 0.29, so all years with drift was level with 12 months (0.04 points better, 98.33% interval from 0.30 better to 0.21 worse, 2 of 5 substations better), and the planned comparison is inconclusive. A first version of the page had the opposite sign for two contrasts, because its forecast spread carried the previous year's mean bias; the page now carries a Correction section. The experiment belongs mainly to the demand: calendar and weather theme.
  • 00106 - Differentiable physics, part 4: A Kalman filter that corrects each day-ahead forecast with the errors observed up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points in the scored year and 1.02 in the year before, at all five long-history substations. More years of history gave -0.22 points in the scored year and +0.32 in the year before, so the verdict is partly supported. With the filter running, a drift term added nothing measurable and refitting made the score slightly worse. Against lagged XGBoost at the same lead, the filtered model was 0.138 points better, which is not significant. The filter's residuals use estimates of past weather.
  • 00107 - Differentiable physics, rolling-origin history and tails: Refitting the convex model every quarter, 12 times from 2023 to 2026, adding a drift term to the model trained on all years lowered the score at 10 of 12 refits (0.45 points, 99% interval 0.23 to 0.68 better). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer, with winter-quarter refits favouring more years. A spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantile coverage worse. The verdict is partly supported.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: long history and drift: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00170 dp-bg-stage3-drift-and-holiday-scoring The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, ensemble-mean weather, the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, and the pinned solar capacity (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when it gets a drift term (experiment 167's D1) on top of the two post-forecast corrections of experiment 155's arm D (a winter night offset and recipe R's 14-day mean error profile). The mechanism is that the drift term removes a slow demand-level error that the monthly refit on 24 months of history leaves in, and neither the offset (winter nights only) nor recipe R (a 14-day profile held to 0.75 of its size) removes that error. Training on every year of history adds a further gain, because the drift term and the pinned capacity let the old years teach the heating and calendar terms. refuted not-for-production A slowly varying demand level (a drift term) improved the forecast by 0.40 points in experiment 167 but worsened it by 0.03 points once the forecast has the Kalman filter on recent errors (lower scores are better), and training on all years of history did not change that. The filter already appears to remove the slow level error that the drift term fixes, because without the filter the drift term improves the score by about 0.2 points. The drift term should not be added to experiment 155's arm D. Christmas (24 December to 2 January) scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday at the same half-hours, below the 1.5 times predicted, and recipe R improved the Christmas score by 0.04 points. also relevant 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. primary 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. primary 00135 differentiable-physics-n10-joint-kalman-and-demand-fit Fitting the convex demand model (GAM-K) so that its coefficients minimise the day-ahead error after the Kalman correction, instead of the plain error before it, lowers the day-ahead quantile score at 12 to 36 hours below the two-stage fit (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals), without moving the fitted shapes to explain recent-level structure that the filter already tracks. not supported not-for-production We fitted the demand model so that its coefficients minimise the error left after a Kalman filter (a running correction of recent errors) has adjusted the forecast. That made the day-ahead forecast much worse, because the filter can absorb a shift in the slow parts of the demand model, so the fit barely constrains those parts. Tying the fit to the two-stage coefficients removed the damage and also removed any gain: the quantile score was within 0.013 points of the two-stage score, in either direction. The two-stage design (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals) stays. primary 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. also relevant 00108 differentiable-physics-shared-anomaly-factor-across-substations The residuals of the frozen convex demand model carry a component shared across Primaries, and a shared state estimated from the other substations' residuals, available at the forecast origin, lowers the day-ahead quantile score by more than the per-site Kalman filter of Part 4 already does. inconclusive not-for-production The experiment stopped at its known-answer gate, where three of seven tests failed, so it cannot say whether a shared factor improves the forecast. On injected anomalies the shared filter, tuned on 2023-24, carried under 5% of the injected points (the plan asked for 40% or more), and it corrected no better than the per-site filter (2.402 against 2.397 points of mean absolute error over days 2 and 3 of the episodes). Part of the test was mis-specified, so a corrected test would be needed before any real score. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. primary 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. primary 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series models Primary substation demand from physical terms. This theme covers what the connections between Primary substations add: power flowing along the interconnections between neighbouring Primary substations when the network operator switches load from one to another, and a forecast of demand under the normal running arrangement (NRA), with those transfers removed. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. also relevant 00204 dp-bsp-full-bottom-up-with-signed-mva-children A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down when the sum covers every child Primary. Experiment 161 summed only the three children per BSP that report real power (MW) and have a long history, which reached 42% of D13's effective capacity and 56% of D17's, and the bottom-up forecast scored 0.5% to 0.6% worse than the top-down forecast. This experiment adds the children that report apparent power (MVA). A child's apparent-power reading is the magnitude of its flow, so a child with reverse flow at midday needs a signed flow before it can enter a sum. The fold-aware model of experiment 152 supplies that signed flow as a latent variable. inconclusive not-for-production Adding every child Primary to the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point: the bottom-up score matched the top-down score (+0.1% at D13, -0.15% at D17), and the intervals include zero. Converting the children that report apparent power to signed flow changed the score by at most 0.03 points, at the one bulk supply point where a child has reverse flow. Even with every child's reading known exactly the BSP's score gains only 12% to 24%, and the children's forecasts gave no detectable gain over the BSP's own chain, so the next gain may lie in forecasting the generators and the unmetered load beneath each BSP. also relevant 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. primary 00131 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-drift-term Adding a slowly varying offset to each substation, fitted jointly with the flows on the interconnection edges, lets the flow fit find injected transfers that last hours to days without putting flow on pairs of substations that are not connected, which experiment 116's fit could not do. inconclusive not-for-production Letting each substation drift slowly did reduce the load that the fit wrongly moves between substations that are not connected, by half to three quarters at an equal or higher detection rate. It did not remove that false load, and the settings that keep it near zero find only about half of the transfers we added artificially and report them too small. In the replicate year part of the false load sits in two jumps in one substation's data that nobody had labelled. We therefore cannot yet read these flows as switching events. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: research plan
docs.text: The proposed next steps are a topology check on candidate flows, or a smaller level penalty combined with a check for unlabelled jumps; neither option is planned. Experiment 116 ended inconclusive because the known-answer gate failed: every setting that found injected transfers also found flow between substations with no interconnection. Experiment 131 added a per-substation drift term. At equal or higher recall the drift term cuts the flow on unconnected pairs by half to three quarters, but no setting meets the recall targets and the placebo limit together, and the level penalty shrinks the flows the fit finds.
