docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling
docs.text:
One XGBoost model shared by a group of Primary substations forecasts almost as well as one model per substation (0.15 points of capacity worse, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), but the one test of a substation outside the pool (8 Primaries, one seed) found fingerprints made it worse, and forecasts of the series beneath 2 bulk supply points added nothing.

Pooling means training one XGBoost model on the rows of several series, with the series identifier as a column, so that 20 models become 3 or 4. The pooling results are from one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026) on 16 Primary substations and 4 supply points, with ENS weather. The hierarchy results cover 2 bulk supply points and 2 grid supply points, and 4 series cannot separate the designs.

Every pooled arm scores worse than one model per series (positive is worse), by 0.15 to 0.29 points with the series identifier and 0.8 to 1.0 without it. Source: experiment 24; C1 to C3 and C5 to C7 use 16 Primary series, and C4, C8, and C9 use all 20 series.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Three or four pooled models score 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models on the 16 Primaries, inside the pre-registered margin of 0.30. The scores are the quantile score over all leads after the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 (the stack of experiment 19, with a half-life of 0.5 years). Per-series models score 5.32, one model per substation type 5.47 (C1, +0.15, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), and one model per capacity band 5.47 (C3, +0.15, +0.05 to +0.26). The type pools beat manual_heuristic (5.89) by 0.42 (exploratory, -0.68 to -0.19). The verdict is supported (experiment 24).

One model for all 20 series falls outside the margin. It scores 5.61 on the 16 Primaries (C2, +0.29, +0.19 to +0.42). On the 2 bulk supply points alone it loses 0.80 (0.64 to 1.00, exploratory, 95%), and the 4 supply points are too few to separate the type pools from per-series models (+0.03, -0.15 to +0.15, exploratory, 95%; experiment 24).

For Primaries, the number of models matters more than which series share one. Random groups of 5 score 5.47 on the 16 Primaries, the same as the type pools. On all 20 series the type pools beat random groups by 0.06 (C9, -0.13 to -0.01), and on the 4 supply points by 0.29 (exploratory, interval not given; experiment 24).

The series identifier is essential. Dropping it raises the score of the type pools by 0.82 (C7, +0.46 to +1.23) and of the all-series pool by 0.85 (C8, +0.72 to +1.00) (experiment 24).

Describing each substation with numbers added nothing to the identifier for series seen in training. Adding a substation's location, its mean level and shape over the training window, or its level over the previous 14 days to the identifier moved the score by at most 0.02 points (C1 to C4; C4, +0.02, 99.375% interval -0.05 to +0.10). The verdict is inconclusive by the pre-registered rule, though the data exclude a gain above 0.05. Training-window statistics alone, without the identifier, scored 0.01 points worse than the identifier (C5, 99.375% interval +0.00 to +0.02, inside the 0.15 margin; experiment 32).

A substation held out of the pool was forecast worse with training-window statistics than with no fingerprint (C7, +1.39, +0.99 to +1.91), and better with recent power statistics alone (post hoc, -0.23, -0.29 to -0.16, 95%). The test used 8 held-out Primaries, one seed, and a pool of 7 other series. The write-up suggests, without testing it, that 7 distinct fingerprints act as 7 identifiers (experiment 32).

Forecasts of the series beneath a bulk supply point did not lower its score. Adding the summed median forecasts of the Primaries and generators beneath a bulk supply point changed its score by +0.04 (99.17% interval -0.18 to +0.25) at Boston and +0.19 (-0.10 to +0.73) at Skegness. At the 2 grid supply points, generic wind and solar columns changed it by -0.02 (-0.06 to +0.03) and -0.04 (-0.13 to +0.07). The pre-registered rule marks the bulk-supply-point family and the wind-and-solar family refuted and the ERA5-trained family inconclusive, so the experiment is inconclusive (experiment 36).

The six planned contrasts all include zero; the two exploratory rows are the ERA5-trained N1 at the bulk supply points, and Boston's excludes it.

An N1 trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40, but its intervals span -1.8 to +1.0. N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model. Only Boston, a bulk supply point, resolved a gain, of 0.41 (0.15 to 0.66, exploratory, 95%) (experiment 36).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the pooled designs tested, one model per capacity band or per substation type scored best, and with the 14-day correction none beat one model per series on the 16 Primaries.

  1. Train an XGBoost quantile model (experiment 24's recipe, N1 fitted per group instead of per series: 9 quantile levels, ENS control member, lead hour, calendar columns, three power lags, power scaled by each series' effective capacity) on 3 capacity bands (the series split into thirds by effective capacity) or 4 substation types. Each pool holds all 20 series, including the 4 supply points.
  2. Give every XGBoost model the series identifier as a categorical column.
  3. Apply the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 to each series' quantiles.

The capacity-band and type pools score the same to two decimals (experiment 24). The pre-registered rule chose capacity bands because they have fewer models.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiment 24 is candidate; experiments 32 and 36 are not-for-production.

  • Pooled XGBoost models for Primary demand (experiment 24). The XGBoost forecaster would train 3 or 4 models instead of 20 and store them at 73 to 94 MB instead of 435 MB, for a loss of 0.15 points of quantile score on the 16 Primaries, with the 14-day correction. Each model would need the series identifier, and a new series would need a retrain. The test covered 20 series, so it says nothing about 2,500 substations.
  • Nothing from experiments 32 or 36 is ready. No fingerprint helped a series seen in training, and no forecast column lowered a bulk or grid supply point's score.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Keep the series identifier in every pooled model. Without it, the type pools lost 0.82 and the all-series pool 0.85 (experiment 24). Re-check with a different model type or a different pool of substations.
  • Score pooled arms with and without the 14-day correction. The correction lowers per-series models by 1.0 and type pools by 0.6, so type pools beat per-series models by 0.30 uncorrected (exploratory, 95%, -0.56 to -0.03) and lose 0.15 corrected (experiment 24). A ranking measured on one stack may not carry to another. Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Scale boosting rounds (the number of trees) with the pool size, or say they were not scaled. Experiment 24 fixed 500 rounds and depth 6, so the all-series loss may be partly lower capacity per series. Re-check with rounds scaled to rows.
  • Do not compare fit seconds across arms. Other sessions loaded the machine during the capacity-band and random-group fits of experiment 24, so only model counts and saved sizes are reliable. Re-check with timings on an idle machine.
  • Match a held-out substation's fingerprint window to the pool's. The held-out substation's 28-day statistics differed from the pool's 15-month ones, and using the whole window removed about two thirds of the C7 damage (post hoc; experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Do not read the oracle's gain as headroom for forecasts. The oracle is the same XGBoost model given the observed values of the series beneath a bulk supply point. It lowered the score by 5.6 and 3.4, while forecasts of those series lowered it by none (experiment 36). Re-check if the child forecasts come from a different weather source.
  • Note how the columns of forecasts of the series beneath a supply point were built. Experiment 36 fitted them by time block, so a block's forecasting model saw months on both sides, and training used the ENS control member while validation used each member. Look for a gain that changes when the columns are fitted strictly out of time, or when training uses every member.
  • Do not compare supply-point scores across experiments 24 and 36. Experiment 24 applies the 14-day correction to all 20 series, including the 4 supply points. Experiment 36 left it off at supply points because experiment 21 found it unproven there, so its scores are uncorrected. Re-check when a supply-point experiment states which stack it used.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether pooling holds at hundreds of series, and for substations the pool never saw.
  • Whether supply points pool at all; 4 series cannot say.
  • Whether an N1 trained on ERA5 helps at supply points beyond Boston.
  • Whether one model shared across substations, with drift and long history, beats separate models. That is the subject of the differentiable-physics background and the sub-themes long history and drift and demand calendar and weather.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and Experiments lists every experiment. Experiment 103 appears there as also relevant: its data look fixes the rows and dates the pooled differentiable-physics model uses, and it has no pooling result.

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. primary 00204 dp-bsp-full-bottom-up-with-signed-mva-children A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down when the sum covers every child Primary. Experiment 161 summed only the three children per BSP that report real power (MW) and have a long history, which reached 42% of D13's effective capacity and 56% of D17's, and the bottom-up forecast scored 0.5% to 0.6% worse than the top-down forecast. This experiment adds the children that report apparent power (MVA). A child's apparent-power reading is the magnitude of its flow, so a child with reverse flow at midday needs a signed flow before it can enter a sum. The fold-aware model of experiment 152 supplies that signed flow as a latent variable. inconclusive not-for-production Adding every child Primary to the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point: the bottom-up score matched the top-down score (+0.1% at D13, -0.15% at D17), and the intervals include zero. Converting the children that report apparent power to signed flow changed the score by at most 0.03 points, at the one bulk supply point where a child has reverse flow. Even with every child's reading known exactly the BSP's score gains only 12% to 24%, and the children's forecasts gave no detectable gain over the BSP's own chain, so the next gain may lie in forecasting the generators and the unmetered load beneath each BSP. primary 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) fitted jointly across six Primary substations, so that each substation's heating curve, lighting curve, daily profile, holiday effects, and Christmas shape are a fleet mean plus a penalised deviation of its own, forecasts better than the same model fitted to each substation alone, now that the solar capacity is pinned and the filter handles recent switching. The mechanism is that a substation sees only two winters and two Christmases in a 24-month window, so its own curves are noisy, and five other substations carry information about the shapes that physically are shared. Capacity, level, and the band means stay per substation. The gain is largest for a substation with 3 months of history and on Christmas rows, and no pooled arm is worse than the per-site fit by more than 0.02 points on ordinary rows. partly supported candidate In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. also relevant 00154 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-2-heating-error-against-truth When the partly pooled convex regression model of experiment 109 is fitted to only 4 winter weeks of one substation, its fitted heating curve is closer to the injected truth than the curves of the no-pooling and complete-pooling fits. The curve is as close to the truth as a fair oracle's curve (within 10%). The model recovers the sign of the substation's own heating offset relative to the fleet's curve. The fleet's shared curve is recovered as well as an average of per-site fits recovers it. partly supported not-for-production On synthetic substations with a known answer, a partly pooled demand model fitted to 4 winter weeks of one substation estimated that substation's heating response with a smaller error than fitting the substation alone (2.8 to 3.6 against 4.1 to 11.5 points of capacity) and than copying the fleet's curve (3.4 to 4.6), on every seed. It recovered the fleet's shared curve about as well as separate fits did. Neither the pooled fit nor the fair oracle recovered the sign of the substation's own heating offset reliably (the pooled fit got the sign right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds), so on these synthetic fleets and one January, a partly pooled model can share the heating curve but cannot learn a substation's own offset from 4 weeks. also relevant 00150 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-rerun-fair-oracle-five-seeds When the reference estimator estimates every coefficient from the same 4 weeks of rows (so that no coefficient is fixed at its true value), the partially pooled convex model of experiment 109 recovers the injected truth about as well as that reference on most of 5 random seeds, and its tuning rule picks a deviation penalty within one grid step of the best one on most of the 5 seeds. inconclusive not-for-production The rerun of the synthetic known-answer test could not say whether the pooled model shrinks substation deviations correctly, because a control that keeps no deviation at all passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when 4 June weeks were held. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 synthetic substations on every seed, the tuning rule picked a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error was below a fair reference estimator's on 5 of 5 seeds. The full-history line passed on only 2 of 5 seeds. A post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks separated the controls, so a test that scores heating error against the injected truth in winter should settle the question. also relevant 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. also relevant 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00036 hierarchy-aware-bsp-gsp-forecasts For the two bulk supply points (BSPs) Boston and Skegness and the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, forecasts of the series beneath each point, and an N1 model trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members, lower the quantile score below that of N1 trained on ENS. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasts of the series beneath two bulk supply points added nothing (+0.04 and +0.19 points of capacity), nor did wind and solar columns at two grid supply points; an N1 trained on ERA5 lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40 with intervals spanning -1.8 to +1.0. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. primary

docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction
docs.text:
On 16 Primary substations over one validation year, both recent power fed to a second-stage calibrator and a correction by the mean error of the last 14 days lower the forecast error, by similar amounts against different reference forecasts; on solar farms, wind farms, and supply points neither has been shown to help.

Recent measured power can enter the forecast as input, or shift the forecast by its recent errors. The experiments put lagged power into stage 1b (a second model that corrects the weather-only forecast) or into the stage 2 calibrator, and tested variants of the 14-day correction. All scores are the quantile score in points of capacity, and lower is better. The five experiments of this theme scored 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days from July 2025 to June 2026. Other experiments cited use other run sets, stated where cited. Stage 1a is the weather-only forecast, trained on ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather.

Lagged power in the calibrator scored better than lagged power in stage 1b in every lead band (C1, stage 1b with a lag-free calibrator minus the calibrator with lags, where positive means stage 1b is worse; 99% intervals; 16 Primary substations). Source: experiment 5.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Recent power lowers the error, and it lowers it more in the calibrator than in stage 1b. For 16 Primary substations up to 48 hours ahead, the calibrator with lagged power scored 5.31, stage 1b with a calibrator that sees no lags scored 6.14, and a calibrator with no lags scored 7.11. The contrast is +0.84 (+0.28 to +1.50 at 99%), so the pre-registered idea that stage 1b is the better place was refuted. Using both placements lowered the score by at most 0.12 more. Stage 1b scored better at 8 of the 16 series, so the average hides a mixed result (experiment 5).

Summaries of recent power added no resolvable gain to the raw lags. Adding the minimum, mean, and maximum of the last 24 hours and of the same weekday changed the score by -0.02 (-0.14 to +0.13 at 98.75%; inconclusive). Replacing the raw lags with the summaries worsened it by 0.29 (+0.11 to +0.51). Summaries alone still beat no recent power (-1.18, -1.83 to -0.58) (experiment 8). Experiment 30 tested more lag columns in N1 and is on the demand inputs page.

With only the data a live service has, the two-stage chain is not distinguishable from N1. The lagged inputs of experiments 5 and 8 use estimates of past weather that a live service lacks, so they are ceilings. Experiment 18 rebuilt them from weather available at the forecast origin and from NGED's real telemetry delay (the wait before a power reading arrives; 7 hours). Over all leads the chain minus N1 was +0.08 (-0.11 to +0.25 at 99.17%; inconclusive). Up to 48 hours it was -0.27 (-0.62 to +0.03), and beyond 3 days +0.15 (-0.07 to +0.36). The chain scored 0.52 above the manual_heuristic baseline (-0.25 to +1.25; interval includes zero). Lag anomalies lowered the score by only 0.04 against raw lagged power (-0.12 to +0.07).

The chain is level with N1, and above manual_heuristic beyond 3 days (point estimate; the interval includes zero). Source: experiment 18.

The 14-day correction lowered the Primary score by about 1 point, a gain of similar size to lagged power in the calibrator against a different reference. Experiments 19 and 21 scored the correction on the same 73 runs and 16 Primary substations as experiments 5 and 18. N1 plus the correction scored 5.34 over all leads, against 6.33 for N1. The chain of experiment 18 scored 6.41, and lagged power in that chain gained -1.05 (-1.64 to -0.58) against a calibrator without lags (experiment 18, C2). The references differ and no paired interval compares them. Experiment 19 (power 3.5 hours old) gave -0.99 (-1.84 to -0.15 at 99.44%). Experiment 21 gave -0.99 (-1.82 to -0.18 at 99.375%) with power 2 days old. Experiment 19 is on the production reference and best guess page.

The correction lowered the Primary score, no variant beat the plain 14-day additive form, and the correction did not lower the score of the 4 bulk and grid supply point series. Source: experiment 21.

No variant of the correction beat the plain 14-day additive form on Primary substations. A 7-day window was worse (+0.19, +0.11 to +0.28), a 28-day window was level or slightly better (-0.07, -0.15 to +0.01), a multiplicative form was far worse (+2.28, +0.50 to +5.46), and a per-half-hour shift (+0.02) and recency weights (+0.04) changed nothing (experiment 21).

The correction is unproven for supply points, solar farms, and wind farms. On 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98 at 99.375%; inconclusive; experiment 21) and by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594) in the BG2 ablation on 292 daily runs (experiment 87). On 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms (53 Tuesday runs), lagged power left the calibrator's CRPS unchanged to about 0.1 points, and the correction raised it for solar (+0.437, +0.215 to +0.664) and did not clearly change it for wind (+0.413, -0.003 to +0.924) (experiment 23).

Lags near switching were tested in two other themes. Training with lags hidden at random did not widen the 5% to 95% band where a lag is missing. On 292 daily runs, the band covered 0.799 of real masked half-hours (37,394) for the plain model and 0.802 with lags hidden in 10% of rows, against 0.90 nominal (+0.003, -0.093 to +0.101 at 98.75%; inconclusive; experiment 100). Telling a monthly-refitted XGBoost model how unusual each lag is raised the score outside switching by 0.355 (+0.209 to +0.513 at 97.5%; refuted; experiment 90).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the designs tested in this theme, the stage 2 calibrator with raw lagged power is the best use of lagged power, and the additive 14-day correction is the best correction.

  1. Give the stage 2 calibrator (arm L3, the calibrator with lagged power, of experiment 5) the power 24, 48, 168, and 336 hours before the target, the four stage 1a residuals at those times, and five residuals at the newest observation. Keep the raw lags (experiment 8).
  2. For a live service, build the lag residuals from weather available at the origin (experiment 18), and apply a spread factor of 1.15 (-0.04, -0.08 to -0.00). This design did not beat N1.
  3. For Primary substations, add the mean error of the last 14 days of the forecast median to every quantile, using a window of 14 days or longer and an additive shift (experiment 21). No experiment combined the chain with the correction.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: No experiment in this theme is marked candidate; all five are not-for-production. The correction for Primary demand is a candidate in experiments 19, 33, and 87, described on the production reference and best guess page, and experiment 30 is a candidate on the demand inputs page. Experiment 21 supports the correction with power 2 days old, which gave the same all-lead gain as power 3.5 hours old, so the service need not wait for fresher telemetry. It supports no use at supply points.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Compare a lagged arm with a calibrated arm that has no lags. A calibrator without lags lowered the stage 1a score by 1.02 up to 48 hours (exploratory contrast E4, whose interval includes zero at some leads), and stage 1a alone scored 8.12 against 8.14 for day-type climatology. Against stage 1a alone, lags look about 1 point better than they are (experiment 5). Look for a lagged arm whose comparison has no calibrator.
  • Label an arm a ceiling when its lag residuals use estimates of past weather. The arms of experiments 5 and 8 used ERA5 at lag times, and rebuilding them from serving sources worsened the score by 0.13 (+0.02 to +0.25; experiment 18). Re-check with a different weather source for the lag times.
  • State the telemetry delay of every lagged arm. Experiment 5 used 0.5 hours (the newest half-hour before the origin), experiment 13 3.5 hours, and experiment 18 7 hours. Three and a half hours more delay worsened the chain by 0.13 over all leads and 0.16 up to 48 hours, so scores with different delays do not compare (experiment 18). Re-check on a different delay.
  • Report how many series agree with the mean. C1 of experiment 5 (above) was +0.84 on average while stage 1b was better at 8 of the 16 Primary substations (experiment 5). Look for a mean over series with mixed signs.
  • Do not correct a skewed target by the mean of observed minus median. That shift raised the solar CRPS by 0.437 and the wind CRPS by 0.413 (interval includes zero) and cut the 5% to 95% coverage to 53% to 77%. A median shift was tried once, post hoc, and moved the CRPS by +0.010 for solar and -0.064 for wind, with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). Re-check with a pre-registered median shift.
  • Check the base forecast's bias before applying the correction. N1's two bulk supply point series had a bias of +0.01, so the correction only added noise (experiment 21), and in experiment 87 a frozen model with the correction scored 13.559 against 13.369 without it (experiment 87). Look for a base forecast with little bias.
  • Build the correction's error history from the runs a live service would have. Experiments 19 and 21 measured each past half-hour's error from a run 0 to 5 days earlier, with runs 5 days apart, and applied it up to 15 days ahead. A daily service sees smaller errors at shorter leads, and experiment 87 scored the correction on 292 daily runs (experiment 19, experiment 21). Look for a run schedule other than every 5 days.
  • Keep a control that keeps the event rows when testing masked lags. Dropping event and closure rows from training (the mask arm, which also sets lags inside labelled events to missing) narrowed the band on unmasked rows by 4% and lowered its coverage from 0.906 to 0.894, so the masked arms differ from the plain model in more than the dropout (experiment 100). The masked rows came from an estimated 15 to 20 events, mostly at three substations. Look for a masked arm without a control that keeps the rows.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether lagged power helps once the correction is in place: no experiment here combined them.
  • Whether the staged chain beats N1 at leads up to 2 days. Its point estimate was lower there, but the interval includes zero.
  • Whether the correction helps supply points when more than 4 series are scored, or helps solar and wind farms when it uses a median shift.
  • Whether an input that flags a missing lag, or a separate model of the band width, widens the band where a lag is missing. Experiment 100 tested only random dropout.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00222 dp-network-before-filter-order Experiments 200 and 201 correct arm D after the Kalman filter. Their gain is mostly a systematic error of the convex model at some temperatures and loads, not a recent-error effect, and that systematic error currently sits in the filter's level state. A network that reads only the convex model's own output and inputs, and corrects the convex model before the filter, leaves the filter a cleaner residual stream and so beats the same kind of network applied after the filter. inconclusive not-for-production The gain of the network after the filter does not come from the convex model's own systematic error as seen in its past residuals. A network trained on those residuals learned patterns that do not carry to the next year, and when it was stopped on a later year it learned nothing and left the score unchanged. The test could not settle the order question, because the network failed to recover a known injected error. also relevant 00205 dp-gamk-gap-robustness-coast-or-frozen-gam When power readings go missing, a Kalman filter that coasts (keeps running with no update, so the transient decays and the level holds) beats the frozen convex model (GAM) alone for short gaps and loses to it for long gaps, so a crossover gap length exists between 6 and 72 hours. The mechanism is that the level is a random walk, so a short gap leaves it nearly right, while a long gap lets it drift away from the demand. Widening the quantile bands by the filter's own growth in predictive variance keeps the 5% and 95% quantiles calibrated at the gap lengths where coasting is still better than the frozen model. inconclusive candidate When readings stop for 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours, keep running the Kalman filter, which corrects the convex demand model using its recent forecast errors, without feeding it new readings, and widen the quantile bands. At each of those four gap lengths that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction (a quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better; the gain is 8% to 14% of the uncorrected model's score). At 72 hours the 99.4% bootstrap interval for the gain runs from 0.04 to 0.48 points, so the gain may be small. The data cannot show whether dropping only the filter beats coasting after a gap of about 72 hours: at every gap length the difference between the two forecasts is smaller than the variation between months. The forecast with the filter, winter night offset, and recipe R was still 0.025 points worse than its no-gap score 48 hours after a 24-hour gap ended. The filter alone was within 0.02 points of its no-gap score 24 hours after the gap ended. also relevant 00201 dp-gam-residual-mlp A small neural network that reads the convex model's own design features, and later the calendar, the ensemble-mean weather, and lagged power, can learn an interaction the additive convex model lacks, and so lowers the quantile score of the best-guess convex forecast (arm D of experiment 155) when it adds a correction to the median and rescales the band widths. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network that reads the convex demand model's forecast lowers that forecast's quantile score by about 0.09 points (3%), and adding weather, calendar, or recent power does not help further. The neural network corrects an under-forecast on very hot and very cold days. That points to a missing temperature term in the convex demand model. The correction also scores worse on bank holidays and, in point estimate, on Christmas. also relevant 00200 dp-pooled-correction-head-on-kalman-state Experiment 142's small network failed its known-answer gate with about 1,100 samples from one year at five substations. The same kind of network, trained on rows pooled across many Primary substations and years, learns to correct arm D's forecast from the recent errors, the calendar, the lead, and the ensemble-mean weather, and so beats recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days) at day D+1. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network trained on arm D's own past errors lowers the day-ahead score by 0.07 to 0.12 points at five substations, but a copy that sees no recent error gets most of that gain. The gain comes from correcting how arm D's error depends on its forecast level and the calendar, and a pinball-loss table comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the network on one year of data. also relevant 00197 dp-kalman-level-adaptation-retest Experiment 190's known-answer gate could not be passed by a filter with one state per hour band, because the target's band is usually unread since an offset began. Scored only on pairs the filter can know about, (a) a faster per-band filter (A1) recovers at least 50% of a 0.10-size, 16-hour offset on target bands already read, and (b) a filter whose bands share one level while a same-sign run lasts (A3) recovers at least 50% on target bands not yet read, because it moves bands that no reading has reached. not supported not-for-production Making the Kalman filter's level state faster does not fix offsets that last for hours. Faster settings recover a long offset only late, and only by scoring worse on quiet days, and a level shared across the four hour bands recovered under a fifth of the offset, because its run counter cannot tell an offset from noise. No setting on the grid tried recovered an injected offset without scoring worse on quiet days, so level adaptation is dropped. also relevant 00190 dp-kalman-level-adaptation-gated-boost The Kalman filter of the convex demand model (GAM-K) has a level state that is a random walk with one shared process-noise setting. A single setting must trade speed on a real level shift against noise on ordinary days. A gate that multiplies the level's process noise by m only while the last k one-step innovations (pooled over the four hour bands) share one sign and their mean exceeds z times the day-before innovation spread gives speed when a shift looks real and keeps the quiet setting otherwise. The mechanism predicts that the gate lowers the excess loss on days where the residual keeps one sign for hours (the 15 smooth-offset days of experiment 175), without harming ordinary days. inconclusive not-for-production A Kalman filter whose level state speeds up when the residual keeps one sign scored the same as the current filter (+0.0002 points), and an always-fast version scored 0.023 points worse. The test cannot say that filter speed is useless: its known-answer gate could not have been passed by any filter with one state per hour band, and a faster filter did recover offsets where they were visible. A fair test needs a redesigned gate and a wider grid of multipliers. also relevant 00168 dp-gamk-production-cadence-and-3-5-hour-delay The GAM-K forecast of experiment 155's arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, the winter night offset, and recipe R) keeps its score when it is issued the way production would issue it. Production refreshes the forecast every 6 hours from the newest ECMWF run, so the weather forecast is 12 to 30 hours old, and the filter reads only power readings that are at least 3.5 hours old. Experiments 136 and 155 issued one forecast a day, 9 hours after the run. The mechanism is that a fresher filter state makes up for an older weather forecast, so the score at a given lead changes little. inconclusive not-for-production Issued every 6 hours from the newest weather forecast with power readings 3.5 hours old, the stage 2 forecast scores about the same as the once-a-day forecast over the next 24 hours (-0.007 points, 99% interval -0.076 to +0.037). The largest loss, 0.073 points, falls between 09:00 and 12:00 UTC, when the new weather run has arrived and the 6-hourly schedule has not yet used it. The pre-registered same-lead contrast read +0.076 but is confounded with the hour of the day, so the formal verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) that already has the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, the pinned solar capacity, and the ensemble mean as its weather input (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when two post-forecast corrections are added: a winter night offset (experiment 137) and the 14-day mean error profile of recipe R (experiment 115). The mechanism is that the two corrections remove different errors, a level error that repeats on winter nights and a half-hour-of-day shape error that repeats day to day, so their gains add. The assembled arm then scores below experiment 111's GAM-K and BG2 (experiment 87) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, and its tails on cold nights and on holidays are no worse than the uncorrected arm's. inconclusive candidate Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. also relevant 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k Averaging GAM-K's past day-ahead errors over the days most similar to the target day (same day type, with holiday identity for holidays, similar forecast daily mean temperature, and a season window of a few weeks either side of the date) gives a better correction than averaging the last 14 days alike (recipe R of experiment 115) or the same-day-type days of the last few weeks (experiment 134). The reasoning is that demand errors repeat on days that resemble each other. The errors that repeat most, on holidays and on cold days, are the ones that a 14-day average dilutes. small gain candidate Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. also relevant 00144 differentiable-physics-weather-forecast-bias-persistence-on-gam-k The day-ahead error of the ensemble weather forecast (temperature and irradiance) repeats from one day to the next, so the trailing mean of recent weather errors can correct GAM-K's demand forecast beyond what the Kalman filter already does. refuted not-for-production In this test, the day-ahead temperature and irradiance forecasts did not repeat their errors from one day to the next: the correlation between one day's error and the next day's was at most +0.11, against a stop threshold of 0.2. A correction that feeds recent weather errors into the demand forecast therefore has little signal to use, so no demand forecast was fitted. Two caveats apply: wind was not tested, because experiment 111's ensemble store does not hold it, and the reference was a later forecast (the analysis proxy), not observed weather, so a bias against observations is not ruled out. also relevant 00143 differentiable-physics-holiday-aware-updating-of-the-gam-k-filter The Kalman filter of GAM-K lets a holiday's reading error teach it a wrong level, which carries into the days after the holiday; leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update (and nothing else) lowers the day-ahead score on those following days, and does not hurt the holiday targets or the rest of the year. not supported not-for-production Leaving holiday readings out of the day-ahead filter's update does not reliably help the days after a holiday: the effect had the opposite sign after Christmas 2024 and Christmas 2025, and its 99% interval in the scored year (-0.309 to +0.036 points) includes zero. In 10 of 12 holidays, the holiday readings' error had the same sign as the error on the following days, so these readings are not usually contamination. Setting the correction to zero on holiday days, as experiment 118 did, is the action that hurts (+0.62 points on holiday days). Two Christmases give no basis for changing the filter this Christmas. also relevant 00142 differentiable-physics-sequence-model-on-gam-k-residuals A small neural network that reads GAM-K's last 14 days of residuals, the calendar, and the target day's forecast weather predicts the day-ahead residual better than the hand-built Kalman filter with the 14-day error profile (recipe R of experiment 115), and gives better tails when it is trained with the pinball loss at the 11 quantiles. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the last 14 days of GAM-K's errors did not learn to adapt to changes in them: when we added a known step or a Saturday-evening shift to real errors, it recovered none of it, so we did not score it on the scored year. Nothing was scored, so this result does not compare it with the hand-built Kalman filter and recipe R. also relevant 00135 differentiable-physics-n10-joint-kalman-and-demand-fit Fitting the convex demand model (GAM-K) so that its coefficients minimise the day-ahead error after the Kalman correction, instead of the plain error before it, lowers the day-ahead quantile score at 12 to 36 hours below the two-stage fit (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals), without moving the fitted shapes to explain recent-level structure that the filter already tracks. not supported not-for-production We fitted the demand model so that its coefficients minimise the error left after a Kalman filter (a running correction of recent errors) has adjusted the forecast. That made the day-ahead forecast much worse, because the filter can absorb a shift in the slow parts of the demand model, so the fit barely constrains those parts. Tying the fit to the two-stage coefficients removed the damage and also removed any gain: the quantile score was within 0.013 points of the two-stage score, in either direction. The two-stage design (fit the demand model, then filter its residuals) stays. also relevant 00134 differentiable-physics-same-weekday-error-profile-on-gam-k Adding a same-weekday component to the 14-day all-days error profile (recipe R of experiment 115) lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score, because demand errors repeat from week to week (Saturdays differ from Tuesdays) and the all-days profile averages that structure away. not supported not-for-production The gain is too small to count: using the same weekday's recent errors, instead of the last 14 days' errors alike, lowers the day-ahead error by about 0.011 points (0.5%) at five Primary substations, and the scored-year interval includes zero. The gain is on Mondays and Fridays and is absent midweek. Grouping days into five day types did better than seven separate weekdays, so day types are the version to test next, with the profile limited to day D+1. also relevant 00133 differentiable-physics-vk-learned-noise-and-observation-variance-in-gam-k On GAM-K's filter (a level and a transient per hour band, per substation), noise settings chosen per substation by day-ahead score lower the day-ahead quantile score below the fixed settings of experiment 111, which were chosen by marginal likelihood on 184 non-contiguous days. An online observation variance in the manner of VIKING (de Vilmarest and Wintenberger, 2022), used to scale the spread, then improves the coverage of the 0.95 quantile on cold nights, which experiment 125 found at 73% to 78%, because recent large errors widen the spread. The mechanism under test is that the size of recent proxy-driven residuals predicts the size of the next day's error on cold nights. inconclusive not-for-production Choosing the filter's noise settings for each substation by how well they forecast the next day did not improve the forecast on later months: the gain of 0.044 points on the months used to choose shrank to 0.009 on the scored year, inside the noise. A single setting shared by every substation did at least as well as the per-substation settings, so tuning the filter's noise per substation looks unnecessary, although the grid did not find a minimum. Letting the observation variance follow recent errors did not widen the forecast where it matters, on cold nights, where the 0.95 quantile still covered only 86% to 88% of readings. also relevant 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. also relevant 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. also relevant 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00108 differentiable-physics-shared-anomaly-factor-across-substations The residuals of the frozen convex demand model carry a component shared across Primaries, and a shared state estimated from the other substations' residuals, available at the forecast origin, lowers the day-ahead quantile score by more than the per-site Kalman filter of Part 4 already does. inconclusive not-for-production The experiment stopped at its known-answer gate, where three of seven tests failed, so it cannot say whether a shared factor improves the forecast. On injected anomalies the shared filter, tuned on 2023-24, carried under 5% of the injected points (the plan asked for 40% or more), and it corrected no better than the per-site filter (2.402 against 2.397 points of mean absolute error over days 2 and 3 of the episodes). Part of the test was mis-specified, so a corrected test would be needed before any real score. primary 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00100 drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals An XGBoost quantile model for Primary substation demand that is trained with labelled switching half-hours removed from its targets and with its lagged power inputs set to missing at random intervals, and that has those lags set to missing when they lie inside a labelled switching event, widens its 5% to 95% band on the half-hours whose lags are missing, so that the band's coverage moves from 0.784 towards the nominal 0.90, without widening the band elsewhere. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand forecast with lags hidden at random did not make its band wider on half-hours where a lag is missing: on real rows the band covered 0.80 (hidden in 10% of training rows) to 0.84 (30%) of actuals, against a nominal 0.90. Hiding lags in 30% of rows did remove the accuracy loss that masking alone causes on injected transfers (-0.02 points, 95% interval -0.35 to +0.38 against the plain model). Hiding lags in 10% of rows left +0.26 (98.75% interval -0.15 to +0.85), not separable from zero or from the loss. An input that tells the XGBoost model a lag is missing, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, are untested routes to a wider band. also relevant 00021 error-correction-variants-bsp-gsp-demand A recent-error correction of N1's quantiles, measured with power that is 2 days old, lowers the quantile score of the 4 bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) demand series as it does for the 16 Primary substations, and some variant of the correction (a 7-day or 28-day window, multiplicative, per-half-hour-of-day, or weighting recent days more) beats the plain 14-day additive correction. inconclusive not-for-production The 14-day additive correction lowered the Primary quantile score by 0.99 points of capacity (99.375% interval -1.82 to -0.18) when the newest power was 2 days old, as it did with 3.5-hour-old power in experiment 19. On the 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98), so it is unproven there. No variant beat the plain additive 14-day form: a 7-day window was worse (+0.19) and a multiplicative form far worse (+2.28). primary 00018 staged-chain-vs-n1-serving-latency-lag-anomalies-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, the staged chain (an ERA5-trained stage 1 and the stage 2 calibrator, with lag anomalies built only from weather that serving has at the forecast origin, and NGED's real telemetry delay) beats the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 and manual_heuristic on the quantile score. inconclusive not-for-production With lagged inputs built only from data a live service has, including NGED's real telemetry delay, the two-stage chain was not distinguishable from the single-stage N1 over all leads: 6.41 against 6.33, a difference of +0.08 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.11 to +0.25; positive means the chain is worse). Up to 48 hours the chain was 0.27 lower (-0.62 to +0.03). It scored 0.52 above the stored manual_heuristic baseline (-0.25 to +1.25), so the staged design is not supported for demand on this evidence. primary 00008 lag-summaries-in-stage2-calibrator-demand For Primary substation demand series, giving the stage 2 calibrator the minimum, mean, and maximum of the most recent 24 hours of power, and of the most recent day on the same weekday as the target, lowers the probabilistic forecast's error below that of the calibrator with only the raw power lags (experiment 00005's L3). inconclusive not-for-production Adding the minimum, mean, and maximum of the last 24 hours of power, and of the same weekday, to a calibrator that already had raw power lags changed the quantile score by -0.02 points of capacity up to 48 hours ahead (98.75% interval -0.14 to +0.13), which cannot be told from no change. Replacing the raw lags with the summaries worsened the score by 0.29 (+0.11 to +0.51), so keep the raw lags. Summaries alone, with no estimate-of-past-weather residual, beat no recent power by 1.18 (-1.83 to -0.58). primary 00005 lag-placement-stage1b-vs-stage2-demand For substation demand series, recent observed power improves a two-stage probabilistic forecast more when it enters stage 1 through a residual-persistence XGBoost model (stage 1b) than when it enters only the stage 2 calibrator, when both placements are given identical inputs and both outputs are calibrated. refuted not-for-production For Primary substations, recent power lowered the forecast error more when it went into the second-stage calibrator than when it went into a stage 1b correction model. Up to 48 hours ahead the calibrator scored 5.31 against 6.14, so stage 1b was worse by 0.84 points of capacity (99% interval +0.28 to +1.50); using both added at most 0.12 points. These are ceilings, because the lagged inputs used estimates of past weather that a live service lacks, and stage 1b was better at 8 of the 16 series. primary
