docs.title: LSC detectors
docs.text:
The best switching detector, RO-NC, finds most of the moved power (the megawatts a transfer moves) of injected load transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, but only about a third of that of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, and no experiment yet shows that using a detector improves a forecast.

A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. Detectors find these transfers from power readings alone. We score them on injected transfers, whose start, end, and size are known, and on 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day that a language model and a hand filter judged visible. The real transfers include 21 under 25% of the receiving load, so the two scores are not like for like. All results are from the lab, on 16 Primary series, and use hindsight to place the end of each transfer.

RO-NC and the refit-offset detector (X) find the most moved power on the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day (RO-NC 0.357), and the 35 are too few to rank them. Source: experiment 101.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
On injected transfers, RO-NC finds 0.770 of the moved power, against 0.656 for the benchmark PF14. The difference is +0.114 (+0.074 to +0.182; experiment 82). Neither part helps transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. Recall here is MW-weighted.

  • Not ignoring alarms near the monthly refit of the demand model removes PF14's blind spot: a second model refitted half a month later gave +0.050 (+0.012 to +0.107), and lifting the suppression alone gave +0.056 (+0.016 to +0.113), so the second model adds nothing on injected transfers (experiment 71).
  • Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation: +0.048 (+0.021 to +0.096; experiment 70).

On real transfers, RO-NC finds fewer than injected transfers of the same step size and metering predict: 12 of the 35 lasting over 1 day (0.357 of their moved power; 0.169 to 0.553), against 18.8 expected, and none of the 31 shorter ones. On the 14 real transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, it finds 0.559 (0.203 to 0.816), an interval that includes 0.770, so that band alone shows no gap, but it finds 6 of those 14 where 10.5 are expected. Of the 35, 6 sit where the detector's residual panel holds no readings and 12 have a step under 4 noise units, and even the 17 with readings and a larger step are found less often than injected ones; the verdict is partly supported (experiment 101).

RO-NC finds none of the real transfers shorter than 1 day, and more of those moving 25% or more of the receiving load than of those without a metered receiver (all 66 real transfers).

RO-NC misses small steps, mostly where the receiver is unmetered. Of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, it finds 6 of 14 of 25% or more of the receiving load and 2 of 10 with no metered receiver. Among injected transfers that step by 4 noise units or more, the single-series detector D0 found 0.56 with a metered receiver and 0.35 without (experiment 58). Before the PF14 end rule, a wrong interval end was most of D0's misses among large transfers with a metered receiver, and about a third of its misses among transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more (experiment 59, experiment 60).

The early detectors D0 and D1 each found under a fifth of 600 injected transfers (experiment 43). Moving D0's interval end to the strongest opposite step found +0.191 more (+0.148 to +0.237; experiment 61), and the post hoc rule PF14 did better (0.688 against 0.646, no paired interval; experiment 66).

The changes listed here found no clear gain. Each was tested against a detector without it, at the same number of unexplained alarms. Refuted: several averaging windows (experiment 59), profile-weighted steps (experiment 60), whitening the residual (experiment 62), scoring onset and return steps as a pair (experiment 61), and one joint fit across substations (experiment 67). Inconclusive or partly supported: a bank-holiday column (experiment 47), a neighbour veto (experiments 55 and 58), refitting without detected transfers (experiment 68), solar and heating corrections (experiment 98), a joint linear fit of solar and transfer terms (experiment 63, of the differentiable-physics demand sub-theme), and accepting weaker onset alarms (experiment 69), and adding neighbours' opposite-sign steps to a substation's own step (+0.019, -0.011 to +0.062; experiment 65).

Using a detector has not yet improved a forecast, in one validation year (experiments 44 and 86) or four (experiment 38) on 16 Primary series. In each result below, a positive change means a worse forecast.

  • Masking: leaving the half-hours that D1 flags out of the 7-day error correction of the stack (experiment 17's H0.5 proxy, with a half-life of 0.5 years) raised the tail error outside logged switching by 57% (0.4% to 134%), because one interval ran for 60 days. A mask from NGED's logs lowered it on the 14-day correction by 8.9% (-21.8% to 0.0%), 95% of that in one closure (experiment 38).
  • Ceiling: in the band of events the labeller finds most reliably (3 of the 16 Primaries), a perfect detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (-0.47% to 1.96%) (experiment 44).
  • Corrected lags: lags corrected with RO-NC's labels raised the score by 0.056 points of capacity outside switching (0.016 to 0.126) and did not lower it inside logged events (experiment 86, of the switching-labels-in-the-forecast theme).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
RO-NC is PF14 with two changes (experiment 82).

  1. Subtract an XGBoost demand model's forecast, which uses no past power, from each Primary's power, and refit the model monthly.
  2. Take the 24-hour step of that residual from whichever of two such models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours of the stamp. Lifting the suppression alone does as well on injected transfers (experiment 71), but RO-NC was tested only with two models.
  3. Score each candidate alarm with a logistic regression on its own step, the largest opposite neighbour step, the number of neighbours, and the number that step the same way.
  4. Set the threshold to allow 80 unexplained alarms over all 16 Primary series on odd months, and end each interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Nothing is ready for the serving path. Experiments 70, 71, and 82 are marked candidate, but each is training-time only: the residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days after the event, and the end rule uses hindsight.

  • Experiment 71: +0.050 on injected transfers. Experiment 70: +0.048, unconfirmed on real transfers (7 found against 8 for PF14). Experiment 82: +0.114, and 12 against 8 on the 35 real transfers, a weak signal.
  • An untested option is to run RO-NC retrospectively to build a table of switching events for NGED. Experiment 44 found that a perfect detector would improve the best guess's quantile score by little, so the table would serve NGED's own use of the events (roadmap page: switching events).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Count events, not half-hours, and show every event. In experiment 37, 99.9% of the stack's confirmed tail score lay on two series, almost all in one 370-hour closure, and in experiment 38 one closure in January 2026 held 95% to 105% of every masking gain (experiment 37, experiment 38). A pooled half-hour total then reads as many closures when it is one. Re-check on a longer period or other series.
  • Match the unexplained-alarm count on every month a rule reads. A threshold matched on odd months left even months 15% under the first round's alarm count (experiment 68), and a shared threshold grid left D0 at 0.14 alarms per series-month and D1 at 0.38 (experiment 37). Otherwise a detector looks better by raising more alarms. Re-check if the demand model or period changes.
  • Spread injected transfers across series and time before training on them. Experiment 58's 620 even-month transfers shrank to 103 once no two on one series lay within 1 day (experiment 68). Otherwise a few overlapping events count many times. Re-check if the injection sampler changes.
  • Compare like with like when quoting injected and real recall. 0.770 is MW-weighted recall on large injected transfers, and 0.34 is a count over all 35 real transfers, 21 of them under 25% of the receiving load (experiment 101). Otherwise a gap the sample cannot show is reported as a finding. Re-check if the labelled real set grows.
  • Score on several injection shapes and by donor step. Recall depends on the donor step in noise units (experiment 58), and experiment 60 tested one step statistic on five shapes. Otherwise a mix of small and large steps hides which transfers are missed. Re-check if the injection builds transfers a new way.
  • Interval ends need hindsight. The strongest-opposite-step end rule needs up to 14 days of later data (experiment 65), and an interval that started at a return step ran for 60 days (experiment 38). Otherwise a detector scored with hindsight is mistaken for one that could run live. Re-check when a detector is run on live data, or an end rule without hindsight is tried.
  • Recompute moved_share_of_receiver before scoring against the experiment 41 labels. 62 of 81 stored values are NaN, partly because series ids were written as strings (experiment 44). Otherwise a filter on that column silently drops most events. Re-check if the labelled set is rebuilt.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether any detector finds real transfers with a step under 4 noise units, or shorter than 1 day.
  • How RO-NC does on real transfers once the readings missing for two Primary substations are restored.
  • Whether the detector's labels improve a forecast of the normal running arrangement; the logged events in experiment 86 are too few to show it.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: LSC detectors: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00332 lsc-curtailment-cost-of-label-free-mask Treating as missing the readings that a label-free load shift detector flags (arm A of experiment 327) lowers curtailment cost during and after load shifts, against no mask (arm C), without raising it on ordinary half-hours. not supported not-for-production Masking the load shifts that a label-free detector finds lowers curtailment cost by about a third when the forecast is judged against the normal running arrangement. Judged against the power the electricity network actually carried, which is what a curtailment instruction responds to, the mask changes cost by -3.0% with an interval from -24% to +30%, and it costs 1.3% more on ordinary half-hours. Adding the true moved megawatts to the true spans lowered cost during a shift, but adding them to the label-free mask did not, so this result cannot say what a live service needs. primary 00331 primary-demand-recency-weights-on-gam-and-kalman When the additive (GAM) model with a Kalman filter on its daily residual is refitted monthly, giving older training rows exponentially less weight forecasts the next month better than equal weights on the full history, and no worse than training on the last 24 months only. not supported not-for-production Training the monthly refit mostly on recent data improves the next month's forecast by about 0.025 points of capacity, but a plain 24-month window gets the same gain, so smooth recency weights add nothing and no weights should go into the research default. Half of the gain comes from one Primary substation whose demand shifted in 2023. Giving extra weight to rows from the same time of year in earlier years gave a further 0.012 points and is worth its own test. This is a lab result on past weather with a Kalman filter that already adapts to level changes. also relevant 00328 lsc-regime-changes-detect-then-model-part-1 A permanent change in the configuration of an electricity network (a large new generator, a new factory) can be found offline from a Primary's own history, and a forecast that keeps the effects of the old behaviour fitted on the full history and adds new effects that exist only from the change onward scores better after the change than the same forecast refitted on a recent window only. not supported not-for-production Adding effects for a detected permanent change does not forecast better than refitting the additive model on the last 24 months, in a lab setting where the model is given past weather. The detectors find a 10% step of a Primary's load within 60 days only 26% of the time at an acceptable false-alarm rate, so there is little time after the alarm for the extra effects to help. On this base, handling a regime change comes down to how often the model is refitted. The rolling-GAM detector might still help when building substation cards, which this experiment did not test. primary 00327 lsc-label-free-detect-mask-train-pipeline A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) can be trained and corrected on power with the load shifts set to missing, where a label-free detector finds the load shifts. The detector reads only how unusual the observed power is inside the predictive bands of a demand model that uses no lagged power, and no NGED switching label enters any threshold, mask, or training row. partly supported candidate A forecast of the normal running arrangement recovers faster after a load shift when the readings that a label-free detector flags are treated as missing: during and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04 points of capacity. On ordinary days the masked forecast is no worse, and slightly better. Without one site (D11) the gain shrinks to 0.30 points, and retraining the demand model on masked power adds nothing beyond masking the filter. primary 00315 lsc-neighbour-residual-filter A real load shift moves load between neighbouring Primary substations, so the 24-hour mean residuals at the two substations have opposite signs, while weather and forecast error give the same sign at neighbours. Keeping a 24-hour mean residual alarm only when a neighbour does not contradict it therefore cuts the alarms per matched shift at equal recall. small gain not-for-production Checking whether neighbouring substations' residuals contradict an alarm removes about a third of the 24-hour residual detector's false alarms and loses none of the real load shifts it found. The gain in alarms per found shift is about a quarter, which is a real but modest improvement, and the two substations that raise 17% to 20% of its false alarms (D8 and D9) keep the same number. The filter is usable for event labels for NGED, but it does not change the detector's accuracy much. primary 00312 lsc-how-good-must-a-detector-be-against-the-band-head A load shift detector that is far from perfect can still beat the best forecast that uses no detector, so a detector need not be near-perfect to be worth building. The one detector-based arm in experiment 297 that beat that forecast was the one that subtracts the true megawatts from the readings during a shift and adds them back to the forecast. This experiment degrades that arm one axis at a time to find where it stops beating the no-detector forecast. It also asks whether the surprise of recent readings against GAM_ONLY's residual bands (band position), or perfect knowledge of a shift, added as inputs to the no-detector quantile head, improves the head. This is question 3 of the LSC decision program, redefined by the Discuss ruling of 2026-10-23. not supported not-for-production A load shift detector does not need to be near-perfect to improve on the best forecast that uses no detector: with the true megawatts added back, finding half the shifts, learning of each up to 3 days late, or misjudging the megawatts by half still lowers curtailment cost against that forecast. The detector tested earlier (RO-NC) finds only a third of the shifts, below the break-even of one half (measured with every other property perfect). The surprise of recent readings against the forecast's bands (band position) found more, 37% of shifts on even months, but still under one half and with about 90% of its alarms false, so the next step is a detector that finds more shifts. primary 00309 lsc-two-forecast-gap-choosing-without-truth NGED sees two forecasts and not the true switching state. A forecast with no lagged power (GAM_ONLY) forecasts the normal running arrangement, and a forecast with lags (K0) forecasts what will flow while an abnormal arrangement lasts. A rule that reads only the gap between the two forecasts, how long it has lasted, and a neighbour check can choose between them nearly as well as knowing the truth. This experiment is part 2 of the brief briefs/sw_lsc_two_forecasts_divergence_and_selection_brief.md, and it builds on experiment 308. not supported not-for-production NGED cannot pick between the two forecasts from the gap alone. A rule on the gap, or on the 24-hour mean of measured power minus the no-lag forecast, did no better than always using the no- lag forecast in the injected worlds, and worse than always using the forecast with lags in the real record. An oracle that knows the true switching state gained little, except in the 72 hours after a real shift ended, so the most promising signal to test next is a flag for the end of a shift. The gap is a filtered copy of the measured-power residual, so it adds no information that the measured power lacks. primary 00308 lsc-two-forecast-gap-as-a-detector The gap between the forecast with lags (K0, the Kalman filter on recent power) and the forecast without lags (GAM_ONLY, which forecasts the normal running arrangement) at a forecast origin already works as a load shift detector. NGED cannot see the true switching state, so this gap is the only signal it has. This is part 1 of the brief briefs/sw_lsc_two_forecasts_divergence_and_selection_brief.md. supported not-for-production The gap between the two forecasts flagged 11 of 35 real load shifts while they were still on, about as many as the learned score (10) when both thresholds are set to the same false alarm rate on odd months. The median alarm came 41 hours after the onset. On the held-out even months the gap raised about twice the learned score's false alarms (1.21 against 0.55 per Primary-year). A 24-hour mean of recent forecast error flagged 20 of 35. Experiment 309 tests whether the gap can choose between the two forecasts. primary 00302 lsc-learned-score-without-nged-labels Experiment 227's carried alarm source (the re-ranker of experiment 195 at a budget of 20 unexplained odd-month candidates, "LR_b20") uses NGED labels twice: its training negatives drop every logged or labelled span, every D8 drop, and the 17 block days, and its threshold counts "unexplained" candidates, which means no logged closure within 24 hours. A re-ranker trained on every real candidate as a negative, and thresholded by a rule that reads no label, still matches about as many of the 35 logged load shifts lasting over 1 day at about the same number of alarms per match, with ordinary-day harm inside the limit. not supported not-for-production A learned load-shift alarm trained without NGED labels matched 14 of the 35 logged load shifts, against 20 to 21 with labels, so the pre-registered test failed. The whole loss sits (post hoc) in load shifts that start in the months the score trained on, because every real candidate there, real load shifts included, was taught as a negative. On the 20 load shifts in months the score never saw, the label-free score found 13 to 14, against 13 for the labelled one, a difference too small to resolve with 20 load shifts. The next test should score a label-free score only on months it never trained on, with more than 20 load shifts. primary 00298 lsc-long-deep-detector-and-refit-cleaning A trivial detector on the daily mean residual of the lagless convex additive model (GAM_ONLY) finds load shifts that last days to weeks and cover at least 10% of a Primary substation's load, which the existing hour-scale detectors miss, and excluding the days it flags from the monthly refit stops the forecast learning those shifts as the normal pattern. not supported not-for-production A simple detector on the daily mean error of the forecast that uses no recent power finds about as many of the long, deep real load shifts as the learned score LR_b20 (10 to 12 of 19 for four of the six variants). The cumulative-sum variant B also finds 27 of the 29 multi-day drops at D8, which are probably a gas engine and not load shifts; variant C finds 11. Leaving the days a detector flags out of the monthly refit cuts the share of a 30-day transfer that the forecast learns as normal from about 19% to about 10% to 13%. Excluding the true shift days instead cuts the share to 2.8%. The detectors recover less because each needs 1 to 3 days to fire and misses about 40% of long injected transfers and over half of the real ones. Tell NGED that transfers of 14 days or more are partly learned as normal, and try a detector that fires on the first day next. primary 00297 lsc-need-a-detector-no-detector-arms-against-the-mask A forecast that never learns which readings are load shifts can match a forecast that uses a detector, because its bands and its recent-power correction can be made to tell a load shift from ordinary variation by themselves. This is question 2 of the LSC decision program. not supported not-for-production A forecast with no detector that recalibrates its bands and reads how far the recent-power correction has moved scores better than the RO-NC detector near load shifts, so with RO-NC a detector is not shown to be needed. Perfect knowledge with the true megawatts added back still lowers curtailment cost by 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2) against that forecast, so the next step is to run the better LSC detector (LR_b20) on the same simulated shifts and judge it against a forecast that has the recalibrated bands. primary 00296 lsc-benefit-by-event-class-long-deep-versus-small-shifts Load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a Primary substation's load carry most of the benefit of knowing every load shift exactly, and shifts that are shorter than 12 hours or under 10% of load carry little. This is the question behind the "long-and-deep" detector of the LSC decision program. supported not-for-production A detector that finds only load shifts of at least 2 days and at least 10% of a substation's load would deliver about 96% of the upper-tail forecast benefit and about 90% of the curtailment-cost benefit of knowing every shift, if it were perfect. Detecting shifts from 6 hours to 2 days would add 3% to 8% more, and detecting shifts down to 5% of load would add 1% to 2%. The next step is to weight these shares by how often a real long-and-deep detector finds each class, which waits for Part 1 of the long-deep detector experiment. primary 00295 regime-segmentation-part-b-persistent-regimes-without-labels A segmentation of a Primary's whole history with hindsight, using only changes in the distribution of the residual of a lagless convex additive model (GAM), finds regime changes without labels. A regime is the whole period, without gaps, during which one configuration holds. For D8's gas engine, the regime is the whole period in which the engine is installed and included in the meter, including the spells when the engine is off. Whether the engine is running, and whether a load shift is in force, are states inside a regime. A boundary is a regime change when the distribution does not return to its earlier form and no neighbouring Primary shows the opposite change, and a state change otherwise. not supported not-for-production Looking only at the residual of a forecast that uses no recent power, a segmentation finds a lasting change of 25% of a Primary's load and dates it with a median error of 0 days, but it misses about half of 10% changes and cannot reliably tell a 14 to 60 day load shift from a lasting change. At D8 it finds the 2023-08-15 break exactly, but only at penalties that also find 2.5 or more regime changes per Primary-year at the other Primaries. An offset for the latest regime lowers the forecast error after a step by 2.2 points of capacity, but a plain 60-day mean residual does as well, so the segmentation is not worth adding for that purpose. primary 00294 regime-aware-model-at-d8-engine-state-term D8's metered power excludes a gas engine's output (experiment 194) while the engine, which runs in spells (experiment 291), takes net load below what the weather and calendar predict. A single model trained across those spells has no way to know which half-hours the engine ran, so its forecast and its bands carry the engine as noise. A model that keeps the calendar, weather, and solar shapes shared across the whole history but adds one regime-specific term, an offset per half-hour the engine runs (non-negative, taking power off net load), forecasts D8 better than the single model. The offset is estimated from the data, and its size is not assumed. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast when D8's gas engine is running would make it much better when the state is read at the half-hour being forecast, but the detector builds that state from the very reading being forecast. With only the state of the last settled day, the engine term made the forecast 10% worse; trained on that stale state, it gained only 3%, no better than widening the bands from past residuals. A forecast of whether the engine runs, or NGED's own record of its running hours, would be the data to test next. also relevant 00291 d8-drops-engine-spells-load-shift D8's 29 multi-day drops (experiment 159) are spells in which a gas engine of up to three units runs, and D8's own metered power no longer includes the engine's output (experiment 194). If so, the engine detector of experiment 196 flags the drops' half-hours far more often than matched windows elsewhere on D8, the drops' depths cluster at multiples of one engine unit, and most of D8's load-shift alarms that fall inside drops are engine edges. partly supported not-for-production D8's multi-day drops coincide with the engine detector's running states, which is consistent with the gas engine running: the detector flags 27 of the 28 drops that began after the engine left D8's reading, against about 1 in 5 comparable stretches of D8, and it flags almost nothing at three other Primaries on the same dates. This cannot be called proved, because the drops and the detector both read D8's residual, and the depths of the drops do not fall at whole multiples of the engine's 1.97 MW unit. D8's drops should be flagged as a probable generator regime and reported apart from the load-shift scoring until NGED confirms the engine's running hours, and the next step is a forecast model for D8 that is told when the engine is running. primary 00290 lsc-long-shift-cut-date-robustness The 19% of a 30-day transfer that experiment 274 found learned as normal is stable across fit-cut dates, so that the share learned lies within 15% to 25% at every cut date. not supported not-for-production The forecast with no recent power learns about a fifth of a 30-day load transfer as normal, but the share depends on the date: it ranges from 9% to 29% across 12 end dates, so experiment 274's 2.49-point bias is a typical value, not a fixed one. Quote the share as a range of about 9% to 29%. The cause of the spread is not located. primary 00283 lsc-perfect-knowledge-value-to-forecast-and-curtailment Knowing every load shift exactly (its true start and end) lowers the error of the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) in the 48 hours after a shift, and lowers the curtailment cost of the forecast of observed power in the days around a shift, while leaving ordinary rows unchanged. This is question 1 of the LSC decision program. partly supported not-for-production Perfect knowledge of load shifts lowers the forecast's error most in the 48 hours after a shift ends (23% lower upper-tail score, 95% interval 9% to 39%) and by under 1% over a whole year, because shifts are rare. Curtailment cost against observed power falls by 8% (6% to 10%) near a shift only when the known shift's megawatts are added back to the forecast, and does not fall when recent readings are merely set aside. The next step is to ask how good a detector must be to keep that gain, using the megawatts-added-back arm as the target. primary 00277 lsc-curtailment-metric-on-existing-forecasts The curtailment-cost metric of experiment 268 (studies.node_curtailment, sorted quantiles) ranks the four existing forecasts as the other metrics do, and can resolve the differences between them well enough to judge the load-shift questions of the decision program. supported not-for-production Over a year of ordinary days, the curtailment metric ranks the four existing forecasts the way the other scores do, and it can tell the GAM stack from BG2 (BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more on the six Primaries at the 0.5 limit, a figure that ranks forecasts and is not money saved). Inside the windows around the 7 logged load transfers, the GAM stack cannot be separated from BG2, because those windows hold only 926 to 2,923 scored half-hours. Questions about load shifts need injected worlds with many more shifts, not the real record. also relevant 00274 lsc-long-arrangement-audit-gam-refit A forecast with no lagged power learns a long-lasting change of running arrangement as the normal pattern, because the monthly refit trains on whatever the meter recorded. The learned share grows with the duration of the arrangement, and the duration beyond which the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) is wrong by more than a stated tolerance sets the limit that can be told to NGED. not supported not-for-production A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal, and the forecast learns the transfer quickly: a transfer lasting only 7 days leaves the forecast 1.2 points of effective capacity too high for the next 2 days, and a transfer lasting 30 days leaves it 2.5 points too high (about a fifth of the transfer). No tested duration, down to 7 days, was short enough to avoid this. Masking known transfers out of training is the obvious remedy, but this experiment did not test it, and the next experiment should test it together with transfers of 1 to 6 days. primary 00271 lsc-load-shifts-net-out-at-bulk-supply-points A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point (BSP) leaves the power flow at the BSP unchanged, so it barely changes the curtailment cost at the BSP, and only a load shift that crosses from one BSP to the other changes the cost noticeably. The step 7 program brief for the load-shift (LSC) decision program asks this in order to know whether the money question can be asked at BSP level. partly supported not-for-production A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point changes the curtailment cost at that bulk supply point by 0.2% at a random time and 0.7% just before days that would be curtailed (interval up to 1.08%), because the two Primaries' forecast errors partly cancel. A load shift across the boundary between the two bulk supply points changes it by 1.4% at a random time and 5.5% just before curtailed days. Only 4 of the 54 hand-filtered real events that involve two Primaries cross the boundary, so the curtailment metric at bulk supply points cannot say whether detecting load shifts is worth money, and that question has to be asked at Primary substations. primary 00268 lsc-curtailment-metric-v2-member-wise-ens A member-wise input path added to studies.node_curtailment (ensemble members of the node's demand and of each farm's output, paired by member, reduced to the quantiles the rule reads) gives the same avoidable cost as the quantile path when the members are drawn from the same quantile function, and scores nodes that experiment 255 could not (Primaries that connect a farm, and the bulk supply points D13 and D17 with member-wise inputs). partly supported not-for-production The curtailment metric can now take ensemble members for a substation's demand and for each solar farm, and on experiment 255's rows it reproduces the earlier answer. A third of the stored solar-farm forecasts list their quantiles out of order. Sorting them moves the cost of some forecasts by up to 3.7% and leaves every comparison between forecasts with the same sign, but it swaps which of two near-equal forecasts is cheapest. Forecasts that are already quantile sets can be scored now. Forecasts driven by ensemble members need member frames that we did not find in the experiment folders we searched. also relevant 00258 lsc-mask-out-of-sample-all-primaries-whole-history Experiment 227 found that LR_b20 (the learned alarm score of experiment 195, at the threshold that leaves 20 unexplained odd-month candidates) with a mask recovers 83.5% of the logged-oracle gain in the 72 hours after a logged load shift and raises the ordinary-day score by -0.007 points (-0.039 to +0.014). That rests on 11 load shifts at 6 Primary substations, 27 months of cached ensemble forecasts, a threshold chosen on the scored rows, and months that were the re-ranker's training negatives. On all 15 Primary series with a residual from the frozen convex model of experiment 130 (arm B), over the whole residual history of about 4.5 years, and scored only on rows the learned score was not trained on, the LR_b20 mask keeps at least half of that gain and keeps its ordinary-day harm inside +/-0.05 points. inconclusive not-for-production On rows it was never trained on, the carried load shift mask recovers about half of the best-case gain after a load shift (47%, with a wide range of 18% to 85%) and changes ordinary days by less than 0.05 points. Over every row of 4.5 years it scores slightly worse than no mask, because a few long alarms over logged closures add more excess score than the mask removes elsewhere. The check against simulated load shifts failed, so the result is inconclusive, and this page gives no support for porting the mask. primary 00254 lsc-alarm-precision-against-full-log-with-chance-base-rate Experiment 195's loose rule (a logged closure within 24 hours "explains" an alarm) overcounts real alarms, because a random window is explained about 45% of the time (experiment 159, which counts any time inside a closure or within 24 hours of it), and the strict rule (experiment 195's step-and- end match) undercounts them, because the log's times are approximate. Once the share expected by chance is removed, a large share of the alarms from LR_b20, the learned alarm source, that are not strict matches still coincide with a logged closure. supported not-for-production We estimate that about 45% of the alarms from the learned load shift screen at its strictest threshold (LR_b20) are real load shifts, with 2.7 false alarms for each logged load shift it finds. The looser sources, LR_b80 and RO_b80, which keep 80 candidate alarms, are real about 28% and 25% of the time. An event table built from LR_b20 would carry an estimated precision of about 45%. primary 00253 lsc-end-time-pair-rule When a load shift moves demand between two metered Primary substations, the end of the shift is estimated better from the pair than from either substation alone, because the true end restores the pair's summed demand and an unrelated step on one substation does not. Using the pair removes most of the disagreement between the end times that the two substations' cards show (a real shift between D5 and D16 on 14 January 2026 is shown as ending after 9.2 days on one card and 2.0 days on the other). inconclusive not-for-production Reading the two substations together makes their end times agree when an unrelated step follows the true end: the median gap falls from 8.5 to 2.5 hours and the share of moved MW with a correct end rises by 0.04 (from 0.593 to 0.633). On ordinary transfers the same rule falls by about 0.02 (from 0.788 to 0.770), so the experiment cannot say the pair rule is safe to port. The pair rule does not change the end times of the real 14 January 2026 shift between substations D5 and D16, because D16 shows no demand step large enough to be the end, and none of D5's 13 candidate steps is matched by an opposite step on D16. primary 00249 lsc-self-training-on-consistent-events The learned load-shift score of experiment 195 is trained only on injected transfers. If it is retrained on injected transfers plus the real events that pass a label-free consistency rule (balanced opposite steps at a metered neighbour, a high round 1 score, and a clean return step), it finds more of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day than the round 1 score, at the same 80 unexplained odd-month alarms, because the pseudo-positives show it what real events look like. refuted not-for-production Retraining the learned load-shift score on its own consistent real events found no extra real transfers: the score still finds 24 of 35. Only 38 to 47 real events per fold pass the consistency rule, against about 2,000 injected transfers per fold, so the extra rows probably could not move the score. The candidate end is the largest opposite step seen so far, and the end is fixed once no later step beats it within the lookahead. A lookahead of 24 hours or less is enough, so a live service need not wait 2 days. supported candidate On injected transfers, a live service needs only 6 hours of data after the candidate end to fix the end of a switching interval, with no loss of recall against the offline rule. The call then comes a median 30 hours after the true end, and 24 of those hours are the step statistic's own window, so a longer lookahead of 24 or 48 hours only delays the call to 48 or 72 hours without finding more. The 35 real transfers give the same 18 found at every lookahead from 1 hour up. A lookahead of 0 hours is wrong in six transfers in ten, because the end is called about 8 hours early. primary 00147 causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc The end of a switching interval that RO-NC has alarmed on can be called from data available at the time, with no lookahead, at a small loss of the share of moved MW found, a low rate of false ends (an end called before the transfer has ended), and a lag of a few days at most. Merging alarms that overlap on one Primary substation, and treating a return step as the end of an open event instead of a new transfer, lowers the share of transfers with 2 or more intervals without losing recall. The offline end rule of experiments 61 and 130 picks the largest opposite step within 24 hours after the first return step, which needs data from up to 48 hours after that first step, so its "known from" time is up to 24 hours too early. supported candidate The end of a switching interval can be called from data available at the time, with no loss of recall against the offline rule, by waiting until the step statistic falls to 0.8 of its running peak. The call comes a median 29 hours after the true end. Ending the interval at the first sign of a return step is wrong in about six transfers in ten, because it fires about 8 hours early. Merging overlapping alarms on one Primary substation cuts the share of transfers reported as 2 or more intervals from 0.57 to 0.03. primary 00146 ro-nc-arm-b-on-the-35-real-transfers-over-1-day Descriptive, with no hypothesis to test beyond the prediction below. Experiment 130 reported only the count of the 35 real transfers over 1 day that RO-NC finds on the frozen convex residual (18 of 35). This experiment reports, for each of the 35, whether and when the detector alarmed, how much of the moved power it covers, and why it missed the transfers it missed. partly supported not-for-production On the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, RO-NC finds 18, and those 18 carry about two thirds (0.657) of the moved power. When it finds a transfer, its alarm starts within half an hour of the labelled start. Only 7 of the 17 misses are small or unreadable starts. 8 have a first step of 4 noise units or more but no alarm, and 2 have an alarm with the wrong end. The next experiment should find out why those 8 got no alarm, before anyone builds detectors for weaker onsets. primary 00141 switching-detector-fed-into-gam-k Telling GAM-K's Kalman filter when the RO-NC detector has seen a load transfer lowers the forecast's quantile score on days after a transfer begins, because the filter's level then adapts within hours instead of over days. The same signal given as plain features (event age and signed step size) does the same, more weakly. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast's filter when a load transfer started and ended helped inside the transfer and hurt in the 72 hours after it, because the filter holds the transfer's step over the whole 7-day forecast. The switching detector's alarm arrives 48 hours after the step and did no better than a random placebo. The next test is a correction that decays over the typical transfer duration. also relevant 00138 weaker-onset-detector-on-the-ro-nc-convex-residual A detector that also considers weaker and slower onsets finds a larger share of the moved megawatts (MW) of injected load transfers than the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) on the frozen convex residual (experiment 130, arm B), at the same 80 unexplained odd-month alarms. In experiment 130, most of the remaining misses were donor steps of 2 to 4 noise units with no metered receiving substation, which the 24-hour step statistic cannot separate from noise. refuted not-for-production Making the detector more willing to fire on weak, slow starts did not help on injected transfers: all three changes found the same 0.79 of the moved power as before (differences of -0.008 to +0.001, no interval above +0.018) at the same 80 false alarms. Most of the weak starts that remain missed (a first step of 2 to 4 noise units at a donor with no metered receiving substation) look too much like noise for any of the three logistic scores to separate them from noise. On the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day the new arms found 21 to 23 against 18, which is a possible gain worth checking on a bigger labelled set, since the injected transfers show no such gain. primary 00132 ro-nc-rescored-with-p12-and-p13-residuals-in-2025 Post hoc and descriptive. In experiment 101, the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) did not find 6 real load transfers lasting more than 1 day at P12 and P13, the two transformers of one Primary substation. Those transfers are found about as often as injected transfers of the same step size and metering once P12 and P13 have a residual in 2025 and the zero readings inside the transfers are no longer flagged as faults. If so, the missing readings, and not a property of the transfers, explain the 6 misses. partly supported not-for-production The detector missed the 6 real transfers at P12 and P13 mainly because the cleaning rule had flagged as faults, and removed, the zero readings that a switched-out transformer reports. With those readings restored from the cleaned power table, the detector finds 4 of the 6, and 17 of all 35 transfers lasting more than 1 day, up from 12. The cleaning rule removes real periods when a transformer is switched out. The thresholds were not re-tuned, and the unexplained alarms on odd-numbered months rose from 80 to 95 (PF14) and from 80 to 87 (RO-NC), so the recall comes with a higher false-alarm count. The next step is to re-tune the alarm thresholds on the new residuals and check that the 4 found transfers survive. With only 6 transfers, the result is descriptive. primary 00131 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-drift-term Adding a slowly varying offset to each substation, fitted jointly with the flows on the interconnection edges, lets the flow fit find injected transfers that last hours to days without putting flow on pairs of substations that are not connected, which experiment 116's fit could not do. inconclusive not-for-production Letting each substation drift slowly did reduce the load that the fit wrongly moves between substations that are not connected, by half to three quarters at an equal or higher detection rate. It did not remove that false load, and the settings that keep it near zero find only about half of the transfers we added artificially and report them too small. In the replicate year part of the false load sits in two jumps in one substation's data that nobody had labelled. We therefore cannot yet read these flows as switching events. also relevant 00130 ro-nc-detector-on-the-gam-k-residual The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) finds more of the moved megawatts (MW) of injected load transfers when its residual is the one-step innovation of the convex demand model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K), than when it is the residual of the lagless XGBoost model of experiment 82. A lower residual noise should lift more of the donor steps of 2 to 4 noise units over the 4.0 threshold. In experiment 82, 401 of the transfers that RO-NC missed had no metered receiver and a donor step of 2 to 4 noise units. inconclusive not-for-production A detector of load transfers found about 2 more of every 100 megawatts moved when it was built on a demand forecast from the convex model without recent power than when it was built on the lagless XGBoost forecast (a difference of +0.023 in the share found, interval -0.001 to +0.046, under the +0.03 bar). It found 18 of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day against 12, but the convex model was trained with those real transfers masked, so that count flatters it. Built on the Kalman filter's one-step errors the detector found far less (0.488 of the moved power against 0.772), most likely because the filter follows a transfer's step within hours and so absorbs it, which we did not test. Most of the detector's remaining misses are small steps with no metered receiving substation, so a stronger signal for those transfers is the next idea to try. The maintainer has chosen to treat the gain as an improvement and to build later detector work on the frozen convex residual; that decision lies outside the pre-registered rule, so the verdict stays inconclusive. primary 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. also relevant 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00101 ro-nc-detector-on-real-hand-filtered-switching-events Post hoc, and descriptive: the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) finds less of the moved power on the 66 real, hand-filtered switching transfers than on injected transfers (0.770 of the moved MW) because most real transfers are small, short, or have no metered receiver, and not because the detector fails on a real transfer of the size the injected ones have. partly supported not-for-production The refit-offset neighbour-count detector found 12 of the 35 real load transfers lasting over 1 day and none of the 31 shorter ones, against 0.770 of the moved power on injected transfers. Of the 35, 6 sit where the detector's residual panel holds no readings and 12 have a step under 4 noise units. primary 00098 det-bg-solar-and-heating-offsets-in-switching-detector-residual The refit-offset neighbour-count switching detector (RO-NC) subtracts a lagless XGBoost demand forecast (experiment 17's H0.5, trained on ERA5) from each Primary substation's measured power. Giving that forecast the best guess's two explicit offsets, an embedded-solar term (capacity times a solar anomaly) and a heating degree-hour term, removes structured weather error from the residual, so the detector finds more of the moved MW at the same number of unexplained alarms. inconclusive not-for-production Giving the demand forecast behind the switching detector explicit solar and heating corrections did not detectably raise the share of moved power that the detector finds. The solar correction made the summer midday residual 12% smaller at the 5 solar series, but recall moved by only +0.003, because most remaining misses are small transfers from substations whose neighbours are unmetered. primary 00086 sw2-12-detector-labels-for-nra-forecast On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of experiment 48, giving the monthly-refitted (P-roll) Primary demand model the lags minus the MW that switching moved, together with that MW as three columns, lowers the quantile score on the half-hours whose lag sits inside a switching event, when the events and MW come from the RO-NC load-transfer detector of experiment 82 instead of NGED's logs, and the gain is smaller than with the oracle labels of experiment 41 by the share of events RO-NC misses. inconclusive not-for-production Lags corrected with the detector's labels did not lower the quantile score on rows with a lag inside a logged event. also relevant 00082 sw2-18-19-combined-refit-offset-and-same-sign-count Experiment 71's refit-offset detector X (the 24-hour step statistic taken from whichever of two monthly-refit residual models did not refit within 24 hours of the stamp) and experiment 70's logistic score with the same-sign neighbour count (LOGIT_SAME) fix different misses of the benchmark PF14. Applying the logistic score to the candidates of X (RO-NC) therefore finds more of the moved MW than PF14, and more than either part alone, at the same count of unexplained alarms, on a fresh draw of injected transfers. supported candidate Using the refit offset and the same-sign neighbour count together found 0.770 of the moved power on injected transfers, against 0.656 for the benchmark detector. The gain of 0.114 is about the sum of the gains of 0.056 and 0.050 from each change alone. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day the combined detector found 12 and the benchmark 8, which is a weak signal on a small sample, and transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days gain nothing. primary 00071 sw2-18-refit-offset-and-gap-bridging The detector D0M with the end rule PF14 (experiment 69's benchmark) cannot raise an alarm, or accept a return step, within 24 hours of the monthly refit of the residual's XGBoost model. Computing the step statistic from whichever of two monthly-refit models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours of the stamp removes that blind spot, and finds more of the moved MW than PF14 at the same number of unexplained alarms. Bridging data gaps is a side check with no verdict, because the panel holds almost no gaps to bridge. supported candidate The detector ignored every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its forecasting model, which lowered recall by about 5% of the moved power. Lifting that rule recovers the loss, and the second residual model added to replace the ignored alarms adds nothing on injected transfers. primary 00070 sw2-19-same-sign-neighbour-count One alarm score that adds the count of neighbouring substations stepping the same way as the alarming substation to the substation's own 24-hour step and the largest opposite neighbour step (LOGIT_SAME) finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the single-series detector D0M, with the same first-return end rule (PF14), at the same count of unexplained alarms on odd months, on a fresh draw of injected transfers. supported candidate Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation found 0.048 more of the moved power on injected transfers than the single-series detector, at the same number of unexplained alarms. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain (7 found, against 8 for the benchmark), and the gain does not extend to transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. primary 00069 sw2-17-missed-onsets-of-the-end-rule An onset rule that accepts a weak alarm only when a matching opposite step follows within 14 days (the paired low-threshold onset, PP) recovers more of the moved MW than D0M with the same end rule, at the same number of unexplained alarms. The labelled real transfers that raise no alarm at their onset are examined separately, because PP is scored on injected transfers and the cause of the real misses is a separate question. inconclusive not-for-production Of the 24 real load transfers lasting over 1 day that raised no alarm at their start, 12 are not a threshold problem: 6 lie in data gaps, 3 in a monthly refit that suppresses the alarm, and 3 have an alarm 2 to 12 hours from the labelled start. Accepting weaker alarms that a step back confirms recovered 0.146 of the moved power, but the stricter threshold needed to hold the alarm count lost 0.140. primary 00068 sw2-5-train-detect-retrain-loop When the lagless XGBoost model (the model whose forecast residual the switching detector reads) is refitted with zero weight on the half-hours inside detected switching intervals, and the detector is then run again on the new residual, three times over, the detector finds a larger share of the MW moved by load transfers at the same number of unexplained alarms. The refit also lowers the forecast error on half-hours outside logged switching. The mechanism is that a lagless XGBoost model trained through a transfer partly learns the transfer. That shrinks the transfer's step in the residual and biases the forecast. inconclusive not-for-production Refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the load transfers that the detector had found barely changed what the detector finds or the forecast error. In these 16 series the limit on the detector is therefore not that the forecast has learned the transfers. primary 00067 sw2-15-joint-edge-flow-estimator A single convex fit of block-shaped load flows across every boundary between neighbouring Primary substations, fitted to all the residuals at once, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the best sequential detector (D0M, the 24-hour single-series detector with the strongest-opposite-step end rule), at the same count of unexplained alarms on odd months. refuted not-for-production Fitting one flow of power across every pair of neighbouring Primary substations at once found 0.108 of the moved power, against 0.646 for the single-series detector when both raised about 80 unexplained alarms. A change to the loss made after seeing the result lifted that to 0.527, still 0.120 lower, so a joint fit would have to start from the 24-hour step statistics. primary 00066 sw2-16-end-rule-as-baseline Experiment 61's end rule (each alarm interval ends at the strongest opposite step within a cap of 14 days) can be improved by a longer cap, a shorter step window, or both. A cap of 30 or 60 days finds more of the MW moved by transfers that last over 14 days, with a loss of at most 0.01 on the shorter transfers of experiment 58. The 4-hour step window finds more of the moved MW than the 24-hour window at the same number of unexplained alarms. The winning window and cap then become the benchmark for every later switching-detector experiment. inconclusive not-for-production A post hoc rule that ends each alarm interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step found more of the moved power than searching 14 days for the strongest opposite step, and a 24-hour averaging window beat a 4-hour window. A longer search cap repairs transfers lasting over 15.6 days but picks a wrong end for some shorter ones, so the pre-registered verdict is inconclusive. primary 00065 sw2-14-combined-single-series-and-neighbour-score One alarm score that adds a substation's own 24-hour step evidence to the opposite-step evidence from its neighbouring substations, with neither acting as a gate, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the 24-hour single-series detector (D0M), the neighbour-confirmation gate (D1), and the neighbour veto (D2, experiment 55), at the same count of unexplained alarms on odd months. inconclusive not-for-production Adding the neighbouring substations' opposite-sign steps to a substation's own step did not find clearly more of the moved power than the own step alone (0.665 against 0.646; 99.17% interval -0.011 to +0.062 on the difference). In a post hoc variant, adding the count of neighbours that stepped the same way raised the share found. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00062 sw2-9-whitened-residual-step-detector Removing the half-hour-to-half-hour memory of the residual before the step statistic is taken (a first-order autoregressive filter, fitted per series and half-hour of day on odd months) makes the switching detector find a larger share of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the same detector on the unfiltered residual (D0M), at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain holds on transfers whose shape the detector does not assume. refuted not-for-production Removing the residual's half-hour-to-half-hour memory made the switching detector find fewer load transfers: 0.34 to 0.37 of the moved power against 0.44 to 0.47 without the filter. The filter shrinks a day-long step faster than it shrinks the noise, and a first-order filter cannot fix that. primary 00061 sw2-6-paired-step-intervals A detector that looks for an onset step and its opposite return step together, scoring the pair and choosing the return stamp with a prior on the duration of real transfers, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the best single-window detector (D0M, the 24-hour step with a tracked end), at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain comes from interval ends: about a third of D0M's transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more have the right start and a wrong end (experiment 60). refuted not-for-production Taking the end of each alarm interval from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days found 0.19 more of the moved power than the single-step detector. Scoring the onset step and the return step as one pair found 0.13 to 0.21 less, so the end of the interval is the main limit on the single-step detector's recall. primary 00060 sw2-7-profile-weighted-step-detector A step statistic that weights each half-hour by the series' expected power (the daily profile of the fitted weather model), D3, finds more of the MW moved by injected load transfers than the constant-step statistic, D0M, at the same rate of unexplained alarms. The gain holds on transfers whose shape D3 does not assume (a constant MW, a share of the receivers' own profiles, and a mix of the two fitted to real transfers), not only on a share of the donor's profile, which is how the injection built every transfer in experiments 43, 55 and 58. refuted not-for-production A switching detector that weights each half-hour by the substation's predicted power found the same share of the moved power as one that expects a constant step, within 0.005 on five shapes of transfer (0.44 to 0.47). The shape of the moved load is therefore not why transfers are missed: among transfers with a large step, about a third have an alarm at the right start but the wrong end. primary 00059 sw2-13-several-windows-in-one-detector One detector that combines the step statistic of experiment 43's detector D0 at windows of 4, 12, 24, and 48 hours, after calibrating each window to the same false-alarm rate on odd months, finds more of the injected load transfers, weighted by the MW each moves, than the best single window at the same false-alarm rate on even months. refuted not-for-production Neither the maximum nor the sum of four window lengths found more of the moved power than the 24-hour window alone (0.423 and 0.451 against 0.473). Among large transfers with a metered receiver, most misses are an interval end placed outside tolerance and not a missed alarm. primary 00058 sw2-8b-donor-step-recut-and-stronger-veto (1) The gap in recall between injected load transfers with a metered receiver (0.50) and without one (0.17), seen in experiment 55, comes mostly from the injection giving the second group a smaller donor step, so the gap shrinks to under half its size when the two groups are compared at the same donor step in noise units. (2) A neighbour veto stronger than experiment 55's strongest (1.5 noise units), at 1.25 or 1.0, lets the 24-hour threshold fall further and finds more injected transfers than no veto. partly supported not-for-production Much of the gap in recall between injected transfers with a metered receiver (0.50) and without one (0.17) comes from the injected step being too small to see: 211 of 274 transfers without a metered receiver step by less than the alarm threshold, and the gap falls from 0.33 to -0.002 at equal step size (interval -0.166 to +0.119). A stronger neighbour veto raised the share found by 0.013, which cannot be told from no gain (98.33% interval 0.000 to +0.029). primary 00055 sw2-8-neighbour-veto-single-series-detector Keeping every alarm of the single-series detector D0 at the 24-hour window, except those vetoed because at least two neighbouring Primary substations stepped the same way and none stepped the opposite way, lets the alarm threshold fall at the same rate of unexplained alarms, and the detector then finds more injected load transfers than D0 alone. inconclusive not-for-production A neighbour veto removed the alarms that look like a weather or calendar miss and let the detector's threshold fall from 4.00 to 3.70, but the share of 620 injected transfers found rose only from 0.355 to 0.363 (98.75% interval -0.003 to +0.022). The result is inconclusive, and a stronger veto was not tried. primary 00047 sw2-4-better-residual-switching-detector Adding one column, the signed days to the nearest bank holiday in England, to experiment 17's lagless ERA5-trained XGBoost demand model H0.5 (refitted monthly, with H0.5's absolute-error loss unchanged) gives a residual in which the single-series detector D0 at the 24-hour window finds more injected load transfers at the same rate of unexplained alarms. inconclusive not-for-production Adding a bank-holiday column to the demand model raised the share of 89 simulated transfers that the detector found by 0.011 (98.75% interval -0.010 to +0.044), which the experiment is too small to tell from zero. The column lowered the demand error on bank holidays by about 1.15 points of capacity, but the detector's matched threshold rose instead of falling. primary 00044 sw2-2-switching-share-of-best-guess-score Half-hours in labelled switching events, and half-hours whose lagged power falls inside one, carry a larger share of the best guess's quantile score and tail score than their share of half-hours, and a perfect switching detector could lower the Primary quantile score or tail score by 3% or more. refuted not-for-production In the band of events the labeller finds most reliably, a perfect switching detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and its tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3%. Switching in that band touches 3 of the 16 Primary series and few half-hours, in one validation year. also relevant 00043 sw2-1-detector-scoreboard Experiment 37's neighbour-balance detector D1 finds injected load transfers between Primary substations more often than its single-series detector D0, when a transfer counts as found only if both its start and its end are placed correctly. refuted not-for-production Two simple switching detectors each found under a fifth of 600 simulated transfers, and no more than 0.29 in any size group. Over a 24-hour window the neighbour check found fewer large transfers than the single-series detector (0.21 against 0.29), and it helped only over the 4-hour window. primary 00041 sw2-0a-labeller-gate A labeller that reads features computed from raw power and the switching logs, and that uses no forecasting model as its deciding evidence, can find injected load transfers and reject placebo windows well enough to label the real logged closures of the 16 Primary substation demand series. partly supported not-for-production The AI model Sonnet called none of 120 placebo windows a switching event and timed starts and ends well, but it found 0.74 of the large, long fake transfers, under the 0.80 bar. It found 0.89 of them where the receiving substation has its own power readings and 0.60 where it does not. primary 00038 switching-mask-value For the 16 Primary substation demand series, excluding the half-hours of detected switching events from the history of the stack's error correction lowers the stack's threshold-weighted error at each series' historical 99th percentile on half-hours outside logged switching, by enough to justify adding a detector to the serving path. refuted not-for-production Leaving the half-hours that an early switching detector (D1) flags out of the 7-day error correction made the forecast worse on half-hours outside logged switching: the error rose 57% (95% interval 0.4% to 134%), where a 5% fall was needed. The rise came from an interval builder that ran one interval for 60 days, so masking with this detector is refuted as built. primary 00037 switching-first-look For the 16 Primary substation demand series, logged network switching (normal open points closed for hours or days) moves load that appears in the telemetry as a pair of opposite steps whose sum is conserved across the donor and its receiving neighbours, and a detector that tests that balance against the static interconnection list finds those transfers at a lower false-alarm rate than a detector that looks at each series alone. inconclusive not-for-production A detector that compares each substation with its neighbours found 0.33 of the switched power in the 18 visible validation transfers, and beat a single-series detector by about 0.14 in a rough post hoc comparison at equal alarm rates, which has no interval. The 18 transfers are too few to show whether the detector meets the 0.35 bar, so the result is inconclusive. primary
