docs.title: SW2: switching-event detection
docs.text:
The SW2 line improves the switching-event detector first, scored by event-level F1 against a labelled set of visible events, and leaves the use of the detector until the detector works. The detector serves two purposes later. The first is a lower forecast error, if switching periods act as unexplained noise for the XGBoost model and corrupt its lagged power inputs. The second, and the more important to NGED, is a forecast under the normal running arrangement (NRA), into which NGED can add its own switching. The switching events roadmap page proposes building that forecast by excluding switching periods from the training target. An event table for NGED is a third purpose, at lower priority. The production detector has to run on power alone, because the switching logs exist only for the trial area, so the logs are used here for evaluation only.

The line reopens a question that experiment 00038 closed, because experiment 00038 tested a different use of the detector. Experiment 00038 masked detected switching from the history of the error correction that runs after the XGBoost model, and the mask made the forecast worse. No experiment has yet masked switching from an XGBoost training target or from a lagged input. Experiment 00037 confirmed 37 of 612 logged closures of 2 hours to 60 days as visible in its own residual, and scored its detectors on the 18 of them in the validation months. That reference set is small, about 6 of the 37 are expected by chance, and the label was built from the residual the detectors use, so a detector that shares the residual's blind spots is flattered by the label. The line therefore starts by building a reference set independent of the detectors.

The full labeller design is in the private file data/ml-experiments/briefs/sw2_labeller_design.md.

docs.title: SW2-4 to SW2-9: detector iterations
docs.text:
Each iteration tests one change to the detector against the experiment 43 scoreboard, tuned on injections and odd months, scored on even months, with recall weighted by the MW moved as the headline from SW2-7 onwards. The order below is a proposal, by expected gain per hour of work, for the plan of each iteration to confirm:

  • SW2-5 (done, experiment 68): three rounds of refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the detected intervals changed the share of the moved MW found by +0.011 and the forecast error by -0.175%, and a random mask did as well.
  • SW2-6 (done, experiment 61): pairing the onset and return steps into one alarm score finds less than D0M at the same alarm rate, but taking the end of D0M's interval from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days finds 0.19 more of the moved MW.
  • SW2-7 (done, experiment 60): a step statistic that weights each half-hour by the expected power found the same transfers as the constant step on five injection shapes, so the step's shape does not limit the 24-hour detector. About a third of the transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more have the right onset and the wrong end, which SW2-6 (paired-step intervals) addresses.
  • SW2-8 (done, experiment 55): a single-series detector first, with neighbour balance as a sense check, not a gate. Every single-series alarm stands. A metered neighbour's opposite step raises the alarm's confidence and names the receiver, a same-sign step on the neighbours vetoes the alarm as a common-mode weather or calendar miss, and an alarm with no metered neighbour keeps its single-series confidence. Experiment 00043 found the neighbour-balance detector D1, which uses the neighbour test as a gate, finding almost none of the injected transfers without a metered receiver. The sum of the neighbourhood's residuals and a subset-sum over neighbours for a split feed the confidence score.
  • SW2-9 (done, experiment 62): whitening, experiment 00037's proposed F4, an autoregressive model of order 1 per series and hour of day fitted to the residual. The filtered detector found less of the moved MW (-0.097 at 24 hours), because the filter shrinks a day-long step faster than the noise of the 24-hour step.

docs.title: Metered solar farms
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. This theme covers the six solar farms whose output NGED meters in the trial area (labelled A to F). The experiments ask what shape each farm's output has, what physical plant (panel tilt, azimuth, ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, heat loss, and inverter clip) reproduces it, and what that implies for the unmetered solar behind Primary substations. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Metered solar farms: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00321 metered-farm-lower-tail-recalibration-and-tail-head Metered solar farms research default 1 (the blend assembled by experiment 300, scored to 10 days by experiment 310) lets the actual output fall below its 0.01 quantile 3.3% to 3.7% of the time, and no mixture-density head tried in experiment 318 changes that. Default plus a recalibration table, a zero-inflated lower tail, or a tail-targeted head brings the share of actual values strictly below the 0.01 quantile close to 1% at leads of 1 to 10 days, without raising the quantile score and without losing experiment 318's 0.99 gain. partly supported candidate The solar-farm forecast's lowest quantile was already close to correct: only 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below the 0.01 quantile, because the earlier 3.3% counted the 3.0% of half-hours that read exactly zero. A recalibration table, a zero-inflated head, and a tail head each lower the own-history score by 0.04 points or less (the unshrunk table raises it by 0.03 to 0.05 points), so none is adopted. A shrunk recalibration table does lower the score by about 0.05 points for a farm with no history, and two heads lower the 0.99 pinball loss by 3.7% to 8.5% while covering the 0.99 quantile only 98.3% to 98.9% of the time. primary 00318 metered-farm-mdn-head-more-features Giving the mixture-density head of Metered solar farms research default 1 the forecast lead (lead in whole days), the hour of day and day of year as sine and cosine pairs, and the ensemble spread of the shortwave irradiance lowers its quantile score, mostly beyond 36 hours and in the lower tail, and one head trained on all lead bands beats one head per band. partly supported candidate Giving the solar-farm head more inputs does not improve its overall score at any lead from 1 to 10 days, so the head's inputs are not what limits the forecast. The extra clock and cloud-spread inputs do lower the loss at the 0.99 quantile (the tail that matters for curtailment) by about 5% at days 3 to 7, and none of the changes fixes the lower tail, where 3.3% to 3.7% of actual values fall below the 0.01 quantile, where 1% is expected. Training one head for all leads makes the network with no plant nearly as good as the plant-based head at days 8 to 10 (0.4% worse), so the plant adds little there. primary 00313 metered-farm-pure-xgboost-and-mdn-vs-plant A predictor built only from weather and calendar inputs, with no plant model anywhere in the pipeline (not even as an input column), scores close to the plant-based forecast in own history and falls behind it where the plant carries what missing history or a long lead cannot. partly supported candidate A forecast that sees only weather and the calendar, with no physical plant model anywhere, scores almost as well as the plant-based forecast for the six solar farms, up to 10 days ahead, even when the farm has no history. The plant's added value is small, between 0% and 3.4%, and its intervals include zero except for XGBoost. For wind, the same kind of network also matches the best plant-based forecast, so a plant model is not needed to be competitive on these farms. primary 00310 metered-farm-long-lead-scoring Experiment 300's candidate (spread-binned plant, additive band, mixture head, blend with XGBoost) still beats XGBoost at every day band from 1 to 10 days ahead, and its margin over climatology shrinks as the lead grows. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast still beats the seasonal-average forecast (climatology) at every lead up to 10 days, by 39% at day 1 and 10% at days 8 to 10, so NGED can use it across its whole horizon of 1 to 10 days ahead. A plant-fed XGBoost model loses its skill by day 8, so a simple first production forecast should be the mixture-density neural network on the plant, which is the best single family at every lead, and the blend of the GAM, MDN, and XGBoost adds more than 1% only at days 1 and 2. primary 00304 metered-farm-node-sum-tail For the solar farms that share a bulk supply point, adding each farm's quantiles overstates the upper tail of the farms' summed output, adding independent bands understates it, and summing the 51 ensemble members' farm forecasts member by member gives calibrated 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles, because the ensemble carries the farms' shared dependence on cloud. not supported not-for-production The band for the combined output of the three farms beneath one substation comes out too wide if the weather forecast's 51 members are summed member by member, because the members' forecasts for the three farms move together almost perfectly while the farms' actual forecast errors are less closely linked. That band is almost the same as the band from adding each farm's quantiles. A band that assumes the farms' errors are unrelated is too narrow. A band from a Gaussian copula with a correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months comes closest to the stated probability. Only 5 half-hours in the scored year exceed 0.75 times a substation's maximum export, so this experiment cannot say what the band widths mean for curtailment cost. primary 00301 metered-farm-outage-state-band A small availability state (online, partly down, offline) estimated from the last 6 to 48 hours of a solar farm's power against its plant forecast improves the forecast band's lower tail during and after an outage. inconclusive not-for-production Solar-farm outages are too rare in the scored year to test an availability state: five of the six farms have at most 34 outage half-hours, and the sixth has 165. Too few half-hours remain to separate a 10% gain from chance, so the experiment stopped before fitting anything. If outages matter, the next test needs a longer period, such as the full history of farms A, B, and F. primary 00300 metered-farm-best-guess-assembly The assembled candidate (spread-binned plant P2, a generalised additive model (GAM) band on the plant's residuals, a mixture-density head (MDN), blended per quantile with XGBoost) scores better than plant-fed XGBoost on the quantile score and at the 0.99 quantile, and its advantage is larger for a farm with no history because the plant carries what the missing history cannot. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast (a physical power model, two correction stages, and a blend with XGBoost) scores 3.3% better than plant-fed XGBoost (XGBoost on the plant forecast, its ensemble spread, the unit mean, and the availability ratio, with no weather features of its own) on the quantile score, which averages the pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, when each farm trains on its own history. It is 43% better at the 0.99 quantile, which bounds how much output NGED may need to curtail. With no history for a farm, the gain over XGBoost is smaller (2.0%) and below the 3% we predicted, so the physical model helps less than we expected when a farm's history is missing. primary 00293 metered-farm-plant-tilt-and-clip The six metered farms fit best at a 15 to 20 degree tilt (experiment 282), while the spread-binned plant (P2 of experiment 270) assumes 35 degrees and caps its forecast at the 0.995 quantile of the tuning months' output. Replacing the fleet tilt with 20 degrees and the hard cap with a higher, soft cap lowers P2's April to July under-prediction and its 0.99 pinball loss. not supported not-for-production Changing the solar power model's panel tilt from 35 to 20 degrees fixes most of its winter over-prediction on clear days and improves the lowest 1% quantile of the forecast by 4%, but it leaves the overall forecast band and the 99% quantile unchanged and slightly worsens summer. A higher or softer cap on the power does nothing, so the shape of the power model is not what limits the upper tail of the forecast band. A tilt between 20 and 35 degrees, or a tilt that varies with the season, is the next tilt to test. primary 00292 metered-farm-ens-neighbourhood A day-ahead cloud field is often right in shape and wrong in position by tens of kilometres, so summaries of the ensemble's irradiance over the hexagonal cells around a metered solar farm carry information that the farm's own cell lacks. Giving H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) those summaries lowers its quantile score at 12 to 36 hour leads. not supported not-for-production At the six metered solar farms tested, the ensemble's irradiance on the cells around a farm adds almost nothing to the day-ahead forecast: the quantile score improves by 0.36%, against the 2% the plan needed, and the gain is not robust to dropping one farm. Adjacent cells, 15 km apart, differ from the farm's own cell by only about 3% of the irradiance, so the ensemble mean is too smooth between them to show where a cloud edge will fall. A weather source of a different kind is the next experiment to run, rather than more processing of the same ensemble. primary 00287 metered-farm-spread-binned-plant-heads On top of the spread-binned plant (experiment 270's P2), an additive model of the residuals gives a band as good as a neural head with monotone quantile output, so the additive model is the explainable candidate and the neural head adds nothing worth porting. supported candidate On top of the spread-binned solar-farm power model, an additive model gives a better forecast band than a neural network that adjusts each quantile, so the explainable model is the candidate. A neural network that outputs a three-component Gaussian mixture scores 1.3% better than the additive model in own history, mostly in the upper tail, but not clearly in zero history, so it needs one more test before it is preferred. A blend of the additive model, a neural network, and XGBoost scores 0.8% better than XGBoost alone and fixes XGBoost's weak 0.99 quantile. primary 00286 metered-farm-drift-soiling-injection A yield index that divides each farm's output by the output of the other farms, on half-hours when the other farms are near clear-sky output, reads a yearly trend more precisely than the monthly yield index of experiment 179, and it can recover a soiling loss that the monthly index cannot. partly supported not-for-production Comparing each metered solar farm with the other farms does not make the yearly trend of its output more precise overall, but of the two indices only the comparison can read soiling, because the plain index shows a false loss slope from weather alone. A loss of 1 %/yr or more is visible at 4 to 5 of the 6 farms, and a loss under about 0.4 %/yr is visible at only 2 farms (C and F). Whether these limits are the best that output alone can give is open: a panel-level or inverter- level record would test it. primary 00284 metered-farm-tail-head-past-weather Experiment 275 found that adding years of past-weather rows lowered the 0.99 pinball loss of the neural head H5 by 4.6% while its overall score moved by 0.47%. A small neural network trained with a loss restricted to the tail quantiles (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99), on the same past-weather plus ensemble rows with an era flag, lowers the 0.01 and 0.99 pinball loss of a metered solar farm's forecast below that of XGBoost trained on the same rows. partly supported not-for-production A neural network trained only to forecast the extreme edges of a solar farm's output band does beat XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile (the upper edge that matters for curtailment) by 30%, but the existing H5 network does slightly better still, and most of the gain comes from building the band around the physical power model and not from tail-only training. The years of past-weather rows add under 1% at the 0.99 quantile, and at the 0.01 quantile the share of half-hours below it is outside 0.5% to 1.5% at three farms (marginally at A, because of exact zeros at D, and clearly only at E). primary 00282 pv-plant-curve-audit The curve that turns sunshine into power in our solar models departs from the metered farms' measured curve by more than 5% of capacity somewhere in the clear-sky range, and the departure is the flat-top level (the inverter limit), not the panel tilt or the temperature loss. not supported not-for-production The curve that turns sunshine into solar power stays within 5 percentage points of capacity at 3 of the 6 metered solar farms and departs from their measured output at the other 3 in different directions, so no single fix to the inverter limit repairs it. The best-guess demand stack assumes panels tilted 35 degrees and the farms fit best at about 20 degrees, which makes the stack over-predict output on clear half-hours in December (measured is 0.66 of the stack, median over farms) and under-predict it from April to July by 5 to 8%. Swapping in the pooled shape of the other farms does not help, so the next experiment should try the 20 degree tilt inside the stack. primary 00275 metered-farm-long-history-neural-head Experiment 243 fitted H5 (the solar-farm power model plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) on about 17 months of ensemble forecasts. Adding each farm's rows built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature, back to 2019-09) as extra training rows, with a flag that marks them, lowers H5's quantile score on the ensemble-driven scored year, and the neural head gains more from the extra rows than XGBoost does. not supported not-for-production Training the neural network that corrects a metered solar farm's power forecast on nearly six years of past-weather rows, as well as on 17 months of ensemble forecasts, lowers the quantile score by only 0.5%, far under the 2% we predicted. The same rows improve XGBoost by 1.7%, so the neural network is not the better way to use extra history. The extra rows do lower the loss at the 99% quantile (the upper edge of the forecast band, which matters for curtailment) by 4.6%. primary 00273 metered-farm-sorted-quantile-rescore Some stored forecasts of experiments 224, 243, 248, 257, and 260 have quantiles that cross (a lower quantile above a higher one). Sorting the 11 quantiles in each row can only lower the pinball loss, so the stored scores are pessimistic for the arms that cross, and the arms that cross most gain most. not supported not-for-production The stored forecasts of seven metered-farm experiments have no crossing quantiles, because every fit script already sorted the 11 quantiles before writing them. Sorting the quantiles again therefore changes no score and no verdict. The 26,344 crossing rows found in experiment 268 are not farm forecasts: they belong to three generators that are not solar farms. Future heads should still be monotone by construction. primary 00272 metered-farm-weather-adapter-gam-vs-neural Extra weather variables that the solar-farm power model (the plant) ignores, fed through a learned correction to the plant's irradiance and temperature, close part of the gap between the plant driven by the ensemble weather forecast (about 0.91 of output fitted on sunny half-hours) and the plant driven by observed weather (0.973), and a small neural network does this better than additive curves. not supported not-for-production The extra ensemble weather variables (longwave radiation, humidity, precipitation, pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height) showed no usable information for the solar-farm power model at these six farms, whether they enter through additive curves or a small neural network, and the real variables do no better than placebo copies. A neural network with no plant, given the lagged power and the ensemble spread, scores 2.7% better than the plant but not better than the linear fit of experiment 257, so a correction to the plant's weather is not the route to a better forecast. primary 00270 metered-farm-xgboost-vs-plant-diagnostic XGBoost beats the plant (the solar-farm power model of experiments 218 and 224) on the six metered farms because of inputs the plant never sees, namely the farm's own lagged power and the ensemble spread, and not because of a better map from the ensemble-mean weather to power. Calendar columns and extra weather variables add little once those two are present. partly supported candidate XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model by about 3% in the quantile score even when it sees only the power model's own weather inputs, and the gain is in the width of the forecast band (the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles), not in the median forecast. The same gain comes from giving the power model a forecast band that depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index, and that band also beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile. Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. primary 00260 metered-farm-quantile-combination The three best solar-farm forecasters of experiment 243 win at different quantile levels (the neural network without physics at 0.99, H5 at 0.01), so convex per-level weights fitted on earlier months beat H5 alone, and a rolling adjustment of the outer levels brings their coverage to the nominal level without hurting the quantile score. partly supported candidate Blending the three stored forecasters with a separate weight at each quantile level scores 2.1% better than H5 alone, and every one of the six farms improves, because the neural network without the plant is best at the top quantile and H5 is best at the bottom one. About a quarter of the gain comes from averaging the five seeds, not from the weights. The rolling adjustment of the outer quantiles corrects the coverage of both tails but raises the error by 1.2%. primary 00257 metered-farm-fair-plant-arm The 4.4% gain of H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) over the plant alone in experiment 243 came from the inputs that H5 saw and the plant did not (the lagged power and the ensemble spread), so a convex linear quantile regression of the 11 offsets on those same inputs (arm P2) recovers most of it, and the neural network is not needed. supported candidate The neural network was not needed. Giving the solar-farm power model the lagged power and the spread of the ensemble members, through a plain linear fit, recovers about 90% of the neural network's gain and scores within half a percent of it. The linear fit is no worse at the 0.99 quantile (the 99% interval of the gap includes zero) and is simpler to serve, so it is the metered-farm candidate. primary 00255 metered-farm-node-curtailment-value When six metered solar farms beneath two bulk supply points are curtailed by the node-plus-generators rule of studies.node_curtailment, a forecast of each farm's output (the plant, XGBoost, or the plant with a neural head) avoids more curtailment cost than the NGED baseline, which assumes every generator runs at full capacity, and the neural head's lower 0.99 pinball loss does not show in the metric, because the rule uses only a farm's median. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting each solar farm's output instead of assuming every farm runs at full capacity cut the cost of curtailing at one of two substations (Boston, 40% lower) and raised it at the other (Skegness, 24% higher), so across both the saving is about a quarter, smaller than the uncertainty in the estimate. The neural network's better upper tail does not show in this cost, because the rule reads only each farm's median, and it lowers the cost by 3% against XGBoost, far under the 10% that would justify serving a neural network. Ranking farm forecasts by curtailment cost needs many more substations. primary 00248 metered-farm-architecture-ukv-inputs UKV irradiance and cloud, given as extra inputs to the two best neural heads of experiment 243 (H5, the plant plus 11 quantile offsets, and H2, the plant plus a correction), lower a metered solar farm's quantile score at 12 to 36 hours by more than the 1.8% that experiment 229 found for a blend of ensemble and UKV irradiance, because a neural head can use UKV cloud layers that a blend cannot. small gain not-for-production Giving the neural head on the solar-farm power model the Met Office's UKV irradiance and cloud forecasts lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, the same small gain that XGBoost gets from the same columns. At these six farms, a neural head gained no more from UKV than XGBoost did, so UKV is not worth a second weather source on this evidence. The UKV archive used is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so the 1% gain is an upper limit. primary 00246 metered-farm-ens-ukv-icond2-blend The DWD ICON-D2 regional weather forecast (2 km grid, run every 3 hours, 48 hours ahead) carries information about cloud over a metered solar farm that neither the ECMWF ensemble nor the Met Office UKV carries, so adding it to the ensemble plus UKV lowers the farm's day-ahead error. The evidence against is that at day 1 every single product lost to the ensemble mean for solar in the matched-lead study, and ICON-D2's errors are likely to be correlated with UKV's. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used is the CEDA research archive. small gain not-for-production Adding the German ICON-D2 weather forecast to the ECMWF ensemble and the Met Office UKV lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, which is under the 1.5% we set as worth a fourth weather source. ICON-D2 is available for only 12 to 29 hours of the day ahead at an 08 UTC forecast time, and the UKV archive used is a research archive, so this is an upper limit for production. primary 00243 metered-farm-architecture-comparison A solar-farm power model (the plant) as the base prediction, with a small neural network that adapts its inputs, its output, or both, forecasts a metered solar farm 12 to 36 hours ahead better than the plant alone and better than XGBoost, and keeps the plant's advantage on a farm it has never seen, while a neural network with no physics does not beat XGBoost on six farms. partly supported candidate A small neural network sitting on top of a solar-farm power model forecasts a metered solar farm about as well as XGBoost and improves on the power model alone by 4.4% in the quantile score, when the network outputs the whole forecast band. Networks that adjust a single number (the scale, a correction, or the sunlight fed to the power model) gain under 1%. The hybrid is far better than XGBoost at the upper tail (0.99 quantile, 29% lower pinball loss), which matters for curtailment. The neural network without physics does better still at that tail (32% lower pinball loss than XGBoost). primary 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 A small XGBoost residual model on the plant forecast's median error, an XGBoost spread model for the quantile offsets around it, or both, close at least half of the gap in quantile score between the XGBoost-free metered solar forecast (the plant fed the mean and spread of 51 ensemble members, experiment 224's arm 3) and the full XGBoost forecast (experiment 224's arm 5) at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. also relevant 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 For Primary substation demand, a metered solar farm, and a metered wind farm, the best forecast that uses no XGBoost anywhere scores within 2% of the quantile score of the best forecast that uses XGBoost, at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. also relevant 00229 metered-farm-ens-ukv-blend The Met Office UKV weather model (2 km grid, 54 hours) carries information about cloud over a solar farm that the 51-member ECMWF ensemble lacks, so giving a metered solar farm's forecast both products lowers its day-ahead error against the ensemble alone, and closes part of the gap between the ensemble-driven fit (0.91 of output on sunny half-hours) and the fit with observed weather (0.973) of experiment 218. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used here is the research archive on CEDA, which differs statistically from the live UKV. small gain not-for-production Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ECMWF ensemble lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1% to 2%. The gain is under the 3% we set as worth a second weather source, and the farms' fit on sunny half-hours moves only about 6% of the way to the fit with observed weather. The UKV archive used here is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so this result is an upper limit for production; a weather product of a different kind is the option we see for a larger gain. primary 00224 metered-farm-dayahead-two-number Passing each of the 51 ensemble members through a solar farm's plant model gives the farm's day- ahead output a spread that the ensemble-mean forecast does not have, and the mean and standard deviation of the 51 plant responses keep most of that information, as they did for Primary substations in experiment 193. A two-number plant forecast therefore forecasts a metered solar farm 12 to 36 hours ahead about as well as XGBoost, and gives calibrated tails. partly supported not-for-production The 51 members of the weather ensemble help a single solar farm's day-ahead forecast only a little: passing each member through a solar-farm power model lowers the quantile score by 1.8% against feeding the model their mean, and two numbers (their mean and spread) carry 95% of that. An XGBoost model on the same weather scores 2.8% better overall, and the solar-farm model beats it only at the 0.99 quantile, the upper tail of the forecast, which matters for curtailment (switching a generator off when the electricity network is overloaded). primary 00218 metered-solar-farm-plant-fit The six metered solar farms differ in panel tilt, panel azimuth, ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, heat loss, and inverter clipping, so a plant model with those parameters fitted per farm reproduces each farm's output better than the one fleet shape (tilt 35 degrees, facing south, DC:AC ratio 1.15, 0.4% loss per kelvin, cell temperature equal to air temperature plus 25 K times the shape), and explains why the flat top of farms C, D, E, and F falls 6% to 9% from spring to summer (experiment 183). not supported not-for-production Giving each metered solar farm its own panel tilt, azimuth, heat loss, and inverter limit fits its output only 0.003 better than one fleet shape (a fraction of output fitted of 0.953 against 0.950), so the plant is probably not what limits the fit. About 5% of the squared metered output stays unexplained, and the sunshine data is the likelier source. Per-farm plant parameters look unpromising for forecasting; a better sunshine forecast looks more promising, because the same plants fit only 0.91 with the ensemble forecast. primary

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Better irradiance for the metered farms
docs.text: Experiment 218 found that the plant's shape is not what limits the fit: giving each farm its own plant parameters raised the fraction of output explained by only 0.003 over one shape shared by all farms. The next question is whether a solar-irradiance product other than the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), or a blend of products, raises the fraction of the six farms' output explained by the plant model. The experiment fails if the best blend raises that fraction by less than 0.02 over CAMS alone.

docs.title: XGBoost with the plant's mean and the members' spread
docs.text: Experiment 224 found that an XGBoost model scores lower pinball loss at the 0.01 to 0.95 quantiles and the plant at the 0.99 quantile. The proposal is to give an XGBoost model two extra input columns, the plant's mean response and the standard deviation of the 51 plant responses, and to refit it weekly. The experiment fails if the quantile score improves by less than 2% over plain XGBoost, or if the 0.99 pinball loss stays above the plant's.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess
docs.text:
On one validation year, the best recipe tested so far beats the stored production-style forecast at Primary substations, supply points, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms. Most of the gain at Primary substations comes from correcting each forecast by its mean error over the previous 14 days, and refitting weekly adds a little more. The experiments scored one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026), and several settings were chosen on that year, so the gains are probably optimistic. Nothing from this theme is adopted in production, and the best training source for solar and wind farms is unsettled.

Over all lead times, BG2 has a lower mean absolute error of the median than manual_heuristic for all four target classes, for example 7.43 against 8.70 at Primary substations (experiment 87).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The stored production-style forecast loses to a simple rule. In experiment 13, the xgboost_baseline forecast had an error of the median 1.69 points of capacity above manual_heuristic's (99% interval +0.98 to +2.59; 16 Primaries). N1 was level with manual_heuristic (+0.22, -0.54 to +0.97), so that verdict was inconclusive.

The 14-day correction supplies nearly all of the early gain. In experiment 19, the correction lowered N1's quantile score by 0.99 points, and the stack of experiment 19 (N1 with the correction, a half-life, and a spread factor) beat manual_heuristic by 0.56 (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). The half-life added nothing to a frozen model. In experiment 87, the correction on a frozen XGBoost model lowers the Primary score by 1.38 of the 1.67 points that BG2 gains, and weekly refitting lowers it by a further 0.12 (95% interval 0.05 to 0.20).

The best guess of experiment 33 beats the production-style forecast by 3.8 to 6.3 points. The experiment 33 contrasts are 4.89 for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar farms (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind farms (-7.65 to -5.28), all at the 98.33% level. The farm contrasts use 53 Tuesday runs and the Primary contrast 73 runs. The correction applied to production explains 1.38 of the 4.89 Primary points. No arm widened production's band, so the share due to calibration is untested. The production-style 0.95 quantile was exceeded in 49% of Primary cases, against 7% for the best guess.

BG2 beats the previous best forecast at Primaries and supply points. BG2 lowered the score by 0.283 at the 16 Primaries (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and by 0.634 at the 4 supply points (-1.111 to -0.279). Adding the five-model blend lowered the Primary score by 0.086 (0.038 to 0.135). The solar offset lowered it by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on the rows it can touch, which are the daylight rows from April to September at the 5 of 16 Primaries that carry an offset. Over all scored rows the gain dilutes to 0.010.

The correction is the largest step, and weekly refitting, the blend, and the solar offset add small steps (experiment 87).

The solar and wind farm models cannot yet be ranked. The ensemble-trained model scored 0.050 points worse than the ERA5-trained mixture at 6 solar farms (98.75% interval -0.125 to +0.168) and 0.228 worse at 3 wind farms (-0.178 to +0.653). Neither interval rules out a loss above the margin we would accept (0.10 and 0.30), which is why the verdict of experiment 87 is partly supported.

Better weather would add little for Primary demand. In experiment 22, ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the score by 0.10 points (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), and not at all within 2 days. A demand model retrained on ERA5 lowered the score by 0.27 against an ENS-trained N1 with the correction (experiment 33). Both are ceilings, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late.

Whether the metering unit causes the MVA-only skill gap is unsettled. In experiment 56, skill was 10.5 percentage points lower at the 8 MVA series than at the 8 MW series over all hours (95% interval 2.1 to 17.5, resampling months), and the gap was smaller at sunny middays (April to September, 10:00 to 13:30 UTC: 5.6, -5.0 to 14.6). Resampling series instead of months gives -2.0 to 20.2 over all hours, so the data cannot separate the metering from which series were chosen. The experiment found no evidence of a need for special handling and cannot rule out a loss of about 15 points at sunny middays.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
BG2 is the best of the recipes tested here for Primaries and supply points, and no recipe is ranked for farms.

  • Primaries: a five-member quantile blend with a solar offset at 5 of 16 Primaries, scoring 5.260 against 5.543 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Supply points: the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no correction, scoring 12.925 against 13.559 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Solar and wind farms: the ERA5-trained mixture of experiment 33 and the ensemble-trained model of experiment 87 are within each other's intervals.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 19, 33, and 87 are marked candidate; none is adopted.

  • Primary demand: add the 14-day correction and the spread factor of 1.15 to N1 (experiment 19, experiment 33). Applied to the production forecast, the correction raised the threshold-weighted CRPS above the 99th percentile of history from 0.067 to 0.107 (higher is worse), and on N1 from 0.058 to 0.064, so check the tail when porting it.
  • Primaries and supply points: refit weekly, and blend five models at Primaries (experiment 87). Serve supply points without the correction.
  • Solar and wind farms: either the ERA5-trained mixture or the ensemble-trained model beats the production-style forecast, and which to serve is unresolved. Adding the power-curve base margin lowered the wind score by 0.057 (95% interval 0.024 to 0.098), and the solar bands need recalibration (experiment 87).

Experiments 13, 22, and 56 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Score every arm on the same cases. Without it, arms with missing forecasts are compared on different rows. The stored production forecast lacked 124 of 282,916 solar and wind cases and manual_heuristic lacked 195 (experiment 33). Look for arms with different run sets or ensemble members.
  • Compare with manual_heuristic as well as production. The quantile score at the 16 Primaries over 73 runs was 9.52 for production and 5.89 for manual_heuristic, so a gain over production alone overstates a new XGBoost model (experiment 13, experiment 33). Look for a changed production recipe.
  • Do not add the correction to supply points without a new test. It raised the supply-point score by 0.305 (0.060 to 0.594) in experiment 87, and experiment 33 found no gain there (+0.38, -0.12 to +0.92). The farms were not tested. Look for a second validation year or more than 4 supply points.
  • Build the correction history from daily forecasts. Experiment 19 used runs 5 days apart, so past errors were probably larger than a daily service would see, whereas experiment 87 scored 292 daily runs and its assembly script builds each correction from earlier runs. Look for a forecast service that runs less often than daily, which would make the history sparser.
  • Treat settings tuned on the scored year as optimistic. The spread factor, the blend scheme, the choice of which Primaries get the solar offset, and the half-life were chosen on the validation year (experiment 87). Look for results on a later year.
  • Read a staircase and a drop-one ablation separately. Adding the blend lowers the staircase score by 0.086, whereas removing it from BG2 raises the score by 0.091, because each starts from a different forecast (experiment 87). Look for a new member of the blend.
  • Report tail coverage and pinball loss as well as the quantile score. The quantile score hid that BG2's solar bands are too wide (experiment 87) and that production covers only 10% to 20% of cases (experiment 33). Look for a new weather source or target class.
  • Do not rely on the production-style row until its origin is confirmed. It was read from a stored table of unconfirmed origin, so its 10.54 may not match the deployed forecast (experiment 87). Look for a comparison with the current production forecasts.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the correction and the weekly refit hold their gains on a second validation year.
  • Which training source suits solar and wind farms, which needs more than 6 solar and 3 wind farms.
  • Whether the solar offset helps on daylight rows from April to September.
  • Whether the 10.5-point all-hours skill gap of MVA-only Primaries (2.1 to 17.5 over months, -2.0 to 20.2 over series) is caused by the metering, which needs more than 8 MVA series.
  • Whether monthly retraining without the correction beats the best guess of experiment 33: it scored 5.12 on one seed against 5.32, and needs a test on three seeds and more than one validation year.

The Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00333 primary-demand-foundation-model-zero-shot A pre-trained time-series foundation model (Chronos-2, 120 million parameters, Apache-2.0) forecasts a Primary substation's half-hourly demand from the substation's own history. Without weather inputs Chronos-2 cannot match Primary demand research default 3 at leads of 1 to 10 days. With the ensemble-mean temperature, the sun's elevation, and calendar columns passed as covariates, Chronos-2 closes part of the gap, but not all of it. partly supported not-for-production A pre-trained time-series foundation model, used without any training on our data, forecasts Primary demand clearly worse than Primary demand research default 3 at every lead from 0.5 to 240 hours. Giving the foundation model the temperature forecast, the sun's elevation, and the calendar recovers about one sixth of the gap, and makes sunny-daylight half-hours worse. Chronos-2, the one foundation model we tested, is not a candidate to replace the default, and a foundation-model forecast would have to be scored alone against the default before use as a blend member. primary 00330 primary-demand-standard-architecture-arm The maintainer prefers one standard architecture (a physics core, an optional neural input adapter, an optional mixture-density output head) across demand, wind, and solar forecasts, unless a different architecture gains strongly. Primary demand has the physics core already (the convex stack with a Kalman filter). One small network, trained jointly to correct the median and to give a mixture-density band, fed through a learned two-layer adapter of the ensemble summaries, scores within 0.03 points of Primary demand research default 3, so demand can share the standard architecture at little or no loss. partly supported not-for-production A single neural network with a learned input adapter and a mixture-density output, placed on top of the frozen convex stack, forecasts Primary demand at least as well as the current research default from 0.5 to 168 hours, so demand does not need a different architecture from wind and solar at those leads. The gain comes from the mixture-density output (the median-only version gains nothing), and most of it comes from one Primary, D10. The 7-to-10-day range is untested, and the cold-night and sunny-daylight tails are too uncertain to call the architecture safe. primary 00329 primary-demand-default-3-member-solar-distribution-at-7-to-10-days At 168 to 240 hours the 51 ensemble members have little skill for individual days, so the forecast centres on average sunshine and the half-hours that turn out sunny have realised demand below the median. The weakness of Primary demand research default 3 on sunny daylight (5.07 against the manual heuristic's 4.82 in experiment 317, for the convex chain before any blend) is therefore a fault of the predictive distribution (the lower tail on realised-sunny half-hours), not of the median. Replacing the two-number Gaussian summary of the members' solar responses with the 51 responses themselves (X1), mixing them with a climatology of the response (X2), or adding the members of the two previous daily runs (X3) fixes the distribution. not supported not-for-production The 7-to-10-day weakness on sunny half-hours no longer exists in the research demand forecast: the two-number solar summary and the daylight-only blend with the manual heuristic already took it from 5.2% worse than the heuristic to 6.6% better, so no new distribution method is needed there. What remains is one coastal Primary (D5), where the forecast is 11% worse than the heuristic, which points back at the solar term and not at the width of the bands. primary 00325 primary-demand-default-3-sunshine-response-refit-and-restriction Experiment 323's sunshine response (F1) harmed all daylight half-hours because the Kalman filter's level, the winter night offset, and the median correction were estimated on the errors of a fit without a response and so counted the same error twice (double counting), or because the response acts too widely, at forecast clear-sky index where the damped ensemble-mean forecast index mis-applies the response. Refitting those corrections on the response's own errors (F1r) removes the first cause, and restricting the response to clear-sky index above 0.6 and sun elevation above 15 degrees (F1s) removes the second. small gain not-for-production The sunshine response, once the rest of the forecast chain is refitted around it, no longer makes daylight forecasts worse, but the response improves the overall forecast by under 0.01 points, too little to adopt. The response improves spring daylight at two Primaries (D5 and D9) by about 0.11 points. primary 00323 primary-demand-default-3-flexible-sunshine-response-in-the-convex-fit Primary demand research default 3 trails the depth-1 XGBoost refit on April-to-June daylight half-hours because its solar term (the pinned capacity times the derated unit shape, with the D5 clip) is too high on clear spring middays. Experiment 322 grafted the refit's sunshine response onto the default and recovered 0.50 of the refit's advantage. A smooth correction in clear-sky index and sun elevation, fitted in the same bounded least-squares fit as the solar term, recovers a useful part of that gain with no model of other inputs. not supported not-for-production Adding a flexible sunshine curve to the solar part of the demand forecast does not recover the gap to the better-performing XGBoost model: it helps the sunniest half-hours but worsens the pooled score by about 0.4%. The advantage seen in experiment 322 is therefore not recovered by adding a smooth curve in clear-sky index and sun elevation on top of the existing level corrections, and most of the harm sits in the level shift. A boosted-tree sunshine term could use more inputs at once, and whether to test it is a decision for the research plan. primary 00322 primary-demand-default-2-daylight-only-heuristic-blend-and-sunshine-graft-replication (Stages 1 and 2) In experiment 320 the heuristic blend's gain at 168 to 240 hours sits on sunny daylight (-0.236 points) and in April to October, while its harm sits on cold winter nights, which are night half-hours. Confining the blend of experiment 319 to half-hours with the sun above 5 degrees (D1) keeps the gain with no harm on cold winter nights by construction, and a night weight that is a function of the share of the 51 ensemble members below 3 degrees C (D3) recovers the nights where the heuristic helps without harming cold ones. (Stage 3, a diagnostic) Experiment 316's sunshine graft, which recovered 0.36 of the depth-1 XGBoost refit's advantage on the worst April-to-June half-hours, replicates in April and June 2025. partly supported candidate At 7 to 10 days the blend with the manual heuristic gains about 4% at all hours, and about 2.4% when it is used only by day, which is the version with no harm on the coldest winter nights. Counting how many of the 51 ensemble members are cold finds 72% of those nights (the ensemble mean finds 41%), and a hard switch on that count keeps the whole 4% with almost no cold-night harm, but that switch was not pre-registered. The sunshine response of the depth-1 XGBoost refit explains about half of the refit's advantage on the worst April-to-June half-hours in both years, so a flexible sunshine term in the convex fit is worth testing. primary 00320 primary-demand-default-2-night-aware-heuristic-blend-and-night-band-width Primary demand research default 2 has two weak spots. (1) At 168 to 240 hours a blend with the manual heuristic lowers the score by 4.5%, but a single weight per lead band and season harms cold winter nights, where the convex chain is the better forecast. Default plus B1 (the blend switched off on half-hours forecast to be cold winter nights) or default plus B2 (a chain weight that is a logistic function of the ensemble-mean temperature, per lead band and day or night) keeps the gain without the harm. (2) The prediction bands are too wide at night, most clearly at one Primary (D10, whose band heads gained 0.144 points, 88% of it at night). Default plus N (a width multiplier on the quantile offsets from the median, fitted per Primary and per night or day block from the previous 90 days) removes that excess width at every Primary. partly supported candidate A blend with the manual heuristic still improves the 7 to 10 day Primary demand forecast by about 4%, and the harm it does on the coldest winter nights cannot be removed by switching it off when the weather forecast says the night will be cold, because at 7 to 10 days that forecast spots only between one and two cold nights in three. Narrowing the night prediction bands helps one Primary (D10, by 0.25 points on night half-hours), leaves the other five unchanged or slightly worse, and makes the cold-night tails worse. primary 00319 primary-demand-default-1-solar-summary-and-heuristic-blend-at-7-to-10-days Primary demand research default 1 has two weak spots at 168 to 240 hours: sunny daylight half-hours, where it scores 5.2% worse than the manual heuristic, and April to October, where it beats climatology by only 4%. Default plus x1 (the two-number solar summary S, the mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses, extended from 0.5 to 168 hours out to 240 hours) lowers the sunny-daylight score at 168 to 240 hours. Default plus x2 (a blend of the convex chain's median with the manual heuristic's, with the weight fitted per 24-hour lead band and season group) lowers the pooled score at 168 to 240 hours, mostly in April to October. partly supported candidate The demand forecast for 7 to 10 days ahead improves by about 2% when its solar term also uses the spread between the 51 weather-forecast members, and the gain is largest on sunny days (6.6%), where the forecast had been worse than the manual heuristic that National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) staff use. Blending in the manual heuristic improves the forecast by 4.5%, but the blend worsens the coldest winter nights beyond the agreed tolerance, so only the solar change is adopted. primary 00317 primary-demand-default-1-at-7-to-10-days The ensemble weather already reaches 10 days, so the convex model of Primary demand research default 1 can be driven to 240 hours, and with a spread table fitted per 24-hour lead band its quantile score stays better than the manual heuristic and climatology through day 9 and ties climatology on day 10. partly supported not-for-production The demand forecast we use for research still has a lower error than a table of typical demand by month and time of day (climatology) at 9 to 10 days ahead, by about 11%, because the temperature forecast keeps some skill there. Its advantage over NGED's manual heuristic shrinks to 5% to 9% beyond 7 days, and the 95% interval of that advantage includes zero. The advantage sits in winter and at two of the six substations. The forecast is useful out to 10 days on cold winter nights and no better than the heuristic on sunny daylight half-hours. primary 00316 primary-demand-night-level-and-single-input-terms (Stage 0) The gain of the band heads of experiments 311 and 314 at D10, an anonymised Primary substation, is mostly a night-time level error of Primary demand research default 1 and not a better description of the uncertainty. (Stage 1) The April-to-June gap between arm D and BG2 at D5 and D9, two anonymised Primaries, sits mainly in arm D's response to sunshine and not in its recent-power or calendar terms. inconclusive not-for-production The band heads help at one Primary substation mainly by narrowing its night-time bands, not by correcting a level error: a night level offset reproduces only 14% of the gain, with a wide interval. For the April-to-June gap to BG2, a post hoc test points at the sunshine response of the best-guess model (0.36 of the gap recovered on the worst half-hours, but only 0.19 at one of the two Primaries), and a differently fitted surrogate in the audit did not reproduce it, so the ranking of the families is unreliable. primary 00314 primary-demand-gated-or-pinball-band-head Experiment 311's mixture-density band head lowered the quantile score of Primary demand research default 1 but harmed sunny daylight half-hours, and its gain rested on D10. Keeping the default's bands on sunny daylight half-hours (gate), training the head directly on the 11-level pinball loss (quantile network), or both, removes the harm and leaves a gain that does not depend on one Primary. partly supported candidate Experiment 311's neural band head was stopped by harm on sunny daylight half-hours. Keeping the current bands on those half-hours fixes that harm, and the gated head scores 0.041 points better than the current Primary demand forecast bands (research default 1, lower is better). The gain is still almost entirely one substation, D10: without it the gain is 0.015 points and its interval touches zero, so the gated head is a candidate and not an adoption. Training the head on the quantile score directly gave no improvement. also relevant 00311 primary-demand-mixture-density-band-head Primary demand research default 1 (the GAM stack A+H+S of experiments 220 and 251) gets its bands from a smooth spread table and a cold-day widening of the upper offsets, around a median shifted by the neural head. A mixture-density neural network, which reads the weather state and may be skewed, gives bands with a lower quantile score, and the gain sits in the protected tail groups. partly supported candidate A neural network that sets the forecast bands from the weather state scores 0.037 points better than the current Primary demand bands over the scored year, and 0.034 better in the year before, but the gain comes almost entirely from one substation (D10) and the new bands are worse on sunny daylight half-hours. The band head is a candidate, not an adoption; the next test should keep the current bands on sunny daylight half-hours or train the head on the quantile score directly. also relevant 00310 metered-farm-long-lead-scoring Experiment 300's candidate (spread-binned plant, additive band, mixture head, blend with XGBoost) still beats XGBoost at every day band from 1 to 10 days ahead, and its margin over climatology shrinks as the lead grows. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast still beats the seasonal-average forecast (climatology) at every lead up to 10 days, by 39% at day 1 and 10% at days 8 to 10, so NGED can use it across its whole horizon of 1 to 10 days ahead. A plant-fed XGBoost model loses its skill by day 8, so a simple first production forecast should be the mixture-density neural network on the plant, which is the best single family at every lead, and the blend of the GAM, MDN, and XGBoost adds more than 1% only at days 1 and 2. also relevant 00306 summer-gap-solar-interactions-with-temperature-and-day-type The April-to-June daylight excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is an additive-structure problem. On cold clear spring days heating demand and rooftop solar output are both large, and an additive model must give the solar term one weight on every day. Experiment 299 found the D5 excess largest on clear midday half-hours (+1.67 points). Letting the solar shape interact with temperature (shape times the heating hinge) and with day type (shape times a weekend indicator) lets the model give those days a different solar weight. refuted not-for-production Letting the rooftop-solar term vary with temperature and with weekdays versus weekends does not close the April-to-June gap to BG2: at the two substations with the gap, the extra columns close about 0% of it. Two linear interaction columns therefore do not explain the gap. The next test is what BG2 uses that the convex demand model does not (item 5 of the summer-gap brief). primary 00305 summer-gap-what-bg2-knows-that-arm-d-does-not BG2 (experiment 87's production-style XGBoost forecast) beats the convex best-guess model (arm D) at the Primary substations D5 and D9 in April to June mainly through interactions of the sunshine inputs with temperature or with recent power, and not through the main effect of sunshine. refuted not-for-production The production-style forecast does not beat the convex best-guess model in April to June at two Primary substations through interactions of sunshine with temperature or with recent power: forbidding them removes under 3% of its advantage on the half-hours where the convex model trails most, and 16% on all daylight half-hours. A refit allowed no interactions at all keeps 92% of the advantage on the worst half-hours but only 45% on all daylight half-hours, so the worst half-hours come from the shape of single inputs and typical ones partly from other interactions. primary 00300 metered-farm-best-guess-assembly The assembled candidate (spread-binned plant P2, a generalised additive model (GAM) band on the plant's residuals, a mixture-density head (MDN), blended per quantile with XGBoost) scores better than plant-fed XGBoost on the quantile score and at the 0.99 quantile, and its advantage is larger for a farm with no history because the plant carries what the missing history cannot. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast (a physical power model, two correction stages, and a blend with XGBoost) scores 3.3% better than plant-fed XGBoost (XGBoost on the plant forecast, its ensemble spread, the unit mean, and the availability ratio, with no weather features of its own) on the quantile score, which averages the pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, when each farm trains on its own history. It is 43% better at the 0.99 quantile, which bounds how much output NGED may need to curtail. With no history for a farm, the gain over XGBoost is smaller (2.0%) and below the 3% we predicted, so the physical model helps less than we expected when a farm's history is missing. also relevant 00299 summer-gap-timing-night-level-and-error-correction The April-to-June excess of arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors) over BG2 (the production-style XGBoost forecast) at the substations D5 and D9 is a step that starts at the March clock change and sits at short leads, which would point at a local-time mismatch or at BG2's use of recent power. D10's night-time level offset of about -2 points (21:00 to 07:30 UTC) is a step on one date, not a smooth drift with temperature. The Kalman filter and the correction head are net harmful at D5 and D9 in April to June. not supported not-for-production The spring excess of the best-guess demand forecast over BG2 grows with sunshine, appearing on clear midday half-hours at D5 and across the whole day at D9. It is not concentrated in the 4 weeks after the clock change or at short leads, so the next test is the solar term's response on clear half-hours at D5. The Kalman filter and the correction heads are not the cause: removing the filter changes little, and at D5 the heads reduce the excess. D10's night-time offset varies partly with month and has no single date on which it changes. primary 00289 summer-gap-weather-input-discriminator The best-guess stack's weaker April to June score than BG2 at the decision Primaries comes from the ensemble's sunshine forecast (or its ratio calibration), and not from demand absorbing the solar term or from the error-correction layers. partly supported not-for-production Giving the best-guess stack the sunshine that actually happened would close about 70% of its April to June gap to BG2, but the same change helps the stack nearly as much in July to September, when the stack already matches BG2. Most of the April to June gap beyond the July to September gap therefore stays. That points to the solar term in the demand model, or to the error-correction layers, and away from the ensemble sunshine forecast. A refit with realised sunshine as the solar driver, and a check of the solar term at D5 and D9 in April to June, are the next steps. primary 00281 economy7-night-step-smooth-in-temperature A forecast of primary substation demand whose night level is a set of free levels for each UTC night half-hour (experiment 121's NS-U), and then a step whose size is a monotone function of the cold, scores better in the Economy 7 step hours and on cold winter nights than the same forecast with only the winter night offset (experiment 155), when the weather input is the ensemble-mean forecast and not past weather. Economy 7 is the tariff that switches storage heaters on shortly after 00:30 UTC. Experiment 121 found a gain of 0.233 points on winter nights on past weather and asked for a test on weather forecasts. inconclusive not-for-production Fitting the Economy 7 night levels inside the demand model, and not adding a winter night offset afterwards, lowered the day-ahead error by about 0.02 to 0.03 points of rated demand over all rows in both years and by about 0.04 points on winter nights, but the gain in the two hours after the step starts could not be shown: it changes sign between the two years and depends on two or three substations. Letting the step grow with the cold added almost nothing over free night levels. The Economy 7 term does not explain the night-time gap at D10 in April to June. also relevant 00280 pv-empirical-shape-and-capacity-in-arm-d The April to June 2026 gap between arm D (the monthly-refit generalised additive model of experiments 155 and 220, scored on experiment 178's rows) and BG2 comes from its solar term: the pinned solar capacity is too high and the south-facing fleet shape is not the shape the metered farms show. Replacing the fleet shape by the pooled empirical shape of experiment 269, at the capacity that shape's real-series fit supports, lowers arm D's April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looks too high (D5, D9, and D16). not supported not-for-production Putting the empirical solar shape into the forecast, at the pinned capacity or at the lower capacity the real series supports, does not lower the April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looked too high. The change is under 0.01 MW against an error of about 0.5 MW, and the intervals are wide. A capacity cut that is correct for the whole of April to June is not the fix either: at D5 it raises the error. This experiment finds no sign that the shape or the capacity of the solar term closes the summer gap to BG2. also relevant 00279 dp-heating-curve-monotone-lagged-temperature-and-wind The heating response of the convex demand model T-all-K (a hinge at 15.5 C on four trailing-mean temperatures, split by day type) is too rigid. A smooth, monotone, non-negative curve on the same temperatures (A1), the same curve also on exponentially weighted and previous-day mean temperatures that carry the building's thermal lag (A2), or a small monotone neural network on three daily mean temperatures and the wind speed (A3), lowers the day-ahead quantile score on cold nights and winter days at the five decision Primaries, and the fitted curve is not a straight line. not supported not-for-production A smooth heating curve, a thermal lag, and wind each leave the day-ahead forecast within about 0.02 points of the straight-line heating response, so the evidence does not justify adding any of them. A small neural network learns a plausible curved heating response and lowers the error on cold nights by 0.13 points, but that gain comes from one cold spell in January 2026, did not appear in the previous year, and the network failed a test on synthetic data, so the substation card keeps the straight line for now. also relevant 00278 stack-retraining-cadence The best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the two-number solar summary) needs its neural network head retrained at least quarterly, but its convex model (a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its coefficients) tolerates quarterly instead of monthly refits, because the filter absorbs the drift between refits. not supported not-for-production Retraining the small neural network that corrects the demand forecast's median, every quarter or every month, scored no better than training it once before the scored year, so it needs no retraining schedule over a year. The convex demand model should keep its monthly refits, which take 0.4 s per substation: refitting quarterly instead scored 0.010 points worse overall (not shown to be acceptable) and weekly refits gained nothing. Refitting the two solar factors quarterly instead of monthly changed nothing. primary 00277 lsc-curtailment-metric-on-existing-forecasts The curtailment-cost metric of experiment 268 (studies.node_curtailment, sorted quantiles) ranks the four existing forecasts as the other metrics do, and can resolve the differences between them well enough to judge the load-shift questions of the decision program. supported not-for-production Over a year of ordinary days, the curtailment metric ranks the four existing forecasts the way the other scores do, and it can tell the GAM stack from BG2 (BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more on the six Primaries at the 0.5 limit, a figure that ranks forecasts and is not money saved). Inside the windows around the 7 logged load transfers, the GAM stack cannot be separated from BG2, because those windows hold only 926 to 2,923 scored half-hours.
