The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. also relevant 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) that already has the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, the pinned solar capacity, and the ensemble mean as its weather input (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when two post-forecast corrections are added: a winter night offset (experiment 137) and the 14-day mean error profile of recipe R (experiment 115). The mechanism is that the two corrections remove different errors, a level error that repeats on winter nights and a half-hour-of-day shape error that repeats day to day, so their gains add. The assembled arm then scores below experiment 111's GAM-K and BG2 (experiment 87) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, and its tails on cold nights and on holidays are no worse than the uncorrected arm's. inconclusive candidate Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. also relevant 00136 dp-bg-stage1-assembly-on-the-ensemble-mean A convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K, experiment 111), given experiment 114's heating split by day type (T-all) and experiment 133's single shared filter noise setting (POOL), and driven by the ensemble mean of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) instead of its 51 members, forecasts Primary demand 0.5 to 168 hours ahead at least as well as BG2 (experiment 87) and better than experiment 111's GAM-K. The mechanism is that the three gains came from different parts of the model (the hinge, the filter noise, the weather input) and so add, and that experiment 125 found that the members' own spread adds no tail skill, so one forecast on the mean loses nothing. inconclusive not-for-production Putting everything that has helped so far into the convex demand model and driving it from the ensemble mean gives a forecast that scores the same as the production recipe (BG2) and as experiment 111's GAM-K, and the experiment cannot tell any of the three apart. Using the ensemble mean makes the score about 0.04 points worse than using all 51 members, and the heating split and the shared filter noise improve it by about 0.05, so the assembly did not add up to the hoped-for gain. also relevant 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. primary 00087 bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations Assembling the best ideas of the last experiments into one forecast beats the previous best forecast of each target class on the 292 daily forecast runs of the validation year (July 2025 to June 2026). For the 16 Primary substations the assembly is a five-member quantile blend of weekly-refitted and monthly-refitted XGBoost models, an analogue model, a pooled-by-type model, and the frozen stack, with an explicit solar offset at the 5 substations that have a clean solar capacity. For the 4 bulk and grid supply points it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no error correction. For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model trained on the ensemble forecast's own history. partly supported candidate BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). primary 00056 mva-only-primaries-skill-against-mw-primaries The best guess (experiment 33's N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor) forecasts the 8 trial Primary substations metered in MVA clearly worse, relative to manual_heuristic, than the 8 metered in MW, and the gap is largest at sunny middays, when embedded solar can push net flow through zero and an MVA meter reads the magnitude of that flow with no direction. inconclusive not-for-production At sunny middays the best guess has 5.6 percentage points less skill at the 8 Primary substations metered only in MVA than at the 8 metered in MW, but the 95% interval (-5.0 to 14.6) includes zero. The experiment found no evidence of a need for special handling of MVA-only Primaries and cannot rule out a loss of up to about 15 percentage points. primary 00033 best-guess-architecture-vs-production The best-guess architecture that the first 32 experiments point to lowers the quantile score below the deployed production recipe by more than the threshold set for each technology (1.0 point of capacity for Primary substation demand, 0.5 for solar farms, 1.0 for wind farms), each scored on its own rows. supported candidate The best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), each wholly below its threshold. primary 00022 era5-weather-ceiling-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the winning recipe of experiment 00019 (the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 with a recency half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day error correction, and the 1.15 spread factor) ERA5 weather in place of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather at serving time lowers the quantile score by at least 0.3 points of capacity over all leads. refuted not-for-production ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score over all leads by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the rule asked for is ruled out. primary 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic For the 16 Primary substation demand series, stacking three changes on the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 (a 14-day correction from the model's own recent errors, a recency half-life of 0.5 years, and a spread factor of 1.15) beats manual_heuristic on ENS weather, which N1 alone does not. supported candidate C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). primary 00013 primary-demand-against-stored-baselines For the 16 Primary substation demand series, a single-stage XGBoost quantile model trained on the ENS control member (N1: the 00006 columns, recency weights, and power lags measured from the forecast origin) beats manual_heuristic, the best stored baseline, and the production recipe loses to manual_heuristic because it has no usable power persistence at short leads. inconclusive not-for-production C1, N1 minus manual_heuristic, Primary substations, mean absolute error of the median: +0.22 points of capacity over all leads (99% interval -0.54 to +0.97) and -0.57 up to 48 hours (-1.33 to +0.27). primary

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Retraining and training history
docs.text:
On 16 Primary substations, refitting the XGBoost demand model every week with no error correction scored 0.20 to 0.24 points of capacity below a model fitted once with the correction, on two separate sets of forecast runs (292 runs at 16 Primaries, and 274 control-member-only runs at 13). The gain is fragile: three substations carry much of it, and refitting weekly instead of monthly adds only 0.04 to 0.13 points. Models trained on one old year scored worse than ones trained on a recent year, but one substation drives most of that gap.

This theme asks how often to refit the demand forecast of Primary substations, and how much history to train on. The comparison throughout is the stack: an N1 model fitted once, with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity, and a negative contrast is an improvement. Refitting solar and wind models gained little, and the cause of the penalty on older training years is not yet found.

Monthly and weekly refitting scored below the stack, though monthly minus the stack has a 99.375% interval of -0.44 to +0.08, and the 14-day correction did not help a refitted model (16 Primaries, 73 runs; experiment 34).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A 12-month window, a half-life of 1 year or less, or the 14-day correction beat training on all history, and a model never retrained lost most (experiment 17). Against an all-history model retrained monthly, the mean absolute error of the median changed by -0.84 for a 12-month window (99.44% interval -1.19 to -0.53), -0.92 for a half-life of 0.5 years (-1.22 to -0.64), +0.52 for yearly retraining (+0.30 to +0.81), and +3.80 for never retraining (+3.12 to +4.47). The test used ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late, so these are ceilings.

Refitting monthly scored 0.20 below the stack in experiment 34, and the pre-registered interval included zero. The contrast was -0.20 (95% interval -0.38 to -0.01; 99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08), so the verdict is inconclusive. Weekly minus monthly was -0.07 (99.375% interval -0.18 to -0.00).

Weekly refitting beat the stack again on two further sets of runs. In experiment 48, on the 292 daily runs that experiment 34 left out, the contrast was -0.20 (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035) and weekly minus monthly was -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.03). In experiment 81, on 274 runs from July 2023 to March 2024 at 13 Primaries, scored with the control member only, the contrast was -0.240 (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145) and weekly minus monthly was -0.039 (-0.064 to -0.012). On an earlier set, July 2022 to March 2023, it was -0.080 (99.17% interval -0.187 to +0.051 in the text; the figure draws 95% intervals, -0.165 to +0.017): the same sign, with an interval that includes zero.

Weekly refitting beat the stack in July 2023 to March 2024 and had the same sign, with intervals that include zero, in July 2022 to March 2023 (13 Primaries, experiment 81).

Three substations carry much of the gain, so it is not established across all 16. In experiment 48 the contrast without D8 was -0.14 (99.44% interval -0.34 to +0.04), and without D8, D12, and D5 -0.08 (-0.24 to +0.10). A t-interval over the 12 months gave -0.43 to +0.04. In experiment 81, D8 alone gained 2.05 (95% interval -2.60 to -1.44), and without D8, D12, and D5 the contrast was -0.093 (95% interval -0.189 to -0.014). Experiment 81 found no sign that the weekly gain grows as 9 km weather data accumulates: it fell from -0.552 in December to -0.137 in March.

The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once in experiments 17, 19, and 48, and stops helping a refitted one. It lowered the frozen model's score by 1.45 (95% interval -1.87 to -0.98; experiment 48), though it did not help the frozen model on experiment 81's runs (+0.091, -0.005 to +0.187). On a weekly model it raised the score by 0.23 (99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44; experiment 34) and by 0.08 to 0.16 with intervals that include zero (experiment 48). It supplied nearly all of the stack's gain over N1: -0.99 of -1.00, and the stack scored 0.56 below manual_heuristic (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26; experiment 19).

Averaging the quantiles of several models gained 0.04 to 0.10 points. Three models gave -0.097 against the best member (98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026; experiment 35). Five models gave -0.076 against weekly refitting (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023; experiment 49), and four gave -0.038 (99.17% interval -0.070 to -0.007), short of the 0.05 threshold (experiment 81). The three-model and five-model averages include the frozen stack as a member.

Refitting solar and wind models gained little. Monthly refitting minus a frozen model was -0.044 at 6 solar farms (99.44% interval -0.158 to -0.003) and +0.007 at 3 wind farms (-0.001 to +0.014), for ERA5-trained models (experiment 48). Six and three farms cannot say more.

Older training years hurt in models trained once on a single year, mostly through one substation, and neither the average level nor the weather product explains it. A model trained on 2021-07 to 2022-06 scored 1.57 worse than one trained on 2024-07 to 2025-06 on 13 Primaries with control-member weather (98.3% interval 1.14 to 2.00), but 0.61 (95% interval 0.41 to 0.81) without one substation, and removing each substation's trailing 365-day level took off 42% of that, under the half predicted (experiment 93). The gap was 1.71 with ERA5 weather in both years (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29), as large as with forecast weather, so the 18 km to 9 km change of weather product is not the main cause (experiment 95). The long-history sub-theme tests a physics-based model that may use old years. Experiment 95 also gave 0.61 without D8 on the control member and 0.78 on ERA5. Half-life contrasts under refitting were unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

The old-year penalty was as large on ERA5 as on forecast weather, so the weather product is not the main cause (13 Primaries, experiment 95).

These changes did not help a refitted model. Re-tuning the spread factor moved the score by -0.0001 (99.17% interval -0.012 to +0.018), and substation fingerprints in a pooled model by +0.009 (-0.037 to +0.050; experiment 49). A zero starting value moved it by -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054; experiment 80). Dropping the Christmas column and changing the half-life from 0.5 to 2 years were unresolved (experiments 49 and 81).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: The best of the recipes tested here for Primary demand is an N1 per substation, refitted weekly with no correction, with an average of quantiles over other models that includes the frozen stack. Weekly refitting scored 5.44 against 5.64 for the stack on 292 daily runs (experiment 48), and the five-model average scored 4.968 against 5.044 for weekly refitting on 73 runs (experiment 49). The half-life, the Christmas column, and the correction were not shown to help a refitted model (experiments 34, 49, and 81). BG2 builds on this recipe.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 17, 19, 34, 35, 48, 49, and 81 are marked candidate; none is adopted. The other experiments of the theme are not-for-production.

  • Refit the Primary demand model weekly and drop the 14-day correction (experiments 34, 48, and 81). This adds a scheduled job that refits 16 series at about 10 seconds each on a graphics card (experiment 34). Monthly refitting gets most of the gain over the stack (-0.20 in experiments 34 and 81; -0.08 with an interval that includes zero in experiment 48), so the case for weekly over monthly is 0.04 to 0.13 points.
  • Refit the bulk and grid supply point models weekly (experiment 48: -0.66 against the stack, 99.44% interval -1.23 to -0.27, on 4 series).
  • Serve an average of quantiles at Primaries (experiments 35 and 49). It needs several models, and experiment 81 found a four-model version short of its threshold.
  • The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once (experiments 17 and 19). A 12-month window or a 0.5-year half-life beat all history under monthly refitting in experiment 17, on ERA5 weather; their value under weekly refitting is unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Use a monthly 12-month-window refit for contrasts of 0.05 or more, and quote absolute and tail scores from weekly refits. The window (150 rounds, learning rate 0.15) reproduced the monthly-minus-weekly gap to within 0.01 at 0.03 to 0.10 of the fit time, but scored 0.16 above full weekly refitting (experiment 85, experiment 34). For contrasts about cadence, retraining rules, or the correction, window, or half-life, use the weekly refit on all history with 150 rounds instead, because conclusions about them change with the schedule (experiment 85). Re-check for another model family or a contrast under 0.05.
  • Do not use quarterly refits to compare arms. Quarterly minus weekly was +0.381 (95% interval +0.207 to +0.565) on the 12-month window, three times the monthly gap (experiment 85). Re-check on other row sets.
  • Compare a refit arm only with a same-code repeat of its control. In experiment 75 only 9% of per-case scores matched the stored weekly run to 0.001, with a largest gap of 4.39 points, although the mean matched to 0.0001. Repeats moved the mean by 0.004 to 0.007 in experiment 80 and by 0.001 in experiment 85. Otherwise a per-case or per-event contrast reads fit noise. Re-check on CPU fits.
  • Retest the 14-day correction after any change of refit cadence or target class. It helps a frozen model, hurts a weekly one in experiment 34 (+0.23, 99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44), and stopped helping in experiment 48 (intervals include zero). Experiment 81's frozen model gained nothing from it. At supply points adding it raised the score by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594; experiment 87). For farms, a correction by the mean error raised the continuous ranked probability score by 0.437 (solar, 99.58% interval +0.215 to +0.664) and 0.413 (wind, -0.003 to +0.924), and a median of the window's errors moved it by +0.010 and -0.064, post hoc with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). A 7-day window and a multiplicative form were worse than the 14-day additive form, and the correction did not help 4 supply-point series (experiment 21). Re-check with another correction window or model.
  • Report every contrast with and without the series that carries it. D8 alone gained 2.05 (experiment 81) and has a 13.1-point old-year gap while the other 12 substations range from 0.0 to 2.6 (experiment 95). Otherwise a pooled interval reads as a gain across all series. Re-check on other substations.
  • Do not screen features on a frozen model. The weekly-analogue columns gained 0.05 on a frozen model and 0.01 under monthly refitting (experiment 34). Re-check with other recent-demand features.
  • Do not stand in warm-start boosting for refitting. Warm starts got worse with more updates (7.76 against 6.21 for the weekly chain over the daily months; +1.55, +0.33 to +3.21), and a proxy that sees later data is a screening device, not a forecast score (experiment 34).
  • Quote absolute scores only within one experiment's runs. The stack scored 5.32 on experiment 34's 73 runs and 5.64 on experiment 48's 292, and experiment 81's control-only scores match neither. The stack of experiment 19 has a half-life of 0.5 years, and the stacks of experiments 33, 34, 48, and 87 use the 2-year weighting. Re-check which stack a new experiment uses.
  • Check that a 12-month window can test an input. The COVID indicator is constant inside the window, so it cannot be tested (experiment 49). Look for the input's variation within the window.
  • A single month cannot show a weather-product change. The frozen model's lead over manual_heuristic swings from 11.6% in April to 1.2% in June to 8.8% in August (experiment 81). Re-check with a model trained on one product.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether weekly refitting beats the stack at all 16 Primaries on a year the project has not scored, and with the full ensemble; the Research plan lists the longer ENS history.
  • Whether any of the gain is adaptation to the 9 km weather product (experiment 81 could not separate them).
  • What makes older training years worse. Drift differs by series (experiment 92, inconclusive), and experiment 95 suggests changes in solar, heating, or the electricity network without testing any.
  • Whether the Christmas column and the half-life matter under weekly refitting.

The Experiments page lists every experiment of the theme.

docs.title: Retraining and training history: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00331 primary-demand-recency-weights-on-gam-and-kalman When the additive (GAM) model with a Kalman filter on its daily residual is refitted monthly, giving older training rows exponentially less weight forecasts the next month better than equal weights on the full history, and no worse than training on the last 24 months only. not supported not-for-production Training the monthly refit mostly on recent data improves the next month's forecast by about 0.025 points of capacity, but a plain 24-month window gets the same gain, so smooth recency weights add nothing and no weights should go into the research default. Half of the gain comes from one Primary substation whose demand shifted in 2023. Giving extra weight to rows from the same time of year in earlier years gave a further 0.012 points and is worth its own test. This is a lab result on past weather with a Kalman filter that already adapts to level changes. primary 00328 lsc-regime-changes-detect-then-model-part-1 A permanent change in the configuration of an electricity network (a large new generator, a new factory) can be found offline from a Primary's own history, and a forecast that keeps the effects of the old behaviour fitted on the full history and adds new effects that exist only from the change onward scores better after the change than the same forecast refitted on a recent window only. not supported not-for-production Adding effects for a detected permanent change does not forecast better than refitting the additive model on the last 24 months, in a lab setting where the model is given past weather. The detectors find a 10% step of a Primary's load within 60 days only 26% of the time at an acceptable false-alarm rate, so there is little time after the alarm for the extra effects to help. On this base, handling a regime change comes down to how often the model is refitted. The rolling-GAM detector might still help when building substation cards, which this experiment did not test. also relevant 00298 lsc-long-deep-detector-and-refit-cleaning A trivial detector on the daily mean residual of the lagless convex additive model (GAM_ONLY) finds load shifts that last days to weeks and cover at least 10% of a Primary substation's load, which the existing hour-scale detectors miss, and excluding the days it flags from the monthly refit stops the forecast learning those shifts as the normal pattern. not supported not-for-production A simple detector on the daily mean error of the forecast that uses no recent power finds about as many of the long, deep real load shifts as the learned score LR_b20 (10 to 12 of 19 for four of the six variants). The cumulative-sum variant B also finds 27 of the 29 multi-day drops at D8, which are probably a gas engine and not load shifts; variant C finds 11. Leaving the days a detector flags out of the monthly refit cuts the share of a 30-day transfer that the forecast learns as normal from about 19% to about 10% to 13%. Excluding the true shift days instead cuts the share to 2.8%. The detectors recover less because each needs 1 to 3 days to fire and misses about 40% of long injected transfers and over half of the real ones. Tell NGED that transfers of 14 days or more are partly learned as normal, and try a detector that fires on the first day next. also relevant 00295 regime-segmentation-part-b-persistent-regimes-without-labels A segmentation of a Primary's whole history with hindsight, using only changes in the distribution of the residual of a lagless convex additive model (GAM), finds regime changes without labels. A regime is the whole period, without gaps, during which one configuration holds. For D8's gas engine, the regime is the whole period in which the engine is installed and included in the meter, including the spells when the engine is off. Whether the engine is running, and whether a load shift is in force, are states inside a regime. A boundary is a regime change when the distribution does not return to its earlier form and no neighbouring Primary shows the opposite change, and a state change otherwise. not supported not-for-production Looking only at the residual of a forecast that uses no recent power, a segmentation finds a lasting change of 25% of a Primary's load and dates it with a median error of 0 days, but it misses about half of 10% changes and cannot reliably tell a 14 to 60 day load shift from a lasting change. At D8 it finds the 2023-08-15 break exactly, but only at penalties that also find 2.5 or more regime changes per Primary-year at the other Primaries. An offset for the latest regime lowers the forecast error after a step by 2.2 points of capacity, but a plain 60-day mean residual does as well, so the segmentation is not worth adding for that purpose. also relevant 00290 lsc-long-shift-cut-date-robustness The 19% of a 30-day transfer that experiment 274 found learned as normal is stable across fit-cut dates, so that the share learned lies within 15% to 25% at every cut date. not supported not-for-production The forecast with no recent power learns about a fifth of a 30-day load transfer as normal, but the share depends on the date: it ranges from 9% to 29% across 12 end dates, so experiment 274's 2.49-point bias is a typical value, not a fixed one. Quote the share as a range of about 9% to 29%. The cause of the spread is not located. also relevant 00278 stack-retraining-cadence The best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the two-number solar summary) needs its neural network head retrained at least quarterly, but its convex model (a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its coefficients) tolerates quarterly instead of monthly refits, because the filter absorbs the drift between refits. not supported not-for-production Retraining the small neural network that corrects the demand forecast's median, every quarter or every month, scored no better than training it once before the scored year, so it needs no retraining schedule over a year. The convex demand model should keep its monthly refits, which take 0.4 s per substation: refitting quarterly instead scored 0.010 points worse overall (not shown to be acceptable) and weekly refits gained nothing. Refitting the two solar factors quarterly instead of monthly changed nothing. also relevant 00275 metered-farm-long-history-neural-head Experiment 243 fitted H5 (the solar-farm power model plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) on about 17 months of ensemble forecasts. Adding each farm's rows built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature, back to 2019-09) as extra training rows, with a flag that marks them, lowers H5's quantile score on the ensemble-driven scored year, and the neural head gains more from the extra rows than XGBoost does. not supported not-for-production Training the neural network that corrects a metered solar farm's power forecast on nearly six years of past-weather rows, as well as on 17 months of ensemble forecasts, lowers the quantile score by only 0.5%, far under the 2% we predicted. The same rows improve XGBoost by 1.7%, so the neural network is not the better way to use extra history. The extra rows do lower the loss at the 99% quantile (the upper edge of the forecast band, which matters for curtailment) by 4.6%. also relevant 00274 lsc-long-arrangement-audit-gam-refit A forecast with no lagged power learns a long-lasting change of running arrangement as the normal pattern, because the monthly refit trains on whatever the meter recorded. The learned share grows with the duration of the arrangement, and the duration beyond which the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) is wrong by more than a stated tolerance sets the limit that can be told to NGED. not supported not-for-production A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal, and the forecast learns the transfer quickly: a transfer lasting only 7 days leaves the forecast 1.2 points of effective capacity too high for the next 2 days, and a transfer lasting 30 days leaves it 2.5 points too high (about a fifth of the transfer). No tested duration, down to 7 days, was short enough to avoid this. Masking known transfers out of training is the obvious remedy, but this experiment did not test it, and the next experiment should test it together with transfers of 1 to 6 days. also relevant 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. also relevant 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00095 age2-old-year-penalty-with-the-same-weather-product-demand The extra forecast error of an old training year (experiment 93) comes mostly from the change of weather product between the old years (18 km grid spacing) and the recent year (9 km), not from the age of the training data, so an old year and a recent year that use the same weather product score about the same. refuted not-for-production The old-year penalty does not shrink when both years use ERA5: the 2021-07 year is 1.71 points worse than the 2024-07 year on ERA5 (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29) and 1.57 worse on the control member (1.12 to 2.03), so the weather product is not the main explanation and the penalty goes with how old the training year is. primary 00093 age1-old-training-year-after-level-normalisation-demand A year of training data hurts a Primary substation demand forecast with its age only because the substation's average demand level differed in that year, so subtracting a trailing 365-day level from the targets and the power lags removes most of the penalty for an old training year. refuted not-for-production Subtracting a trailing 365-day level removes 42% of the old year's penalty (C1 1.57, C2 0.91 points), under the half the prediction required, and without the one series that carries most of the penalty it removes none (0.61 to 0.68). primary 00092 lv0-drift-diagnostics-on-stored-predictions-demand Most of the drift in Primary substation demand since 2022 is a per-series level or smooth trend, not a change of daily shape, so a slow per-series level term, not a new weather response, is what a long-history or pooled XGBoost model is missing. inconclusive not-for-production Drift is large and differs by series, but a level shift alone does not explain the loss from extra history or the pooling gap. primary 00085 cheaper-retraining-schedules-rank-arms-like-weekly-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, a cheaper retraining schedule ranks two pairs of arms the way full weekly retraining ranks them: the cadence pair (monthly minus weekly retraining) and the starting-value pair (a zero starting value minus XGBoost's estimated starting value, the contrast of experiment 80). The cheaper schedules are (a) a monthly refit on a rolling 12-month window with 150 rounds and eta 0.15 (P-roll), (b) the same refit every quarter, (c) a monthly refit at the full setting (whole history, 500 rounds, eta 0.05), and (d) a weekly refit on the whole history with 150 rounds and eta 0.15. A schedule that passes can replace weekly retraining in research experiments. partly supported not-for-production Monthly minus weekly retraining is +0.125 (95% interval +0.036 to +0.229) at the full setting, +0.118 (+0.033 to +0.216) with a 12-month window, and +0.125 (+0.038 to +0.227) with 150 rounds. primary 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand The Primary substation demand findings of experiments 48 and 49 keep their sign on forecast runs the project has not scored: the daily 00:00 UTC ECMWF ensemble (ENS) control-member runs of 2023-07-01 to 2024-03-31 (July to March, with no April to June). For the 13 Primary substations that have power data throughout, weekly refitting of the XGBoost demand model N1 without error correction scores below the stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor 1.15), and weekly refitting scores below monthly refitting. supported candidate C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). primary 00080 bm0-zero-base-margin-xgboost-quantile-models XGBoost starts a quantile model from a base score that it estimates from the training labels, one value for each of the nine quantile levels (experiment 78 found 0.403 at the 5% level to 0.899 at the 95% level for one series, with 500 boosting rounds and no early stopping). Replacing that start with zero (a base margin of zero in every row, which is the same as a base score of zero) lowers the quantile score of the production-style models for Primary substation demand (retrained weekly), bulk supply point and grid supply point demand (retrained weekly), solar farms, and wind farms. The gap is not a symptom of too few boosting rounds, so four times as many rounds, or early stopping, does not remove it. inconclusive not-for-production Starting XGBoost from zero did not lower the quantile score of any production-style XGBoost model: Primary substations -0.017 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054), bulk and grid supply points +0.006 (-0.091 to +0.092), the frozen Primary stack -0.033 (-0.084 to +0.031), solar farms -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028). also relevant 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, once the XGBoost quantile model N1 is refitted every month without the 14-day error correction, (a) a spread factor chosen on earlier months only lowers the quantile score below the fixed factor 1.15, (b) an average of the quantiles of retrained and stored XGBoost models, with one weight vector chosen per month on earlier months, still lowers it below the best single member, and (c) each adopted input (the Christmas column, the COVID indicator, a half-life of 0.5 years) changes the score when dropped, and the substation fingerprints of experiment 32 change it when added to a pooled XGBoost model, all under the cheap rolling-window refit P-roll. supported candidate B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). primary 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of the validation year that experiment 34's 73 runs leave out, weekly retraining of the Primary substation demand model N1, with no error correction, lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than zero points of capacity; monthly retraining of the ERA5-trained solar and wind stage 1a models changes the score by less than 0.05 points; and, once the model retrains weekly, neither a 7-day nor a 14-day error correction helps. supported candidate C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). primary 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models For Primary substation demand, solar farms, and wind farms, averaging the quantiles of two or three forecast models that experiments 19, 20, 30, and 33 already scored (N1 is the ENS-trained single-stage XGBoost model, and the stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15), with one weight per lead band chosen only on earlier months, lowers the quantile score below the best single member by more than the threshold set for each technology (0.05 points of capacity for Primary demand and solar, 0.10 for wind). supported candidate Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. also relevant 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, retraining the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 monthly (half-life 0.5 years, no 14-day error correction) lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than 0.10 points of capacity; the gain from retraining more often flattens between monthly and weekly retraining; and the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained. A second, separately reported claim is that at least one cheap proxy for monthly retraining ranks arms the way full monthly retraining ranks them. inconclusive candidate C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). primary 00023 lagged-power-and-error-correction-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving the stage 2 calibrator the farm's recent observed power (lagged power, or summaries of the latest day), or shifting the forecast by its own recent error (the 14-day correction of experiments 00017 and 00019), lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) below that of the same calibrator without recent power. inconclusive not-for-production C1, lagged power added to the calibrator: solar -0.012 (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146). also relevant 00021 error-correction-variants-bsp-gsp-demand A recent-error correction of N1's quantiles, measured with power that is 2 days old, lowers the quantile score of the 4 bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) demand series as it does for the 16 Primary substations, and some variant of the correction (a 7-day or 28-day window, multiplicative, per-half-hour-of-day, or weighting recent days more) beats the plain 14-day additive correction. inconclusive not-for-production The 14-day additive correction lowered the Primary quantile score by 0.99 points of capacity (99.375% interval -1.82 to -0.18) when the newest power was 2 days old, as it did with 3.5-hour-old power in experiment 19. On the 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98), so it is unproven there. No variant beat the plain additive 14-day form: a 7-day window was worse (+0.19) and a multiplicative form far worse (+2.28). also relevant 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic For the 16 Primary substation demand series, stacking three changes on the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 (a 14-day correction from the model's own recent errors, a recency half-life of 0.5 years, and a spread factor of 1.15) beats manual_heuristic on ENS weather, which N1 alone does not. supported candidate C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). also relevant 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand For the stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained on ERA5 weather, Primary substation demand drifts (experiment 13 saw every arm under-forecast its validation year by 1.3 to 3.1 points of capacity), so a model trained on a recent window, weighted towards recent rows, retrained monthly, or corrected by the error of the last 14 days, has a lower error than the same model trained on the whole history and never retrained. supported candidate C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). primary
