docs.title: P16: a longer ENS history
docs.text: The ENS backfill from Source Cooperative (2021-03 to 2024-03) could give an earlier validation fold, and the full fetch cannot run autonomously. Issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history) describes the fetch. The archive is in us-west-2. Fetching the control member alone is about 530 GB and 4 to 5 hours, and fetching all 51 members is about 30 TB, which needs a cloud machine in that region and the maintainer's approval of the cost. The issue also ties autonomous use of the fetch to the scorer-protection work in issue 958. Every experiment since 00003 scores the same year on the same 16 series, so choices tuned there overfit it, and an earlier fold is the remedy. For demand, a longer training history has hurt so far, so the backfill is valuable first as validation data.

docs.title: Solar disaggregation
docs.text:
At the 5 Primary substations with a clean solar-capacity estimate, giving the XGBoost demand forecast a forecast of the output of the solar panels behind the substation lowered its daylight April-to-September error by 0.15 points of capacity in one validation year; against a reference that also starts from zero the gain is 0.08 (post hoc, 95% interval -0.11 to -0.05).

A Primary substation's meter reads demand minus the output of the solar panels connected below it, and NGED does not meter those panels. A least-squares fit of calendar-and-temperature demand minus a solar capacity times a satellite-based sunshine shape recovers most of the solar capacity of solar-farm output that we added to real series. The forecast gain depends on the sunshine forecast: a term built from the true sunshine lowers the error by about a fifth, and a term built from the ECMWF ensemble forecast gains little beyond 2 days ahead.

Arm am (the forecast solar output, given to XGBoost as a base margin) scores 4.467 against 4.620 for d0, the best guess of experiment 33, and every arm scores better than its own placebo twin (the same arm given the sunshine of another date). Source: experiment 64. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity; lower is better. The rows are daylight half-hours of April to September at the 5 Primaries (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), from July to September 2025 and April to June 2026.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A simple fit finds most of the solar capacity that we inject, and the capacity is close to unbiased on pure solar output. On the 8 Primaries metered in both directions, the daily fit recovers 0.854 (95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand, and the half-hourly fit 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818). Six of the 8 pass four checks on their real series: placebo sky, season, cloud term, and day type (experiment 39). A misfit test gives a median capacity of 0.992 of the truth on pure solar output (0.951 to 1.032), but detects a load that follows the day's mean cloud in only 0.35 of trials (experiment 40).

An explicit solar term lowers the error of the XGBoost forecast, and the sunshine forecast limits the gain. Built from the true sunshine, the term lowers the score of d1l (d0 without its radiation inputs) by 0.966 (97.5% interval -1.431 to -0.595). Built from ENS sunshine with a coefficient fixed at 1, it lowers it by 0.056 (-0.191 to +0.064), short of the 0.35-point gain the plan required (experiment 46, refuted). With a weight fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and the term given as a base margin, the score of d0 falls by 0.152 (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111), and by 0.272 (-0.420 to -0.145) under 48 hours. With monthly refits the explicit term gains 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and three same-time sunshine analogues gain 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007); the two are not separated, and the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 74).

Beyond 10 days all of the gain, and over all leads about half of it, is XGBoost starting from zero. Beyond 10 days the fitted weight is zero, yet a refit with a base margin of zero and no solar term scores 0.102 below d1l and am 0.098 below d1l (both uncorrected, 95% intervals; experiment 76). Over all leads am is 0.152 below d0 and 0.082 below a d0 that starts from zero (-0.113 to -0.052; post hoc, 95%; experiment 78). Whether a zero start matters in production-style forecasts is not settled: see the gotcha below.

The starting-point read in this figure is for am_sy (am with a capacity re-estimated each season-year), which is 0.100 below d0 started from zero, not the 0.082 of am. Source: experiment 78.

Neither the panel shape nor a fresher capacity is where the next gain lies. A fitted blend of east-, south-, and west-facing shapes changed the score of am by -0.001 (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014) (experiment 77, refuted). A capacity re-estimated before every forecast run lowered it by 0.018 (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold (experiment 78, small gain).

A weekly capacity series, the panel mix, and a loss monitor were not shown to work. A weekly capacity fit that penalises falls more than rises recovered none of a 30% fall and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year, against a limit of 0.5 (experiment 45, refuted). The east-south-west shares were not identified: the median share error with noise was 0.200 against a limit of 0.15, although the blend predicted held-out blocks 1.3% better than all-south panels (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%; experiment 73, partly supported). A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days (experiment 72, refuted).

At the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA, the real readings showed almost no reverse flow, so the fit could not be tested on them. In the injection test at the 8 MW-metered Primaries, with the sign of the readings hidden, the unfolding fit's median capacity error was 0.092 against 0.290 for a naive fit, and its balanced accuracy for the direction of flow 0.78 to 0.81, below the 0.80 the rule needed. On the real MVA-only Primaries the fit found no reverse flow at 7 of 8; at the eighth the flow is negative on 75% to 87% of daylight half-hours from 2021, and signed power is needed to check it (experiment 79, partly supported).

The data could not tell us whether the gain holds in a second year, at Primaries without a clean capacity estimate, or on rows outside April to September. The weights of experiment 64 rest on one July-to-September period.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best of the recipes tested in this theme gives XGBoost a solar offset built from a solar capacity per season-year and a calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly. The steps are:

  1. Fit one solar capacity per Primary per season-year, by least squares, and refresh it once per season-year (experiment 39, experiment 45, experiment 78).
  2. Multiply the capacity by the calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly: how much sunnier or cloudier the day is than average for that month and half-hour, rescaled by a slope fitted on the training window. The weight is fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and is zero from 10 days (experiment 64).
  3. Give the product to XGBoost as a base margin, not as an input column or a shift after the fit: am beats the input-column arm by 0.093 (95% interval 0.057 to 0.129, exploratory; experiment 64).
  4. Use an all-south panel shape (experiment 77).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 64 and 78 are candidate.

  • The solar offset (experiment 64). Production would need a capacity table, a table of weights, the ENS calibration slopes at predict time, and a base margin set on each prediction matrix; the write-up says the live service cannot supply these as built.
  • Refresh the capacity table once per season-year (experiment 78). A weekly vintage differs from the season-year vintage by -0.005 (95% interval -0.013 to +0.003, exploratory).
  • A zero start is untested in production-style forecasts, so it is not yet a candidate. Experiment 78 advised testing it; experiment 80 could not tell the two starts apart.
  • The offset's gain inside the full forecast is 0.114 on the rows it can touch. In BG2 (a blend of XGBoost forecasts, with the offset at 5 of 16 Primaries) the offset lowers the score by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on April-to-September daylight rows of the 5 offset Primaries, and by 0.010 (0.000 to 0.019) over all rows of the 16 Primaries, because only 8.5% of those rows can carry an offset. The gate was chosen on the same validation year (experiment 87).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
Score a zero-start twin before crediting an input. XGBoost's estimated starting prediction (its base score) raised the score of d0 by 0.071 over all leads (zero start minus estimated start -0.071, -0.099 to -0.047), and the gain of am where its weight is zero is reproduced by a refit with a zero margin and no solar term (experiment 76, experiment 78). Experiment 80 (inconclusive) could not tell a zero start from the default at the 16 Primaries refitted weekly (-0.017, 98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054, which does not exclude -0.07). Re-check: the zero-start twin of whichever recipe, correction, and number of boosting rounds you use (experiment 80).

Give every solar-term arm a placebo twin. The twin of am scores 0.300 worse (0.198 to 0.407), so the gain comes from the timing of the sunshine. Shift the twin cyclically and do not permute it at random: a random permutation paired runs that forecast the same valid time, so the permuted anomaly stayed correlated with the real one (experiment 64, experiment 77). Re-check: a different sunshine source. These experiments ran no shuffled-capacity control.

Report each contrast with and without the 14-day correction. The correction carried the base margin's effect from shorter leads into leads beyond 10 days: am minus am0 was -0.035 corrected (98.33% interval -0.074 to +0.003) and +0.004 uncorrected (95% interval -0.012 to +0.021) (experiment 76). Re-check: a forecast with a different correction window.

Score a solar term on daylight April-to-September rows that have both a CAMS shape and an observed power, and name the row set. Experiments 46, 64, 74, 77, and 78 share 68,903 rows per seed. Experiment 87's headline scored all rows of all 16 Primaries, so its 0.010 cannot be compared with 0.15; on the matching gated rows it found 0.114 (experiment 46, experiment 87). Re-check: a study that scores winter or night rows. CAMS is the Copernicus satellite sunshine estimate (glossary).

Check a contrast's sign in each valid month before reading the pooled interval. The ENS solar term lowered the score of d1l in April, May, and September (-0.204, -0.232, -0.262) and raised it in June, July, and August (+0.117, +0.183, +0.024) under a pooled interval of -0.191 to +0.064 (experiment 46). Re-check: a validation period longer than 6 valid months.

Use one capacity per season-year, which runs from September to August in these experiments. The differentiable-physics code runs it from July to June. The latest week of a real-time weekly estimate had 3.63 times the path error of the same week in the final fit, and no penalty pair met the limits (experiment 45). Re-check: a penalty set per Primary, which experiment 45 did not test.

Do not treat a fitted capacity as a measurement. The fit can absorb cloud-driven demand, and the misfit test misses a load that follows the day's mean cloud. Run the placebo-sky, season, cloud-term, and day-type checks on the real series, and inject more than one farm: the ratios of Solar farm E left the capacity at 0.825 of the truth (experiment 39, experiment 40). Re-check: an independent register of installed solar.

Do not publish the fitted orientation shares. They changed by a median 0.24 between consecutive season-years, and the 1.3% fit gain did not reach the forecast (-0.001; experiment 73, experiment 77). Re-check: shares fitted on a longer record, or a known answer with the real noise that they recover to within 0.15.

Do not fit a signed model to an MVA-only series. The magnitude folds reverse flow into positive power, and in the injection test at the 8 MW Primaries the naive fit's capacity error was 0.29 to 1.00 (experiment 79). Re-check: a few weeks of signed power at the Primary in question.

Read coverage as well as the score. The ENS solar term moved the share of sunny-row actuals below the 0.05 quantile from 0.151 to 0.045, though the score barely changed (experiment 46). Re-check: coverage on sunny and cloudy rows for any new solar term.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the gain holds in a second validation year and beyond the 5 Primaries with a clean capacity estimate.
  • Whether a better sunshine forecast closes the gap to the true-sunshine oracle. The NOAA GEFS ensemble was refuted as a replacement for ENS. The Met Office UKV blended with ENS gave a small gain in squared error of the sunshine-anomaly forecast (not of demand), and the UKV archive used has a non-commercial licence (experiment 50, experiment 53).
  • Why the true-sunshine term loses at sunny summer middays: the coefficient of 1 is too large, and the cause is not identified (experiment 51).
  • Whether a solar term helps a joint demand fit (experiment 63, experiment 104).

The Research plan lists the proposed next experiments.

docs.title: Solar disaggregation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00289 summer-gap-weather-input-discriminator The best-guess stack's weaker April to June score than BG2 at the decision Primaries comes from the ensemble's sunshine forecast (or its ratio calibration), and not from demand absorbing the solar term or from the error-correction layers. partly supported not-for-production Giving the best-guess stack the sunshine that actually happened would close about 70% of its April to June gap to BG2, but the same change helps the stack nearly as much in July to September, when the stack already matches BG2. Most of the April to June gap beyond the July to September gap therefore stays. That points to the solar term in the demand model, or to the error-correction layers, and away from the ensemble sunshine forecast. A refit with realised sunshine as the solar driver, and a check of the solar term at D5 and D9 in April to June, are the next steps. also relevant 00282 pv-plant-curve-audit The curve that turns sunshine into power in our solar models departs from the metered farms' measured curve by more than 5% of capacity somewhere in the clear-sky range, and the departure is the flat-top level (the inverter limit), not the panel tilt or the temperature loss. not supported not-for-production The curve that turns sunshine into solar power stays within 5 percentage points of capacity at 3 of the 6 metered solar farms and departs from their measured output at the other 3 in different directions, so no single fix to the inverter limit repairs it. The best-guess demand stack assumes panels tilted 35 degrees and the farms fit best at about 20 degrees, which makes the stack over-predict output on clear half-hours in December (measured is 0.66 of the stack, median over farms) and under-predict it from April to July by 5 to 8%. Swapping in the pooled shape of the other farms does not help, so the next experiment should try the 20 degree tilt inside the stack. also relevant 00280 pv-empirical-shape-and-capacity-in-arm-d The April to June 2026 gap between arm D (the monthly-refit generalised additive model of experiments 155 and 220, scored on experiment 178's rows) and BG2 comes from its solar term: the pinned solar capacity is too high and the south-facing fleet shape is not the shape the metered farms show. Replacing the fleet shape by the pooled empirical shape of experiment 269, at the capacity that shape's real-series fit supports, lowers arm D's April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looks too high (D5, D9, and D16). not supported not-for-production Putting the empirical solar shape into the forecast, at the pinned capacity or at the lower capacity the real series supports, does not lower the April to June error at the substations where the pinned capacity looked too high. The change is under 0.01 MW against an error of about 0.5 MW, and the intervals are wide. A capacity cut that is correct for the whole of April to June is not the fix either: at D5 it raises the error. This experiment finds no sign that the shape or the capacity of the solar term closes the summer gap to BG2. also relevant 00269 pv-capacity-gain-decomposition Most of the 0.090 gain that experiment 238 found from using a nearby farm's recorded output as the solar shape comes from the farm's plant shape (tilt, orientation, flat top) and from the capacity unit in which recovery is read, and little comes from the farm's measured sunshine. partly supported not-for-production For the five substations and six farms tested, the measured sunshine at a nearby farm explains almost none of the extra solar output that its recorded output helped to find. The extra output found comes from the farms' plant shape (panel tilt, panel orientation, and the flat top of the output curve). A table learned from other farms' output and driven by the satellite irradiance reproduces that plant shape. Using the table finds 0.966 of an injected solar farm's output when recovery is read as the capacity ratio of experiment 231 (0.826 with the physical fleet shape), and 0.995 when it is read over clear-sky daylight energy. In these tests the satellite irradiance was not the limit, and a metered farm beside each substation was not needed. Switching to the table lowers the fitted solar capacities of the five decision substations by 0.2 to 0.4 MW. The effect on the sunny-half-hour forecast score has not been run. also relevant 00267 pv-capacity-early-years-and-register-floor The inferred capacity of unmetered solar at the five decision Primaries falls below the register floor in season-year 2021 (July 2021 to June 2022) because the capacity fit recovers only about 0.78 of an injected farm and the 2021 fit window is thin, not because the register is shared to the wrong district. Dividing by the median recovery of the metered farms, and using the output of a metered farm within 25 km as the sunshine shape, lifts the estimates to the floor. not supported not-for-production The 2021 shortfall at D10 and D11 is not a missing recovery correction and not a thin fit window: the card already divides by the metered farms' recovery, and the 2021 season-year has 12 months of data at every Primary. Using a nearby metered farm's output as the sunshine shape makes the shortfall no smaller (the estimates fall by 7% to 22%, partly because the two shapes are divided by different recoveries), so the shortfall at those two Primaries remains unexplained. Candidate causes are the register's postcode-district share, a gap of about 20 months in the early data, and a fit that is too low in its first full year. Show 2021 at D10 and D11 as a known shortfall. also relevant 00266 summer-gap-diagnostics-solar-term The best-guess demand stack (experiment 251's arm 1) trails BG2, the production-style XGBoost forecast, in April to June 2026 mainly because of its explicit solar term (the subtracted estimate of unmetered rooftop solar output), and not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response, the Kalman filter, or the heating and lighting terms. The same defect explains the loss at D5, an anonymised Primary substation, on sunny half-hours. partly supported not-for-production The best-guess stack trails BG2 in April to June because of the solar term at two of the six substations (D5 and D9 on daylight half-hours) and a night-time error at a third (D10), not because of the neural-network head, the two-number summary, the Kalman filter, or the ensemble sunshine forecast; the head and summary actually reduce the gap. The pinned solar capacity looks too high in those months, not too low, and clear mornings are forecast worse than clear afternoons. Candidate next experiments are the export clip at D9, a morning-and-afternoon solar shape, and a look at D10's night residuals; the stack's added parts need no change for this gap. also relevant 00241 pv-capacity-calibrated-interval The recoveries that experiment 129 measured when it injected real solar farms into a Primary substation's power can be turned into a calibrated estimate of unmetered solar capacity: dividing the capacity found by the Primary's median recovery over the other farms corrects its bias, and the spread of those recoveries gives an 80% interval that covers the truth about 80% of the time. partly supported not-for-production Dividing the solar capacity found by the typical recovery of other real farms removes most of the bias: the estimate lands within 10% of the truth at all five Primaries, against a typical error of 19% without the correction. The 80% interval built the same way covers the truth 59% to 79% of the time, which is too uncertain to label as an 80% interval, and it fails completely when the demand follows cloud (0% to 2%). Keep showing the range as a spread over scenarios, with the correction applied. also relevant 00239 pv-capacity-seasonal-efficiency-curve The metered solar farms' output falls 6% to 9% from spring to summer by a pattern that no clip or heat term explains. A seasonal efficiency curve of 12 monthly factors, shared by all farms, fitted on the farms' own output, and then applied to the solar shape in a Primary substation's capacity fit, lets that fit find more of an injected real solar farm. not supported not-for-production Twelve monthly efficiency factors fitted on the metered farms' output do not close the recovery shortfall. The farm-only fit rises by 0.003, below its target, and the recovery of an injected farm rises by 0.039 or 0.025 depending on whether the injected farm keeps its low-sun output. The farms fall below the satellite shape in November to January, and show no fall of 6% to 9% from spring to summer. Keeping the injected farm's low-sun output, which experiment 231 zeroed, raises the recovery by 0.033 (paired median over farms) on its own. also relevant 00238 pv-capacity-nearest-farm-sunshine-reference Using the recorded output of a metered solar farm within 30 km of a Primary substation as the measure of sunshine, in place of the CAMS satellite irradiance, lets the capacity fit of experiment 129 find more of an injected real solar farm. partly supported not-for-production A nearby farm's measured output finds more of an injected solar farm than the satellite irradiance does: 0.867 against 0.780 of its output, and at least 0.05 more at all five Primaries. The gain is 0.02 to 0.14 when the two farms are 5 to 25 km apart and 0.17 to 0.24 for the one pair of farms 2 km apart, and it falls to 0.052, reaching 0.05 at 3 of 5 Primaries, when recovery is read in the capacity unit of experiment 231. The farm may carry plant effects as well as sunshine, so the result does not yet show that the satellite irradiance is the limit. also relevant 00236 pv-capacity-clear-sky-fit Fitting the capacity of the unmetered solar behind a Primary substation only on half-hours with a clear sky and a high sun, where the irradiance error is smallest, finds more of an injected real solar farm than the fit of experiment 129 on all rows. refuted not-for-production Fitting the solar capacity only on clear, high-sun half-hours did not find more of an injected solar farm: 0.818 against 0.827 for all rows, with an interval 1.8 times wider. The farm alone fits better on those half-hours (0.965), so the demand terms seem to absorb more of the solar signal when only clear half-hours are used (0.147 against 0.104). Do not restrict the rows by sky condition; reduce demand absorption instead. also relevant 00235 pv-capacity-matched-day-pairs The capacity of unmetered solar behind a Primary substation can be read from the difference in net power between a sunny day and a cloudy day of the same day type and the same temperature, because ordinary demand cancels in the difference. That estimator should find more of an injected real solar farm than the convex fit of experiment 129 (arm 2), which finds 0.78 to 0.88. refuted not-for-production Pairing sunny and cloudy days removed none of a synthetic load that follows cloud, so the pairs give no evidence that a real cloud-following demand cancels. With the load added, the load adds 0.3 of the injected capacity to the pair estimator's recovery, against 0.2 for the convex fit, and a December-and-January test finds 0.33 of the farm. Pairs of days with at least 10 hours of daylight find 0.91 of the farm, which agrees with experiment 231's finding that winter rows weaken the fit. The load is built to follow the pairing variable exactly, so 0.3 is a worst case. also relevant 00231 pv-capacity-audit-where-recovery-goes Of the roughly 0.2 of an injected solar farm's capacity that the capacity estimator of experiment 129 (arm 2) does not find, most is lost because demand terms absorb part of the solar signal, a quarter or more is lost to the irradiance input, and neither the winter rows nor the definition of capacity (the divisor) explains much. partly supported not-for-production The capacity estimator misses 0.17 of an injected solar farm mainly for two reasons: the demand terms of the fit absorb part of the solar signal (58% of the miss), and the fixed solar shape does not reach the farm's flat top (47%). Better sunshine data does not help, because fitting the farm alone on clear half-hours finds no more than fitting it on all daylight. The next experiments should target demand absorption and the shape's seasonal flat top, not the irradiance input. also relevant 00218 metered-solar-farm-plant-fit The six metered solar farms differ in panel tilt, panel azimuth, ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, heat loss, and inverter clipping, so a plant model with those parameters fitted per farm reproduces each farm's output better than the one fleet shape (tilt 35 degrees, facing south, DC:AC ratio 1.15, 0.4% loss per kelvin, cell temperature equal to air temperature plus 25 K times the shape), and explains why the flat top of farms C, D, E, and F falls 6% to 9% from spring to summer (experiment 183). not supported not-for-production Giving each metered solar farm its own panel tilt, azimuth, heat loss, and inverter limit fits its output only 0.003 better than one fleet shape (a fraction of output fitted of 0.953 against 0.950), so the plant is probably not what limits the fit. About 5% of the squared metered output stays unexplained, and the sunshine data is the likelier source. Per-farm plant parameters look unpromising for forecasting; a better sunshine forecast looks more promising, because the same plants fit only 0.91 with the ensemble forecast. also relevant 00215 dp-pv-step-scan-real-series-register-match The step path of experiment 207 (total-variation weight 3, April to August rows), run on the real 2019 to 2026 series of the Primaries, finds real changes in solar capacity, and the steps that increase capacity fall near the dates when feed-in tariff solar installations were commissioned in the Primary's area. partly supported not-for-production The method that finds jumps in solar capacity finds about as many in the real Primary series as it invents when none exists, so we cannot call any of them real. The only list of dated installations we hold ends in March 2021, before the months the fit uses, so no change could be checked against it. The changes do not alter the forecast, but they should not appear on the substation cards as confirmed. A list covering 2021 to 2026, or the metered record of a known installation, would settle the question. also relevant 00207 dp-meter-regime-steps-e2-step-capacity-known-answer A convex solar-capacity path that allows a few sudden jumps (a total-variation penalty on the month-to-month change) finds both the size and the date of a known solar-farm step added to a Primary's power, where a smooth path blurs the step and a path that steps once a year places it within the wrong month. partly supported not-for-production A solar capacity that is free to change each month finds a known solar-farm step added to a Primary's power, to within 2% of its size at the pre-registered penalty, and places it within one month of the true date. At that penalty the fit also invents steps above 0.5 MW in a year without any, at 2 of 5 Primaries, and a stronger penalty that avoids them still finds 89% to 96% of the step. A capacity that changes once a year finds only 24% to 49% of the step. also relevant 00206 dp-meter-regime-steps-e1-farm-outages-in-primary When a metered solar farm's meter reads zero for days while the sun is high, the farm's output stays in the Primary substation's supplied power, so the Primary reads more solar generation (lower net power) during the outage than in the 14 days either side. not supported not-for-production When a metered solar farm's meter reads zero for days, the power of the Primary substation we could test (D10) does not change by that farm's output. Meter failures at farms A and C therefore do not explain capacity steps at D10, and the other decision Primaries could not be tested. The farms may connect to substations we could not test, so the connection list from NGED would settle it. also relevant 00183 metered-farm-flat-top-cause The flat top at farms C, D, E, and F is a fixed export cap, so its level does not change with season or with the sun's azimuth. not supported not-for-production The flat top of solar farms C, D, E, and F is lower in summer than in spring (by 6% to 9% of its mean level at the 90th percentile, in even and odd years alike), so the flat top does not behave like a fixed export cap. The per-farm plant fit should therefore fit panel tilt, panel azimuth, and a loss that grows with heat or a gradual flattening near the inverter limit, not only one clip level. More cloud in summer half-hours could lower the 90th percentile, because the clear-sky filter is modelled and not observed; the 99th percentile falls by less (1% to 6%). primary 00182 switching-d8-disaggregated-farms-and-drops D8 (Marsh Lane) is a disaggregated Primary: the metadata says the output of two solar farms was added back to its reading, and that both farms' analogues are not working. When an analogue fails, D8's reading loses that farm's output, so D8's multi-day drops (experiment 159) coincide with a stuck, zero, or missing reading at the farms, and the drop depth matches the farms' lost output. inconclusive not-for-production We cannot tell from the farms' own readings whether D8's multi-day drops are the two disaggregated farms dropping out, because the readings for the farms are almost entirely absent from the power table and so look the same inside and outside the drops. D8's shortfall is larger in daylight than at night in 24 of 29 drops, which is consistent with lost solar output, but it is also large in the evening, so the daylight pattern does not settle it. The next step is to ask NGED for the farms' output and capacity, or to model the farms from weather and compare the modelled output with the drop depth. also relevant 00179 metered-solar-farm-exploration At least 4 of the 6 metered solar farms show AC clipping, meaning output that flattens below the level that clear-sky irradiance alone would give, so that the AC limit can be separated from the DC capacity. not supported not-for-production Four of the six metered solar farms have output that flattens at about 1.05 times their effective capacity once clear-sky irradiance passes about 650 W/m² (read off Figure 1), but the pre-registered test was too strict to say so, and the flat top could be an export cap (a limit on grid export set by the network operator), a panel-angle effect, or a summer-heat effect rather than a limit in the inverters. Before any DC-versus-AC follow-up, check each farm's export-cap record and get an independent DC capacity. primary 00157 differentiable-physics-joint-pv-capacity-known-answer Letting the convex demand model (studies.dp_gam) fit the solar capacity as a smooth non-negative path across months, with a penalty on growth, finds more of a known solar farm's injected output than the two-stage capacity of experiment 129, which steps once per season-year and was recovered at 0.78 to 0.88. not supported not-for-production In this test, letting the solar capacity change month by month did not find more of an injected solar farm than a capacity that changes once a year. For the five farms tested, one scale of the fixed fleet solar shape fits a median of 93% of a farm's output, so the target of 0.95 to 1.05 was out of reach for most farms before the fit ran. No forecast was run, and the monthly capacity is not worth taking to the forecast stage. also relevant 00152 dp-mva-fold-aware-gam-k-at-mva-only-primaries At the MVA-only Primaries, the GAM-K forecast driven by the ensemble mean (experiment 136's arm A2) forecasts the MVA reading better when it models the fold: it fits the demand model through the meter (experiment 110's L0), corrects the forecast with a Kalman filter whose state is the signed flow, and builds its quantiles by folding a signed predictive distribution. The gain is concentrated at Stickney (D12), the one trial Primary where reverse flow is the usual state on sunny middays, and the change is harmless at the Primaries without reverse flow. inconclusive not-for-production At Stickney (D12), the one Primary with clear reverse flow, drawing the quantiles around a signed flow and folding them at zero lowered the score by about 0.4 points on sunny middays against the same fit with symmetric quantiles, and it did no harm at the other seven Primaries. The whole-year gain against reading the apparent power as signed power is of similar size, but its interval in the scored year includes zero. The known-answer test on five Primaries with hidden farms passed on the sign at the larger injection and failed at the smaller injection and on the upper tail's coverage, so the experiment does not support a port yet. also relevant 00139 differentiable-physics-pv-as-of-capacity-in-gam-k Feeding the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) the as-of solar capacity of experiment 129 in place of experiment 45's pinned capacity lowers the quantile score on the sunniest third of half-hours, and does not raise it on the darkest third. The mechanism is that the pinned capacity is a hindsight growth prior, and the as-of capacity is read from each Primary's own power before the forecast origin. refuted not-for-production Replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not improve the forecast, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm) only matched the pin, so the accuracy of the capacity number is not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error; it did not test the ensemble's cloud forecast, the solar shape, the Kalman filter, or the non-solar load. also relevant 00129 differentiable-physics-pv-capacity-known-answer-test The AC capacity of the unmetered solar behind each of the five decision Primaries can be inferred offline, one value per September-to-August season-year, from CAMS irradiance, ERA5 temperature, and the Primary's net power, with an 80% range that holds its coverage when the real panels differ from the assumed south-facing shape and when a day-long cloud-driven demand is present. partly supported not-for-production The capacity of the small solar panels behind five Primary substations can be read from the substations' power. For 2025/26 the arm 2 estimate is 3.3 to 4.5 MW of AC capacity per Primary, and it grew by 0.4 to 2.8 MW since 2021/22. The range around each estimate is 1.2 to 1.6 MW wide, but it is a spread over test scenarios and not a calibrated 80% interval. The method has not been shown to work on real panels that face other ways or on overcast-day demand, so a card should show the range with those caveats. also relevant 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00079 pvdis-7-mw-at-mva-only-primaries At a Primary substation (a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV) whose meter records only the magnitude of apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA), a least-squares fit of the magnitude of "calendar-and-temperature demand minus capacity times a solar shape" recovers the solar capacity and the direction of flow, as long as the power factor is near 1. The fit alternates between choosing a sign for each half-hour and fitting the signed model to the signed series. It is tested first on the 8 Primaries that are metered in MW, by hiding the sign of their readings (taking the absolute value) and recovering it. partly supported not-for-production Hiding the sign of the MW series and recovering it works for the solar capacity (median error 0.09 to 0.11 of the signed fit's, against 0.29 to 1.00 for the naive fit) but not to the pre- registered level for the direction of flow (balanced accuracy 0.78 to 0.81, rule 0.80), so the verdict is partly supported. At 7 of the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA, the fit found no reverse flow. primary 00078 pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages Experiment 00064's arm am (the XGBoost model given a forecast solar output as a base margin) used one embedded-solar capacity per Primary substation, fitted on data up to 2025-06-30 and held for the whole validation period. That capacity is 5% to 19% below experiment 00045's 2025/26 constants at the five series. Giving am a capacity that is re-estimated before each forecast run, using only data from before the run (a real-time vintage of the season-year constant), lowers its quantile score further, and the fitted solar term still carries solar information, because the same arm with the forecast sunshine taken from another date scores worse. small gain candidate Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowered the error of experiment 64's best forecast by only 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold, and by 0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012, an interval that includes zero) at leads under 48 hours. primary 00077 pvdis-6b-fitted-solar-shape-in-arm-am At the 5 Primary substations (33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substations in the distribution network) of experiment 00064, replacing the all-south solar shape of arm am with a fitted solar shape (a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing output, one set of shares per Primary, fitted on the training window only and held fixed across training years) lowers the quantile score of the forecast, and the gain comes from the timing of the forecast sunshine and not from the shape alone. refuted not-for-production Replacing the all-south solar shape with a fitted east-south-west shape changed the score of experiment 64's arm am by -0.001 points of capacity (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014), so a gain of 0.5% (0.022 points) is excluded. primary 00076 pvdis-5-leak-check-beyond-10-days Experiment 00064's arm am (the XGBoost model given the forecast solar output as a base margin) scored 0.082 points of capacity below d0 at leads of 10 days and beyond, where its margin is zero. That gain does not come from information that was unavailable at forecast time. If it is real, it comes from the offset in the training rows at shorter leads, which removes the solar swings from the training target so that the trees fit demand better at every lead (the cleaner-target effect), or from the fit starting at zero instead of at XGBoost's estimated base score. supported not-for-production No route for a leak was found, and a refit with no solar term at all reproduces the gain of experiment 64's arm am at 10 days and beyond (0.102 below d1l without the 14-day correction, against 0.098 for am). The gain matches XGBoost starting from zero when a base margin is supplied, and not the solar offset, with the caveat that the reference d1l came from another pipeline. primary 00074 an1-same-time-analogues-vs-explicit-solar-forecast-demand At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, when the XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data (P-roll), an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output, given to the model as a starting offset (experiment 64's arm am), lowers the daylight April-to-September quantile score by more than same-time-of-day analogues do. An analogue is a recent day, at the same half-hour of the day and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday), whose satellite-based sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target. The model receives the observed power on the K nearest such days (K is 1, 3, or 5) as input columns. Once the explicit offset is in the model, the analogue columns add less than 0.05 points of capacity. inconclusive not-for-production Both ways of telling the monthly-refitted model about sunshine lowered the daylight error: the explicit forecast of the panels' output by 0.149 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and the 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007) against the reference. also relevant 00073 pvdis-6-orientation-mix-and-dc-ac-ratio On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, (a) the share of east-, south-, and west-facing solar behind each Primary can be recovered from its half-hourly power, and (b) the ratio of DC to AC capacity of that solar can be recovered from a clipping level fitted on clear days. Both are tested first on known answers: synthetic east-south-west mixes of solar output, and the output of the six metered solar farms, added to the real demand. partly supported not-for-production A blend of east, south, and west shapes lowers held-out error by 1.3% against all-south panels (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%, better at all 8 Primaries), although the shares themselves are not identified: with noise added to the known answer the median share error is 0.200 (limit 0.15), and the shares of the free fit change by a median 0.24 between consecutive season-years. primary 00072 p35-step-loss-monitor-for-solar-farms For the 5 metered solar farms with a long record (labelled A, B, C, D, and F), a monitor can find a loss of generating capacity, such as a lost inverter, from the farm's own power telemetry. The monitor divides each day's power by the power a physics model expects on clear, unclipped hours, divides that ratio again by the same day's ratio at the other farms, and fits a piecewise-constant level to the result with an L0 penalty (an optimal-partitioning change-point fit). It finds a 25% loss that lasts 30 days, starting from April to September, within 28 days of its onset in at least 80% of injections, at no more than 0.5 false alarms per farm-year. It finds more injected losses of 10% than two simpler monitors that are tuned to the same false-alarm rate: a rolling median of the same signal, and the hysteresis rule of the capacity studies (called HYST here) run on the same signal. refuted not-for-production A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, below the 0.80 the plan needed, so the verdict is refuted. On 10% losses it did not beat a rolling median by an interval that excludes zero (+0.045, 97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). also relevant 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, a demand forecast that carries an explicit solar term (the substation's embedded solar capacity times a calibrated forecast of the solar output) scores no worse than experiment 00033's best-guess recipe d0 by more than 0.10 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows, and the solar term carries real solar information, because the same arm with the forecast sunshine taken from another date scores worse. The solar term is built in four ways: added to the forecast after the fit with a coefficient fitted on the training window (sf), given to the XGBoost model as an input column (a), given to it as a starting offset so that the trees fit only the remainder (am), or removed from the training target and added back after the fit (b, "demand minus solar"). supported candidate Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00051 pvdis-3b-midday-loss-of-the-solar-term At June-to-August midday on day+2 and day+3, the solar term of experiment 00046 scores worse than the best guess d0 (C6 +0.477 and +0.172 points of capacity) mainly because the fixed coefficient of 1 is too large for the sunniest rows, which a PV inverter clips, and not because the ENS members add noise. partly supported not-for-production At June-to-August midday the oracle shift's coefficient of 1 is too large in effect: the residual of the d1l median has a slope of -0.42 to -0.69 on it in every month and hour bin, and a fitted coefficient lowers the median's error by 0.991 points (-1.473 to -0.495). primary 00046 embedded-solar-share-of-primary-forecast-error At the five Primary substations metered in MW that have a clean 2023/24 capacity estimate, an explicit solar term lowers the error of the demand forecast that experiment 00033's best-guess recipe produces without its shortwave and longwave radiation inputs (arm d1l) by at least 0.35 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows. The solar term shifts every forecast by minus the capacity of experiment 00040 times the calibrated ENS forecast of the solar anomaly (a fitted slope on the ensemble mean, plus each member's own deviation from the mean), with the coefficient fixed at 1. The contrast is against d1l and not against the best guess. refuted not-for-production The ENS solar term lowers the quantile score of d1l by 0.056 points (97.5% interval -0.191 to +0.064), against a threshold of 0.35, so the verdict is refuted. primary 00045 pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1 On the 8 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) metered in MW, a least-squares fit of the daylight power to a calendar-and-temperature demand term minus a weekly capacity times one PV shape from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), with weekly capacity increments under an asymmetric L1 penalty (a penalty on the sum of absolute increments, light on rises and heavy on falls), meets six conditions. It recovers a known injected capacity path (ramps, steps, and temporary falls, injected into a semi-synthetic baseline) with a median error of at most 0.15 of the path's mean capacity. It beats a capacity that is constant within each season-year by at least 20% on ramps and steps. It produces at most 0.5 false steps of 10% of capacity per Primary-year at the median Primary, and at most 1.0 at the worst Primary, on the placebo sky and on a constant injected path. Its path drifts upward on noise by at most 0.05 of capacity over 5 years. It recovers a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks at 0.5 or more of its depth, and an 8-week fall at under 0.5. Its 90% bootstrap interval covers 0.85 to 0.95 of non-step weeks and at least 0.60 of step weeks. Capacity is the 99th percentile of the half-hourly AC output, in MW, of the embedded solar (solar connected inside the distribution network, mostly unmetered by NGED) behind a Primary. refuted not-for-production No weekly capacity fit met the limits fixed in advance for tuning: the best penalty pair recovered none of a 26-week fall of 30% and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year at the median Primary, against a limit of 0.5. Weekly changes in embedded solar capacity cannot yet be read from Primary-substation data at the accuracy a weekly series needs, so the next experiment should use one capacity per season-year and read it as a range. primary 00040 pv-capacity-error-bars On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, comparing the PV capacity that six least-squares arms fit to the same series (they differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows) detects a cloud-driven demand load that pushes the half-hourly fit's capacity at least 25% off, with at least 80% power and a false-positive rate of at most 10% on pure injected PV, so that a bounded error bar can be attached to the capacity at every Primary where no such load is detected. partly supported not-for-production The misfit test is calibrated (median capacity over truth 0.992, 95% interval 0.951 to 1.032; false-positive rate 0.055) and detects four of the five confound shapes that no fit contains at 25% of capacity, but it detects a day-long cloud load in only 0.35 of draws, so the pre-registered power rule fails and the verdict is underpowered. primary 00039 pv-disaggregation-cams-injection On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, a calendar-plus-temperature demand term minus one PV shape driven by Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance recovers the P99 capacity of real solar-farm output injected into the real demand series to within 25%, and the same fits on the un-injected series pass four checks that a weather-correlated demand confound would fail. partly supported not-for-production A fit of calendar-plus-temperature demand minus one satellite-driven solar shape recovers 0.854 (daily fit, 95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand of the 8 directional Primaries. On the real series 6 of the 8 pass four checks that a demand confound would fail, and one fails the placebo-sky check, so the verdict is partly supported. primary
