docs.text:
No proposal in this theme is waiting.

Experiment 00116 (differentiable physics, NRA) also bears on this theme. It fits flows on the interconnection edges between Primary substations and scores them on injected transfers; see the Network research plan.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Weather products and blending
docs.text:
Of the weather changes tested, only training on estimates of past weather (ERA5) clearly lowered the error in a test without power lags, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to 6 days ahead, and no extra weather forecast has yet been shown to help in a way a live service could use.

A weather product is a source of weather data, such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS), the Met Office's UKV (a 2 km forecast of the UK), the US ensemble GEFS, or ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional forecast). The experiments trained XGBoost models on one product's history, then added a second product as extra input columns or as a blend. They scored 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and 16 Primary substations, each over one validation year. For Primary demand, even weather as accurate as ERA5 lowered the score by only 0.10 points.

Training on ERA5 lowered the mean absolute error of the ensemble-mean forecast at 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to day 6, and not beyond. Source: experiment 1. Lower is better.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Training on ERA5 lowered the solar and wind farm error up to day 6. Over all leads, the ERA5-trained XGBoost model scored 15.39 against 17.09 for wind (-1.70, 95% interval -2.33 to -1.08) and 7.67 against 8.25 for solar (-0.57, -0.83 to -0.32), in points of capacity, with no calendar or lag columns (experiment 1). The contrasts were revised after two reviews, so they are not pre-registered. A later test used the quantile score and power lags at 24 to 54 hours. It found the ENS-trained model 0.218 points lower than the ERA5-trained best guess for wind (-0.472 to +0.069) and 0.107 lower for solar (-0.327 to +0.053). Both differences are unresolved (experiment 54, experiment 57).

For demand series it did not carry over. On 22 series that are not wind or solar farms, 16 of them Primaries, the ERA5-trained model scored 1.37 points worse (+0.68 to +2.17) with weather columns only. Starting the ERA5 history in 2023-09 instead of 2019-09 lowered the error by 1.32 (-1.81 to -0.90), a post hoc read that does not separate drift in the series from bad early data (experiment 3).

Weather as accurate as ERA5 gave a small gain for Primary demand, measured only for a model trained on ENS. Swapping ENS for ERA5 weather in the stack of experiment 19 (a half-life of 0.5 years) lowered the quantile score by 0.10 (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04) at 16 Primaries over 73 runs. Shortwave radiation alone gave -0.084, and inside 2 days there was no gain (experiment 22). Training on CAMS sunshine instead of ERA5 shortwave gave -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), against a planned 0.2 (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS first (stage 0) gave a further -0.067 (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039). The CAMS-trained arm with stage 0 scored 0.102 below the ERA5-trained arm. The verdict stays inconclusive because the monthly mismatch to CAMS reached 18.6% (experiment 14).

A second global ensemble, GEFS, did not improve the sunshine anomaly. The anomaly is a forecast's sunshine minus its own monthly mean, scored against the CAMS anomaly at 5 Primaries on daylight rows from April to September. Cross-validated squared error was 1.109 times ENS's for GEFS (worse in all 9 held-out months) and 1.002 times for a fitted blend, against the 0.99 needed (refuted, experiment 50).

GEFS correlated worse with the CAMS anomaly than ENS did, and the blend matched ENS. Source: experiment 50.

A UKV and ENS blend lowered the squared error of the same anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours in cross-validation, and the validation year cannot confirm it. The validation correlation gain was +0.011 (-0.006 to +0.027), and the blend beat ENS in 3 of the 6 months of forecast origin that the intervals resample. The test was post hoc. Six or 7 origin months understate the uncertainty (experiment 53).

UKV wind lowered the wind-farm quantile score by about 0.2 points at 24 to 54 hours, a small gain that is an upper limit. An ENS-trained XGBoost model given UKV wind as extra columns, trained on UKV's own history, scored -0.198 (-0.316 to -0.069) at 3 wind farms. The interval's end nearest zero does not reach the pre-registered 0.15, and a shuffled-UKV placebo scored +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040). One farm gained clearly (-0.413) and one did not (+0.018), post hoc. The UKV data come from the CEDA archive, which differs statistically from the live feed (experiment 54; UKV-CEDA study).

Giving UKV wind to an ENS-trained model lowered the wind-farm score, and the shuffled-UKV placebo did not. Source: experiment 54.

The same test with UKV shortwave, cloud, and temperature at 6 solar farms was inconclusive. The score changed by -0.035 (-0.119 to +0.037), so a gain of 0.10 can be neither shown nor ruled out (experiment 57). Averaging the wind best guess with ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast (IFS) gave -0.055 (-0.200 to +0.072) at days 1 and 2, also inconclusive, and the products' runs were half a day older than ENS (experiment 52).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best recipe tested here depends on the target, and none beat the reference by a resolved margin. For farms the reference is the best guess, as the generator-forecasting Summary explains.

  • Solar and wind farms, up to day 6: train the weather-to-power model on ERA5 and apply it to each of the 51 ENS members (experiment 1). This was measured without power lags, and experiments 54 and 57 found the ENS-trained model within an unresolved margin at 24 to 54 hours. For solar, CAMS sunshine as the training input scored -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044), short of the planned -0.15 and inconclusive (experiment 12).
  • Wind farms, 24 to 54 hours: add UKV wind as columns to an ENS-trained model, trained on UKV's history (experiment 54). This is an upper limit, measured on the CEDA research archive.
  • Primary substations: keep the model trained on ENS. If training on estimates of past weather, start in 2023-09 (experiment 3) and map the ENS shortwave onto CAMS (experiment 14).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Two experiments are marked candidate, and neither is ready to port as it stands.

  • ERA5-trained weather-to-power model for solar and wind farms (experiment 1). Production would train on ERA5 and CAMS history and serve ENS members, which needs the staged design. The caveat under "Best design so far" about power lags applies.
  • Stage 0 mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for Primaries (experiment 14). Production would fit the mapping on 14 or more months of ENS and CAMS pairs. The mapping left monthly mismatches, widened the member spread by 27%, and needs a CAMS-trained model.

No second weather product (GEFS, UKV, ICON-EU, IFS) is ready. Experiments 50, 52, 53, 54, and 57 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Train each product on its own history. The arms are ENS-trained, ENS plus the other product as columns, and the other product alone; an ERA5-trained model is only a reference. A model trained on ENS and fed ERA5 weather understates what ERA5 training would give (experiment 22). The ERA5-trained wind model fed uncorrected ICON-EU winds alone scored 2.5 points worse than the best guess, and IFS winds 1.3 points worse, at days 1 and 2 (experiment 52). Re-check when the model, the product, or the bias correction changes.
  • "Better weather adds little" was measured only for a model trained on ENS. Experiment 22 trained on the ENS control member, and ERA5 differs from ENS in bias (mean shortwave 132.6 against 139.1 W/m2). Experiment 9's CAMS-trained arm gained 0.88 daylight points at observed weather and 0.04 over all leads with ENS input (experiment 9). Look for a Primary demand model trained on ERA5 and scored on experiment 22's stack.
  • Pass a shuffled-product placebo through every step. In experiment 54 the placebo showed that extra columns alone do nothing. In experiment 52 it scored +0.343 because July's equal weights and the spread factor, not the shuffled forecasts, drove the score, so fit the spread factor on blends made under the same weights (experiment 54, experiment 52). Re-check if the blend weights or the spread factor are fitted a different way.
  • Use the live feed, and check its variables on a recent run. The CEDA UKV archive has no 100 m wind and lacks four hourly steps, UKV was upgraded on 2026-01-21, and Open-Meteo's UKV history stops at lead day 0 (experiment 54, experiment 57). Feeds gain fields over time, so an old date gives a wrong answer. Re-check when a live UKV history exists.
  • Feed the run the service would have. Experiment 52 fed runs half a day older than ENS, and experiment 53 assumed a 3-hour UKV delivery time without measuring it (experiment 53). Look for a measured delivery time before reading a blend's gain. Re-check once the live delivery time is known.
  • Give a guard arm the variant it guards. A guard arm is a control built to catch one artefact; in experiment 3 it was the ENS-trained arm with one row per valid time. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, so calendar columns let an ENS-trained model memorise the calendar position, and a one-row-per-valid-time guard arm with lags failed by construction (experiment 1, experiment 3). Re-check when the input columns or the training rows change.
  • Calibrate each source's anomaly, and cross-validate by whole months. GEFS's raw anomaly was about 15% too large, and the interval width follows the number of origin months (experiment 50, experiment 53). Re-check with a longer validation period, which gives more origin months.
  • Check the hour-of-day peak of every source. CAMS and ENS are means labelled at the period end and UKV is instantaneous, so a mislabelled UKV control peaked at 10 UTC instead of 12 UTC (experiment 53). Re-check for any new product whose shortwave is instantaneous.
  • Take the planned threshold from a contrast between like arms. Experiment 9 planned 0.2 and resolved 0.035 (experiment 9). Report a pooled share with and without the largest series: a fixed CAMS correction removed 46.6% of the daylight squared residual, one substation set the pooled figure, and a fixed bias alone removed 39.1% (experiment 7, inconclusive). Re-check whenever a pooled share is quoted.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text: Whether a live UKV history gives the wind-farm gain, whether ICON-EU and IFS help when read at the service's own time, and whether a source of a different kind helps solar farms. Experiment 50 tested GEFS against the CAMS solar anomaly at 5 Primaries only. The open proposals are in the research plan.

docs.title: Weather products and blending: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00333 primary-demand-foundation-model-zero-shot A pre-trained time-series foundation model (Chronos-2, 120 million parameters, Apache-2.0) forecasts a Primary substation's half-hourly demand from the substation's own history. Without weather inputs Chronos-2 cannot match Primary demand research default 3 at leads of 1 to 10 days. With the ensemble-mean temperature, the sun's elevation, and calendar columns passed as covariates, Chronos-2 closes part of the gap, but not all of it. partly supported not-for-production A pre-trained time-series foundation model, used without any training on our data, forecasts Primary demand clearly worse than Primary demand research default 3 at every lead from 0.5 to 240 hours. Giving the foundation model the temperature forecast, the sun's elevation, and the calendar recovers about one sixth of the gap, and makes sunny-daylight half-hours worse. Chronos-2, the one foundation model we tested, is not a candidate to replace the default, and a foundation-model forecast would have to be scored alone against the default before use as a blend member. also relevant 00329 primary-demand-default-3-member-solar-distribution-at-7-to-10-days At 168 to 240 hours the 51 ensemble members have little skill for individual days, so the forecast centres on average sunshine and the half-hours that turn out sunny have realised demand below the median. The weakness of Primary demand research default 3 on sunny daylight (5.07 against the manual heuristic's 4.82 in experiment 317, for the convex chain before any blend) is therefore a fault of the predictive distribution (the lower tail on realised-sunny half-hours), not of the median. Replacing the two-number Gaussian summary of the members' solar responses with the 51 responses themselves (X1), mixing them with a climatology of the response (X2), or adding the members of the two previous daily runs (X3) fixes the distribution. not supported not-for-production The 7-to-10-day weakness on sunny half-hours no longer exists in the research demand forecast: the two-number solar summary and the daylight-only blend with the manual heuristic already took it from 5.2% worse than the heuristic to 6.6% better, so no new distribution method is needed there. What remains is one coastal Primary (D5), where the forecast is 11% worse than the heuristic, which points back at the solar term and not at the width of the bands. also relevant 00325 primary-demand-default-3-sunshine-response-refit-and-restriction Experiment 323's sunshine response (F1) harmed all daylight half-hours because the Kalman filter's level, the winter night offset, and the median correction were estimated on the errors of a fit without a response and so counted the same error twice (double counting), or because the response acts too widely, at forecast clear-sky index where the damped ensemble-mean forecast index mis-applies the response. Refitting those corrections on the response's own errors (F1r) removes the first cause, and restricting the response to clear-sky index above 0.6 and sun elevation above 15 degrees (F1s) removes the second. small gain not-for-production The sunshine response, once the rest of the forecast chain is refitted around it, no longer makes daylight forecasts worse, but the response improves the overall forecast by under 0.01 points, too little to adopt. The response improves spring daylight at two Primaries (D5 and D9) by about 0.11 points. also relevant 00323 primary-demand-default-3-flexible-sunshine-response-in-the-convex-fit Primary demand research default 3 trails the depth-1 XGBoost refit on April-to-June daylight half-hours because its solar term (the pinned capacity times the derated unit shape, with the D5 clip) is too high on clear spring middays. Experiment 322 grafted the refit's sunshine response onto the default and recovered 0.50 of the refit's advantage. A smooth correction in clear-sky index and sun elevation, fitted in the same bounded least-squares fit as the solar term, recovers a useful part of that gain with no model of other inputs. not supported not-for-production Adding a flexible sunshine curve to the solar part of the demand forecast does not recover the gap to the better-performing XGBoost model: it helps the sunniest half-hours but worsens the pooled score by about 0.4%. The advantage seen in experiment 322 is therefore not recovered by adding a smooth curve in clear-sky index and sun elevation on top of the existing level corrections, and most of the harm sits in the level shift. A boosted-tree sunshine term could use more inputs at once, and whether to test it is a decision for the research plan. also relevant 00319 primary-demand-default-1-solar-summary-and-heuristic-blend-at-7-to-10-days Primary demand research default 1 has two weak spots at 168 to 240 hours: sunny daylight half-hours, where it scores 5.2% worse than the manual heuristic, and April to October, where it beats climatology by only 4%. Default plus x1 (the two-number solar summary S, the mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses, extended from 0.5 to 168 hours out to 240 hours) lowers the sunny-daylight score at 168 to 240 hours. Default plus x2 (a blend of the convex chain's median with the manual heuristic's, with the weight fitted per 24-hour lead band and season group) lowers the pooled score at 168 to 240 hours, mostly in April to October. partly supported candidate The demand forecast for 7 to 10 days ahead improves by about 2% when its solar term also uses the spread between the 51 weather-forecast members, and the gain is largest on sunny days (6.6%), where the forecast had been worse than the manual heuristic that National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) staff use. Blending in the manual heuristic improves the forecast by 4.5%, but the blend worsens the coldest winter nights beyond the agreed tolerance, so only the solar change is adopted. also relevant 00307 wind-farm-power-as-wind-sensor The wind that the three metered wind farms' own power implies (the fitted physics core's power curve run backwards) is closer to a high-resolution analysis than to ERA5 at 9 to 14 m/s, and at least half of the ensemble's shortfall (observed power below the forecast's median on 34.1% of rows instead of 50%) is in the spread and timing of the members, not in their mean speed. not supported not-for-production The ensemble's low wind-power forecast comes mostly from wind speeds that are too slow, by about 1.1 m/s on average and more at longer leads. Multiplying every member's wind speed by a factor fitted on the 14 months before the scored year closed about 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle, while widening the members or shifting them in time closed almost none. The median is slightly better calibrated when the factor is fitted to the wind that the farms' power implies than when it is fitted to ERA5 on the same rows (1.7 percentage points), but the quantile score is not better. also relevant 00292 metered-farm-ens-neighbourhood A day-ahead cloud field is often right in shape and wrong in position by tens of kilometres, so summaries of the ensemble's irradiance over the hexagonal cells around a metered solar farm carry information that the farm's own cell lacks. Giving H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) those summaries lowers its quantile score at 12 to 36 hour leads. not supported not-for-production At the six metered solar farms tested, the ensemble's irradiance on the cells around a farm adds almost nothing to the day-ahead forecast: the quantile score improves by 0.36%, against the 2% the plan needed, and the gain is not robust to dropping one farm. Adjacent cells, 15 km apart, differ from the farm's own cell by only about 3% of the irradiance, so the ensemble mean is too smooth between them to show where a cloud edge will fall. A weather source of a different kind is the next experiment to run, rather than more processing of the same ensemble. also relevant 00272 metered-farm-weather-adapter-gam-vs-neural Extra weather variables that the solar-farm power model (the plant) ignores, fed through a learned correction to the plant's irradiance and temperature, close part of the gap between the plant driven by the ensemble weather forecast (about 0.91 of output fitted on sunny half-hours) and the plant driven by observed weather (0.973), and a small neural network does this better than additive curves. not supported not-for-production The extra ensemble weather variables (longwave radiation, humidity, precipitation, pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height) showed no usable information for the solar-farm power model at these six farms, whether they enter through additive curves or a small neural network, and the real variables do no better than placebo copies. A neural network with no plant, given the lagged power and the ensemble spread, scores 2.7% better than the plant but not better than the linear fit of experiment 257, so a correction to the plant's weather is not the route to a better forecast. also relevant 00270 metered-farm-xgboost-vs-plant-diagnostic XGBoost beats the plant (the solar-farm power model of experiments 218 and 224) on the six metered farms because of inputs the plant never sees, namely the farm's own lagged power and the ensemble spread, and not because of a better map from the ensemble-mean weather to power. Calendar columns and extra weather variables add little once those two are present. partly supported candidate XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model by about 3% in the quantile score even when it sees only the power model's own weather inputs, and the gain is in the width of the forecast band (the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles), not in the median forecast. The same gain comes from giving the power model a forecast band that depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index, and that band also beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile. Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. also relevant 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a lead-dependent mixture of the ECMWF ensemble's member forecasts, the AIFS ensemble's member forecasts (both run through experiment 230's ERA5-trained XGBoost wind model A0r), and climatology lowers the quantile score and the 0.99 pinball loss against the ECMWF members alone, after both are corrected by a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm; and a small neural gate that reads the two ensembles' spread and disagreement chooses better weights than weights by lead alone. partly supported candidate Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. also relevant 00246 metered-farm-ens-ukv-icond2-blend The DWD ICON-D2 regional weather forecast (2 km grid, run every 3 hours, 48 hours ahead) carries information about cloud over a metered solar farm that neither the ECMWF ensemble nor the Met Office UKV carries, so adding it to the ensemble plus UKV lowers the farm's day-ahead error. The evidence against is that at day 1 every single product lost to the ensemble mean for solar in the matched-lead study, and ICON-D2's errors are likely to be correlated with UKV's. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used is the CEDA research archive. small gain not-for-production Adding the German ICON-D2 weather forecast to the ECMWF ensemble and the Met Office UKV lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, which is under the 1.5% we set as worth a fourth weather source. ICON-D2 is available for only 12 to 29 hours of the day ahead at an 08 UTC forecast time, and the UKV archive used is a research archive, so this is an upper limit for production. also relevant 00237 dp-two-number-solar-summary-with-clip The mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses lower the daylight quantile score of the demand forecast also when each member is passed through the clipped solar term, because cloud uncertainty and the clip both act at midday only partly on the same rows. supported candidate At D5, in one year of data, summarising the ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation keeps at least about 90% of its gain when the solar output is clipped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (110%, interval 91% to 141%). On the sunniest third of daylight rows the point estimate of the remaining gain is about half (interval -12% to 88%). A post hoc arm using the standard deviation alone kept the gain there, which suggests testing that form. also relevant 00229 metered-farm-ens-ukv-blend The Met Office UKV weather model (2 km grid, 54 hours) carries information about cloud over a solar farm that the 51-member ECMWF ensemble lacks, so giving a metered solar farm's forecast both products lowers its day-ahead error against the ensemble alone, and closes part of the gap between the ensemble-driven fit (0.91 of output on sunny half-hours) and the fit with observed weather (0.973) of experiment 218. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used here is the research archive on CEDA, which differs statistically from the live UKV. small gain not-for-production Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ECMWF ensemble lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1% to 2%. The gain is under the 3% we set as worth a second weather source, and the farms' fit on sunny half-hours moves only about 6% of the way to the fit with observed weather. The UKV archive used here is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so this result is an upper limit for production; a weather product of a different kind is the option we see for a larger gain. also relevant 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay Experiment 193 found that two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses) lower the daylight quantile score by 2.20% in the scored year. Its two fitted factors per lead band were fitted on interleaved months (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), some of them later than the replicate months they were applied to, and its numbers were held in float64. A replay of the live weather layer, which stores the two numbers as float32 columns computed from the one ensemble run published before each origin and refits the factors each month on history that has completed before that month, keeps most of the gain. supported candidate A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. also relevant 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary Experiment 187 found that passing each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term lowers the daylight quantile score of the full best-guess stack by 2.23%, and that a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the 51 responses recovers 95% of that gain. Two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the members' solar responses) therefore carry nearly all of the gain, so a serving path can store two columns instead of running 51 passes. supported candidate Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. also relevant 00192 dp-ens-members-temperature-cold-nights Experiment 187 found that passing the 51 ECMWF ensemble members through the solar term of the demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. The demand response to heating is also nonlinear (a hinge at 15.5 degrees C), and the ensemble mean smooths away the cold tail. Passing each member's temperature through the temperature terms therefore lowers the quantile score on cold winter nights. not supported not-for-production Running each ensemble member's temperature through the demand model gave no detectable improvement in the forecast bands on cold winter nights, because the 51 members' temperatures differ too little to signal the day's error. The cold-night bands are already too narrow. The cause of the cold-night error is still unknown; widening the bands directly, and testing wind, night cloud cover, and switching as inputs, are the candidates. also relevant 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack Experiment 184 found that running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term of the convex demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%, but its verdict was capped at inconclusive because a monotone gate failed on rows where the unit PV shape itself falls as irradiance rises. With a gate that matches that shape, the same arm passes, and its gain lies where the best-guess stack leaves the largest sunny-daylight error, at the substation D5. supported candidate Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. also relevant 00184 dp-ens-daylight-calibration Experiment 169 found that passing the ensemble's spread to the width of the forecast's bands adds nothing when scored over all half-hours. The benefit may be confined to daylight half-hours, especially sunny and partly cloudy ones, where the clouds that the 51 ensemble members disagree about change the output of embedded solar generation, and so the demand. Passing each member's irradiance through the convex model's solar term (arm M), or using the spread of the members' irradiance as a fraction of clear-sky to set the band width in daylight (arm S), calibrates the daylight bands better than the existing bands (arm A). inconclusive not-for-production Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2%, mostly in the lower tail and on partly cloudy half-hours, while night is untouched. Placebos that widen the bands the same way but without the real members gain little, so most of the benefit is information about cloud. The next step is a production-cost check of the member pass and a test of its gain on top of the best-guess forecast. also relevant 00174 dp-unlabelled-worst-days-weather-shared-or-single-site Most of the excess loss on the unlabelled worst days of experiment 172 is weather error, and the unlabelled worst days are mostly shared with other Primaries. Replacing the ensemble-mean weather with the estimate of past weather (ERA5 temperature and CAMS irradiance) in arm D's forecast removes at least 50% of the unlabelled days' excess loss, and at least a third of the unlabelled days are also in the worst 5% of days of at least one other Primary. partly supported not-for-production Most of the forecast's error on its worst unlabelled days is not weather error: with past weather in place of the forecast weather, about 69% of the excess loss stays. Other Primaries share these days about as often as random shifting gives, so the data show at most a weak shared cause. The remaining loss could therefore come from events at one substation, such as undetected switching, a change in behaviour, or a metering fault. The next place to look is the substation's own recent readings and the switching records on those days. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00057 product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms For the six metered solar farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's shortwave radiation, total cloud, and temperature as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead hours 24 to 54 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. inconclusive not-for-production Giving UKV forecasts to an ENS-trained solar-farm model changed the quantile score by -0.035 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), which is too small to resolve. The data cannot show a gain and cannot rule out the 0.10-point gain that would justify a new weather feed. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms. also relevant 00054 product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. small gain not-for-production Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to an ENS-trained wind-farm model lowered the quantile score by about 0.2 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval 0.07 to 0.32), and a shuffled-UKV placebo shows the gain is information and not extra columns. The UKV data come from a research archive and not the live feed, so the gain is an upper limit on what a service could get. also relevant 00053 ukv-vs-ens-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW that decide experiment 00046's verdict (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), the Met Office UKV forecast of the solar anomaly (the output of a generic solar fleet minus its own month-by-half-hour mean), alone or blended with the ECMWF ensemble mean (ENS) using weights fitted on the training window, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone does within the UKV's lead range of 120 hours. small gain not-for-production At 5 Primary substations, a fitted blend of the Met Office's UKV and ENS lowered the cross-validated squared error of the sunshine anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours (3.8% to 13.8% in each band), but the validation year cannot confirm it (correlation gain +0.011, 95% interval -0.006 to +0.027). The test was post hoc and its intervals rest on 6 or 7 origin months, so they understate the uncertainty. UKV alone was worse than ENS, and the UKV data are a research archive, so any gain is an upper limit. primary 00052 more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, averaging the quantiles of the experiment 33 wind best guess (the ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve margin and the spread factor) with the quantiles of the same ERA5-trained model fed ICON-EU's and IFS 0.25 degree's forecast wind lowers the quantile score at 1 to 2 days ahead, with weights chosen only on earlier months. inconclusive not-for-production Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts, ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast, scored 0.055 points of capacity better at lead days 1 and 2, but the 95% interval (-0.200 to +0.072) includes zero. Three wind farms cannot show whether the extra forecasts help, and the blend scored 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6. also relevant 00050 second-weather-forecast-for-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW in experiment 00046's verdict set (anonymised series D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), an anomaly forecast that blends the NOAA GEFS ensemble mean with the ECMWF ENS ensemble mean, with weights fitted on the training window only, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone. Laid into experiment 00046's solar term with its fitted lead-dependent coefficient, the blended anomaly lowers the quantile score by at least 0.1 points of capacity against the same term built from ENS alone. refuted not-for-production The stage 1 gate stopped the experiment: in cross-validation on the training window GEFS's squared error against the CAMS anomaly is 1.109 times ENS's (worse in all 9 held-out months) and the fitted blend's is 1.002 times, against the 0.99 needed. primary 00022 era5-weather-ceiling-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the winning recipe of experiment 00019 (the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 with a recency half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day error correction, and the 1.15 spread factor) ERA5 weather in place of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather at serving time lowers the quantile score by at least 0.3 points of capacity over all leads. refuted not-for-production ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score over all leads by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the rule asked for is ruled out. also relevant 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. primary 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. primary 00003 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained-demand A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 (2019-09 onward) and applied to the 51 ENS members, with the member forecasts averaged, has a lower mean absolute error on electricity demand series than the same columns trained on ENS weather. not supported not-for-production D1, s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, weather only, all leads: +1.37 (+0.68 to +2.17), 22 series; with calendar +1.38 (D2, against the one-row-per-valid-time arm: +1.67); with calendar and lags +0.10 (-0.26 to +0.50). primary 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 and CAMS (2019-09 onward) and applied to ENS weather has a lower point-forecast error than the same columns trained on ENS weather. supported candidate P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond. primary

docs.text: A lower number in the "Priority" column runs sooner.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text: Id Question Priority Waits for State P11 Do ensemble statistics (the member mean, spread, and percentiles of temperature and irradiance) beat control-member rows? 5 Nothing Deferred; an ERA5-trained stage 1 cannot take ensemble spread as an input, and experiment 00018 found the staged chain level with N1 for demand P13 Does a stage 1 trained on ENS early leads beat the ERA5-trained stage 1 at long leads, and how much skill remains with ERA5, CAMS, or short-lead fields as inputs? 5 Nothing Deferred; 00001 found no gain beyond day 6, and 9 generator series cannot resolve smaller gains P15 For solar and wind, does a shared stage 2 calibrator with a learned blend let a second weather product already on disk (CEDA UKV or Open-Meteo) enter without retraining? 5 A decision on the shape of the production model Deferred; run for solar and wind only, ENS against ENS plus one product, because demand depends less on weather than generation does

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: P11: ensemble statistics as inputs
docs.text: The arms are the member mean, spread, and 10th and 90th percentiles of temperature and irradiance, against rows from the control member only. The planned contrast is the statistics arm against the control-member arm.

docs.title: P13: perfect-prognosis and ceiling checks
docs.text:
Experiment 00001 found no gain from ERA5 training beyond day 6. The arms are the ERA5-trained stage 1, a stage 1 trained on ENS early leads, and ceiling inputs (ERA5, CAMS, both, and each product's short-lead fields).

Resolution limit. 9 generator series cannot resolve gains smaller than about 0.3 points of capacity, and few solar farms share a weather cell.

docs.title: P15: a second weather product already on disk
docs.text:
Blending products is the maintainer's strongest hunch for improving the forecast, and it can be tested before any ingest. CEDA UKV and products downloaded from Open-Meteo are already on disk. The CEDA UKV archive differs statistically from the live feed, so a result may not carry over. The arms are ENS alone; ENS plus the second product with the shared calibrator and the learned blend; the per-product-columns control; a fixed equal-weight mixture; and a learning curve at 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 months of the second product's history, rotated across seasons. The planned contrast is ENS plus the second product against ENS alone, with a safe-entry check at 1 and 2 months (the interval lies inside plus or minus 0.15 points).

Resolution limit. With 9 generator series, a safe-entry interval of plus or minus 0.15 points is not reachable at 1 or 2 months of history. The experiment compares ENS alone with ENS plus one product, and does not run the learning curve.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
This roadmap outlines the planned order of development toward the v1.0 live forecast release (January 2027) and beyond. This page was last substantially revised July 2026, following a full codebase review and a reprioritisation (decided 2026-07-01) that made getting any forecast running on AWS the top priority over scientific-improvement work. That shipped as v0.1 in July 2026; the live service is now on v0.2 (deployed 13 August 2026), and work continues on the milestones below toward v1.0. Technical plans change as we learn more — treat this as a best-estimate, not a guarantee.

For how this page relates to GitHub issues, docs/architecture/, and the rest of the docs — and which place to put new planning content — see the Documentation Guide.

Status legend (used throughout these design docs): ✅ Implemented — exists in code today · 🚧 Planned — designed, not yet built · 🔬 Research — exploratory / v2.

docs.title: Design documents
docs.text:
• Delivery tables — the five Delta Lake tables OCF delivers to NGED (power_forecast, power_forecast_warnings, asset_health_history, effective_capacity, substation_switching), with full field-level schemas.
  • Forecast building blocks — "normal" vs. "prevailing conditions" forecasts, sign conventions, and worked examples.
  • Metrics & leaderboard — cross-fold validation protocol, evaluation metrics, horizon time-slices, and leaderboard grouping tags.
  • Estimating the money a better forecast saves — the two £ leaderboard metrics (flexibility procurement and curtailment), the equal-risk method that avoids needing a price for a network breach, their limitations, and the open questions for NGED.
  • Data sources — NGED power data + supporting files, network topology, and the weather datasets (ECMWF ENS, CAMS, ERA5, and the CEDA UKV archive that version 1 does not ingest), with the dated list of upgrades to each weather model.
  • Live service — the AWS deployment: the live_forecasts inference asset, the champion-model container, the costed AWS architecture options, production monitoring, and the handling of NWP model upgrades.
  • Handover to NGED — the operating model after the Network Innovation Allowance (NIA) project ends (the working assumption is that NGED runs the service on its own AWS account): the operator-contract design constraint, and the handover workstreams (runbooks, alert-on-absence, infra-as-code, confirming NGED's cloud and security standards, and game days).
  • XGBoost improvements — the v0.5 experiment backlog: four effort tiers, ordered best bang-for-the-buck within each tier, targeting the 3–10 day user band.
  • Extending the training history — using estimates of past weather, CAMS for irradiance and ERA5 for other variables, to train on the power data that predates the ECMWF ENS archive: the era-confounding hazard that dictates the ingest's scope, the reconciliation and pooling variants, how a weather product with a few months of history could enter the forecast, the COVID covariate, and why scoring against estimates of past weather is a diagnostic rather than a promotion criterion.
  • A staged probabilistic forecast — 🔬 a design under test: a stage 1 that turns weather into power, a stage 2 that calibrates, uses lagged power, and blends weather products, and coupling that restores coherent ensemble members. The experiments that test it are on the ML experiments pages.
  • Experiments run by an LLM agent — a large language model (LLM) agent searching for improvements to the XGBoost forecasting model in two phases: experiments run overnight from a plan agreed the day before, then a careful search in which the agent runs as a separate Unix user that never sees the leaderboard's validation window. The page also summarises what published research agents found. A person re-implements every idea that survives either phase.
  • Engineering health — scientific-rigor tests and cleanup.
  • Capacity estimation — the v0.7 head-to-head between candidate estimators of the time-varying effective capacity of metered generators: a convex (CVXPY) censored quantile-envelope estimator, a differentiable-physics variational estimator, and cheap baselines — the winner ships in v1.
  • Net-demand disaggregation — the canonical v2 research arc: graph-structured disaggregation of net substation power into latent demand and DER generation, the convex dictionary baseline, MVA metering, prior art, and the novelty claims.
  • Switching events — the canonical treatment of switching events and estimating latent demand under the normal running arrangement: the v0.6 unsupervised statistical detector and the v2 mixture models (the graph is a data structure).

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text: The milestone sections below show the order in which this work is planned. Each maps 1:1 to a GitHub epic issue.

docs.title: v0.1 — "Naive" MVP (internal only)
docs.text:
Epic: #137 — deploy the naive forecast on AWS. ✅ Shipped July 2026 (v0.1.0), superseded on AWS by v0.2 on 13 August 2026.

Goal: A simple XGBoost forecast that lets us test infrastructure end-to-end and establish a baseline. Intentionally does not detect switching events or estimate effective capacity — hence "naive" (assumes the grid is always in perfect health). The data pipeline, per-series XGBoost models, and CV leaderboard were already built; the remaining work was deployment, now running on AWS — see Live service.

docs.title: v0.2 — Code Quality & Documentation
docs.text:
Epic: #138 — code quality, reproducibility, and observability hardening. ✅ Shipped 13 August 2026 (v0.2.0) — running on AWS.

  • More unit tests, including feature-level lag-leakage and forecaster-level determinism tests ✅ (#62; exercised by test_nullify_leaky_lags, test_engineer_features_weather_lag_leakage_prevention and test_random_seed_makes_training_deterministic, alongside new package coverage for dynamical_data (#163) and geo (#164)). The CV-windowing no-lookahead, leaderboard-fairness and fold-level determinism guardrail tests remain unwritten — see Engineering health
  • CI on GitHub (ruff + ty + pytest on every PR) ✅ (per-PR gate + nightly network tests; see Testing → Continuous integration)
  • Improve documentation ✅ (#139)
  • Verify daylight savings time handling is correct ✅ (#84; test_apply_local_time_features_dst_transitions covers both the spring-forward and fall-back transition instants)
  • Reproducibility stamping: git SHA + Delta table versions on every MLflow run ✅ (implemented in ml_core.repro; every MLflow run carries the stamp)
  • Drop Hydra in favour of plain YAML + importlib + pydantic ✅ (contracts.config_schemas owns the _target_ round-trip; dropping the two dependencies also unpinned antlr4-python3-runtime, which had been breaking Dagster's asset-selection strings)
  • Asset check on live_forecasts reporting missed NWP runs at forecast time (#424) ✅ (live_forecasts_are_healthy: it also reads the slot's rows back off disk, so every production asset now has a check — including the one NGED consume)
  • Start the intervention log ✅ (started with the v0.1 AWS period; its measurement window opens at v1.0, but it cannot be reconstructed retrospectively, which is why it exists now)

docs.title: v0.3 — Leaderboard / Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Epic: #6

  • Implement the ML energy forecasting "leaderboard" (cross-fold validation metrics in MLflow), ready for systematic cross-validation runs ✓ (CV assets added)
  • Metrics: MBE, MAE, NMAE, RMSE, Pinball loss, PICP, interval width, CRPS, Spread-Skill Ratio — all ✅ (definitions in the evaluation-metrics reference; plan and remaining 🚧 items in Metrics & leaderboard)
  • Time-slice filters: nowcasting (0–6 h), day-ahead (6–36 h), medium range (Day 2–7), extended range (Day 8–14), peak events (top 5%)
  • Baseline forecasters (the manual heuristic and climatology, with persistence in v0.9 as #1087) so leaderboard scores are interpretable
  • Cost-savings metrics (£) — two figures per leaderboard row, for flexibility procurement and for curtailment, scored against manual review and against a perfect forecast; see Estimating the money a better forecast saves. Expected to be the metrics NGED read first, so they land early in this milestone.
  • Production monitoring of the live service (production_monitoring metrics scope)
  • Failure-scenario evaluation — the evaluation machinery must precede the v0.5 experiments it is meant to judge, or v0.5 picks a champion blind to how it behaves when inputs degrade:
    • Canonical failure-scenario suite: named, versioned degradation transforms (#437) — see Scoring under failure scenarios
    • Degradation smoke-tests in CI (#436)
    • Score every leaderboard CV run under each scenario, against manual_heuristic (#438)
  • Phase 1 of agentic ML research — Claude runs experiments overnight, each testing one hypothesis and ending in a verdict; an experiment whose output fits the scorer may post its scores to the leaderboard as a study/ MLflow experiment, and the scorer drops the checks that exist only to stop deliberate cheating (#1031); see Experiments run by an LLM agent
  • One-command rollback for promoted_model (#440), plus the runbooks that pin down what "one command" means (#448)

docs.title: v0.4 — Automatic Data Cleaning
docs.text:
Epic: #150

  • Automatic cleaning of NGED's power data. Versions 0.1 to 0.3 do none: the models train on, and the live service forecasts from, uncleaned telemetry. What has been measured about the trial area's faults, including the one commissioning cut-off already established, is in cleaning the trial-area telemetry
  • power_forecast_warnings Phase 1 — STALE NWP and STALE POWER, with warning_source (#439)
  • power_forecast_warnings Phase 2 — the meter-error warning types, which are this milestone's cleaning detections surfaced to NGED (#441)
  • The asset_health_history table — the historical view of the same detections (#442)

docs.title: v0.5 — XGBoost Upgrades ("Quick Wins")
docs.text:
Epic: #145

Establish a strong XGBoost baseline before investing in capacity estimation and switching event detection.

The full experiment backlog — four effort tiers, ordered best bang-for-the-buck within each tier — is in XGBoost improvements.

This milestone also carries the ingest of estimates of past weather (ERA5: #143, moved here from v0.7) and the pre-training experiments that ingest unlocks (#167) — see Extending the training history. The version-1 plan is CAMS for irradiance and ERA5 for other variables, and CEDA UKV is not ingested (see the CEDA UKV against ERA5 study). Our power data reaches back to late 2019 while the ENS archive starts 2024-04-01, and Dynamical.org's ENS back-fill is not expected until ~November 2027, so an estimate of past weather is how the seasonal experiments on this page get more than one winter to learn from. The Tier-1 and Tier-2 config wins do not wait for it.

This milestone also carries the quantile-ensemble pipeline (per-member quantile forecasts pooled into delivered percentiles — Phase D of Delivering the probabilistic metrics; theory in Probabilistic forecasting from NWP ensembles), which builds directly on the lead-time-feature and ensemble-member-training wins in that backlog.

It also carries the degradation half of the inherent-stability work, which is gated on that same quantile pipeline:

  • Degradation-conditional interval calibration — conformal prediction per regime (#443), so the bands widen honestly when the inputs degrade rather than staying over-confident
  • The weather-blind guarantee: outage-shaped training augmentation (#445), which is what makes "never worse than the manual heuristic" true rather than hopeful
  • Clear-sky as the zero-data floor (#444), extending #168
  • Make live_forecasts degrade rather than raise when NWP is absent (#446) — deliberately gated on the two items above, since degrading earlier would emit output no scenario has tested

Phase 2 of agentic ML research: once an XGBoost model beats manual_heuristic on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), an LLM agent screens the XGBoost backlog, and possibly larger ideas from other roadmap pages, as a separate Unix user that never sees the leaderboard's validation window (#1169). The maintainer leans towards screening every idea. Experiments run by an LLM agent gives the published evidence, and a design in which the agent screens ideas on data before the leaderboard's validation window, an idea is implemented again whenever the idea's score is close to a competitor's, and a person re-implements every idea that survives in a reviewed pull request.

docs.title: v0.6 — Switching Events
docs.text:
Epic: #151. Internal only for first month, then shared with NGED. (v0.6 vs v0.7: we don't yet know which of switching events and capacity estimation will actually land first — but naming one v0.6 and the other v0.7 beats the ambiguity of "v0.6 or v0.7"; we'll swap them later if reality disagrees.)

  • Build the shared switching infrastructure: the stage-1 weather/calendar baseline, normalised residuals, the labelled event table, and the synthetic-injection harness — see Switching events & latent demand
  • Ingest the NGED supporting files this needs (substation adjacency, switching logs)
  • Make the forecaster switching-aware with residual, event-age, and pooled-neighbour features, and run the v1 label-exclusion experiments — the feature-based mainline
  • Conditional — see the decision point: the discrete detector (changepoint detection and attribution), training-data cleaning from detected events, and the substation_switching Delta table

docs.title: v0.7 — Dynamic Generator Capacity
docs.text:
Epic: #141. Internal only for first month, then shared with NGED.

Dynamic effective capacity estimation for metered generators (capacity estimation)

The estimator is chosen by racing candidates head-to-head on the same data, and the winner ships in v1. What they estimate is the effective capacity of the metered wind and solar PV generators over time, which bumps up and down with maintenance, faults, and build-out. The contenders are a convex (CVXPY) censored quantile-envelope estimator, a differentiable-physics (PyTorch) variational estimator, and cheap baselines. The judging criteria — including uncertainty quality and robustness to missing inputs, scored against the same failure-scenario vocabulary the forecasting leaderboard uses — are on the capacity estimation page.

Capacity estimation is the first model family we must actively build for missingness. A differentiable-physics estimator degrades most gracefully of all, and that should count in the judging.

A deliberate secondary goal of the contest is building hands-on CVXPY experience, to inform v2 tooling choices and our advice to NGED.

The "clever" latent-demand and abnormal-running-arrangement inversion is explicitly not in scope here. That inversion is v2 research.

The remaining work items for metered-generator capacity:

  • Two-pass approach: first pass estimates effective capacity; second pass normalises the time series by effective capacity before training the power forecast model
  • Ingest CAMS (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service) solar radiation — satellite-derived irradiance, used to estimate solar PV capacity (data sources). Wind-farm capacity estimation takes its wind from the planned estimate of past weather for variables other than irradiance, which is ERA5 in the version-1 plan
  • Populate the effective_capacity Delta table

CAMS is an offline source: it feeds historical capacity estimation, and the production serving path does not depend on it, so its near-real-time freshness is not the reason we chose it. The reasons are that its values accumulate over the metering interval rather than sampling an instant, that it draws on 3-hourly aerosol analyses, and that it offers steps down to 1 minute — which is what the dynamic thermal model would need.

The ingest is small. CAMS serves one point per request rather than a grid, but the v1 trial area needs at most 32 requests, and 6 of those requests cover its solar farms. CM SAF SARAH-3 stays on the list as a v2 comparison.

Dynamic effective capacity estimation for substations:

  • For now, while we're forecasting substations top-down, just use the 99th percentile per year as the effective capacity. Later, in v2, the system should already capture everything we need to know about substation capacity, as a function of all the weather, demand, and topology drivers of the substation's behaviour.

"Prevailing conditions" building block (needs both the v0.6 switching and v0.7 capacity blocks):

  • Produce example Python code for NGED to construct a "prevailing conditions" forecast from OCF's building blocks

docs.title: v0.8 — Improve Live Service
docs.text:
Epic: #323

The bucket for operational improvements to the running live service — efficiency, robustness, and operability polish discovered during early live running, as distinct from the forecast-skill milestones above. Items so far:

  • Replace the polling schedules with Dagster sensors (#324): cheap "is there new data?" detection runs on the control-plane box, and Fargate tasks launch only when there is real work to do. Design context: Production Deployment — Design.
  • Codify the AWS infrastructure as infra-as-code (#326): the Terraform-vs-CDK question and the sequencing (start at access-phasing Stage 2) are in the live-service plan; the account-portability requirement is in Handover to NGED.
  • Consider seven pieces of industry best practice we currently lack (#449): input-drift detection, shadow deployment of a challenger model, a schema-evolution policy for the delivery contract (which may need pulling forward to v0.6), statistical process control on forecast error, naming poka-yoke among the design principles, a retraining cadence and trigger, and monitoring how NGED uses the delivered forecasts — each discussed in Design Principles → Industry best practices we have not yet absorbed. A holding issue: the task is to consider them once the live service has run for a while, not a commitment to build them.

docs.title: v0.9 — Nice-to-haves if we have time
docs.text:
Epic: #361

Genuinely optional experiments worth trying if the schedule allows, sitting between the operational polish of v0.8 and the v1.0 trial-service milestone. Nothing downstream depends on any of them — if we are short on time, none of it blocks v1.0. Each lands as its own registered leaderboard CV run or controlled ad-hoc ablation, so we keep the result either way.

  • Neural net vs XGBoost as a leaderboard CV run (#362): does a simple neural net — an MLP with a per-series embedding and quantile-regression heads — beat gradient-boosted trees? XGBoost suits the current per-series regime (one model per series, on the order of 10⁴–10⁵ rows), and the recurring "trees are bad at maths" pain is already handled cheaply by the physics and residual features on the XGBoost improvements page. So the decisive, cheap test is the sibling of the global model per time_series_type win: a global MLP against a global XGBoost on the identical feature frame, run once that win's prerequisites (per-series target normalisation, static per-series features, and init-time-anchored features) exist, so the comparison isolates the model family. A negative result de-risks the neural approaches on the post-v2 research list before we spend research time on the fancier ones. The spike must also state and test how it handles missing inputs: XGBoost gets NaN routing for free and an MLP does not, so a zero-filled MLP would lose the comparison for a reason that has nothing to do with model family (zero is a real physical value — see Encoders → Handling missing inputs), and it should be scored under the failure-scenario suite like any other CV run.
  • Additional NWP source, e.g. ICON-EU (#363): explore whether adding ICON-EU from Dynamical.org improves forecast skill over ECMWF ENS alone — the v1 nice-to-have version of the broader v2.1 multi-source item. The v0.5 perfect-weather ceiling sizes the forecast-error headroom, but that ceiling does not bound resolution, so ICON-EU's ~6.5 km grid could still beat a coarser estimate of past weather, such as the 31 km ERA5, on representativeness. Because ICON-EU's history starts early 2026 (shorter than the canonical CV folds) it is assessed via a controlled ad-hoc ablation, not the leaderboard, until it has ~1–2 complete years of history. A product calibrator, under research, could let ICON-EU into the forecast sooner. See Evaluating a data source whose history is shorter than the folds.
  • Handle NWP model upgrades (#851): an upgraded weather model arrives on time and passes validation, so nothing in the live service notices it, yet the promoted model was trained on the old version. The plan records the NWP model cycle on every row, keeps a dated list of upgrades, treats an upgrade as a degradation that widens the uncertainty bands, and retrains early. It starts with a study measuring how fast a model recovers after the Met Office's January 2026 upgrade of UKV. See Live service → NWP model upgrades.

docs.title: v1.0 — Stable Live Service for NGED's Trial Area
docs.text:
Epic: #133

Target: January 2027

  • All features listed above (v0.1–v0.8), plus fixes discovered during live running
  • 32 time series in the NGED trial area (scope)
  • Five Delta Lake output tables delivered to NGED every 6 hours:
    1. power_forecast — [−1, +1] ensemble power forecasts
    2. power_forecast_warnings — meter, generator, and feed-health warnings per time_series_id (the nine warning types)
    3. asset_health_history — complete historical record of each time series's health state
    4. effective_capacity — half-hourly probabilistic effective-capacity estimates (mean + std after the v0.7 upgrade, #247; a static scalar per series in v0.1)
    5. substation_switching — estimated power diverted between substation pairs (mean + std)

docs.title: v2.0 — Scale-Up
docs.text:
Epic: #156 (WP5: delivery of the v2 live service)

Required:

  • Scale to approximately 2,500 time series: all of NGED's primary substations (1,161), BSPs (271), GSPs (52), and most customer meters (~1,000)
  • Estimate the installed capacity of unmetered solar PV and wind on each primary substation (by disaggregating net primary substation power flows)

Stretch goals:

  • Forecast unmetered solar and wind power at each primary substation
  • Disaggregate additional DERs (price-sensitive assets like batteries) from substation power flow
  • Build a REST API on top of the Delta Lake delivery mechanism (purely additive — see when a REST API would earn its keep)

docs.title: v2.1 — XGBoost Improvements at Full Scale
docs.text: v2.1 is about a month of XGBoost work, once the v2 live service runs for all 2,500 time series. v2.1 picks up whatever XGBoost improvements v0.5 left undone, and adds further NWP sources as features, or through a product calibrator if the study of that design shows promise.

docs.title: Model cards for promoted models
docs.text: Deferred until after v2 ships. Every model promoted to production should get a model card recording detailed feature importance, calibration behaviour, and the population it was trained and validated against — the record an operator or an auditor needs to trust a specific promoted model. The Energy Systems Catapult DNO Forecasting Forum names model cards under the same "Explainability" characteristic as the feature attributions below, as what supports operator trust and incident investigation. A model card is a heavier, promotion-time record, distinct from the lightweight per-training-run feature attributions every model gets (see Log feature importances for every trained model). Model cards are a stretch beyond what v2 needs in order to ship live, so this workstream starts once the v2 service is running.

docs.title: After v2.1 — Research (Advanced ML)
docs.text:
The research items run roughly in the order listed. The weather encoder trains through the differentiable-physics modules, so the encoder comes after the physics and disaggregation work.

  • Differentiable physics for power forecasting (not just capacity estimation): use DP models to directly forecast power, handling MVA metering natively (see the graph-structured engine and MVA metering), and to calibrate each weather product in weather space by gradient descent (see the weather-space arm)
  • Graph-structured disaggregation: Model substations, metered generators, and unmetered generator fleets as nodes in an electrical/spatial graph, with edges representing physical connections. The graph is a data structure — a structural prior on who can exchange load and which sites share weather: each substation is reconstructed as a sum of per-site differentiable-physics modules with inferred capacities, and cross-site gains come from hierarchical parameter sharing. (See Net-demand disaggregation — the canonical page for this arc, including the convex dictionary baseline it must beat — and the switching-events approaches.)
  • Top-down forecast coherence checking: check whether independently-produced primary, BSP, and GSP forecasts sum consistently up the substation hierarchy — a lighter check than the comparison below, worth running first because it needs no new modelling, only the forecasts v2 already produces. The Energy Systems Catapult DNO Forecasting Forum names hierarchy coherence as its own forecast characteristic, for exactly this reason.
  • Bottom-up vs top-down substation forecasts: compare a substation forecast built by summing the forecasts of the assets behind that substation (metered generators, disaggregated demand, and disaggregated unmetered generation) against a forecast of the substation's own net power taken directly, to see which is more accurate.
  • Latent-demand recovery under switching: reconstruct the demand each substation would have metered under the normal running arrangement, using a time-varying neighbourhood mixture (optionally type-resolved into demand / PV / wind) over the network graph. This neighbourhood-mixture approach reconstructs the topology-normalised demand NGED requires, and goes beyond the v0.6 statistical detector — which only flags and masks switching periods. See Switching events & latent demand.
  • Synthetic telemetry from fitted models, for the problems whose labels are missing: three of this project's problems are scored against labels that are incomplete or absent — disaggregating unmetered distributed energy resources (DERs), detecting switching events, and estimating the effective capacity of metered generators. Fitting the per-site generation modules (differentiable physics) and the shared demand-profile basis (the BasisLoadNode), then running them forward on real weather and summing the sites, produces a simulated substation whose generation, demand, and capacity are all written down by construction. Editing the simulated sum writes the labels the other two problems need. Reassign a site from one substation's sum to a named neighbour over a known window to label a switching event; step a site's capacity down on a known date to label a capacity change. Both edits are exact in simulation, where the real-data harnesses can only approximate them by scaling a fraction of net power. The hazard is circularity: an estimator scored on data generated by its own model family measures whether the parameters are identifiable, not whether that model family matches reality. Two consequences follow. Parameters must be drawn afresh rather than frozen at their fitted values wherever the fitted value is the quantity under test — a capacity estimator scored against its own earlier answer measures only that the fit reproduces, and simulating with the same biased irradiance hides the weather-bias aliasing that page names as the dominant systematic error. And a passing score never stands alone, because the simulated telemetry carries none of the meter noise the switching detector's thresholds are normalised against. The simulator therefore supplements the real-data harnesses rather than replacing them: injection into real telemetry stays the primary evidence for switching detection, and the other disaggregation spokes stay the primary evidence for disaggregation.
  • JEPA (Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, à la Yann LeCun): adapt to demand forecasting using JEPA's encoder and predictor as the "load" module in the graph-structured disaggregation engine
  • Pre-trained neural network encoders: "weather encoder" and "time encoder" pre-trained on large datasets, then fine-tuned for substation forecasting
  • Multi-sequence alignment with axial attention: find "similar" historical days and feed them as additional context to the forecasting model
  • CRPS training objective: train the ensemble power forecast model to directly optimise CRPS for sharper probabilistic forecasts (issue #1156 plans a test, run only if cheaper calibration steps leave the forecast poorly calibrated)
  • Modelling DER response to market signals (stretch goal, only if time remains well after v2): extend the differentiable-physics DER modules to react to a price signal directly — battery charge/discharge and other price-sensitive dispatch as a function of the market signal, rather than as unexplained residual behaviour

docs.title: Handover to NGED (post-NIA operating model)
docs.text:
Epic: #309 — see Handover to NGED for the design.

The working assumption is that, after the NIA project, NGED runs the Flexpectation service on its own AWS account (see Requirements → Operating model & handover). This handover is not a single late milestone: it sets a standing design constraint from today (NGED staff who did not develop the code must be able to run the service day to day, working from the runbooks — the operator contract), one workstream that must start early (confirming NGED's cloud and security standards, because the Tailscale-based access design has to fit those standards), and a cluster of late-project work (runbook hardening, game days, and progressive transfer of control). The gate: OCF runs the full v2 service for a few months before NGED decides on the operating model after the NIA project.

docs.title: Experiments run by an LLM agent (agentic ML research)
docs.text:
Status: 🚧 Phase 1 under way; phase 2 planned. Phase 1, in which Claude runs experiments overnight, each testing one hypothesis, is tracked in issue #1031 (Tracking: phase 1 of agentic ML research) in the v0.3 milestone. Phase 2, the careful search that the rest of this page describes, is tracked in issue #1169 (Tracking: phase 2 of agentic ML research) in the v0.5 milestone. Phase 2 starts once an XGBoost model beats manual_heuristic on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), and none of phase 2's infrastructure is built yet.

We plan to have a large language model (LLM) agent search for improvements to this project's XGBoost forecasting model, in two phases. Flexpectation is the forecasting system this project builds for National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED). Flexpectation's current forecaster is an XGBoost model, and XGBoost is a standard machine-learning method. In phase 1, which is under way, Claude runs experiments overnight from a plan that the maintainer and Claude agreed the previous day. In phase 2, the agent screens the XGBoost improvements backlog, the list of ideas for improving the XGBoost forecasting model, so that people implement properly only the promising ideas. The phase 2 agent implements each idea, scores each implementation, and combines the ideas that help, in the style of Karpathy's autoresearch, with no human in the loop during a round. In neither phase does the agent write production code.

Every forecasting experiment here is trained on one stretch of past data and scored on a later stretch, the validation window, that the training never saw. A training stretch paired with its validation window is called a fold. The leaderboard, the table that ranks every CV run, scores every CV run on the same fold. In phase 2, the agent never sees the leaderboard fold's validation window, and scores ideas on earlier folds. The maintainer then scores the best implementation of each of the most promising ideas on the leaderboard fold, and re-implements the ideas that survive.

Each attempt at an idea is kept as a git branch, a separate copy of the code where a change can be tried without touching the reviewed code on main. A change reaches main only through a pull request, which a person reviews before merging.
