Comparison Reference value, primary setting 2% threshold, primary setting Primary setting (99% interval) Sensitivity setting (99% interval) Rules out a gain that large P1, the lag minus B0 8.93 0.18 −0.001 [−0.075, +0.073] +0.012 [−0.043, +0.058] yes P2, the chosen arm minus the lag, 8 months 8.39 0.17 +0.012 [−0.243, +0.278] −0.088 [−0.356, +0.164] no P3, S2 minus L2 8.98 0.18 +0.039 [−0.059, +0.143] +0.047 [−0.050, +0.142] yes P4, the CRPS of the lag minus that of B0 6.15 0.12 +0.009 [−0.020, +0.036] +0.002 [−0.014, +0.015] yes P5, the lag minus B0, one shared model 9.09 0.18 −0.059 [−0.151, +0.029] −0.022 [−0.081, +0.030] yes

The plan's verdict is "unresolved" for all five comparisons, and a post hoc reading rules out a gain as large as the 2% threshold for P1, P3, P4, and P5. For those four, the 99% interval lies wholly between minus and plus the threshold at both settings. A t-interval over months gives the same verdict. P5's margin is thin: its lower bound is −0.151 from the bootstrap and −0.171 from the t-interval, against a threshold of −0.182. P2 rests on 8 months and cannot rule out a gain of the threshold's size. The 2% threshold is about half of what an oracle gains from knowing a 10% power loss in half the months, so the study can rule out only a large gain.

docs.title: A single day's lag neither detects a planted power loss nor beats a random-day lag
docs.text: A random-day lag changes the error as much as the real lag does. The shuffled-lag control N2 minus B0 is +0.011 points [−0.025, +0.051], and the lag minus N2 is −0.013 points [−0.066, +0.037] (exploratory). Two extra random-day lags raised B0's error by 0.038 points [−0.005, +0.085], and three by 0.033 [−0.024, +0.092] (post hoc), so extra columns alone may raise the error by up to about 0.04 points, although neither interval excludes zero. The planted-loss control detects no recovery by the lag at 2%, 5%, or 10%: the lag minus B0 is −0.036 points [−0.126, +0.049] at 10% (the first run, exploratory), where the oracle changes the error by −0.392 points [−0.708, −0.052] (post hoc; both intervals 99%).

docs.title: For a 10% loss at every plant, the satellite ratio recovers 74% of the oracle's gain; one day's lag, 9%
docs.text:
When every plant's power is cut by 10% in the same 9 months, the satellite ratio recovers 0.74 of the oracle's gain and the lag 0.09 (post hoc). The other shares are 0.39 for weekly statistics [0.21, 0.73], 0.23 for the analogue ensemble [0.05, 0.46], 0.16 for the 30-day percentiles [−0.04, 0.36], and 0.17 for the transfer ratio [−0.13, 0.48] (95% intervals). A 5% loss is too small for even the oracle to be statistically detectable (−0.110 points, 99% interval [−0.214, +0.013]), so no share is computed for it. The 2% rule cannot be the pass criterion for a control. The control cuts every plant in the same months, so it cannot tell an input that tracks one plant's level from an input that tracks a change shared by every plant.

The control that cuts each plant separately for 4 to 12 weeks gives the oracle too small a gain to separate the arms. The oracle's gains there are statistically detectable but small (0.057 and 0.096 points at 5% and 10%), so every arm's share interval includes zero, including the satellite ratio's (−0.21 [−0.67, 0.41] at 10%).

docs.title: The screen picked the analogue ensemble on these months, so its 0.23-point gain is biased upward
docs.text: The analogue ensemble had the lowest error in the screen (8.97 points against 9.20 for B0), and beat B0 by 0.231 points [−0.392, −0.102] in the paired comparison. The analogue ensemble was the best of 11 eligible arms, so some of that gain is a winner's curse. Six arms were worse than B0 by a statistically significant amount: L2 by 0.105, RP by 0.130, S2 by 0.132, CK by 0.156, CTX7 by 0.246, and S3 by 0.286 points (post hoc 95% intervals; with 17 paired comparisons, about 1 would reach statistical significance by chance).

docs.title: On the 8 unselected months, three level-tracking inputs gained most; the analogue ensemble did not
docs.text:
Outside the screen the analogue ensemble's gain over the baseline fell from 0.231 points to 0.046 points [−0.243, +0.169]. The satellite ratio (−0.234 points [−0.507, −0.031]), weekly statistics (−0.165 [−0.353, −0.005]), and transfer ratio (−0.141 [−0.281, −0.015]) gained most on those 8 months. These three arms were picked on the same 8 months they are scored on, so their gains carry the same upward bias as the analogue ensemble's 0.231. The t-intervals over the 8 months include zero for all three arms (for example [−0.486, +0.023] for the satellite ratio). At 99%, the weekly statistics' and transfer ratio's intervals include zero and the satellite ratio's is borderline. The era rows of the figure rest on 3 or 5 months, so their percentile intervals are unreliable and can be too narrow.

Waiting 2 days for CAMS throughout leaves the satellite ratio's 8-month gain unchanged. Three of the 8 months fall before February 2026, when the CAMS latency was 2 days. PC2 gains 0.240 points [−0.554, −0.012] on the same 8 months, against 0.234 for PC (the difference is −0.006 points [−0.062, +0.059]).

A perfect monthly rescale applied in hindsight gains 0.35 to 0.44 points on the 8 months, which is a bound for monthly corrections only. The 0.35 to 0.44 points is the gain from a perfect monthly scale and not a ceiling for finer corrections.

docs.title: One plant's 3 low-output training months carry most of the satellite ratio's and weekly statistics' gains
docs.text:
Most of the satellite ratio's and weekly statistics' gain on the 8 months comes from one plant in one month, March 2026, where the baseline under-forecast the plant's output by 14.6 points of capacity on average. That plant produced as much as the other 5 plants relative to their output in that month. In March 2025 the plant produced about two thirds as much (the baseline over-forecast it by 15.6 points), and in December 2024 and April 2026 it produced two thirds to three quarters as much. The cause of the low output is unknown: an outage, curtailment, or a metering or capacity-table fault would each give the same ratio. The cleaning removed none of those months. The baseline is given the day of the year, so it learned the low March and under-forecast a normal March. The inputs that see the plant's recent output corrected that error.

Against a baseline without the day of the year, none of the satellite ratio, weekly statistics, or transfer ratio gained over 18 months. Their errors minus the baseline's were +0.02, +0.04, and +0.06 points (slightly worse), with intervals that include zero. Dropping the day of the year from the baseline lowered its error in that plant-month by 3.96 points, and over all 18 months by 0.117 points [−0.308, +0.063].

Removing the plant's 3 low-output months from its training lowered the baseline's error in that plant-month by 5.17 points and removed most of the satellite ratio's and weekly statistics' gains. The 5.17 varies between 4.74 and 5.81 across fitting seeds. A single month gives no interval over months. The gain of the satellite ratio in that plant-month fell from 6.19 to 0.50 points and of weekly statistics from 4.61 to 0.57. Across all 6 plants the 8-month gains fell from 0.234 to 0.040 points for the satellite ratio (95% interval [−0.141, +0.040]) and from 0.165 to 0.046 for weekly statistics ([−0.137, +0.047]), and the transfer ratio's from 0.141 to 0.109. The 30-day percentiles' gain did not change: −0.081 points [−0.127, −0.048] on the 8 months and −0.062 [−0.109, −0.013] on all 18.

A month counted as low-output when the plant produced less than 80% of the other plants' output, and the same 3 months qualify under both ratios computed. The ratio was computed over the hours at which all 6 plants are scored, and again over the hours at which the plant and at least 2 other plants are scored. No other way of computing the ratio was tried.

The plant and its 3 months were chosen after the first run's results were known, from the whole record including the 8 unselected months on which the gains are scored, so removing the 3 months is an after-the-fact cleaning that a live service could make only once a month had ended. The refit tests whether low-output training months explain the plant-month's error. It does not estimate what a live forecast would gain. A live service would also have trained on the low March a year earlier, so the baseline's error in that plant-month is not only an artefact of cross-validation. Whether a live service would make an error of the same size was not tested.

Against random-day controls of the same width, the satellite ratio, the transfer ratio, the 30-day percentiles, and weekly statistics still gained 0.07 to 0.10 points over 18 months with the dominant plant-month left out of scoring. The satellite ratio minus the 2-column control is −0.078 points [−0.143, −0.009], the transfer ratio −0.085 [−0.166, −0.009], the 30-day percentiles −0.097 [−0.145, −0.057], and weekly statistics minus the 3-column control −0.070 [−0.125, −0.017]. The gain over the baseline is what a service would see. The gain over a random-day control of the same width estimates what an input's information adds once the extra columns are allowed for, from one random draw per width. Both gains are below the 0.18-point threshold. The satellite ratio's and the weekly statistics' gains are also biased towards zero, because the removed plant-month, in which these two inputs gained most, was chosen after the results were known.

docs.title: Month by month, the paired difference from the baseline at the day-ahead lead
docs.text: At lead-days 0 and 1, no lag arm beat B0 by more than 0.1 points except the analogue ensemble. The analogue ensemble gained 0.164 points [−0.281, −0.044] at day 1, over 18 months that include the 10 on which it was selected. Four arms (CK, CTX7, RP, and S3) were worse by 0.12 to 0.19 points.

docs.title: With IFS HRES as the weather input, the single-lag null also holds
docs.text: With IFS HRES as the weather input, the single-lag null also holds (post hoc). IFS HRES is ECMWF's single high-resolution forecast. Since Cycle 50r1 on 2026-05-12, that single forecast is the ENS control member. The lag minus B0 was +0.014 points [−0.030, +0.053] at lead-day 1 and −0.027 [−0.101, +0.047] at lead-day 2, on the same rows. B0's error was 9.86 with IFS HRES against 8.95 with the ENS mean. That difference is not a ranking of the products, because an ensemble mean is smoother than a single forecast and usually scores lower on absolute error.

docs.title: At lead-day 14 the baseline is 1.2 points worse than climatology from earlier years, and a random-day lag gains too
docs.text:
At lead-day 14 the baseline XGBoost model's error (15.35 points) is above that of a climatology built from earlier years (14.18), a difference of −1.17 points [−1.82, −0.50] on the rows where that climatology exists. The comparison is between an XGBoost model trained on 18 months and a median over up to 6 earlier years of the same plant's power. A climatology built from the study's own 18 months was not distinguishable from the baseline at day 14 (−0.73 points [−1.52, +0.17] on the same rows). Most of the gap therefore reflects how much history each forecast has and not the ENS mean alone, and the study does not separate history depth from the ENS mean.

At days 10 and 14, weekly statistics and the 30-day percentiles gain 0.20 to 0.45 points (exploratory). Only weekly statistics were tested against a random-day control of the same width at those leads. The 30-day percentiles were not, so their gain cannot be separated from the effect of extra columns. Weekly statistics gain 0.45 points [−0.74, −0.16] at day 14 on all rows and 0.20 points [−0.37, −0.004] at day 10, and the 30-day percentiles 0.22 points [−0.34, −0.10] at day 10 and 0.22 points [−0.35, −0.07] at day 14. Weekly statistics minus the 3-column control is −0.058 points [−0.173, +0.048] at day 10 and −0.275 [−0.508, −0.048] at day 14. At lead-day 2 the lag raised the error by 0.080 points [+0.015, +0.147] (exploratory, one of many such rows).

docs.title: Blending the baseline with climatology lowers long-lead error more than any lag arm shown does
docs.text:
A 50/50 blend of the baseline with a climatology built from earlier years lowers the error by 0.54 points [−0.90, −0.16] at day 7, 0.90 [−1.20, −0.59] at day 10, and 1.16 [−1.50, −0.80] at day 14. A blend of the weekly-statistics arm with it lowers the error by 1.31 points [−1.74, −0.85] at day 14. The earlier-years climatology is the plant's median capacity-normalised power by calendar month and hour. On the same rows at day 14 the blend beats weekly statistics by 0.646 points [−0.939, −0.390], more than weekly statistics beat the baseline (−0.512 [−0.819, −0.208]). The same blends at lead-day 1 raise the error by about 1.6 points. Adding the climatology as one input column gains little (−0.060 points [−0.234, +0.109] at day 14).

The figure's climatology reads months after the target day, which a live service would not have, so its blends are about 0.2 points weaker than the earlier-years blends (0.17 to 0.23). The earlier-years climatology reads up to 6 earlier years from 2019, whereas the figure's climatology reads the 18-month record, so the gap mixes look-ahead with history depth.

Random-day lag controls gain at long leads because they sample the plant's own power from other months, which acts as a weak climatology. N2 refitted on a fixed seeded draw gained 0.069 points [−0.147, +0.018] at day 14, the first run's N2 draw 0.120 points [−0.213, −0.032], and a random-day control as wide as weekly statistics 0.174 points [−0.334, −0.006]. The first run's draw cannot be regenerated, because its build did not fix the draw order.

docs.title: A shared XGBoost model scored worse than one XGBoost model per plant
docs.text: On the same folds, one shared XGBoost model given no input describing the plant scored 0.255 points [+0.078, +0.450] worse than one XGBoost model per plant. Adding a plant code (a column identifying the plant) closed the gap (+0.002 points [−0.113, +0.137]).

docs.title: Plant information lowers a shared model's error; the clipping ceiling raises it for unseen plants
docs.text:
The transfer ratio and the daily shape together lower a shared XGBoost model's error by about as much as a plant code does. Compared with the shared baseline, a plant code lowers the error by 0.252 points [−0.368, −0.137], a plant code with the transfer ratio by 0.435 points [−0.567, −0.308], the transfer ratio and the daily shape together by 0.311 points [−0.485, −0.144], and the fingerprint (the transfer ratio, the daily shape, and the clipping ceiling) by 0.402 points [−0.596, −0.209]. For a plant left out of training the fingerprint gains 0.172 points [−0.381, +0.055] and the version without the ceiling 0.321 points [−0.510, −0.136].

The clipping ceiling acts as a plant code: it barely helps plants seen in training and raises the error for a plant left out. Adding the ceiling changes the error by −0.091 points [−0.188, +0.017] for seen plants and +0.149 points [+0.018, +0.290] for unseen plants. The ceiling is nearly constant within a plant and differs between plants, so in training it acts as a plant code, which cannot transfer to an unseen plant. These intervals resample months, not plants, so with 6 plants they do not show how a seventh plant would fare. Six plants also say nothing about whether a fingerprint scales to hundreds of plants, because the trees have only 5 training plants to interpolate between.

docs.title: The 10%–90% forecast band holds about 69% of hours rather than 80%, with and without the lag
docs.text: The 10%–90% forecast band held 68.9% of hours without the lag and 68.5% with it, against a nominal 80%.

docs.title: Both forecast bands are too narrow: too many hours fall below the 10% or above the 90% quantile
docs.text:
The share of hours below the 10% quantile is 14.0%, and above the 90% quantile 17.0%, for B0, and the lag changes neither.

Building the band from recent residuals made the CRPS 0.562 points [+0.415, +0.693] worse. Adding the quantiles of recent residuals to the baseline's point forecast gave that result.

docs.title: Where each arm's trees split (descriptive)
docs.text: Importance is descriptive, not evidence. The lagged power of the lag arm carries 1.3% of the total split gain [0.8%, 2.5% across refits].

docs.title: Discussion: what to use
docs.text:
For the day-ahead solar forecast at these 6 utility-scale plants, do not add the same-hour lag. The recommendation would change with more plants, a longer record, or a power feed that is minutes old. The training data kept whole months in which one plant ran at two thirds to three quarters of its usual output, which favours inputs that track a plant's level. Even so, the lag did not help.

A same-hour lag from 2 days earlier is the wrong input for tracking a lasting drop in a plant's output. The study cannot say whether any input helps when a single plant is partly offline in the month being forecast, because the per-plant test was too weak and the data held too few months in which a plant was partly offline.

Remove low-output months from training, in the service and in any further study of lag inputs. A rule that flags a finished month in which a plant produced less than 80% of its neighbours' output needs only metered power, whereas the satellite ratio needs a CAMS feed. The rule can flag a month only once it has ended, and needs other plants nearby.

The 30-day percentiles are the one lagged input worth a planned test. Of the arms tested, they gave the most consistent small gain, about 0.06 points (0.7% of the baseline's error), far below the threshold. The gain did not show in either planted-loss control. With both the baseline and the 30-day percentiles arm stripped of the day of the year, the gain fell to 0.04 points [−0.12, +0.05], so the 30-day percentiles are a hypothesis to test and not a recommendation.

At days 10 to 14, test a blend with a climatology built from earlier years before testing lag inputs. The blend beat every lag arm shown in Figure 14 at those leads and needs no extra data feed. The blend raises the error at day 1, so it belongs only at the longest leads.

For an XGBoost model shared by many plants, test the transfer ratio and daily shape on more plants before relying on them. At these 6 plants they described each plant about as well as a plant code, and still helped a plant left out of training (post hoc).

Recalibrate the 10%–90% forecast band before adding inputs; a lag does not widen it. The study did not test adding the ensemble's spread (see Limitations).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Sample: 18 scored months at 6 plants in one box 25 km across. P2 rests on 8 months (2025-10 to 2026-06, without 2026-01), spanning the matched-lead study's second and third fold eras and with no July to September.
  • Day of year with 18 months: the baseline sees each calendar month once or twice, so its day-of-year column can memorise one plant's anomalous month. The post hoc lag gains depend on that memorisation. A baseline without the day of the year scored 0.117 points [−0.308, +0.063] lower over all 18 months.
  • Intervals: a percentile bootstrap that resamples 18 one-month clusters tends to give intervals narrower than their stated coverage. Plants are pooled and weighted by row count, and the test does not cover differences between plants. A 99% bound within 0.01 points of zero changes with the bootstrap's random-number stream, so a result whose 99% bound lies that close to zero is called borderline at 99%, neither significant nor not significant.
  • Selection: the analogue ensemble was chosen on the screen, and the arms and the plant highlighted in the follow-ups were chosen after seeing the first run, so those results are hypotheses.
  • Low-output months: the study has too few months in which a plant is partly offline to say whether a lag helps in the scored month (see Figure 11).
  • Controls: the month-level control cannot separate one plant's level from a change shared by every plant, and the plant-steps control is too weak to separate the arms (see Figure 8).
  • Weather-product changes: the record holds one ENS change, ECMWF's Cycle 50r1 on 2026-05-12, with about 7 weeks of power after it, so the study does not test whether a lag absorbs a change in the weather forecast product.
  • Ensemble spread: every arm is given the ENS mean only, never the ensemble's spread, so the forecast band cannot follow the ensemble's own estimate of each day's uncertainty. The study did not test adding the spread.
  • Latency: the study assumes observed power up to the issue time, and CAMS with a 1-day delay. A delay of up to 9 hours in the power feed leaves every whole-day input unchanged, and only the issue-morning arm would lose hours. Before February 2026 the CAMS latency was 2 days, so in the 13 scored months from 2024-12 to 2025-12 the backtest reads CAMS a day fresher than the CAMS service then offered. The version of the satellite ratio that waits 2 days throughout gained the same (a difference of −0.019 points [−0.056, +0.020] over 18 months). The CAMS point service recomputes each request with its current processing, so the backtest reads values fetched after the fact, which may differ from those a live service would have received the next day.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The study does not cover domestic solar, wind, other regions, a plant that is partly offline in the scored month, a change in the weather forecast product, intraday updates from runs later than 00 UTC, a power feed that is minutes old, histories longer than 18 months, or hundreds of plants.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: The ENS-mean forecasts, CAMS irradiance, and the matched-lead study's rows are inputs the project holds. NGED's power data are private, and no plant's name, identifier, or coordinates appear on this page. The scripts are in studies/lag_features/, at the commit that merged this page. XGBoost 3.4.1 (from the repository's lock file) fitted every model on a GPU with 4 workers, at the primary setting (maximum depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 500 rounds, and row subsampling 0.8) and the sensitivity setting (maximum depth 4, learning rate 0.03, and 1,200 rounds). A refit of one plant's baseline on the GPU reproduced the first run's per-row losses bit for bit (the plant-control section of the third follow-up round's report, which the study folder's README describes).

docs.title: Claude Sonnet 5.5 found about 1 in 7 planted one-month solar losses and all 12 of a 60% loss lasting 90 days; the planned contrasts are untested
docs.text:
The question. A solar plant's usable capacity can fall for weeks (a failed string of panels, a network operator's export limit). A forecast that divides by a fixed capacity then errs, and the first capacity study had no way to tell real falls from noise. This study hides synthetic losses ("planted losses") in six real plants' power records and asks whether Claude Sonnet 5.5 can write down when each plant's capacity changed. The model is given the output of fixed calculations (the "tools": tables and two charts, such as the ratio of power to a physics-model estimate and a list of candidate change dates). The model answers with a list of dated capacity values (a "labeller"). A "hit" is an answer that marks a drop near the loss's start and a recovery near its end. "Static power" is a plant's fixed 99th-percentile output, so "holding static power" means estimating no change. Flexpectation is this project's forecast product.

Bottom line. In the planned round, the model hit 0 of 32 planted one-month losses and a fixed rule on the tools hit 1. The planned comparisons (C1 to C3) are untested, because the positive control, a set of 30% losses the model should be able to find, needed a pass mark of 80% and the model found 2 of 17. Later rounds were designed after seeing results ("post hoc"), except round 3, whose one new rule was written down before it ran ("pre-registered"). In round 3 the model hit 2 of 32 events (6%; 95% interval 2% to 20%), and pooled with six further fresh draws it hit 18 of 129 (14%; 9% to 21%), against 13 of 129 (10%; 6% to 17%) for the best fixed rule and 0 for holding static power. Its capacity error (5.6 points) was no better than the fixed rule's (5.3) or static power's (5.4). For larger losses it did better: it hit all 12 of a 60% loss lasting 90 days, 5 of 12 of a 30% loss lasting 90 days, and 5 of 12 of a 60% loss lasting 30 days. For Flexpectation, a language-model labeller is not ready to serve as a reference for small losses. With two prompts, one model, and two samples, no arm passed the 80% control, so the study cannot say whether the model can follow a 30% one-month loss.

docs.title: What the figure and the rounds show
docs.text:
Figure 1 shows the estimators this study compares on one planted loss. Each panel draws one estimator's capacity (orange line) over the plant's daily maximum power (grey dots), both as a share of static power, with the planted month shaded. The panels are static power, three estimators from the first study rerun with a seasonal correction (HYST2, HM2, CX2S), the fixed rule on the tools, the model's labels from the whole record ("hindsight"), and the model's labels from data up to each issue date ("causal", shown only for the last 6 months).

The four rounds. Round 1 (planned) gave the model the tools and a prompt. Round 2 (post hoc) added a local scan (each 30-day window against its neighbours) and a softer prompt. Round 3 (pre-registered) fixed one flaw that round 2 exposed: round 2's hard checks, which drop implausible labels, rejected labels the scan supported. Round 4 (post hoc) repeated round 3's arm on six more draws and added an easy case and a size-by-duration grid. Each "draw" is a fresh set of planted losses, one of each shape at each plant, 16 or 17 events. Hit rates are for events with at least one hit, with Wilson 95% intervals that treat events as independent although events in one draw share a plant record and its weather. The design details, the checks, the model route, and the spend guard are in the study folder's README. The four rounds cost US\(12.15 of a US\)15 ceiling. Round 4 stopped on the spending guard during draw 13, so the pooled draws are 05 to 12 and not the planned 05 to 14. The guard's per-call cap was lowered from US\(1 to US\)0.25 for round 4, because the dearest earlier call cost US\(0.07 and a US\)1 cap would have stopped the run after about US$3.00. The stop was arithmetic and not a function of any answer. The partial draw 13 answers are excluded from every table.

docs.title: Part 1: only HYST2 stayed within the false-movement gate, and it recovered nothing
docs.text:
Estimator Mean absolute capacity error, 32 planted losses (points) Days that moved, 23 quiet plant-months Mean delay to find a step (days) Static power 5.17 0.0% not applicable HYST2 (drop 15%, 3 days) 5.31 4.1% 12.4 HM2 (stay 0.95, spread 0.2) 3.59 13.8% 6.2 CX2S (the first study's tuned CX2) 2.39 59.7% 2.1

The gate is 10% of quiet days moving, and no HM2 setting passed it, so the HM2 row is its least-moving setting. The 23 quiet months both tune and score the gate, so HYST2's pass is in-sample. The seasonal correction cut HM's false movement from the first study's 31.5% to 13.8%.

docs.title: Round 1 (planned): the model found no planted loss, and the control failed
docs.text: The model with the tools hit 0 of 32 losses (95% interval 0% to 11%), and the model on weekly summaries hit 0. The tools' changepoint list had a down candidate near the start for 3 of the 32 losses, and the model marked none of them; for two it answered no change, and round 1's prompt asked for no reason. The planned contrasts were C1 (tools plus model against tools only, +0.64 points [−0.34, +2.11] resampling events) and C2 (against the model on weekly summaries, +1.04 [+0.00, +2.62]). They are untested because the positive control failed: the model found 2 of 17 steps of 30%, and rescored per run of adjacent planted months (post hoc) 5 of 13, both under the 80% pass mark. No model arm hit any loss, so C2's nominal "worse" verdict (its lower bound is +0.004) is not a difference in detection. A set of 32 events could never have powered C1 or C2, which need about 90 to 100.

docs.title: Round 2 (post hoc): a local scan helped the fixed rule, and conflicting checks cost the model its hits
docs.text: On draws 03 and 04 (34 losses) the fixed rule on the scan hit 5 (15%; 6% to 30%) against 0 for round 1's rule, and the model hit 6 events (18%; 8% to 34%) before the hard checks and 1 after them. The checks conflicted with the evidence: a step had to lie near a changepoint candidate, but the model now also saw scan episodes. The fixed rule beat round 1's by 1.1 points of error (interval −2.3 to −0.03), and the model was no better than the fixed rule (+0.25 [−0.5, +1.0]). Null-record answers scored against the same dates hit none of the 34, so the hits are not chance. Of the 12 no-change notes on these draws, 5 call the scan's episodes seasonal or weather, for example "the local-scan episodes are mostly winter/summer seasonal-correction artifacts that recur every year".

docs.title: Rounds 3 and 4: with the amended check, the model's hit rate was about 14%
docs.text:
The amended check also accepts a label when a scan episode starts or ends within 14 days. The amended check was written down and tested before round 3 ran, and round 3's draws 05 and 06 are its only pre-registered test.

Arm (events with a hit; Wilson 95%) Round 3 alone (32) Draws 07 to 12 (97) Pooled draws 05 to 12 (129) Mean error, pooled (points) Holding static power 0 0 0 (0% to 3%) 5.4 Fixed rule on the scan 3 (9%) 10 (10%) 13 (10%; 6% to 17%) 5.3 Model, original checks 0 4 (4%) 4 (3%; 1% to 8%) 8.1 Model, amended checks 2 (6%; 2% to 20%) 16 (16%; 10% to 25%) 18 (14%; 9% to 21%) 5.6

The model's pooled rate is above the fixed rule's, but no paired test is given, and the model's error is higher (5.6 against 5.3). By planted size the model hit 0% of losses under 15%, 5% of those from 15% to 25%, and 26% of those of 25% or more (answers, pooled).

docs.title: Easy case and grid (post hoc): size and duration both help
docs.text:
Design (12 losses each) Model, amended checks: events hit Model, no checks Fixed rule on the scan Error, static / model amended / fixed rule (points) 60% for 90 days (easy case) 12 (76% to 100%) 12 1 36.0 / 5.4 / 32.0 30% for 90 days 5 (42%; 19% to 68%) 7 0 18.0 / 11.9 / 17.5 60% for 30 days 5 (42%; 19% to 68%) 6 6 20.0 / 17.3 / 15.7

A large or long loss helped the model, but at 60% for 30 days the fixed rule beat it (6 against 5 hits, 15.7 against 17.3 points). Losses started on random days. The easy case changed size and duration together against the 30% one-month control, so the grid separates them, with only 12 losses per design.

docs.title: Exploratory: the real record, the plant under network management, and the causal role
docs.text: These are the model's opinions, with no ground truth. In the lag study's 3 low-output plant-months at one plant, round 1's model gave 0.77, 0.81, and 0.91 of static power, and round 2's gave 0.77, 1.00, and 0.93. For the one plant under active network management, the tools-only rule wrote 3 knots and named no curtailment, although the export cap bound on 134 days. The causal role ran only in round 1 and was not scored for detection.

docs.title: What this means for the next version, and for wind
docs.text: A labeller is limited first by its detector, and the hard checks must use the detector's candidates. The first study found that estimators that recover a planted loss also move when nothing changes; here the model's hits depended on candidates the tools listed. A wind study (speculation beyond the first page's sourced points) would plant losses of several sizes and durations, share one candidate list between detector and checks, and judge a labeller against a fixed rule, not against holding the capacity constant.

docs.title: Where else a language model could help in the NGED data pipeline
docs.text:
Each idea is speculation unless a page is cited, and each follows the pattern this study tests: deterministic tools first, the model reads their output.

  • Labelling faulty metering and switching events. The requirements list both as objectives. A model could read changepoint candidates, stuck-run flags, and neighbours' power and propose a label; the risk is a confident label with no evidence.
  • Reading outage, curtailment, and distribution network operator notices. A model could turn text into dated rows; the risk is a mis-parsed date or substation entering the data unnoticed.
  • Explaining data-quality warnings and forecast misses, and writing the daily health summary. The inherent-stability design already sends attributable events to developers; a model could write the paragraph. The risk is a plausible explanation that names a cause nobody tested.
  • Cleaning the substation metadata table. A model could propose fixes for a human to accept; the risk is a silent edit to a table the system trusts.

Every use shares three risks (non-determinism, leakage of what a model learned about real dates, and cost; a case file here cost about US$0.03) and three requirements: answers cached by prompt hash, every prompt and answer logged, and a guarded fallback to the path without a model. The three requirements follow the degradation rules: an absent or invalid answer is missing input, widens the uncertainty, and is recorded on the row. A capability that could live in the training loop belongs there, so the model's output would be a training label.

docs.title: Proposed follow-up study
docs.text: The follow-up would add what this study excluded: a stronger deterministic baseline, a weekly-summary arm on the round 2 prompt, and a larger model, then test on fresh draws that include losses starting mid-month. In this study, fixed rules hit about 10% of one-month losses and the model about 14%. The model hit more of the large or long losses. The follow-up would add (a) a matched one-month filter with its threshold set on the null record, so that "the model beats the fixed rule" is not against a rule that found 1 of 12 easy losses; (b) a weekly-summary arm on the round 2 prompt, to separate tools from prompt; and (c) a larger model, run only because the grid showed the model finds mid-size losses. A rough cost is two days of agent time, no downloads, and US\(10 to US\)15 (an estimate for an Opus-class model at about five times Sonnet's price). The case against is that no planted loss was persistent and small, and 129 losses still give wide intervals. The proposal commits the project to nothing.

docs.title: Limitations and scope
docs.text: The numbers rest on 12 to 129 planted losses in one record shared by all draws, with a prompt written for one-month, calendar-aligned losses (the easy case and grid start on random days). The planted test is optimistic: the physics model never saw a planted loss, and a real deployment fits on data that contains it. Round 2's scan, threshold, prompt, and the amended check followed earlier results. The model sees real dates, so it can use what it learned about UK weather. Only Sonnet 5.5 was tested. This page says nothing about wind plants, forecasts, or plants outside the six.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: The satellite irradiance and the lag-features study's rows are held by the project. National Grid Electricity Distribution's (NGED's) power data are private, and no plant's name, identifier, or coordinates appear here. The prompt and answer log pairs plant letters with dates, so it stays in the private data store. The scripts are in studies/llm_capacity_labeller/, with the reproduction commands, and the shared code is in packages/studies/. The model is Claude Sonnet 5.5 through claude -p (version 2.1.296).

docs.title: How the matched-lead study reads its extra products, and what they show at other lead days
docs.text: This page holds the parts of the matched-lead study that concern its exploratory products: how the study reads each product, and the two results sections that have no figure. The main page carries the planned contrasts, the blends, Figures 1 to 20, the discussion, and the limitations, which apply to every number here. Every result on this page is exploratory and fitted at the primary setting only. The main page's Introduction names the products. An arm is one XGBoost model given one product's forecast, and the primary setting is the first of the two hyperparameter settings that the main page defines.

docs.title: The extra lead days, day 0, and the products added later
docs.text:
The extra arms are fitted on a graphics processing unit (GPU), in four batches, and every one is exploratory. Each extra arm is the same XGBoost model given one product's forecast, at the primary setting only, on the same shared rows, folds, and eras as every other arm, except that IFS HRES 9 km loses its gap days (below) and the AIFS arms have rows of their own (How AIFS is read). The batches are:

  • Batch 1: the ENS mean at days 5, 10, and 14; the ENS control member at day 0; the GEFS mean at days 0, 5, 10, and 14; IFS 0.25° and GFS (Open-Meteo) at days 0, 5, and 7; ICON global at days 0 and 5; and every other Previous Runs product at day 0.
  • Batch 2: the ENS mean and the GEFS mean at day 7, the ENS control member at days 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14, and GPU refits of the published arms that batch 1 left on the CPU.
  • Batch 3: GFS (native) at days 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14.
  • Batch 4: IFS HRES 9 km at days 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7.

Each product has the lead days below, and the horizons in this table come from public specifications that the study did not confirm. Where the archive holds no value, the table gives the share of hours with a value.

Product Lead days fitted Days not fitted, and why ENS mean, ENS control member, GEFS mean, and GFS (native) 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14 Days 4, 6, 8, 9, and 11 to 13 were not fitted. Each of these products reaches day 14. IFS 0.25° and GFS (Open-Meteo) 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 Days 4 and 6 were not fitted. Open-Meteo's Previous Runs archive stops at day 7, so days 10 and 14 are not in the archive. IFS HRES 9 km (Open-Meteo Single Runs) 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7 Days 4, 6, 8, and 9 were not fitted. The runs end at lead 240 hours, so day 10 is beyond the runs. ICON global 0, 1, 2, 3, and 5 Days 4 and 6 were not in archive. Day 7 is 0% non-null in the archive, so day 6 is the last day with values. ICON-EU 0, 1, 2, and 3 Day 4 was not in archive. Day 5 is 0% non-null in the archive, so day 4 is the last day with values. ARPEGE Europe (solar only) 0, 1, 2, and 3 Beyond the product's horizon from day 4. UKV 0 and 1 Day 2 is 0% non-null in the archive, and the study could not verify UKV's horizon locally. The UKV-CEDA page tests UKV at days 1 to 4 from the CEDA archive. ICON-D2, AROME France (solar only), DMI HARMONIE-AROME, and KNMI HARMONIE-AROME 0 and 1 Beyond the product's horizon from day 2.

Day 0 reads the freshest run that covers each hour, and its served lead is checked for only ICON-EU and ICON-D2, and only for radiation. The past-weather studies matched ICON-EU's served radiation to ICON's own files within 1 W/m² at 9 of 9 hours (one day, one place). For ICON-D2 the freshest run was the closest match at 7 of 9 hours, and differed by up to 44 W/m². The wind lead of 0 to 2 hours for both products is inferred from where the hour-to-hour jumps of the served series fall and from the 3-hourly run cycle, and the radiation lead is 1 to 3 hours. This study's day-0 series for the two products equals those studies' series on every shared hour (the largest absolute difference is 0.0000). The day-0 lead of every other Previous Runs product is estimated from the product's own run cycle, not measured. ENS, GEFS, and IFS HRES 9 km read the 00 UTC run of the hour's own day at day 0, so their day-0 marks cover hours before that run is published. GFS (native) reads the freshest of four runs a day, at a lead of 1 to 6 hours for solar and 0 to 5 hours for wind, which ignores the hours GFS takes to publish a run.

GFS (native) reads Dynamical.org's store of NOAA's GFS at each generator's nearest 0.25° cell, and differs from GFS (Open-Meteo) in its source, run cycle, and lead. The store holds four runs a day (00, 06, 12, and 18 UTC), with hourly leads to 120 hours and 3-hourly leads after. Day N of 1 or more reads the 00 UTC run issued N days before the hour's own day, at ENS's own leads. The store's radiation is the mean since the last 6-hourly reset, and the build converts it to the mean over each hour, or over each 3 hours after lead 120 hours. Days 5, 7, 10, and 14 lie on 3-hourly leads and are upsampled to hourly as the ENS and GEFS arms are.

IFS HRES 9 km is Open-Meteo's Single Runs archive of ECMWF's IFS HRES on its native O1280 grid, the same forecasting system as IFS 0.25° on a finer grid. The archive (ecmwf_ifs, on ECMWF's O1280 grid) holds one 00 UTC run a day, with hourly leads 0 to 240 hours. Day N reads the 00 UTC run issued N days before the hour's own day, at ENS's own leads. The archive publishes every 3 hours after lead 90 and every 6 hours after lead 144, and Open-Meteo interpolates those steps to hourly, so the hourly values at days 5 and 7, and at the last hours of day 3, are interpolated. Radiation is clipped at zero (the archive holds 244 values below zero, the lowest -1.0 W/m²), and wind is the served speed and the sine and cosine of the served direction. Each solar generator reads its nearest cell and each wind generator its nearest land cell, and sites B and D share a source cell and carry identical series. Open-Meteo's processing of HRES was not checked against a native archive. IFS Cycle 50r1 began on 2026-05-12, inside the span, and these arms add no era feature, so the shared rows' era code has no boundary at that date.

IFS HRES 9 km is scored on the shared hours minus the target days its archive lacks. The archive holds 919 of 926 run days, so seven run days are absent. Those gap days are never filled from another run. The six solar arms score 34,751 to 34,786 rows, and the six wind arms 36,957 to 37,008, against 35,263 and 37,407 shared rows. Every contrast that involves IFS HRES 9 km is computed on the rows both arms score, from the existing out-of-fold errors with no refit of the other arm, whose training rows included the gap days. Dropping the gap days of the day-1 arm moves the ENS mean's day-1 error from 8.771% to 8.792% for solar (+0.022 points) and from 8.350% to 8.379% for wind (+0.029 points).

Part of the rise in ENS's and GEFS's error with lead may come from coarser time steps. ENS serves 6-hour steps beyond 144 hours and GEFS beyond 240 hours. ENS at days 7, 10, and 14 and GEFS at days 10 and 14 therefore fall on 6-hour steps, and ENS at day 5 touches a 6-hour step only in the margin its upsampling reads beyond lead 144. Part of the rise in the error of those arms with lead may come from the coarser steps and not only from an older run. verify_extra_leads.py checked, before the build, that GEFS's radiation beyond 240 hours is a 6-hour window mean.

Every mark in Figures 3 and 4 is a GPU fit, and a GPU fit is not bit-identical to a central processing unit (CPU) fit. Every contrast among the extra arms therefore uses reference arms (the arms each contrast subtracts) refitted on the same device. The device noise floor is the difference between a GPU refit and the published CPU fit of the same arm. For solar it lies between -0.024 and +0.014 points, and every interval includes zero. For wind every point estimate is negative, between -0.090 and -0.040 points, and one difference, ICON-EU at day 3 (-0.079 points [-0.167, -0.005]), is statistically significant at the 5% level. A wind mark from a GPU fit may therefore sit slightly below where a CPU fit would put it. A GPU fit repeats itself: the 23 solar arms and 23 wind arms that both an earlier GPU run and batch 1 fitted have identical per-row errors, to 0.0 on every row (a comparison of the two runs' saved losses that no committed script prints). The published headline contrasts, the blends, and the per-generator contrasts (Figures 5, 6, and 9 to 12) rest on the CPU fits of the published run.

The ENS numbers at the extra leads are not comparable with the ENS horizons study. Days 5, 7, 10, and 14 of ENS, and ICON's day 0, use this study's rows, which start after the IFS Cycle 49r1 change. The ENS numbers here are therefore not comparable with the ENS horizons study, whose ENS rows span that change.

docs.title: How AIFS is read
docs.text:
AIFS is read at the same lead as ENS, on 6-hourly steps. For a target hour on UTC day D, the day-d band reads the 00 UTC run of day D minus d, so the lead is 24d plus the hour, at days 1 and 2. AIFS Single and AIFS ENS serve one value every 6 hours, where ENS serves one every 3 hours to 144 hours, so an XGBoost model given ENS at full resolution would be favoured by its finer steps alone. The like-for-like references are therefore ENS's control member (against AIFS Single) and ENS's mean (against AIFS ENS's mean), both averaged to the same 6-hourly steps. Hourly IFS 0.25° is a one-sided reference, because its hourly steps and its shorter lead both favour IFS 0.25°. The positive control is ENS's mean on 6-hourly steps minus ENS's mean on 3-hourly steps, which should be positive: it is +0.243 points [+0.153, +0.332] for solar and +0.321 points [+0.206, +0.419] for wind.

AIFS Single's radiation is a 6-hour mean that ends at the lead, and its wind is instantaneous. Against ERA5, the mean absolute difference of AIFS Single's radiation from ERA5's 6-hour mean is smallest, at 16.36 W/m², when the window ends at the lead (39.55 W/m² one hour earlier and 37.97 W/m² one hour later). The correlation of AIFS Single's 100 m wind speed with ERA5's instantaneous 100 m wind speed is highest, at 0.9422, at the same hour. The units and the grid orientation also passed their checks.

Every AIFS arm reads the same spatial average that ENS reads. Each generator's value is the mean of the 0.25° cells under its H3 resolution-5 hexagon, weighted by overlap. A nearest-cell AIFS Single arm shows how far the spatial read moves the result.

AIFS arms have rows of their own. AIFS Single carries radiation and 100 m wind from the 2025-02-24 06 UTC run, and AIFS ENS from 2025-07-02, so neither covers the hours every other product is scored on. The single row set holds the hours whose 00 UTC run is inside one AIFS Single version, and the ens row set is the part of that AIFS ENS also covers. Every arm on a row set is scored on the same hours, and the study fits the reference arms again on each row set. The Dynamical.org store carries no model-version marker, so the study assigns each run to a version by its run date, taken from ECMWF's release pages. Folds are cut inside each version era, and the months that hold a version switch (2025-08 and 2026-05) are dropped. The single row set holds 28,570 solar rows and 28,873 wind rows over 16 months, and the ens row set holds 16,911 solar rows and 18,555 wind rows over 11 months. The ens row set starts in 2025-09, because July 2025 would form a one-month version era. Each AIFS arm has the same seven columns as an ENS arm.

One contrast was planned before any AIFS fit: AIFS Single against ENS's control member at day 1, for solar and for wind. The page calls this AIFS contrast a deciding contrast, and it is planned. The study also refits it at the sensitivity setting, without day of year in either arm, and at a 97.5% interval (a Bonferroni correction across solar and wind), and drops each month in turn. The AIFS ENS contrasts are descriptive only, because about 84% of the scored (generator, fold, calendar month) cells of the ens row set have no training row of their calendar month (55 of 65 solar cells and 27 of 33 wind cells). Every other AIFS number is exploratory and post hoc. Every AIFS fit is on the GPU.

The conventions of AIFS Single's radiation and wind were checked at days 1 and 2 only. The script verify_aifs_steps.py compares AIFS Single with ERA5 at several offsets to find the hour at which each field is stamped. At days 7 and 14 the check fails, because AIFS Single's correlation with ERA5's wind speed is only 0.43 at day 7 and 0.15 at day 14, so an offset test cannot tell one offset from another. The checks pass at days 1 and 2, and the wiring check, which compares the built columns with the raw store, passes at every day. This study therefore assumes, and did not check, that the same radiation window and wind reading hold at days 7 and 14.

AIFS Single is also read at days 7 and 14, and blended with ENS's mean at days 1, 2, 7, and 14. Days 7 and 14 read the 00 UTC run 7 and 14 days before the hour's own day, at ENS's own leads, so the ENS control member and the ENS mean are natively 6-hourly there and share AIFS Single's steps. A row is dropped when its run lies outside the AIFS version era of its hour. That drops 362 solar and 454 wind hours at day 7 and 1,121 and 1,433 at day 14. The single row set then holds 28,208 solar and 28,419 wind rows at day 7, and 27,449 and 27,440 at day 14, all over 16 months. A blend gives one XGBoost model ENS's mean and AIFS Single's forecast at the same day. A solar blend has 9 columns and a wind blend 11, against 7 for ENS's mean alone, so the study also fits two controls with the blend's number of columns. The blend's control shuffles AIFS Single's weather among hours of the same generator, year-month, and hour of day, and the mirror control shuffles ENS's mean instead. Because two shuffles of the same weather can differ (see the AIFS section), a shuffled arm's interval may understate the noise. The blends fit and the P4 second-seed refit below were fitted on the GPU.

Four contrasts per technology are deciding contrasts, and the page does not call them planned. Each was named before the fit of this section, but after the day-1 and day-2 AIFS results and the ENS results at days 7 and 14 were known. They are:

  • H7 and H14: AIFS Single minus the ENS control member at day 7 and at day 14.
  • B7 and B14: the blend of ENS's mean and AIFS Single minus ENS's mean alone at day 7 and at day 14, with the blend minus its control as the guard.

A deciding contrast is claimable only if its interval is statistically significant at the 5% level at both hyperparameter settings with the same sign, and every dropped month keeps the sign. For H7 and H14 the refit without day of year in either arm must also agree in sign. For B7 and B14 the guard must also be statistically significant at both settings. The report also prints each deciding contrast at 99.375%, the Bonferroni level across the eight deciding contrasts (four per technology). Every other contrast in the section is exploratory and post hoc, and AIFS ENS rows are descriptive.

A day-14 reading rule decides whether there is any skill to compare at day 14. Skill exists at day 14 only if AIFS Single or the ENS control member has an error that is statistically significantly below both shuffled-AIFS arms (two seeds, primary setting, 95% interval). Where the rule finds no skill, the page does not read H14 or B14, and prints their intervals only for completeness. A second reading rule applies beside H7 and H14: AIFS Single having a lower error than the control member but not than the ENS mean is consistent with smoothing, and is not described as a better weather forecast.

docs.title: How WeatherNext 3 is read
docs.text:
WeatherNext 3 (WN3), Google's machine-learned ensemble weather model, is read at the same lead as ENS, at days 1, 2, 7, and 14, on hourly steps. For a target hour on UTC day D, the day-d band reads the 00 UTC run of day D minus d, as for ENS and AIFS. The WN3 store holds 360 hourly leads of the ensemble mean only, on a 0.1° grid, for runs from 2026-01-01. The study copies the 00 UTC runs and the cells that cover the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, and averages the cells over each farm's H3 cell in the same way as for ENS and AIFS. Radiation is the accumulation over the hour ending at the target time, in joules per square metre, so the study divides it by 3,600 s to get watts per square metre. For solar, the 2 m temperature at an hour's midpoint is the mean of the two hourly values on either side of it, as ENS's is.

WN3's wind speed is the length of the mean wind vector, which is biased low relative to ENS's. The store holds the ensemble mean of the eastward and northward wind components and no member values, so WN3's speed is the length of the mean vector. ENS's speed is the mean of the members' speeds, which is larger when the members disagree in direction. The study therefore also fits, for wind at every day, a matched ENS reference: ENS's mean whose speed is the length of the mean of its members' wind vectors. That reference, and not ENS's mean speed, is the one the wind contrasts against WN3 use as the like-for-like comparison. ENS's members' speed and direction at 100 m and 10 m are on local disk for every day, so the reference needs no download. If a run lacked members, the build would drop that run and the fit would stop, naming the run.

The WN3 rows cover about 7 months, so every WN3 contrast is descriptive. The row set holds February to April and June to 10 September 2026. September holds 10 days only, and counts as a whole month when the intervals resample months. Each calendar month occurs in one year only, so no scored month has a training row of its own calendar month. The contrast of interest is WN3's mean minus ENS's mean on the same rows, at days 1, 2, 7, and 14, for solar and wind, each with the sensitivity setting and each read as descriptive. Each is paired with a negative control that shuffles WN3's weather within farm, year-month, and hour of day, under two seeds. The day-14 gap minus the day-1 gap is exploratory, and is read from the two intervals, not tested. A difference whose 95% interval spans 0 is reported with the interval's bounds, because a null at day 14 excludes only differences larger than the interval, and is never described as no difference. AIFS Single and the AIFS ENS mean keep the days they were fitted at (1, 2, 7, and 14), on their own row sets.

docs.title: What is known about WN3's lookahead
docs.text:
Which WeatherNext 3 (WN3) weather-model version made the 2026 archive is not documented, so the in-sample months (before July) may or may not overlap its training data. Rasp et al. (2026) state "For the production model, we train until June 30 2026". Their Appendix A.1.3 also lists versions trained until the start of 2025 and until the start of 2026, and the paper does not say which version produced the archive. We found no statement from Google of which version made the 2026 archive. Every WN3 result on this page is therefore reported for three groups of rows: the months before July (February to June), which may overlap training; the months from July (July to September), which lie after every training end the paper lists; and a pooled group of every scored row from February to September 2026, including the rows that fall in neither of the first two groups. The July to September rows are the check for a version change and for overlap with training data, and the leaderboards draw the pooled group, whose 7 months clear the study's minimum of 6 months for an interval. WN3 against AIFS or ENS on the months before July may not be a fair comparison, because WN3's weights may have seen those months and the other products' had not. The pooled group mixes both kinds of month, so its lead over ENS may include such overlap, and the leaderboards' captions say so. The folds are unchanged, and each group selects rows that were already scored out of fold. The July to September group is still not fully clean: the out-of-fold models train on the February to June WN3 rows, which may overlap WN3's training data, and the direction of that effect is unknown.

Hypothesis, not documented and stated by no source we found: the archive for January to June 2026 was made by a WN3 weather model trained on data from before 2026, and the archive from July 2026 onwards by the production WN3 weather model, trained on data from before July 2026. The reasoning behind the hypothesis is that an archive from a weather model that had seen the months it forecasts would overstate its skill. If the hypothesis holds, no archived forecast comes from a model that had seen the period it forecasts. The three groups of rows are motivated by this hypothesis. The split checks whether a version change at the start of July shows in the scores, and makes no claim about which version made any row. A difference between the groups is weak evidence either way, because every product's error differs between the months (see the absolute-skill paragraph in the results).

A row is out-of-sample only if its valid month is July or later and the 00 UTC run it reads was issued after 30 June. A day-14 row that verifies in July from a run issued in the last two weeks of June sits in neither group. The report gives the count of such rows for every technology and lead day. The out-of-sample group holds 3 calendar months, fewer than the study's minimum of 6 for an interval, so its intervals give the range of the months and are indicative only.

WN3's archive is labelled real-time, and the copy cannot show when Google produced each run. Google's dissemination guide gives a latency of 7 hours 45 minutes (Cloud Storage) to 8 hours 10 minutes (BigQuery) for the 6-hourly runs, and the Cloud Storage guide labels the archive "real-time operational data for 2026 to present". The store's run_written and source_init_time records show that the 271 runs at 00 UTC from 2026-01-01 to 2026-09-28 are all present, with no gap and no run whose source_init_time differs from its init_time. Our own download wrote those records, so they show that the copy is complete and say nothing about when Google produced each run. If Google produced the runs after the fact, WN3's error is optimistic. The --lookahead-cleared flag of fit_aifs.py --wn3 stops the fit from starting until whoever runs it has read this section.

docs.title: Why the WN3 paper's gains over ENS are not directly comparable with this study
docs.text: The WN3 paper's gains over ENS and this study's results answer different questions, so they do not conflict. Rasp et al. (2026) compare WN3 against 48 ENS members, scored with the fair continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). For single-level variables, the ENS members are regridded to 0.1° from the TIGGE (THORPEX Interactive Grand Global Ensemble) and MARS (Meteorological Archival and Retrieval System) archives. Rasp et al. note that TIGGE's reduced storage resolution adds roughly 0.02 K to ENS's 2 m temperature CRPS at 6-hour multiples in the paper's analysis evaluations. We found no mention of statistical post-processing applied to ENS. The paper reports no ensemble-mean error for ENS, so its results cannot separate the accuracy of the ENS mean from the calibration of its spread. The ensemble-mean errors we found in the paper are cyclone track, intensity, and extent errors for WN3 and its predecessor. For short lead times, the WN3 station head lowers station 2 m temperature CRPS by up to 40% against ENS, and Figure 3 shows the gain narrowing with lead time. Rasp et al. describe the station head as building station calibration into the model, so that WN3 needs no separate calibration stage. A comparison with post-processed ENS would therefore be a natural extension of their work. This study trains one XGBoost model per weather product on the ensemble mean, which can absorb each product's systematic bias but not differences in spread, because the XGBoost model sees only the mean. The study scores the error of the generators' power forecast in percent of capacity. This study does not test the paper's claim.

docs.title: How the AIFS papers and an independent study compare AIFS with ENS
docs.text:
The ECMWF papers on AIFS (Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System) score raw ensembles with probabilistic scores, and find AIFS ahead of the IFS ensemble for most upper-air variables. Lang et al. (2026) train AIFS-CRPS on the almost fair CRPS (afCRPS) and compare it with the 9 km, 50-member IFS ensemble. We found no mention of post-processing of the IFS ensemble in the medium range. For most upper-air variables the paper reports lower CRPS and ensemble-mean root mean squared error and higher anomaly correlation, with improvements "in the range of 5–20%". Lang et al. discuss AIFS-CRPS's over-dispersion, and we found no discussion of under-dispersion in the IFS ensemble.

The ECMWF Newsletter on the operational AIFS ensemble reports a similar comparison. Lang and Magnusson (2025) compare AIFS ENS with IFS ENS on the same four scores, and we found no mention of post-processing. The authors write that improvements "reach up to 25%" for upper-air variables, and that for 10 m wind speed verified against surface synoptic observation (SYNOP) stations "IFS ENS is more skilful". They describe AIFS ENS as "currently overdispersive for a range of upper-air variables".

An independent study finds raw AIFS ENS less skilful than raw IFS ENS for 10 m wind speed. Kocsis and Baran (2026) verify 10 m wind speed at 9,246 SYNOP stations from July to November 2025. They score raw and post-processed versions of both ensembles. Raw AIFS scores worse than raw IFS at every lead time, with a CRPS skill score near -4% and a mean absolute error skill score near -3%. Post-processing shrinks the gap, which stays significant only at short lead times and in some cases at days 14 and 15. Both raw ensembles are strongly under-dispersive.

These papers rank weather forecasts against weather observations, which is a different question from the one this page answers. This study fits an XGBoost model for each generator and each arm, from one product's forecast and calendar columns, and scores the power forecast in percent of capacity. The question is how much information an XGBoost model fitted to power can extract from each product. An arm reads ENS's mean, ENS's control member, AIFS Single, or AIFS ENS's mean. The XGBoost model can therefore learn a product's stable bias at each generator, but it never sees a product's spread. This page makes no comparison of calibrated probabilistic forecasts.

docs.title: Day 0 is lower than day 1 for every product, and ICON-D2's day 0 is the lowest (exploratory)
docs.text:
ICON-D2's day-0 marks are the lowest wind error in Figure 4 and tie with IFS 0.25°'s day 0 for the lowest solar error in Figure 3, and each product's day-0 error is lower than the same product's day-1 error. ICON's day 0 is read from the run that starts 0 to 3 hours before the hour it describes. That run is delivered about 1.5 hours (ICON-D2) or 3.5 hours (ICON-EU) after it starts, so day 0 is not a day-ahead forecast a service could read. The XGBoost model given ICON-D2's day-0 value has an error of 7.776% of capacity [7.201, 8.305] for solar and 6.826% [5.901, 7.864] for wind. ICON-EU's day-0 errors are 8.487% [7.850, 9.071] and 7.224% [6.329, 8.221]. ICON-D2 minus ENS at day 0, both fitted on the GPU, is -0.349 points [-0.496, -0.189] for solar and -0.600 points [-0.771, -0.432] for wind (exploratory). ENS at day 0 minus ICON-EU at day 0 is -0.362 points [-0.538, -0.199] for solar and +0.201 points [+0.023, +0.401] for wind, so for solar ENS's day-0 error is lower than ICON-EU's. ICON-D2 minus ICON-EU is -0.711 points [-0.871, -0.557] for solar and -0.398 points [-0.503, -0.290] for wind at day 0, against +0.302 points [+0.061, +0.665] and +0.046 points [-0.079, +0.166] at day 1 (exploratory, both GPU refits).

Day 0 minus day 1 is negative and statistically significant for every product whose difference the batch reports print. Those are 14 arms for solar and 12 for wind. The difference runs from -0.682 [-0.892, -0.462] points (GEFS) to -2.101 [-2.598, -1.686] points (ICON-D2) for solar, and from -1.042 [-1.309, -0.784] points (the ENS control member) to -2.157 [-2.433, -1.927] points (UKV) for wind. IFS 0.25°'s solar day-0 error, 7.793%, is within 0.02 points of ICON-D2's.

At day 0, ICON-D2, IFS 0.25°, and for wind UKV and ICON-EU have a lower error than the ENS mean, and the day-0 leads of every one of these products but ICON-D2 and ICON-EU are estimated, not measured. A Previous Runs product's day 0 reads the freshest run, a lead of a few hours. ENS's day 0 reads the 00 UTC run of the day, a lead of 0 to 23 hours, so the comparison favours the Previous Runs products.

Exploratory: product at day 0 minus ENS mean at day 0 (points, primary) Solar Wind GEFS mean +1.233 [+0.940, +1.521] +0.473 [+0.310, +0.620] ENS control member +0.190 [+0.111, +0.267] +0.201 [+0.126, +0.282] UKV -0.017 [-0.266, +0.240] -0.446 [-0.673, -0.218] IFS 0.25° -0.332 [-0.524, -0.139] -0.184 [-0.309, -0.059] GFS (Open-Meteo) +1.969 [+1.671, +2.230] +0.143 [-0.001, +0.276] ICON global +0.513 [+0.362, +0.662] +0.373 [+0.073, +0.727] ARPEGE Europe +1.441 [+1.098, +1.796] no wind arm AROME France +0.716 [+0.441, +1.001] no wind arm KNMI HARMONIE-AROME +0.828 [+0.657, +1.002] +0.415 [+0.179, +0.648] DMI HARMONIE-AROME +0.838 [+0.632, +1.052] +0.569 [-0.077, +1.723]

For solar, ICON-D2's advantage over ICON-EU at day 0 shrinks as the served lead grows; for wind the intervals overlap. For solar, ICON-D2 minus ICON-EU is -1.071 points [-1.241, -0.898] at a served lead of 1 hour, -0.599 points [-0.786, -0.428] at 2 hours, and -0.462 points [-0.670, -0.246] at 3 hours. For wind the advantage is the same at 0 and 1 hours (-0.454 points [-0.582, -0.317] and -0.454 points [-0.573, -0.336]) and smaller at 2 hours (-0.287 points [-0.413, -0.158]), but the intervals overlap. The subsets are different hours, so the study computed no paired test between served leads.

The day-0 served lead is checked for ICON-D2 and ICON-EU, radiation only, and estimated from the run cycle for every other product. ICON-D2 runs every 3 hours, so the served lead of a radiation value at label hour h is ((h-1) mod 3) + 1 hours and of a wind value h mod 3 hours. The past-weather studies checked the radiation lead against ICON's own files at 9 hours on one day and at one place, and took the wind lead from where the hour-to-hour jumps of the served series fall and from the 3-hourly run cycle.
