Solar power (% of capacity) In-sample WN3 In-sample ENS mean July to September WN3 July to September ENS mean Pooled WN3 Pooled ENS mean Day 1 9.055% 9.281% 8.841% 9.127% 8.964% 9.208% Day 2 10.063% 10.919% 9.731% 10.049% 9.879% 10.482% Day 7 16.284% 16.656% 12.476% 12.359% 14.533% 14.697% Day 14 17.437% 17.912% 13.669% 13.796% 15.679% 16.014% Solar power: WN3 minus ENS mean (points) In-sample July to September Pooled Day 1 -0.226 [-0.494, -0.056] -0.286 [-0.570, +0.007] -0.243 [-0.440, -0.069] Day 2 -0.856 [-1.241, -0.496] -0.318 [-0.584, -0.064] -0.603 [-0.966, -0.306] Day 7 -0.371 [-0.988, +0.518] +0.117 [-0.365, +1.034] -0.165 [-0.630, +0.343] Day 14 -0.475 [-1.654, +0.489] -0.127 [-0.347, +0.258] -0.334 [-0.996, +0.194] Wind power (% of capacity) In-sample WN3 In-sample ENS reference July to September WN3 July to September ENS reference Pooled WN3 Pooled ENS reference Day 1 7.861% 8.683% 6.348% 6.706% 7.129% 7.730% Day 2 9.615% 10.606% 7.429% 7.758% 8.580% 9.381% Day 7 20.093% 21.462% 11.512% 11.926% 16.345% 17.395% Day 14 23.065% 25.014% 10.861% 11.359% 17.939% 19.098% Wind power: WN3 minus ENS mean-vector reference (points) In-sample July to September Pooled Day 1 -0.821 [-1.089, +0.010] -0.358 [-1.185, -0.002] -0.601 [-0.979, -0.192] Day 2 -0.991 [-1.378, +0.105] -0.329 [-1.528, +0.219] -0.801 [-1.206, -0.321] Day 7 -1.369 [-4.618, +2.891] -0.413 [-0.501, -0.302] -1.050 [-2.870, +0.917] Day 14 -1.949 [-9.023, +1.946] -0.498 [-0.609, -0.359] -1.159 [-4.480, +0.829] Wind power, July to September: WN3 minus ENS mean speed (points) Difference Day 1 -0.468 [-1.175, -0.099] Day 2 -0.382 [-1.388, +0.129] Day 7 -0.050 [-2.213, +0.849] Day 14 -0.070 [-0.248, +0.519]

At days 7 and 14, the mean-vector reference has a higher error than ENS's mean speed, in July to September, by 0.36 and 0.43 points, so the wind contrasts against the reference at those days partly measure the reference's definition. Against ENS's mean speed, WN3's differences at days 7 and 14 are -0.050 and -0.070 points, and both intervals span 0.

Absolute skill falls steeply with lead, and a gap of a few tenths of a point sits beside errors of 6 to 25% of capacity. At solar day 1 in July to September, WN3's error is 8.841% and ENS's is 9.127%, a gap of 3% of ENS's error. The months before July have errors 1.3 to 2.2 times those of July to September at days 7 and 14, for WN3 and ENS alike, so a difference between the groups' errors is not evidence about WN3's training data.

The negative control shows that WN3's weather carries the skill at days 1 and 2 for both technologies and at day 7 for solar, and carries none detectable at solar day 14 or wind day 7 in July to September. In the control, WN3's weather is shuffled within farm, year-month, and hour of day, under two seeds. At day 1 and day 2, WN3's error minus the shuffled arm's is between -3.4 and -9.8 points for solar and between -4.6 and -17.6 points for wind, in every group, with intervals that exclude 0. At solar day 7 the July to September differences are -1.124 [-1.953, -0.317] and -0.759 [-1.443, -0.320]. At solar day 14, the July to September differences are +0.096 [-0.054, +0.442] and +0.568 [+0.218, +0.781]. At wind day 7 the July to September differences are -0.005 [-0.154, +0.113] and +0.002 [-0.297, +0.273]. At solar day 14 the XGBoost model given the second-seed shuffled weather has the lower error, and at wind day 7 the shuffled arms' error (11.517% and 11.511%) equals WN3's (11.512%) and beats the mean-vector reference's (11.926%). So WN3's mean adds no detectable skill at those two cells, and the wind day-7 contrast of -0.413 points measures the reference doing worse than no weather. The wind day-14 July to September differences, -0.526 [-0.711, -0.314] and -0.405 [-1.010, -0.177], favour the real weather, on 3 months. The two shuffle seeds also differ from each other: the interval of their difference excludes 0 in 5 of the 24 cells of technology, day, and group, and the largest such difference is -2.240 points [-7.471, -0.196], for wind day 2 in the months before July. Shuffling noise is therefore not negligible next to the differences read here. In the pooled rows, no failure of the control is detectable at solar day 14 (+0.124 [-0.600, +0.598]) or at wind day 14 (-0.402 [-1.603, +0.369]), because both intervals span 0.

The sensitivity setting removes the exclusion of 0 from three July to September wind contrasts, at days 1, 7, and 14, and moves the solar day-1 interval off 0. The sensitivity refits fire on contrasts whose interval lies near the 5% line. In July to September, at solar day 1 the difference is -0.409 [-0.700, -0.122] at the sensitivity setting, against -0.286 [-0.570, +0.007] at the primary setting, and at solar day 2 it is -0.300 [-0.579, -0.035]. At wind day 1 the matched contrast is -0.358 [-1.185, -0.002] at the primary setting and -0.303 [-0.898, +0.032] at the sensitivity setting. At wind day 7 the difference is -0.413 [-0.501, -0.302] at the primary setting and +0.011 [-0.536, +0.726] at the sensitivity setting, so the wind day-7 difference depends on the XGBoost setting and is not claimable. At wind day 14 the sensitivity setting gives -0.201 [-0.436, +0.735], against -0.498 [-0.609, -0.359] at the primary setting, so the wind day-14 difference depends on the XGBoost setting too.

The number of rows in each group, and the rows in neither group, are in the report. The months before July hold 6,335 rows for solar and 5,415 for wind at every lead day. The July to September group holds 5,069, 4,995, 4,602, and 4,129 solar rows at days 1, 2, 7, and 14, and 4,773, 4,701, 4,349, and 3,863 wind rows. The pooled group holds 11,479 solar rows and 10,260 wind rows at every day. The rows in neither group are those whose valid month is after June but whose 00 UTC run was issued on or before 30 June: 75, 149, 542, and 1,015 rows for solar at days 1, 2, 7, and 14, and 72, 144, 496, and 982 for wind. In each cell, the two groups' rows plus the rows in neither group sum to the pooled rows. Across the 42 solar and 21 wind (farm, fold, calendar month) cells, none has a training row of its own calendar month. No loss in any saved file is NaN, and the only nulls are the continuous ranked probability scores that a single-valued arm does not have.

docs.title: WN3 and AIFS at days 0, 3, 4, and 10 (exploratory)
docs.text: In the pooled rows, WN3's mean has a lower error than ENS's mean at days 3 and 4 for solar and wind, every AIFS point error is lower than ENS's mean at days 3 and 4, and at day 0 the AIFS point errors are higher. At day 10 the AIFS sign changes with the row set and the technology, and WN3's wind error is higher than ENS's in the pooled rows. No AIFS difference is claimed, because the fits give no paired interval. The WN3 differences are against a same-rows ENS mean, and the months before July may overlap WN3's training data. The companion page holds the tables for the three row groups.

docs.title: Discussion: what to use
docs.text:
Each recommendation below is about a product as this study reads it, and rests on an XGBoost model fitted at nine generators in one area. Each paragraph gives the size of the effect beside ENS's own error, and says whether the live lead, which the study did not measure, would strengthen or weaken the verdict. A live service reads ENS at 09:00 UTC. The Previous Runs day-1 lead of UKV, ICON-EU, and IFS 0.25° is probably shorter than the lead a 09:00 UTC service would get from those products, so the live lead would probably make those products look worse than this study does.

For solar, keep the ECMWF ENS ensemble mean as the day-ahead weather input. UKV and ICON-EU lose to ENS at a matched lead at both settings (P1a and P2a, planned; solar results). Their gaps are +14.2% and +9.3% of ENS's own day-1 error (exploratory shares). UKV's solar radiation is also the study's own reconstruction from two snapshots. What would change the recommendation: a weather product that beats ENS's day-0 error, which no Previous Runs product did (the closest Previous Runs product, IFS 0.25°, is +0.666 points [+0.462, +0.852] behind, exploratory).

For solar, adding ICON-EU and IFS 0.25° to ENS shows no detectable gain at the conservative lead, so the study gives no reason to ingest a second weather model. The contrast that decides the blend verdict, P4b (planned), includes zero at both settings (blend results), and is -0.4% [-1.2%, +0.4%] of ENS's own error (exploratory share). A gain as large as 0.106 points is therefore not excluded, and neither is a loss as large as 0.068 points. Scored on daily means, P4b is -0.097 points [-0.190, -0.016] (exploratory), so a small gain in daily solar energy is possible even though no hourly gain was detected. The optimistic contrast, P4a (planned), shows a gain, but the P4a permutation guard is uninformative and P4a's IFS 0.25° value can come from a run newer than ENS's 00 UTC run. The study did not test how the live lead would move P4b, so the effect of the live lead on this verdict is unknown. What would change the recommendation: a test that separates a second weather model from a newer ECMWF run, such as a solar blend given ICON-EU alone. The blends page fits that blend: at the conservative lead it shows no detectable solar gain at day 1 or day 2.

For solar, the free GEFS ensemble is not a substitute for ENS. At the same lead, an XGBoost model given GEFS's mean has a higher error than an XGBoost model given ENS's mean at both settings (P3, planned; solar results), by +14.5% of ENS's own error (exploratory share). GEFS's own error, 10.039% of capacity, is still well below climatology's 14.458%, so GEFS carries real information. GEFS and ENS have the same lead, so the live lead does not change this verdict.

IFS 0.25° is the closest to ENS of the individual products tested, but the study does not show that IFS 0.25° would match ENS in a live service. IFS 0.25° day 1 cannot be told apart from ENS day 1 for solar or wind (exploratory). IFS 0.25°'s Previous Runs lead is shorter than ENS's on most hours, and its day-1 value can come from a 12 or 18 UTC run published after the 09:00 UTC issue time, so both comparisons favour IFS 0.25°.

For wind, keep ENS and do not use UKV. UKV loses to ENS at a matched lead at both settings (P1a, planned; wind results). On an ENS day-1 error of 8.427% of capacity, the gap is +9.1% of ENS's own error (exploratory share). The study did not test the Met Office's ensemble, the Met Office Global and Regional Ensemble Prediction System for the UK (MOGREPS-UK), so this finding is about UKV as one deterministic run and not about the Met Office's forecasts as a whole. The loss is the same before and after UKV's 2026-01-21 upgrade (exploratory). The gap also shrinks when the forecasts and measurements are averaged over whole days, to +0.303 points [-0.119, +0.666], which is no longer statistically significant at the 5% level (exploratory). What would change the recommendation: a comparison that reads UKV at ENS's exact lead, which the Previous Runs archive cannot supply and Open-Meteo's Single Runs archive might.

For wind, ICON-EU is unresolved against ENS, so the study gives no reason to swap ENS for ICON-EU. The upper side of the bracket (P2a, planned) includes zero and the lower side (P2b) is well above zero (wind results), so ICON-EU sits between ENS's day-0 and day-1 errors. The upper end of the P2a interval means that ICON-EU could be up to 0.384 points worse than ENS, which is 4.6% of ENS's own error of 8.427% (exploratory share). On the night hours where the two leads are exactly equal, 00 to 05 UTC, ENS wins (exploratory). Against a single ENS control run, which has no ensemble averaging, ICON-EU cannot be separated from ENS (exploratory). ICON-EU's Previous Runs day-1 lead is shorter than the control run's lead on most hours of the day, so the control-run comparison favours ICON-EU. ICON-EU's Previous Runs day-1 lead is also probably shorter than the lead a 09:00 UTC service would get. The unmeasured live lead would therefore probably move ICON-EU towards a "loses" verdict, and would strengthen the case for keeping ENS.

For wind, adding ICON-EU and IFS 0.25° to ENS is the one planned contrast against ENS alone that shows a gain at the conservative lead, and the gain is about 0.2 points of capacity. The contrast that decides the blend verdict, P4b (planned), is -0.184 points [-0.282, -0.087] at the primary setting, on an ENS day-1 error of 8.427% of capacity, which is -2.2% [-3.3%, -1.0%] of ENS's own error (exploratory share). The guard is negative and the controls are not significantly worse than ENS alone at both settings (blend results), so the gain comes from the weather of ICON-EU and IFS 0.25° rather than from extra columns. The gain is not the same at every generator: at W1 the P4b interval reaches zero, and each per-generator interval covers month-to-month weather and the fitting seed, not differences between generators (exploratory). The study did not test how the live lead would move P4b, so the effect of the live lead on this verdict is unknown.

A service that ingests one added product would probably get most of the wind gain from ICON-EU (exploratory and post hoc). ICON-EU at day 2 alone, added to ENS, gives -0.169 points [-0.250, -0.090], which is not statistically distinguishable from P4b. Against P4b, ENS plus ICON-EU alone is +0.015 points [-0.033, +0.065], so it could be up to 0.065 points worse than P4b. What would change the recommendation: a different result at more wind generators than the three tested here.

ICON-D2 read at its freshest run has the lowest error of any forecast fitted, but that skill does not carry to day-ahead use (exploratory). A value from a run that started 0 to 3 hours before the hour is not available to a service issuing at 09:00 UTC for the rest of the day. At day 1 ICON-D2 is mid-ranking (Figures 3 and 4), and ICON-D2's domain does not cover all of Great Britain.

Beyond day 3, keep the ENS mean, and do not treat a day-10 or day-14 forecast as skilled beyond climatology at these farms. At days 5 to 10, every product fitted has a higher error than the ENS mean in the point estimates. At day 14, GEFS, native GFS, and the ENS control member have point estimates within 0.2 points of the ENS mean's for solar, and none of them can be told apart from the ENS mean. The ENS mean's error is lower than climatology's at day 7 and cannot be told apart from climatology's at day 10 or day 14 (Error and lead). What would change the recommendation: a test at more generators, or over more months, than these nine farms and 21 months provide. Every lead-day result is exploratory and fitted at the primary setting only.

For day-ahead use, IFS HRES 9 km and native GFS give no reason to replace the ENS mean. Native GFS has a higher error than the ENS mean at equal lead from day 1 to day 10, and IFS HRES 9 km has a higher error at every lead day fitted (native GFS and IFS HRES 9 km). The study did not check Open-Meteo's processing of IFS HRES against a native archive, so the IFS HRES 9 km result is about the archive as served.

On this evidence a service that reads the ENS mean has no reason to switch to AIFS Single, and no AIFS result shows AIFS Single forecasting worse than the ENS mean. AIFS Single has a lower wind error than ENS's control member at day 1 on 6-hourly steps, and no solar difference is claimable. Against the ENS mean on the same steps AIFS Single is not better. The literature we surveyed gave no like-for-like evidence that AIFS improves faster than the physics-based IFS, and each AIFS version is scored separately. Assigned by run date from ECMWF's release pages, this study's rows span AIFS Single v1.0, v1.1, and v2 and AIFS ENS v1 and v2, one version at a time, and the study did not check whether Dynamical.org's archive holds any period backfilled with a later version, so its data cannot measure a rate of improvement. The study did not measure when AIFS ENS is published, so a live service's lead from AIFS ENS is unknown.

A distribution-network planner acting on these recommendations needs answers to two questions the study does not cover. The study is a comparison of archived forecasts scored against past output, and not a test of a live service. Scope lists what else the study does not cover.

  • Fetch latency and outage behaviour. Previous Runs values come from an archive, so the study says nothing about how late a live feed arrives or what happens when a second feed is down.
  • Licence and cost. The study did not check the licence terms or the cost of any second weather source.

docs.title: What Figures 1 to 4 do not show
docs.text:
The zero line in Figures 1 and 2 is an ENS mean fitted on the same rows, which is a weaker zero line for three products. AIFS Single, AIFS ENS mean, and WeatherNext 3 cover 16, 11, and 7 months, so each is compared with an ENS mean refitted on those months (the filled dot) and with the 21-month ENS mean on the same hours (the hollow diamond). The refitted ENS mean scores a higher error than the 21-month ENS mean. Key findings gives the marks that differ between the two zero lines. WeatherNext 3's intervals cover 7 months, are dashed, and sit in the WeatherNext 3 results, which list the July to September rows separately.

Most products in Figures 1 and 2 read a fresher run than ENS does, which favours those products. At days 0 to 7, the Previous Runs products (read from Open-Meteo's archive of past forecasts) read the freshest run at least a day old, which is a shorter lead than ENS's on most hours (How the leads are matched). The products are UKV, ICON-D2, ICON-EU, ICON global, GFS through Open-Meteo, IFS 0.25°, Météo-France's ARPEGE and AROME, and the HARMONIE-AROME runs of the Danish and Dutch weather services; native GFS does so at day 0. A lower error than ENS's is therefore not evidence of skill at equal lead, and a higher error is conservative for those products. Day 0 is a hindcast, because each product reads a run that started before the hour it describes, and a live service cannot use day 0. IFS 0.25°'s lower wind error at day 2 is the one dot of 114 on the 21-month rows at days 1 to 14 with a lower error and an interval clear of zero, and its shorter lead favours it.

The intervals in Figures 1 and 2 are not tests of independent rows. An interval from fewer than 12 months is dashed and too narrow, because resampling whole months draws few distinct months, and a row with fewer than 6 months has no interval. Every comparison uses the same farms and weather, every product is compared against the same ENS mean, and the figures make no adjustment for the number of comparisons. About 1 in 20 comparisons with no true difference is statistically significant at the 5% level by chance. Every row in the two figures is exploratory.

Figures 3 and 4 give no test of a gap, and they rank only rows that share a window. WeatherNext 3, AIFS Single, and AIFS ENS mean are scored on their own, smaller row sets, and IFS HRES 9 km is scored without the target days its archive lacks. The ENS mean errors in Figures 3 and 4 (8.771% and 8.350% at day 1) are GPU fits. Climatology (14.458% and 18.460%) and smart persistence (15.274% and 17.799% at day 1) come from the CPU fits of the published run, and a GPU fit is not bit-identical to a CPU fit.

docs.title: What this study cannot separate
docs.text:
A blend's gain cannot be split between a second weather model and a newer run. P4a reads ICON-EU and IFS 0.25° at day 1 and P4b at day 2, so the two contrasts differ in lead and in the age of the run behind each value at once. IFS 0.25°'s day-1 value can come from a run newer than ENS's 00 UTC run, and the 12 and 18 UTC runs are published after the 09:00 UTC issue time. P4a's gain (-0.347 points for solar, -0.656 for wind) may therefore reflect newer ECMWF information. Only P4b (-0.033 and -0.184) is a conservative bound.

At the wind farms, a Previous Runs product's gap to ENS may include timing noise and ENS's spatial averaging, and the study cannot say how much (exploratory). The study cannot say whether timing noise or grid-point sampling accounts for more of the wind gaps, which shrink relative to ENS's own error as the averaging block lengthens (the block-average contrasts). For solar the gaps do not shrink, so the block averages give no support for a timing-noise reading of the solar gaps.

ENS's standing cannot be separated from ensemble averaging. The error given the mean of ENS's members is lower than the error given its single control run, for solar and for wind (the control-run contrast, exploratory). Mean absolute error rewards a smoother forecast, so part of ENS's advantage over each single-run product is averaging rather than weather-model quality. The comparisons against the control run favour the Previous Runs products, whose leads are shorter than the control run's on most hours, so ICON-EU's deficit is probably larger at equal lead and IFS 0.25°'s advantage probably smaller. UKV, a single deterministic run, is behind the control run too, so UKV's loss to ENS is not only ensemble averaging. The study cannot say how much of UKV's loss is ensemble averaging.

ICON's "100 m" wind is not an independent 100 m level. ICON-D2, ICON-EU, and ICON global serve a native 120 m wind rescaled by about 0.98. An XGBoost model treats the rescaled speed exactly as the 120 m speed, so the ICON arms read a wind from a different height than the other products' native 100 m wind. The study cannot say how much of any ICON gap comes from the height.

GEFS against ENS cannot be separated from the two ensembles' spatial sampling. P3 is exact in lead, because both ensembles' 00 UTC runs are read at 09:00 UTC. The two ensembles are not sampled alike, though. ENS is averaged over each generator's H3 cell, GEFS is read at the nearest cell of its own grid, and the two ensembles have different numbers of members. Relative to ENS's own error, the GEFS gap does not shrink as the averaging block lengthens, whereas the wind gaps of the Previous Runs products do (see the block-average tables). A gap that keeps its share of ENS's error as the block lengthens points away from timing noise (exploratory). The study cannot separate weather-model quality from the sampling differences.

This study fits no XGBoost model given ECMWF's ERA5 reanalysis or Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) data, so the study has no past-weather ceiling. The earlier past-weather studies score ERA5 and CAMS as descriptions of hours that have already happened, and no forecast could have had that information. Without an XGBoost model given either product, the study cannot say how far the best day-ahead forecast lies from perfect weather. The study does report a reference given no weather at all: climatology, whose error is 14.458% of capacity for solar and 18.460% for wind.

docs.title: What the numbers depend on
docs.text:
The WeatherNext 3 rows span about 7 months of 2026, each calendar month in one year only, so every WN3 result is descriptive: no scored month has a training row of its own calendar month. September 2026 holds 10 days of rows and counts as a whole month in the month resampling. February to June may overlap WeatherNext 3's training data, because Google has not documented which weather-model version made the archive. A wind difference against ENS's mean speed partly reflects how WN3's speed is built, and the matched mean-vector reference removes that part. The WN3 rows take their capacities from the same effective_capacity table as every other row on this page (version 1, committed on 2026-09-22), which was committed after the last WN3 row of 10 September 2026.

The UKV day-1 requirement removes 47.8% and 50.5% of the solar rows of April and May 2026, and 86.8% and 89.4% of the wind rows. The shared rows require UKV's day-1 value, because UKV is a planned product. The study did not investigate why the value is missing. The values are missing from the Open-Meteo Previous Runs feed that the study reads. Unless shown otherwise, the study presumes that the gap lies in that feed and not in the Met Office's forecasts. UKV's day-1 value is missing on 6.8% of the solar candidate rows (2,659 of 39,030) and 11.1% of the wind candidate rows (4,678 of 42,144). The gaps fall on 38 calendar dates between April and June 2026 for solar (16 in April, 18 in May, and 4 in June) and 70 for wind (27, 29, and 14), plus 1 date in 2025 for solar and 2 for wind. For solar, the requirement removes 47.8% of the rows of 2026-04, 50.5% of 2026-05, and 11.1% of 2026-06; for wind, 86.8%, 89.4%, and 47.0%. The removal is nearly uniform across the hours of the day for wind (about 11% each hour) and heaviest at 05 and 06 UTC for solar (12.4% and 12.6%). Every arm is scored on the rows that remain, so spring 2026 is under-represented in every figure on this page. The 8 months after UKV's 2026-01-21 upgrade hold 12,642 solar rows and 10,484 wind rows.

An XGBoost model that never trained on the calendar month scores 20 solar cells and 9 wind cells. The coverage table has 124 (generator, fold, calendar month) cells for solar, of which 20 are not covered by training data, and 63 for wind, of which 9 are. Every uncovered cell holds a calendar month that occurs in one year only at that generator, so no other fold can hold the month. January is a single-year month, because the part-month that straddles UKV's upgrade on 2026-01-21 is dropped. October and November are single-year months too, because the rows run from December 2024 to September 2026 and hold each of October and November once. Two of the 20 uncovered solar cells, at generator E (August in fold 1, September in fold 2), arise because E's rows cover 19 months, not 21. The uncovered cells hold from 69 to 356 scored rows for solar and from 539 to 729 for wind. raise_on_uncovered_months allows only single-year cells and raises on any other uncovered cell, so the study scores the single-year cells rather than dropping them. The errors in those seasons come from an XGBoost model that has not seen the season.

Four facts about the study's inputs limit what the numbers mean.

  • The capacity table is the effective_capacity table at version 1, committed on 2026-09-22. The report records the table's version and commit time, and that the study's inputs were built on 2026-09-24, after the commit. A rebuilt table would move every number.

  • The GEFS build stops if a run the rows need is missing or incomplete. The build script raises unless every 00 UTC run the rows need holds all 31 members, so a gap in the GEFS download cannot become empty GEFS columns. The September 2026 GEFS month is a partial month, and the build accepts the partial file for that last month only, after the same check that every run the rows need is complete. The report does not print this check.

  • The downloaded GEFS store holds missing 100 m wind values at long leads, which the study does not read. In the store, wind_u_100m and wind_v_100m are missing (NaN) for some runs from 2026-01-15 onwards, at leads of 16 d 6 h and beyond. The planned arms read leads to 95 h and the extra arms read leads to 366 h, so none of the rows the study reads holds a missing value. The download's README does not list this gap; it was found by reading the store.

  • The exploratory arms carry a small share of missing weather values, and the planned arms carry none. The planned arms define the shared rows, so they hold every value. The published exploratory arms are fitted on the same rows with their gaps left as missing values, which XGBoost routes natively. IFS HRES 9 km drops its gap days from the rows instead, and the AIFS arms have rows of their own. For solar the largest shares are 0.83% (KNMI HARMONIE-AROME), 0.35% (ICON-D2), and 0.27% (ICON global); for wind, 1.48% (DMI HARMONIE-AROME) and 0.25% (KNMI HARMONIE-AROME). The extra arms add ICON global at day 5 for solar (0.27%) and DMI HARMONIE-AROME at day 0 for wind (1.24%). IFS HRES 9 km lacks 1.35% to 1.45% of the shared solar rows and 1.07% to 1.20% of the shared wind rows. Every other exploratory arm is at 0.05% or lower. An exploratory contrast involving those arms therefore rests on a slightly different information set from a planned one.

The extra arms rest on inputs the study could not check natively, and the AIFS rows are short.

  • Open-Meteo's processing of IFS HRES was not checked against a native archive. The archive holds 919 of 926 run days, so seven run days are gaps, and the arms score the shared hours minus those days. The hourly values at days 5 and 7 are interpolated from 3-hourly and 6-hourly steps, and sites B and D share a source cell, so the two generators' series are identical (how IFS HRES 9 km is read).
  • The day-0 leads of most products are estimated, and native GFS's day 0 ignores publication time. Only ICON-EU's and ICON-D2's day-0 radiation leads were checked against source files, ICON-D2's less cleanly. Every day-0 mark is a nowcast that a live service could not read in advance.
  • The AIFS rows span several AIFS versions, and the version dates come from ECMWF's release pages, not from the data or a check for backfilled periods. The 2026-05-12 change to AIFS Single v2 coincides with IFS Cycle 50r1, so an AIFS change cannot be separated from an IFS change. The v2 era holds 4 months.
  • Most calendar months have no training row of their own in the AIFS row sets. Of the (generator, fold, calendar month) cells, 37 of 95 solar cells and 18 of 48 wind cells of the single row set have no training row of their calendar month, and 55 of 65 and 27 of 33 of the ens row set.
  • AIFS Single's radiation window and wind reading were not checked at days 7 and 14, because the offset check cannot discriminate there.

The rows cover 21 months at 6 solar and 3 wind generators in one trial area, so the sample is small. Neighbouring generators share their weather, so the sample is 21 months of weather rather than 21 months of independent generators. An interval covers month-to-month weather and the fitting seed, and not differences between generators. Each interval resamples the 21 year-months as whole blocks, and all nine generators lie in one small area, so the intervals are probably too narrow. An exploratory interval with no real effect behind it has a nominal 5% chance of being statistically significant at the 5% level, and a higher chance if the intervals are too narrow. How many significant exploratory intervals are spurious is unknown, because how many have no real effect behind them is unknown. The intervals rest on overlapping months of weather and often share an arm, so spurious results tend to arrive together. An isolated exploratory result therefore deserves less weight than a planned one.

Four statistical caveats limit how far the intervals can be trusted.

  • No multiplicity correction. The study has 18 planned contrasts (9 for solar and 9 for wind, including the 4 blend guards), the two planned AIFS day-1 contrasts, which carry their own Bonferroni interval, the eight deciding contrasts of the AIFS blends and days 7 and 14 (four per technology, printed at a 99.375% Bonferroni interval beside the 95% one), and many exploratory contrasts, among them which product carries the wind blend gain, the 00-05 UTC subset, and the result at wind generator W3. Apart from the Bonferroni intervals named above, no interval is adjusted for the number of comparisons.
  • The sensitivity setting is not independent confirmation. It changes the XGBoost hyperparameters and keeps the same rows, folds, and weather. Agreement between the two settings shows only that a verdict does not depend on the hyperparameters.
  • The voiding rule reacts to noise. A band is voided when its point estimate is zero or below, which a noisy estimate can reach by chance.
  • A shuffled control can carry shuffle noise that its interval does not show, and the P4 blends' second-seed refit found none. Two shuffles of the same AIFS Single weather differ by +0.453 [+0.223, +0.696] points for solar. Two shuffles of the P4 blends' added weather differ by +0.059 [-0.008, +0.125] and +0.039 [-0.021, +0.096] points for solar and by -0.031 [-0.099, +0.031] and -0.013 [-0.087, +0.055] points for wind, at the primary setting, so the P4 guards' verdicts agree across two seeds. The AIFS-blend guards each subtract one shuffled control, and their seed noise was not measured.

One month can move a point estimate a little, and no month reverses one. With each year-month dropped in turn, and no refit, P1a runs from +1.127 to +1.343 points for solar and from +0.713 to +0.871 for wind. P2a runs from +0.769 to +0.870 and from +0.128 to +0.226, P3 from +1.183 to +1.361 and from +0.784 to +0.941, and P4b from -0.042 to -0.009 and from -0.205 to -0.162 (exploratory, primary setting). Every dropped-month estimate keeps the sign of the full-sample estimate. The dropped month still trained the XGBoost models that scored the other months.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: This study says nothing about the skill of any ensemble's spread, about the Met Office's ensemble MOGREPS-UK, about leads beyond day 14, or about generators outside the trial area. The study scores point forecasts, made by an XGBoost model fitted separately for each generator, of hourly solar and wind output at 6 solar and 3 wind generators, at day-ahead leads that depend on each Previous Runs product's run cycle, at exact leads for ENS and GEFS, and, in exploratory arms, at days 0, 5, 7, 10, and 14 for the products listed in the extra arms, and at days 1, 2, 7, and 14 for AIFS. The study says nothing about substation demand, and because it scores generators and not substations, it does not show how the gaps carry into a forecast summed over a substation's generators. The study gives the XGBoost model ENS's mean and none of ENS's spread, so the uncertainty information in ENS is unused. The study says nothing about a forecast issued at any time other than 09:00 UTC, apart from the exploratory day-0 arms, which read the freshest run (ICON, UKV, native GFS, and the other Previous Runs products) or the 00 UTC run of the hour's own day (ENS, GEFS, and IFS HRES 9 km). The study also says nothing about the values an Open-Meteo archive would have served live rather than as a Previous Runs value. The study does not test any product's grid, physics, or resolution as a cause of a gap, and it does not test the live service.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text:
Most inputs are public, but the generator telemetry and the capacity table are private. The public inputs are ECMWF ENS (from 2024-04-01), NOAA GEFS (from 2020-10-01), NOAA's native GFS store, and ECMWF's AIFS Single and AIFS ENS from Dynamical.org, and the Previous Runs values and the IFS HRES Single Runs archive of Open-Meteo. Open-Meteo's day-offset archive starts on 2024-01-19 for ICON-EU and ICON-D2, on 2024-03-06 for IFS 0.25°, and on 2024-08-06 for UKV (start dates from the weather-products survey). Dynamical.org's access ends on 2026-09-30. The generator telemetry and the effective_capacity table are private, because a single generator's output can be commercially sensitive.

The code is in the repository, at a fixed commit and with fixed XGBoost settings. The scripts under studies/nwp_forecast_comparison/ and the shared code under packages/studies/ last changed at commit 1e5ec75acbba956c4c6bd2d7efd3102c9417c3b4. The XGBoost version is 3.4.1. The primary setting has a maximum depth of 6, a learning rate of 0.05, 500 boosting rounds, a row subsample of 0.8, a minimum child weight of 20, and an L2 penalty of 1. The sensitivity setting has a maximum depth of 4, a learning rate of 0.03, 1,200 rounds, a row subsample of 0.8, a minimum child weight of 50, and an L2 penalty of 5. Both settings use the absolute-error objective, no column subsampling, and the seeds 0, 1, and 2. Every extra and AIFS fit uses the primary setting on a GPU, and the AIFS deciding pair, every deciding contrast of the blends fit, and every AIFS pair near the 5% line are also fitted at the sensitivity setting, and the P4 refit is fitted at both settings.

The outputs of the extra arms are in seven write-once folders. Each folder is under data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/. Batches 1 to 4 write to leads_day10, leads_day10b, leads_day10c, and leads_day10d, the day-1 and day-2 AIFS arms write to aifs, the AIFS blends and the day-7 and day-14 AIFS arms write to aifs_blends, and the GPU refit of the P4 blends with two shuffle seeds writes to p4_seeds. Each folder holds the extra inputs, the losses and predictions, report.md, and a verification/ directory. The folder leads holds an earlier run of batch 1's arms, and the charts and tables do not read it.

docs.title: Reproducing this page
docs.text:
Every number on this page comes from one of nine report.md files, the verification/ files beside them, the report.md of the leaderboard script or of the dot script, or is derived from them, except the three the page marks in place (the GEFS store's missing long-lead wind, the day-by-day coverage shares in the lead-day table, and the repeat of the 23 GPU arms), and the commands below rebuild the reports and the figures. The nine files are the published run's, one for each of the four extra-lead batches, the day-1 and day-2 AIFS arms', the AIFS blends and long leads', the P4 refit's, and the WN3 fit's. Run the commands from the repository root, in this order. The verification scripts write the verification/ directories that the reports quote.

P=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/original
D1=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/leads_day10
D2=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/leads_day10b
D3=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/leads_day10c
D4=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/leads_day10d
A=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/aifs
AB=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/aifs_blends
PS=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/p4_seeds
W=data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/wn3
R=studies/nwp_forecast_comparison

# The published run
uv run python $R/verify_previous_runs_leads.py --output-dir $P/verification
uv run python $R/check_input_steps.py --output-dir $P/verification
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py
uv run python $R/nwp_forecast_comparison.py
uv run python $R/nwp_forecast_comparison.py --report-only

# Batch 1: extra lead days and day 0
uv run python $R/verify_extra_leads.py --output-dir $D1
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --extra-leads --published-dir $P --output-dir $D1
uv run python $R/fit_extra_leads.py --check --published-dir $P --output-dir $D1
uv run python $R/fit_extra_leads.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $D1 --workers 2

# Batch 2: more ENS and GEFS days, and GPU refits of the published arms
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --extra-leads --batch second --published-dir $P --output-dir $D2
uv run python $R/fit_extra_leads.py --batch second --published-dir $P --output-dir $D2 \
    --context-dir $D1

# Batch 3: native GFS
uv run python $R/verify_gfs_native.py --output-dir $D3
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --extra-leads --batch third --published-dir $P --output-dir $D3
uv run python $R/verify_gfs_native.py --output-dir $D3 --built-dir $D3
uv run python $R/fit_extra_leads.py --batch third --published-dir $P --output-dir $D3 \
    --context-dir $D1 --context-dir $D2

# Batch 4: IFS HRES 9 km
uv run python $R/verify_ifs_single.py --output-dir $D4
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --extra-leads --batch fourth --published-dir $P --output-dir $D4
uv run python $R/verify_ifs_single.py --output-dir $D4 --built-dir $D4
uv run python $R/fit_extra_leads.py --batch fourth --published-dir $P --output-dir $D4 \
    --context-dir $D1 --context-dir $D2

# AIFS Single and AIFS ENS
uv run python $R/verify_aifs_steps.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $A
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --aifs --published-dir $P --output-dir $A
uv run python $R/verify_aifs_steps.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $A --wiring
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --check --published-dir $P --output-dir $A
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $A

# AIFS blends, days 7 and 14, and the P4 second-seed refit
uv run python $R/build_forecast_inputs.py --aifs --aifs-days 1 2 7 14 --published-dir $P \
    --output-dir $AB
uv run python $R/verify_aifs_steps.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $AB
uv run python $R/verify_aifs_steps.py --wiring --published-dir $P --output-dir $AB
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --blends --check --published-dir $P --output-dir $AB
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --blends --workers 1 --published-dir $P --output-dir $AB
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --p4-controls --check --published-dir $P --output-dir $PS
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --p4-controls --workers 1 --published-dir $P --output-dir $PS

# WeatherNext 3: read the trial area from the store (needs Google Cloud credentials), build, verify, fit
uv run python $R/build_wn3_inputs.py --read-store --bucket BUCKET
uv run python $R/build_wn3_inputs.py --build --published-dir $P --output-dir $W
uv run python $R/verify_wn3_steps.py --published-dir $P --output-dir $W
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --wn3 --check --lookahead-cleared --published-dir $P --output-dir $W
uv run python $R/fit_aifs.py --wn3 --lookahead-cleared --workers 1 --published-dir $P --output-dir $W

# Figures
uv run python $R/nwp_forecast_charts.py --input-dir $P --extra-dir $D1 --extra-dir $D2 \
    --extra-dir $D3 --extra-dir $D4 --aifs-dir $A --wn3-dir $W --output-dir docs/studies/assets
uv run python $R/leaderboard_by_day.py --replace-svgs --first-figure-number 3 \
    --wn3-groups-figure-number 19 --headline-figure-number 5
uv run python $R/nwp_forecast_charts.py --aifs-blends-dir $AB --output-dir docs/studies/assets
uv run python $R/dot_interval_vs_ens.py --first-figure-number 1

The third command writes solar_forecast_inputs.parquet and wind_forecast_inputs.parquet under data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/original/. The fourth command fits every arm and saves <domain>_losses.parquet and <domain>_predictions.parquet there. The fifth command rewrites report.md from the saved losses without fitting again. In each batch, the build writes the extra inputs on the published inputs' own (site, time) keys, and --check fits one arm at one generator twice on a GPU and stops unless the two runs agree. Each later batch takes one --context-dir for each earlier batch whose arms its contrasts name. Batches 3 and 4 run their verification script before the build and again, with --built-dir, after it. The AIFS commands check AIFS Single's radiation window, wind reading, units, and grid orientation, build the AIFS columns, check the wiring, and fit. The blends commands do the same at days 1, 2, 7, and 14, and the P4 commands refit the published blends on the GPU with two shuffle seeds. The third chart command draws only the two AIFS lead charts (Figures 17 and 18). The dot command draws the two dot-and-interval figures (Figures 1 and 2) and writes its own report.md and intervals.parquet to data/studies/per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/vs_ens_dots_final. Every extra folder is write-once: the scripts refuse to overwrite it, and never write to the published folder. The chart script runs npx svgo@4 --multipass --precision=1 --final-newline on every SVG it writes and reads every folder. The dot command runs last, and its script runs the same svgo command.

The inputs are on disk and cannot all be downloaded again. The build reads the finished GEFS download in data/studies/downloads/NWP/windows/GEFS_window_2024-11-01_None/, each Previous Runs product's combined.parquet, and the native GFS, IFS HRES 9 km, and AIFS downloads under data/studies/downloads/NWP/. Dynamical.org's access ends on 2026-09-30. Every worktree writes to the main checkout's data/studies/, so move the saved outputs to superseded/ before re-running the fourth command.

docs.title: Production feature faults: diagnosis and forecast effects
docs.text:
Draft study. The diagnostic audit is complete. Forecast experiments and the final scientific and prose reviews are still in progress. Forecast-effect conclusions will follow.

This audit describes the polar pipeline at commit 5ac2e16a7088d13f2f7103f0385a58f54388bfba. Reproduction uses the matching polar archive and engineered caches. References to the current calculations below mean that audited implementation. The component pipeline interpolates u/v before deriving speed and bearing; the historical wrap results below do not describe its behaviour.

Two reproducible calculation problems affected conversion to the half-hourly timestamps used by that power forecast. Radiation values are averages over the interval ending at their timestamp, but the audited conversion treats them as measurements at that instant. Wind directions near north can be interpolated through south. Windchill is also evaluated outside the formula’s stated domain. Temperature loses some extrema on the coarser weather grid; precipitation has a historical availability boundary; and the checked two-week lag gaps correspond to absent observations.

This study investigates Part 1 of issue 1156, following the suspicious input plots in quick wins. It includes a diagnostic audit and study-only corrected-feature experiments. No production code was changed.

The diagnostic audit covers 9,762,768 training control-member rows from April 2024 through June 2025 and weekly validation weather runs from July 2025 through June 2026, across 31 series. Its prevalence statements apply to the unperturbed ensemble member 0. Forecast experiments train on that member and predict all 51 members of the same weekly runs. They use observed power.

A series is one power time series being forecast. Forecast lead is the time from issuance to the forecasted time. The control member is the unperturbed member of the weather ensemble. Training and validation refer to the two periods above.

docs.title: Forecast baseline and comparisons
docs.text:
The baseline is a newly trained XGBoost forecast for each power time series, using production’s input features and training settings. XGBoost fits an ensemble of decision trees. Every corrected comparison uses the same saved training examples. This baseline is distinct from the stored quick-wins forecasts and from a production deployment. Every fit uses the graphics processor (GPU).

The primary comparison retains all 24 input columns and makes every column available when each decision tree is fitted. This setting, called column subsampling of 1, follows the study protocol. Otherwise it uses production’s 500 trees, depth 6, learning rate 0.05, minimum child weight 1, and row subsampling 0.8. The separate production-hyperparameter comparison uses production’s column subsampling of 0.8. A second, more regularised setting checks the planned contrasts. Each setting uses fitting seeds 0, 1, and 2.

The five forecast contrasts were planned before fitting:

Contrast What it measures All corrections versus baseline (planned) Combined candidate effect All corrections versus all except radiation (planned) Radiation’s contribution with the other corrections enabled All corrections versus all except wind direction (planned) Wind’s contribution with the other corrections enabled All corrections versus all except guarded windchill (planned) Windchill’s contribution with the other corrections enabled Precipitation masked versus all corrections (planned) Sensitivity to the availability mismatch

The effects of removing individual corrections need not add to the effect of applying them all. Ordinal-weekday masking, with weekday sine and cosine retained, is exploratory. Missing history and the true extrema between native weather samples cannot be reconstructed from these inputs, so neither receives an invented “corrected” score.

docs.title: Radiation: interval means are displaced and flattened
docs.text:
The radiation probe below records production behaviour before interval-aware resampling. The saved figure and numbers remain a historical snapshot, reproduced from the pinned checkout above. See radiation resampling for the current policy and before/after comparison.

Each native radiation value is a mean over the interval before its timestamp. Here, “native” means the weather forecast’s original sampling grid. The upsampler at the time of this study filled the half-hourly grid by drawing straight lines between the timestamped means. The interpolation spread daylight energy later and flattened the daily peak. The independent synthetic probe aggregated half-hour backward means into three- or six-hour means before calling that production upsampler. The probe has a known answer, rather than treating a different interpolant as observed truth.

On the complete interior day, the radiation-weighted mean time is late by 1.25 hours for three-hour inputs and 2.75 hours for six-hour inputs. Both reconstructions preserve this probe’s daily energy of 6.115915 kWh/m². Energy conservation therefore does not establish correct timing. The synthetic reference labels each half-hour by its ending timestamp.

The cached engineered profiles show the same broad flattening at longer leads. This comparison is descriptive: the lead groups differ in weather and forecast error, so it cannot by itself measure the resampler’s causal effect.

A positive native mean at a dark endpoint can be legitimate: the preceding interval may contain daylight. The audit separately checks fully dark native intervals, and finds no native radiation above 1 W/m² in those checked intervals. Do not repair native means by setting every dark endpoint to zero.

Recommended production change: give interval-mean fields a dedicated resampling path in ml_core/features/_nwp.py. For short-wave, divide each native mean by the clear-sky mean over the same native window, anchor that ratio at the window midpoint, interpolate daylight ratios, hold the nearest daylight ratio outside daylight, and multiply by the backward half-hour clear-sky mean. Validate timing, nighttime output, and interval energy independently. The experiment uses the existing reviewed study helper with Haurwitz clear sky and 15-minute midpoint quadrature. It is a candidate shape reconstruction, not recovery of the unknown sub-grid truth.

Long-wave and precipitation rates also need their interval convention respected, using a suitable conservative policy. Long-wave is absent from the current 24-feature forecast recipe, so correcting it alone cannot change the XGBoost forecast’s predictions. Review the generic continuous-field set’s storage, rounding, and dashboard callers when implementing the resampling change.

See variable conventions and the resampling roadmap.

docs.title: Wind: interpolation crosses the wrong side of the circle
docs.text:
Between 350° and 10°, a linear numeric interpolant passes through 180°, although both endpoints are near north. A shortest-arc reference passes through 0°. This is an interpolation problem; the additional choice of how to represent direction to a tree model is a separate question.

In the audited control member, roughly 3–7% of interpolated wind directions differ from the shortest-arc reference by more than 1°, depending on height, training or validation period, and forecast lead. The percentage counts inserted half-hours with supported native samples on both sides. Original sample times and ambiguous pairs separated by 180° are excluded. These discrepancies are measured against shortest-arc reconstruction, not observed wind. Every lead band has affected series.

Current implementation: the component pipeline retains and interpolates u/v, then derives speed and bearing. The score experiment isolates the wrap problem by changing direction through shortest-arc interpolation at both heights while leaving speeds unchanged. Its result therefore does not measure every effect of the component interpolation pipeline.

See the documented wind convention.

docs.title: Windchill: the formula runs beyond its intended conditions
docs.text:
The cached values exactly match the current windchill expression. The problem is its unrestricted use, rather than a discrepancy between the cache and that expression. Its stated domain is air temperature at most 10°C and wind at least 4.8 km/h. Outside those conditions, the expression can produce a value warmer than air temperature.

Across lead bands, about 53–59% of finite validation inputs lie outside that domain; training shares are about 58–61%. This is not an estimate of forecast damage: temperature and wind are already features, and the XGBoost forecast may use the unrestricted expression as a nonlinear transform.

Recommended production change: specify the feature’s semantics explicitly and guard the formula. The studied candidate falls back to air temperature outside the domain, preserving missing inputs. A renamed unconstrained nonlinear feature would be a different modelling choice, requiring its own evaluation.

docs.title: Temperature: the six-hour grid omits extrema
docs.text:
Retaining every second three-hour temperature sample reduces the mean daily range from 5.427829°C to 4.565359°C. The comparison covers 8,060 complete days, counted separately for each power time series and weather forecast run in the validation period. The mean loss is 0.862471°C. These days use native weather leads above zero through 144 hours and the actual six-hour grid phase. Each day has eight finite three-hour samples and four retained six-hour samples.

This emulation measures information lost by thinning short-lead weather, not the error in real long-lead temperature forecasts. It also does not establish the true atmospheric daily range. A shape-preserving cubic interpolant cannot recover an extremum absent from the retained samples.

Recommended production change: preserve higher-frequency native temperature where available. Treat any diurnal reconstruction beyond the native grid as a separately validated model. Do not claim that switching interpolants alone restores the omitted extrema.

See instantaneous-variable amplitude loss.

docs.title: Precipitation: training spans an availability boundary
docs.text:
Precipitation type is entirely missing in the early training months, partly missing in November 2024 and complete in the later training and validation months. The audit groups by weather-run start, so long forecasts crossing a calendar boundary do not move the apparent source boundary.

The XGBoost forecast trains with precipitation type missing for part of training and available throughout the forward validation year. Missing-value branches can absorb some of this difference; that does not make the availability shift disappear. The masked-feature contrast measures whether using the available history helps this recipe. It cannot estimate the benefit of obtaining the missing historical categories.

Recommended production change: record availability eras, monitor missingness by run, and backfill only from a source with verified compatible semantics. Evaluate availability explicitly in both chronological directions before relying on the feature. Do not invent categories or replace missing precipitation type with “no precipitation”.

docs.title: Two-week power lags: the checked gaps have missing source observations
docs.text:
The two-week power lag uses observed power 336 hours before the forecasted time. It is eligible only when that observation precedes forecast issuance. Among eligible control-member rows, roughly 3–6% of lag values are missing, depending on training or validation period and lead. The lookup audit compares each cached lag with the guarded current power source at valid_time − 336 hours.

Every checked eligible row is either a matching value or an absent observation key. There are no unexplained cache/source value mismatches in this audit. This comparison with the current source does not establish why a historical observation is absent, or prove every historical join was correct. Repeated training lookups are counted as rows; unique lookup counts are only unique within their reported group and must not be summed as global distinct counts.

At issuance lead 336 hours and later, the lag would use an observation at or after issuance and must be missing. The cached control-member rows respect that constraint. The current-code probe also checks the equality boundary with a nonzero nine-hour weather publication delay.

Recommended production change: retain the leakage guard, distinguish absent observations from failed joins in monitoring, and investigate upstream gaps only where the missing readings should exist. Avoid forward filling or using observations at/after issuance to hide the gaps.

docs.title: Weekday and overall completeness
docs.text:
Production already supplies weekday sine and cosine alongside the ordinal weekday. The ordinal code is an encoding choice, not evidence that the weekly cycle is absent. Its masking experiment keeps the two cyclic columns and all 24 feature positions.

The completeness plot includes all forecast leads. Consequently, short power lags have high missing shares because they are intentionally unavailable beyond their leakage horizon. Compare eligible lag rows separately before interpreting these shares as faulty data.

docs.title: Scope, reproducibility and limits
docs.text:
The radiation and direction candidates reconstruct cached native-grid values, which are not guaranteed original native observations: production interpolation can already have filled a native null. Linear reconstruction is checked against the cached production values before correction. Unsupported boundaries and originally missing inputs retain production values. The clear-sky candidate may change individual interval energy; the generated score report prints that discrepancy. A positive score result would support this candidate policy, not every possible implementation of an interval-aware resampler.

All comparisons preserve training targets, sorted training order, forecast cases, and member labels. Losses are normalised by each series’ effective capacity before averaging, with series given equal weight. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) uses the fair ensemble estimator. Mean absolute error (MAE) is calculated from the ensemble mean. Errors and changes are percentage points of effective capacity, so a 0.15-point improvement is not a 15% relative improvement.

Whole-month bootstrap intervals include sensitivity over the three fitting seeds; they are not uncertainty over all possible fits or future weather regimes. Subgroup results are descriptive and involve multiple comparisons.

The backwards fold is a stress test trained on July 2025–June 2026 and evaluated on April 2024–June 2025. Its future-trained chronology is not a prospective validation result. The production-hyperparameter cached-data refit is also not a reproduction of the entire serving pipeline. No official leaderboard score is claimed.

Full real-data bulk-versus-single-run feature equivalence and power/weather clock-offset correlations remain untested. Synthetic probes establish their stated mechanisms, not those wider properties. The study also makes no causal estimate for temperature information that was never retained, historical precipitation that is unavailable, or power readings that do not exist.

Scripts and commands are in the study README. The generated diagnostic and score reports are the numerical evidence for this page. Input, source, and configuration hashes bind the outputs to their runs. Reviews use fresh available reviewers in place of the study skill’s unavailable Claude models; the PR records the review findings and triage.

The proposed follow-up is a production PR for interval-aware radiation resampling, with feature-path equivalence and energy controls; allow roughly two to three engineering days, then repeat the same forecast contrasts on its actual engineered outputs. Component interpolation ordering is implemented; matched power-forecast evaluation remains pending.

docs.title: Production implementation handoff
docs.text: Implement the confirmed resampling faults first, then the windchill guard and availability monitoring. The order below reflects the diagnostic evidence and implementation dependencies. The forecast experiments are still running, so the order is not a final ranking of forecast-score improvements. The next session should read this section alongside the generated diagnostic report in studies/production_feature_faults/results/diagnostics.md and the completed score reports when available.

docs.title: 1. Give radiation an interval-aware resampler
docs.text:
Production implementation: the radiation resampling policy uses midpoint clear-sky indices for short-wave and piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial (PCHIP) interpolation through native-window midpoint means for long-wave. Unlike this study candidate, the production helper conserves each short-wave window's energy and preserves source-missing windows. Historical study results below remain measurements of the study's candidate, not of that production helper.

Replace point interpolation of short-wave interval means in packages/ml_core/src/ml_core/features/_nwp.py. On the synthetic probe’s complete interior day, point interpolation shifts the radiation-weighted mean time by 1.25 hours for 3-hour inputs and 2.75 hours for 6-hour inputs. Both reconstructions preserve that day’s energy. Use the study’s clear-sky-index candidate as a design reference: divide native radiation means by clear-sky means over the same intervals, interpolate the ratios at interval midpoints, and multiply by clear-sky means over the target half-hours. Define the production policy for native-interval energy explicitly. Implement the production helper in a reviewed production package; production code must not import studies. The candidate can change individual interval totals; copying the candidate does not establish energy conservation.

Respect the interval ending at each timestamp and its actual width, including the three-hour to six-hour transition. Treat short-wave separately from long-wave and precipitation rates, whose interval means need suitable conservative resampling without a solar shape. Long-wave is absent from the current forecast recipe, so its correction has no direct forecast effect here.

Gotchas: a dark endpoint can legitimately label an interval containing daylight; do not zero native values solely from the endpoint’s solar elevation. Handle low clear-sky denominators, missing native samples, the first supported interval, and trailing boundaries explicitly. Preserve source missingness separately from newly inserted grid points. Read original native inputs for implementation and regression checks: the study reconstructs native-grid values from engineered caches, where interpolation may already have filled a native null. Keep interpolation within each series, weather run, and ensemble member. Review the continuous-variable classification’s storage, rounding, and dashboard callers before changing shared behaviour.

docs.title: 2. Interpolate wind on the circle
docs.text:
Correct both 10 m and 100 m bearings in the same resampling path. Numeric interpolation between 350° and 10° passes through south; the shortest path crosses north. Around 3–7% of eligible inserted bearings differ from shortest-arc reconstruction by more than 1° in this audit.

The current converter retains signed u/v components. Feature engineering interpolates those components before deriving speed and meteorological bearing at both heights. Component interpolation resolves the historical arithmetic wrap fault; the study's shortest-arc scores do not evaluate every effect of component interpolation. The separate archive migration reconstructs historical components from archived speed and bearing.

Gotchas: vector interpolation changes speed as well as direction. The study’s shortest-arc experiment holds speed fixed, so its score difference does not estimate the complete vector change. Specify behaviour for calm wind, opposing vectors, exactly 180° separation, missing inputs, and unsupported boundaries. Changing the tree model’s direction encoding is a separate experiment; weekday sine and cosine already exist, so there is no missing cyclic-weekday feature to repair.

docs.title: 3. Guard the windchill formula
docs.text:
Apply the domain guard in packages/ml_core/src/ml_core/features/_parsed_features.py. The cached expression matches the code, but about 53–59% of finite validation inputs fall outside its stated domain. Use the studied policy: evaluate windchill at air temperature at most 10°C and wind speed at least 4.8 km/h; otherwise return air temperature when both inputs are present.

Gotchas: the stored wind speed is in metres per second; convert units before checking the threshold. Preserve missing inputs, including a missing wind speed in warm conditions. Test both threshold equalities. The unrestricted expression may be useful to XGBoost as a nonlinear transform, so improved physical semantics do not guarantee an improved forecast score.

docs.title: 4. Track precipitation availability and investigate recoverable gaps
docs.text:
Add per-run availability monitoring and document the historical precipitation-type boundary. Early training months have no precipitation type, whereas forward validation has complete coverage. Backfill only if a source with compatible categorical meanings and timestamp conventions is available. A masking experiment cannot measure the benefit of obtaining missing history.

Gotchas: missing precipitation type does not mean “no precipitation”. Do not interpolate precipitation-type category codes as numbers or fill them across weather-run boundaries. Evaluate any backfill or feature-policy change on both availability eras; the backwards study fold is a stress test, not prospective validation.

docs.title: 5. Preserve temperature information and the power-lag leakage guard
docs.text:
Continue retaining native temperature samples wherever the source provides them. The current production upsampler retains those sample times. Deliberately thinning the checked 3-hour samples to 6 hours reduces mean daily range by about 0.86°C; this emulation does not demonstrate a production thinning defect. Interpolation cannot restore unobserved extrema. Any diurnal reconstruction needs a separate evaluation.

Monitor absent power observations separately from failed lag joins. Every checked eligible two-week lag matched its source value or had no source observation. There is no demonstrated lag join defect to patch. Retain _nullify_leaky_lags in packages/ml_core/src/ml_core/features/_lags.py: an observation at or after issuance is ineligible. Do not forward fill gaps to conceal missing history. Preserve the distinction between weather-run initialisation, publication delay, forecast issuance, and target time in regression tests.

docs.title: Acceptance checks before deployment
docs.text:
Validate the actual production feature paths, regenerate affected feature caches, and retrain before assessing forecast gains. Add regression cases for radiation timing and interval energy, wind wrap and calm/opposing vectors, windchill thresholds and nulls, and the lag equality boundary. Check native and inserted timestamps, the three-hour to six-hour transition, all ensemble members, and group isolation. Compare bulk feature generation with single-run inference on real cases; this study has not yet established their equivalence.

Repeat the baseline and corrected comparisons on those actual engineered outputs with identical forecast cases, three fitting seeds, and whole-month uncertainty intervals. Keep correction effects separate where possible. Update the variable-convention documentation with the chosen boundary, missingness, and conservation policies. The rough estimate of 2 to 3 engineering days above covers the initial radiation and wind work and its checks. Broader backfilling or new diurnal reconstruction models require separate estimates.

docs.title: Quantile training and other cheap changes lowered the production XGBoost forecast's probabilistic error by about a third at 31 NGED series
docs.text:
A combination of four cheap changes to the production XGBoost forecast lowered its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) from 11.3% to 7.9% of capacity, and its mean absolute error (MAE) from 12.1% to 10.7%, over a validation year at 31 series in the trial area of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED). The four changes are quantile training, a forecast-lead-time column, leaner columns for wind farms, and one XGBoost model per series type with a site identifier. Quantile training gives each of the 51 ensemble members a spread of its own, and lowered CRPS by 2.4 points on its own. Rescaling the members' spread with factors learned from past outcomes is a separate fifth change for point forecasts, and lowered CRPS by 1.3 to 1.9 points. Two other planned changes, the absolute-error objective and early stopping, each lowered CRPS by about 0.4 points on their own. The study chose quantile training, the wind columns, and pooling after seeing the first results, so their gains are biased upward. The page labels them "post hoc".

After the changes, the point forecast beats the manual_heuristic baseline at days 0 to 2 and ties it at days 3 to 10, and the CRPS still sits above the heuristic's from day 3 on.

Removing the power lags from solar and wind farms, which the plan asked about, made both worse. For solar, the result differs from the lag-features study's day-ahead result (see Round 1).

Terms used on this page.

  • Production forecast: the point-valued XGBoost forecast in conf/model/xgboost.yaml. It fits one XGBoost model per series, trains on the control member of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' (ECMWF) 51-member ensemble (ENS), and runs the model over every member. "Production" in a table means the study's refit of it, and "production with cleaning" adds the cleaning rule chosen in round 0.
  • Arm: one copy of the production recipe with one named difference, such as a different objective. A combination arm has several differences.
  • Points: percentage points of a series' effective capacity, its 99th percentile of absolute power. A difference is an arm's error minus a reference's error, so a negative difference means a lower error.
  • CRPS: the fair continuous ranked probability score (Ferro, 2014) of all 51 ensemble members, as ml_core.metrics computes it. MAE: the absolute error of the members' mean. Both divide by the series' effective capacity before averaging. Smaller is better for both.
  • Fold A: the leaderboard fold. Training uses April 2024 to June 2025, and the 12 scored months run from July 2025 to June 2026. Fold B: the same 31 series trained on July 2025 to June 2026 and scored from April 2024 to June 2025.
  • Round, seed, control: round 0 compared cleaning rules, round 1 tried ideas one at a time, round 2 combined the winners, and round 3 repeated the key arms on more seeds and on fold B. A seed changes the random row subsampling. The control arm for later arms is production with cleaning, and the control member is the ensemble's unperturbed run.
  • Reading the tables: [a, b] is the 95% interval from resampling whole months, and "12 of 12 months" counts the months in which the arm beat its reference. P0 to P3 are the four planned contrasts (see the Introduction).
  • ERA5: ECMWF's reanalysis, an estimate of past weather.
  • Planned, post hoc: a planned arm was in the plan approved before any fit. A post hoc arm or rule came later, after earlier results or after reading the training data.
  • manual_heuristic: the baseline forecaster that treats the power at the same weekday and time on each of the last 6 weeks, and 49 to 55 weeks back, as 13 ensemble members. It uses no weather. climatology: the baseline that takes 51 quantiles of past power for each calendar cell.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5). Independent Claude reviewers checked the method, the numbers, and the prose. The study had one scientific-validity review by Claude Opus 5.5, where the study's own rules ask for two.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• The production forecast has a spread problem and a point-forecast problem, and the spread problem is larger. The refit's 10% to 90% member band holds the outcome in 10.5% of half-hours, where an ideal band holds 80%. Its CRPS is 11.3% of capacity, against 7.2% for manual_heuristic, and its MAE of 12.1% is also above the heuristic's 11.0%.
  • Quantile training lowered CRPS by 2.4 points, and combined with three other changes by 3.5. The combination scores a CRPS of 7.85% [7.43, 8.24] and an MAE of 10.74% on fold A, averaged over three seeds, and a CRPS 3.44 points lower than production on fold B. The combination's CRPS is the lowest among the arms fitted with three seeds, and 0.6 points above the heuristic's. One arm fitted with one seed, which adds the heuristic's weekly inputs, scores 7.63%. Of the 3.5 points, about 1.3 come from a better point forecast (the MAE falls by 1.35) and about 2.2 from the spread.
  • The quantile gain is smaller against spread rescaling, and the quantile forecast's band is still too narrow. Quantile training takes about 8 times longer. Against spread rescaling on the same 45 later runs, the quantile gain is smaller: 0.4 points for the plain arm and about 1.0 for the best arm. The 459-value distribution is still too narrow (57% coverage of a nominal 80% band), and the control member's 9 quantiles alone score 0.33 points better than the crossed sample. The fair CRPS may account for part of that gap, because it gives a set of 9 values a larger spread term than a set of 459.
  • The point forecast is good at short leads and loses its edge from day 3. At days 0 to 2 the best point-forecast arm's MAE is 9.5% against the heuristic's 11.3%, and for wind farms 10.0% against 19.2%. The 9.5% and 10.0% figures are point estimates, and the study computed no paired interval against the heuristic. At days 3 to 10 the two tie (10.8% and 10.9%), and from day 11 the heuristic is ahead (11.1% against 11.8%).
  • The absolute-error objective and early stopping are the two best planned single ideas. The objective lowers CRPS by 0.42 points [−0.48, −0.37] and early stopping by 0.38 points [−0.52, −0.24], against production with cleaning (fold A, three seeds).
  • Leaner columns for wind farms lower wind CRPS by 3.3 points, and a matching cut for solar farms raises solar CRPS. A similar cut for solar farms, and removing the power lags from solar and wind farms, raised their errors.
  • Rescaling the ensemble spread lowers CRPS by 1.9 points for production and 1.3 to 1.4 points for the best point-forecast arm (post hoc). The rescaled forecast still scores worse than the heuristic.
  • More training months help little beyond 12. Cutting the training window from 15 to 12 months raises CRPS by 0.07 points [−0.01, 0.14], and to 6 months by 0.48.
  • Showing the model the 6 weekly analogue observations the heuristic uses helps demand substations a little. The weekly observations lower CRPS by 0.24 points [−0.39, −0.07] over all series.
  • Cleaning the training data matters for 2 of 31 series. Dropping every half-hour up to 6 weeks after a new meter first reads live lowers CRPS by 0.31 points. Rules for zeros, spikes, dropouts, switching days, and commissioning ramps changed it by 0.07 points or less.
  • Four input columns have faults worth fixing in production, none of which the study tested. Precipitation type is missing from half of the training rows and none of the scored rows, windchill is computed outside its valid range, wind direction and the weekday are fed as numbers that wrap around, and short-wave radiation is positive after sunset.

docs.title: Why the XGBoost forecast scores worse than the heuristic
docs.text:
The evidence supports four answers, each with a limit.

  • Is it a calibration problem? Largely, for CRPS. The 51 members differ only through the weather inputs, so their spread is far narrower than the forecast's real error. Rescaling that spread lowered CRPS by 1.3 to 1.9 points, and quantile training lowered it by 2.4. Calibration alone does not close the gap: the best arm with rescaled spread scores 8.9% on later runs, against the heuristic's 7.4% on the same runs.
  • Should we train on CRPS? Quantile loss is the nearest cheap proxy, and it helped on both folds and on every series type except the single biofuel generator. The study did not train on CRPS itself, which needs a custom objective or a neural network, and it did not measure whether the 9 quantile levels are the right number.
  • Is the feature pipeline broken? The study found four column faults (see Input features) and did not audit the pipeline beyond that visual check. The point forecast beats the heuristic by 1.8 points of MAE at days 0 to 2, which argues against a gross mis-join, but a lead-dependent or one-hour offset would not be excluded. Some columns still mislead the model: removing 8 columns judged irrelevant to wind farms lowered wind CRPS by 3.3 points, although the matching 11-column cut for solar farms raised solar CRPS by 0.26 points.
  • Do we need more years, or an ERA5 first stage? The study cannot say. Over the 15 months available, a longer window helps with diminishing returns: removing the oldest 3 months raises CRPS by 0.07 points on fold A. The 15 months hold one winter, so the gain from a second winter, or from pre-training on ERA5 and then learning the weather forecasts' errors, is untested.

Two tests of "give XGBoost what the heuristic has" are in the results, and a third was not run. First, a combination of the heuristic's members with the XGBoost members lowered CRPS against XGBoost alone but scored worse than the heuristic alone. Second, showing XGBoost the heuristic's six weekly analogue observations lowered CRPS by 0.24 points. A climatology column was not tested, because a climatological mean computed from the training window includes each training row itself, so the follow-up needs a leave-one-week-out construction.

docs.title: Recommendations for the production forecast
docs.text:
These are the changes to try first, in order of evidence and then effort. "Effect" is the paired CRPS difference against production with cleaning on fold A (three seeds, 12 months), with fold B (15 months, one seed) beside it. Each effect is in points of capacity.

Order Change Planned? Effect on fold A Effect on fold B Effort 1 Train with reg:absoluteerror planned −0.42 [−0.48, −0.37], 12 of 12 months −0.37 [−0.46, −0.28], 15 of 15 One config line 2 Choose the tree count by early stopping on the last 6 training weeks, then refit planned −0.38 [−0.52, −0.24], 11 of 12 −0.77 [−0.98, −0.55], 15 of 15 Small change in the training loop. Early stopping roughly doubles the CRPS of the single biofuel generator (+1.16 [0.80, 1.54]), so exclude that series or check its score 3 Train with quantile loss at 9 levels instead of squared error, and score every member times every level post hoc −2.39 [−2.52, −2.27], 12 of 12 −2.60 [−2.74, −2.46], 15 of 15 Training takes about 8 times longer; the forecast becomes 51 × 9 values.
